# 1 Peter

## 1:1 Introduction
[Johann Gerhard, Commentarius super Priorem D. Petri Epistolam (Jena, 1660). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
Σὺν Θεῷ. PROLEGOMENA.

1. The author of the Epistle, the Apostle Peter. In the Syriac Paraphrase, the Syriac name Cephas is emphatically repeated, which, however, the Greek name Peter had already expressed before. The Epistle of Peter the Apostle Simon Cephas. Concerning him we shall advise certain things later.

2. The kind of writing, which is to say, that it is an Epistle. The books of the N.T. are distinguished into Historical, Doctrinal & Prophetic. Historical ones hand down the history either of Christ, as the four Evangelists, or of the Apostles, as the Acts. Doctrinal ones are the Apostolic Epistles. There is one Prophetic one, namely the Apocalypse. Therefore, this Epistle belongs to the second class of N.T. books. Although indeed the whole Scripture of the O. & N.T. is rightly called by Augustine in enarr. Ps. 90. & serm. 56. ad frat. in erem. Macarius homil. 33. & Greg. lib. 4. epist. 40. the Epistle of the omnipotent GOD to His creature in which the words of GOD sound and the heart of GOD is learned, properly however and peculiarly the Canonical Those New Testament books, which Paul, James, Peter, John, and Jude left to the Church, are called Epistles, since they were written in the form of letters to the Church, whether Catholic, or particular, or even to certain specific persons. It is a beautiful observation of the pious ancients that only in the New Testament, in which GOD has spoken to us familiarly through his SonHebr. 1. v. 1.did the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom begin to be written down through Epistles, since an Epistle is nothing other than a familiar conversation with a friend.

3. The denomination sought from the breadth of the object, because it is a Catholic Epistle. It has this name in common with the one of James, the other of Peter, the three of John, and the one of Jude, so that in total seven Catholic Epistles are numbered, in which way Gregory Nazianzen calls and numbers them in his heroic poem on Scripture, Athanasius in his Synopsis, Jerome in his book on illustrious men, in Peter, James, and Jude. Augustine in book 2 of Christian doctrine, chapter 8. Cyril of Jerusalem, catechism 5. Damascene, book 4 of the orthodox faith, chapter 18. Sophronius, the interpreter of Jerome, Origen in Eusebius, book 6 of History, chapter 19. Dionysius of Alexandria in the same, book 7, chapter 20. Eusebius himself, book 2, chapter 22. The opinions of the interpreters vary concerning the reason for the denomination. Some judge them to be so called because they are of the Apostles, whom God set over the whole world as Catholic Doctors, because they contain the Catholic doctrine handed down and commended by the Apostles to the Church, and because they have been received by all who profess the faith of Christ as divine and Apostolic, with other Apocryphal works being repudiated and ψευδεπιγράφοις formerly sold under the name of the Apostles. But these Catholic Epistles have all these things in common with the Pauline Epistles. Some seek the reason in the septenary number, which is of perfection and universality; and from that they establish that these Epistles are called Catholic, because they contain a perfect and universal doctrine, on account of which they are compared they might be with the seven planets in the firmament, with the seven golden lampstandsApoc. 1. v. 13.with the seven loaves, satisfying four thousand menMatt 15. v. 34.with the seven pillars hewn in the house of wisdomProv. 9. v. 1.with the seven horns of the Lamb, by which the ferocity of heretics is suppressedApoc. 5. v. 6. But they have this perfection of Catholic doctrine in common with other books of the O. & N. T. taken together. Therefore, it is answered most simply from Oecumenius, that those are called Catholic or Universal, because they are not inscribed to certain specific persons or particular Churches, nor is the name of a region or city added to them, to which they might be directed in particular, but they are inscribed in general to all Christians, in which sense also the Church of the N. T. first began to be called Catholic, because it was gathered to Christ not from one particular race or nation, but from all nations in the whole world. But against this opinion it is urged. 1. That the Epistle to the Hebrews ought likewise to be called Catholic, since it was written to those converted from the Jews. Resp. from cap. 10. v. 34. it can be gathered that it was written particularly to the converted Jews who were dwelling in Jerusalem and in Judea, for they are said to have accepted the plundering of their goods with joy.

2. The first to the Corinthians is inscribed to all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christcap. 1. v. 2. Resp. it is signified that the use of this Epistle ought to be common to all Christians, meanwhile it is inscribed particularly to the Church of GOD, which is at Corinth.

3. James and Peter write to those converted from Judaism. Resp. they themselves constituted the entire people, comprising no weak part of the Catholic Church, for the Church was gathered from Jews and Gentiles.

4. This first Epistle of Peter was once called the Pontic. Resp. that it was not inscribed to the Pontics alone, but that it was inscribed to them principally, for they are named in the first place.

5. That the first Epistle of John was formerly called the Epistle to the Parthians. Resp. In the title it is called καθολικὴ. Those who say it was written to the Parthians wish to include under the name of Parthians the other Oriental peoples among whom the Christians were dispersed, namely the Medes, the Elamites, and the inhabitants of Mesopotamia, who are joined to the Parthians Acts 2. v. 9..

6. The second of John was written to the elect Lady and her children; the third to Gaius. Resp. The name καθολικῆς is not added to the third Johannine Epistle even in Greek codices; they are numbered among the Catholic Epistles because they are considered as certain parts of the first Catholic Epistle of John.

It must be admitted, therefore, that in this appellation not everything can be exacted according to ἀκρίβειαν. The same must be said concerning the name Canonical already attributed long ago to these seven Epistles. Jerome in the prologue upon the Catholic Epistles, which is found in the most ancient editions of the Bibles and in Lyranus. John Huss in his commentary on the first of Peter says, that they are called Canonical either to distinguish them from those Epistles which false apostles wished to foist upon the Church, or because they have been received into the canon of divine Scripture, or because they contain the rules and precepts of the Christian life. Some add, that they were written without any obliquity of error, and that they are a canon and rule, both of Ecclesiastical Scriptures and of our intellect, will, and works. But anyone can see that all these things are common to the Pauline Epistles themselves. Therefore, that they are called Canonical is not to be taken exclusively, but ἐξοχικῶς & ἐξαιρέτως. Jerome, Epistle to Paulinus: James, Peter, John, and Jude published Epistles as mystical as they are succinct, and equally brief and good; brief in words, long in meanings, so that there is rarely anyone who does not go blind in the reading of them. Dionysius in the proem to the Catholic Epistles: Although for these reasons the Epistles of Paul could also be called Canonical, yet this name was imposed more upon these epistles, because they are from diverse authors let them be written together, and thus they could not obtain any particular name from one of them, but some common name had to be attributed to them, and that a worthy and venerable one.

Something must also be mentioned concerning the order of those seven Catholic Epistles. Jerome, in the aforementioned work, records that in Latin codices the first place was formerly given to the Petrine Epistles, which order he changed based on Greek codices. The order is not so, he says, among the Greeks, who are sound in their understanding and follow the right faith, of the seven Epistles which are called Canonical, as it is found in Latin codices, so that, because Peter is first in the order of the Apostles, his Epistles should also be first in the order of the others. But just as we have long since corrected the Evangelists to the line of truth, so we have restored these to their proper order with God's help. For the first of them is one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude. Jerome would not have dared to change this order if he had judged the hypotheses, which the Papists defend today with great effort, to be true, namely that Peter was the Monarch of the Church, and that the Latin edition is authentic. Hence the Fathers of the Council of Florence in the decree given to the Armenians, and of Trent in the decree concerning Canonical Scripture, session 4, place the Epistles of Peter in the first place against the authority of the Greek codices. But not only do the Greek codices support Jerome, but also the most ancient Doctors of the Church, and the very Latin editions of the Bibles of today, in which the Epistle of James is placed in the first position, either because it was written in the first place, as Lyranus maintains, or because James the son of Alphaeus, the brother of the Lord, the author of this Epistle, was the Bishop of the Jerusalem Church, which they honored as the mother and origin of the remaining churches. Esai. 2 v. 3.Mich. 4. v. 2. Indeed, in the last of the canons of the Apostles and in Augustine, book on faith and works, chapter 14, as also in the German version of Luther, the Catholic Epistles are listed in this order: The Epistles of Peter, John, James, and Jude in the 3rd Council of Carthage, canon 47, and in Augustine, book 2, On Christian Doctrine, chapter 8, are placed such that the Epistle of James is in the last position, perhaps because it was at first doubted by some, and finally received in the last place; Innocent I in Epistle 4 to Exuperius places the Epistles of John before the others. Meanwhile, because the Epistle of James is placed in the first position in the Council of Laodicea, last canon, in Jerome in the Epistle to Paulinus prefixed to the Bibles, and in Gelasius, c. Sancta Romana dist. 15, and because the canons of the Apostles, following a different order, are supposititious, and the Greek Codices consistently grant the first place to the Epistle of James, therefore we deservedly insist upon that order. What Estius establishes, that those who numbered the Epistles of Peter in the first place had regard for the primacy of Peter among the Apostles, if that is taken concerning a certain primacy of honor, we leave in the middle; but if it is taken concerning a primacy of Monarchical power, we reject it as contrary to the Scriptures and to this very first Epistle cap. 5. v. 1..

4. The series. It is called πρώτη first, with respect to the latter written by the same Apostle. For these alone, out of all the remaining writings which are attributed to Peter by ψευδεπιγραφὴν, have been received into the pinnacle of Canonical authority, yet with this distinction, that the latter is referred to the second order of Canonical books. Jerome in the prologue upon the Epistles of Peter: Peter wrote two Epistles, which are named Canonical, of which the second is denied by many to be his on account of the dissonance of style with the former. But also the Gospel according to Mark, who was his hearer and interpreter, is said to be his. However, his books, of which one is written of his Acts, another of his Gospel, a third of his preaching, a fourth of his Apocalypse, a fifth of his Judgment, are reputed among the Apocryphal Scriptures. It is doubted by some whether this Epistle is truly Peter's first, since he seems to have written another before this one. Erasmus, in the argument which he prefixed to the paraphrase of this Epistle and in the paraphrase itself, last chapter, thinks, that Peter before these two he wrote yet another and to the same people, since at the end of the formercap. 5. v. 12.he says: By Silvanus, a faithful brother, I have written briefly. But we cannot rise to this reasoning. For Peter is speaking not of another, but of this very Epistle, as is shown not only by the Syriac version, which notably rendered it, [consult facsimile image] These few things I have written to you, but also by the subjoined description of the argument, which most exactly agrees with this Epistle, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of GOD, in which you stand. Thus when Paul says 1. Corinth. 5. v. 9.I wrote to you in an Epistle, he does not understand some other, but that very Epistle given to the Corinthians, as Chrysostom and Theophylact teach on that passage. When the same person Hebr. 13. v. 22. says, I have written to you in very few words, it is most manifest that he likewise understands not another, but this very Epistle. What of the fact that in the later Epistle cap. 3. v. 1. it is held thus: Behold, dearly beloved, I write this second Epistle to you. But if he had sent another before the former, he ought to have called that one the third.

And let these things be said concerning the exposition of the title, to which for the sake of completing προλεγόμενα can be added the writing. 1. Occasion. 2. Time. 3. Place. 4. Original idiom 5. Argument of the Epistle & 6. General disposition. 1. The occasion of the writing Lyranus thinks it was the arrival of Silvanus to Peter. Silvanus, he says, through whom Peter wrote, who is Silas, perhaps wished to go to the places to confirm the faithful, for the reason that he had been there in preaching with Paul, as is evident from the Acts. It can therefore be thought that Silvanus, who in those very regions in which those to whom Peter writes lived dispersed, had together with Paul taught and planted churches,Act. 15. v. 40cap. 17. v. 4cap 18. v. 5.2. Cor. 1. v. 19.about to return to confirm the same, had passed through Babylon and there met Peter, from whom he received this Epistle. Augustine In his book on faith and works, chapter 14, he thinks that the occasion for writing was given to John, James, and Jude, just as it was to Peter, by the erroneous opinion of those who preached faith without works. Since, therefore, he says, this opinion of Simon Magus, Nicolaus, and others, who preached faith without works, had then arisen, the other Apostolic Epistles of Peter, John, James, and Jude direct their intention especially against it, so that they might vehemently assert that faith without works profits nothing, just as Paul himself defined not just any faith, by which one believes in God, but that wholesome and clearly Evangelical faith, whose works proceed from love. And faith, he says, which works through love. And afterwards. Whence evidently in the second Epistle Peter, when he was exhorting to the holiness of life and morals, knowing that some wicked men had taken occasion from certain somewhat obscure sentences of the Apostle Paul, so that, as if secure concerning the salvation which is in faith, they did not care to live well, he mentioned that some things were very difficult to understand in his Epistles, which men were perverting, as they did also the other Scriptures to their own destruction, when nevertheless that Apostle also felt the same things concerning eternal salvation, which would not be given except to those living well, as the other Apostles. From the very argument of the Epistle and from the state of the Church of those times, as also from the purpose for which Paul went up to Jerusalem to Peter and James Gal. 1. v. 18. & 19.cap. 2. v. 2., it is gathered that there were some who doubted whether Peter taught the same things as those which were taught by Paul and Silas or Silvanus, especially since huge struggles were being stirred up on account of the Levitical Ceremonies abrogated in the New Testament. Therefore, to testify to the consensus of doctrine with Paul and Silas, and to confirm in the faith those to whom he had preached the Gospel by word of mouth, and to excite the same to the study of good works, i.e., to bringing forth the fruits of the Gospel, he wrote this Epistle, which he gave to Silvanus to be delivered, whence he also makes express mention of Paul in 2. Epist. 3. v. 15.

2. Time Baronius in the Year of Christ 45, no. 16, maintains that this Epistle was written in the year of Christ which we have mentioned, by which reasoning it would be the most ancient of all the Apostolic Epistles, because the first to the Thessalonians is believed to have been written in the Year of Christ 52. But anyone can see that this is uncertain. That can be gathered from chapter 4, v. 16 of this Epistle, that it was written when the disciples of Christ had already begun to be called Christians, which Luke chapter 11, v. 26 records to have happened at Antioch, which the founder of the Annals judges to have occurred in the year of Christ 43, no. 10. Lyranus in the prologue upon the Catholic Epistles maintains that both Epistles were written by Peter after the death of James, a little before the end of his life.

3. The Apostle himself expresses the place chapter 5, v. 13 The church that is in Babylon, saluteth you. Most Papists argue with great effort that Rome is to be understood by it, concerning which matter what is to be determined will be examined in its own place.

4. Some gather from Jerome, Epistle 150 to Hedibia, q. 11, that this Epistle was written by Peter in the Hebrew idiom, but translated into the Greek language by Mark. But Jerome says nothing else than that the two Epistles which are attributed to Peter differ in style and character, and in the structure of the words, where by character he does not understand the language in which each was written, but the manner of speaking and the propriety of the discourse. Therefore, this Epistle is said to have been written by Peter in the Hebrew language with the same truth as Mark, the interpreter of Peter, is maintained by Baronius, year 45, no. 38, Bellarmine, book 2 of the Word of God, chapter 7, Adrian Fin., book 6 of the scourge against the Jews, chapter 80, book 8, c. 62, Petr. Anton. Beuter, annot. 9 to the Scriptures, to have written the Gospel in the Latin language.

5. The Apostle explains the argument chapter 1, v. 13 Hope perfectly for the grace that is offered you, and chapter 5, v. 12 by Sylvanus, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and testifying that this is the the true grace of GOD in which you stand. The Apostle therefore has a twofold goal proposed for himself in this Epistle. 1. Διδασκαλικὸν, for he wishes to confirm those to whom he writes in the faith, and to testify that the Evangelical doctrine concerning the grace of GOD through Christ, which they had embraced and in whose faith and profession they stood, is infallibly true. 2. Νουθετικὸν, because he seriously and gravely warns them that they should lead a life worthy of that profession, and adorn the doctrine with holy morals. Oecumen. in argum. He confirms those who had believed from among the Jews in faith and integrity of life.

6. General disposition. The Latins divide the Epistle into five chapters, the Greeks into eight. Ederus lib. 4. Oecon. Bibl. p. 521. brings forward such a partition. The sum of this Epistle is split into two parts, in which it is treated 1. Specifically concerning the giving of thanks, chap. 1. & 2. up to verse 11. 2. Generally concerning other virtues of a Christian man from the said v. 11. chap. 2. up to the end of the whole Epistle. The Apostle completes the first part of the Epistle in three members. First, he touches upon six benefits, in whose name each one for himself ought to give perpetual thanks. The first is Baptism, by which we are regenerated into a living hope into an incorruptible inheritance.cap. 1. v. 3.The second is the power of GOD, by which we are guarded through faith unto salvationv. 5.The third is the ability of resisting every kind of temptation, by which our faith is proved much more rightly than gold.v. 6.The fourth is the salvation of souls, which causes us to love Christ even though not seen.v. 8.The fifth is the gift of prophecy, by which not only the sufferings of Christ were announced to us, but also the glory to be revealed hereafter,v. 10.The sixth is the mission of the Holy Spirit, by whose benefit those things which were promised through the Prophets have all been perfected and completed.v. 12.

Secondly, he prescribes the manner by which we may most rightly show ourselves grateful to God, which the Apostle asserts will come to pass if we flee every kind of vice and pursue the holiness of morals. Thirdly, he teaches that there are seven things which move us to both, as much to the giving of thanks, which they ought to impel toward the holiness of life, namely. 1. The grace, which was offered to us freely, and by which we have been called and adopted into such a holy conversation of Christ v. 13. 2. The obligation, by which we are stirred to return gifts, and are held to obey a vocation so worthy and honest, whoever we are who desire to enjoy the privilege of sons. v. 14. 3. The mutual connection between GOD the Father and us his sons, which consists in this, that we should revere him, whom we know to love us as sons, in turn, as a Father. v. 17. 4. The magnitude of the price, by which we are, v. 18. 5. The dignity of our regeneration v. 22. 6. The most sweet taste of the Lord, by which those are refreshed, who lay aside all malice and all guile, cap. 1. v. 1. 2. & 3. 7. The certainty of our faith, which is built upon the living stone. v. 4. up to 11.

In the latter part of the Epistle, which deals with the reforming of the morals of Christians, must be considered 1. The civil order, about which in cap. 2. v. 11. up to the end cap. 4. 2. The ecclesiastical, the reason of which is explained in cap. 5. The civil condition of men is threefold. 1. Servile from v. 11. cap. 2. up to the end of the chapter. 2. Conjugal from the beginning of cap. 3. up to v. 9. 3. Political from v. 9. of that chapter, up to the end of the same. The duties and morals of those who are in a servile condition are described thus, that they ought to practice for themselves abstinence from fleshly desires cap. 2. v. 11. to provide a good example to their neighbor v. 12. obedience to the Magistrate v. 13. religion, reverence, and fear to GOD v. 16. to yield even to unjust and froward masters, and to bear their importunity with a patient mind. v. 18. imitation to Christ v. 21. up to the end of the chapter. The duties of spouses are explained in cap. 3. in which the Apostle exhorts 1. Wives to humility and obedience v. 1. to honest conversation, that by the comity of their morals they may win their husbands, v. 2. to seek the cultivation and adornment of the mind rather than of the body v. 3. 2. Husbands, that they may dwell with their wives according to knowledge. v. 8. that they may yield meanwhile something to their morals on account of the infirmity of the sex, ibid. that they may show them honor, as fellow-heirs of the grace of life, ibid. that they may abstain sometimes even from the lawful use of them, so that they may be able to devote themselves to prayer. ibid. The Apostle measures the duties of any man living in the Christian Republic from the various circumstances of things, especially from two. 1. From the comparison of man first to man i. e. his neighbor of whatever order he may be, with whom we shall then be able to converse rightly, if we embrace concord chap. 3. v. 9. humanity, ibid. piety v. 10. justice v. 12. innocence v. 15. Secondly to himself & his own body or flesh, the lusts of which must be resisted. chap. 4. v. 1. up to 7. 2. From the contemplation first of the end, to which all things must be directed. In which again two things are to be considered. First the means, by which one arrives at that end, which are prudence v. 7. watchings ibid. Prayer ibid. charity v. 8. hospitality v. 10. the liberal dispensation, or communication, of the gifts of GOD. v. 10. Secondly the sum, that in all our actions GOD may be glorified through Christ. v. 11. Secondly of the Christian name. For in a Christian man, who desires to sustain this name by right, are required constancy in faith v. 12. fortitude in enduring persecutions for the name of Christ vers. 14. diligent caution, lest he either fall into sin, or become presumptuous. vers. 18.

In the Ecclesiastical state others preside as pastors, whose duty it is to teach with faith & diligence chap. 5. v. 1. not by constraint but willingly v. 2. nor for the sake of base gain, ibid. without pride v. 3. by the good example of an honest conversation. ibid. Others are subject, as sheep, whom it becomes to have obedience v. 5. humility and mutual reverence & compliance among them ibid. fear of GOD v. 6. firm hope v. 7. sobriety & vigilance v. 8. fortitude & constancy. v. 9. And to men the glory of eternal life is promised. v. 10.

Although indeed this partition can be usefully applied in some respects, yet in it two things are especially rightly desired. 1. That only a single scope of the Epistle is established, namely an exhortatory one to a holy conversation of life and morals, since it is evident from the argument of the Epistle that the Apostle wished furthermore to teach that the Evangelical doctrine, which they had embraced by faith, is infallibly true, and on this account to exhort them to constancy in the faith. 2. That he refers duties common to all Christians only to certain states and orders. Certainly the imitation of Christ prescribed in chapter 2, verse 21, is required not only of those who are established in a servile kind of life, but of all Christians altogether.

We proceed therefore in this order, that we may establish three parts of this Epistle. 1. προίμιον. 2. ἐργασίαν. 3. ἐπίλογον. The prologue contains the inscription & salutation. chapter 1, verse 1 & 2. ἐργασὶα is completed in two parts. The former is διδασκαλικὴ, that the doctrine concerning Christ, which those converted from Judaism had received from the Apostles, is altogether most true and most certain. The Apostle proves this in two ways. 1. By the commemoration of spiritual benefits partly already conferred through it, partly still to be hoped for. 2. By the demonstration of the most exact consensus with the Prophetic doctrine, the truth of which was undoubted to those converts. chapter 1, verse 3 up to verse 13. The latter is νουθετικὴ, for with this foundation of the truth of the Evangelical doctrine laid, the Apostle exhorts those to whom he writes that they should persevere constant in the profession of that doctrine, and adorn the same with holiness of life and morals, and thus show themselves grateful to GOD not only in words, but also in reality. That exhortation is either general, looking to all Christians, or special, directed to certain states and orders of life. For some duties are common to all Christians, but some are proper to certain states of life. In general, the Apostle exhorts all Christians to the pursuit of good works and the tolerance of evils. Good works are either of the first table, such as constancy in faith, humility, serious prayer, etc., or of the second table, such as love of neighbor, mercy, according to the fifth commandment; temperance, sobriety, chastity according to the sixth commandment; hospitality according to the seventh; the bridling of the tongue according to the eighth. Evils to be tolerated are either private injuries or public persecutions. Specifically, he addresses persons established in certain offices and kinds of life, and exhorts them γενικῶς, that they may solicitously administer the function committed to them; εἰδικῶς in the political state, subjects; in the economic state, husbands, wives, and servants; in the ecclesiastical, he admonishes presbyters of their duty. These exhortations are proposed scatteredly and mixedly from v. 13 of the first chapter up to v. 10 of the fifth chapter. The Epilogue consists of: 1. ἀνακεφαλαιώσει of the principal chapters treated in this Epistle, v. 12. 2. ἀσπασμοῖς. v. 13. 3. προτροπῇ & 4. εὐχῇ. v. 14.

The summary and parts of this chapter are evident from the preceding. The Proem of the Epistle is proposed in v. 1 & 2 Peter, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, to the elect sojourners of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father, unto sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace be multiplied. Most people constitute three members of this proem, subscription, inscription, and salutation. They look to the customs of our times and regions, in which the name of the author of an Epistle is accustomed to be subscribed. But the thing itself shows that Peter the Apostle did not subscribe his name, but according to the custom then of the time received among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Romans, he prescribed it in the frontispiece of the Epistle. More correctly, therefore, two members are established. Inscription and salutation. The inscription expresses both the efficient cause, or the author of the Epistle, and the object, namely those to whom it is written.

CHAPTER I.

The author of the Epistle is Peter the Apostle of Jesus Christ. This author is described: 1. by name. He was otherwise called Simon from obedience. Hieron. de vir. illustr. Peter the son of John, brother of Andrew the Apostle, born in the village of Bethsaida of the province of Galilee, which is near the lake of Gennesaret, who was first called Bar-Jona. The surname Peter was promised to him when he was first led to Christ by his brother Andrew John 1. v. 43., given when he was elected to the Apostleship with the other twelve Mark 3. v. 15., and confirmed when he confessed Christ as the true and only rock of salvation in the name of all the Apostles Matt. 16. v. 18.. Very frequent mention is made of this Peter in the Evangelical and Apostolic History.

2. By office. The Apostle of Jesus Christ. For he had been called by Christ to the Apostleship Matt. 4. v. 18 Mark 3. v. 15. Luke 6. v. 14., instructed in the School of Christ for over three years, and on the day of Pentecost, through the Holy Spirit miraculously and visibly poured out, most fully taught concerning the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Only Peter and Paul in the inscription of their Epistles call themselves Apostles. James and Jude call themselves servants of Christ.

It is asked here: 1. Why did Peter wish to express his name in the frontispiece? Resp. So that he might distinguish this genuine Epistle of his from supposititious and ψευδεπιγράφοις Pseudo-Apostolic writings.

2. Why does he call himself the Apostle of Jesus Christ? 1. To show that he does what he does in this Epistle by virtue of his office. For it was the duty of the Apostolic office not only to teach the Church by living voice, but also by writings. Matt. 28. v. 19. John 21. v. 24. 1 John 1. v. 3 & 4. Rev. 1. v. 2. & 3. 2. To win authority and goodwill for himself. For who would not wish to hear an Ambassador of Christ? He is an Ambassador of Jesus the Savior. Therefore, he seeks solely the salvation of those to whom he writes. Didymus in comm. Epist. Cathol. Just as mortals desiring the glory of men place before their writings the dignities which they are thought to have, Thus holy men in the Epistles which they write to the Churches principally set themselves forth as servants of our Lord Jesus Christ, esteeming that this title stands above the rule of the whole world. John Huss in his commentary on this passage not absurdly establishes that Peter by this title expresses his dignity, authority, and infallible truth. 3. To show that he does not bring forward any new doctrine, but teaches the same things in all respects with Paul and other Apostles. In Clement, book 2 of the Recognitions, Peter is introduced speaking to Simon Magus thus: For we, the Apostles of Him who sent us, are sent to expound the words, and we have no command to say anything of our own, but, as I have said, to open the truth of His words. Tertullian, book on Prescription: The Apostles chose nothing at all of their own judgment to introduce, but faithfully assigned to the nations the discipline received from Christ.

1. Ἔλεγχος. 1. Peter in this inscription is content with the designation of Apostle, but by no means calls himself the prince of the Apostles and Monarch of the whole Church. It is therefore false what Bellarmine, book 1 on the Roman Pontiff cap. 10. and the remaining Papists establish that monarchical dominion over the whole Church was bestowed upon him by Christ. Salmeron, Disp. 1 on this Epistle, objects in various ways. First, that Peter was not entirely forgetful of his power, since it pertained to the supreme Pastor to admonish the Presbyters of their duty, which Peter does cap. 5. v. 1. and following. I answer: nay, rather, Peter in that same place contradicts this dream in express words. For he calls himself συμπρεσβύτερον v. 1. and forbids κατακυριεύειν τῶν κλήρων v. 3. Who, therefore, would believe that he arrogated to himself κυριότητα and dominion, the use of which he forbade to other pastors? But he also calls Christ alone in that same place v. 4. the Prince of pastors, but he by no means arrogates such dignity to himself. Nor can any monarchical power be proven from the fact that Peter admonishes other Pastors of their duty; otherwise, the same power would have to be attributed to the Apostle Paul for the same reason Act. 20. v. 28. 1. Timoth. 3. v. 2. Tit. 1. v. 7. Secondly, since he knew very well that Christ the Lord had predicted and ordained many things concerning his keys for opening the kingdom of heaven, and concerning his pastorate and the confirmation of his brethren, he did not think it necessary, with all those great testimonies of Christ being known and revealed, to bring forward another testimony of himself concerning himself. I answer: did Christ by those words, I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, feed my sheep, you being converted confirm your brothers, etc. whether he conferred a monarchical primacy over the universal Church upon Peter is still in question; for the contrary can be clearly demonstrated from those very passages. In this place we urge this: if for this reason brought forward by Salmeron, Peter did not wish to call himself the Monarch of the Church, he certainly should not have called himself an Apostle of Christ either, because it is likewise known to all concerning his Apostleship.

Thirdly, since Peter was not only the universal pastor of the Church, but also an Apostle, whose proper duty it was to traverse the whole world and illuminate it with the Gospel, he nevertheless preferred to perform the Apostolic duty by running through all the provinces, erecting churches, and ordaining ministers and Bishops, rather than the pastorate, in which he was only the leader and judge of all Christ's sheep and of the particular Pastors under him, so that he seemed in a certain way to neglect his pastorate and primacy; and he chose to conduct himself with the other Apostles as a brother and equal, and not as a superior and their head and ruler. Resp. We invert the argument, because Peter nowhere arrogated to himself the power of dominion, but wished to perform the same duty as the rest of the Apostles; because he suffered himself to be sent away together with John as an equal to the Samaritans Acts 8. verse 14. he admitted with an even mind the expostulation of the Jews, because he had entered unto the Gentiles, and excused himself before them. Acts 11. v. 3. he decided the controversy concerning the observation of the Mosaic law not by praetorian authority, but by common votes with the rest of the Apostles Acts 15. v. 5. he suffered himself to be rebuked by Paul on account of dissimulation, Gal. 2. v. 14. in the election of Matthias Acts 1. v. 23. in the constitution of the Deacons, Acts 6. v. 5. he acted having communicated his counsel with the rest of the Apostles, therefore he showed in reality that a monarchical dominion did not belong to him in the least. Furthermore, if Peter for the sake of the Church's salvation preferred to neglect his primacy, and chose to conduct himself with the rest of the Apostles as a brother and equal, and not as a superior and their head and ruler, namely by preaching the Gospel, why does the Pontiff, who calls himself Peter's successor, abstain from the duty of teaching on account of the primacy? Nor does what Salmeron has in the same Disputation agree with these things. Peter (he says) preached more rarely, so that he might be occupied in instituting the ministers of the churches and other great affairs. And afterwards. Peter ascribed his preachings to other ministers out of charity. Bellarm. book 1. on the Pontiff chapter 15. Although most Pontiffs do not preach, yet they exercise many other pastoral acts, while they bind, loose, dispense, judge controversies, create Bishops, and what they do not do by preaching themselves, they do through others.

Fourthly, if Peter had written as Roman Pontiff, and Vicar of Christ, and Pastor of the universal Church, it would seem that in his writings he had dictated Ecclesiastical law, or what is the same, Canon and Pontifical law, rather than divine. Blessed Peter therefore wrote as a mere Apostle of Christ, handing down those things which are of Christ, which have divine and indispensable authority. Resp. Salmeron himself detracts from this little argument when he adds: The Supreme Pontiffs, whatever they establish in their decretals, do not immediately establish divine law, and institute mandates as if they were given by Christ ἀμέσως except, however, for those things which it is established that the Lord in the Gospel handed down to all the faithful concerning faith, hope, charity, and the Sacraments, and the keeping of His law. And afterwards. Nothing forbids that there be found sometimes in divine and canonical Scriptures Ecclesiastical or Canonical precepts, which the Apostles, with Luke as witness in the Council of Jerusalem, handed down to the Antiochenes concerning not eating what is strangled; Paul also handed down a precept concerning not promoting a bigamist to Bishop, concerning a neophyte, etc. But if divine precepts are found in the decretals of Pontiffs, and Ecclesiastical precepts in the Apostolic writings, it would not have been incongruous for Peter to have called himself Pontiff, even if he had most especially wished to propose divine precepts in this Epistle. Furthermore, if an Apostle, as such, proposes divine law; and a Pontiff, as such, Ecclesiastical law, then certainly the Apostleship is greater than the Papacy, and yet Salmeron argues that Peter as Pontiff was greater than the rest of the Apostles. Estius, having passed over those reasons of Salmeron, attributes to modesty that Peter called himself an Apostle of Christ, but not the Prince and head of the Apostles. But he who expresses an office divinely committed to him does not in the least transgress the limits of modesty, otherwise Peter could not even have named himself an Apostle. 2. The Roman Pontiff in many things proposes things contrary to those which are contained in this Epistle, as we shall see in the progress. Therefore he is not the true successor of Peter. Nazianz. in orat. de laudibus Athanas. tom. 2. p. 502. τὸ ὁμόγνωμον, καὶ ὁμόθρονον; τὸ δὲ ἀντὶδοξον καὶ ἀντίθρονον. He who embraces the same faith is also a participant of the same throne. But he who embraces a contrary faith ought to be considered an adversary also in the throne. Ambros. lib. 1. de poenit. c. 6. tom. 1. p. 156. They do not have the inheritance of Peter, who do not have the faith of Peter.

3. Peter in the writing itself calls himself Apostle of Christ: Therefore the Apostles wrote by the command of Christ. Against Bellarmine, book 4, on the Word of GOD, chapter 4.

4. He who wrote this Epistle was an Apostle. Therefore it cannot be proven that Stephen 3, Roman Pontiff, pressed by the Lombards, wrote an Epistle in the name of Peter to King Pepin, which Baronius recites in the Year of Christ 755, no. 18.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Bellarmine in the place most recently cited argues thus. If the Apostles had wished to commit their doctrine to writing by design, they certainly would have composed a Catechism or a similar book. But they wrote either History, as the Evangelists; or Epistles from some occasion, as Peter, Paul, James, Jude, John, and in them they treated of dogmas not except incidentally. Response: the occasions of writing offered to the Apostles externally do not remove the internal command of writing, otherwise they would also remove the command of preaching, since an occasion was sometimes offered to them for preaching as well, Acts 17, v. 16. One should rather acknowledge in this the wonderful arrangement of divine providence, that to those occasions offered externally, an internal divine impulse was added. That the disputes concerning dogmas are not treated incidentally and ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, but by design in the Apostolic Epistles can be confirmed by induction.

2. Fevardentius in chapter 1 of the Epistle of James, from the fact that Peter adds his name, lashes out at the light-shunning beasts of the heretics, who have woven their pernicious books under foreign and fictitious names, or have published them entirely without a name, to whom for that reason the new name of Neminists could be appropriate. Response: this accusation can be retorted upon the Papists themselves. The author of Autonomia calls himself Franciscus Burchardus, although Antonius Possevinus, book 1, Bibl. p. 125, testifies that the name is supposititious, and the true author of the book is Andreas Ernstenberger. Conradus Vetterus, under the name of Conradus Andreae, wrote books filled with insults, and lied that he was the brother of that great Theologian D. Iacobus Andreae. The Congratulation of Christophorus ab Ungersdorff to the Evangelical estates in Austria assumes a false name of the author. We ourselves teach that writings ἀνώνυμα & ψευδώνυμα are not to be approved simply, meanwhile the name of the author can sometimes be omitted, if it is done without evil intent and for some necessary cause, The Epistle to the Hebrews and the first of John show this, which did not have the names of their authors inscribed at first.

3. The author of this Epistle calls himself Peter, because he is that rock upon which Christ promised that He would build His Church. Resp. He who was called Simon from the rock, was Peter, because through faith he built himself, and through confession and preaching he also built others upon Christ, the true and unique rock of salvation; just as all believers are built as living stones upon Christ, 1. Petr. 2. v. 4. & 5. but not because the Church was to be built upon him by reason of his person and successors. August. serm. 13. de verb. Domini. Rock is the primary name, therefore Peter is from the rock, not the rock from Peter, just as Christ is not called from the Christian, but the Christian from Christ. You are therefore, he says, Peter, and upon this rock, which you have confessed, upon this rock, which you have acknowledged, saying, you are Christ the son of the living GOD, I will build my Church; I will build you upon me, I will not build me upon you. For men wishing to be built upon men were saying: I indeed am of Paul, I of Cephas. And others, who did not wish to be built upon Peter, but upon the rock, were saying: I am of Christ.

Διδασκαλίαι 1. Peter had denied Christ, yet nevertheless he was restored to the Apostleship. This is an example of divine grace proposed to repenting sinners. 1. Tim. 1. v. 16.

2. Without a legitimate calling, no one ought to claim for himself the role of teaching in the Church. Hebr. 5. v. 4.

3. That writings ἀνώνυμα and ψευδώνυμα are not to be simply approved is evident from the saying of Christ Iohan. 3. v. 20. from the inconveniences which are accustomed to arise from the suppression or variation of a name, from the examples of the Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles, who prefixed their names to their writings, from civil laws, 1. Falsi 13. ff. de leg. Corn. de falsis. Luth. tom. 4. f. 508. tom. 5. f. 551.

4. This Epistle is of the Apostle Peter. Therefore it obtains Canonical authority. Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. cap. 3. & 4. testifies, that there was never any doubt about it in the Church; and as many as enumerate the Canonical books of the N. T., expressly count this Petrine one among them. Petrus Damianus serm. 28. tom. 2. Does not the Epistle of Peter and that sublime doctrine of his discourses wonderfully feed the Church of GOD? Boniface the Martyr requested from Eadburga or Eadeburga the Abbess, a relative of the King of the Kentishmen, that the Epistles of Peter be written out for him in golden letters, as Baronius records Vol. 9. Annal. p. 39. just as once a certain Platonist said that the beginning of the Gospel of John ought to be written in golden letters and set up in the most prominent places throughout all the Churches, as Augustine reports from the holy old man Simplicianus, who presided as Bishop over the Church of Milan, lib. 10. de Civ. DEI cap. 29. A comparison with the Pauline Epistles clearly shows that both those and this one proceeded from the same Spirit. Erasmus in his annotations deservedly bestows upon it this eulogy, that it is an Epistle worthy of the Prince of the Apostles (by reason of dignity, not of Monarchical power, as it is so called by the ancients, as Marsilius of Padua teaches in defens. pacis p. 203.) full of Apostolic authority and majesty, sparing in words, stuffed with meanings.

Latin:

Σὺν Θεῷ. PROLEGOMENA.

1. Epistolae autorem, Petrum Apostolum. In Syriaca Paraphrasi emphaticè repetitur nomen Cephae Syriacum, quod tamen Graecum nomen Petrus iam antè expresserat. Epistola Petri Apostoli Simonis Kiphae. De eo postea quaedam monebimus.

2. Scriptionis genus, quod sc. sit Epistola. Distinguuntur libri N. T. in Historiales, Doctrinales & Propheticum. Historiales tradunt Historiam vel Christi, ut quatuor Evangelistae, vel Apostolorum, ut Acta. Doctrinales sunt Epistolae Apostolicae. Propheticus unus est, videlicet Apocalypsis. Ad secundam igitur librorum N. T. classem haec Epistola pertinet. Quamvis verô tota v. & N. T. Scriptura ab Augustino in enarr. Ps. 90. & serm. 56. ad frat. in erem. Macario homil. 33. & Greg. lib. 4. epist. 40. rectè vocetur Epistola omnipotentis DEI ad creaturam suam in qua verba DEI sonant & cor DEI discitur, propriè tamen & peculiariter Canonici illi N. T. libri, quos Paulus, Iacobus Petrus, Iohannes & Iudas Ecclesiae reliquerunt, Epistolae vocantur, cum ad Ecclesiam vel Catholicam, vel particularem, vel etiam certas quasdam personas, in forma Epistolarum conscripti sint. Pulchra est piorum veterum observatio, quod in novo demum Testamento, in quo DEUS familiariter, per Filium suum nobis locutus estHebr. 1. v. 1.mysteria regni coelestis per Epistolas conscribi coeperint, cum Epistola nihil aliud sit quàm familiare cum amico colloquium.

3. Denominationem ab obiecti latitudine petitam, quod sit Epistola Catholica. Hoc nomen commune habet cum Iacobi unâ, Petri altera, Iohannis tribus & Iudae unâ, ut sic in universum septem Epistolae Catholicae numerentur, quo modo eas vocant & numerant Gregor. Nazianz. in carm. heroico de Scriptura, Athanasius in Synopsi, Hieronymus in lib. de viris illustribus, in Petro, Iacobo & Iuda. Augustinus lib. 2. de doctr. Christ. cap. 8. Cyrill. Hierosol. catech. 5. Damasc. lib. 4. orth. fid. cap. 18. Sophronius Hieronymi interpres, Origenes apud Euseb. lib. 6. Hist. cap. 19. Dionys. Alexandrinus apud eund. lib. 7. cap. 20. Eusebius ipse lib. 2. cap. 22. De ratione denominationis variant Interpretum sententiae. Quidam eas sic appellatas censent, quod sint Apostolorum, quos Deus Catholicos Doctores toti mundo praefecit, quod contineant doctrinam Catholicam ab Apostolis Ecclesiae traditam & commendatam, quodque ab omnibus, qui Christi fidem profitentur, tanquam divinae & Apostolicae sint receptae, repudiatis aliis Apocryphis &ψευδεπιγράφοιςsub Apostolorum nomine olim venditatis. Sed haec omnia cum Paulinis Epistolis hae Catholicae habent communia. Quidam rationem quaerunt in numero septenario, qui est perfectionis & universitatis; atque ex eo Epistolas hasce Catholicas dictas statuunt, quod contineant perfectam & universalem doctrinam, propter quod conferri possint cum septem planetis in firmamento, cum septem candelabris aureisApoc. 1. v. 13.cum septem panibus, quatuor hominum millia saturantibusMatt 15. v. 34.cum septem columnis in domo sapientiae excisisProv. 9. v. 1.cum septem cornibus Agni, quibus haereticorum ferocia deprimiturApoc. 5. v. 6. Sed hanc doctrinae Catholicae perfectionem cum aliis V. & N. T. libris simul sumtis communem habent. Simplicissimè igitur respondetur ex Oecumenio, illas vocari Catholicas seu Universales, quia non sint inscriptae certis quibusdam personis vel particularibus Ecclesiis, nec addatur illis nomen regionis vel civitatis, ad quam in specie sint directae, sed in genere omnibus Christianis inscriptae, quo ferè sensu etiam Ecclesia N. T. Catholica primùm dici caepit, quia non ex particulari quadam gente vel natione, sed ex omnibus gentibus in universo orbe Christo fuit collecta. Sed contra hanc sententiam urgetur. 1. Epistolam ad Hebraeos itidem dici debere Catholicam, cum ad conversos ex Iudaeis sit scripta. Resp. ex cap. 10. v. 34. colligi potest, quod peculiariter ad conversos Iudaeos, qui Hierosolymis & in Iudaea commorabantur, perscripta fuerit, dicuntur enim rapinam bonorum suorum cum gaudio suscepisse.

2. Priorem ad Corinthios inscribi omnibus, qui invocant nomen Domini nostri Iesu Christicap. 1. v. 2. Resp. significatur, usum huius Epistolae omnibus Christianis debere esse communem, interim peculiariter inscribitur Ecclesiae DEI, quae est Corinthi.

3. Iacobum & Petrum scribere ad conversos ex Iudaismo. Resp. illi ipsi integrum constituebant populum, partem Ecclesiae Catholicae non infirmam complectentem, Ecclesia enim ex Iudaeis & gentibus fuit collecta.

4. Priorem hanc Petri Epistolam ad Ponticos olim fuisse vocatam. Resp. quod non solis Ponticis, sed quod praecipuè illis inscripta, nominantur enim primo loco.

5. Primam Iohannis olim Epistolam ad Parthos dictam fuisse. Resp. in titulo vocatur καθολικὴ. Qui ad Parthos scriptam dicunt, Parthorum nomine caeteros populos Orientales, in quibus dispersi erant Christiani, videlicet Medos, Elamitas, incolas Mesopotamiae, qui Act. 2. v. 9. Parthis subiunguntur, complecti volunt.

6. Secundam Iohannis ad electam Dominam & filios eius; tertia ad Gaium scripta. Resp. Epistolae tertiae Iohanneae nomen καθολικῆς etiam in Graecis Codd. non adiicitur, annumerantur Catholicis Epistolis, quia primae Iohannis Catholicae quasi quaedam partes censentur.

Fatendum igitur, in hac appellatione non posse omnia ad ἀκρίβειαν exigi. Idem dicendum de nomine Canonico Epistolis hisce septem iam olim attributo. Hieronymus in prologo super Epist. Cathol. qui habetur in Bibliorum edition. antiquissimis & apud Lyranum. Iohannes Huss. in comm. prioris Petri dicit, vocari eas Canonicas vel ad differentiam illarum Epistolarum, quas Pseudo Apostoli Ecclesiae obtrudere voluêre, vel quia in canonem divinae Scripturae sunt receptae, vel quia regulas & praecepta vitae Christiana continent. Quidam addunt, quod sine obliquitate erroris sint exaratae, ac sint canon & regula, tum Ecclesiasticarum Scripturarum, tum nostri intellectus, voluntatis & operum. Sed quilibet videt, haec omnia cum Epistolis Paulinis ipsis esse communia. Quod ergo Canonicae dicuntur, non exclusivè, sed ἐξοχικῶς & ἐξαιρέτως accipiendum. Hieronym. Epist. ad Paulin. Iacobus, Petrus, Iohannes & Iudas Epistolas ediderunt tam mysticas, quam succinctas & breves pariter & bonas; breves in verbis, longas in sententiis, ut rarus sit, qui in earum lectione non coecutiat Dionys. in prooem. Cathol. Quamvis propter has rationes etiam Pault Epistolae possent dici Canonicae, magis tamen hoc nomen his impositum est epistolis, quod à diversis autoribus sint conscriptae, & ita ab uno eorum peculiare aliquod nomen sortiri nequirent, sed commune eis aliquod nomen tribuendum erat, idque condignum & venerabile.

De ordine septem istarum Epistolarum Catholicarum etiam aliquid monendum. Hieronymus d. l. memorat, Petrinis Epistolis in Latinis Codd. olim primum fuisse datum locum, quem ordinem ex Graecis Codd. mutaverit. Non ita (inquit) ordo est apud Graecos, qui integrè sapiunt & fidem rectam sectantur Epistolarum septem, quae Canonicae nuncupantur, sicut in Latinis Codicibus invenitur, ut, quia Petrus est primus in ordine Apostolorum, primae sint etiam eius Epistolae in ordine caeterarum. Sed sicut Evangelistas dudum ad veritatis lineam correximus, ita hos proprio ordini Deo iuvante reddidimus, Est enim prima earum una Iacobi, duae Petri, tres Iohannis & una Iudae. Hunc ordinem Hieronymus non fuisset mutare ausus, si hypotheses, quas Pontificii hodie magno conatu defendunt, veras iudicasset, videlicet Petrum fuisse Ecclesiae Monarcham, ac Latinam editionem esse authenticam. Inde Patres concilii Florentini in decreto Armenis dato, & Tridentini in decreto de Script. Canon. sess. 4. Petri Epistolas contra Graecorum Codicum fidem primo loco ponunt. Sed Hieronymo suffragantur non solùm Graeci Codices, verùm etaim antiquissimi Ecclesiae Doctores, & ipsae editiones Bibliorum Latinae hodiernae, in quibus Iacobi Epistola primo loco ponitur, vel quia primo loco fuit scripta, ut vult Lyranus, vel quia Iacobus Alphaei filius, frater Domini, Epistolae huius autor, fuit Hierosolymitanae Ecclesiae Episcopus, quam reliquarum Ecclesiarum veluti matrem & originem honorarunt. Esai. 2 v. 3.Mich. 4. v. 2. Sanè in canon. Apostolorum ultimo & apud Augustinum lib. de fide & operibus cap. 14. uti etiam in Germanica Lutheri versione, Catholicae Epistolae recensentur hoc ordine; Epistolae Petri, Iohannis, Iacobi & Iudae in Concilio Carthaginensi 3. can. 47. & apud Augustinum lib. 2. de doctr. Christ. c. 8. Iacobi Epistola ultimo loco ponitur, fortè quia de eâ à quibusdam primò fuit dubitatum, ac ultimo demum loco recepta; Innocentius primus in Epist. 4. ad Exuperium Iohannis Epistolas caeteris anteponit. Interim quia Epistola Iacobi in Concil. Laodiceno can. ult. apud Hieronymum in Epistola ad Paulinam Bibliis praefixa & Gelasium c. Sancta Romana dist. 15. primo loco ponitur, quia canones Apostolorum diversum ordinem sectantes sunt supposititii, ac Graeci Codices constanter Iacobi Epistolae primas deferunt, ideò ordini isti meritò insistimus. Quod Estius statuit, illos qui primo loco Petri Epistolas numerarunt, rationem habuisse principatus Petri inter Apostolos, illud si de principatu quodam honoris accipitur, in medio relinquimus; sin de principatu Monarchicae potestatis, tanquam Scripturis & huius ipsius Epistolae prioris cap. 5. v. 1. contrarium repudiamus.

4. Seriem. Vocatur πρώτηprior, respectu posterioris ab eodem Apostolo scriptae. Hae enim solae ex reliquis omnibus scriptis, quae Petro per ψευδεπιγραφὴν attributa, in Canonicae autoritatis fastigium sunt receptae, cum eo tamen discrimine, ut posterior ad secundi ordinis Canonicos referatur. Hieronymus in prologo super Epist. Petri. Petrus scripsit duas Epistolas, quae Canonicae nominantur, quarum secunda à plerisque eius esse negatur propter styli cum priore dissonantiam. Sed & Evangelium iuxta Marcum, qui auditor eius & interpres fuit, huius dicitur. Libri autem eius, è quibus unus Actorum eius scribitur, alius Evangelii, tertius praedicationis, quartus Apocalypsis, quintus Iudicii, inter Apocryphas Scripturas reputantur. Dubitatur à quibusdam, an haec Epistola reverà sit Petri prima, cum aliam ante hanc scripsisse videatur. Erasmus, in argumento, quod praemisit paraphrasi huius Epistolae & in ipsa paraphrasi cap. ult. existimat, Petrum ante has duas aliam adhuc & ad eosdem Epistolam scripsisse, cum in fine prioriscap. 5. v. 12.dicat. Per Sylvanum fidelem fratrem breviter scripsi. Sed huic ratiocinationi assurgere non possumus. Loquitur enim Petrus non de alia, sed de hac ipsa Epistola, ut ostendit non solùm versio Syriaca, quae notanter reddidit, [consult facsimile image]Haec pauca scripsi vobis, sed etiam subiuncta descriptio argumenti, quod exactissimè huic Epistolae congruit, exhortans & testificans hanc esse veram gratiam DEI, in qua statis. Sic quando Paulus dicit 1. Corinth. 5. v. 9.scripsi vobis in Epistola, non intelligit aliam quandam, sed illam ipsam ad Corinthios datam Epistolam, uti docent Chrysostomus & Theophylactus in illum locum. Quando idem Hebr. 13. v. 22. dicit, perpaucis scripsi vobis, manifestissimum est, quod itidem no aliam, sed hanc ipsam intelligat Epistolam. Quid quod in posteriore Epistola cap. 3. v. 1. sic habetur. Hanc ecce carissimi secundam vobis scribo Epistolam. At si ante priorem aliam misisset, tertiam illam dicere debuisset.

Atque haec de expositione tituli dicta sunto, quibus ad προλεγόμενα complenda addi potest scriptionis. 1. Occasio. 2. Tempus. 3. Locus. 4. Idioma originarium 5. Epistolae argumentum & 6. Dispositio generalis. 1. Occasionem scriptionis Lyrianus existimat fuisse ad adventum Sylvani ad Petrum Sylvanus, inquit, per quem Petrus scripsit qui est Silas forsan volebat adire loca ad confirmandum fideles, eo quod ibi fuerat in praedicatione cum paulo ut patet ex Actis. Cogitari igitur potest, Sylvanum, qui in illis ipsis regionibus, in quibus dispersi habitabant illi ad quos Petrus ferbit, unà cum paulo docuerat & Ecclesias plantaverat,Act. 15. v. 40cap. 17. v. 4cap 18. v. 5.2. Cor. 1. v. 19.ad easdem confirmandas rediturum Babylonem transivisse & isthic Petrum covenisse, à quo hanc Epistolam acceperit. Augustinus lib. de fide & operibus cap. 14. ut Iohanni, Iacobo ac Iudae, ita quoque Petro scribendi occasionem datam existimat ab erronea eorum opinione, qui fidem sine operibus praedicabant. Quoniam ergò, inquit, haec opinio Simonis Magi, Nicolai & aliorum, qui fidem sine operibus praedicabant, tunc fuerat exorta, aliae Apostolicae Epistolae Petri, Iohannis, Iacobi, Iudae contra eam maximè dirigunt intentionem, ut vehementer astruant, fidem sine operibus nihil prodesse, sicut & ipse Paulus non quamlibet fidem, quâ in Deum creditur, sed eam salubrem, planeque, Evangelicam definivit, cuius opera ex dilectione procedunt. Et fides, inquit, quae per dilectionem operatur. Et postea. Unde evidenter in secundâ Epistolâ Petrus, cum ad vitae & morum sanctitatem hortaretur, sciens, de Apostoli Pauli quibusdam sub obscuris sententiis nonnullos iniquos accepisse occasionem, ut tanquam securi de salute, quae in fide est, benè vivere non curarent, commemoravit, quaedam ad intelligendum difficilima esse in Epistolis eius, quae homines perverterent, sicut & alias Scripturas ad proprium suum interitum, cum tamen & ille Apostolus de salute aeterna, quae nisi benè viventibus non daretur, eadem sentiret, quae caeteri Apostoli. Ex ipso Epistolae argumento & ex statu Ecclesiae illorum temporum, uti etiam ex fine, propter quem Paulus Hierosolymam ad Petrum & Iacobum ascendit Gal. 1. v. 18. & 19.cap. 2. v. 2. colligitur, fuisse quosdam, qui dubitarent, an Petrus eadem doceret cum iis, quae à Paulo & Sila sive Sylvano docebantur, praesertim cum ob Ceremonias Leviticas in N. T. abrogatas ingentia certamina moverentur. Ad testificandum igitur doctrinae cum Paulo & Sila consensum, & ad confirmandos in fide eos, quibus Evangelium vivâ voce praedicaverat, eosdemque ad studium bonorum operum i. e. ad proferendos Evangelii fructus excitandos, hanc Epistolam scripsit, quam Sylvano perferendam dedit, unde etiam in 2. Epist. 3. v. 15. disertam Pauli mentionem facit.

2. Tempus Baronius Anno Christi 45. n. 16. Epistolam hanc eo, quem diximus, anno Christi scriptam fuisse statuit, qua ratione foret omnium Epistolarum Apostolicarum antiquissima, quia prior ad Thessal. Anno Christi 52. scripta creditur. Sed hoc incertum esse quilibet videt. Illud potest colligi ex cap. 4. v. 16. huius Epistolae, scriptam eam esse, cum discipuli Christi iam coepissent vocari Christiani, quod Antiochiae factum, Lucas cap. 11. v. 26. memorat, Anno Christi 43. contigisse, Annalium conditor ann. 43. n. 10. factum esse censet. Lyranus in prolog. super Cathol. Epist. statuit, utramque Epistolam post Iacobi mortem paulo ante finem vitae à Petro scriptam esse.

3. Locum exprimit ipse Apostolus cap. 5. v. 13.Salutat vos Ecclesia, quae est in Babylone. Per eam v. Romam intelligendam esse, mágno conatu plerique Pontificii disputant, quâ de re quid statuendum sit, suo dispicietur loco.

4. Idiomate Hebraeo hanc Epistolam à Petro scriptam, in Graecum vero sermonem à Marco translatam quidam colligunt ex Hieronymo Epist. 150. ad Hedib. q. 11. Sed Hieronymus nihil aliud dicit, quàm duas Epistolas, quae feruntur petri, stylo & charactere discrepare, structuraque, verborum, ubi per characterem non intelligit linguam, quâ utraque scripta est, sed dicendi genus & sermonis proprietatem. Eadem ergo veritate haec Epistola Hebraeo sermone exarata à Petro dicitur, quâ Marcus Petri interpres Evangelium Latino sermone scripsisse statuitur à Baronio ann. 45. n. 38. Bellarm. lib. 2. de verbo DEI cap. 7. Adrian. Fin. lib. 6. flagelli contra Iud. cap. 80. libro 8. c. 62. Petr. Anton. Beuter. annot. 9. ad Script.

5. Argumentum exponit Apostolus cap. 1. v. 13.Perfectè sperate in eam, quae vobis oblata est, gratiam &cap. 5. v. 12.per Sylvanum breviter vobis scripsi, exhortans & testificans, hanc esse veram gratìam DEI in qua statis. Duplicem igitur Apostolus in hac Epistola propositum sibi habet scopum. 1. Διδασκαλικὸν, vult enim eos, ad quos scribit, in fide confirmare, & testificari doctrinam Evangelicam de gratiâ DEI per Christum, quam amplexi erant & in cuius fide ac professione stabant, esse in fallibiliter veram. 2. Νουθετικὸν, quia seriò & graviter ipsos monet, ut vitam professione illâ dignam agant, & doctrinam sanctis moribus exornent. Oecumen. in argum. Eos qui ex Iudaeis crediderant, in fide & vitae integritate confirmat.

6. Dispositio generalis. Latini secant Epistolam in quinque capita, Graeci in octo. Ederus lib. 4. Oecon. Bibl. p. 521. talem affert partitionem. Summa huius Epistolae in duas scinditur partes, in quibus agitur 1. In specie de gratiarum actione, cap. 1. & 2. usque ad versum 11. 2. In genere de aliis Christiani hominis virtutibus à dicto v. 11. cap. 2. usque ad finem totitus Epistolae. Priorem Epistolae partem absolvit Apostolus tribus membris. Primò sex tangit beneficia, quorum nomine pro se quisque perpetuas debet agere gratias. Primum est Baptismus, quo sumus regenerati in spem vivam in hereditatem incorruptibilem.cap. 1. v. 3.Secundum virtus DEI, quâ custodimur per fidem in salutemv. 5.Tertium facultas resistendi omnis generis tentationibus, quibus fides nostra multò rectius probatur, quam aurum.v. 6.Quartum salus animarum, quae efficit, ut Christum diligamus etiam non visum.v. 8.Quintum donum prophetiae, quo nobis non passiones tantum Christi praenunciatae, sed futura etiam posthac gloria revelata est,v. 10.Sextum Spiritus sancti missio, cuius beneficio ea, quae per Prophetas promissa fuerunt, perfecta sunt omnia & absoluta.v. 12.

Secundò modum praescribit, quo rectissimè nos Deo gratos exhibere possimus, quod Apostolus futurum asserit, si omne genus vitiorum fugiamus & morum sanctitatem sectemur. Tertiò septem esse docet, quae nos ad utrumque tam ad gratiarum actionem, quàm ad vitae sanctimoniam impellere debent, videlicet. 1. Graetiam, quae nobis ultrò fuit oblata, & quâ in tam sanctam Christi conversationem vocati & adoptati sumus v. 13. 2. Obligationem, quâ ad antidora excitamur, & vocationi tam dignae & honestae parere tenemur, quicunque privilegio filiorum gaudere cupimus. v. 14. 3. Mutuam inter DEUM Patrem & nos filios eius coniunctionem, quae consistit in eo, ut eum, quem nos ut filios diligere scimus, revereamur vicis sim, ut Patrem. v. 17. 4. Precii, quo sumus, maginitudinem, v. 18. 5. Regenerationis nostrae dignitatem v. 22. 6. Gustum Domini dulcissimum, quo reficiuntur ii, qui deponunt omnem malitiam & omnem dolum, cap. 1. v. 1. 2. & 3. 7. Certitudinem fidei nostrae, quae aedificata est super lapidem vivum. v. 4. usque ad 11.

In posteriore Epistolae parte, quae de moribus Christianorum reformandis agit, considerandus est 1. Ordo civilis, de quo in cap. 2. v. 11. usque ad finem cap. 4. 2. Ecclesiasticus, cuius ratio explicatur in cap. 5. Civilis hominum conditio triplex est. 1. Servilis à v. 11. cap. 2. usque ad cap. finem. 2. Coniugalis à princ. cap. 3. usque ad v. 9. 3. Politica à v. 9. illius capitus, usque ad eiusdem finem. Officia & mores eorum, qui in servili sunt conditione, sic describuntur, quod debeant sibiipsis abstinentiam à carnalibus desideriis cap. 2. v. 11. proximo bonum praebere exemplum v. 12. Magistratui obedientiam v. 13. DEO religionem, reverentiam & timorem v. 16. Dominis etiam iniquis & dyscolis morem gerere, ac eorum importunitatem patienti animo ferre. v. 18. Christo imitationem v. 21. usque ad cap finem. Officia coniugum explicantur in cap. 3. in quo Apostolus hortatur 1. Uxores ad humilitatem & obedientiam v. 1. ad honestam conversationem, ut morum comitate viros lucrifaciant, v. 2. ad cultum & ornatum potius animi quàm corporis quaerendum v. 3. 2. Viros, ut cohabitent uxoribus secundum scientiam. v. 8. ut cedant interim aliquid earum moribus proter sexus infirmitatem, ibid. ut exhibeant eis honorem, ut coheredibus gratiae vitae, ibid. ut abstineant interdum etiam à legitimo earum usu, ut orationi vacare queant. ibid. Officia hominis cuiusvis in Christiana Republ. versantis metitur Apostolus ex variis rerum circumstantiis, praecipuè ex duabus. 1. Ex collatione hominis primò ad hominem i. e. proximum suum cuiuscunque sit ordinis, quo cum tunc rectè conversari poterimus, si amplectamur concordiam cap. 3. v. 9. humanitatem, ibid pietatem v. 10. iustitiam v. 12. innocentiam v. 15. Secundò ad seipsum & corpus sive carnem suam propriam, cuius concupiscentiis resistendum. cap. 4. v. 1. usque ad 7. 2. Ex contemplatione primò finis, ad quem omnia sunt dirigenda. In quo iterum consideranda sunt duo. Primò media, quibus ad eum finem pervenitur, quae sunt prudentia v. 7. vigiliae ibid. Oratio ibid. charitas v. 8. hospitalitas v. 10. donorum DEI liberalis dispensatio, sive communicatio. v. 10. Secundò summa, ut in omnibus actionibus nostris honorificetur DEUS per Christum. v. 11. Secundò nominis Christiani. In homine enim Christiano, qui hoc nomen iure sustinere cupiat, requiruntur constantia in fide v. 12. fortitudo in persecutionibus pro Christi nomine perferendis vers. 14. cautio diligens, ne vel inpeccatum incidat, vel praesumtuosus fiat. vers. 18.

In statu Ecclesiastico alii praesunt ut pastores, quorum est docere cum fide & diligentia cap. 5. v. 1. non coactè sed sponte v. 2. nec turpis lucri gratiâ, ibid. absque superbia v. 3. bono exemplo honestae conversationis. ibid. Alii subsunt, ut oves, quas decent obedientia v. 5. humilitas ac mutua inter eas reverentia & obsequium ibid. timor DEI v. 6. spes firma v. 7. sobrietas & vigilantia v. 8. fortitudo & constantia. v. 9. Virisque gloria vitae aeternae promittitur. v. 10.

Quamvis vero haec partitio in quibusdam utiliter adhiberi possit, tamen in ea duo potissimùm iure desiderantur. 1. Quòd unicum duntaxat Epistolae scopum statuat exhortatorium scilicet ad sanctam vitae & morum conversationem, cum ex argumento Epistolae constet, quod Apostolus insuper docere voluerit, doctrinam Evangelicam, quam fide amplexi erant, esse infallibiliter veram, atque hoc nomine ad constantiam in fide eos exhortari. 2. Quòd officia omnibus Christianis communia ad certos duntaxat status atque ordines referat. Certè imitatio Christi cap. 2. v. 21. praescripta non tantum ab illis, qui in servili vitae genere constituti sunt, sed ab omnibus omninò Christianis requiritur.

Progredimur igitur hoc ordine, ut Epistolae huius tres constituamus partes. 1. προίμιον. 2. ἐργασίαν. 3. ἐπίλογον. Prooemium continet inscriptionem & salutationem. cap. 1. v. 1. & 2. ἐργασὶα absolvitur duabus partibus. Prior est διδασκαλικὴ, quòd doctrina de Christo, quam ab Apostolis conversi ex Iudaismo acceperant, sit omninò verissima ac certissima. Probat hoc Apostolus dupliciter. 1. Commemoratione beneficiorum spiritualium partim iamdum per eam collatorum, partim adhuc sperandorum. 2. Demonstratione exactissimi consensus cum doctrina Prophetica, cuius veritas conversis illis erat indubitata. cap. 1. v. 3. usque ad v. 13. Posterior est νουθετικὴ, posito enim isthoc de veritate doctrinae Evangelicae fundamento exhortatur Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit, ut in professione illius doctrinae constantes perseverent, eandemque vitae & morum sanctitate ornent, sicque non verbis solum, sed etiam reipsâ DEO gratos exhibeant. Exhortatio illa vel est generalis ad omnes Christianos spectans, vel specialis ad certos vitae status atque ordines directa. Quaedam enim officia sunt omnibus Christianis communia, quaedam vero certis quibusdam vitae statibus propria. In genere Apostolus omnes Christianos exhortatur ad studium bonorum operum & tolerantiam malorum. Bona opera sunt vel primae tabulae, ut constantia in fide, humilitas, seria precatio &c. vel secundae tabulae, ut dilectio proximi, misericordia, iuxta praeceptum quintum; temperantia, sobrietas, castitas iuxta praeceptum sextum; hospitalitas iuxta septimum; linguae refrenatio iuxta octavum. Mala toleranda sunt vel iniuriae privatae, vel persecutiones publicae. In specie compellat personas in certis officiis ac vitae generibus constitutas, easque hortatur γενικῶς, ut functionem sibi commissam solicitè administrent; εἰδικῶς in statu politico subditos; in statu oeconomico viros, uxores & servos; in Ecclesiastico Presbyteros officii sui admonet. Hae exhortationes sparsim ac mixtim à v. 13. capitis primi usque ad v. 10. capitis quinti proponuntur. Epilogus constat. 1. ἀνακεφαλαιώσει praecipuorum capitum in hac Epistola tractatorum v. 12. 2. ἀσπασμοῖς. v. 13. 3. προτροπῇ & 4. εὐχῇ. v. 14.

Summa & partes huius capitis patent ex praecedentibus. Prooemium Epistolae proponitur in v. 1. & 2.Petrus Apostolus Iesu Christi electis advenis dispersionis Ponti, Galatiae, Cappadociae, Asiae & Bithyniae, secundum praescientiam DEI Patris in sanctificationem Spiritus, in obedientiam & aspersionem sanguinis Iesu Christi. Gratia vobis & pax multiplicetur. Prooemii huius plerique tria constituunt membra, subscriptionem, inscriptionem & salutationem. Respiciunt illi ad mores nostrorum temporum & regionum, in quibus nomen autoris Epistolae subscribi solet. Sed res ipsa ostendit, Petrum Apostolum nomen suum non subscripsisse, sed more tum temporis inter Hebraeos, Graecos & Romanos recepto, in frontispicio Epistolae praescripsisse. Rectiùs ergo duo statuuntur membra. Inscriptio & salutatio. Inscriptio exprimit tum causam efficientem, sive autorem Epistolae, tum obiectum, ad quos scilicet ea sit perscripta.

CAPUT I.

Autor Epistolae est Petrus Apostolus Iesu Christi. Describitur hic autor. 1. ex nomine. Vocatus alioqui fuit Simon ab obedientia. Hieron. de vir. illustr. Petrus filius Iohannis, frater Andreae Apostoli, ortus in vico Bethsaida provinciae Galilaeae, quae est iuxta stagnum Genezareth, qui primò vocatus est Bariona. Petti cognomen ipsi promissum, cum primùm ad Christum à fratre Andrea adduceretur Iohan. 1. v. 43. datum, quando ad Apostolatum cum aliis duodecim electus Marcus. 3. v. 15. confirmatum, quando Christum veram & unicam salutis petram omnium Apostolorum nomine confessus Matth. 16. v. 18. Plurima huius Petri in Historia Evangelica & Apostolica fit mentio.

2. Ex officio. Apostolus Iesu Christi. Vocatus enim erat à Christo ad Apostolatum Matth. 4. v. 18Marc. 3. v. 15.Luc 6. v. 14. in Schola Christi ultra triennium institutus, ac die pentecostes per Spiritum sanctum miraculosè & visibiliter effusum de mysteriis regni coelorum plenissimè edoctus. Solus Petrus & Paulus in Epistolarum inscriptione se vocant Apostolos. Iacobus & Iudas se vocant Christi servos.

Quaeritur h. l. 1. Quare Petrus nomen suum in frontispicio exprimere voluerit? Resp. ut genuinam hanc suam Epistolam à supposititiis & ψευδεπιγράφοις Pseudo. Apostolorum scriptis distingueret.

2. Quare se Apostolum Iesu Christi vocet? 1. Ut ostendat, se id quod in hac Epistola facit, ex officio facere. Apostolici enim muneris erat, non solùm viva voce, sed etiam scriptis Ecclesiam docere. Matth. 28. v. 19.Iohann. 21. v. 24.1. Iohann. 1. v. 3 & 4.Apoc. 1. v. 2. & 3. 2. Ut autoritatem & benevolentiam sibi conciliet. Ecquis enim Legatum Christi audire nollet? Est Legatus Iesu Salvatoris. Ergo Salutem eorum, ad quos scribit, unicè quaerit. Didynius in comm. Epist. Cathol. Sicut mortales gloriam hominum appetentes in suis conscriptionibus dignitates, quas putantur habere, praeponunt, ita sancti viri in Epistolis, quas scribunt ad Ecclesias, principaliter proserunt se esse servos Domini nostri Iesu Christi, aestimantes, hanc appellationem supra regnatotius mundi consistere. Iohannes Huss in comm. h. l. haud absurdè statuit, Petrum hac appellatione exprimere suam dignitatem, autoritatem & infallibilem veritatem. 3. Ut ostendat se non afferre novam aliquam doctrinam, sed cum Paulo & aliis Apostolis eadem per omnia docere. Apud Clementem lib. 2. Recognit. Petrus ad Simonem Magum sic loqui introducitur. Nos enim Apostoli illius, qui misit nos, verba exponere missi sumus & affirmare sententias, proprium vero dicere aliquid non habemus in mandatis, sed verborum illius, ut dixi, aperire veritatem. Tertull. lib. de praescript. Apostoli nihil quicquam ex suo arbitrio, quod inducerent, elegerunt, sed acceptam à Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignaverunt.

1. Ἔλεγχος. 1. Petrus in hac inscriptione contentus est Apostoli denominatione, nequaquam vero sese vocat Apostolorum principem & totius Ecclesiae Monarcham. Falsum igitur est quod Bellarm. lib. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap. 10. & reliqui Pontificii Monarchicum dominium in totam Ecclesiam ipsi à Christo tributum statuunt. Salmeron Disp. 1. in hanc Epistolam variis modis excipit. Primò Petrum non fuisse potestatis suae penitus oblitum, cum ad summum Paestorem spectaverit Presbyteros sui admonere officii, quod faciat Petruscap. 5. v. 1. & seqq. Resp. imò vero Petrus ibidem disertis verbis huic somnio contradicit. Vocat enim se συμπρεσβύτερονv. 1. ac prohibet κατακυριεύειν τῶν κλήρωνv. 3. Ecquis ergò credat, ipsum, κυριότητα ac dominatum sibi arrogasse, cuius usu aliis pastoribus interdixit? Sed & solum Christum ibidem v. 4. vocat Principem, pastorum, sibi vero eiusmodi dignitatem minimè arrogat. Neque ex eo, quod Petrus alios Pastores sui admonet officii, Monarchica, quaedam potestas evinci potest, aliàs Paulo Apostolo eadem ob eandem rationem effet tribuenda Act. 20. v. 28.1. Timoth. 3. v. 2.Tit. 1. v. 7. Secundò, cùm optimè novisset, multa Christum Dominum praedixisse, & constituisse de eius clavibus ad aperiendum regnum coelorum, deque eius pastoratu & fratrum suorum confirmatione, non putavit, illis tantis Christi testimoniis omnibus compertis & patefactis necessarium esse aliud ipsum de seipso testimonium afferre. Resp. an Christus verbis illis, dabo tibi claves regni coelorum, pasce oves meas, tu conversus confirma fratres tuos &c. Monarchicum in universam Ecclesiam primatum Petro contulerit, adhuc in quaestione; contrarium enim ex illis ipsis locis liquidò demonstrari potest. Hoc loco illud urgemus, si propter hanc causam à Salmerone allatam, Petrus seipsum, Ecclesiae Monarcham appellare noluit, utique nec Apostolum Christi sese vocare debuisset, quia de Apostolatu ipsius itidem omnibus constat.

Tertiò cum Petrus non tantum esset pastor universalis Ecclesiae, sed etiam Apostolus, cuius proprium erat munus, universum orbem, lustrare & Evangelio illustrare, maluit tamen perfungi Apostolico munere, discurrendo per omnes provincias, erigendo Ecclesias, & ministros & Episcopos ordinando, quàm pastoratu, in quo tantùm Coryphaeus & universarum Christi ovium iudex & sub se peculiarium Pastorum, ita ut videretur quodam modo pastoratum suum negligere & primatum; & cum caeteris Apostolis tanquam frater atque aequalis se gerere elegit, non autem ut maior & ipsorum caput & rector. Resp. invertimus argumentum, quia Petrus nuspiam potestatem dominii arrogavit, sed eodem cum reliquis Apostolis munere perfungi voluit; quia passus est se ablegari unà cum Iohanne tanquam aequali ad Samaritanos Actor. 8. vers. 14. aequo animo admisit Iudaeorum expostulationem, quod ad gentes ingressus fuerit, seque coram illis excusavit. Actor. 11. v. 3. controversiam de observatione legis Mosaicae nequaquam praetoriâ autoritate, sed communibus cum reliquis Apostolis suffragiis decidit Actor. 15. v. 5. passus est à Paulo ob simulationem sese reprehendi, Gal. 2. v. 14. in electione Matthiae Actor. 1. v. 23. in constitutione Diaconorum, Actor. 6. v. 5. communicato cum reliquis Apostolis consilio egit, ideò reipsâ ostendit, Monarchicum dominatum sibi minimè competere. Praetereà si Petrus ob Ecclesiae salutem maluit primatum suum negligere, & cum caeteris Apostolis tanquam frater & aequalis, non autem ut maior & ipsorum caput, & rector se gerere elegit, Evangelium sc. praedicando, eccur Pontisex, qui se Petri successorem vocat, à docendi munere propter primatum abstinet. Nec cum his congruit, quod in ead. Disp. Salmeron habet. Petrus (inquit) rarius praedicavit, ut in instituendis Ecclesiarum ministris & aliis magnis negotiis occuparetur. Et postea. Petrus suas praedicationes aliis administris ex charitate ad scripsit. Bellarm. lib. 1. de Pont. cap. 15.Tametsi plerique Pontifices non concionantur, tamen alios multos actus pastorales exercent, dum ligant, solvunt, dispensant, controversias iudicant, Episcopos creant & quod per se concionando non faciunt, per alios faciunt.

Quartò si Petrus ut Romanus Pontifex, Christique vicarius, atque, universalis Ecclesiae Pastor scripsisset, videretur in suis scriptis ius Ecclesiasticum, sive quod idem est, ius Canonicum ac Pontificium dictasse potiùs quàm divinum. Scripsit ergo B. Petrus ut merus Christi Apostolus, tradens, quae Christi sunt, quae divinam & indispensabilem habent autoritatem. Resp. huic ratiunculae derogat ipse Salmeron, quando subiungit: Summi Pontifices quaecunque in decretalibus suis statuunt, non statim ius divinum condunt, ac instituunt mandata tanquam à Christoἀμέσωςdata sint: exceptis tamen illis, quae Dominum constat in Evangelio de fide, spe, caritate, & Sacramentis, servandaque lege sua omnibus fidelibus tradidisse. Et postea. Nihil vetat, in divinis & canonicis Scripturis inveniri interdum praecepta Ecclesiastica sive Canonica, quae Apostoli, teste Luca in Concilio Hierosolymitano tradiderunt Antiochenis de suffocato non edendo, Paulus quoque praeceptum tradidit de non promovendo in Episcopum digamo, de neophyto &c. At si in Pontificum decretalibus inveniuntur praecepta divina, & in Apostolicis scriptis praecepta Ecclesiastica, non fuisset incongruum, Petrum se appellasse Pontificem, si vel maximè divina praecepta in hac Epistola proponere voluisset, Praeterea, si Apostolus, quâ talis, proponit ius divinum; Pontifex, quâ talis, ius Ecclesiasticum, utique Apostolatus maior est Papatu, & tamen Salmeron disputat, Petrum ut Pontificem reliquis Apostolis fuisse maiorem.
