Estius praetermissis illis Salmeronis rationibus, modestiae tribuit, quod Petrus se Apostolum Christi, non autem Apostolorum Principem & caput vocaverit. Sed qui officium divinitus sibi commissum exprimit, modestiae limites minimè transgreditur, aliàs ne quidem Apostolum sese Petrus potuisset nominare. 2. Pontifex Romanus in multis, contraria illis, quae in hac Epistola continentur, proponit, ut in progressu videbimus. Ergo non est verus Petri successor. Nazianz. in orat. de laudibus Athanas. tom. 2. p. 502. τὸ ὁμόγνωμον, καὶ ὁμόθρονον; τὸ δὲ ἀντὶδοξον καὶ ἀντίθρονον.Qui eandem fidem amplectitur, eiusdem quoque throni particeps est. Qui autem contrariam fidem amplectitur, adversarius quoque in throno censeri debet. Ambros. lib. 1. de poenit. c. 6. tom. 1. p. 156. Non habent hereditatem Petri, qui fidem Petri non habent.

3. Petrus in ipsa scriptione se vocat Apostolum Christi: Ergo Apostoli ex mandato Christi scripserunt. Contra Bellarm. lib. 4. de verbo DEI. cap. 4.

4. Apostolus fuit, qui hanc Epistolam scripsit. Ergo probari nequit, quod Stephanus 3. Pont. Rom. à Longobardis pressus Petri nomine Epistolam ad Pipinum Regem scripsit, quam recitat Baronius Ann. Christi 755. n. 18.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Bellarminus loco proximè citato sic disseret. Si Apostoli doctrinam suam literis consignare ex professo voluissent, certè Catechismum aut similem librum confecissent. At ipsi vel Historiam scripserunt, ut Evangelistae; vel Epistolas ex occasione aliqua, ut Petrus, Paulus, Iacobus, Iudas, Iohannes, & in iis non nisi obiter disputationes de dogmatibus tractaverunt. Resp. occasiones scribendi exteriùs Apostolis oblatae non tollunt internum scribendi mandatum, aliàs etiam praedicandi mandatum tollerent, cum ad praedicationem quoque occasio interdum ipsis fuerit oblata, Actor. 17. v. 16. Agnoscenda potius in eo mirabilis providentiae divinae dispositio, quòd ad occasiones illas oblatas exteriùs impulsus divinus interior accesserit. Quod disputationes de dogmatibus non obiter & ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, sed ex professo in Epistolis Apostolicis tractentur, inductione confirmari potest.

2. Fevardentius in cap. 1. Epist. Iacobi ex eo, quod Petrus nomen suum addit, perstringit lucifugas bestias haereticorum, qui perniciosos libros suos alienis & fictis nominibus contexerunt, aut omnino absque nomine vulgaverunt, quibus idcirco novum nomen Neministarum possit convenire. Resp. accusatio haec in ipsos Pontificios retorqueri potest. Autor Autonomiae vocat se Franciscum Burchardum, cum tamen Antonius Possevinus lib. 1. Bibl. p. 125. testetur, nomen esse supposititium, ac verum libri autorem esse Andream Ernstenbergerum. Conradus Vetterus sub nomine Conradi Andreae libros convitiis refertissimos scripsit, seque magni illius Theologi D. Iacobi Andreae fratrem mentitus est. Gratulatio Christophori ab Ungersdorff ad status Evangelicos in Austria falsum autoris nomen supponit. Ipsimet docemus, scripta ἀνώνυμα & ψευδώνυμα non esse simpliciter approbanda, interim posse aliquando nomen autòris omitti, si fiat sine dolo malo & ob causam aliquam necessariam, ostendit Epistola ad Hebraeos & prima Iohannis, quae autorum nomina non habuêre primùm adscripta.

3. Autor huius Epistolae vocat se Petrum, quia est petra illa, supra quam Christus promisit se aedificaturum suam Ecclesiam. Resp. Simon à petra dictus, fuit Petrus, quia per fidem seipsum, per confessionem & praedicationem etiam alios super Christum veram & unicam salutis petram aedificavit; sicut omnes credentes tanquam vivi lapides super Christum aedificantur, 1. Petr. 2. v. 4. & 5. non autem, quia Ecclesia super ipsum ratione personae & successorum erat aedificanda. August. serm. 13. de verb. Domini. Petra principale nomen est, ideò Petrus à petrâ, non petra à Petro, quomodo non à Christiano Christus, sed à Christo Christianus vocatur. Tu es ergo, inquit, Petrus, & super hanc petram, quam confessus es, super hanc petram, quam cognovisti, dicens, tu es Christus filius DEI vivi, aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, super me aedificabo te, non super te aedificabo me. Nam volentes homines aedificari super homines dicebant. Ego quidem sum Pauli, ego Cephae. Et alii, qui nolebant aedificari super Petrum, sed super petram, dicebant. Ego sum Christi.

Διδασκαλίαι 1. Petrus Christum abnegaverat, nihilo tamen minus in Apostolatum restitutus fuit. Exemplum hoc est divinae gratiae peccatoribus resipiscentibus propositum. 1. Tim. 1. v. 16.

2. Sine vocatione legitima nemo sibi partes docendi in Ecclesia vendicare debet. Hebr. 5. v. 4.

3. Scripta ἀνώνυμα ac ψευδώνυμα non esse simpliciter approbanda, patet ex dicto Christi Iohan. 3. v. 20. ex incommodis, quae ex suppressione vel variatione nominis oriri solent, ex Prophetarum, Evangelistarum & Apostolorum exemplis, qui scriptis suis nomina praefixerunt, ex legibus civilibus, 1. Falsi 13. ff. de leg. Corn. de falsis. Luth. tom. 4. f. 508. tom. 5. f. 551.

4. Epistola haec est Petri Apostoli. Ergo Canonicam autoritatem obtinet. Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. cap. 3. & 4. testatur, de ea nunquam in Ecclesia fuisse dubitatum; ac quotquot Canonicos N. T. libros enumerant, hanc Petrinam disertè illis accensent. Petrus Damianus serm. 28. tom. 2. Epistola Petri & sublimis illa sermonum doctrina nunquid mirabiliter pascit Ecclesiam DEI. Bonifacius Martyr ab Eadburga vel Eadeburga Abbatissa, Cantiorum Regis affine, petiit describi sibi literis aureis Petri Epistolas, uti memorat Baronius tom. 9. Annal. p. 39. perinde ut olim Platonicus quidam initium. Evangelii Iohannis aureis literis conscribendum, & per omnes Ecclesias in locis eminentissimis proponendum esse dicebat, ut ex Simpliciano sancto sene, qui Mediolanensi Ecclesiae praesedit Episcopus, refert August. lib. 10. de Civ. DEI cap. 29. Collatio cum Epistolis Paulinis luculentè ostendit, & illas & hanc ab eodem Spiritu profectas. Erasmus in annot. ei meritò hoc defert elogium, quod sit Epistola digna Apostolorum Principe (ratione dignitatis, non Monarchicae potestatis à veteribus sic dicto, ut docet Marsilius Patavinus in defens. pacis p. 203.) plena autoritatis ac maiestatis Apostolicae, verbis parca, sententiis differta.

## 1:1
TO THE ELECT SOJOURNERS OF THE DISPERSION OF PONTUS, GALATIA, CAPPADOCIA, ASIA & BITHYNIA,

The object, or those to whom this Epistle was written, are described 1. by their miserable external state 2. by their most happy internal state. By reason of their external state they are called παρεπίδημοι διασπορᾶς Πόντου, Γαλατίας, Καππαδοκίας, Ασίας καὶ Βιθυνίας.

Διασπορᾶς In Asia the metropolis was Babylon, from which Peter wrote this Epistle. For it must be known, as Scaliger advises in his notes to the N. T., that for the Jews there was one metropolis of religion, καὶ θρησκείας Jerusalem: but there were three πολιτείας metropolises, Jerusalem, Babylon, Alexandria. For there were two διασποραὶ, Asian, to which Peter writes; European, of which mention is made John 7. v. 95. The head of the Asian διασπορᾶς was Babylon, and those Jews used, and still use today in their Synagogues, the Chaldean paraphrase of Onkelos. Peter writes to them from the very metropolis of Babylon. διασπορᾶς The metropolis of the European was Alexandria. Those Jews had a temple almost as great as the Jerusalemites and used the Greek paraphrase of the LXX Interpreters, for that reason called ἑλληνισταὶ Acts 6. v. 1.c. 11. v. 20. for ἑλληνίζειν is not to dwell in Greece, as a certain Interpreter annotated, but to use the Greek language. The third kind πολιτείας were Jews attributed to the Jerusalemite metropolis as in the same c. 6. ἑβραῖοι they are distinguished from those who ἑλληνισταὶ, they used the Jerusalemite paraphrase, which exists today. Whom James calls τοὺς ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ that is ὄντας chap. 1. v. 1. them Peter calls παρεπιδῇμους διασπορᾶς strangers dispersed through Hebraism. The Ordinary Gloss renders placed in dispersion, for the noun dispersion is used in the customary phrase of Scripture for the dispersed themselves, just as election is used for the elect Rom. 11. v. 7. and circumcision for the circumcised Galat. 2. v. 7., in which meaning the noun dispersion is used Ioh. 7. v. 35. διασπορὰ τῶν ἑλλήνων. And from this noun διασπορᾶς it is understood that by strangers here are not understood either proselytes, who had converted themselves to the true God of Israel, in which meaning the Latin Interpreter uses this noun when he calls Nicolaus a stranger of Antioch Act. 6. v. 5., or Gentiles, who through the preaching of the Gospel had been called to the kingdom of Christ and had arrived at the heavenly Jerusalem, but Jews dispersed into those regions whose names are subjoined, who are therefore called strangers because they had arrived from elsewhere to the region in which they lived, in which meaning the Latin Interpreter uses this word Actor. 2. v. 12. where Roman stranger Jews are distinguished from proselytes. Thus also the little word παρεπιδήμων is used for foreigners and guests Hebr. 11. v. 13. and by Peter himself 1. Epist. 2. v. 11. where they are joined with παροίκοις παρεπίδημοι, which two words are also associated Gen. 23. v. 4. Psal. 39. v. 17. where it corresponds to the Hebrew תושב which signifies a sojourner, a guest, who in that place where he lives does not have his own house or possession. Moreover, Peter expresses the names of the regions in which those strangers lived in a scattered manner.

The first is Pontus, a maritime region, which embraces the whole shore of the Euxine sea as far as Colchis, lying upon the Mediterranean regions of Galatia and Cappadocia. It received its name from the fact that it was nearest to the Euxine sea. It had many distinguished cities and among them Caesarea.

The second is Galatia, a region near to Pontus. Oecumenius reads these two words conjunctively, of Pontus of Galatia, i.e., of that region which was called the Galatia of Pontus, because there was also another Galatia near the Celts, which is Celtic Gaul. Hence the Interpreter of Oecumenius translates, to those inhabiting the Galatia of Pontus. But nowhere else is Galatia of Pontus read. Nor is Galatia, which is called by another name Gallo-Graecia, a region of Pontus, but it has Pontus lying adjacent to it from the North.

The third is Cappadocia, so called from a river of lesser Asia, likewise a neighbor of Pontus, hence it is joined with Pontus in this place, as also Act. 2. v. 9..

The fourth is Asia, namely the minor, not that greater one, which constitutes the third part of the world along with Africa & Europe.

The fifth is Bithynia, at the beginning of the Pontus, opposite Thrace. Bede in this place: There is also another Bithynia in Europe, from which those who are in Asia are said to derive their origin. But that which is in Asia is called Bithynia and greater Phrygia, which is separated from Galatia by the river Hiera. All these nations were Greek and belonged to Asia Minor, from which it is gathered that by the name of those regions which he enumerates, Peter comprehends the whole tract of Asia Minor from the Euxine Sea as far as Cappadocia.

It is asked in this place: 1. Who are those peoples to whom Peter wrote this Epistle? Four opinions occur regarding this matter.

First, some wish that it was written to all Christians in general, since all are sojourners and pilgrims in this world, and all are also dispersed throughout the whole world. To confirm this opinion, it could serve that in ἐπιγραφῇ this Epistle is called Catholic, and that Peter in this Epist. cap. 2. v. 11. addresses all Christians: Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims. But one must distinguish between the proper object of the inscription, which in this place is determined as the inhabitants of Asia Minor, and the common use of the written Epistle. By reason of common use, both this Petrine Epistle and all the Epistles of the remaining Apostles pertain to us, of which, however, it is certain that some were inscribed to specific regions and cities, and some even to specific persons.

Secondly, Augustine, book 22 against Faustus, chapter 89, Ioh. Hesselius in his commentary, and from our own, B. Luther, Osiander, Winckelmann, etc., maintain that it was written to converted Gentiles.

1. Because in chapter 2. v. 10. the testimony is cited Oseae 2. v. 23. Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of GOD, which Paul Rom. 9. v. 25. interprets concerning the calling of the Gentiles.

2. In the same cap. v. 5. he says: Καὶ αὐτοὶ Ye also as lively stones are built up, i. e., not only those who are from the Jews, but also you who have been converted to Christ from the Gentiles, are built up upon that cornerstone, just as Paul Eph. 2. v. 19. says to the converted Gentiles: Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of GOD. v. 20. And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ himself being the chief cornerstonev. 22.in whom you also are being built together.

3. Incap. 1. v. 8.he says that they believe in Christ, whom they have not seen, and love him. This properly applies to the Gentiles, since the Jews are called blessed by this name, because they saw the Messiah teaching in the flesh and performing miracles.Luc. 10. v. 23.

4. In the samecap. v. 14.it is said, not conforming to the former lusts in your ignorance. But such a thing as this ἄγνοια properly belongs to the Gentiles.Act. 17. v. 30.Eph. 4. v. 18.

5. In cap. 4. v. 3.he says. The past time is sufficient to have wrought the will of the Gentiles when you walked in lasciviousness. He signifies, therefore, that they were Gentiles before their conversion.

6. In the same place he testifies that they walked in the illicit worship of idols. But idolatry was proper to the Gentiles.Gal. 4. v. 8.1. Thess. 1. v. 9.

7. The occasion of the writing seems to prove the same. For he wrote this Epistle for this reason, that he might not seem to dissent from Paul, through whom they had been called to the Gospel. Now, indeed, Paul was properly and especially the Apostle of the GentilesGal. 2. v. 7.

Thirdly, Bede, the Author of the ordinary gloss, Lyranus, John Huss, etc., wish it to have been written to the proselytes, whom they think are signified by the name of strangers. But those to whom Peter writes are not called προσήλυτοι, but παρεπίδημοι. Nor was there a reason why he should write particularly to them, since after the preaching of the Gospel it was not necessary for the Gentiles that they should become proselytes by undergoing circumcision, but they were converted immediately to the Christian faith.

Fourthly, Eusebius, book 3 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 4; Jerome in the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers; Athanasius in the Synopsis; Didymus in his commentary on the Canonical Epistles; Oecumenius in this place; Baronius, Annals, year 45, numbers 20, 21, wish it to have been written to the Jews.

1. They are called strangers of the dispersion, who are the same as those whom James calls τοὺς ἐν διασπορᾷ. But those were Jews, as is evident from the fact thatIac. 1. v. 1.the name of the twelve tribes is added.

2. The Gentiles were not strangers of those regions which Peter lists there, nor did they dwell dispersed only in those regions, but throughout the whole world. But the Jews dwelt in those places as if they were foreigners and guests.

3. Cap. 2. v. 12. he says, having your conversation honest among the Gentiles. Therefore they lived in the midst of the Gentiles.

4. Cap. 3. v. 7.Sara obeyed Abraham, whose daughters you are &c. that is thus you will answer to your race and to your ancestors. The Jews were accustomed to boast of their father Abraham.Matt. 3. v. 9.Luke 16. v. 24.

5. Cap. 1. v. 10.he proves the truth of the Christian doctrine from the consensus with the doctrine of the Prophets. But their authority was sacrosanct not to the Gentiles, but to the Jews.

6. In the same cap. v. 18.mention is made of paternal traditions. Of those the Jews boasted most of all, and they embraced them tightly.Matt. 15. v. 2.Mark 7. v. 2.Gal. 1. v. 14.

7. The later Epistle was written to the same ones to whom the former was, as is evident from2. Epist. cap. 3. v. 1.Now indeed that later one was written to those converted from Judaism, for it is said in itcap. 1. v. 19.we have a more sure Prophetic word.cap. 2. v. 1.there were indeed also False Prophets among the people.cap. 3. v. 15.as also our most dear brother Paul wrote to you, namely in his Epistle to the Hebrews.

8. To Peter was committed chiefly and peculiarly the Gospel of the circumcision i. e. to be preached to the circumcised JewsGal. 2. v. 7.

And indeed these arguments, although not all have equal strength, show that this Epistle was written primarily to the Jews, meanwhile because after the conversion to Christ not only proselytes, but also Gentiles communicated with the Jews believing in Christ as brothers, and constituted one Church with them, and thus had common Bishops with them, therefore it can also be said that it was written secondarily and less primarily to the converted Gentiles. For just as to the Gentiles converted to Christ living at Rome, Corinth, etc., those converted from the Jews were mixed in, and nevertheless the Epistles written to the Romans and Corinthians are said to have been written primarily by Paul the Apostle of the Gentiles to the converted Gentiles; so also conversely this Epistle of Peter is rightly said to have been written primarily to those converted from Judaism, although it pertains in a certain way to the converted Gentiles and proselytes joined to them by an internal unity of faith and an external unity of place.

Q. 2. Why did Peter write peculiarly to the faithful of these provinces? Resp. Peter himself 2. Epist. 1. v. 12. 13. & cap. 3. v. 1. ὐπόμνησιν he established the end of his writing. Moreover, ὑπόμνησις is a calling back into memory of those things which one has heard before, whence that ὑπομιμνήσκειν Peter in the same chapter 2, verse 15 ἐξηγητικῶς declares through μνήμην ποιεῖ σθαι. From which it is gathered that Peter had previously preached with a living voice to those to whom he directed this Epistle for the sake of ὑπομνήσεως. Epiphanius in the heresy of the Carpocratians Peter often visited Pontus and Bithynia. Jerome in book 1 against Jovinian likewise maintains that Peter himself had traveled through those provinces and had joined them to the Church of Christ by his preaching. Leo in sermon 1 on the birthday of the Apostles Peter and Paul addresses Peter thus: Already you had filled Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia with the laws of evangelical preaching. The same is the opinion of our Chemnitz in chapter 50 of the Harmony: That Peter taught, he says, in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia, and in Babylon, is evident from his own former Epistle chapter 1, verse 1 and chapter 5, verse 13. Estius opposes this opinion in vain, that the peoples of Asia and Galatia were converted to Christ by the preaching of Paul. For it was not unusual for several Apostles to have preached in one and the same region at distinct times. Thus, Irenaeus and others among the ancients testify that the Roman Church was planted by Paul and Peter. Nor can it be denied that John also preached in Asia Minor. What Estius argues, that there was another reason for Peter's writing, namely that he himself, as the Apostle of the circumcision and pastor of all the faithful, because of the grave persecutions stirred up against the faithful, especially the Jews in those parts, might exhort them through this Epistle to patience and confirm them in the faith, that does not yet prove that Peter had not previously preached the Gospel to those to whom he writes; otherwise it would follow that Paul also had not preached to those whom he would exhort in his Epistles to constancy in the faith and patience. That Peter wrote as the common pastor of all the faithful can be accepted in a double way: either that by reason of his Apostolic office he was the pastor of all the faithful, for to him just as to the other Apostles it had been entrusted by Christ that he should preach the Gospel to every creature and teach all nations Matthew 28, verse 19 Mark 16, verse 15, in which sense Paul also asserts that he is touched by the care and solicitude for all the churches 2 Corinthians 11, verse 28, or that by reason of a Monarchical primacy he was the pastor of all the faithful, in which sense Boniface VIII in the chapter Unam sanctam 10, on superiority and obedience, accepts the words of Christ brought to Peter John 21. The former sense we concede, the latter we deny.

Q. 3. Why is no mention made of Babylon in this inscription, when nevertheless the Jews living in Babylon were the head of the dispersion? Resp. because he writes this Epistle from Babylon 1. Epist. 5. v. 13. which very thing proves that the name of Babylon is to be taken properly there, not metaphorically and symbolically for the city of Rome.

Q. 4. What was that dispersion of the Jews? Most understand the dispersion made after the killing of Stephen. Act. 8. v. 1. but Luke notably adds that the faithful were then dispersed through the regions of Judea and Samaria. Baronius objects in Ann. 45. n. 21. that some of the faithful had gone even to Antioch and into Cyprus Actor 11. v. 19. and that Ananias, one of them, had arrived at Damascus Act. 9. v. 10. But those who betook themselves to distant regions in that dispersion were fewer than to constitute entire Churches, to which Peter writes. More correctly, therefore, it is said that the dispersion is understood which had already been made long before the coming of Christ, to wit, at that time when they had departed, having been led away or having fled of their own accord into Assyria, Babylonia, Egypt, and other kingdoms through captivities and wars, of which dispersion mention is made Iohan. 7. v. 35. Act. 2. v. 9. & 10. Those who were dispersed in that way remained joined to the Jewish people by the profession of religion, observed circumcision and the Levitical rites, and ascended to Jerusalem every year for the feasts. Ioh. 7. v. 35. cap. 12. v. 20.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι 1. Asia is placed in this passage as a region distinct from Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, and Bithynia. But all these were regions of Asia Minor. Resp. by the name of Asia, the region neighboring Ephesus is understood specifically in this passage, which in its circuit comprised, besides others, those seven cities to which John is commanded to write Apoc. 1. v. 11. In this meaning the name of Asia is taken Actor. 16. v. 6. & 7. where Phrygia, Galatia, Mysia, and Bithynia, which all are regions of Asia Minor, are distinguished from this Asia, Item Act. 19. v. 10. where Paul is said to have taught at Ephesus for two years with such fruit, that all who dwell in Asia heard the word of the Lord.

2. The Jews are said in this passage to be dispersed into various regions. And yet it had been promised to Abraham, Gen. 17. v. 8. To your seed I will give the land of Canaan for a perpetual possession. Resp. those promises had the condition of obedience annexed, as appears from the threats Lev. 26. v. 33. Deut. 28. v. 64. and the word עולם does not always signify absolute eternity, but according to the nature of the subject matter a long time, the end of which is hidden.

Ἔλεγχος. 1 The faithful converted from Judaism to Christ are called strangers of the dispersion. Therefore, the Church in the N. T. is not bound to a certain place or to a certain nation. Hence also, with respect had to the Israelite Church of the O. T., it is called Catholic.

2. The condition of those converted from Judaism was miserable; they lived dispersed among the nations, torn away from their ancestral seats, they experienced the fervor of temptations. 1. Petr. 5. v. 12. Therefore, temporal happiness is not a true & proper mark of the Church. Against Bellarm. lib. 4. de Eccles. cap. 18. Bellarmine himself admits, that the Church in the beginning suffered great straits, lib. eiusd. cap. 2. & grew from persecutions, lib. eiusd. cap. 6. how therefore can temporal happiness be a property of the Church.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. This Epistle was written to παρεπιδήμους. And yet we all are in these lands πάροικοι καὶ παρεπίδημοι Psal. 39. v. 17.Hebr. 11. v. 13. by which name Peter addresses us in this very Epistle cap. 2. v. 11. Therefore the use of this Epistle pertains to us also. Bede in h. l. But also if we can truthfully say with the Prophet to God, since we are inhabitants with you in the land & pilgrims, we ought to believe that the Epistles of Blessed Peter were written to us also & read them as sent to us.

2. The Church in this world is παθουμένη καὶ πατουμένη.

3. In Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia &c. there were once most flourishing Churches, but today Turkish idolomania reigns in the same place. Let us beware, therefore, lest on account of contempt for the word the kingdom of GOD be taken away from us alsoMatth. 21. v. 43. and our lampstand be moved from its place.Apoc. 2. v. 5.

4. GOD has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew; even after the Jerusalemite destruction, a remnant according to the election of grace has been made.Rom. 11. v. 2. & 5.

Latin:

ELECTIS ADVENIS DISPERSIONIS PONTI, GALATIAE, CAPPADOCIAE, ASIAE & BITHYNIAE,

Obiectum sive illi, ad quos haec Epistola exarata, describuntur 1. à statu externo miserabili 2. à statu interno felicissimo. Ratione status externi vocantur παρεπίδημοι διασπορᾶς Πόντου, Γαλατίας, Καππαδοκίας, Ασίας καὶ Βιθυνίας.

Διασπορᾶς in Asia metropolis erat Babylon, ex qua Petrus', hanc Epistolam scripsit. Sciendum n. ut monet Scaliger in notis ad N. T. Iudaeis unam religionisκαὶ θρησκείαςmetropolin fuisse Hierosolymam: tres a.πολιτείαςmetropoles fuisse, Hierosolymam, Babylonem, Alexandriam. Duae enimδιασποραὶ,Asianae ad quam scribit Petrus; Europaea, cuius mentio fit Iohan. 7. v. 95. Asianae διασπορᾶς caput erat Babylon, iique Iudaei utebantur, utunturque adhuc in Synagogis paraphrasi Chaldaicâ Onkelos. Ad eos scribit Petrus ex ipsa metropoli Babylone. διασπορᾶς Europaeae metropolis erat Alexandria. Ii Iudaei habebant templum quasi quantum Hierosolymitani & Graecâ paraphrasi LXX. Interpp. utebantur, ob id dicti ἑλληνισταὶActor. 6. v. 1.c. 11. v. 20. nam ἑλληνίζειν non est habitare in Graecia, ut quidam Interpres annotavit, sed Graecâ linguâ uti. Tertium genus πολιτείας erant Iudaei attributi metropoli Hierosolymitanae ut eodem c. 6.ἑβραῖοι distinguuntur ab iis, qui ἑλληνισταὶ, ii paraphrasi Hierosolymitanae, quae hodie extat, utebantur. Quos Iacobus vocat τοὺς ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ sc. ὄντας cap. 1. v. 1. eos Petrus vocat παρεπιδῇμους διασπορᾶς advenas dispersos per Hebraismum. Gloss. ord. in dispersione positos reddit, nomen enim dispersionis usitatâ Scripturae phrasi ponitur pro ipsis dispersis, sicut electio pro electis Rom. 11. v. 7.circumcisio pro circumcisis Galat. 2. v. 7. ponitur, in qua significatione nomen dispersionis usurpatur Ioh. 7. v. 35.διασπορὰ τῶν ἑλλήνων. Atque ex hoc nomine διασπορᾶς intelligitur, per advenas hic non intelligi vel proselytos, qui ad verum Deum Israëlis sese converterant, in qua significatione Latinus Interpres hoc nomine utitur, quando Act. 6. v. 5. Nicolaum vocat advenam Antiochenum vel gentiles, qui per Evangelii praedicationem ad Christi regnum vocati ad coelestem Hierosolymam pervenerant, sed Iudaeos in regiones illas, quarum nomina subiiciuntur dispersos, qui propterea vocantur advenae, quia ad regionem, in qua habitabant, aliunde advenerant, in qua significatione Latinus Interpres hac voce utitur Actor. 2. v. 12. ubi advenae Romani Iudaei à proselytis distinguuntur. Ita quoque vocula παρεπιδήμων pro peregrinis & hospitibus Hebr. 11. v. 13. & ab ipso Petro 1. Epist. 2. v. 11. ubi cum παροίκοις παρεπίδημοι coniunguntur, quae duo vocabula etiam consociantur Gen. 23. v. 4.Psal. 39. v. 17. ubi respondet Hebraeo תושב quod significat inquilinum, hospitem, qui in eo loco, ubi vivit, non habet propriam domum aut possessionem. Exprimit autem Petrus nomina regionum, in quibus advenae illi sparsim habitabant.

Prima est Pontus, regio maritima, quae totam oram maris Euxini usque ad Colchidem complectitur, Galatiae & Cappadociae mediterraneis regionibus incumbens. Nomen accepit ex eo, quod ponto Euxino fuerit proxima. Habuit multas insignes civitates & inter eas Caesaream.

Altera est Galatia, Ponto proxima regio. Oecumenius has duas voces legit coniunctim, Ponti Galatiae i. e. eius regionis, quae vocabatur Galatia Ponti, eò quod essect etiam alia iuxta Celtas Galatia, quae est Gallia Celtica. Inde Interpres Oecumenii vertit, incolentibus Ponti Galatiam. Sed nuspiam alibi legitur Galatia Ponti. Nec Galatia, quae alio nomine Gallo-Graecia dicta, Ponti regio est, sed à Septentrione Pontum habet adiacentem.

Tertia est Cappadocia, à fluvio minoris Asiae sic dicta, Ponti itidem vicina, inde cum Ponto hoc loco, uti etiam Act. 2. v. 9. coniungitur.

Quarta est Asia, minor scilicet, non illa maior, quae tertiam orbis partem cum Africa & Europa constituit.

Quinta est Bithynia in exordio Ponti Thraciae adversa. Beda in h. l. Est etiam alia Bithynia in Europa, de qua illi, qui in Asia sunt, Bithyni originem ducere perhibentur. Illa autem quae in Asia est Bithynia vocatur & maior Phrygia, quae Hiera flumine est à Galatia disterminata. Omnes hae gentes erant Graecae ac pertinebant ad Asiam minorem, ex quo colligitur, quod nomine illarum, quas enumerat, regionum Petrus totum Asiae minoris tractum à Ponto Euxino usque in Cappadociam comprehendat.

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quinam sint illi populi, ad quos Petrus hanc Epistolam scripsit? Quatuor hac de re occurrunt sententiae.

Primò quidam volunt, in genere ad omnes Christianos scriptam esse, cum omnes sint advenae & peregrini in hoc mundo, omnes etiam per totum orbem sint dispersi. Huic sententiae confirmandae inservire. posset, quod in ἐπιγραφῇ haec Epistola vocatur Catholica, quodque Petrus in hacEpist. cap. 2. v. 11.omnes Christianos alloquitur. Carissimi obsecro vos tanquam advenas & peregrinos. Sed distinguendum est inter proprium inscriptionis obiectum, quod hoc loco determinatur ad inquilinos Asiae minoris, & inter communem scriptae Epistolae usum. Ratione communis usus tùm haec Petrina, tum omnes reliquorum Apostolorum Epistolae ad nos pertinent, quarum tamen quasdam certis regionibus & civitatibus, quasdam etiam certis personis inscriptas esse constat.

Secundò Augustinus l. 22. contra Faustum cap. 89. Ioh. Hesselius in comm. Ex nostris B. Luthèrus, Osiander, Winckelmannus &c. ad gentiles conversos eandem scriptam esse statuunt.

1. Quia in cap. 2. v. 10.Citatur testimoniumOseae 2. v. 23.Qui aliquando non populus, nunc autem DEI populus, quod PaulusRom. 9. v. 25.de vocatione gentilium interpretatur.

2. In eod.cap. v. 5.dicit.Καὶ αὐτοὶetiam ipsi tanquam lapides vivi super aedificamini i. e. non tantum qui ex Iudaeis, sed etiam vos qui ex gentibus ad Christum conversi estis, super aedificamini in lapide illo angulari, perinde ut PaulusEph. 2. v. 19.ad conversos gentiles dicit. Iam non amplius estis hospites & advenae, sed estis cives sanctorum & domestici DEI.v. 20.superaedificati super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum existente summo lapide angulari Christov. 22.in quo & vos coaedificamini.

3. Incap. 1. v. 8.dicit, quod in Christum, quem non viderunt, credant, eumque diligant. Hoc propriè convenit gentilibus, cum Iudaei hoc nomine beati praedicentur, quod Messiam in carne docentem & miracula edentem viderint.Luc. 10. v. 23.

4. In eodemcap. v. 14.dicitur, non configurati prioribus in ignorantia vestra concupiscentiis. Atqui eiusmodiἄγνοιαpropriè competit gentilibus.Act. 17. v. 30.Eph. 4. v. 18.

5. In cap. 4. v. 3.dicit. Sufficit praeteritum tempus ad voluntatem gentium consummandam his qui ambulaverunt in luxuriis. Significat igitur, illos ante conversionem fuisse gentiles.

6. Ibidem testatur, illos ambulasse in illicitis idolorum cultibus. Atqui gentilibus idololatria fuit propria.Gal. 4. v. 8.1. Thess. 1. v. 9.

7. Idem videtur probare scriptionis occasio. Ideò enim hanc Epistolam exaravit, ne à Paulo, per quem ad Evangelium vocati erant, dissentire videretur. Iam vero Paulus propriè ac praecipuè fuit gentium ApostolusGal. 2. v. 7.

Tertiò Beda, Autor glossae ordinariae, Lyranus. Iohan. Hussus &c. ad proselytos eam scriptam volunt, quos nomine advenarum significari arbitrantur. Sed illi, ad quos Petrus scribit, non vocantur προσήλυτοι, sed παρεπίδημοι. Nec erat ratio, cur peculiariter ad eos scriberet, cum post Evangelii praedicationem gentibus non fuerit necessarium, ut susceptâ circumcisione proselyti fierent, sed immediatè ad Christianam fidem convertebantur.

Quartò Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. Eccl. cap. 4. Hieronymus in catalog. script. Eccles. Athanas. in Synopsi. Didymus in comm. Epist. Canon. Oecumenius in h. l. Baronius Ann. 45. n. 20. 21. volunt esse scriptam ad Iudaeos.

1. Vocantur advenae dispersionis, qui sunt iidem cum illis, quos Iacobus vocatτοὺς ἐν διασπορᾷ.Illi vero fuêre Iudaei, ut constat ex eo, quodIac. 1. v. 1.additur nomen duodecim tribuum.

2. Gentiles non erant advenae illarum regionum, quas Petrus ibi recenset, nec in illis duntaxat regionibus, sed per totum orbem dispersi habitabant. Sed Iudaei in illis velut peregrini & hospites commorabantur.

3. Cap. 2. v. 12. dicit, conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam. Ergo habitarunt in medio gentilium.

4. Cap. 3. v. 7.Sara oboediebat Abrahae, cuius filiae estis &c. h. e. sic respondebitis vestro generi ac vestris maioribus. Iudaei solebant dae patre Abrahamo gloriari.Matt. 3. v. 9.Luc. 16. v. 24.

5. Cap. 1. v. 10.veritatem doctrinae Christianae probat ex consensu cum doctrina Prophetarum. Illorum vero autoritas non gentilibus, sed Iudaeis erat sacrosancta.

6. In eod. cap. v. 18.mentio fit paternarum traditionum. De illis Iudaei vel maximè gloriabantur, easque arctè complectebantur.Matth. 15. v. 2.Marc. 7. v. 2.Gal. 1. v. 14.

7. Posterior Epistola ad eosdem scripta, ad quos prior, ut constat ex2. Epist. cap. 3. v. 1.Iam vero posterior illa scripta est ad conversos ex Iudaismo, dicitur enim in illacap. 1. v. 19.habemus firmiorem Propheticum sermonem.cap. 2. v. 1.fuerunt vero & Pseudo Prophetae in populo.cap. 3. v. 15.sicut & carissimus frater noster P. aulus vobis scripsit, in sua sc. ad Hebraeos Epistola.

8. Petro praecipuè ac peculiariter commissum est Evangelium circumcisionis i. e. circumcisis Iudaeis praedicandumGal. 2. v. 7.

Et sanè haec argumenta, quamvis non omnium sit aequale robur, ostendunt principaliter hanc Epistolam esse ad Iudaeos scriptam, interim quia post conversionem ad Christum non solùm proselyti, sed etiam gentiles cum Iudaeis in Christum credentibus tanquam fratribus communicabant, ac unam cum illis Ecclesiam constituebant, adeoque communes cum illis Episcopos habebant, ideò etiam secundariò & minus principaliter ad conversos gentiles eandem esse scriptam dici potest. Quemadmodum enim gentilibus ad Christum conversis Romae, Corinthi &c. habitantibus conversi ex Iudaeis erant admixti, ac nihilominus Epistolae ad Romanos & Corinthios scriptae, principaliter à Paulo gentium Apostolo ad conversos gentiles dicuntur scriptae; ita quoque vice versâ haec Epistola Petri ad conversos ex Iudaismo principaliter scripta rectè dicitur, quamvis ad conversos gentiles ac proselytos fidei interna ac loci externa unitate illis coniunctos quodammodo pertineat.

Q. 2. Quare ad harum provinciarum fideles peculiariter Petrus scripserit? Resp. Petrus ipse 2. Epist. 1. v. 12. 13. & cap. 3. v. 1.ὐπόμνησιν scriptionis suae finem constituit. Est autem ὑπόμνησις eorum, quae quis prius audivit, in memoriam revocatio, unde illud ὑπομιμνήσκειν Petrus ibidem cap. 2. v. 15.ἐξηγητικῶς declarat per μνήμην ποιεῖ σθαι. Ex quo colligitur, quod Petrus vivâ voce illis prius praedicaverit, ad quos hanc Epistolam ὑπομνήσεως causâ direxit. Epiphanius in haeres. Carpocrat. Petrus saepe Pontum & Bithyniam visitavit. Hieronymus lib. 1. contra Iovinian. itidem statuit, quod Petrus provincias illas ipse peragrasset & suâ praedicatione Ecclesiae Christi coniunxisset. Leo serm. 1. in natali Apost. Petri & Pauli Petrum sic alloquitur. Iam Pontum, Galatiam, Cappadociam, Asiam atque Bithyniam legibus Evangelicae praedicationis impleveras. Eadem est sententia nostri Chemnicii cap. 50. Harm. Docuisse, inquit, Petrum in Ponto, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia & in Babylone, constat ex prioris Epistolae ipsiuscap. 1. v. 1. & cap. 5. v. 13. Frustra opponit Estius huic sententiae, quod Asiae & Galatiae populi Pauli praedicatione ad Christum fuerint conversi. Insolens enim haud fuit, in una eademque regione distinctis temporibus plures Apostolos praedicasse. Sic Romanam Ecclesiam à Paulo & Petro plantatam esse, Irenaeus & alii ex veteribus testantur. Nec potest negari, etiam Iohannem in minori Asia praedicasse. Quod Estius disputat, aliam fuisse Petro scriptionis causam, videlicet ut ipse velut Apostolus circumcisionis & omnium fidelium pastor, ob graves persecutiones adversus fideles maximè Iudaeos in illis partibus excitatas, eos per hanc Epistolam ad patientiam exhortaretur & in fide confirmaret, illud nondum probat, Petrum illis, ad quos scribit, priùs non praedicasse Evangelium, aliàs consequens foret, etiam Paulum illis non praedicasse, quos in suis Epistolis ad constantiam in fide & patientiam exhortaretur. Petrum scripsisse ut communem omnium fidelium pastorem duplici modo accipi pòtest, vel quod ratione muneris Apostolici fuerit omnium fidelium pastor, ipsi enim aequè ac aliis Apostolis à Christo demandatum erat, ut praedicaret Evangelium omni creaturae, ac doceret omnes gentesMatth. 28. v. 19.Marc. 15. v. 15. quo sensu etiam Paulus omnium Ecclesiarum curâ ac solicitudine se tangi asserit2. Cor. 11. v. 28. vel quod ratione primatus Monarchici fuerit omnium fidelium pastor, quo sensu Bonifacius VIII. in c. Unam sanctam 10. de maiorit. & obed. verba Christi ad Petrum prolataIoh. 21. accipit. Priorem sensum concedimus, posteriorem negamus.

Q. 3. Quare Babylonis in hac inscriptione nulla fiat mentio, cùm tamen caput dispersionis fuerint Iudaei in Babylone habitantes? Resp. quia ex Babylone hanc Epistolam scribit 1. Epist. 5. v. 13. quod ipsum probat, Babylonis nomen propriè ibi accipiendum esse, non metaphoricè ac symbolicè pro urbe Romana.

Q. 4. Quaenam fuerit illa Iudaeorum dispersio? Plerique intelligunt dispersionem factam post necem Stephani.Act. 8. v. 1. sed Lucas notanter addit, fideles per regiones Iudaeae ac Samariae tunc fuisse dispersos. Regerit Baronius Ann. 45. n. 21. aliquos fidelium perrexisse etiam Antiochiam atque in CyprumActor 11. v. 19.ac Ananiam unum ex illis pervenisse DamascumAct. 9. v. 10. Sed qui in regiones dissitas in illa dispersione sese contulerunt, pauciores fuêre, quàm ut integras Ecclesias, ad quas Petrus scribit, constituerent. Rectiùs igitur dicitur, intelligi dispersionem, iam olim ante Christi adventum factam, eo sc. tempore, quo in Assyriam, Babyloniam, Aegyptum & alia regna per captivitates & bella abducti vel sponte profugi discesserant, cuius dispersionis mention fit Iohan. 7. v. 35.Act. 2. v. 9. & 10. Qui eo modo dispersi erant, professione religionis populo Iudaico manebant coniuncti, circumcisionem ac ritus Leviticos observabant, & quotannis Hierosolymam ad festa ascendebant. Ioh. 7. v. 35.cap. 12. v. 20.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι1. Asia hoc loco tanquam distincta regio à Ponto, Galatia, Cappadocia & Bithynia ponitur. At hae omnes fuêre Asiae minoris regiones. Resp. nomine Asiae specialiter hoc loco intelligitur regio vicina Epheso, quae ambitu suo praeter alias complectebatur septem illas civitates, ad quas Iohannes scribere iubetur Apoc. 1. v. 11. In hac significatione nomen Asiae accipitur Actor. 16. v. 6. & 7. ubi Phrygia, Galatia, Mysia & Bithynia, quae omnes sunt minoris Asiae regiones, ab hac Asia distinguuntur, Item Act. 19. v. 10. ubi Paulus Ephesi per biennium tanto cum fructu docuisse dicitur, ut omnes, qui habitant in Asia, audirent verbum Domini.

2. Iudaei hoc loco dicuntur in varias regiones dispersi. Atqui Abrahae promissum erat,Gen. 17. v. 8.Semini tuo dabo terram Canaan in possessionem perpetuam. Resp. promissiones illae annexam habuêre conditionem oboedientiae, ut apparet ex comminationibus Lev. 26. v. 33.Deut. 28. v. 64. ac vox עולם non semper significat absolutam aeternitatem, sed pro ratione subiectae materiae tempus longum, cuius finis est absconditus.

Ἔλεγχος. 1 Fideles ex Iudaismo ad Christum conversi vocantur advenae dispersionis. Ergo Ecclesia non est ad certum locum vel ad certam gentem in N. T. alligata. Inde etiam respectu ad Israeliticam V. T. Ecclesiam habito vocatur Catholica.

2. Misera fuit conversorum ex Iudaismo conditio, habitabant dispersi inter gentes, avulsi à patriis sedibus, experiebantur fervorem tentationum. 1. Petr. 5. v. 12. Ergo felicitas temporalis non est vera & propria Ecclesiae nota. Contra Bellarm. lib. 4. de Eccles. cap. 18. Fatetur ipse Bellarminus, Ecclesiam in principio magnas fuisse passam angustias, lib. eiusd. cap. 2. & ex persecutionibus crevisse, lib. eiusd. cap. 6. quomodo igitur felicitas temporalis poterit esse Ecclesiae idioma.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. Scripta est haec Epistola ad παρεπιδήμους. Atqui nos omnes in his terris sumus πάροικοι καὶ παρεπίδημοιPsal. 39. v. 17.Hebr. 11. v. 13. quo nomine in hac ipsa Epist. Petrus nos compellat cap. 2. v. 11. Ergo ad nos quoque usus huius Epistolae pertinet. Beda in h. l. Sed & nos si veraciter cum Propheta Deo dicere possimus, quoniam incolae nos sumus apud te in terra & peregrini, ad nos quoque Epistolas B. Petri scriptas credere & ut nobis missas legere debemus.

2. Ecclesia in hoc mundo est παθουμένη καὶ πατουμένη.

3. In Ponto, Galatia, Cappadocia &c. olim fuêre Ecclesiae florentissimae, hodie vero Turcica idolomania ibidem regnat. Caveamus igitur, ne propter verbi contemtum etiam à nobis regnum DEI auferaturMatth. 21. v. 43. ac candelabrum nostrum de loco suo moveatur.Apoc. 2. v. 5.

4. Non repulit DEUS plebem suam, quam praescivit; etiam post excidium Hierosolymitanum reliquiae secundum electionem gratiae factae sunt.Rom. 11. v. 2. & 5.

## 1:2
ACCORDING TO THE FOREKNOWLEDGE OF GOD THE FATHER IN SANCTIFICATION OF THE SPIRIT, UNTO OBEDIENCE & SPRINKLING OF THE BLOOD OF JESUS CHRIST.

By reason of their most happy internal state they are called elect according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father, unto sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ. Προσδιορισμὸν κατὰ πρόγνωσιν. Oecumenius, following Cyril in his book on the true faith, connects it with the words, Apostle of Jesus Christ, so that the sense may be that according to the foreknowledge of God the Father he is an Apostle of Jesus Christ, just as Paul Gal. 1. v. 15. says that he was set apart from his mother's womb, that he might preach Christ among the Gentiles, and Rom. 1. v. 1. speaks thus, Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an Apostle, separated unto the Gospel of God. But the following words, in sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Christ, show προσδιορισμὸν that it must be joined with the word elect, which Bede, Lyranus, and almost all interpreters do, so that there is a certain transposition in the Greek text in this place, since between the elect according to foreknowledge are inserted the strangers scattered, whence also the Syriac paraphrast not without emphasis repeats that. v. 2. Who were elect in foreknowledge. And in the first verse he inserts a copulative, To the elect and strangers. The name of the elect is taken either for eternal election to salvation, or for temporal election, which is threefold: to the fellowship of the Church, to the communion of the reborn, and to some certain ecclesiastical or political office. By reason of the first signification among those in which it is taken for temporal election, the elect are the same as the called; by reason of the second signification, the same as the reborn; by reason of the third signification, the same as persons established in a public office. And all these things have a place when the name of the elect is taken concerning men, but in a general signification it is also attributed to Christ Isa. 42. v. 1. chap. 43. v. 10. Matt. 12. v. 18. who is called the elect servant of God, both because he is peculiarly beloved by God the Father, and because he was established in the eternal counsel of God as Mediator and Redeemer of the human race. Likewise to the holy Angels, 1. Tim. 5. v. 21. who are called elect because they are exceptional, excellent, preeminent, beloved by God, and separated from the evil Angels.

Because, therefore, the name of the elect is taken in so many ways, thence Salmeron and others take it concerning temporal election to the fellowship of the Church, or as they say, to hearing the word of God, not to the saving hearing of the word. But because the elect are said to be according to the foreknowledge of God the Father in sanctification of the Spirit, etc., from that it is manifest that the name of the elect is taken here concerning eternal election to salvation. For this Apostolic passage is parallel to the Pauline passage 2. Thess. 2. v. 13. We are bound to give thanks always to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth, where this election is notably said to be made εἰς σωτηρίαν & ἄπ᾽ ἀρχῆς i. e. from eternity, before the foundations of the world were laid, because the beginning is not understood there as ἔναρχον but as ἄναρχον Mich. 5. v. ult.Hab. 1. v. 12. The Royal Codex has in this place, to the elect κατὰ πρόθεσιν, just as also Rom. 8. v. 28. the elect are called κλητοὶ κατὰ πρόθεσιν. But all the remaining Codices read κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, so that it is joined with the election πρόγνωσις which agrees with the Apostolic passage Rom. 8. v. 29. οὓς προέγνω καὶ προώρισε. By this πρόγνωσιν some understand the eternal decree of GOD concerning the saving of the elect. 1. Because the Apostle Rom. 11. v. 2. seems to use the word προγινώσκειν in that meaning. GOD has not cast away his people whom he foreknew, which is v. 7. thus expounded, the election has obtained it i. e. the elect have obtained it. 2. Because Peter in this very chapter v. 20. says Christ was foreknown i. e. foreordained before the foundation of the world.

3. Augustine in the book on the gift of perseverance, chapter 18, teaches that foreknowledge, when it is placed among good things, is the same as predestination. Hence Erasmus translates predefinition, Lyranus predestination. But πρόγνωσις is distinguished from ἐκλογῇ in this place, which also happens in the parallel passage Rom. 8. v. 29. Therefore foreknowledge cannot be taken precisely and formally concerning election. But if anyone should wish to say that by πρόγνωσιν is understood here not the ἐκλογὴν itself but the πρόθεσιν according to which the election was made, this is deservedly objected to him, because πρόγνωσις à προθέσει is distinguished in the article concerning divine providence. Nor can the contrary be demonstrated from the adduced passages of Scripture, because Rom. 11. v. 2. πρόγνωσις likewise is not placed absolutely and formally for election, but for foreknowledge, according to which the election was made, which we shall see presently how it is compared. Nor is Christ said by Peter to be elected or predestined by that election by which believers in Christ are said to be predestined to salvation, but foreknown or foreordained, as will appear below in its own place.

Others therefore understand by foreknowledge the special love of GOD, hence Estius translates predilection. As a place of argument he brings forward that, that to know or to recognize is most commonly taken in the Scriptures for to love, to approve, to acknowledge as one's own, therefore also in this place the elect are said to be according to foreknowledge i. e. by the eternal foreordination and predilection of GOD. And yet although τὸ to know is used for knowledge of approval, it signifies the same as to love, yet an example will scarcely occur concerning foreknowledge where it is used for love or predilection, since the word προγνώσεως even exists as used concerning the evil works of men, Act. 2. v. 23. Πρόγνωσις therefore, according to the nature of the subject matter, because it is a question of those elected to eternal salvation, it signifies not only the eternal foreseeing of certain individuals and persons to be saved, but also the ordination of the means by which GOD has decreed to save men, which are the preaching and hearing of the word, the institution and use of the Sacraments, and faith to be drawn, increased, and preserved from the hearing of the word and the use of the Sacraments, and likewise the foreknowledge of both faith itself and μελλόντων πιστεύειν 1. Tim. 1. v. 16. For those whom GOD from eternity foresaw would use the means ordained by Him for salvation and through the operation of the Holy Spirit would perseveringly believe in Christ the Mediator and Savior, those and only those and all those He elected to eternal salvation. This explanation is gathered from those sayings of Scripture which testify that the intuition of persevering faith enters into the decree of election to salvation. For election was made in Christ Eph. 1. v. 4. but we are not in Christ except through faith Eph. 3. v. 17. Therefore, just as in Christ, so also in faith GOD is said to have elected us, because we could not be elected in Christ except under the intuition of faith apprehending Christ and applying His benefits to itself. Hence GOD is said to have elected the poor, rich in faith Iac. 2. v. 5. and the faith of Christ is called the faith of the elect Tit. 1. v. 1. For those whom GOD glorifies and saves in time, those He determined to glorify and save from eternity. Now indeed, GOD glorifies and saves in time only and all those who perseveringly believe in Christ. Therefore, only and all those who perseveringly believe in Christ, or as the Apostle 1. Tim. 1. v. 16. speaks emphatically, μέλλοντας πιστεύειν, GOD determined to glorify and save from eternity and consequently also elected to salvation. That Apostolic oracle is of entirely eternal and immovable truth. It is impossible to please GOD without faith Hebr. 11. v. 6. the reason for which pronouncement depends on the stain of original sin, from which no one can be freed except through faith in Christ. Now indeed, the elect pleased GOD from eternity and pleased Him in such a way that He elected them to eternal salvation, which is the highest degree of divine love toward men. Therefore, they did not please GOD except by the intuition of faith in Christ and consequently they were not elected except by the intuition of faith in Christ.

Furthermore, the Apostle adds that those to whom he writes are chosen according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father in the sanctification of the Spirit. In the Greek it is not εἰς ἁγιασμὸν, but ἐν ἁγιασμῷ in sanctification, just as it is also said in 2. Thess. 2. v. 13.: GOD chose you for salvation έν ἁγιασμῷ πνεύματος, where the Vulgate translation itself rendered it, in the sanctification of the Spirit. Salmeron explains it concerning the passive holiness of our spirit, since the word πνεύματος does not have an added article. The same pleases Tossanus and others. They think, therefore, that by these words is explained both the end of election, that election was made to that end, that we might be holy and blameless before GOD Eph. 1. v. 4. and the sign of election, that those who are chosen by GOD for salvation should strive for holiness. 2. Tim. 2. v. 21. Some also go further, that that sanctification of our spirit, i.e., the pursuit of holiness, is both the means and the merit of eternal salvation. Estius is ambiguous. He determines that it can be explained either concerning the human spirit or the divine Spirit. In the former way, the sense is: chosen, that your spirit may be sanctified. In the latter way, the sense is: chosen through the Holy Spirit, that He may sanctify you, as if he had said, in the spirit of sanctification, that is, in the sanctifying Spirit Rom 1. v. 4. by a certain kind of hypallage. But from the parallel passage 2. Thess. 2. v. 13. and from the whole context of this place, it is gathered that by the sanctification of the Spirit is not understood in this place the passive sanctification of our spirit, but the active sanctification of the Holy Spirit. The preposition ἐν according to the customary idiom of the Hebrew language is placed for διὰ, in which way Erasmus also rendered it, so that thus the instrumental cause of salvation is expressed, which is the ministry of the word and Sacraments, through which GOD works faith in the hearts of the elect, just as Christ says Iohan. 17. v. 17. sanctify them in truth, thy word is truth. This ministry is called the sanctification of the Spirit, because it is the ministry of the Spirit 2. Corinth. 3. v. 6. which GOD ordained from eternity, that it might be a salutary and efficacious means, through which men might be gifted with faith, and in it be preserved unto salvation. Nor is it explained either in this place or in 2. Thessal. 2. v. 13. as the effect of election, which is our sanctification through the Holy Spirit, as Estius wishes, whom the very series of the Apostolic context refutes, since that holiness does not precede faith in the order of nature but follows it. But the means of faith and our sanctification is understood, which is the ministry of the word and Sacraments, through which GOD faith and holiness in the hearts of the elect. works. And since that ministry of the Holy Spirit is the means of salvation on the part of GOD, therefore Peter immediately adds to it the means of salvation on the part of men, when he says we are elected unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Christ. Some take it of the active obedience of Christ, i. e. by which Christ was obedient to his heavenly Father even unto the death of the cross Phil. 2. v. 9., to which opinion Salmeron also inclines. They prove this exposition from the fact that it is added, & sprinkling of the blood of Christ. As therefore the sprinkling of the blood of Christ is understood as active, i. e. by which he sprinkles and cleanses us with his blood, so also the active obedience of Christ seems to be understood, so that thus both merit and efficacy, or what is the same thing, both the acquisition and application of the benefits of Christ may be described. But Estius deservedly refutes this exposition, since we are not rightly said to be elected unto the obedience by which Christ obeyed his Father, but rather through it and because of it. Others therefore understand it of the passive obedience of Christ, i. e. by which we are obedient to Christ, which exposition is approved not only by Estius, but also by Calvin, who by obedience here understands the newness of life. Strength is sought for this exposition from those sayings of Scripture in which the pursuit of holiness and filial obedience is required of the elect. For as we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which GOD has prepared, that we should walk in them Eph. 2. v. 10., so also we are elected in Christ, that we should be holy Ephes. 1. v. 4. & that we might serve GOD in filial obedience Luc. 1. v. 74.. But if they wish that pursuit of holiness and obedience to be understood by the sanctification of the Spirit, how can it be understood again by obedience? Furthermore, the sprinkling of the blood of Christ is added to this obedience, which by the consent of all is done through faith. Now indeed filial obedience does not precede faith, but is its consequence, for it is necessary that we first be made children of GOD through faith, before we render filial obedience to him. Therefore, by the name of obedience is understood faith in Christ, which is also called elsewhere the obedience of faith Rom. 1. v. 5. Cap. 16. v. 26. the obedience of the Gospel Actor. 6. v. 7. Rom. 10. v. 16. the obedience of Christ Hebr. 5. v. 9., which exposition not only corresponds to the whole context and the analogy of faith, which teaches that faith is the only means through which we apprehend the benefits of Christ offered in the ministry of the word, but is also confirmed from the parallel passage 2. Thessal. 2. v. 13. For as there the means of salvation on the part of GOD and on the part of men, the sanctification of the Spirit and the faith of the truth, are joined together:

So also in the same sense clearly in this place we are said to be chosen in the sanctification of the Spirit, and unto obedience or in the obedience, namely, of faith; and just as Paul in the cited place calls that faith of the elect the faith of the truth either because it is true faith, or what is more fitting, because through it faith is had in the truth of the Gospel Mark 1. v. 14.Acts 6. v. 7.Rom. 10. v. 16. so also Peter in this very chapter calls that obedience the obedience of the truth, because through it obedience is exhibited to the truth. Estius mentions a certain explanation, through which προσδιορισμὸς τοῦ αἳματος Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ, is referred to both members, unto the obedience of the blood of Christ and the sprinkling of the blood of the same. This exposition would wonderfully confirm our opinion, because the obedience of the blood of Christ cannot be other than the obedience of faith, by which we obey the word of the Gospel, in which the benefits obtained by the death and blood of Christ are offered to us. But because this construction is more forced, therefore we more rightly understand the noun faith from Rom. 1. v. 5. and chap. 16. v. 26. The same judgment applies to that exposition, which Estius likewise mentions, and which he approves more than the former, by which προσδιορισμὸς Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ is referred to both preceding members. Unto the obedience of Jesus Christ and the sprinkling of the blood of the same Jesus Christ, which exposition likewise would not differ from ours, since in Heb. 5. v. 9. faith is called the obedience of Christ. But there is no need that we descend to that, since the name of obedience even when placed absolutely is rightly accepted according to the Pauline exposition concerning the obedience of faith. For this opinion is confirmed most of all by what is immediately added, and unto the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. By this sprinkling of the blood of Christ it is manifest that the application of the benefits obtained by the death and blood of Christ is understood, which is done through that obedience of faith, or through faith, applying to itself the merit of Christ for righteousness and the remission of sins. For because no one is cleansed from sins by the blood of Christ, unless he has been sprinkled with it, i.e., unless he applies to himself the benefits obtained by the passion and death of Christ, or what is the same thing, the shedding of the blood of Christ, which application is made through the obedience of faith Rom. 3. v. 25. GOD set forth Christ as a propitiation through faith in his blood, therefore with the sanctification of the Spirit the Apostle joins obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, i.e., faith, by which our hearts are sprinkled with the blood of CHRIST and are cleansed from sins, he joins in an individual bond in the matter of election & salvation. For by faith hearts are purifiedActs 15. v. 9. and the blood of Christ, that is, sprinkled upon us by faith, cleanses our conscience from dead worksHeb. 9. v. 14. and thus cleanses us from all sin1. John 1. v. 7. by which reason there occurs in the Apostolic phrase the figure which they call ἑνδιαδύο.. The Apostle, however, by the little word of sprinkling, looks back both to the phraseology of the Holy Spirit in the O. T. Ps. 51. v. 9. you shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed, (where in the Hebrew is held the verb חטא he has purified, he has expiated, he has taken away sin, but the Chaldean rightly rendered it by דכי and the LXX by ῥαντίζειν, because that expiation was made by the sprinkling of the blood of sacrifices.) Isa. 52. v. 15. he shall sprinkle many nations, where in the Hebrew is כזה which is used concerning the sprinkling of the blood of sacrifices Lev. 8. v. 30. and also to the types of the O. T. because the Priests were sprinkled with the blood of sacrifices poured out upon the altar and by this sprinkling were consecrated to God Exod. 29. v. 21.Lev. 8. v. 30. but with the first things a regard is held to Exod. 24. v. 8. where Moses sprinkled the blood of sacrifices taken from the altar upon the people, saying, This is the blood of the covenant, which the Lord has made with you, which the Epistle to the Hebrews Chap. 9. v. 20. applies to the blood of Christ as the antitype, by which both the N. T. was initiated and believers are cleansed from their sins and consecrated to God, so that as Spiritual Priests Rev. 1. v. 6. they may offer spiritual sacrifices to God.Rom. 12. v. 1.

Q. in this place 1. Why did Peter wish to make mention of election immediately at the beginning of the Epistle? Resp. because a little later he was about to enumerate the spiritual benefits conferred upon believers on account of Christ, among which election made from eternity in Christ stands out most of all.

Q. 2. From where did the Apostle know that those to whom he was writing were elect? Resp. not a priori from some immediate and peculiar divine revelation, but a posteriori, because they had been called through the Gospel to the kingdom of Christ, and they had given place to that calling by believing in Christ, and rendering their faith testified both by the pursuit of good works and by the tolerance of persecutions.

ἘναντιοΦανείαι 1. Peter calls those to whom he writes elect. But no one can be infallibly certain of the election of others. The Lord knows who are his2. Tim. 2. v. 21. Man sees those things which appear, but the Lord looks upon the heart1. Sam. 16. v. 7. Resp. Peter knew the election of others not a priori with certainty, as the Scholastics speak, but a posteriori probably, not by an infallible judgment of faith, but by a probable judgment of charity. Thence when afterwards in chap. 5. v. 12. he called Silvanus faithful, he adds προσδιορισμὸν, ὡς λογίζομαι.

2. Peter calls those to whom he writes elect. But not all to whom he writes were elect. Resp. The title of elect belongs to the churches to which he writes, not by reason of all, but by reason of the principal members, by a synecdoche customary in the Scriptures. August. book on the unity of the Church, chap. 12, & in the book which he published after the conference with the Donatists, chap. 20, The Prophets and Apostles are accustomed to argue in this way those who are blameworthy in some people, so that all in some people are argued, and thus to address the praiseworthy, so that all there are praised.

Ἔλεγχος 1. Election was made according to foreknowledge. Therefore not from some absolute decree. The reason for the consequence is because that foreknowledge looks to faith in Christ, as we have shown from a comparison of parallel passages. Against the Calvinists.

2. Election was made according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father in the sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ. Therefore not on account of foreseen merits. The force of truth compelled Estius to comment thus on this place. The Apostle says they are elect according to foreknowledge, that is, by the eternal predestination and love of GOD, so that every thought of merits of whatever kind preceding this election, which can be imagined on our part, may be excluded, and so that the faithful may understand with thanksgiving that they were predestined to salvation by the grace of GOD alone. And a little later at v. 3 he annotates thus. Election is not from merits. Salmeron vol. 16. Disp. 1. on the Epistle of Peter in the same way. Election to possess the end of eternal life is firm and certain in itself and does not depend on our works.

3. If the election of others can be known probably from the judgment of charity, much more can one's own election be known with certainty from the judgment of faith. But that is so, as Peter witnesses in this place and Paul 1. Thess. 1. v. 4. Therefore.

4. Scripture establishes the remission of sins and our cleansing from them in the sprinkling of the blood of Christ. It knows nothing of lustral water, the sprinkling of which is believed in the Papacy to purge offenses.

Έκδίκησις. 1. Calvinists desire to prove from this place that faith depends on election as from the first cause, since we are said to be elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father. Piscator on this place. But this proof rests on the false hypothesis that πρόγνωσις signifies an absolute decree.

2. Estius strives to prove from this passage that our righteousness before GOD consists not only in faith and the remission of sins, but also in works. Of obedience, he says, the Apostle adds the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, i.e., the expiation of sins made by the blood of Christ, which is the other part of our justification, so that he may intimate that our whole righteousness, which consists partly in faith and the operation of virtues, and partly in the remission of sins, is of divine election. But this proof rests upon a false hypothesis, that by obedience is understood the operation of virtues, whereas it is to be taken concerning the obedience of faith, which Estius himself acknowledges when he writes thus in the same place. That remission of sins is called the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, because no one is cleansed from sins through the blood of Christ unless he has been sprinkled with it, i.e., unless through the applied merit, which application is made through the obedience of faith. From this arises such an argument. Through which obedience the application of the merit of Christ is made, that and indeed that alone is understood by the Apostle here by the name of obedience. Through the obedience of faith, and not through the operation of virtues, is the application of the merit of Christ made. Therefore, the obedience of faith, and indeed that alone, is understood by the Apostle here by the name of obedience.

3. The Photinians attempt to evince from this passage that election was made according to the foreknowledge of works: for those whom God foresaw would rightly use free will and would walk in the precepts of Christ to the best of their ability in all their life, those they say were elected to eternal life and elected for this reason indeed, because they were to receive Christ and obey his commandments. Catech. Racov. p. 295. Socinus in his commentary 1. John 1. wishes by obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ nothing else to be understood than that the righteous were elected by God so that they might be participants of the covenant of Jesus Christ, and thus through obedience would attain eternal life. But 1. it is true that being received into the covenant and being sprinkled with blood as a symbol or confirmation of it are connected Ex. 24. v. 8.Heb. 9. v. 20. but it cannot be inferred from that that the sprinkling of blood itself signifies reception into the covenant. 2. Socinus sins, seeking the reason for the covenant only in exemplary demonstration, with the satisfaction of Christ excluded.

4. The same people desire to evince from this passage that justifying faith consists in trust and in new obedience. Both proofs rest upon a false hypothesis, that by the name of obedience is understood the obedience of a holy life, when the Apostle is speaking of the obedience of faith.

5. Salmeron writes thus on this passage. The blood of Christ is sprinkled upon us when it is offered in the sacrifice of the Mass for the living and the dead. But by the sprinkling of blood, which is done through the word and the Sacraments, which are the δοτικὰ, means, and through faith, which is the ληπτικὸν, means; the Apostle speaks here; concerning the sprinkling, which is done through an offering for the living and the dead, we have nothing in the Scriptures.

6. Piscator desires to prove from this place, that the blood of Christ shed with a sense of divine wrath, and therefore the passive obedience of Christ alone, is that which is imputed to us for righteousness before the judgment of GOD. But the inclusion of one is not the exclusion of the other. Scripture therefore makes mention especially of the blood, i.e., of the passion and death of Christ, because the passion and death was the highest degree of obedience rendered to GOD.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. Election was made according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father in the sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ. Therefore the foundation of our election is the grace of GOD founded in the merit of Christ, offered to us through the ministry of the word and the Sacraments, apprehended by us through faith.

2. Election was made in the sanctification of the Spirit. Therefore the ministry of the word, which is the ministry of the Spirit, is to be highly esteemed, inasmuch as through it the Holy Spirit wills to kindle, increase, and preserve in us the faith of the elect.

3. Of faith, in which we are chosen, and through which we are justified and saved, the principle is the grace of GOD choosing; the form consists in obedience, not legal but Evangelical, not of works but of knowledge, assent, and fiducial apprehension; the medium is the ministry of the Spirit; the fruit and effect is the remission of sins.

4. To God the Father is attributed foreknowledge, to Christ the sprinkling of the blood, to the Holy Spirit sanctification, i.e., the ministry of the word. We have therefore the mystery of the Trinity insinuated. God the Father grants salvation to us through gratuitous election; the Son merits it through the shedding of blood; the Holy Spirit applies those benefits of the Son through the preaching of the Gospel.

5. The sprinkling of blood, which was Ceremonial in the O. T., was a figure of the spiritual sprinkling in the N. T., through which the blood of Christ is sprinkled upon us in the word and Sacraments, as if by divinely ordained salutary sprinklers. He who withdraws himself from this sprinkling cannot be purged from the uncleanness of his sins.

6. The obedience of faith looks to the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, i.e., the word of the Gospel, in which the benefits obtained by the passion and death of Christ are offered to us, which is the proper and adequate object of justifying faith. And conversely, the sprinkling of the blood of Christ requires faith. Hebr. 4. v. 2.

The greeting is appended to the inscription.

GRACE TO YOU AND PEACE BE MULTIPLIED, Χάρις ὐμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη πλῃθυνθείη.

Πληθυνθῆναι signifies to be multiplied, to be dilated, to take the most abundant increase, to be fulfilled, so that it may be taken both concerning multiplication in discrete quantity and concerning augmentation in continuous quantity. Matth. 24. v. 12.Act. 6. v. 1. & 7.c. 7. v. 17.c. 9. v. 31.c. 12. v. 24.2. Cor. 9. v. 10.2. Petr. 1. v. 2. from there some render it, be multiplied, but others be fulfilled. A similar greeting exists in Epist. Iudae v. 2. Mercy to you and peace and charity πληθυνθείη, where the Latin version rendered it, be fulfilled, whereas in this place it rendered it be multiplied. In almost all the Pauline Epistles, grace and peace are joined in the greeting prefixed to them, with the word πληθυνθείη, omitted and of grace and peace added, both at the beginning and by merit. Grace to you and peace from GOD our father and the Lord Jesus Christ Rom. 1. v. 1.1. Cor. 1. v. 3. &c. from which it appears that this form of greeting is Apostolic. Indeed, it is read concerning Darius Dan. 6. v. 25. that he used this formula of greeting at the beginning of royal letters. Peace to you be multiplied. But that varies greatly from this Apostolic one, as will be manifest from the explanation of the same. By grace some μετωνυμικῶς understand benefits conferred out of grace, directed toward the eternal salvation of man, such as faith, hope, charity, and the remaining virtues, and likewise perseverance in good works. But it is more correctly understood as the source of all those benefits, namely the gratuitous favor of GOD, by which He embraces us in Christ, remitting sins to us, justifying and saving us out of grace. For 1. in the parallel passage Iudae v. 2. χάρις is explained by τὸ ἔλεος. 2. Peter himself v. 13. of this chapter says, that grace is offered in the word of the Gospel, in which GOD offers His fatherly favor, the remission of sins, justice, and eternal life to those who believe. 3. Peace in this greeting is distinguished from grace as fruit and effect from its cause. By the name peace the Hebrews are accustomed to embrace every happiness and prosperity, Gen. 43. v. 27.Psal. 119. v. 165.Ierem. 29. v. 7. from there some establish that by peace in general here are taken any benefits whatsoever, bodily and spiritual, temporal and eternal. Lyranus distinguishes grace from peace thus, that he refers grace to the present life, peace to the future life. But in the greeting of Christ Luc. 24. v. 36.Iohan. 20. v. 19. & 21. and of Paul the Apostle Rom. 1. v. 7.1. Cor. 1. v. 3. &c. by the name of peace is understood that chief benefit of divine grace, which being justified by faith we have peace with GodRom. 5. v. 1. which is peace in GOD & with GOD. Peter therefore celebrates that singular benefit of the Gospel, that in it the grace of GOD is offered on account of Christ the Mediator, so that for the future we may have a quiet & tranquil conscience, inasmuch as we are reconciled to GOD through Christ, and he prays for the preservation and increase of these goods.

Q. Why does the Apostle pray for the multiplication of grace & peace for those to whom he writes? Resp. 1. Because although they had been made partakers of both grace & peace, yet those goods were not yet perfect, but there was need of their daily increase. 2. Because they did not possess them immutably, but they could be taken away again in this life.

ἘναντιοΦανία Grace be multiplied to you. But that fatherly favor of GOD, by which He embraces us in Christ, is not multiplied, but always remains the same. Resp. just as the love of God is said to be poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us,Rom. 5. v. 5. both because the sense of that love is poured out into our hearts, for we feel that we are loved by GOD, and we taste how good the Lord is: and because the effects of this love, namely the gift of the Holy Spirit, is poured out into our hearts: so also the grace of GOD is said to be multiplied, when πληροφορία concerning the grace, goodness, and mercy of GOD, by which He embraces us in Christ, it is increased, so that we may stand more and more strengthened in that grace of GOD, and when the gifts bestowed upon us from grace are increased and multiplied.

Ἐλεγχος Peter prays that grace and peace be multiplied in the hearts of believers, i.e., he wishes for them an efficacious and intimate sense of divine grace and peace of conscience. The Pope commands one to doubt concerning the remission of sins and the grace of GOD, which doubt is diametrically opposed to the peace of conscience and the sense of divine grace.

Ἐκδίκησις. Baronius in the Year of Christ 45. n. 27. taking the occasion from this Petrine salutation, discourses thus concerning the blessing of the Roman Pontiff, which they are accustomed to call Apostolic. That the Apostle Peter at the end of his first Epistle, just as also in its beginning, greets by imparting grace, just as it is evident he did also in the second Epistle, and that furthermore it is evident he did the same in the second Epistle, and that furthermore by the same salutation That the Apostle Paul often uses &c. and that John also uses the same greeting, is clearly signified, having been introduced into the Church by the example of the Apostles, so that in Apostolic letters grace may be imparted in greeting. n. 28. From Apostolic tradition and example, therefore, it flowed that the Roman Pontiff, in greeting someone in Apostolic letters, imparts grace together with the Apostolic blessing. Resp. 1. That the prayer for grace and peace is placed at the beginning in the Epistles of the Roman Pontiff, no one among us disapproves in itself and by itself. 2. But we do disapprove of this, that he claims this belongs peculiarly to himself as the successor of Peter, when it is common to all Bishops, as successors of the Apostles, to pray for grace and peace for the faithful. Baronius himself, d. 1, confesses, that Ignatius in his Epistle to the Ephesians and the other Bishops of Antioch after him used the same formula of greeting. Just as not only Peter, but also the remaining Apostles Paul, James, and Jude use this form of greeting. Now, however, they do not seek the successors of Peter in the Antiochene see, but solely in the Roman. 3. A certain peculiar efficacy is ascribed to this Pontifical blessing from the work performed. For if indeed the blessing of a Bishop, the striking of the breast, the sprinkling of holy water, &c., without any other good movement, suffices for remitting venial sins, as Francisco à Victoria teaches, summ. Sacr. poenit. n. 100. p. 63, how much greater will the power be, according to their own hypothesis, in the blessing of the Pontiff, who is the head of all Bishops.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. Without the grace of Christ one never comes to the peace of reconciliation, therefore grace and peace are so joined in the Apostolic greeting, that grace is placed before peace. Beda in h. l.

2. The Jews today call upon the name of peace, and they used to greet in this way in the Scriptures. But I understand that he (the Apostle) defended the preaching of the creator by his office. How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize good things, who evangelize peace. For the evangelizer of good things, i. e. he knew that grace of GOD was to be preferred to peace. Tertull. lib. 5. adv. Marc. cap. 5. The sense is that up until the ascension of Christ it was the custom to greet someone only with the word of peace, as many examples in the old Testament supply, such as Gen. 43.Iud. 6. & 9.1. Reg. 25.1. Paral. 12.Tob. 12. & in the new concerning Christ, who was accustomed to greet his disciples with the same name of peace Luc. 24.Ioh. 14. & 20. whom he also admonished that they should greet in the same way when they entered into foreign houses and were staying in them Marc. 10.Luc. 10. But to the same greeting of the name of peace the Apostles also added grace they added, nay even prefixed, that they were indeed the announcers of so sublime a grace, restored to the human race through Christ. Baron. d. l.

3. The sum of the whole Gospel is contained in this Apostolic salutation. For in the Gospel the grace of GOD is offered to us in Christ and on account of Christ, which he who receives by faith, obtains peace toward GOD, in GOD, and with GOD.

4. It is not enough to have been made a participant of divine grace and peace once, but there is need of preservation and daily increase.

5. Hence the saints pray for one another for the increase of spiritual gifts.Rom. 1. v. 11.Eph. 1. v. 17.Phil. 1. v. 9.

6. But if we ought to pray for the increase of spiritual goods for others, much more does it behoove us to groan daily to God, that He may perfect the good work which He began in us until the day of Christ Jesus.Psal. 68. v. 29.Phil. 1. v. 6.

Latin:
