Omnes homines post lapsum, cum sint peccatores, egent gloriâ coram DEORom. 3. v. 23.non possunt coram DEO consistere per suam iustitiam, sed debetur eis confusio faciei,Dan. 9. vers. 7. & quamdiu sunt extra Christum, aedificant super arenam, ac tales ferunt fructus, in quibus erubescunt Rom. 6. v. 21. sed DEUS in Sion, i. e. in Ecclesia posuit lapidem angularem, electum & preciosum, qui in eum credit, i. e. ut Petrus ipse versu praeced. 5. 10. quitur, qui tanquam lapis vivus super eum verâ fide aedificatur, ille aedificat super petram, ideò non confunditur, habet firmum ac stabile fundamentum, & erexit firmam ac stabilem structuram, ideò non nutat nec vacillat, nec necesse habet trepidare ad insultus pluviarum, fluminum & ventorum, sed persistit immobilis ac firmus.

Descendente pluviâ, i. e. tentationibus, quae sunt à Daemonibus existentibus in aëre, & flantibus ventis ambitionis & inanis gloriae, qui mittuntur à mundo, & supervenientibus fluminibus concupiscentiarum, quae erumpunt à carne, & irruentibus in illam domum, non cecidit, sed stetit, quia fundatu erat supra petram seu Christum, inquit Weidn. in loc. fid. praecip. tract. 2. p. 383. Quinimò qui fide super Christum firmam illam petram extructus est, ille adversus omnes mortis, Diaboli & inferni insultus persistit, nec est, quod coram DEO vel hominibus pudefieri metuat. Beda adhuc aliam monstrat connexionis rationem. Praeclarè, inquit, convenit hic Prophetae & Apostoli sermo, quo dicitur, accedentes ad lapidem vivum, vel credentes in eo non confundi illius Psalmi versiculo, in quo, cum dictum esset, accedite ad eum, & illuminamini, continuò subiunctum est, & vultus vestri non erubescent. Quamvis vero LXX. Interpp. versio à Petro hoc loco citata, quoad verba discrepet à textu Hebraeo, tamen quoad sententiam consensus est pulcherrimus. Qui credit, inquit Propheta, non festinabit. Esaias simpliciter dicit, Qui credit, sed LXX. Interpp. & Petrus eos secutus, illud complent expresso fidei obiecto. Qui credit in eum, quem προσδιορισμὸν ostendit connexio horum verborum cum praecedente promissione de lapide illo angulari & fundamentali in Ecclesia ponendo. Futurum non festinabit, quidam accipiunt positum more Hebraeorum pro imperativo, quâ ratione proponeretur in his verbis exhortatio. Qui credit ea, quae dico de lapide fundamentali in Sion ponendo, non festinet, ut ea videat (uti ἐξηγήσεως causâ Pagninus addit) i. e. non festinet ad rem promissam morae impatiens, quasi statim ea debeat exhiberi, neque si differatur, spem abiiciat, sed patienter expectet. Confirmari videtur haec expositio ex contextu. praecedit enim v. 10. praeceptum ad praeceptum, linea ad lineam, ubi μιμητικῶς repetuntur eorum voces, qui promissionum divinarum complementum expectare renuebant, & propter dilationem complementi reddebantur impatientes, ut & ex Habac. 2. v. 3. Sed rectiùs accipitur, ut promissio, ac futurum in propria significatione relinquitur. Qui credit, non festinabit, i. e. non opus habebit ad alia remedia confugere, vel ex anxietate & trepidatione cordis fugere, sicut ex adverso de illis, qui alienum sequuntur, dicitur Psalm. 16. v. 4.multiplicarunt molestos labores suos, postea acceleraverunt. Qui enim alibi, quàm in Christo salutem suam quaerunt, in propriis sc. operibus, vel in aliis confictis Salvatoribus, illi perpetuò fluctuant tanquam de salute sua incerti, ac eorum tandem finis confusio Phil. 3. v. 19. sed qui in Christum credunt, in quo solo DEUS salutem nostram reposuit Actor. 4. v. 12. illi non frustrantur expectatâ salute, sed eam suo tempore certissimè consequuntur. Atque hac ratione verbum pudefiet, quo Apostoli ex LXX. Interpp. versione utuntur, pulcherrimè congruit cum verbo festinabit, quo Propheta utitur. Qui enim pudore suffunduntur, fugam capessunt, & ex conspectu hominum sese protinus subducunt. Haec expositio confirmatur ex V. seq. Quia enim illi, qui in Christum non credunt, non pudefiunt, ex eo Petrus infert. Vobis igitur credentibus hic lapis est honor, i. e. quia fide in hunc lapidem aedificamini, ideò non metuendus vobis pudor & ignominia, sed expectandus honor & gloria. Confirmatur etiam ex allegatione Paulina Rom. 9. v. 31. & seqq. Israël sectando legem iustitiae, in legem iustitiae non pervenit. Quare? quia non ex fide, sed q. ex operibus, offenderunt enim in lapidem offensionis, sicut scriptum est. Ecce pono in Sion lapidem offensionis, & petram scandali, & omnis, qui credit in eum, non confundetur, i. e. incredulis quidem hic lapis est lapis offensionis & confusionis, sed credentibus est salutatris, à confusione eos prohibens, qui locus huic nostro est planè parallelus. Idem elucet ex allegatione Rom. 10. v. 11 ubi postquam dixisset Apostolus. Corde, creditur adiustitiam, subiungit, dicit enim Scriptura, omnis qui crediderit in illum, non confundetur, quae omnia manifestè ostendunt, non exhortationem, sed promissionem in hisce Prophetae & Apostolorum verbis contineri.

## 2:7-8
TO YOU THEREFORE HONOR WHO BELIEVE: BUT TO THOSE WHO DO NOT BELIEVE THE STONE, WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED, THIS HAS BEEN MADE INTO THE HEAD OF THE CORNER & A STONE OF STUMBLING & A ROCK OF SCANDAL. TO THOSE WHO STUMBLE AT THE WORD NOR BELIEVE, INTO WHICH ALSO THEY WERE PLACED.

Connection. 1. After the Apostle had brought forward the Prophetic testimony Isa. 28. v. 16. in the verse immediately preceding, now transferring the thesis to the hypothesis he accommodates it to the believers from the Jews and Gentiles, to whom he writes. That stone, which the heavenly Father, he promised that he would place in Sion, is ἒντιμος to believers, inasmuch as they are kept by him from shame and confusion. Wherefore, since you also believe in Christ, therefore this stone is also to you τιμὴ or honor.

2. He had said in V. 4. that this stone was indeed chosen and honored by God, but rejected by men, he confirms this very thing from Psal. 118. v. 22. and Esai. 8. v. 14. and on this occasion he brings forward two other testimonies concerning this stone from the Scripture of the O. T.

3. Moreover, he wished to meet by the allegation of both sayings the scandal which was born among the more unlearned and weak from the fact that Christ had been repudiated and rejected by the leaders of the Jews. For since this very thing was equally predicted by GOD, as that some are to be built upon this stone by faith, and to be freed from eternal ignominy, therefore this very thing ought to move no one to scandal.

Exposition of the text. Ὑμῖν οὖν ἡ τιμὴ τοῖς πιστέυουσιν. Most people take the word τιμῆς as placed for ἒντιμος,, the abstract for the concrete, in which way Erasmus also rendered it. To you therefore, who believe, he is precious viz. this stone, which exposition agrees with the preceding and following. For it precedes. I lay in Sion a precious stone. Therefore, so that the Apostle may show that it is not enough that this stone be precious before God, but that it is required furthermore that it also be precious to us through faith, which manifests to us the price and excellence of Christ, and transfers the salutary use of this stone to us, therefore the Apostle adds. To you therefore, who believe, this stone is precious. It follows, but to them that do not believe, the stone which the builders rejected and a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal i. e. To you believers he is precious, but to the unbelieving he is vile and abject, nay a stone of scandal and stumbling. But indeed the little word τιμὴ can be retained in its proper and native signification, so that it may be joined with the immediately preceding sentence. He that believeth in him, shall not be confounded, in this way. He who shall have been built upon this stone by faith, for him confusion and ignominy is not to be feared. Therefore to you believers this stone is honor i. e. it yields to your honor and advantage, that you believe in Christ. Bede on this place. To you therefore honor, believers, that honor indeed, that you may not be confounded by him at his coming, but as he himself says, if any man serve me, my father will honor him. Ioh. 12. v. 26. And even if it should be established that the Apostle looked to the word ἒντιμος, nevertheless it can none the less be the proper the meaning of the little word τιμῆς is to be retained. That stone placed by GOD in Sion is called by the Prophet ἒντιμος. Therefore to you who are built up through faith as living stones upon him, there is honor before GOD and his judgment. The Syrian rendered it in this way. To you therefore is given [consult facsimile image] [consult facsimile image] this precious thing who believe. He therefore implies for the completion of the sentence the word to have been given. But because this stone was given or placed not only for believers, but for all men, so that they might be built up upon him by faith unto salvation, therefore that completion is not sufficiently convenient, unless it is explained concerning application, or concerning the gift of faith, just as Paul says Phil. 1. v. 29. To you it is given, that you may believe in Christ.

Ἀπειθοῦσι δὲ, λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ ὀικοδομοῦντες, οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας καὶ λίθος προσκόμματος καὶ πέτρα σκανδάλου. By τοὺς ἀπειθεῖς some understand the unyielding and disobedient. But if it is taken concerning the disobedience opposed to the obedience of faith Rom. 1. vers. 5. cap. 16. v. 26., it is rightly said, for the antithesis shows τοὺς ἀπειθεῖς to be opposed to τοῖς πιστέυουσι, and consequently those are understood, who do not wish to receive Christ offered in the Gospel by faith, but through unbelief repel him. To those unbelievers the stone, which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner. The Syriac version omits this whole thing, and simply reads. But to those who do not acquiesce, he is a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal. But the Greek Codices consistently read this passage, and it agrees best with v. 4. where Peter says, this stone to be rejected by men, but with GOD chosen and honored, both of which he confirms by the testimony of David. Without a doubt it seemed absurd to the Syrian Interpreter, that Christ should be said to have become the head of the corner to those not believing, when to them he has become a rock of scandal and a stone of stumbling. In order that this apparent absurdity may be met, some include those words, οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας in a parenthesis, and explain them separately in this sense. To those not believing Christ has become the stone rejected by the builders (namely that same one, who afterwards became the head of the corner) he has also become to them a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal. But this construction is by no means suitable, because in the Greek the first case is not had λἰθος, but the fourth case λίθον, as the LXX Interpreters also read Psal. 118. v. 22.Matthaeus cap. 21. v. 42.Marcus cap. 12. v. 10.Lucas cap. 20. v. 17. which case cannot be adapted to τοῖς ἀπειθοῦσι, if those words ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ ὀικοδομοῦντες are included in a parenthesis. Robertus Stephanus indeed makes mention of one Codex, in which it is read, λίθος, in the first case. But the reliability of one Codex, without a doubt conformed to the Latin version, does not prejudice the remaining Codices, and the reading received among the Evangelists. Some therefore render this sense, which leaves the construction unchanged. To the incredulous, however, that stone, which the builders rejected, has become the head of the corner that is to them, however unwilling and resisting, a judge and King has been given, who may coerce the rebels with a hard rule. But anyone notices that this is also forced. Most simply, therefore, it is established that, regarding the word άπειθοῦσι, it must be understood that what follows is said, or it is fitting, which is written elsewhere concerning this stone. The stone, which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner, because by the name of those who reject this stone are understood not only the Chief Priests, Scribes, and Pharisees among the Jews, who as spiritual architects ought to have erected the building of the Church upon this stone by their ministry, but with blind judgment and perverse affection rejected him, but also all the incredulous, who ought to have been built upon this stone by faith, but by incredulity repudiated him. Notwithstanding that rejection, however, this stone has become the head of the corner, and thus the foundation of the spiritual building, which it props up and sustains with its strength and firmness. Some explain the phrase itself, by which the word λίθος. is placed in the fourth case, in such a way that the accusative is established as placed absolutely in this sense. As regards the stone, of which phrase a similar example is hadActor. 10. v. 36. & 38. 1.Ioh. 2. v. 24. & 27. But it is answered more simply that there is in it a customary Hebraism, which the LXX Interpreters frequently imitate Gen 31. v. 16.Num. 32. v. 4.Ios. 1. v. 3.1. Reg. 6. v. 31.2. Reg. 1. v. 4. Among the Latins this formula of speaking is less customary, whence some here establish antiptosis, some change the collocation of the words in this way. Which stone the builders rejected. But there is no need to descend to that, since similar examples occur among approved writers. The city, which I am establishing, is yours. The eunuch whom you gave, I have sent. Furthermore, through this That the stone is understood to be Christ is shown not only by the Petrine allegation, but also by the whole context of the Psalm. David predicts two things concerning him: first, that the builders are to reject him, and second, that he is to be established by God as the head of the corner. For although David uses verbs of past time, they nevertheless have the meaning of the future, because in the prophetic manner David prophesies about a future thing with past verbs on account of the certainty of the thing. By the builders are properly and directly understood the Priests, Scribes, Pharisees, and in general all those upon whom the office of teaching in the Israelite people rested Acts 4. v. 8. & 11. For they were established upon the chair of Moses and Aaron, so that they might build the Church of the O. T., i. e., teach and rule the Israelite people, for to build is to teach Jer. 1. v. 10.Rom. 15. v. 20.1. Cor. 3. v. 10.Gal. 2. v. 18. whence Paul calls himself an architect 1. Cor. 3. v. 10. Moreover, by a Hebrew phrase, the present participle is put for a verbal noun signifying an office, so that the builders are builders or architects, just as ὁ πειράζων is the tempter Matt. 4. v. 3. Similar examples occur Ps. 14. v. 2.Prov. 10. v. 20.Gal. 2. v. 11.1. Tim. 5. v. 21. Furthermore, these builders are truly called foolish, for having rejected the stone, which was fit not only for the building but also for the foundation of the building, i. e., having rejected it as useless and inept for the building, and thus harmful, as one who would be worthy of no place in the structure of the building. For ὰποδοκιμάζειν signifies to repudiate something in an election, or also to reject someone from an office as unworthy Wis. 9. v. 4.Sir. 20. v. 20. Symmachus in his version Ps. 35. v. 4. and the LXX Interpreters Jer. 6. v. 30.ch. 7. v. 28.ch. 8. v. 9.ch. 14. v. 19.ch. 31. v. 36. use it for מאס,, which signifies to reject some thing or person with a certain disgust and indignation, as vile and despised, which word David also uses in Ps. 118. v. 22. And because Christ uses this word in the prediction of his passion and death Mark 8. v. 31.Luke 9. v. 22.ch. 17. v. 25. it is gathered from it that in this very Davidic oracle is contained a prophecy concerning the passion and death of the Messiah, to be inflicted upon him by the very leaders of the Israelite people. These architects or Jewish Princes rejected Christ with calumnies, snares, blows, and torments, but Christ, that solid and corner stone, remained firm, unmoved, and unshaken against them in their insults. Nay, he was made εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας i. e. the head of the corner by a Hebrew phrase Gen. 2. v. 7.22. & 24.Matt. 19. v. 5. To be the head of the corner, because γίνεσθαι here is the same as εἲναι. Peter In v. 4. the preceding, and Paul Eph. 2. v. 20. express this with one word, when they call Christ a stone ἀκρογωνιαῖον, both because he is the fundamental and most strong stone of the whole building, containing and preserving that whole in himself Es. 28. v. 16.Eph. 2. v. 21. and because he connects the two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, to one another, and associates them into one Church. Eph. 2. v. 14. and because for many he is a stone of stumbling: for corner stones are accustomed to protrude outside the building, and so those who walk less providently easily strike against them. Whence also Peter from Es. 8. v. 14. adds that this stone for those unwilling to believe is a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, which prophecy is also alleged Luc. 2. v. 34.Rom. 9. v. 33. πρόσκομμα signifies properly a stumbling block, or an obstacle in the way, against which we strike our foot, for properly ἐπὶ ποδῶν is called πρόσκομμα, as ὑπώπιον ἐπ᾽ ὀφθαλμῶν, with Eustathius as witness: Σκάνδαλον likewise is called everything that is thrown in the way of those making a journey, against which striking they fall, or at least find an occasion for striking, from σχάζειν which signifies to limp, because the object of stumbling makes a man limp. Certain Grammarians say σκάνδαλον that it is that curved wood by which a trap is sustained, and against which an animal striking overturns the snare itself upon itself in a sudden ruin. The former explanation agrees with the word προσκόμματος, which Peter uses from the version of the LXX Interpreters, and presents such a comparison. Just as a fundamental and corner stone not only props up and sustains a building, but also the weary can rest upon it, if it protrudes, and those fainting under a burden can raise themselves upon it, but for those who walk improvidently, or out of drunkenness run into it, it becomes a stone of stumbling: so Christ is set for the resurrection of many, who namely lean upon him with true faith, and are built upon him as living stones; but he is also set for the ruin, namely of those who not only reject this stone, but also run into it, and attempt to overturn it. The latter explanation agrees with the word נגף, which the Prophet uses, that it is a stone of percussion, by which those upon whom it falls are to be crushed and ground to pieces, for thus Christ explains Matth. 21. v. 44.Luc. 20. v. 18. Whoever shall fall upon that stone, shall be broken, but upon whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder. But who those are, who fall upon this stone, and strike against it, Peter further explains that, adding. Οἱ προκόπτουσι τῷ λόγῳ ἀπειθοῦντες, εἰς ὃ καὶ ἐτέθησυν. By τὸν λόγον Drusius and others understand λόγον ὑποστατικὸν the Son of GOD himself, Ioh. 1. v. 1. and following 1. Ioh. 1. v. 1.cap. 5. v. 7.Apoc. 19. v. 13. And indeed those who stumble and

they strike against the word of the Gospel, they strike against Christ himself, who is offered to them in the Gospel Matth. 11. v. 5. meanwhile, however, properly and directly here is understood λόγος προφορικὸς the word of the Gospel. For the Apostle explains the manner in which that stone placed for the resurrection and salvation of men becomes for many a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, namely because they do not receive the sermon of the Gospel, and because they are ἀπειθοῦντες unwilling to believe, on account of the despised appearance of the Gospel, thence they strike heavily against it, not only contradicting it, but also blaspheming it Actor. 13. v. 45. which sin of theirs, so that the Apostle may exaggerate it more, he adds, εἰς ὃ καὶ ἑτέθησαν. Some Latin Codices read, in which, but some into which, which version agrees more with the Greek text. Bede mentions both readings. But in various ways this προσδιορισμὸς added in the place of an appendix is explained.

1. Bede and from him the interlinear gloss explain it thus. In which also they were placed, which is understood according to this, which Paul speaking about GOD says. For in him we live, and move, and are. But the Greek Codices constantly read εἰς ὃ, nor will the word ἐτέθησαν used concerning divine conservation easily occur.

2. Some refer it to the word of the Gospel, of which mention had been made in the immediately preceding. They do not believe the word of the Gospel, to which they were placed to be heard and received by faith, that is ordained through the law and the Prophets announcing Christ beforehand. But in the Greek the gender does not correspond, for λόγος is masculine, the relative ὃ is neuter.

3. Some refer the relative ὃ to the stone, of which mention had been made several times in the preceding verses, so that the sense may be. Even those unbelievers were placed into this stone, i. e. called to the recognition and kingdom of Christ through the preaching of the Gospel. But λίθος is likewise masculine, to which the neuter ὃ. does not agree. It remains therefore, that τὸ εἰς ὃ is not to be referred to any one word, but to the whole complex of the preceding speech, and therefore is to be taken indeterminately, to which, i. e. to which thing they were also placed. But here again arise divisions of opinions, what that complex may be, or that thing, to which the unbelievers are said to be placed, 1. Gagnaeus, Salmero, Lorinus, Estius, Franciscus Lucas and most Calvinists refer to the words immediately preceding, οἱ προκόπτουσι τῷ λόγῷ ἀπειθοῦντες, so that the sense may be: Those unbelievers were placed, that they might stumble at the word, and not believe, which exposition they prove. First, from the series of the context. Second, from the collation of parallel passages Rom. 9. v. 17.1. Thessal. 5. v. 9.Jude v. 4. Third, from the scope of the Apostle, for Peter speaks of the Jews reprobated by GOD, which reprobation of theirs he explains in such a way as to say that they were permitted by GOD to fall into this sin. Fourth, from the particle καὶ, which leads us to the will of GOD. Fifth, from the suffrage of the ancient Doctors of the Church, Didymus and Oecumenius. Although, indeed, we do not entirely disapprove of this exposition, if it be purged from the leaven of the absolute decree of reprobation, and be taken concerning the consequent and judiciary will of GOD punishing preceding sins by a just judgment, in the sense that unbelievers, on account of their prior crimes, deserve by the just judgment of GOD to be left, blinded, and hardened by GOD, so that subsequently they might stumble the more at this stone; yet we prefer that by which most of our own refer that εἰς ὃ to what is more remote, namely to v. 6. For in that verse it is said that the foundation stone and precious Christ, to wit, is placed in the Church, to this end, that everyone who believes in him may not be confounded. Peter therefore adds that even the unbelievers were placed for this, namely that they too might be built up in this stone by faith, i.e., that they might believe in Christ, and by this means be delivered from eternal ignominy and confusion, but that they themselves, by their own fault through voluntary unbelief in the word of the Gospel, and consequently also in this stone, stumbled and brought upon themselves eternal destruction. We prove this exposition. 1. From the collation of the word τίθημι in v. 6. and the word ἐθέτησαν in this v. 8. which shows such a connection. Even the unbelievers were placed, i.e., called through the Gospel, that they might be built up upon this stone placed by GOD in the Church. 2. From the collation of other passages of Scripture. GOD through the word of the Gospel calls all to the participation of the benefits of Christ, He wills all to be saved1. Timoth. 2. v. 4. He wills to gather all, as a hen gathers her chickensMatth. 23. v. 36. Therefore, He also placed the unbelievers who spurn this counsel of GOD against themselves Luke 7. v. 30., that they might believe in Christ. Especially pertinent here is the notable passage Acts 13. v. 46. which, since it likewise treats of the unbelieving Jews, is not undeservedly considered parallel to this one of ours. It was necessary that the word of GOD should be spoken to you first, but since you repel it (by contradicting and blaspheming) And you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold we turn to the Gentiles.v. 47.For so the Lord has commanded us. Behold I have set you for the salvation of the Gentiles. 3. From the analogy of faith. Although GOD, on account of foreseen final unbelief, reprobates some, yet He is nowhere said to place or predestine them to the sin of unbelief, which is the cause of reprobation and damnation. Indeed, some sayings are brought forward, from which the architects of absolute reprobation labor to prove that, but what is to be determined concerning them will be explained in its own place. 4. From the suffrage of the Interpreters. Although Bede explains the word ἐτέθησαν too generally concerning creation, yet he correctly explains the relative εἰς ὃ. In this, he says, placed, that is, in this by Nature men were made, that they might believe in GOD, and obey His will, Solomon attesting, when he says: Fear GOD, and keep His commandments, this is, every man, that is, in this naturally every man was made, that he might fear GOD, and comply with His commandments; which words the Glossa ordinaria repeats. Lyranus in the same way. For this the law was given to them, that they might be disposed toward Christ, according to what is said, Gal. 3. The law was our schoolmaster in Christ, and they for the greater part remained unbelieving. Caietanus also accepts it in the same sense. Erasmus likewise. In which they were placed. For to this Judaism was prepared, that one might believe in Christ, whom the Mosaic law prefigured. What of the fact that Calvin himself by no means repudiates this exposition? For thus he comments on this passage. They commonly interpret that they were placed to believe, because the promise of salvation was destined for them. But the other sense can equally square, that they were ordained to unbelief, just as Pharaoh is said to be placed for this, that he might resist GOD,Exod. 9. vers. 16.& all the reprobate are destined to their end. And that I incline to this sense, the particle καὶ interposed makes it so. But if, however, the former exposition pleases more, it is a vehement reproach. For thence Peter exaggerates the unbelief of the people chosen by GOD, because they rejected the salvation peculiarly ordained for them. Nicol. Hemmingius in h. l. The sense is. Although to them (the unbelieving Jews) the promise of salvation was destined, yet they did not believe.

Q. in this place. 1. Why is Christ here compared to a stone? Resp. 1. on account of the oracles of the O. T. Psal. 118. v. 22.Esa. 8. v. 12.cap. 28. v. 16.Dan. 2. v. 34.Zach. 3. v. 9. from which Peter in this place brings forward the first three. 2. on account of the types. Jacob, having set out for Mesopotamia, places a stone under his head, on which he sleeps sweetly, and sees a ladder stretched to the heavens, on which Angels were descending and ascending. Gen. 28. v. 11. Thus we can cast all our care upon Christ Ps. 37. v. 5.1. Pet. 5. v. 7. and in death we can fall asleep sweetly in Him, believing in Him. Jacob pours oil upon the same stone, and promises that it will come to pass that it grows into the temple of GOD Gen. 28. v. 18. and 22. thus the structure of the spiritual building to be erected in our hearts relies solely upon Christ. Jacob sets up a stone as a sign of the covenant initiated between himself and Laban Gen. 31. v. 44. thus in Christ and through Christ GOD initiates a covenant of grace with us. Moses, obtaining victory for Joshua and the Hebrews against the Amalekites, has a stone placed under his hands, upon which he supported his weary arms. Ex. 17. v. 12. Thus our prayers must rely upon faith in Christ, if they are to be pleasing to God, and obtain victory against spiritual enemies. Ioh. 16. v. 23. The stony rock struck by the rod of Moses poured forth most abundant waters Num. 20. v. 11. which type Paul himself applies to Christ 1. Cor. 10. v. 4. he who believes in Him and strikes this rock with the rod of prayers, will draw forth life-giving water from it. Ioh. 4. v. 13. Moses standing upon the rock or stone of the cave, sees the glory of GOD passing by Exod. 33. v. 21. thus in Christ and through Christ we can see the friendly face of GOD, Ioh. 14. v. 9. when the Israelites were being led through the Jordan into the promised land, Joshua by divine command sets up stones in the middle of the riverbed, Ios. 4. v. 22. Christ is that unique way, which leads us through the Jordan of this life to the heavenly fatherland. Ioh. 14. v. 6. Joshua sets up a stone as a testimony, that the Israelites wish to adhere solely to GOD, Ios. 24. v. 26. thus Christ is that faithful witness Apoc. 1. v. 5. who promises that He will give a good testimony to those who believe Apoc. 2. v. 17. when the ark of the covenant was being brought back by the Philistines, the Bethshemites were offering sacrifices upon a great stone, 1. Sam. 6. v. 14. thus in Christ and through Christ our spiritual sacrifices are to be offered, if they are to be pleasing and acceptable to God, as Peter teaches in this place. David, about to engage with the giant Goliath, places five most clear stones taken from the torrent into his shepherd's bag, and with one of them struck into the forehead of the enemy, he kills him, 1. Sam. 17. v. 40. Christ overcame the infernal Goliath by the merit of His passion, when He drank from the torrent in the way Ps. 110. v. ult. Hebr. 2. v. 14. Cyprian gathered these Prophetic sayings and almost all these types in book 2 against the Jews, chapters 15 and 16. 3. On account of the suitability. Stones are firm, they provide a solid foundation for a building Matth. 7. v. 24. thus Christ is the immovable foundation of the Church against sustaining it against the very gates of hell Matth. 16. v. 18.1. Cor. 3. v. 11. the Apostle himself provides this reason, when he calls Christ the corner and foundational stone. A stone is carried downward from on high by its own weight: thus Christ, impelled by the weight of his own love, descended from the heavens to the earth to us. A refuge is open to fugitives and exiles at a rock: thus Christ is the rock of our salvation, to which we can flee by true faith. 2. Sam. 22. v. 2. A stone placed in a road or in the foundation of a building is to some a stone of stumbling: thus also is Christ to the unbelieving. A stone crushes those upon whom it falls with force from above: thus Christ will grind and crush all his enemies in the final judgment.

Q. 2. Why is Christ called a living stone? Resp. 1. Just as water is called living which bubbles up from its source or vein, so a stone is called living which is born in its own rock or vein, and is cut from thence. This can be applied to Christ, cut from the mountain without the hands of men, Dan. 2. v. 24. when he was born of an untouched virgin without marital embrace, like a living stone he was formed in the lower parts of the earth. Psal. 139. v. 15. 2. By this epithet the Apostle signifies that the discourse is not about any natural or earthly stone, which is inanimate, but about a spiritual and heavenly stone, animated and living. 3. Christ according to his divine Nature is αὐτοζωὴ life itself 1. Ioh. 5. v. 30. he has life in himself Ioh. 5. v. 26. he is the living and eternal Son of the living and eternal GOD, Matth. 16. v. 16. According to his human Nature he dies no moreRom. 6. v. 10. but is living and lives for ever and everApoc. 1. v. 18. 4. Nor is he only living himself, but also life-giving. For he confers life both naturally upon the living Actor. 17. v. 28. and spiritual life upon those believing in him in this age Ioh. 6. v. 58. and heavenly and eternal life in the future age Ioh. 5. v. 28. 29.cap. 10. v. 28. He vivifies souls in this life through grace, he will vivify bodies on the day of judgment through resurrection. 5. He is therefore our life not only by reason of merit, but also by reason of efficacy, not only by reason of acquisition, but also by reason of application. By his death he merited spiritual and eternal life for us who were dead in sin, and he communicates and gives the same to all who truly believe in him.

Q. 3. In what sense is this stone said to be chosen and precious before GOD? Resp. 1. He is called chosen not in respect of the reprobate, but by comparison with the remaining stones of the same building, to which in many ways he is more excellent. 2. Electus in the Hebrew phrase is the same as excellent and outstanding, for in a true and free election those things which are more outstanding are accustomed to be chosen. 3. He is elect before God because he is the beloved Son of the heavenly Father Esai. 42. v. 1. My elect, in whom my soul has taken pleasure. Matth. 12. v. 18. Behold my servant, whom I have chosen: my beloved, in whom my soul has taken pleasure. 4. He is precious, because the heavenly Father has raised him to the highest sublimity Phil. 2. v. 9. by placing him according to his human Nature at his right hand in the heavenly places above everything that is named not only in this age but also in the future. Eph. 1. v. 20. Lyranus in this place This stone was honored in the working of miracles, in the resurrection, in the ascension, and in the mission of the Holy Spirit. 5. The interlinear Gloss adds that he is called precious, because he was given as a price. 1. Petr. 1. v. 19. 6. Among stones there are certain precious and gem-like ones, which are preferred by far to common ones. Christ is a precious stone of this kind to believers, as Peter adds v. 7. he is that precious pearl, which he who finds, sells all that he has and buys it Matth. 13. v. 46. the gem-like structure of the heavenly Jerusalem is built upon him as the unique gem of our salvation, Apoc. 21. v. 19. the twelve gem-like foundations, that is, the twelve Apostles, lean upon him as the unique foundation. Eph. 2. v. 20.

Q. 4. In what sense are believers called living stones? Resp. 1. Ambrose in chapter 3 of Luke He calls men strengthened in vigor living stones. 2. Interlinear Gloss Solid in faith, living in virtues. 3. By the name of stones the firmness and vigor of this spiritual building is denoted. Not only is the foundation of this structure a firm and immovable stone, but also stones, not mortar, not wood, are built upon this foundational stone, so that in this way a form and solid building may arise. The pious, built upon Christ by faith, become Petrine and stony, that is, they receive vigor and firmness from Christ. Matth. 16. v. 16. 4. And they participate not only in vigor and firmness, but also in life from Christ, whence they are called living stones. Through faith in him they are rendered participants of spiritual life, they are vivified, animated, and quickened by the same Spirit by which the whole body of the Church and the building, which is spiritual, living, and mystical, is vivified. 5. They are also called living stones, because they were not cut by the hands of men, that is, they were not chosen for this building by human will, but were ordained to this spiritual fabric by the eternal counsel of GOD. 6. It is shown, the antitype, that is, the house and temple that spiritual thing which rises up constructed from these living stones is far more excellent than the type, i.e., the external temple of Jerusalem, inasmuch as it was constructed from inanimate and insensible stones, whereas here all things are living. 7. Bede brings forward yet another reason for this denomination. He calls the elect living stones, in order to insinuate the effort of their good intention or action, by which, with the grace of God preceding and accompanying them, they ought always to be exercised. For dead, that is, material stones, when they are prepared or placed in buildings, work no labor themselves to help, nor can they do anything by themselves except fall, but wherever and however they have been placed by the builder, they remain there insensibly, or having slipped, they fall down. But Blessed Peter does not want us to imitate the hardness and insensibility of such stones, but to be built up as living stones upon the foundation of Christ, so that, namely, with grace helping us, we may cooperate by living soberly and justly and piously.

Q. 5. Why is the building constructed from living stones upon Christ the foundational stone, i.e., the Church, called a spiritual house? Resp. 1. By way of difference from the Jerusalem temple, which was a material and corporal house of GOD, and merely a type of this spiritual structure. 2. On account of the signification of the mystery. Spiritual in the Scriptures is sometimes the same as signifying or signified allegorically or mystically. An example of the former is had in 1. Cor. 10. v. 3. & 4. where manna is called spiritual food, and the water flowing from the rock spiritual drink, because, namely, they signified spiritual food, namely the body of Christ, and spiritual drink, namely the blood of Christ. Ioh. 6. v. 49. & following. An example of the latter is had in Apoc. 11. v. 8. where the great city is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt, because, namely, it is prefigured by Sodom and Egypt. In this sense also the Church is called a spiritual house, because it was prefigured by a material house, namely by the Mosaic tabernacle and the Jerusalem temple in the O. T. 3. On account of expressing the condition of the true Church. The Church is a spiritual house and a spiritual and mystical body, because all the true inhabitants of this house, all the true members of this body, are vivified and as it were animated by the Holy Spirit. Nothing in this body is dead, nothing outside this body is living; hence also the Apostle calls the stones from which this spiritual house rises up living, i.e., made participants of spiritual life, and he calls the sacrifices which believers offer spiritual.

Q. 6. What is understood by the stone rejected by the builders inPsal. 118. v. 22.? Lyranus thinks that this statement in the literal sense must be accepted concerning the building of Solomon's temple, that a certain stone offered several times in the building could not be conveniently placed, and therefore was rejected several times, but was finally placed at the completion of the corner, by which stone Christ is signified. But Burgensis in his additions rightly warns that the foundation of this exposition, which exists in the Scholastic History, is fictitious and fabulous, since it is nowhere read in the authentic Scriptures that such a thing happened in the building of Solomon's temple. 2. Some of the Hebrews explain it concerning the people of Israel, that they, having been rejected by the powerful of this world, will be the head of the whole world in the days of the Messiah. But to be the corner and foundational stone in the spiritual building of GOD does not befit the whole Israelite people, otherwise the building would not be distinct from the corner stone. 3. Calvin in the literal sense explains it concerning David. 4. Bellarmine applies it to the Roman Pontiff. We shall examine both perversions a little later in ἐκδικήσει. 5. By that corner stone only Christ is understood here, as is evident. First, from the scope and context of the Psalm. All men are stirred up in this Psalm to acknowledge with a grateful heart the greatest benefits to be prepared for the human race by the passion, death, and resurrection of the Messiah, and the very formal words are described in it with which the Jerusalemite people received Christ, celebrating his royal entry into the city. Secondly, from the parallel passages of the O. T. Esa. 8. v. 12. & 13.cap. 28. v. 16.Dan. 2. v. 34.Zach. 3. v. 9. which befit no one else but Christ. Thirdly, from the allegation of the N. T. Luc. 2. v. 34.Matth. 21. v. 42.Marc. 12. v. 10.Luc. 20. v. 17.Actor. 4. v. 11.Rom. 9. v. 33. & in this Petrine passage. Fourthly, from the predicate. Subjects are such as are signified by the predicates. To be the corner and foundational stone of the Church befits no one else but Christ, who sustains the spiritual building of the Church and associates the two peoples, Gentile and Jewish, with one another in the unity of faith. Eph. 2. v. 14. &c.

Q. 7. Who are understood by the builders? Resp. 1. Some in general understand all the Jews, who ought to have received Christ by faith and to have been built as living stones upon Christ, but through unbelief they rejected him when they cried, Crucify him. For although not all and every single one rejected Christ, yet since the greatest part of the people rejected him, it is therefore rightly attributed to the whole assembly. 2. But by the builders The Priests, Scribes, and Pharisees established in the public office of teaching among the Jewish people are understood directly and properly, as is evident not only from the parable of Christ Matt. 21. v. 33.Mark 12. v. 1.Luke 20. v. 1. in which he compares them both to the tenants of the vineyard and to the builders, just as Paul 1. Cor. 3. v. 9. also joins these two metaphors: but indeed especially from Acts 4. v. 8. & 11. where, having addressed the Princes of the Israelite people, he says expressly. This is the stone, which was rejected by you builders. 3. Secondarily and by a certain extension and accommodation, all unbelievers can be understood as builders rejecting such a stone, whence Peter v. 4. says generally that this stone was rejected by men.

Q. 8. Whence did it happen that the Chief Priests and Elders of the people repudiated Christ? Resp. 1. They desired a Messiah who was rich, opulent, promising the happiness of an earthly kingdom to the Israelite people. 2. They bore with difficulty that the corruptions of doctrine and the impiety of life, especially hypocrisy, were taxed by him. 3. They could not bear that Christ called himself the Son of God and the redeemer of the world. 4. Being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they were unwilling to submit themselves to the righteousness of God and to Christ who inculcated the same. Rom. 10. v. 3.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. The Chief Priests, Scribes, and Pharisees are called builders, and yet they did not build. Resp. They are called such by reason of their office, because they were established upon the chair of Moses and Aaron Matt. 23. v. 2. so that they might build the Church of the O. T., but not by reason of the deed, because they were repudiating the foundation upon which they ought to have built. They are called builders, not because they were such in reality, but because they ought to have been such. Malach. 2. v. 7. & 8.

2. Christ is a rock of scandal. But to give scandal does not befit Christ, who is most just, Matt. 18. v. 6. Resp. it is one thing to be scandal given, another to be accepted. John Huss expresses that thus. Scandal is taken either actively or passively. In the latter signification, Christ is in this place and 1. Cor. 1. v. 23.

3. To those not believing, Christ is a rock of scandal. But how can he be a scandal to those to whom he has not been announced in the word of the Gospel, such as are many of the unbelievers? Resp. it is a question here of positive unbelief, which presupposes the offering of the benefits of Christ in the word of the Gospel.

Έλεγχος, 1. Believers are built as living stones upon the rock Christ. Therefore not Peter alone is built upon this rock, nor is Peter alone so denominated by Christ, the true and unique rock of salvation, which, however, the Papists are forced to presuppose, attempting to evince from Matth. 16. v. 16. that Peter, through these words of Christ, Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, was constituted Monarch of the Church and vicar of Christ. Origen, tract. 1 in Matth.: The rock is whoever is a disciple of Christ, and upon such a rock is built every ecclesiastical doctrine: But if you think that the whole Church is built upon that one Peter alone, what will you say of John the son of thunder and each one of the Apostles? Shall we dare to say that the gates of hell shall not prevail against Peter alone? Or are the keys of the kingdom of heaven given to Peter alone? Truly, therefore, it was said to Peter, Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, yet it seems to have been said to all the Apostles and all perfect believers, since all are Peter and rocks, and in all of them the Church of Christ is built, and against none of them who are such do the gates of hell prevail. tract. 35 in Matth.: Christ is called the spiritual rock, and it is reasonable that all imitators of Christ are likewise said to be rocks. Ioh. Ferus on chapter 16 of Matthew, after he had adduced these words of Peter: Coming to Christ the living stone etc. he adds: You hear what Peter says, namely that Christ is the stone, then he wishes us also to be stones, which happens when we are built upon Christ. But he is built upon Christ who believes in Christ, not only in word, but also in deed, and leans upon those things which Christ has and can do. Therefore, Christ is primarily the rock, upon whom the whole Church is built, according to that: No one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ. Then, because through true faith we are joined to Christ, and thus in a certain way we also know ourselves to be a rock, if it is permitted to speak thus. And afterwards: Peter was so called on account of his confession of faith. But this change of name concerns us also. For thus it was foretold concerning believers: And a new name shall be called for you. It belongs to Christ alone to be the rock. But he who is built upon this rock acquires this new name, just as you see in Peter. Salmero, Disp. 3 on 1 Peter, introduces Peter speaking thus: Therefore I was surnamed Peter by Christ the rock, and not only am I Peter, but you all are also Peters. Just as from Christ the King, Priest, Shepherd, and Teacher, all believers participate in his kingdom and priesthood and pastorate and doctorate. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage Christ is the true and primary rock of the Church, from whom Peter and the rest of the faithful are made rocks.

2. Christ alone is that living, fundamental, and corner stone, upon whom all the faithful are built up. Therefore, Christ alone is the foundation of the Church. To Him alone also belong the properties of a foundation, which are to sustain and support the Church, so that not even the gates of hell can prevail against it, to be the most firm base of our faith and justice, upon which we can safely lean Isa. 28. v. 16. all the faithful are built upon Him, as living stones, as Peter speaks in this place. The Papists object, the wall of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church has twelve foundations, and in them the twelve names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb, Apoc. 21. v. 14. Therefore, besides Christ, another foundation of the Church is also given. I answer, the words of the Apostle are manifest 1. Cor. 3. v. 11. for no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. The Apostles are therefore called the foundations of the Church by reason of the preaching and doctrine concerning Christ, that unique foundation of the Church, in which way the Apostle explains Eph. 2. v. 20. you have been built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, i. e., upon Christ preached by the Prophets and Apostles. And Paul says of his own ministry 1. Cor. 3. v. 10. According to the grace of GOD, which has been given to me, as a wise architect I have laid the foundation. Therefore, we acknowledge no other foundation of the Church besides Christ, whether it be called secondary, or ministerial, or vicarious, such as the Papists establish Peter and his successors in the Roman See to be, because Christ Himself, present and effective in the Church, and sufficient for all the duties of a foundation, does not need any vicarious and ministerial foundation. Ioh. Ferus in the same place When Christ says, upon this rock I will build my Church, He means nothing else than that He is about to build the Church upon a firm and immovable foundation, against which all the insults of adversaries can do nothing. From this it is clear that Christ did not build His Church upon Peter, or any other man whatsoever. For no man is so firm and constant that he cannot be moved, which we also see manifestly in Peter. Another rock must therefore be sought. And indeed in Holy Scripture Christ Himself is frequently called the stone or rock, etc.

3. The Church is a spiritual house. Therefore, the true Church of the Elect is invisible, for everything spiritual, as such, is invisible.

It is also false, what Bellarmine writes in book 3 de Eccles. cap. 2. The Church is a gathering of men so visible and palpable, as is the gathering of the Roman people or the kingdom of France, or the Republic of the Venetians. Luther vol. 2. Lat. fol. 377. book against Ambrosius Catharinus. Just as the head of the Church is invisible and spiritual, perceptible by faith alone: so it is necessary that the Church also be invisible and spiritual, perceptible by faith alone. For it is necessary that the foundation be of the same condition as the building, as we say: I believe in the holy Catholic Church. But faith is of things not appearing. Bellarmine objects in book 3 de Ecclesia cap. 15. that something is said to be spiritual in two ways, in one way according to substance, in which way Angels are called spiritual: in another way according to ordination to the Spirit, just as the body is called spiritual, and good works are called spiritual sacrifices. The Church is called a spiritual house in the second way, since the Apostle means this, that the Church is not a house built of wood and stones, but of men consecrated to GOD. I respond. If the Church is therefore called a spiritual house, because it consists of men regenerated by the Spirit of GOD, and such as are ruled by the Spirit of GOD, certainly the true Church of the elect is invisible. Those men who are true members of the true Church are indeed seen, but they are seen as corporeal men, and not as spiritual men, belonging to the house of the Church, they become men of the spiritual house of GOD and true members of the Church only by the regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Now indeed that operation of the Spirit is interior and by no means exposed to the eyes of men 1. Corinth. 2. v. 11. Therefore it cannot be seen either, which men are truly spiritual. The same thing can be proven from the following words of the Apostle, A holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices etc. Those truly and properly belong to the house of GOD, which is the Church 1. Tim. 3. v. 15. who offer to God spiritual sacrifices acceptable through Christ. Now indeed who such truly are, does not appear to the eyes of men. Therefore the Church of the saints consisting of them is invisible. Compare the place on the Church § 75. William Estius objects thus. It is a heretical commentary, that the Church is called a spiritual house, because it is hidden and invisible, which error fights against the most manifest Scriptures, but it is called spiritual both in distinction to a material house, which consists of corporeal matter, and on account of the signification of a mystery, for by spiritual in the Christian School is signified something allegorical. I respond. The Scriptures which testify, that the Church in a certain respect is visible, do not oppose our opinion, since we say that the Church is κατ᾽ ἄλλον καὶ ἄλλον ὑπολήψεως τρόπον visible and invisible, as is more fully explained in its own place. We do not reject those reasons of Estius, on account of which he asserts that the Church is called a spiritual house; meanwhile, the principal reason must not be omitted, that the Church is therefore called a spiritual house because the inhabitants of this house are temples of the Holy Spirit, and to whom that truly applies is not obvious to external eyes. The difference of this spiritual house from a corporal one confirms the same thing. A material house consists of corporal matter. Therefore, a spiritual house consists of spiritual matter, i.e., of such as are spiritual, or regenerated by the Spirit of GOD. Cornelius à Lapide objects, that a spiritual house is here opposed to a material house, not a visible one. For he calls Christian men the stones composing this house, but Christian men are visible, not invisible. I reply, we invert the argument. A spiritual house is opposed to a material one. Therefore, to a visible one. For a house is visible precisely because it is material. We concede that Christian men are visible, but as corporal men, not as truly Christian men. For to hear and profess the Word externally, and to use the same Sacraments, which all those do who are established in the external and visible society of the Church and are obvious to the eyes of men, does not yet make someone a true Christian and a true and living member of the mystical body of Christ, but there is required in addition true faith in Christ and the interior regeneration of the Holy Spirit, which, since it is not obvious to the eyes of men, therefore it cannot be seen externally who are truly Christians, and consequently the true Church of the elect is invisible. Cornelius retorts. It is called a spiritual house because it worships GOD with spiritual faith, religion, and worship. Very well, I say, therefore the true Church of the elect is also invisible, because that spiritual faith, religion, and worship is invisible. Cornelius denies that this follows, for although that spiritual worship is invisible, insofar as it is internal and hidden in the soul, the same is nevertheless visible, insofar as it betrays itself and exhibits itself to be seen, through the external profession of faith and its worship, by which the faithful visibly communicate in the same Church, assembly, Eucharist, Sacraments, prayers, etc., and manifest their faith and religion. I reply, from that it is indeed very well deduced that the external ministry of the Church is visible, and that the called, who are in the society of the external Church, are visible, but it can in no way be overturned from that which we assert, that the of the elect The Church is invisible, because that external profession of faith and worship, which is common to the elect with hypocrites, does not yet infallibly show who are the true and living members of the true Church, who are truly regenerated by the Holy Spirit, and elected to eternal life. August. lib. 2. contra literas Petiliani cap. 118. The impious are not to be thought to be in the body of Christ, which is the Church, because they become bodily participants of his Sacraments, etc. For they themselves are not in that structure of the Church of Christ, which grows into the increase of God through the connection and contact of the members of Christ. The same author, Epist. 57, teaches that the faithful are gathered into one Spirit and into one body, whose head is Christ, and he says that this congregation is the building of the temple of GOD, and is made through spiritual regeneration.

4. Peter describes the building of the Church thus, that believers as living stones are built upon the living and fundamental stone Christ, a spiritual house, a holy Priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices. Therefore the Church is properly the congregation of the saints and the truly faithful. For this description does not apply to all who are called, since not all are built upon Christ as living stones, nor do all offer spiritual sacrifices to GOD. Unjustly, therefore, Bellarmine, lib. 3. de Eccles. cap. 2., condemns the seventh article of the Augsburg Confession, that it says the Church is the congregation of the saints, who truly believe and obey GOD, which opinion he falsely slanders in the same place as being forged from the heresy of the Pelagians, Novatians, and Donatists. Beautifully Augustine, lib. 7. de Baptismo contra Donatist. cap. 51. All things considered, I think I do not rashly say that some are in the house of God in such a way that they themselves are also the same house of GOD, which is said to be built upon the rock, which is called the only dove, which is the beautiful bride, etc.; but it is certain that others are in the house in such a way that they do not belong to the structure of the house, nor to the society of fruitful and peaceful justice, but just as the chaff is said to be among the grain. lib. de unit. Eccles. cap. 18. In these is the Church who build upon the rock, that is, who hear the words of Christ and do them, etc. Therefore it is not in those who build upon the sand, i. e. who hear the words of Christ and do not do them.

5. Peter calls all the truly faithful and pious spiritual Priests, who offer spiritual sacrifices to GOD. Therefore the name of Priests is not proper to the Ministers of the Church of the N. T., but common to all the truly pious, nor is there given besides the sacrifice offered on the cross. any external sacrifice in the New Testament, such as the Papists establish the Mass-sacrifice to be, but the sacrifices of the New Testament are spiritual. Salmero objects in this place, First, that this ought not to be opposed to the external sacrifice of the Mass, since the sacrifice of the cross was also corporeal and visible, which Christ offered by himself. I respond: it is not simply and absolutely denied that there is a visible and external sacrifice in the New Testament, but that besides Christ, who offered himself as a sacrifice on the altar of the cross, there are such Priests in the New Testament who ought to offer an external and visible sacrifice, this is what we deny, since after the offering by Christ on the altar of the cross, Peter knew of no other Priests than spiritual ones, no other victims than spiritual ones. Secondly, that the sacrifice of the Mass was instituted by Christ himself, when he said: Do this in my remembrance. I respond: neither from the word do, nor from the word remembrance can that Mass-sacrifice be proven. For to do is not to sacrifice. Nor is it yet proven that Christ offered himself in the first institution of the Eucharist in an unbloody manner to the heavenly Father, and commanded the Apostles to do this very thing. But also, without an external sacrifice, a remembrance of the passion and death of Christ can be made. Thirdly, that not all are fit to offer the sacrifice of the altar, but only those sanctified and promoted to holy orders, just as formerly also in the law only the consecrated and anointed sacrificed; but for other spiritual sacrifices, every Christian is fit and has the right. I respond: the principle is begged, for we deny this very thing, that besides spiritual Priests and spiritual victims, there are still other properly called Priests in the New Testament who ought to offer an external victim to GOD. Fourthly, that the sense is this, not that all Christians are equally Priests, as are those who publicly minister in the sacrifice of the Mass, but that the Church of GOD has in itself the dignity and utility of the Priesthood. I respond: on the contrary, the Apostle says not only this, that there is a holy Priesthood in the Church, but also that those very believers are that holy Priesthood, that is, holy and spiritual Priests. For just as they are said to be built as living stones, so that they may be a spiritual house, so also they are said to be built, so that they may be a holy Priesthood. Either therefore it must be denied that they themselves are a spiritual house, or it must be conceded that they themselves are a holy Priesthood. The Apostle teaches this same thing more clearly, when v. 9. he expressly added: You are a royal Priesthood. Fifthly Apoc. 1. v. 5. it is said, he made us a kingdom and Priests to GOD and his father, and you have made us a kingdom and Priesthood to GOD. But just as he did not in reality make all men Kings, having and possessing their own kingdom, so neither did he make all men Priests, but only participants in the gifts and benefits of the Priesthood and kingdom, just as we say that the Romans had a kingdom, a Consulship, an Empire, not indeed in all, but only in certain selected persons: and just as in the Church not all are Apostles, not all Prophets or Teachers, or Bishops, so neither are all Kings or Priests. Resp. This exception fights with the express words of Peter and John. For the pious are not only called participants in the benefits of the kingdom and Priesthood, but also Kings and Priests, namely spiritual ones. As all are Kings, that is to say spiritual ones, so also all are Priests, namely spiritual ones. Estius excepts, that a distinction must be made between that which is said properly, and that which is said figuratively. For as a sacrifice is called specially and properly that which is offered to GOD, as supreme Lord, by an external rite with some change of itself, but generally and improperly everything that is done so that one may adhere to GOD in a holy society: so those are called Priests peculiarly and properly whose office it is to offer sacrifices of the former kind, of which sort indeed there is none in the Church except the unbloody sacrifice of the body and blood of the Lord. But improperly and by a general reason, those who offer to GOD sacrifices of the latter kind, that is, whoever exercises pious and holy works, whether of religion, or of mercy, or of any virtue whatsoever. Resp. Let Estius truly prove that, besides spiritual Priests, there are given in the New Testament more Priests properly so called, who offer a sacrifice properly so called, by an external rite, with some change of itself to GOD. Neither Peter, nor any of the Apostles makes mention anywhere of such Priests. And how does it befit the sacrifice of the Mass that it is offered to GOD by an external rite with some change of itself? For either this is understood of bread and wine, or of the body and blood of Christ. Bread and wine cannot be understood by the hypothesis of the Papists, otherwise the sacrifice of the Mass would not be really the same with the sacrifice of the cross, in which Christ offered not bread and wine, but his body and blood to the heavenly Father. Nor can the body and blood of Christ be understood, for those do not undergo any change of themselves. Cornelius à Lapide excepts, that Peter is not speaking of any believer whatsoever, but of the whole assembly of the faithful, but that assembly of the faithful has a true Priesthood, true Priests for those appointed, that they may offer sacrifices properly so-called to GOD for the people. But this exception has already been satisfied before. The same: A layman, by assisting, serving, and cooperating with true Priests, offers a true sacrifice in the Mass. Resp. By this reasoning, not only the little sacrificers, but all pious people entirely will be Priests properly so-called. Someone could also retort this for the Papists. If from the fact that Peter calls all the faithful spiritual Priests, it can be proven that there are no Priests properly so-called in the N. T. who offer an external sacrifice, it will follow that there are also no Kings properly so-called who administer an external kingdom, since Peter also calls them spiritual Kings. v. 1. Resp. The reason is different. For it can be proven from other sayings of Scripture, and from this very chapter, 2. Epist. 1. Peter, that besides spiritual Kings there are also Kings properly so-called in the N. T., but that besides Christ, the only supreme Priest of the N. Testament, there are still other Priests properly so-called, cannot be proven by any saying of Scripture. Add that in Christianity, as such, there are no Kings properly so-called, whereas the Papists wish for there to be Priests properly so-called in Christianity, as such.

6. Through Christ, spiritual sacrifices offered to GOD are acceptable and pleasing. Therefore, Christ is that Angel, of whom mention is made Apoc. 8. v. 3. & 4., which is acknowledged by Primasius, Ambrose, Ansbertus, Rupertus, Haymo, the interlinear Gloss, Thomas, Hugo Cardinalis, and among the more recent Papists, Blasius de Viegas in Apocal. page 343, and Estius in h. l. Petrinum, who comments on it thus: Through Christ we offer spiritual sacrifices, in that He, as our Mediator and Priest, offers them to GOD the Father as if received from us, and by His intercession commends them,Hebr. 13.Through Him let us offer the sacrifice of praise always to GOD.Apoc. 8.There was given to that Angel much incense, that he should give it to the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar. By which Angel Christ is signified. And afterwards: Christ offers our prayers and other good works to GOD the Father, because by His merit He makes them pleasing and acceptable to Him. This must be opposed to Bellarmine, who in book 1 de beat. sanct. cap. 16, attempts to prove the religious invocation of Angels and saints from that passage of the Apocalypse. The Angel, he says, stood before the altar having a golden censer, and there was given to him much incense, that he should give it to the prayers of the saints &c.Apoc. 8.Therefore Angels offer our prayers to GOD, and consequently they can also be religiously invoked by us. If Angels, therefore also the deceased saints.

7. Peter confirms his doctrine from Prophetic testimonies, three of which he brings forward in this place. The rest of the Apostles did the same in their sermons and writings. Christ himself did the same. What little sheep would not follow these shepherds? Clement of Alexandria, book 6, στρωματ. p. 288, attributes to Peter that he said, οὐδὲν ἄτερ γραφῆς, which seems to be taken from 1. Petr. 4. v. 11. If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of GOD. Origen, book 3, on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 3, before the middle: Paul, as is his custom, wishes to affirm what he had said from the holy Scriptures, at the same time providing an example for the Doctors of the Church, so that those things which they speak to the people, they may bring forth not presumed from their own opinions, but fortified by divine testimonies. This is to be opposed to the Papists, who strive to foist upon the Church traditions ἀγρὰφους, to be accepted with an equal affection of piety as the written word of GOD, and presume to teach ἂτερ γραφῆς certain things in the Church.

8. He who believes in Christ shall not be confounded. Therefore, believers can be certain of the grace of GOD, and have peace of conscience against any assaults of temptations whatsoever. Salmero on this passage: He who shall have believed in him shall not be confounded, because everyone who believes in him will at length arrive at salvation, even if for a time it is necessary that he be confounded among men. In the margin it is noted: The security of the believer in Christ, and the firmness of salvation. This is to be opposed to the Papists, who champion doubt concerning the grace of GOD and the uncertainty of salvation.

9. The Chief Priests, Elders, Scribes, and Pharisees sitting upon the seat of Moses rejected Christ, the foundational stone of the Church. Therefore, even those who are in the ordinary succession can err and repudiate the doctrine of Christ. This is to be opposed to the Papists, who strive to prove the infallibility of the Roman Pontiffs from succession in the Apostolic See.

10. In the Prophet, Jehovah is called a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense Esa. 8. v. 14. Peter calls Christ a stone of stumbling. Therefore, Christ is that true Jehovah of whom the Prophet speaks. This is to be opposed to the Photinians, who deny the Deity of Christ.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Salmeron adapts this to the Eucharist, that the pious are said, by approaching Christ, to be built upon him like living stones, so that he may infer from it that the Eucharist is a sacrifice, since it follows, to offer up spiritual sacrifices. The words are thus, that he said rational milk (The Apostle) now calls him a living stone, because this bread is a certain wonderful foundation. For sacramental bread strengthens the heart of man, and restores spiritual powers, as earthly bread does bodily ones. With this living stone, however, we are joined together through holy communion, if indeed we ourselves are also living stones, and not rather dead through our sins and desires, so that we cannot be glued to him. And although Christ is one living stone, there are nevertheless many Sacraments of the Eucharist, which Peter therefore calls spiritual and acceptable sacrifices on account of the number of many. Resp. 1. We easily concede that through the Sacrament of the Eucharist we are joined to Christ the living stone, and in this way the Apostolic statement can be accommodated to it, just as Fulgentius also applies it in book 2 to Monimus. This, he says, spiritual building is never more opportunely sought than when, from the very body of Christ, which is the Church, the very body and blood of Christ is offered in the Sacrament of bread and wine: meanwhile, the Apostle is not properly and principally dealing with the Eucharist here. 2. If the Eucharist is understood here by spiritual sacrifices. Therefore it is not an external and visible sacrifice, since the Papists themselves oppose it to the spiritual sacrifices of the pious. 3. Those who offer spiritual sacrifices, they are all holy Priests. But those who offer the external sacrifice of the Mass, they are not all holy. Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass cannot be understood by spiritual sacrifices. Estius in his commentary on this passage: The priesthood of which Peter speaks is not properly so-called, but metaphorical, which is insinuated by the epithet Holy. For those who are properly called Priests, namely those deputed to offer external Sacrifices, are not all holy, that is, endowed with internal holiness and purity of soul, even while they perform their Priesthood.

2. The same Salmero thinks Christ is called a stone chosen by GOD, because he was chosen for the union of the Word and ὑπόστασιν. Resp. 1. In what sense Christ is said to be chosen by GOD was explained above in q. 2. 2. When therefore Christ is said to be chosen, he is not then said to be chosen in the sense in which believers are finally said to be chosen by GOD for eternal life, for Christ is not the object of this election, but the efficient and meritorious cause. For Christ is to be considered in the election of those to be saved in a twofold manner. First, as true GOD with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he chose us for eternal life by one undivided action. Second, as the established Mediator of the human race And He is the Redeemer, on account of whom we were chosen, whence we are said to be chosen not only by Christ, but also in Christ Eph. 1. v. 4. 3. When Salmero calls Christ chosen for the hypostasis of the Word, he silently approves that hypothesis by which the election of certain ones is said to have been made first from an absolute decree, and only afterwards followed the counsel concerning the means which are suitable for saving the elect, among which is the incarnation of the Son of GOD. Bellarmin. lib. 2. de grat. & lib. arbit. cap. 9. The order of predestination in the divine mind stands thus. 1. GOD foresaw, if He were to create man, that he would fall with all his posterity &c. 2. He willed to create man, and to permit him to fall, and mercifully to liberate certain ones from the number of the fallen, with others justly left in the mass of perdition. 3. He devised remedies suitable for the elect to be saved, in which the incarnation and passion of the Savior held the first place. But by this reasoning the order of divine decrees is perverted, because the counsel concerning the means of salvation is postponed to the purpose of election, when it ought only to be placed before it. 4. The name of election is taken either καταχρηστικῶς, and in a certain breadth for every preordination and decree, or ίδιως and properly for the decree concerning those finally believing who are to be saved. In the former way Christ, or rather the human Nature of Christ, can be said to be chosen for ὑπόστασιν. Augustine de praedest. sanct. cap. 15. The most illustrious light of predestination and grace is the Savior Himself, the Mediator of GOD and men Himself, the man Jesus Christ, who, in order that He might be this, what merits of works or of faith, pray, did the human Nature, which is in Him, acquire beforehand? &c. Therefore, just as that one was predestined so that He might be our head: so we many were predestined so that we might be His members. 5. Election according to the phrase of Scripture, properly accepted, has persons in the place of the object. The human Nature of Christ is not a person. Therefore it cannot properly be called chosen. The human Nature of Christ is chosen for ὑπόστασιν, but it itself is not ὑπόστασις, but ἐνυπόστατος, nor did it exist before it was chosen, but ἅμα σὰρξ, ἅμα λόγου σάρξ.

3. From the fact that we are said as living stones to be built upon Christ, the Papists gather, the powers of free will in spiritual matters. Resp. 1. In the Greek it is passive, ὀικοδομεῖσθε be built up. 2. In which way also the Vulgate translation has it, which is authentic among them. 3. The ministers of the Church are compared to builders. Therefore by force of the relation the hearers are built up.

4. Meanwhile we willingly concede that those whom Peter addresses also build up themselves, since they are and are called not dead, but living stones, as Bede observes. Moreover, Peter addresses the reborn cap. 1. v. 23. whom we concede to be θεοῦ συνέργους, in the spiritual building. They act, however, not by the natural powers of free will, but by new powers received from the Holy Spirit.

4. Cornelius à Lapide in this place Build yourselves upon Christ through charity, and his works, which vivify faith. Resp. 1. Good works do not vivify faith, but faith demonstrates itself to be alive through works. 2. Those who build themselves up are called living stones, therefore they are already participants in spiritual life. 3. Christ is that living stone, who confers and preserves spiritual life upon the faithful built upon him, and imparts to them spiritual growth in this building.

5. From the fact that good works are called spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to GOD through Christ, Estius gathers that we are saved by good works. Spiritual sacrifices, he says, although they are in themselves pleasing and acceptable to GOD, insofar as they are works of piety, nevertheless just as they cannot be had except through Jesus Christ, so neither are they accepted by God for our salvation and glory, except through the same Jesus Christ. Resp. 1. We do not concede that good works are in themselves pleasing to GOD, for they are imperfect and unclean, therefore they are not pleasing and acceptable to GOD except through faith in Christ. Because of Christ apprehended by faith, not only the person, but also the good works of believers are pleasing to GOD; hence it is that faith is called the form of good works, insofar as they are considered not νομικῶς, but ἔυαγγελικῶς. Evagrius, Bishop of Antioch, said, good works are pleasing to GOD προηγουμένης τῆς πίστεως. Luther, vol. 4, Jena, Latin, fol. 403. All our works are pleasing to GOD, not because of any merit or dignity of ours, for they are all polluted, but because of the gift of faith, by which we believe in Christ. 2. The Apostle teaches that very thing in express words, when he says that spiritual sacrifices are acceptable to GOD through Christ, namely, apprehended by faith. 3. Nor yet is the justice and satisfaction of Christ so imputed to works that we are justified in the judgment of GOD through those works of ours. Since they themselves need to be justified, they certainly can in no way justify us, says Luther. Good works are pleasing to GOD, but they do not appease God. Hence it is not without reason that a distinction is made between the acceptance of the person and of the works. Compare the treatise on good works §. 19.

6. That reasoning, that Christ is called the cornerstone because he connects the two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, to one another and associates them into one Church, Calvin disapproves, and calls it an Augustinian subtlety. In Harm. Evang. and in comm. h. l. he writes thus: That some philosophize more subtly on the word corner, as if this were said because Christ joins the Jews and the Gentiles together as two different walls, is not sufficiently firm. He is so called because he sustains the weight of the building, and is also the rule of the whole building. Resp. 1. This reasoning is handed down in clear words by the Apostle Eph. 2. v. 14. and following. 2. It is handed down not only by Augustine, but also by Origen, Hilary, Jerome, Theophylact in chapter 21 of Matthew, Isidore of Pelusium lib. 1. Epist. 497. and all the ancients. 3. The same metaphor of the building fits most beautifully.

7. Bellarmine in the preface to the 3rd general controversy concerning the Roman Pontiff applies the Prophetic saying Esai. 28. v. 16. to the Roman Pontiff, whom he thinks is called a stone, on account of the firmness of the Roman See divinely founded; but cornerstone, to demonstrate the distinction between the Pontiff of the Jews and of the Christians. For that one was indeed a stone and a foundation, but not a cornerstone. For he did not sustain two walls, but only one. But the Roman Pontiff is a cornerstone. For both Jews and Gentiles, as two walls joined together, and making one Christian Church, are held together by this one cornerstone. Nay, in a manuscript copy he had denied that the Prophetic saying could be understood of Christ, but that it must be understood solely of the Roman Pontiff, since it follows in the Prophet, I will place a stone founded in the foundation i. e. a foundation after a foundation, or a secondary foundation, which cannot pertain to Christ. In the printed copy, however, he corrects himself and inserts certain words. Although, he says, we do not doubt that these things are to be understood principally of Christ, yet they can also not ineptly be referred to Peter (and Peter's successor the Roman Pontiff). But yet 1. we showed above in q. 6 from immovable foundations, that by the cornerstone and fundamental stone only Christ is to be understood. What is clearer than the Apostolic saying 1. Cor. 3. v. 11. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. 2. Bellarmine himself in lib. 1. de Christo Cap. 4. forms an argument for asserting the Divinity of Christ from this Prophetic passage, which he calls indissoluble and he is therefore compelled to acknowledge that this must be expounded concerning Christ alone. 3. Nor is this stone said to be founded upon another foundation, but it is called the foundation of the foundation, a most founded foundation, founding and containing the whole building. For repetition among the Hebrews intensifies the matter.

8. Salmero comments on this passage thus.
