Vocat autem eos dilectos, quia à DEO misericordiam consecuti, inque filios ab ipso adoptati, meritò pro fratribus eos habeat, atque eo ipso φιλαδελφίαν, ad quam eos exhortaturus fuerat, cap. 1. v. 22. demonstret. Respicit etiam ad spiritualem regenerationem per verbum, cuius mentionem fecerat cap. 1. v. 23. cum enim per verbum illud in Christo eos genuerit 1. Cor. 4. v. 15. inde dilectos suos filios ipsos vocat. παρακαλεῖν significat & precari & exhortari. Vulgata versio Latina ut & Syrus priorem, Lutherus in Germanica versione posteriorem significationem amplectitur. Utraque satis congrua est & sine absurditate coniungi potest. Hortor, & si fas est, rogo. Primum hoc est exhortationis argumentum. Aequum est, vos meae petitioni locum relinquere, cum sim vester Apostolus, sincerè in Christo vos diligens. Ὡς παροίκους καὶ παρεπιδήμους. Utraque vox in cap. praecedenti fuit exposita, prior quidem v. 17. posterior vero v. 1. Voculam παρεπιδήμους, Vulgatus Interpres initio Epistolae reddidit advenas, hîc vero vertit peregrinos, utriusque vocis eadem fermè significatio. Denotat enim eos, qui ut peregrini, & adventitii in aliquo loco commorantur. Cyprian. lib. 1. Epist. 5. legit hospites. August. conc. 8. in Psal. 118.Quod est in Graecoπάροικοςaliqui nostri inquilinus, aliqui incola, nonnulli etiam advenam interpretati sunt. Inquilini non habentes domum propriam habitant in aliena. Incolae autem vel advenae utique adventitii perhibentur. Quamvis vero Petrus Iudaeos conversos ad quos scribit, alio sensu in v. 1. appellat παρεπιδήμους, quàm hoc loco, ibi enim vocat eos παρεπιδήμους διασπορᾶς propterea quòd extra terram patriam inter gentes dispersi habitabant, hîc vero in genere conversos Iudaeos & gentes vocat advenas & peregrinos, propterea quòd sint peregrini & hospites in hoc mundo, dubium tamen nullum, quin Apostolus hac appellatione ad versiculum primum cap. 1. alludat. Estis advenae dispersionis, à terra patria extorres, haec conditio vestra vos admoneat, quòd sitis spiritualiter advenae & peregrini in hoc mundo. Alterum hoc est exhortationis argumentum. Hospites & peregrini estis in hoc mundo. Ergò non amate mundum, nec ea quae sunt in mundo, videlicet concupiscentiam carnis, concupiscentiam oculorum & superbiam vitae. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 15. & 16.Versamini in hoc mundo velut in terra exilii. Ergò non concupiscatis ea, quae sunt mundana, quae in mundo & à mundo maximi aestimantur, videlicet voluptates, honores, opes. Peregrini enim & advenae non conformant se regioni, in qua ad tempus duntaxat peregrinantur, nec finem desideriorum suorum statuunt in terra exilii, sed ad patriam perpetuò aspirant. Nec absurdè cogitatur, quod Petrus his verbis eos revocet ad exempla sanctorum Patriarcharum. Abrahamus pater omnium credentium, vocat sese advenam & peregrinumGenes. 23. v. 4. Moses fuit advena in terra alienaExod. 2. v. 22. Israelitae fuerunt advenae in terra Aegypti,Deut. 10. v. 19. David de se dicit Psal. 39. v. 13.advena ego sum apud te & peregrinus, sicut omnes Patres mei.Psal. 119. v. 19.peregrinus ego sum in terra, ac de se & toto populo Israelitico dicit, 1. Paralip. 29. v. 15.Peregrini sumus coram te & advenae, sicut omnes Patres nostri. De Patriarchis omnibus Epistola ad Hebraeos 11. v. 13. sic loquitur. Iuxta fidem defuncti sunt omnes isti non acceptis promissionibus, sed à longè eas aspicientes & salutantes, & confitentes, quia peregrini & hospites sunt super terram.v. 14.Qui enim haec dicunt, significant, se patriam inquirere.v. 15.& siquidem ipsius meminissent, de qua exierunt, habebant utique tempus revertendiv. 16.nunc autem meliorem appetunt, id est, coelestem. Quemadmodum igitur sancti Patriarchae, quando se vocarunt advenas & peregrinos, testati fuerunt, se ad coelestem patriam ex mundi huius exilio aspirare, ita quoque credentes Apostolus hortatur, ut veluti spirituales ipsorum filii, ad coelestem patriam anhelantes concupiscentias suas pravas despicatui habeant. Ἀπέχενσθαι τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμίων, Vulgata reddidit pronomen vos, quod non est in textu Graeco, nec est necessarium ad sententiae complementum, unde etiam in quibusdam Latinis Codicibus omittitur. Per ἀπέχεσθαιabstinere, quidam Codices habent ἀπέ χεσθεabstinete in imperativo, quo modo etiam Syrus reddidit. [consult facsimile image]separate vos ipsos. Sed infinitivus ἀπέχεσθαι magis congruit textui, quia cohaeret hoc verbum cum praecedente παθκαλῶ quo modo etiam legit & ordinat Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 3. Stromatum 2. Per τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας quidam in specie intelligunt carnales libidines. Sed rectiùs in genere intelliguntur quaevis pravae & illicitae carnis concupiscentiae, quae post lapsum protoplastorum ex carnali generatione singulis hominibus insitae, & in carne renatorum adhuc haerent, perque eam sese exerunt, & ad opera carnis hominum solicitant. Earum catalogum benè longum recenset Apostolus Gal. 5. v. 19. 20. & 21. Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image][consult facsimile image]desideria corporis, quo verbo etiam in explicatione praecepti de non concupiscendo utitur Roman. 7. v. 7. De his concupiscentiis carnalibus dicit Apostolus, quòd militent adversus animam. Quidam animae nomine hîc intelligunt salutem animae. existimant igitur, carnales concupiscentias propterea dici pugnare adversus animam, quòd carnis vitiosi affectus, utut anima illis assentiatur, in eius exitium tendant; quodque desideria illa carnalia, quamvis sensibus grata sint, tamen exitiale bellum inferant hominis saluti. Sed rectiùs dicitur, phrasi etiam reliquis Apostolis usitatâ, per animam intelligi totum hominem novum ac interiorem, quatenus est per Spiritum sanctum renovatus, sicut per carnem intelligitur totus homo, quatenus adhuc sub vetustate carnis constitutus est, ex parte carnalis sub peccatum venundatus. Roman. 7. v. 14. Quemadmodum igitur Paulus dicit, in renatis carnem concupiscere adversus Spiritum, & Spiritum adversus carnem, ac proinde inter carnem & Spiritum esse hostilem pugnam,Galat. 5. v. 17. ita quoque Petrus hoc loco dicit, desideria carnalia pugnare adversus animam, i. e. adversus interiorem hominem, adversus Spiritum, adversus mentem, (haec enim omnia Paulo in descriptione huius pugnae hostilis sunt ἰσοδυναμοῦντα,) inde etiam eodem verbo στρατουεσθαι utitur Petrus, quo Paulus in describenda hac Spiritus & carnis pugna usus fuit. Roman. 7. v. 23.Video aliam legem in membris meisἀντιστρατευόμενονlegi mentis meae.Iacobi. 4. vers. 1.Unde bella & lites in vobis? nonne hinc ex concupiscentiis vestris,ἐκ τῶν ἡδονῶν ὑμῶν τῶν στρατευόι των,quae militant in membris vestris. Tertium hoc est exhortationis argumentum. Carnales concupiscentiae militant adversus animam. Ergò ab illis meritò debetis abstinere, ne scil. eas opere compleatis.

## 2:12
HAVING YOUR CONVERSATION GOOD AMONG THE GENTILES, THAT IN THAT, WHEREIN THEY SPEAK AGAINST YOU, AS OF EVILDOERS, THEY MAY BY THE GOOD WORKS, WHICH THEY SHALL BEHOLD IN YOU, GLORIFY GOD IN THE DAY OF VISITATION.

Connection. 1. The Apostle had exhorted those to whom he writes, that they should decline from evil, now furthermore he admonishes them, that they should do good, Psal. 34. v. 15. he had required of them, that they should live σωφρόνως, now furthermore he requires, that they should live also δικαίως, Tit. 2. v. 12.

2. He had commanded, that they should keep the mind pure from fleshly lusts, and thus he had informed the inner man, now he demands, that in external conversation among men they should behave themselves honestly, and not only that they should not offend their neighbor by the wickedness of their manners, but also that by honest and composed manners they should provoke his love toward them and thus he forms and informs the outer man. The effect and end of the mortification of fleshly lusts is an honest and blameless conversation.

3. He confirms the exhortation to an honest conversation among the gentiles by a double argument, both of which are sought from a salutary consequence, first, that they may by this reason refute the false crimes, by which they are burdened by the gentiles beyond merit: second, that the gentiles, converted by their example to the Christian religion, may glorify GOD.

Exposition of the text. By τὴν ἀναστροφὴν καλὴν the Apostle understood an honest and praiseworthy conversation in external society. The Vulgate rendered it good. The Syrian rendered it. Let your conversations be [consult facsimile image] elegant, pleasant and grateful. In place of the participle ἒχοντες Oecumenius reads ἒχειν in the infinitive, so that it may depend on the verb παραχαλῶ just as also ἀπέχεσθαι in the preceding verse depends on it, ἐν τοῖς ἒθνεσιν among the gentiles, as the Vulgate rightly rendered, from which it is gathered, that the Apostle principally wrote this Epistle to Jews converted, living scattered among the gentiles. For writing to the gentiles he would say, among the unbelievers, or among those, who are without. Meanwhile, because this Epistle was written also to those converted from the gentiles constituting one Church together with the converted Jews, therefore the Syrian generally translates, before all the sons of men. Ἐν ᾧ καταλαλοῦσιν ὑμῶν The Vulgate rendered it, in that, wherein they speak against you. καταλαλεῖν properly is to speak against, to slander, to disparage, Jas. 4. v. 11. The LXX use for נדף he has treated with reproach, he has reviled, Ps. 43. v. 18. The Apostle expresses this meaning more clearly by adding, ὡς κακοποιῶν who slander you as evildoers, i.e., who hold you as evildoers and wicked men, harmful to the Republic, and unworthy of the common air. The Syrian thus circumscribed it, who speak against you evil words.

Ἐκ τῷν καλῶν ἔργεν ἐποπτεύσαντες. Ἐποπτεύσαντες looking into more deeply and more perfectly. Clem. Alex. book 2. paedag. 11. looking up. The Vulgate rendered it, considering you from your good works. But the pronoun you is not in the Greek text, which properly has it thus. Having looked upon from good works, or when they shall have inspected, to wit, your good works. The Syrian supplied that relative pronoun yours, they shall see your good works. Cyprian also supplied it in book 3. of testimonies against the Jews chap. 11. reading thus. That while they speak against you as if of evil men, looking upon your good works they may glorify GOD. Some understand the relative ἃ from good works, which they shall have inspected and considered, δοξάσωσι τὸν θεὸν they may praise and glorify GOD. This seems to be taken from the words of Christ Matt. 5. v. 16. Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father, who is in heaven. The sense therefore is. You will be able to stop the mouths of the slanderers, who hold you for evildoers, best of all by the pursuit of good works. For when they shall see your good works, they will not only begin to think more honestly of you, but will also be of a more favorable mind toward the Christian religion, and will glorify GOD, who has such worshippers, and thus they will convert the ignominious and least deserved slander into the praise and glory of GOD. The Apostle repeats the same in chap. 3. seq. v. 16. Having a good conscience, that in that, wherein they slander you, as evildoers, they may be confounded, who calumniate your good conversation in Christ. Ἐν ἡμέρα ἐπισκοπῆς, when the day of visitation shall follow.

Latin:

CONVERSATIONEM VESTRAM INTER GENTES HABENTES BONAM, UT IN EO, QUOD DETRACTENT DE VOBIS, TANQUAM DE MALEFACTORIBUS, EX BONIS OPERIBUS VOS CONSIDERANTES, GLORIFICENT DEUM IN DIE VISITATIONIS.

Connexio. 1. Exhortatus fuerat Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit, ut declinarent à malo, iam porrò illos admonet, ut faciant bonum, Psal. 34. v. 15. requisiverat ab eis, ut viverent σωφρόνως, iam porrò requirit, ut vivant etiam δικαίως,Tit. 2. v. 12.

2. Praeceperat, ut animum servarent purum à carnalibus concupiscentiis, sicque interiorem hominem informaverat, nunc exigit, ut in externa conversatione apud homines honestè se gerant, ac non solùm proximum non offendant improbitate morum, sed etiam moribus honestis & compositis eius amorem erga se provocent sicque exteriorem hominem format & informat. Effectum ac finis mortificationis carnalium concupiscentiarum est honesta & inculpata conversatio.

3. Exhortationem ad honestam inter gentes conversationem confirmat duplici argumento, quorum utrumque à consequente salutari petitum, primò, ut falsa crimina, quibus à gentilibus praeter meritum praegravantur, hac ratione redarguant: secundò, ut gentiles ipsorum exemplo ad religionem Christianam conversi DEUM glorificent.

Expositio textus. Per τὴν ἀναστροφὴν καλὴν intellexit Apostolus honestam & laudabilem in externa societate conversationem. Vulgata reddidit bonam. Syrus reddidit. Sint conversationes vestra[consult facsimile image]elegantes, iucundae & gratae. Loco participii ἒχοντες Oecumenius legit ἒχειν in infinitivo, ut pendeat à verbo παραχαλῶ sicut etiam ἀπέχεσθαι in versu praeced. ab illo pendet, ἐν τοῖς ἒθνεσινinter gentes, ut Vulgata rectè reddidit, ex quo colligitur, Apostolum principaliter hanc Epistolam scripsisse ad Iudaeos conversos, inter gentes sparsim habitantes. Ad gentiles enim scribens diceret, inter incredulos, vel inter eos, qui foris sunt. Interim, quia etiam ad conversos ex gentibus unam cum conversis Iudaeis Ecclesiam constituentes haec Epistola scripta, ideò Syrus generaliter vertit, coram omnibus filiis hominum.Ἐν ᾧ καταλαλοῦσιν ὑμῶν Vulgata reddidit, in eo, quod detrectant de vobis.καταλαλεῖν propriè est obloqui, detrahere, obtrectare,Iac. 4. v. 11. LXX. utuntur pro נדףopprobrio affecit, conviciatus est,Psal. 43. v. 18. Hanc significationem clariùs exprimit Apostolus subiungens, ὡς κακοποιῶνqui detrahunt vobis tanquam maleficis, i. e. qui vos habent tanquam maleficos & sceleratos homines, Reipublicae noxios, & communi aëre indignos. Syrus sic circumscripsit, qui loquuntur contra vos sermones malos.

Ἐκ τῷν καλῶν ἔργεν ἐποπτεύσαντες. Ἐποπτεύσαντες penitiùs & perfectiùs inspicientes. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. paedag. 11. suspicientes. Vulgata reddidit, ex bonis operibus vos considerantes. Sed pronomen vos non est in textu Graeco, qui propriè sic habet. Ex bonis operibus conspicati, vel cùm opera bona, scil. vestia, inspexerint. Relativum illud vestra supplevit Syrus, vide bunt bona opera vestra. Supplevit etiam Cyprianus lib. 3. testimoniorum adv. Iudaeos cap. 11. sic legens. Ut dum detrectant de vobis quasi de malignis, bona opera vestra aspicientes magnificent DEUM. Quidam subintelligunt relativum ἃ ex bonis operibus, quae inspexerint ac considerarint, δοξάσωσι τὸν θεὸν DEUM laudent ac glorificent. Videtur hoc desumtum ex verbis Christi Matth. 5. v. 16.Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona opera vestra, & glorificent Patrem vestrum, qui in coelis est. Sensus igitur est. Maledica calumniatorum, qui pro maleficis vos habent, ora, omnium optimè bonorum operum studio poteritis obturare. Quando enim videbunt bona opera vestra, non solùm honestiùs de vobis sentire incipient, sed etiam aequiore animo erga Christianam religionem erunt, ac DEUM, qui tales habet cultores, glorificabunt, sicque ignominiosam ac minimè meritam detractionem convertent in laudem & gloriam DEI. Idem repetit Apostolus in cap. 3. seq. v. 16.Conscientiam habentes bonam, ut in eo, quod detrahunt vobis, tanquam maleficis, confundantur, qui calumniantur vestram bonam in Christo conversationem.Ἐν ἡμέρα ἐπισκοπῆς, quando dies visitationis subsequetur.

## 2:13-14
BE SUBJECT THEREFORE TO EVERY HUMAN CREATURE FOR GOD'S SAKE, WHETHER TO THE KING AS PREEMINENT. OR TO GOVERNORS, AS SENT BY HIM FOR THE PUNISHMENT OF EVILDOERS, BUT FOR THE PRAISE OF THE GOOD.

Connection. 1. From a general exhortation the Apostle passes to special precepts of holy and honest conversation. And first indeed he prescribes certain rules of life for subjects, because all Christians were then subjects, but the Magistrates were Heathen.

2. The particle οὖν, which is illative, shows that this exhortation is deduced from the preceding. Because it is incumbent upon you to lead an honest conversation among the gentiles, therefore it is also just to show yourselves obedient to the Magistrate, since obedience toward the Magistrate is not the least part of honest conversation.

3. The Apostle had said that the faithful ought therefore to lead an honest life among the nations, so that in that in which the infidels slander them as evildoers, they may glorify God by considering their good works. Among those slanders, calumny held the chief place, by which the Jews converted to Christ, on account of the Jewish nation being prone to seditions, were ill-spoken of among the Gentiles, as if they were law-breakers and adversaries of the Magistrate, since those movements, which the Jews stirred up in the provinces for the sake of shaking off the yoke by which they were oppressed, were the causes of great calamities and the seeds of perpetual strife. Judas the Galilean had taught that tributes were not to be paid to a Gentile Caesar; hence Christians, of a religion related to the Jews, were accused of this error, as witnessed by Jerome in Epist. to Titus, chap. 3, Augustine in Epist. 5, Chrysostom in chap. 13 of Romans. The Apostles themselves were Jews and for the most part Galileans; the Apostle therefore first of all requires subjection to be rendered to the Magistrate by the faithful. This reason is gathered from v. 15.

4. Since Christ and his Apostles had in express words prohibited that Christians should resist evil out of a desire for private vengeance Matt. 5. verse 39.Luke 6. verse 29.Rom. 12. verse 17.1. Corinth. 6. v. 7., they slandered them, saying that all vengeance was prohibited to infidels, and consequently that political government was overturned by Christian doctrine. That the Apostle might meet this calumny, he seriously requires obedience toward the Magistrate from the faithful, by the example of Paul, who delivers similar precepts Rom. 13. verse 1. & following Tit. 3. verse 1., lest the Gentiles should say that Christianity brings about the subversion of the polity, says Oecumenius in this place.

5. Christians professed themselves to be liberated by Christ the Savior and therefore free, John 8. verse 32. & 36.2. Corinth. 3. verse 17.; therefore, lest the Ethnic Magistrates, out of hatred for the Christian religion, should interpret this liberty as if it were opposed to obedience toward the Magistrate, and lest under the pretext of this spiritual liberty ἄτακτοι they should shake off the yoke of the Magistrate and civil burdens among Christians, for that reason the Apostle prescribes subjection here. This reason is gathered from v. 16.

6. Not only the superiors but also the inferior Magistrates, Caesars and Presidents of the provinces, were at that time Gentiles, profane and impious. Therefore, so that Christians would not refuse to obey their rule under this pretext, and would not deform the doctrine of the Gospel by their jurisdictions, for that reason the Apostle exhorts them to obedience. This reason is gathered from v. 13.

Disposition. The Apostle illustrates and confirms the exhortation to obedience toward Magistrates. He illustrates it by a distribution into superior and inferior Magistrates, and teaches that one must obey both. He confirms it. 1. From the principal cause of the Magistrate. Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake. 2. From the effects, which vary according to the diversity of the objects. The Magistrate is ordained by GOD for the punishment of those doing evil and the praise of those doing well. The very obedience of subjects is also a refutation of slanderers, who disparage the faithful beyond all merit. Thus, therefore, some effects of obedience yield to the obedient themselves for their advantage, while others truly benefit others.

Exposition of the text. Ὑποτάττεσθαι properly signifies to be subordinated, to be subjected in a certain order. He hints, therefore, that the order between Magistrates and subjects is divinely constituted, on account of which the subjection of subjects toward the Magistrate is required, and that those who deny obedience to the Magistrate disturb the order divinely constituted, and walk ἀτάκτως 2. Thess. 3. vers. 6. & 11. The Syrian rendered it. Be [consult facsimile image] subject and serving. Oecumenius understands the noun κτίσεως abstractly and really concerning the power and office of the Magistrate. He knows, he says, that Scripture calls a constitution κτίσιν a creature or creation, just as to the Ephesians chap. 2. the Apostle said, to create two peoples into one new man. But he calls human ordination power. Caietanus leans toward the same opinion, who by κτίσιν understands the office of government itself. Others likewise understand it abstractly and really, but accommodate it to the ordinances, constitutions, and laws promulgated by the Magistrate. Luther, at this place, annotates thus. Whatever the Magistrate creates and ordains, he ought to keep. Osiander at this place. Obey the political laws constituted by men who hold the Magistracy. But it is more correctly accepted concretely and personally concerning the men who hold the Magistracy, as is evident. 1. From the subject distribution, whether to the King as excelling, or to Dukes as sent by him. 2. From Didymus and the Greek Scholia, which note, human that the creature is here called the presidents themselves. 3. From the Syriac version, which rendered it, be subject to all sons of man 4. From the usage of Scripture. The Greek word κτίσεως nowhere in the Scriptures signifies constitution or ordination, especially such as is that of laws, but is everywhere taken for a creature, i.e., things and persons created by GOD. Mark 16. Ver. 15.Rom. 1. v. 25.Coloss. 1. v. 23. thus καινὴ κτίσις is a new man 2. Cor. 5. v. 17.5. From the usage of the word κτίζειν. Just as the Latins say to create a Magistrate, to create a Consul; so also κτίσις or creature is called he who is constituted in a Magistracy. The sense therefore is, be subject to every human creature i.e., to every man constituted in the office of a Magistrate, which Magistrate it is agreed is created, who bears the duty of a Magistrate. He adds the little word πάσῃ therefore, to show that not the qualities of the persons, but the very office which they bear, is to be regarded in this subjection. Be subject to every superior constituted in a Magistracy, whether in respect of religion he be a Christian, or an infidel; whether in respect of nation and people he be a Jew, or a gentile; whether in respect of conduct he be good, or bad. διὰ τὸν Κύριον The Vulgate rendered for GOD'S sake, as also the Syrian [consult facsimile image] but the Greek Codices constantly read διὰ τὸν Κύριον for the Lord's sake, in which way it is also read in certain Latin Codices. By the Lord some understand Christ, who not only commanded to give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's Matt. 22. v. 21. but also by his own example commended obedience, not only toward parents Luke 2. v. 51. but also toward the Magistrate, Matt. 17 v. 27. The sense therefore would be. Because you are denominated Christians from Christ, therefore it is fair that, admonished by his command and example, you should perform obedience to the Magistrate. John Huss on this passage. Be subject for the sake of the imitation of GOD, that is, of Christ. Luke 2. But it is more correctly taken concerning GOD the Lord of all, so that this passage may be parallel to the Pauline passage Rom. 13. v. 1. Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, for there is no power but from GOD. Moreover, this προσδιορισμὸς looks 1. To the divine office which the Magistrate performs. Be subject to persons constituted in a Magistracy for the sake of GOD, whose place they hold, so that in them you may not consider the man, but GOD, whose person they sustain, from whom they also received the Power. 2. To the divine command. Be subject for the Lord's sake, that you may honor GOD with this obedience of yours, who commanded this subjection. 3. Regarding divine approval. Because GOD commanded this subjection, therefore it is also pleasing and acceptable to Him; consequently, by rendering service to the Magistrate, you render a service pleasing to GOD Himself, which will be rewarded with temporal and eternal rewards. 4. Regarding the manner of subjection. You ought to be subject not compelled, but willingly, because GOD, who commanded this obedience, demands voluntary services. Psal. 110. v. 3.5. Regarding the term or limits of subjection prescribed by God. For the Lord's sake. Be subject to the Magistrate. Therefore, if the Magistrate commands anything against the Lord, you ought not to render obedience to him. Eph. 6. v. 1. εἴτε βασιλεῖ. By the King is understood Caesar, who at that time was the highest Magistrate on earth, and held in his power those provinces to whose inhabitants Peter writes. For although the Romans at that time did not call their supreme Magistrate King, a name which was hateful to them after the Kings were expelled, but rather Caesar, or Emperor, or Augustus, yet the Greeks, according to the customary manner of other peoples, called him βασιλέα. Iohan. 19. v. 15.Actor. 17. v. 6. Thus Theodoret called Caracalla βασιλέα. However, because the name βασιλεὺς is general, signifying him who, because of the power of command, is βάσις τοῦ λεὼ, in whom the safety of the people is founded, and because Peter's command is likewise general, pertaining not only to those who live in the Roman Empire, but to all Christians everywhere, therefore in an accommodative sense any superior Magistrate is rightly understood by the name of King. Whence also the Syrian rendered it in the plural. Be subject to Kings. ὡς ὑπερέχοντι. The Vulgate rendered it, as to the one excelling. Some think that in the proper and principally intended sense of the Apostle, this pertains to all Magistrates, just as Paul Rom. 13. vers. 1. says generally, let every soul ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις be subject, and 1. Timoth. 2. v. 2. commands prayers to be made for all ἐν ὑπεροχῇ who are in high station, that is, constituted in the office of Magistrate. Thus, therefore, in these words there would not be contained a comparison of Caesar with other Magistrates, since that ὑπεροχὴ power and eminence which Peter inculcates is common to all Magistrates, and the sense would be that obedience is owed to all who preside, because to the dignity and preeminence of government divinely are elevated, and translated from the common lot of men to the pinnacle of power and dignity by GOD himself, the King of Kings, so that they may excel others and exercise authority over them. The Syriac Interpreter seems to lean toward the same opinion, who rendered [consult facsimile image] [consult facsimile image] For their dominion. But because the Apostle manifestly distinguishes between the King and the Governors, as between superior and inferior Magistrates, it is therefore more correctly established that by τὸν ὑπερέχοντα is understood in this place such a pinnacle of power and dignity, which is not common to inferior Magistrates, of whom the latter member speaks, and thus ὑπερέχοντα is called here he who has supreme power in the Republic, and so commands that he himself is not commanded by other men. Ἕιτε ἡγεμόσιν. The Vulgate rendered or to Governors, yet elsewhere it translates τοὺς ἡγεμόνες Presidents, Matth. 10. v. 18. cap. 27. v. 2. 11. &c. Marc. 13. v. 9. Luc. 20. v. 20. Actor. 23. v. 24. &c. which would have been more suitable for this place, for Peter in the proper and principally intended sense speaks of the Presidents of provinces, who were sent by Caesar and the Roman Senate into provinces subject to Roman rule, such as were in Judea Cyrenius, Pilate, Felix, Festus &c. In an accommodative sense, by Presidents any inferior Magistrates can be understood, just as by King any superior Magistrates, because the name ἡγεμόνος itself is general, signifying any ἡγούμενον, Matth. 2. v. 6. cap. 10. v. 18. Marc. 13. v. 9. Luc. 21. v. 12. and it is attributed to Caesar himself ἡγεμονία, Luc. 3. v. 1. whence the Syriac rendered [consult facsimile image] judges. Ὡς δι' αὐτού πεμπομένοις. Most refer the relative pronoun αὐτού to the nearer, in this sense, that those Presidents were sent by Caesar with authority into the provinces, and therefore they, as Caesar's supreme Magistrates' deputies, ought deservedly to be obeyed. But it is more correctly referred to the more remote, namely to GOD, in this sense, that not only the King, that supreme Magistrate, but also the Presidents, those inferior Magistrates, were sent by GOD, and perform a divine office. For 1. Presidents were set over provinces, not so much by the authority of Caesar as by that of the Senate. 2. The scope of the Apostle is to propose that which is to be considered in the Presidents, which to the rendering of obedience to them any should move one, because it itself also pertains to the King as a common reason for commending the authority of the Magistrate. 3. That vengeance of the evil, and praise of the good, which the Apostle established as the end of this mission, not all Kings have as a goal proposed to themselves, but GOD has prescribed this end for all Magistrates, as much for the inferior as for the superior. Therefore the mission to him also is rightly referred. 4. The Apostle had said, that one must obey the Magistrate for the Lord's sake, that very ἐξηγητικῶς declares that the Magistrate was sent by GOD for an end to human society, not only useful, but also necessary, namely εἰς ἐκδὶκησιν μὲν κακοποιῶν, ἔπαινον δε αγαθοποιῶν. A parallel passage exists Rom. 13. v. 3. & 4. Rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Do you wish then not to fear the power? Do good, and you will have praise from it. For he is GOD's minister to you for good. But if you have done evil, fear, for he does not carry the sword without cause. For he is GOD's minister, an avenger into wrath to him who does evil. The Vulgate version rendered this in this place, for the vengeance of evildoers, but the praise of the good, which could be taken concerning things, namely evil and good works, just as Paul also said Roman. 13. v. 3. ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν ἔργων. But from the Greek text it appears that this is to be taken concerning persons, namely concerning those who either do evil or good, just as the Syrian also rendered, [consult facsimile image] for the vengeance of those who commit offenses, and for the praise of [consult facsimile image] those who do good. Τοῖς κακοποιοῖς He says that the Magistrate is constituted εῖς ἐκδίκησιν, by which are understood punishments to be inflicted upon evildoers; Τοῖς ἀγαθοποιοῖς εῖς ἔπαινον, by which are understood rewards to be distributed to the obedient and those who do well, not because obedience is to be commended with bare words, but because praise is a certain species of reward, through which συνεκδοχικῶς rewards of every kind are understood, or because the reward of praise is a sign of honor.

Latin:

SUBIECTI IGITUR ESTOTE OMNI HUMANAE CREATURAE PROPTER DEUM, SIVE REGI Q. PRAECELLENTI. SIVE DUCIBUS, TANQUAM AB EO MISSIS AD VINDICTAM MALEFACTORUM, LAUDEM VERO BONORUM.

Connexio. 1. A generali exhortatione transit Apostolus ad specialia sanctae & honestae conversationis praecepta. Ac primùm quidem certas vitae regulas subditis praescribit, quia Christiani omnes tunc erant subditi, Magistratus vero Ethnici.

2. Particula οὖν, quae illativa, ostendit hanc exhortationem deduci ex superioribus. Quia vobis incumbit, conversationem honestam inter gentes ducere, ideò etiam aequum est, Magistratui vos obsequentes praebere, cum obedientia erga Magistratum honestae conversationis pars sit non postrema.

3. Dixerat Apostolus, fideles propterea debere honestam inter gentes conversationem ducere, ut in eo quod infideles detrahant ipsis tanquam malefactoribus, ex bonis operibus ipsos considerantes glorificent Deum. Inter illas obtrectationes principem locum obtinebat calumnia, quâ Iudaei ad Christum conversi, ob gentem Iudaicam ad seditiones pronam, inter gentiles malè audiebant, ac si essent legum refractarii & Magistratus adversarii, siquidem motus illi, quos Iudaei in provinciis & Romanis excutiendi, quo premebantur, iugi causâ excitabant, erant magnarum calamitatum causae, & perpetuarum simultatum seminaria. Iudas Galilaeus docuerat Caesari gentili non esse tributa pendenda, hinc Christiani cognatae cum Iudaeis religionis huius erroris accusabantur, teste Hieronymo in Epist. ad Tit. cap. 3. Augustino Epist. 5. Chrysostomo in cap. 13. Rom. Apostoli ipsi erant Iudaei ac plerique Galilaei, Apostolus igitur primò omnium subiectionem Magistratui praestandam à fidelibus requirit. Haec ratio colligitur ex. v. 15.

4. Cum Christus eiusque Apostoli disertis verbis prohibuissent, ne Christiani ex cupiditate privatae vindictae malo resisterent Matth. 5. vers. 39.Luc. 6. vers. 29.Rom. 12. vers. 17.1. Corinth. 6. v. 7. infideles omnem vindictam prohiberi, ac proinde per doctrinam Christianam gubernationem politicam convelli calumniabantur. huic calumniae ut Apostolus occurrat, obedientiam erga Magistratum seriò à fidelibus requirit, exemplo Pauli, similia praecepta tradentis Rom. 13. vers. 1. & seqq. Tit. 3. vers. 1.ne dicerent gentiles, quòd politiae subversionem afferat Christianismus, inquit Oecumenius in h. l.

5. Christiani se à Christo Salvator liberatos ac proinde liberos profitebantur, Iohan. 8. vers. 32. & 36.2. Corinth. 3. vers. 17. ne igitur Magistratus Ethnici ex odio Christianae religionis hanc libertatem sic interpretarentur, quasi ea obedientiae erga Magistratum sit opposita, neve sub praetextu spiritualis huius libertatis ἄτακτοι inter Christianos iugum Magistratus & onera civilia excuterent, ideò subiectionem Apostolus hîc praescribit. Haec ratio colligitur ex v. 16.

6. Non solùm superiores sed etiam inferiores Magistatus, Caesares & provinciarum Praesides tùm temporis erant gentiles, profani atque impii. Ne ergò Christiani hoc praetextu imperio eorum parere detrectarent, & doctrinam Evangelii se ditionibus deformarent, ideo Apostolus ad obedientiam eos exhortatur. Haec ratio colligitur ex v. 13.

Dispositio. Exhortationem ad obedientiam erga Magistratus Apostolus illustrat & confirmat. Illustrat distributione in Magistratus superiores & inferiores, ac utrisque parendum esse docet. Confirmat. 1. à causa Magistratus principali. Subiecti estote omni humanae creaturae propter Dominum. 2. Ab effectis, quae pro diversitate obiectorum variant. Magistratus à DEO ordinatus est in vindictam malè agentium & laudem benè agentium. Ipsa quoque subditorum obedientia est redargutio calumniatorum, fidelibus praeter omne meritum detrahentium. Sic ergò quaedam effecta obedientiae cedunt ipsis obedientibus in commodum, quaedam vero aliis prosunt.

Textus expositio. Ὑποτάττεσθαι propriè significat subordinari, ordine quodam subiici. Innuit ergò, ordinem inter Magistratus & subditos esse divinitus constitutum, propter quem subditorum erga Magistratum subiectio requiratur, ac illos, qui obedientiam, Magistratui denegant, turbare ordinem divinitus constitutum, ac ambulare ἀτάκτως2. Thess. 3. vers. 6. & 11. Syrus rèddidit. Estote[consult facsimile image]subiecti ac servientes. Nomen κτίσεως Oecumenius intelligit abstractivè & realiter de potestate & officio Magistratus. Novit, inquit, Scriptura constitutionem vocareκτίσινcreaturam vel creationem, sicutad Ephesios cap. 2.dixit Apostolus, duos populos creare in unum novum hominem. Ordinationem vero humanam vocat potestatem. In eandem sententiam propendet Caietanus, qui perκτίσινipsum officium regiminis intelligit. Alii itidem abstractivè & realiter intelligunt, sed accommodant ad ordinationes, constitutiones ac leges à Magistratu promulgatas. Lutherus, ad h. l. sic annotat. Quicquid Magistratus creat & ordinat, debet is servare. Osiander in h. l. Obedite legibus politicis ab hominibus, qui Magistratum gerunt, constitutis. Sed rectiùs accipitur concretivè & personaliter de homini bus, qui Magistratum gerunt, ut patet. 1. Ex subiecta distributione, sive Regi q. praecellenti, sive Ducibus tanquam ab eo missis. 2. Ex Didymo & Scholiis Graecis, quae annotant, humanam creaturam hic dici ipsospraesides. 3. Exversione Syriaca, quae reddidit, subiecti estote omnibus filiis hominis 4. Ex usu Scripturae. Graeca vox κτίσεως nuspiam in Scripturis significat constitutionem seu ordinationem, praesertim talem, qualis est legum, sed passim accipitur pro creatura i. e. rebus & personis à DEO creatis. Marc. 16. Vers. 15.Rom. 1. v. 25.Coloss. 1. v. 23. sic καινὴ κτίσις est homo novus 2. Cor. 5. v. 17.5. Ex usu verbi κτίζειν. Sicut Latini dicunt creare Magistratum, creare Consulem; ita quoque κτίσις sive creatura dicitur is, qui in Magistratu constitutus. Sensus igitur est, subiecti estote omni bumanae creaturae i. e. cuique homini, in Magistratus officio constituto, quem Magistratum esse creatum constat, qui Magistratus munus gerit. Voculam πάσῃ ideò adiicit, ut ostendat, non qualitates personarum, sed ipsum quod gerunt officium, in hac subiectione respiciendum esse. Subiecti estote cuique superiori in Magistratu constituto, sive respectu religionis sit Christianus, sive infidelis; sive respectu nationis ac gentis sit Iudaeus, sive gentiles; sive respectu conversationis sit bonus, sive malus. διὰ τὸν Κύριον Vulgata reddidit propter DEUM, uti etiam Syrus [consult facsimile image] sed Codices Graeci constanter legunt διὰ τὸν Κύριονpropter Dominum, quo modo etiam in quibusdam Codicibus Latinis legitur. Per Dominum quidam intelligunt Christum, qui non solùm iussit dare Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris Matth. 22. v. 21. sed etiam exemplo suo obedientiam commendavit, non solùm erga parentes Luc. 2. v. 51. sed etiam erga Magistratum, Matth. 17 v. 27. Sensus igitur foret. Quia à Christo denominamini Christiani, ideo aequum est, ut ipsius mandato & exemplo admoniti Magistratui obedientiaem praestetis. Iohannes Hussus in h. l. Subditi estote propter imitationem DEI, hoc est, Christi. Luc. 2. Sed rectiùs accipitur de DEO omnium Domino, ut hic locus sit parallelus loco Paulino Rom. 13. v. 1.Omnis animapotestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit, non est enim potestas, nisi à DEO. Respicit autem hic προσδιορισμὸς 1. Ad divinum, quo Magistratus fungitur, officium. Subditi estote personis in Magistratu constitutis propter DEUM, cuius vices gerunt, ut in illis non hominem consideretis, sed DEUM, cuius personam sustinent, à quo etiam Potestatem acceperunt. 2. Ad divinum mandatum. Subditi estote propter Dominum, ut honoretis hac vestrâ obedientiâ DEUM, qui subiectionem istam praecepit. 3. Ad divinam approbationem. Quia DEUS hanc subiectionem praecepit, ideò etiam illi grata est & accepta, proinde obsequium Magistratui praestantes, ipsi DEO gratum praestatis obsequium, quod praemiis temporalibus & aeter nis remunerabitur. 4. Ad subiectionis modum. Non coacti, sed sponte debetis fubiici, quia DEUS, qui hanc obedientiam praecepit, voluntaria servitia exigit. Psal. 110. v. 3.5. Ad subiectionis terminum sive limites divinitus praescriptos. Propter Dominum. Magistratui subditi estote. Ergò si Magistratus quippiam praecipiat contra Dominum, non debetis ei obedientiam praestare. Eph. 6. v. 1.εἴτε βασιλεῖ. Per Regem intelligitur Caesar, qui tunc summus erat in terris Magistratus, ac provincias illas, ad quarum incolas Petrus scribit, in sua tenebat potestate. Quamvis enim Romani supremum suum Magistratum tunc temporis non vocarent Regem, quod nomen ipsis post Reges expulsos erat exosum, sed vel Caesarem, vel Imperatorem, vel Augustum, Graeci tamen consueto reliquorum populorum more, eum vocabant βασιλέα.Iohan. 19. v. 15.Actor. 17. v. 6. Sic Theodoretus Caracallam vocavit βασιλέα. Quia tamen nomen βασιλεὺς generale est, significans eum qui ob potestatem imperii est βάσις τοῦ λεὼ, in quo fundata est populi salus, ac quia Petri praeceptum itidem generale est, non solùm ad eos, qui in Imperio Romano vivunt, sed ad omnes ubique Christianos pertinens, ideò in sensu accommodatitio per nomen Regis quilibet superior Magistratus rectè intelligitur. Unde etiam Syrus in plurali reddidit. Subiecti estote Regibus.ὡς ὑπερέχοντι. Vulgata reddidit, tanquam praecellenti. Quidam putant in sensu proprio & principaliter ab Apostolo intento hoc pertinere ad omnes Magistratus, sicut Paulus Rom. 13. vers. 1. generaliter dicit, omnis animaἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαιςsit subiecta, ac 1. Timoth. 2. v. 2.preces fieri iubet pro omnibusἐν ὑπεροχῇin sublimitate, id est, in Magistratus officio constitutis. Sic ergò in his verbis non contineretur comparatio Caesaris cum aliis Magistratibus, cum illa ὑπεροχὴ potestas ac eminentia, quam Petrus inculcat, sit omnibus Magistratibus communis, ac sensus foret, deberi omnibus, qui praesunt, obedientiam, quia ad regiminis dignitatem & praeeminentiam divinitus sint evecti, ac ex communi hominum sorte in potestatis & dignitatis fastigium, à DEO ipso Regum Rege translati, ut aliis praeemineant, & in ipsos imperium exerceant. In eandem sententiam videtur propendere Syrus Interpres, qui reddidit [consult facsimile image] [consult facsimile image]Propter dominium eorum. Sed quia Apostolus manifestè distinguit inter Regem & Duces, tanquam inter superiores & inferiores Magistratus, ideò rectiùs statuitur, per τὸν ὑπερέχοντα intelligi hoc loco eiusmodi potestatis & dignitatis fastigium, quod inferioribus Magistratibus, de quibus membrum posterius loquitur, non sit commune, adeoque ὑπερέχοντα hîc vocari eum, qui supremam potestatem habet in Republica, atque ita imperat, ut ab aliis hominibus ipsi non imperetur. Ἕιτε ἡγεμόσιν. Vulgata reddidit, sive Ducibus, alibi tamen τοὺς ἡγεμόνες vertit Praesides,Matth. 10. v. 18.cap. 27. v. 2.11. &c. Marc. 13. v. 9.Luc. 20. v. 20.Actor. 23. v. 24. &c. quod huic loco convenientius fuisset, Petrus enim in sensu proprio & principaliter intento loquitur de Praesidibus provinciarum, qui à Caesare & Senatu Romano mittebantur in provincias, Romanorum ditioni subiectas, quales in Iudaea fuêre Cyrenius, Pilatus, Felix, Festus &c. In sensu accommodatitio per Praesides intelligi possunt quivis inferiores Magistratus, sicut per Regem quivis superiores Magistratus, quia ipsum ἡγεμόνος nomen generale est, quemvis ἡγούμενον significans, Matth. 2. v. 6.cap. 10. v. 18.Marc. 13. v. 9.Luc. 21. v. 12. ac ipsi Caesari ἡγεμονία tribuitur, Luc. 3. v. 1. unde Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image]iudices.Ὡς δι' αὐτού πεμπομένοις. Pronomen relativum αὐτού plerique referunt ad propinquius, sensu eo, quòd Praesides illi à Caesare cum imperio in provincias missi sint, ac proinde illis tanquam Caesaris supremi Magisiratus vicariis meritò sit obtemperandum. Sed rectiùs refertur ad remotius, videl. ad DEUM, sensu eo, quòd non solùm Rex supremus ille Magistratus, sed etiam Praesides inferiores illi Magistratus à DEO missi sint, ac divinum gerant officium. Nam 1. Praesides provinciis praeficiebantur, non tam Caesaris, quàm Senatus autoritate. 2. Scopus Apostoli est, illud in Praesidibus considerandum proponere, quod ad obedientiam illis praestandam quemlibet movere debeat, quod ipsum etiam ad Regem tanquam communis ratio ad commendandam Magistratus autoritatem pertinet. 3. Vindictam illam malorum, & laudem bonorum, quem Apostolus finem huius missionis constituit, non omnes Reges tanquam scopum sibi habent propositum, DEUS autem hunc finem omnibus Magistratibus tàm inferioribus, quàm superioribus praescripsit. Ergò etiam missio ad ipsum rectè refertur. 4. Apostolus dixerat, obediendum esse Magistratui propter Dominum, illud ipsum ἐξηγητικῶς declarat, quòd Magistratus à DEO missus sit ad finem humanae societati, non solùm utilem, sed etiam necessarium, videlicet εἰς ἐκδὶκησιν μὲν κακοποιῶν, ἔπαινον δε αγαθοποιῶν. Locus parallelus extat Rom. 13. v. 3. & 4.Principes non sunt timori bonis operibus, sed malis. Vis autem non timere potestatem? bonum fac, & habebis laudem exilla. DEI enim minister est tibi in bonum. Si autem malum feceris, time, non enim sine causâ gladium portat. DEI enim minister est, vindex in iram ei, malum agit. Vulgata versio hoc loco reddidit, ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum, quod posset de rebus, videlicet operibus malis & bonis accipi, sicut etiam Paulus dixit Roman. 13. v. 3.ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν ἔργων. Sed ex textu Graeco apparet, de personis hoc esse accipiendum, videlicet de illis, qui vel mala vel bona agunt, sicut & Syrus reddidit, [consult facsimile image]ad vindictam delinquentium, & ad laudem[consult facsimile image]opemntium bona.Τοῖς κακοποιοῖς Magistratum constitutum esse dicit εῖς ἐκδίκησιν, per quam intelliguntur poenae maleficis irrogandae; Τοῖς ἀγαθοποιοῖς εῖς ἔπαινον, per quem intelliguntur praemia obedientibus, & benè operantibus distribuenda, non quòd nudis verbis commendanda sit obedientia, sed quia laus est praemii quaedam species, per quam συνεκδοχικῶς omnis generis praemia intelliguntur, vel quia praemium laudis & honoris est signum.

## 2:13-25 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. Why the Apostle wishes servants to be subject to their masters in all fear. Resp. Some take the little word all distributively for discrete quantity, since there is a manifold fear which ought to be in servants, namely first the fear of punishment, lest they be punished by their masters if they are disobedient, secondly the fear of guilt, lest they offend God by their disobedience; thirdly the fear of scandal, lest by their disobedience they provoke their masters to hatred of the Christian faith. But we have warned above that the Apostle does not require fear of punishment, which is servile fear, but fear of guilt, which is filial. More correctly, therefore, the little word πάντι is taken for continuous quantity, with all fear, that is, with much reverence. For the Apostle demands a pure, full, and voluntary affection of reverence, by which they acknowledge that they owe obedience to their masters out of their duty. Col. 3. v. 22.

Q. 2. Whether it is permitted for servants to flee from inclement masters? One must distinguish between slaves and freedmen. Slaves were not of their own right, but the possession of the Master, whence they were dragged back from flight, but freedmen can flee if danger to their life or the safety of their limbs threatens them. August. tract. 15. on John: Every servant of God does not sin if he withdraws himself to another place, laughing at the fury of those following him, or seeking his soul for evil. However, the servant of God would seem to sin if he did so, unless the Lord had preceded him in doing so. That good Master did this, so that he might teach, not because he was afraid.

Q. 3. What the Apostle understands here by the conscience of GOD in v. 19. Resp. 1. Caietanus sic exponit. Si quis propter DEI conscientiam sustinet tristitias i. e. propter applicationem scientiae, quam habet de iis, quae sunt DEO grata. 2. Gagnaeus hanc expositionem reiicit, ipse vero sic exponit. Si quis propter DEI conscientiam sustinet, id est, propter Deum, qui & servilis patientiae & herilis malitiae conscius est, ac utriusque erit iudex & vindex, ut servi patientiam praemiis coelestibus ornet, heri vero saevitiam flammis infernalibus puniat. Conscientia ergò DEI est innocentia coram DEO acuni DEO patens. 3. Quidam sic exponunt. Si quis propter Dei conscientiam sustineat tristitias i. e. quia est veri Dei cultor; eo nomine hero suo exosus, quòd fidem Christianam profiteatur. Quando enim servi ad Christum convertebantur, ab heris Ethnicis in odium fidei Christianae plagis ac verberibus mulctabantur, si ergò propter Dei conscientiam patiebantur i. e. propter Deum & Dei cultum, ex pura conscientia profectum; patiebantur haec omnia propterea quod bonâ conscientiâ Deo servire studerent in fide Christiana, quam amplexi erant ac profitebantur. Huic expositioni à quibusdam obvertitur, quòd Petrus nondum agere videatur de afflictione Christianorum propter fidem Christianam ipsis illata, de qua demum in seqq. capp. agat. 4. Quidam Dei conscientiam intelligunt eam, quae solius Dei gloriam spectat, eidemque sese totam addicit. Fideles servi ab iniustis dominis illatas iniurias patienter tolerantes, patiebantur propter Dei conscientiam, quia in servitio ac tota vita sua Dei solius honorem spectabant, nec hominum sed Dei respectu officio suo fungebantur. 5. Simplicissimè respondetur, conscientiam Dei esse conscientiam ad Deum, ut Lutherus reddidit, vel de Deo, quando scilicet aliquis conscius est, id DEUM velle, idque DEO gratum esse, quod agit. Sic servi patiebantur propter DEI conscientiam, quia iniurias iniustè sibi illatas patienter tolerabant, non tantùm ne graviora incurrerent incommoda, nec ut herorum suorum vel aliorum hominum gratiam sibi conciliarent, sed quia noverant, hanc esse Dei voluntatem, ut iniurias patienter sustineant, patientiam illam esse opus DEO gratum & acceptum, quod etiam temporalibus & aeternis praemiis sit remuneraturus. Obediebant ergò etiam durissimis herorum imperiis, & mores ipsorum asperrimos tolerabant, ut conscientiae satisfacerent, ut bonâ conscientiâ coram DEO ambularent & ipsius voluntati obtemperarent, sicque non hominum, sed Dei timore in officio continebantur.

Q. 4. What is said to have been handed over by Christ to GOD the judge? Resp. 1. The ordinary Gloss accepts it with Didymus concerning the persecutors and enemies of Christ. He handed over his own through the persecutors to GOD the Father by praying for them. Father forgive them, for they know not what they do,Luke 23. verse 34. 2. Some accept it concerning Christ himself. He handed himself over to GOD the Father as a voluntary sacrifice, he was obedient to his Father even unto the death of the cross,Phil. 2. verse 8. 3. Some understand the noun vengeance, so that the sense may be. Christ did not avenge himself, but committed vengeance to GOD the Father, who says. Vengeance is mine, I will repay,Deuter. 32. verse 35.Roman. 12. v. 19. 4. It is most simply accepted concerning the cause itself. Christ, sustaining various sufferings for our sins, was commending his cause to GOD, seeking liberation from distresses, interceding for his crucifiers, and committing the stubborn and incorrigible to the judgment of GOD, for παριδίδον signifies not only handed over, but also committed and commended. Jerem. 11. v. 20.To thee I have devolved my cause.

Q. 5. Who is understood by him who judges justly? Oecumenius accepts it concerning τῷ λόγῳ GOD the Word dwelling in Christ. But Augustine in tract 21 on John and Didymus in his commentary more rightly understand it concerning GOD the Father, by whom he had been handed over unto death,Roman. 8. verse 32.and with whom he dealt through prayers in his passion,Matth. 26. v. 39.Hebr. 5. verse 7. meanwhile it is certain that the Father and λόγου are one essence of Deity.

Q. 6. By what reason is the holiness of life a consequence of the death of Christ? Resp. 1. Ποιητικῶς. Christ by his death not only merited for us the remission of sins, but also the donation of the Holy Spirit, who mortifies sin in our flesh. 2. Ὑποδειγματικῶς. Roman. 6. v. 4.We are buried together with Christ by Baptism into death, that as Christ rose from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life. Ambrose in 2. Cor. 5.Crucify sin, that you may die to sin. For he who dies to sin, lives to GOD. Let us live to him, who did not spare his own Son, that in his body he might crucify our passions. For Christ died for us, that we might die in his revived body. Therefore, it is not our life that died in him, but our guilt.

Q. 7. Why does the Apostle call Christ the Shepherd and Bishop of souls only? Resp. Christ, as true GOD with the Father and the Holy Spirit, also feeds our bodies with bodily food for this life, and as our Mediator and Redeemer leads not only our souls, but also our bodies to eternal life; meanwhile, the Apostle wished to make mention of souls only. 1. That he might distinguish Christ the spiritual Shepherd and Physician of souls from the shepherds and physicians of bodies. Christ is the Shepherd and Bishop of our souls, because he guards us for eternal salvation by spiritual feeding and defense. 2. That he might signify that Christ takes care of our souls, and receives them to himself, when our bodies are killed by persecutors, Matth. 10. v. 28.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. For what glory is it, if when you sin and are buffeted you endure it? v. 20. And yet patience even in deserved punishments has its own praise and reward. Resp. Peter does not speak absolutely, but comparatively. He does not signify that he who patiently sustains punishments inflicted either by GOD or by the Magistrate, the minister of GOD, for his own offenses, will be entirely devoid of all reward of patience before GOD, but he denies that it is a great and illustrious work of patience of its own kind, to which singular glory is owed, such as it is if someone patiently sustains injuries inflicted for good works, or certainly beyond merit. It is a thin and obscure praise to bear a just punishment with an even mind, if it is compared with the praise arising from afflictions unjustly inflicted, but patiently tolerated.

2. If doing good and suffering you endure it, this is grace before God, in the same verse. And yet glory before GOD has no place in punishments. Resp. Truly the Syrian Interpreter repeats the little word κλέος here from the former member. But all Greek Codices read: This is grace before God. Therefore, by singular counsel, the word χάριτος is repeated by the Apostle from the preceding verse, when the antithesis of this little verse seemed to require the word κλέος. For he signifies that we cannot glory before GOD concerning patience in afflictions even unjustly inflicted, since it pertains to the obedience owed to GOD by many names, since it is not our work, but of grace and the Spirit effectively working in us, since it is imperfect and contaminated by vicious affections in the infirmity of this flesh. In nothing is one to glory, because nothing is our own. 1. Cor. 4. v. 7.

3. Christ left us an example, that we should follow his steps.v. 21.And yet Christ walked upon the sea, restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, in which we can by no means follow him. Resp. One must distinguish between the miraculous works of Christ, and the virtuous ones, or virtues. Peter does not propose to us for an example of imitation the miraculous and heroic works of Christ, but patience, obedience, and innocence. In certain works Christ is wonderful to us, in certain others he is imitable.

4. He left us an example, that we should follow his steps,v. 21.And yetEccles. 2. v. 12.What is man, that he should be able to follow the King his maker. Resp. John Huss distinguishes between the divine and human Nature of Christ; not that one, but this one is proposed to us for an example of imitation. It is answered more correctly that it is read otherwise there in the Hebrew. What is man, who is to come after the King, which they have already done to him, where the discourse is not about a heavenly, but a terrestrial King.

5. Christ did no sin.v. 22.And yet Christ was made sin for us,2. Cor. 5. v. 21.GOD made Christ sin for us. Resp. It is one thing for Christ to have committed sin, another for Christ to have been made sin for us. The former denotes the inhesion and operation of sin, but the latter denotes the imputation of sin, the offering made for sins, and the toleration of the punishments owed to our sins. The former is accepted as ἐνυπαρκτικῶς, but the latter as λογιστικῶς. August. book 2 against Pelagius and Coelestius chapter 32. GOD made Christ sin for us, i. e. a sacrifice, through which our sins might be forgiven, since sacrifices for sins are called sins. Fulgentius on faith to Peter chapter 26. Christ conceived without sin, died without sin, was made sin for us, i. e. made a sacrifice for our sins.

6. Christ did no sin,v. 22.And yet Christ is free not only from actual sins, but also from original. Resp. 1. τό to commit sin, is not placed exclusively for actual sins alone, but inclusively, so that it may also include original sin, from which as from a poisonous fountain actual sins arise. 2. For what Peter says, that Christ did not commit sin, Paul expresses thus 2. Cor. 5. v. 21.Christ did not know sin, where Chrysostom notes, the Apostle did not say, who had not committed sin, but who had not known sin, indeed to such an extent had he been separated from sinners, that not even by sight indeed he knew sin.Heb. 7. v. 26. He is called ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῆν ἁμαρτωλῶν. 3. Peter notably adds from Isaiah, that guile was not found in the mouth of Christ. Now truly who does not offend in tongue, this one is perfect, says James ch. 3. v. 2. Therefore by that very thing the highest and most perfect innocence of Christ is denoted. 4. Augustine from the removal of actual sin gathers the removal of original sin, book 5 against Julian ch. 15, thus arguing. Indeed sin would have made him even greater, if the little child had possessed it. For on that account there is no one of men besides him, who did not commit sin with the approach of older age, because there is no one of men besides him, who did not have sin with the rise of infantile age.

7. When he was reviled, he did not revile backv. 23.But yetJohn 8. v. 44.he says to the Jews reviling him. You are from your father the Devil. Resp. 1. This was not a recrimination, because nothing similar had been objected to him before, but it was a true and just accusation. 2. He did not bring this forth from a vicious affection of private vengeance, but from a mind most desirous of their own salvation, so that he might lead them to the recognition of sins, and consequently to conversion and salvation, John Huss in this place. Charitable correction is not an insult, but that which proceeds from hatred, especially if it be for one's own vengeance.

8. When he suffered, he did not threaten.v. 23.But yetMatt. 11. v. 20.he says. Woe to you Chorazin, woe to you Bethsaida.Matt. 23. v. 13. & following Woe to you Scribes and Pharisees.ch. 26. v. 64.Nevertheless I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of GOD, and coming in the clouds of heaven. Resp. 1. He did not denounce woe or eternal curse to the High Priests, Scribes and Pharisees at the very time of his passion, but before the passion, lest he might seem to have done it not from Zeal for justice, but moved by affections of anger and hatred. 2. He denounced to them the judgment of GOD, not on account of himself, nor from impatience or a desire for vengeance, but on account of them and from charity, so that he might recall them from wickedness, and consequently from damnation.

9. He delivered to him who judges justly.v. 23.But Christ is nowhere read to have commended his own cause of vengeance to GOD. Resp. he did not ask for vengeance, but for pardon, when he became an intercessor for his killers and sought their conversion, Luke 23. v. 34. whence his blood is said to speak κρείττονα better things, than the blood of Abel,Heb. 12. vers. 24.For the blood of Abel asked for revenge,Gen. 4. v. 10. but the blood of Christ for reconciliation and expiation.

10. You were as sheep going astray.v. 25. But before conversion they were not sheep, but goats. 1. Bede answers in this place: How does He call them both sheep and wandering, since those who lead their lives in error are reckoned by the name of goats rather than sheep, unless it is because the Lord knows those who are His, whom He also sustains, though they have lived badly for a long time, whom nevertheless He foresees are to be saved in the number of His sheep. 2. It is answered more simply that men not converted to Christ are compared to sheep, not by reason of simplicity, innocence, patience, and the remaining images of virtues, but by reason of the stupidity, danger, and misery in which sheep destitute of a shepherd and exposed to the prey of wolves are involved, whence they are not simply compared to sheep, but to wandering sheep.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. This is grace with GOD, if you endure while doing good and suffering. It is false, therefore, what the Pope teaches, that patience and the remaining virtues of the pious merit heavenly rewards by condignity. For grace and a reward from grace are opposed to a reward from debt, or a reward of merit. Rom. 4. v. 4.

2. Christ suffered for us, not only on account of us and for our utility, but also for us and in our place, because He sustained the punishments owed to our sins, and by this reason He made satisfaction for our sins. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 2. in which sense it is also said that He bore our sins in His body upon the tree, namely that He might offer Himself as a sacrifice for them. It is false, therefore, what the Photinians establish, that the passion and death of Christ are not satisfactory and meritorious, but merely exemplary.

3. Christ bore our sins in His body upon the tree. Therefore our sins were effectively imputed to Him before the judgment of God. It is false, therefore, that the Papists deny that this imputation of our sins was made to Christ. They object, that Christ is said to have been made sin for us2. Cor. 5. v. 21. and to have borne our sins in His body upon the tree, because He offered Himself as a sacrifice for our sins. I answer: that Christ was made a sacrifice for our sins presupposes that an imputation of our sins was made to Christ. For thence and therefore Christ offered Himself as a sacrifice for our sins, because He took upon Himself our sins transferred into Him through imputation. We prove this 1. From the Prophetic phrase Es. 53. v. 4. & following, where Christ is said not only to have borne our sorrows and the punishments owed to our sins, but also our infirmities and our sins it is sometimes said, and emphatically added, that the heavenly Father made the iniquities of us all to rush upon him in a formed battle line. 2. From the Apostolic phrase, Christ is not only said to have been made a curse for usGal. 3. v. 13., which phrase respects the punishment owed to our sins, but also made sin for us.2. Cor. 5. v. 21., which phrase respects the imputation of our sins made to Christ. 3. From the comparison of this Petrine passage with the Apostolic passage Hebr. 7. v. 27.. For as it is said in this place, that Christ in his body ἀνένεγκεν ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν,, so it is said there ἑαυτὸν ἀνένεγκας.. Therefore, when he ascended the cross, he not only ascended to offer himself as a sacrifice to GOD, but also made our sins, imposed and imputed to him, to ascend with him onto the cross, as the Syrian notably rendered in this place, and he bore them together with his body, and in his body, as a great burden imposed upon him, onto the cross. Athanas. orat. 4. contra Arian. bearing our sins onto the cross together with his body. 4. From the saying of John the Baptist Ioh. 1. v. 29. Behold the lamb of GOD ὁ αἴρων the sin of the world. Moreover, αἴρειν signifies not only to take away and remove from the midst, but also to receive into oneself and to carry. 5. From the Greek version Esai. 53. v. 4., where in the Hebrew text it is said: Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our sorrows. But the LXX interpreters rendered: He himself carries our sins and suffers for us, most beautifully joining the imputation of sins and the toleration of punishments as antecedent and consequent. 6. From the type of the scapegoat Lev. 16. v. 21. The priest, having placed both hands upon the head of the goat, shall confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions and sins, which, placing upon his head, he shall send him away by a man prepared into the desert.v. 22. and when he shall have thus carried all their iniquities into a solitary land. 7. Chrysostom on 2. Cor. 5. and from him Theodoret: He permitted him who had committed no sin to be afflicted with punishment for the transgressors. But he did not say that, but something much greater. What? He made him, who had not known sin, who was righteousness itself, sin, that is, he permitted him to be condemned as a sinner, to die as a curse. 8. That Christ was made sin for us λογιστικῶς, i.e., that our sins were imputed to him, is acknowledged by Ruardus Tapperus, Dean of Louvain, art. 8. tom. 2. p. 27. Barradius, tom. 4. Conc. Evangel. lib. 6. cap. 3. in sept. passion. praecellentia.

4. Just as our sins were imputed to Christ, so the righteousness of Christ it is imputed to us through faith, because Christ is said to have been made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of GOD i. e. righteous before God in him. August. enarr. 2. on Psal. 22. He made our offenses his own offenses, that he might make his righteousness our righteousness. in Enchir. cap. 41. Therefore he himself is sin, that we might be righteousness, not our own, but GOD'S: and not in ourselves, but in him, just as he demonstrated sin not his own, but ours; and established not in himself, but in us in the likeness of sinful flesh, in which he was crucified. Therefore the Papists are deceived, when they deny that the righteousness of Christ can be imputed through faith. Salmero tom. 15. p. 20. Bellarm. lib. 2. de iustificat. cap. 7.

5. Christ is said to have borne our sins in his body. Therefore he made most full satisfaction for all sins in general. It is false, therefore, what Thomas opusc. 58. de Sacr. altar. & Ambrosius Catharinus in lib. de incruento sacrificio argue, that the body of the Lord was offered once on the cross for original debt, but is continually offered on the altar for our daily offenses.

6. Christ is said to have borne our sins in his body upon the tree, because he endured the punishments owed to our sins on the cross. It is false, therefore, what the Papists declare, that Christ satisfied for guilt and eternal punishment alone, but that for temporal punishment we ourselves must make satisfaction. Concil. Trid. sess. 6. cap. 14. sess. 14. cap. 12. Bellarminus lib 4. de poenit. cap. 2.

7. Peter says, that Christ bore our sins in his body upon the tree. Therefore Peter includes himself and his own sins, and intimates that Christ also made satisfaction for them, as Beda observes in h. l. He does not say your sins, but with himself added, who himself, he says, bore our sins in his body upon the tree. It is false, therefore, what the Papists teach, that the reborn can perfectly fulfill the law of GOD. For if the Apostle Peter taught that his sins were expiated by Christ, he certainly professed himself a sinner, and consequently also a transgressor of the divine law.

8. We were like sheep going astray. Therefore we could not by our own powers return to the way and be converted to the Lord. It is false, therefore, the dogma of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians, and Synergists.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Lyranus explains the words of the Apostle, This is grace, if for conscience of GOD one endures sorrows, thus. This is a gracious thing, because it is of supererogation. Insisting on his footsteps Cornelius à Lapide comments on this passage thus. This is grace, i. e. your glory, whence explaining he adds. For what is glory. Thus Paul says his glory is not to preach the Gospel, for the necessity of the command of GOD bound him to this, but to preach the Gospel without cost, i. e. freely, for this was a liberal and illustrious work of supererogation, and of counsel, not of command. 1. Cor. 9. v. 16. Resp. 1. This exposition directly opposes the scope of the Apostle. For the name of grace completely excludes the opinion concerning a work of supererogation and merit. 2. To endure injuries inflicted without merit is not a work of counsel and supererogation, required only of Monks, but is a work of command required of all Christians, because those servants, whom Peter specifically addresses here, were not Monks. 3. It is one thing to glory in the Lord, another to glory before the Lord. The former is of Christians, the latter of proud hypocrites. 1. Cor. 1. v. 31. To glory in God is not except from God alone. This glory therefore does not make men proud, but humble; it does not despise the neighbor, but loves; it does not prefer itself to others, but subjects itself in the fear of GOD and charity. 4. It is one thing to glory against men, another to glory before GOD. The Apostle was glorying against men, namely the Pseudo-Apostles, that he had not received a reward from the preaching of the Gospel, but before GOD he was not glorying, but was humbling himself.

2. From the fact that Christ is said to have suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow his steps, Cornelius à Lapide gathers proper satisfactions. Let the soft heretics note this, he says, who wish to follow the faith of Christ, not the steps of his passion, saying that faith alone in Christ suffices for salvation, for Christ has fully satisfied for us, wherefore there are no merits of good works, no satisfactions. Let them hear what S. Peter thunders here and from him Gregory in 1. Reg. 9. v. 24. It remained, he says, because Christ did not fulfill all our things, indeed he redeemed all through his cross, but it remained, that he who strives to be redeemed and to reign with him, should be crucified. This remainder truly he had seen, who was saying, If we suffer with him we shall also reign with him 2. Tim. 2. v. 12. and I fill up those things which are wanting of the sufferings of Christ in my flesh. Coloss. 1. v. 24. Resp. 1. Peter does not speak of afflictions assumed spontaneously in satisfaction for sins, or imposed by Priests, but of passions inflicted by others, which he teaches are to be borne patiently by the example of Christ. For he addresses servants, who were tolerating blows from wicked masters without merit.

2. We follow the footsteps of the passion of Christ, and we ought to follow them, not by making satisfaction for our sins, for this glory belongs to Christ alone, who trod the winepress alone, Is. 63. v. 3. and made purification of our sins by himself, Heb. 1. v. 3. but by patiently bearing the cross divinely imposed. 3. What Cornelius says, that God has ordained that we apply the price of the passion of Christ to ourselves through our own passions, that is said without any testimony of Scripture. Scripture nowhere proposes passions, or patience in passions, as a medium through which the fruit of the passion of Christ is applied to us, but everywhere attributes this application to faith alone. 4. We must therefore suffer with Christ, and be conformed to him through the cross, Rom. 8. v. 29. not for the completion of satisfaction, but for the example of imitation. 5. Guilielmus Estius and Benedictus Iustinianus in their commentary on Col. 1. expressly refute that exposition of Cornelius à Lapide. For Lyranus rightly warns ibid., The passions of Christ are spoken of in two ways: in one way in his own body, in which Christ endured hunger, thirst, and death, and taking it thus, there is nothing to be filled up; in another way as he suffers in his members, which are the faithful, and thus the Apostle speaks in that place. And Thomas, p. 3. q. 48. art. 5. resp. to 3. says, The passions of the Saints profit the Church, not indeed by way of redemption, but by way of example and exhortation, according to that, whether we are afflicted for your exhortation and salvation.

3. From the fact that Christ is said to have left us an example, that we should follow his footsteps, the Papists gather, the Lenten fast. Resp. We warned above that Peter is not speaking of the miraculous works of Christ, but of the virtuous ones. Now, however, the Lenten fast pertains to the miraculous works of Christ. Martinus Delrius, part 1, Disquisit. Magicar. lib. 2. q. 4, some things in divine matters are to be believed, such as the Trinity; some are to be honored with admiration, such as the miracles of Christ and the saints; some are to be imitated, such as the meekness and charity of Christ. To wish to imitate in those prodigious effects is the mark of a foolish and proud mind. Meanwhile, we do not deny that an example of temperance and Christian fasting is proposed to us in the deed of Christ.

4. From the fact that Peter proves CHRIST to be ἀναμάρτητον, because he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth, the Pelagians gathered, that no original sin is given. For if original sin were given, Peter could not have [proven him to be such] from the removal of one of the species to proceed to the removal of the genus. He responds. 1. Augustine, book 5 against Julian, chapter 15: You have certainly said that great and true thing, when you had placed the testimony of the Apostle Peter saying, 'Who did no sin,' it is to be noted that the Apostle judged it sufficient to show that there was no sin in Christ, in order to teach, he says, that he who did not commit it, could not have it. It is entirely most true. For indeed a greater person would have committed sin, if a little child had had it, for on that account there is no one of men besides him who did not commit sin by the approach of a greater age, because there is no one of men besides him who did not commit sin by the rising of infantile age. 2. Certain people respond that this testimony produced from Isa. 53. v. 9., in which it had been said previously concerning the whole human race, v. 6. All we like sheep have gone astray, every one has turned aside into his own way, where also little children are included, who have the stain of original sin, and turn aside into a depraved way. 3. Jerome in chapter 53 of Isaiah rightly warns that concerning no man after the fall of the first-formed can that Prophetic word be said, that he did not commit sin, because as Job teaches, chapter 28, v. 4, no one is clean from filth, not even if his life has been one day upon the earth. For although infants do not yet commit προαιρετικῶς, sin, nevertheless they are not entirely free from actual sins, since the tinder of sin in them is not idle and torpid.

5. From the fact that Peter proves that Christ is also devoid of original sin because he did not commit sin, Salmero gathers in this place that Mary was conceived without original sin. If the rule of Augustine is true, he says, as I think it most true and most solid, it necessarily follows that the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, did not contract or have original sin, since every sin, even actual, indeed venial, is removed by all the Fathers, and by Thomas himself, from the time he began to use free will. But if she is defended from light and smallest sins, why not rather from original, which makes one a child of wrath, and a prey of the Demon? This argument is of great moment to me, nor do I know how it can be well dissolved by those holding the contrary opinion. Resp. 1. Scripture testifies that the Blessed Mary did not lack the blemishes and infirmities of actual sins, Matt. 12. v. 46. Mark 3. v. 20. Luke 2. v. 23. 43. 49. chap. 8. v. 20. John 2. v. 4. Therefore, it should rather be inferred in the contrary way that she too was subject to original sin. 2. It is false that all the Fathers free Mary from actual sins. Chrysostom, homily 12 on Matthew, importunity, He attributes ambition and vain glory to him, in comm. Psal. 13. he writes that the sword of doubt pierced his soul at the time of the passion. in comm. Iohan. 2. he assigns to him a desire for ambition and human glory. Similar things to which are found in Origen homil. 17. on Luke, August. in qq, v. & N. T. q. 73. Theophylact on chap. 2. Lucae. 3. this collection has a place in Christ. Christ did not commit sin. Therefore he is also free from original sin, both because Christ was conceived without male seed, from the special overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, and because in other sayings of Scripture it is clearly established ἀναμάρτητος. But in Mary this collection does not hold, because neither reason for the connection has a place in her.

6. From the fact that Christ is said to have expiated our sins on the cross, so that having died to sins, we might live to righteousness, Estius gathers that sanctification and renewal is the other part of our justification, to which the prior part, which consists in the remission of sins, is ordered as if to an end. Resp. we concede that the effect and fruit of the death of Christ is not only the remission of our sins, but also our sanctification and renewal: We also concede this, that the remission of sins is ordered to a holy conversation of life, as to an end, but from neither of these does it follow that our justification consists in sanctification and renewal. For the benefits of Christ, justification and sanctification, are distinct: justification consists in the remission of sins, not in sanctification and renewal, which is a consequence of justification. But if all the benefits of the death of Christ pertained to our justification before GOD, it would follow that even resurrection to eternal life is a part of our justification, because Christ by his death merited for us resurrection to eternal life.

Didactic observations. 1. In Christ Jesus there is no slave, nor free, but all are one in Christ, Galat. 3. v. 28. Col. 3. v. 11. Therefore the Gospel does not remove the distinction between slaves and masters in the polity, but in Christ through faith it makes them equal before GOD. The condition of slaves, if they are faithful, is not displeasing, Iob. 31. v. 15.

2. Slaves owe obedience to their masters, which also includes the tolerance of injuries. Christ, a faithful servant of GOD, became obedient to his heavenly Father even unto the death of the cross, Phil. 2. v. 8. his example is to be imitated by the faithful.

3. Servants indeed sustain a hard province under unjust masters, ὡς ἀργάλεον πρᾶγμ᾽ ἐστιν ὧ ζεῦ καὶ θεοὶ δοῦλον γενέσθαι παραφρονοῦντος δεσπότου, says Carion the servant in Aristophanes, complaining about the difficult and morose Chremylus; but because GOD has imposed this burden upon servants, it must be borne with an even mind, and one must promptly obey masters even when they command and inflict the harshest things.

4. Injuries are to be borne patiently. This tolerance is pleasing to GOD, which He will also reward with a gratuitous recompense.

5. The same is the part of the duty divinely enjoined upon us. For we have been called in this life to bear the cross patiently, in the future life to attain glory.

6. Christ in His passion proposed to us the most perfect example of patience, charity, meekness, and obedience; therefore it is incumbent upon us that we follow Him as the leader of the way, and insist upon His footsteps. Matth. 16. v. 24.Luc. 9. v. 23.Iohan. 15. v. 20.Roman. 8. v. 29. Beda in h. l. You hear that Christ suffered for us, and you rejoice that He died for you; attend to what follows, leaving us an example, that you should follow His footsteps, an example of tribulations, delights, insults, scourges, pains, reproaches, thorns, the cross, --nerum of death.

7. Of this imitation there is not only great dignity, for what is more honorable than to be conformed to Christ the head through the cross, and to carry the stigmata of Christ in one's body,Galat. 6. vers. 17. but also great utility, for those who carry around the mortification of Christ in their body, in their body also the life of Christ will be manifested,2. Corinth. 4. vers. 10. those who die with Christ in this world, they will live with Him in the future age, those who sustain with Him, will also one day reign with Him,2. Timoth. 2. vers. 11. & 12. those who are rendered conformed to the image of Christ crucified, they will one day be rendered conformed to the image of Christ glorified,Roman. 8. vers. 29. and altogether the highest necessity.
