Oecumenius in this place κτίσιν ἀνθρωπίνην τὰς ἀρχὰς λέγει τὰς χειροτονητὰς ὑπὸ τὡν βασιλέων, ἣ καὶ αὐτοὺς τοὺς βασιλεῖς, καθοτι καὶ αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐτὰχθησαν ἤτοι ἐτέθησαν, οἶὸε γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ καὶ τὴν θέσιν κτίσιν καλέῖν. Meanwhile, it is the ordinance of GOD by reason of the principal cause, of which Paul speaks.

2. Be subject to every human creature. But it is fitting that we be subject not to all men, but only to the Magistrate. Resp. 1. Some take the words of the Apostle generally, as a precept of humility, which from true and sincere humility the truly pious ought not only to subject themselves to superiors and equals, but also to inferiors, in humility to esteem others better than themselves,Phil. 2. v. 3. and by the charity of the spirit to serve one another,Gal. 5. v. 13. to which they accommodate that which is said in the Syriac paraphrase: Be subject to all the sons of men. Dionys. Carth. in this place. But from the distribution that follows, whether to the King, or to governors, it is manifest that the Apostle is speaking here specifically about the political subjection owed to the Magistrate. Cornelius à Lapide opposes this exposition, that such humility is of counsel and perfection, but not of precept. But it is very absurd to refer those Apostolic precepts Phil. 2. v. 3. & Gal. 5. v. 13. to counsels placed in the judgment of each person, and not to precepts required of all. 2. Some understand by κτίσιν the ordinance, constitution, and disposition of civil government. But we showed above that the name κτίσεως is more correctly taken concerning persons. 3. As in other sayings of Scripture, in which the Gospel is said to be preached to every creature, Marc. 16. v. 15. Col. 1. v. 23. a certain restriction is to be understood, that this is to be taken determinately concerning the human creature to whom preaching can be done: so also in this place those words, be subject to every human creature, are to be taken determinately and restrictively, namely by reason of the underlying subject matter concerning all men who are established in power. In vain, therefore, does Innocent III, Roman Pontiff, fear in chapter Solitae de maiorit. and obedience lest any servant be subjected to the Ministers of the Church, if by the word creature the political Magistrate is understood, and from that it is inferred that even the ministers of the Church ought to be subjected to him in political matters. For thus he argues against the Constantinopolitan Emperor, who from these words of the Apostle claimed for himself dominion over the Patriarch of Constantinople. It would follow that even any servant would have received authority over Priests, since it is said, to every human creature.

3. For the punishment of evildoers. But Deut. 32. v. 35. Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, which is repeated, Sirac. 28. v. 1. Rom. 12. v. 19. Hebr. 10. v. 30. Resp. 1. One must distinguish between lawful and ordered vengeance, which is granted by laws, such as if someone repels manifest force from himself and his own, if a Magistrate by reason of his office exacts punishments from evildoers, exercises public judgments, coerces the enemies of the Republic, etc., and between illicit and disordered vengeance, which is exercised against the laws by private desire, such as if someone injured by another does not flee to the aid of the laws and the Magistrate, but inflamed by anger takes penalties from his adversary. The former they call public vengeance, the latter truly private. 2. Where, however, it is to be noted that a private person sometimes also exercises public vengeance, namely when in sudden violence and oppression, where the aid of the Magistrate cannot be implored and had, he kills a robber, for in that case the law and rights hand the sword to the private person, and conversely a public person sometimes also exercises private vengeance, namely when a Magistrate beyond and against the laws oppresses the innocent, not by exercising the judgment of GOD, but by complying with his own desire. 3. That vengeance, which a Magistrate exercises according to the laws and the due order of judgment, is divine. For GOD takes vengeance from enemies sometimes immediately, but sometimes mediately.

4. For the praise of those who do good. But the Magistrate sometimes oppresses obedient subjects, so far is he from providing praise, defense, and rewards to them. Resp. 1. The Apostle speaks of the end, for the sake of which the office of Magistrate is divinely instituted, from which if even the persons established in that office stray greatly, nevertheless nothing is taken away from the divine ordinance, and the precept remains perpetual, that this they ought to do. Bede in this place, Not that all Kings, or Leaders, or evildoers know how to punish or praise the good, but they simply narrate what the action of a good judge ought to be, that is, that he may restrain those doing evil, and reward those doing well. 2. Bede adds, that that very injury, which is inflicted upon the pious by the Magistrate, yields to their reward and advantage. Although, he says, the Magistrate acts unjustly, if he condemns the good, nevertheless what he does pertains to their praise, if they patiently tolerate his wickedness, and patiently resist his folly. Do you wish, he says, not to fear the power? Do good and you will have praise from it. He does not say, by it, because even if human power does not praise, nay, even if it persecutes, if it kills with the sword as it did Paul, if it crucifies as it did Peter, you will have praise from it, while from that which it does evilly against you, who are just and innocent, the patience of your virtue merits a crown of praise. For the following words, by which it is said, teach that Peter also intended this in this sentence: For so is the will of GOD, that by doing good you may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men. This, therefore, is the praise of the good, for which he says leaders are sent by the King, while by doing good they use the ignorance of foolish leaders for their own perpetual praise.

5. That by doing good you may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men. But the pious are never so studious of innocence and obedience, that they stop the mouths of all slanderers. Resp. Meanwhile, however, the material and food for the slander of enemies is withdrawn, and it suffices that the pious have the holy purpose of stopping the mouths of slanderers, even if the outcome does not always follow, nor among all people.

6. Honor all men. But Psalm. 15. vers. 5. it is said of the pious: In his eyes a reprobate is despised, but he honors those who fear the Lord. Resp. 1. Just as in verse 13 something had to be understood according to the reason of the subject matter, so also the same must be done in this place. Honor all men, namely, those whom GOD willed to be honored, to whom honor is due by reason of power, dignity, gifts, office, etc. Rom. 13. vers. 7. honor, to whom honor. 2. We ought not to honor the impious by approving or promoting their worst counsels and deeds: meanwhile, we ought to honor what is divine in them, namely, their office, power, and gifts, and out of true humility serve them for good.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Peter commands that Christians ought to be subject to every human creature, that is, to whatever Superiors there may be. Therefore, they ought to be subject even to a Heathen and heretical Magistrate, for at the time when Peter was writing these things, there were no other than Heathen Magistrates. It is false, therefore, what Bellarmine writes in book 5 de Rom. Pont. cap. 7. It is not permitted for Christians to tolerate an infidel or heretical King who attempts to draw Catholics over to his false religion. Creswell the Jesuit in the book against the edict of the Queen of England, published under the name of Andreas Philopater, sect. 2. n. 160. establishes that subjects are obligated to drive out heretical Kings who are injurious to the Catholic faith, provided that they have suitable forces for this. n. 126. subjects are not only able to lawfully overthrow such Princes of theirs, but are also bound to this by divine precept and a most strict bond and at the extreme peril of their souls. To this seditious doctrine we oppose the confession of the adversaries themselves, that the Apostles, and especially Peter in this place, taught that obedience is owed even to a Heathen Magistrate. Cajetan in h. l. The Apostle says every, not distinguishing between Heathens and the faithful. Estius in h. l. The sense is, obey every human superior, whether he be a Jew or a Gentile; and whether he be a Christian or an infidel; finally, whether he be good or bad. And afterwards. At the time when this Epistle was written, the prince of the Roman Empire was Domitius Nero, the most grave persecutor of Christians, under whom Peter himself, who writes these things, and Paul underwent Martyrdom. It is clear, therefore, from the Apostolic doctrine, that one must be obedient even to infidel and very bad Princes. Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. Catholics for the first three hundred years obeyed Heathen Emperors, even persecutors, in all things, faith and religion excepted, nor did anyone plot death or rebellion against them under the pretext of faith, even though they could often have done so easily, if they had wished. Stapleton in promt. morali Dom. 22. post Pentec. Since by the law of nations and of Nature this was doubtful to no one, the Apostles teach that it is also the will of GOD that even the faithful themselves should obey Kings, even Heathen and infidel ones, for there were no others then. Thus Christ teaches that one must obey Caesar, Peter that one must obey Nero.

2. Be subject to every human creature i. e. to whatever Magistrate, whether he be good or bad, just as the Apostle v. 18. asserts that obedience is to be rendered by servants not only to good and equitable Masters, but also to τοῖς σκολιοῖς perverse ones. It is false, therefore, what certain heretical Pseudo-Apostles they said, as Bernard reports in sermon 66 on the Song of Songs, that all power, as much political as ecclesiastical, is lost through mortal sin, and therefore those who are guilty of mortal fault are not to be obeyed. Hence, in the Council of Constance, Session 8, this article was condemned in Wycliffe: No one is a civil Lord, no one is a Prelate, while he is in mortal sin. Session 15 of the same Council, the same article was condemned in John Hus. Alfonso de Castro, book 12 against heresies, under the word Power, attributes this error also to the Waldensians, Wycliffe, and John Hus. But he does not prove his assertion about the Waldensians with even any conjecture or testimony of the ancients. Rightly, however, he opposes to this error the Prophetic saying Jer. 27, v. 6 I, says the Lord, have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the King of Babylon my servant v. 7 and all nations shall serve him, etc. for it is certain that Nebuchadnezzar was an evil King: as also the saying of Job chap. 34, v. 30 GOD makes a hypocrite man to reign for the sins of the people.

3. Be subject to every human creature i.e., to any Superior whatsoever, whether he be a legitimate Lord or a Tyrant. The Romans had penetrated into Asia by evil arts rather than by legitimate reason, and had subjected to themselves those regions in which the Christians lived, to whom Peter writes. The Caesars, who then held power, had seized the Monarchy for themselves by Tyrannical force. Peter forbids inquiring laboriously into these things, and commanding obedience to the King, i.e., to Nero, who at that time presided over the Empire, he refers the Christians to the hand of GOD, by which he was raised to the empire. But if one must obey a Tyrant who is such by title and occupation, much more must one obey a Tyrant who is such by exercise and administration. This is to be opposed to Brutus, Rossaeus, Boucher, and others, who assert that a Tyrant can be dislodged from the throne by subjects, whom Barclay in his book against the Monarchomachs, Alberico Gentili in his book on the force against Princes always unjust, Cunerus in his book on the office of the Christian Prince, and Arnisaeus in his book on the authority of Princes over the people always inviolable, refute. One must distinguish, however: 1. Between Princes of integral majesty and absolute power, who hold absolute command over subjects, and are not bound by certain agreed-upon pacts or fundamental laws of the kingdom by express promise, and between Princes of limited power and agreed-upon pacts between them and the of the kingdom. The leaders of those who are circumscribed. And likewise between those who are mere subjects and those who are mixed. Jurisconsults and politicians dispute whether it is possible for princes, whose power is limited by those who are not mere subjects, namely by the Estates of the realm, to be resisted, and for their violence to be repelled with an armed hand, whose arguments are enumerated in Volume 7 concerning the political Magistrate, § 485.

4. Peter prescribes this rule not only to the laity, as they are called, but also to the clergy, that they should render obedience to the Magistrate, as is gathered from chapter 5, v. 1. and especially from the parallel Apostolic precept Rom. 13, v. 1. Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. Therefore the Pontiff, who exalts himself above all Kings and Princes and above the Emperors themselves, and wishes the clergy to be exempt from the power of the Magistrate, is not a true and genuine successor of Peter. Bernard, Epistle 42 to the Archbishop of Sens: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. If every soul, then yours too. Who has excepted you from the whole? If anyone attempts to except you, he attempts to deceive you.

5. The Magistrate is established by GOD for the punishment of evildoers, and leaders command not only in time of peace, but also in time of war. It is therefore false, what the Photinians deny, that a Christian Magistrate can inflict punishments upon evildoers, and wage war for the sake of public vengeance. For Paul explains this vengeance thus Rom. 13, v. 4.: He does not bear the sword in vain, for he is God's minister, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. Alphonsus à Castro, book 8 against heresies, under the word Judge, attributes this error to the Waldensians, that no judge can condemn any man to any punishment. And indeed Guido the Carmelite attaches this error to the Waldensians, but Aeneas Sylvius in his book on the origin of the Bohemians, chapter 35, reviewing the errors of the Waldensians, does not mention this. Alphonsus notes in many other places that Guido's credibility is shaky, yet nevertheless, out of partisanship and preconceived hatred, he adds: But if the Waldensians think so, it is not to be wondered at, since it is characteristic of wicked men to desire impunity for their crimes, so that they may be able to commit whatever crimes they wish more freely and securely. In this manner acted the Waldensians, who, so that they might more safely suggest their errors to men, strive to teach this above all else, that no judge can condemn another man to any punishment.

6. As free, and not as having liberty for a cloak of maliciousness. It is therefore false, what the Anabaptists teach, that Christian liberty fights with the subjection owed to the Magistrate.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. The Anabaptists, from the fact that the Magistrate is called a human creature, gather that the Magistrate is not constituted by GOD. Resp. 1. The contrary is rather gathered from the text. Peter repeats the Apostolic precept, that one must be obedient to the Magistrate, as being a divine ordinance, Rom. 13. vers. 1. and warns that in this obedience one must look not to the instrumental cause, namely to the men through whom the Magistrate is constituted, but to the principal cause, namely GOD, from whom is every Magistrate, whence he notably adds, διὰ τὸν Κύριον for the Lord's sake, who namely ordained the Magistrate, and by whom both superior and inferior Magistrates are sent. 2. The Magistrate is called a human creature, not by reason of the first origin, but by reason of the instrumental cause, because human election, birth, laws, and counsels intervene: then by reason of the subject, because men hold the Magistracy. For just as the Ecclesiastical Ministry was not commended to Angels, but to men; so also GOD willed that political rule be administered not through Angels, but through men: a similar phrase exists in this very chapter vers. 2. where by γάλα λογικὸν is understood λόγος cap. 3. vers. 8. where by σκεῦος γυναικεῖον are understood women: finally by reason of the end, because the Magistrate was instituted by GOD for the preservation of human society. 3. To these three reasons explained above can be added a fourth, by reason of the object, that the Magistrate is called a human creature, because he commands men, and is an ordered way of living among men.

2. The same Anabaptists, from the fact that Christians are commanded to be subject to every human creature, gather that a Christian cannot with a good conscience hold the Magistracy, since the Apostle wishes Christians to be subject, not to preside. Resp. 1. The Apostle in this place describes the duty of subjects, from which it cannot be gathered that the Magistracy cannot be administered by a Christian man, but the contrary is rather gathered from it because of the mutual relation. For if the duties of subjects do not fight with the Christian profession, certainly neither do the duties of fight with it. Of Magistrates. If the obedience of subjects is pleasing to GOD, then certainly the power of the Magistrate is also pleasing to GOD. 2. If it could be gathered from this passage that the office of Magistrate cannot be held by a Christian, it could also be gathered from those sayings which describe the duties of hearers that Christians cannot perform the office of teaching.

3. Cornelius à Lapide in his commentary gathers from this passage that not only laymen, but also Princes ought to be subject to Ecclesiastical Princes, i. e. to Bishops and Prelates, because Bishops are creatures of GOD, i. e. Prelates given by GOD to the whole Church, not only to the common people, but also to Princes. Response 1. Cornelius admits that Peter speaks directly about civil Princes, and commands the faithful to be subject to them, lest they think themselves exempt from their dominion through Christ. 2. We do not object to the deduction from this passage that not only laymen but also Princes ought to obey their leaders, Hebr. 13. v. 17. but this obedience in spiritual matters does not prevent the Bishops themselves from being subject to the Magistrate in political matters. For that subjection does not subvert piety, says Chrysostom in homily 23 on the Epistle to the Romans.

4. The same Cornelius à Lapide writes thus on this passage: Learn that the sign and effect of true faith is humility, subjection, and the obedience of subjects toward Magistrates: but the effect of infidelity and heresy is pride, disobedience, and rebellion, as we have seen and see being done by the Lutherans etc. and more so by the Calvinists in Scotland, England, and Germany. Indeed, Luther, the parent of them all, by his rebellion and heresy armed a hundred thousand peasants against their Princes through his disciples, and stirred up the peasants' war, which produced such great disasters for Germany. Response 1. It is a calumny that Luther is the parent of the Calvinists; he was rather their fiercest opponent. 1. Iohan. 2. v. 19. 2. It is a calumny that the Lutherans teach rebellion against the Magistrate. Sermons, writings, and practice itself testify to the contrary. 3. It is a calumny that Luther stirred up the peasants' war. Luther most gravely disapproved of that sedition of the peasants begun in the year 1525. For before the publication of the twelve demands circulated by the peasants, he published a writing by which he recalled subjects from sedition to obedience, vol. 3. Jena German, fol. 108. Sleidan. lib. 5. Comm. page 124. But after the demands were published by the peasants, the same Luther responded to those articles of the peasants without delay, vol. 3. Jena, fol. 113. Sleidan. in the same book and exhorted them lovingly that they should withdraw from arms. A little later another writing he sent forth, the sum of which is, that the Catholic Princes themselves, and especially the Ecclesiastical ones, are the cause of this sedition, because, being about to hinder the sincere doctrine of the Gospel, they press their subjects with intolerable burdens, and he exhorts those Princes to repentance. Sleidanus, same book, page 134. Afterwards he brought to light an Epistle to the Princes and the peasants at the same time, and he exhorted both to settle the controversy peacefully. Sleid., same book, page 137. Finally, another writing having been published, he instigated the Magistrates, that they should hasten as if to extinguish a common fire tom. 3. Ien. Germ. fol. 122. 123. Wider die Ra uderische und Mo rderische Bauren. Sleid. page 130. and when many criticized that booklet as too sharp, Luther defends himself tom. 3. Ien. Germ. fol. 141. where he teaches that mercy is to be shown to none, except to those who, having been warned, have made a surrender. 4. If it is the axiom of heretics that their sect and heresy must be protected and propagated by all means and arts, and especially by arms, and consequently that an orthodox Prince, if he resists, must be resisted with all forces, as Cornelius à Lapide writes in this place, the Popes will be heretics, who absolve subjects from the oath of fidelity and arm them against Magistrates; the Jesuits will be heretics, who in express words teach that Christians cannot tolerate a heretical King if he attempts to draw his subjects toward heresy.

5. Estius on these words. Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake, he comments thus. These things are to be understood concerning legitimate power, even if it perhaps took its beginning from Tyranny and evil arts. Resp. We have warned above that there are two kinds of Tyrants, some by occupation, some by administration. As regards Tyrants by administration only, in them the power is to be distinguished from the abuse of power or Tyranny. The power itself is from GOD, to which they were also raised by legitimate ways and means, but the abuse of power or the Tyranny itself is not from GOD, nor is it approved by GOD. As regards Tyrants by occupation, their power is not legitimate, nor did GOD establish it, nor does He approve it; meanwhile, however, even these Tyrants are from GOD, namely, permitting and by just judgment punishing the sins of the subjects. Jud. 3. v. 8.cap. 4. v. 2.cap. 10. v. 7.1. Reg. 15. v. 27.cap. 16. v. 2.Os. 13. v. 11. Therefore, by those who are merely subjects, not only legitimate power, but also those abusing legitimate power must be obeyed.

6. The same Estius on this place comments thus. Be subject to the King as if ὑπερέχοντι, having supreme power in the Republic. For in those things which pertain to the government of the Church, and what the end of that government is, the salvation of souls, Christ had his vicar, the Apostle Peter, and has now also his successor, the Roman Pontiff. Resp. Hidden in these are the seeds of the indirect power which the Pontiff arrogates to himself over Emperors, Kings, and Princes, concerning which Bellarmine, lib. 5. de R. P. cap. 7., discourses thus: Civil power is subject to spiritual power when both parts are of the same Christian Republic. Therefore, the spiritual Prince can command temporal Princes and dispose of temporal things in order to the spiritual good, for every superior can command his inferior. And afterwards: The spiritual Republic can command the temporal Republic subject to it, and compel it to change its administration, and depose Princes and institute others, when it cannot otherwise protect its own spiritual good. By the force and vigor of this power, which the Jesuits attribute to the Pontiff, the Pontiff has sometimes deposed from the throne Emperors less fair and convenient to him, absolved them from the oath of fidelity, and substituted others in their place at his pleasure. But such power Peter, whose successor the Pontiff desires to be called, never arrogated to himself, never exercised. Otto of Freising, lib. 6. Chronic. cap. 35.: I read and re-read the deeds of Kings and Emperors, and nowhere do I find that any of them, before this Emperor Henry, whom Hildebrand deposed, was deprived of his kingdom by the Supreme Pontiff.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. The word ὑποτάγητε admonishes us that GOD, the creator and preserver, did not leave the human race in confusion, like beasts, but instituted the order of the Magistrate, through which the Polity obtains its τάξιν. Chrysost. homil. 23. in Epist. ad Rom. cap. 13.: That there are Magistrates, that these indeed command, while those obey, that all things are not carried along simply and rashly, nor are peoples driven hither and thither like the waves of the sea, I say is the work of divine wisdom. Nazianz. orat. 3. de Theol. τὸ ἂναρχον ἂτακτον.

2. The little word κτίσεως: sends us back to the same thing; for the word κτίζειν is used not only of the primal creation, in which GOD disposed all things in a most beautiful order, but also of the construction of a building, in which all things are aptly and conveniently ordered for the uses of the inhabitants. It is signified, therefore, that GOD, as if in the fabric of the world and in a building aptly arranged, willed that individual statuses in the human race be ordered and arranged in their own place.

3. The Gospel does not abolish polities, but leaves the order divinely instituted in civil life inviolate.

4. πειθαρχία is the daughter of εὐσεβείας, the mother of εὐτυχίας. Nor can he truly and from the heart revere God, who refuses to obey the Magistrate, for he who resists the power, resists the ordinance of GOD, and brings judgment upon himself. Rom. 13. v. 2.

5. Four most grave causes are proposed by the Apostle, on account of which obedience is to be rendered to the Magistrate. First, that we may honor God, who commanded that obedience. Second, that we may avoid the punishments of violated civil justice. Third, that we may obtain from the Magistrate the praise of justice, and defense against the disturbers of human society. Fourth, that we may blunt the calumnies of evil speakers, and the name of God may not be blasphemed on our account.

6. We should obey not only the equitable and just, but also the impious and harsh Magistrate. Aug. lib. 5. de Civ. Dei c. 21. He who gave power to Marius, the same gave it to Gaius Caesar; he who to Augustus, the same also to Nero; he who to Vespasian, either the father or the son, most gentle Emperors, the same to Julian the Apostate.

7. Although indeed the harsh commands of the Magistrate are to be borne, nevertheless unjust precepts and those fighting against divine laws are not to be put into execution. Act. 5. v. 29. On account of the Lord, obedience is to be rendered to the Magistrate. Therefore, God is to be obeyed more than the Magistrate. Chrysost. hom. 71. in Matth. When you hear that the things which are Caesar's are to be rendered, do not doubt that those things alone are meant which do not hinder piety and religion, for that which stands against faith or virtue is not a tribute and tax of Caesar, but of the Devil. Hence also when Peter repeats the precept concerning the subjection to be rendered to the Magistrate, he places the fear of God before the honor of the King, for thus the King is to be honored, so that we do not sin against God.

8. It is fitting to be subject not only to one or another form of government, but to any whatsoever, whether it be Monarchical, or Aristocratic, or Democratic, for by βασιλὲα Peter insinuates μοναρχίαν, by ἡγεμόνας Aristocracy. Ignatius Epist. 7. ad Smyrnenses. It is necessary to honor the King, for there is no one more excellent than the King, nor anyone like him among all created things.

9. It is not true and perfect obedience to obey only the supreme Magistrate, but to deny obedience to inferior Magistrates; for the Apostle joins Kings and governors.

In inferior magistrates it is fitting to look upon and revere the King as a superior, and in the King to look upon and revere GOD Himself.

10. It is the duty of the magistrate to protect civil society with punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good. Plato used to say, that the Republic is held together by rewards and punishments. Cicero to Brutus praises the opinion of Solon, who, when asked, By what method might the Republic be best governed? replied, If the good are invited by rewards, and the wicked are restrained by punishments. Chemnit. part. 2. Loc. comm. pag. 26. Because God willed there to be degrees in Empires, so that there might be some Orders Superior to private individuals, who are a part of public counsel and government 1. Petr. 2. v. 13. whether to the King as supreme, or to governors as sent by him 1. Tim. 2. v. 2. for Kings and all who are set in high places. Those Superior Orders, therefore, because by their office they ought to contribute counsel and efforts to the defense of discipline and the common safety, do not satisfy their duty by tolerating unjust cruelty, but ought to disapprove and in their own place resist.

11. To the rewards owed to good and obedient citizens belongs also defense, on account of which magistrates are called the shields of the earth Psal. 47. v. 10. Archytas said, that the magistrate is like an altar, to which those affected by injury may flee.

12. The innocence of the good stops the mouths of the slanderous.

13. Men ignorant of the Gospel and destitute of the saving knowledge of GOD are held by the Holy Spirit to be foolish, for true wisdom consists in the saving knowledge of GOD. Right understanding is not found except in the knowledge of GOD.

14. Ignorance and foolishness are joined to one another by a sisterly bond.

15. Let the truly pious not indulge in sins under the pretext of spiritual liberty, nor change spiritual liberty into carnal license. Iohan. 8. v. 32. Rom. 6. v. 18. Gal. 5. v. 1. & 13. 2. Petr. 2. v. 19. Beda in h. l. They turn their liberty into a cloak of malice, who, the less they are restrained by the yoke of human servitude, the more widely they are enslaved to the dominion of sins, and when they serve vices with impunity, they call it liberty, covering their own fault with this name, etc. We are rightly called free who have been absolved from the bonds of sins through Baptism. We who have been redeemed from demonic servitude, who have been made children of GOD, have not received a greater faculty or license for sinning from such a gift of liberty; nay rather, if we sin, we are immediately made servants of sin, having lost our liberty. And whoever he thinks himself freed by the Lord for this purpose, that he may sin more licentiously; such a one changes his liberty into a cloak of malice.

16. Nay rather, spiritual liberty, obtained for us through Christ, ought to be an incitement to the pursuit of piety and good works of every kind. For we have been freed from the curse of the law, from the wrath of GOD, from the servitude of sin, from the captivity of the Devil, from the traditions of men, not so that hereafter we may do what is pleasing to our flesh, but that we may serve GOD according to His will revealed in the law. The end of liberty is that we may be more prompt for the service of GOD. Bede in h. l. As free men they do good things, who, by how much the greater liberty they use among men, by so much the more strictly, nay rather more freely, are they subjugated to divine service. Gloss. interl. h. l. By how much the greater liberty you use among men, by so much the more freely may you be subjugated to divine service.

17. The liberty of Christians is a servile liberty, because they have been freed so that they may serve GOD; and a free servitude, because they obey GOD and the Magistrate not by compulsion but willingly.

18. The truly pious reverently acknowledge the gifts of GOD in others, and therefore they anticipate one another with honor. Rom. 12. v. 10. upon which passage Lyranus comments thus: Anyone is deficient in some good which is in another, and thus he can consider him better than himself, and thus anticipate him by honoring him.

19. This honor does not consist only in gestures, but also in the affection of the heart, as Luther rightly warns in h. l.: it embraces not only external reverence, but duties of every kind. Hence Ambrose on chapter 12 of Romans, regarding what the Apostle said, anticipating one another with honor, explains it thus: anticipating one another with mutual obsequies.

20. Such mutual honor preserves friendship, benevolence, and love of neighbor. In the book Musar. 23. v. 1. a certain meek man, being asked why he was loved by all, answered: I have never seen a man whom I did not honor and consider more pious than I am.

21. There are certain degrees of love owed to one's neighbor. Ἒυνοιαν we owe to all, φιλαδελφίαν to those of the household of faith. 2. Peter 1. v. 7. minister ὲν εὐσεβείᾳ τήν φιλαδελφίαν, ἐν δὲ τῆ φιλαδελφίᾳ τήν ἀγάπην.

22. The fear of GOD does not remain only enclosed within the mind, but it also composes the whole life of man and all the members of the body for the service, piety, and honesty of God. Hence the fear of the Lord is called the beginning of wisdomPsal. 111. v. 10.Prov. 1. v. 7. that is, of true worship, because true wisdom is to rightly acknowledge and worship God.

23. The fear of God and the honor of the King or Caesar are joined together in this place by the Apostle, just as Christ also Matth. 22. v. 21. joins the tribute of God and the tribute of Caesar. For neither does the fear or worship of God hinder the honor or obedience of Caesar, nor does the obedience rendered to Caesar detract anything from divine fear.

24. Therefore, let not one hinder the authority of the other. God has reserved the souls and consciences of men for Himself; He has subjected the bodies and fortunes of men to the King. The souls of men are not commanded in the same way as their tongues; God is the King of minds.

Latin:

OMNES HONORATE. FRATERNITATEM DILIGITE. DEUM TIMETE. REGEM HONORIFICATE.

Connexio. 1. Quidam existimant, Apostolum redire ad generalem exhortationem de honesta conversatione inter gentes sectanda in v. 12. proposita, eandemque in quatuor summa q. capita distribuere, quod omnibus honorem, fratribus amorem, Deo timorem, Regi obsequii specialem honorem exhibere debeant.

2. Quidam volunt, quod exhortationem priorem specialem de obedientia Magistratui praestanda conclusurus, alias quasdam exhortationes speciales, priori cognatas, interspergere, & alia praecepta specialia ad conversationem Christianis dignam subiungere voluerit.

3. Sed res ipsa testatur, Apostolum adhuc versari in exhortatione ad obedientiam Magistratui praestandam. Concludit enim hunc versiculum repetitione exhortationis in v. 13. propositae. Regem honorate, quia honor Regi praestandus subiectionem ibidem requisitam includit. Est ergò haec brevis conclusio proximè praecedentium, ac quia honorem omnibus debitum, amorem fratribus impendendum, & timorem DEO praestandum, cum speciali obsequii honore Regi debito Apostolus coniungit, significat, nec Deum verè timeri, nec ius suum cuique reddi, nec civilem societatem conservari posse, nisi ordo politicus Magistratum & subditos invicem devinciens inviolatè servetur, & Magistratui debita obedientia praestetur.

4. Significat etiam Apostolus, honorem illum obsequii, qui Regibus debetur ac defertur, ex vero Dei timore atque hominum caritate oriri debere, ac proinde cum illis perpetuò coniunctum esse. Qui Deum Magistratus autorem verè & ex animo timet, is etiam Regi sive Magistratui honorem obsequii non denegabit, quia DEUS hunc honorem Regi deferri praecepit. Vicissim qui fratres suos amat, & totum genus humanum, quo decet, humanitatis, benevolentiae & amoris affectu amplectitur, is itidem Magistratui honorem obsequii non denegabit, quia Magistratus in salutem humani generis & fratrum i. e. Ecclesiae commodum est institutus. 1. Tim. 2. v. 1. & 2.

5. Coniungit Apostolus eiusmodi propositiones, quae in speciem videntur pugnare, sed revera inter se sunt optimè coniunctae & connexae, ita ut una sine altera subsistere nequeat. Prima quidem specie pugnare videntur, honor omnibus debitus, & honor soli Regi debitus; timor Dei & honor Regis; amor fraternitatis & honor Regis, sed si accuratâ mentis trutina iuxta normam verbi divini haec omnia expendamus, fraterna caritas, Dei timor & obedientia Magistratui praestanda indivulso nexu invicem sunt coniuncta.

Expositio. 1. Πάντας τιμήσατε. Iudaei despiciebant gentiles Rom. 14. v. 3. ac inter ipsos Iudaeos divites despiciebant pauperes, Iacob. 2. v. 3. huic malo remedium opponit Apostolus, dicens omnes honorate i. e. Dona Dei in aliis reverenter agnoscite, benè & honorificè de omnibus sentite, etiam eos, qui vel ratione donorum, vel ratione status vobis sunt inferiores, honorate, sicque concordiam mutuam conservate, quia concordiae nihil magis adversum, quàm proximi contemtus. Locus parallelus extat Rom. 12. v. 10.τῆ τιμῆ άλλήλους προηγούμενοι.Phil. 2. v. 3.In humilitate superiores vos invicem arbitremini.

2. Τήν άδελφότητα ἀγαπᾶτε.Fraternitatis nomen collectivè sumitur pro tota fratrum multitudine, sicut nobilitas pro toto Nobilium caetu usurpatur. In eadem significatione Apostolus hac voce utitur c. 5. huius Epistolae v. 9. inde Syrus rectè reddidit. Fratres vestros diligite. Intelligit autem fratres, non respectu carnalis generationis, sed respectu spiritualis regenerationis, de qua dixerat C. 1. v. 23.renati non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili &c. Repetitigitur praeceptum φιλαδελφίας,ibidem v. 22. propositum, ac Christianorum, tanquam in Christo fratrum coniunctionem officiis caritatis speciali quodam modo fovendam esse praecipit. Proinde hoc praeceptum subiungitur praecedenti, tanquam speciale generali, debemus omnes homines honorare & amare, interim speciali amore Ecclesiam & cives Ecclesiae complecti, ac dilectionem nostram fraternis officiis testatam reddere. Gal. 6. v. 10.Operemur bonum ad omnes, maximè autem ad domesticos fidei. Locus huic nostro parallelus extat Rom. 12. v. 10.τῆ φιλαδελφὶα εἰς ἀλλήλους φιλόστοργοι, quod φιλαδελφίας praeceptum ibidem cum praecepto de honore aliis tribuendo coniungitur. Beda hoc praeceptum de fratribus diligendis pertinere putat ad deprimendum fastum in animis superiorum. Fraternitatem, inquit, diligere iubet liberos, ut eos quoque, qui sibi temporali conditione subiecti sunt, fratres sibi in Christo factos esse recolant. Cornelius à Lapide hoc praeceptum Apostolicum sic exponit, quòdpii coetum & conventum fidelium ad communes preces, conciones, Synaxes diligere & frequentare debeantHebr. 10. v. 25. Sed manifestum est, φιλαδελφίαν ab Apostolo praecipi.

3. Τὸν θεὸν φοβεῖσθε Syrus reddidit, à DEO timete. Nomine timoris quidam statuunt, universum DEI cultum, imò totum pietatis studium comprehendi, videlicet & veram DEI agnitionem, & filialem fiduciam, & seriam DEI invocationem; Itemque infirmitatis nostrae agnitionem, & seriam coram DEO humiliationem, uti etiam caritatem erga proximum, & omnis generis officia ipsi debita. Sed rectiùs nomen timoris in speciali significatione accipitur de filiali timore ac reverentia, quae DEUM omnium actionum nostrarum inspectorem agnoscit, ipsumque ut supremum Dominum ac iudicem reveretur. Interserit autem Apostolus hoc praeceptum, ut subiectionis & honoris Magistratui debiti certos statuat limites, ac DEO magis obediendum esse doceat, quàm hominibus, Actor. 5. vers. 29. Proinde si Magistratus aliquid praecipiat, quod DEI voluntati adversum, ab eo timore illius, qui est Rex Regum, & Dominus dominantium,1. Tim. 6. vers. 15. revocari nos debere innuit.

4. Τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε. Vulgata reddidit. Regem honorificate. Sed in Graeco est idem verbum cum superiore in primo speciali praecepto. πάντας τιμήσατε, τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε, sicut & Syrus utrobique habet verbum [consult facsimile image] Intelligitur autem specialis honor Regi, imò omnibus Magistratibus debitus, videlicet honor obsequii, tunc enim Magistratus debito modo honorantur, quando excellentia officii, ad quam divinitùs evecti sunt, agnoscitur, & reipsâ, h. e. tùm obedientiâ erga legis à Magistratu promulgatas, tùm praestatione tributorum honor ipsis defertur.

Q. hoc loco. 1. Quare Petrus Magistratus vocet humanamκτίσιν? Resp. 1. Ratione subiecti, quia ex hominibus, adeoque ex vulgari hominum sorte divinitùs ad dignitatem & potestatem Magistratus eliguntur ac evehuntur. 2. Ratione causae instrumentalis quia plerunque per homines ad eum, quem gerunt, principatum evehuntur, praesertim si sint Magistratus inferiores. 3. Ratione termini ad quem, quia in commodum humanae societatis potestas Magistratus instituta est, & eodem fine adhuc conservatur. Luth. tom. 2. Ien. Germ. fol. 181. Ubrigkeit wird weltliche Ordnung genennet/weil solcher Stand zu menschliche/weltliche/politische Ordinantz von Gott geordnet/nicht aber in geistlichen himlischen Sachen/wie der Eehrstand.

Q. 2. An loquatur Apostolus de voluntate DEI praeceptiva, an vero de absoluta? Resp. potest quidem intelligi etiam de voluntate absoluta, quòd DEUS sic disposuerit, ut per bonorum innocentiam calumniatorum ora obturentur, ac maledicae eorum linguae elanguescant, Tit. 2. vers. 8. interim Apostolus propriè loquitur de voluntate DEI praeceptiva, DEUS inter alias bonorum operum causas etiam hoc fine serium eorum studium à fidelibus requirit, ut Magistratui obedientiam praestando, ac omnis generis bonis operibus studendo, omnem calumniandi occasionem hostibus Evangelicae veritatis praecidant.

Q. 3. Quare libertatis mentionem incipiat Apostolus? Resp. 1. Ut occurrat tacitae obiectioni. Christiani per Christum facti sunt liberi. Ergò non tenentur obedire Magistratui. Respondet Apostolus, libertatem spiritualem non debere esse velamen malitiae & licentiae carnalis. 2. Ut ostendat, pios sponte ac liberaliter, non coactè ac serviliter Principibus, & eorum legibus debere parere. 3. Ut novum exhortationis ad obedientiam argumentum inserat. Pii sunt à peccatis per Christum liberati, ut inposterum iustitiae serviant,Rom. 6. v. 22. iustitiae illius pars est non postrema obedientia Magistratui debita. Ergò ipsa libertas debet esse incitamentum ad obedientiam Magistratui praestandam.

Q. 4. Quo sensu Apostolus libertatem nolit esse velamen malitiae? Resp. Quidam statuunt, respectum haberi ad vestem candidam, quam baptizati in Baptismo accipiebant. Ea enim non solùm innocentiae & laetitiae, sed etiam libertatis per Christum partae, & baptizatis per hoc Sacramentum collatae fuit Symbolum. Quia servis, cum manumittebantur, & libertate donabantur, dabatur vestis alba. Tertull. lib. 5. contra Marc. Ipsum quod ait, quâ libertate Christus nos manumisit, nonne eum constituit manumissorem, qui fuit Dominus? alienos enim servos nec alba manumisit. Augustinus lib. 4. de Symbolo ad Catechum. cap. 9. candidae vestis in Baptismo datae, hanc reddit rationem, ut anima libertate novae vitae induta, adversus Diabolum cum adiutorio divino valeat fortiter dimicare. LXX. utuntur pro operimento tabernaculi foederis ex pellibus hyacinthinis parato,Exod. 26. v. 14.cap. 36. v. 16. Quemadmodum externa illa operimenta obtegebant tabernaculum intus pulcherrimum, in quo DEUS ipse suâ gratiâ habitabat: sic exterior piorum conversatio non debet esse operimentum malitiae interioris, sed potiùs cordis sanctificati, ac fide & aliis virtutibus exornati, quòd sit templum DEI pulcherrimum.

Q. 5. Quare Apostolus specialiter Regi honorem deferri praecipiat? Resp. 1. Quia Rex est ὑπερέχων, ideò etiam velut praecipua quaedam species, sive pars ex communi reliquorum numero eximitur, eique cumprimis honor deferri iubetur. 2. Honor Regi debitus includit obsequium, quod iam antè ei deferri Apostolus praeceperat.

Est ergò repetitio prioris exhortationis in v. 13. propositae. 3. Rex sive Imperator tùm temporis non solùm erat Ethnicus, sed etiam omnibus sceleribus coopertus, & verae Ecclesiae persecutor. Apostolus igitur hoc praeceptum de Rege obsequiis honorando repetit, ne propter religionis diversitatem, vitae improbitatem ac crudelitatem minùs honorandus alicui videri posset.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Magistratus est humanaκτίσις.Atqui non est potestas, nisi à DEO,Rom. 13. v. 1. Resp. Magistratus dicitur humanaκτὶσις ratione causae instrumentalis, quia per homines ut plurimùm constituitur. Oecumenius in h. l. κτίσιν ἀνθρωπίνην τὰς ἀρχὰς λέγει τὰς χειροτονητὰς ὑπὸ τὡν βασιλέων, ἣ καὶ αὐτοὺς τοὺς βασιλεῖς, καθοτι καὶ αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐτὰχθησαν ἤτοι ἐτέθησαν, οἶὸε γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ καὶ τὴν θέσιν κτίσιν καλέῖν. Interim est DEI ordinatio ratione causae principalis, de qua loquitur Paulus.

2. Subiecti estote omni humanae creaturae. At qui non omnibus hominibus, sed soli Magistratui subiectos nos esse convenit. Resp. 1. Quidam verba Apostoli generaliter accipiunt, tanquam praeceptum humilitatis, quod ex vera & sincerâ humilitate verè pii non solùm superioribus & aequalibus, sed etiam inferioribus sese subiicere, in humilitate superiores se invicem aestimare,Phil. 2. v. 3.& per caritatem spiritus invicem servire debeant,Gal. 5. v. 13.quò accommodant illud, quod in Syriaca paraphrasi dicitur. Subiecti estote omnibus filiis hominum. Dionys. Carth. in h. l. Sed ex subiecta distributione, sive Regi, sive praesidibus, manifestum est, Apostolum hîc specialiter de subiectione politica Magistratui debita loqui. Cornelius à Lapide huie expositioni opponit, quòd talis humilitas consilii sit & perfectionis, non autem praecepti. Sed perquam absurdum est, praecepta illa Apostolica Phil. 2. v. 3. & Gal. 5. v. 13. referre ad consilia in arbitrio cuiusque posita, non autem ad praecepta ab omnibus requisita. 2. Quidam per κτίσιν intelligunt ordinationem, constitutionem, & civilis gubernationis dispositionem. Sed ostendimus superiùs, nomen κτίσεως rectiùs de personis accipi. 3. Ut in aliis dictis Scripturae, in quibus Evangelium omni creaturae praedicandum, dicitur Marc. 16. v. 15.Col. 1. v. 23. subintelligenda quaedam restrictio, quòd de creatura humana, cui praedicatio fieri potest, determinatè hoc sit accipiendum: ita quoque hoc loco verba illa, subiecti estote omni humanae creaturae, determinatè & restrictè sunt accipienda, ratione scilicet substratae materiae de omnibus hominibus, qui sunt in potestate constituti. Frustra igitur metuit Innocentius 3. Pont. Rom. in c. Solitae de maiorit. & obed. ne cuilibet servo Ministri Ecclesiae subiiciantur, si per vocem creaturae Magistratus politicus accipiatur, & ex eo inferatur, etiam Ecclesiae ministros in politicis illi subiici debere. Sic enim disserit contra Constantinopolitanum Imperatorem, qui ex his Apostoli verbis dominium in Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum sibi vendicabat. Sequeretur, quòd etiam servus quilibet imperium in Sacerdotes accepisset, cum dicatur, omni humanae creaturae.

3. In vindictam maleficorum. AtDeut. 32. v. 35.Mea est ultio, & ego retribuam, quod repetitur,Sirac. 28. v. 1.Rom. 12. v. 19.Hebr. 10. v. 30. Resp. 1. Distinguendum inter vindictam licitam & ordinatam, quae legibus est concessa, utpote si quis vim manifestam à se suisque repellat, si Magistratus ratione officii supplicia de maleficis sumat, publica iudicia exerceat, hostes Reipubl. coerceat &c. & inter vindictam illicitam & inordinatam, quae contra leges privata cupiditate exercetur, utpote si quis ab alio laesus non confugiat ad auxilium legum & Magistratus, sed ira accensus poenas ab adversario sumat. Illam vocant vindictam publicam, hanc vero privatam. 2. Ubi tamen notandum, quòd publicam vindictam quandoque etiam privatus exerceat, quando scilicet in subita violentia & oppressione, ubi Magistratus auxilium implorari & haberi nequit, latronem interficit, eo enim in casu lex & iura gladium privato tradunt, & vicissim privatam vindictam quandoque etiam publica persona exerceat, quando scilicet Magistratus praeter & contra leges innocentes opprimit, non DEI iudicium exercendo, sed cupiditati suae obsequendo. 3. Vindicta illa, quam Magistratus iuxta leges & debito iudicii ordine exercet, est divina. DEUS enim vindictam ab hostibus sumit quandoque immediatè, quandoque vero mediatè.

4. In laudem bene operantium. At Magistratus quandoque obedientes subditos opprimit, tantum abest, ut laudem, defensionem & praemia ipsis praestet. Resp. 1. Apostolus loquitur de fine, propter quem Magistratus officium divinitus institutum, à quo si vel maximè personae in officio illo constitutae aberrent, ordinationi tamen divinae nihil decedit, ac perpetuum manet praeceptum, quod hoc facere debeant. Beda in h. l. Non quòd omnes quidem Reges, aut Duces, vel malefactores punire vel laudare bonos noverint, sed quae esse debeat actio boni iudicis simpliciter narrant, hoc est, ut malefacientes coërceat, benè agentes remuneret. 2. Addit Beda, ipsam illam iniuriam, quae à Magistratu piis infertur, in praemium & commodum ipsorum cedere. Etsi, inquit, Magistratus iniustè agit, si bonos damnat, nihilominus ad laudem eorum pertinent quae facit, si patienter eius improbitatem tolerent, & patienter eius stultitiae resistant. Vis, inquit, non timere potestatem? bonum fac & habebis laudem ex illa. Non dicit, ab illa, quia etsi potestas humana non laudat, imò si etiam persequitur, si occidit gladio ut Paulum, si crucifigit ut Petrum, habebis ex illa laudem, dum ex eo, quod illa malefacit in te iustum & innoxium tuae virtutis patientia coronam laudis meretur. Nam & hoc intendisse Petrum in hac sententia, verba sequentia docent, quibus dicitur. Quia sic est voluntas DEI, ut benefacientes obmutescere faciatis imprudentium hominum ignorantiam. Haec est ergò laus bonorum, ad quam Duces à Rege dicit missos, dum ignorantia ducum imprudentium boni ad laudem suam perpetuam bene agendo utuntur.

5. Ut benefacientes obmutescere faciatis imprudentium hominum ignorantiam. At pii nunquam adeò innocentiae & obedientiae sunt studiosi, ut omnium maledicorum ora obstruant. Resp. interim tamen materia & q. pabulum calumniae hostium subtrahitur, ac sufficit, pios sanctum habere propositum, ora calumniatorum obstruendi, etiamsi eventus non semper nec apud omnes sequatur.

6. Omnes honorate. AtPsalm. 15. vers. 5.de pio dicitur. Contemtus est in oculis eius reprobus, timentes autem Dominum glorificat. Resp. 1. Sicut in vers. 13. pro ratione subiectae materiae aliquid fuit subintelligendum, ita quoque idem hoc loco fieri debet. Omnes honorate, sc. quos DEUS honorari voluit, quibus ratione potestatis, dignitatis, donorum, officii &c. honor debetur. Rom. 13. vers. 7.honorem, cui honorem. 2. Impios non debemus honorare, pessima ipsorum consilia ac facta approbando vel promovendo: interim quod in ipsis divinum, videlicet officium, potestatem ac dona debemus honorare, ac ex vera humilitate ad bonum ipsis inservire.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Petrus iubet, omni humanae creaturae, id est, quibuscunque Superioribus Christianos debere esse subiectos. Ergò etiam Ethnico & haeretico Magistratui subiecti esse debent, quo enim tempore Petrus haec scribebat, nulli erant alii, quàm Ethnici Magistratus. Falsum igitur est, quod Bellarminus lib. 5. de Rom. Pont. cap. 7. scribit. Non licet Christianis tolerarè Regem infidelem, aut haereticum, conantem Catholicos ad suam falsam religionem pertrabere. Cresweil Iesuita in libr. contra edictum Reginae Angliae sub nomine Andreae Philopatris edito sect. 2. n. 160. statuit, obligator esse subditos ad Reges haereticos depellendos, qui fidei Catholicae iniuriosi sunt, si modò vires ad hoc habeant idoneas. n. 126. subditos huiusmodi Principes suos non tantùm legitimè posse deturbare, sed etiam ad hoc praecepto divino & vinculo arctissimo ac extremo animarum suarum periculo teneri. Seditiosae huic doctrinae opponimus confessionem ipsorum adversariorum, quod Apostoli, ac cumprimis Petrus hoc loco etiam Ehnico Magistratui obedientiam deberi docuerint. Caietanus in h. l. Dicit Apostolus omni, non distinguendo inter Ethnicos, & fideles. Estius in h. l. Sensus est, obedite cuicunque, homini superiori, sive Iudaeus ille sit, sive gentilis; & sive Christianus, sive infidelis; denique sive bonus sive malus. Et postea. Quo tempore scripta fuit haec Epistola, princeps Imperii Romani erat Domitius Nero, Christianorum gravissimus persecutor, sub quo Petrus ipse, qui haec scribit, & Paulus Martyrium subierunt. Liquet ergò ex doctrina Apostolica, Principibus etiam infidelibus & valdè malis obediendum esse. Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. Catholici per primos trecentos annos obedierunt Imperatoribus Ethnicis etiam persecutoribus, in omnibus, fide & religione excepta, nec quisquam necem aut rebellionem contra eos machinatus est fidei praetextu, etiamsi saepe id facilè facere potuissent, si voluissent. Stapletonus in promt. morali Dom. 22. post Pentec. Cùm iure gentium & Naturae nemini dubium hoc esset, docent Apostoli, etiam voluntatem DEI esse, ut Regibus etiam Ethnicis & infidelibus, neque enim alii tunc erant, ipsipii & fideles obtemperarent. Sic Christus Caesari, Petrus Neroni obediendum docent.

2. Subditi estote omni humanae creaturae i. e. cuicunque Magistratui sive bonus sive malus sit, perinde ut Apostolus v. 18.non tantum bonis & aequis Dominis, sed etiamτοῖς σκολιοῖςà servis obediendum esse asserit. Falsum est ergò, quod quidam haeretici Pseudo Apostoli dicti, referente Bernhardo serm. 66. in Cant. docuerunt, omnem potestatem tàm politicam quàm Ecclesiasticam amittiper peccatum mortale, ac proinde illis qui mortalis culpae rei sunt, non esse obtemper andum. Hinc in Concilio Constantinensi Sess. 8. in Wiclepho damnatus fuit hic articulus. Nullus est Dominus civilis, nullus Praelatus, dum est in peccato mortali. Sess. 15. eiusd. Concilii in Iohan. Husso idem articulus damnatus. Alphonsus de Castro lib. 12. adv. haereses, in verbo, Potestas, hunc errorem etiam tribuit Waldensibus, Wiclepho & Iohanni Huss. Sed assertionem suam de Waldensibus ne ulla quidem coniecturâ vel veterum testimonio probat. Rectè autem huic errori opponit dictum Propheticum Ierem 27. v. 6.Ego, inquit Dominus, dedi omnes terras istas in manu Nabuchodonosor Regis Babylonis servi meiv. 7.& servient ei omnes gentes &c. constat enim Nabuchodonosorem fuisse Regem malum: uti etiam dictum Iobicap. 34. v. 30. DEUS regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi.

3. Subditi estote omni humanae creaturae i. e. cuicunque Superiori, sive sit legitimus Dominus sive Tyrannus. Romani malis artibus potius, quàm legitimâ ratione penetraverant in Asiam, & regiones illas, in quibus habitabant Christiani, ad quos Petrus scribit, sibi subiecerant. Caesares, qui tunc rerum potiebantur, Monarchiam vi Tyrannica ad se rapuerant. Petrus operosè in haec inquirere prohibet, ac obedientiam Regii. e. Neroni, qui tunc temporis Imperio praeerat, praestari iubens, ad manum DEI Christianos remittit, per quam ad imperium sit evectus. Quòd si vero Tyranno qui titulo & occupatione talis, parendum, multò magis Tyranno, qui exercitio & administratione talis, parendum fuerit. Opponendum hoc Bruto, Rossaeo, Bucherio & aliis, qui Tyrannum è solio à subditis deturbari posse asserunt, quos Barclaius in libr. contra Monarchomachos, Albericus Gentilis in libr. de vi in Principes semper iniusta, Cunerus in lib. de off. Princ. Christ. Arnisaeus in lib. de autoritate Principum in populum semper inviolabili refellunt. Distinguendum tamen. 1. Inter Principes maiestatis integrae & potestatis absolutae, qui absolutum in subditos imperium obtinent, nec tenentur certis quibusdam pactis conventis, vel legibus regni fundamentalibus expressa promissione obstricti, & inter Principes potestatis limitatae & pactis conventis inter ipsos & regni Proceres initis circumscriptae. Itemque inter subditos meros & mixtos. Principibus, quorum potestas est limitata ab illis, qui non sunt merè subditi, ab Ordinibus sc. regni resisti, ac violentiam eorum armatâ manu repelli posse, Iurisconsulti & Politici disputant, quorum argumenta enumerantur Tom. 7. de Magistratu politico §. 485.

4. Petrus non solùm Laicis, quos ita vocant, sed etiam Clericis hanc regulam praescribit, ut Magistratui obedientiam praestent, ut colligitur ex cap. 5. v. 1. cumprimis vero ex praecepto Apostolico parallelo Rom. 13. v. 1.Omnis anima sit potestatibus sublimioribus subdita. Pontifex ergò, qui se supra omnes Reges & Principes ac supra ipsos Imperatores effert, ac Clericos à potestate Magistratus exemtos esse vult, non est verus & genuinus Petri successor. Bernhardus Epist. 42. ad Archiep. Senon. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus sit subdita. Si omnis, & vestra. Quis vos excepit ab universitate? Si quis tentat excipere, conatur decipere.

5. Magistratus à DEO constitutus est in vindictam maleficorum, ac Duces non tantùm pacis, sed etiam belli tempore imperant. Falsum igitur est, quod Photiniani negant, Christianum Magistratum supplicia maleficis irrogare, ac bellum publicae vindictae causa gerere posse. Hanc enim vindictam Paulus Rom. 13. v. 4. sic explicat. Non sine causa gladium gerit, Dei enim minister est, vindex in iram ei, qui malum agit. Alphonsus à Castro lib. 8. adv. haereses, verbo Iudex, Waldensibus hunc errorem tribuit, quòd nullus Iudex possit damnare aliquem hominem ad poenam aliquam. Et sanè Guido Carmelitanus hunc errorem Waldensibus affricat, sed Aeneas Sylvius in lib. de origine Bohemorum cap. 35. errores Waldensium recensens, huius non meminit. Alphonsus in aliis quam plurimis Guidonis fidem sublestam animadvertit, nihilo tamen minus ex partium studio & praeconcepto odio subiicit. Quòd si ita sentiunt Waldenses, non est mirandum, quoniam hoc est sceleratis hominibus proprium, ut impunitatem suis sceleribus optent, quò liberiùs & securiùs, quae voluerint, scelera perpetrare valeant. Ad hunc modum fecêre Waldenses, qui, ut tutiùs suos errores possent hominibus suggerere, hoc ante omnia docere nituntur, nullum iudicem posse alium hominem ad aliquam poenam damnare.

6. Quasi liberi & non quasi velamen habentes malitiae libertatem. Falsum igitur est, quod Anabaptistae docent, libertatem Christianam pugnare cum subiectione Magistratui debita.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Anabaptistae ex eo, quod Magistratus dicitur humana creatura, colligunt, Magistratum non esse à DEO constitutum. Resp. 1. Contrarium potiùs ex textu colligitur. Repetit Petrus praeceptum Apostolicum, quòd obediendum sit Magistratui, utpote divinae ordinationi, Rom. 13. vers. 1. ac monet, non ad causam instrumentalem, ad homines scilicet, per quos Magistratus constituitur, sed ad causam principalem DEUM scilicet, à quo est omnis Magistratus, in hac obedientia esse respiciendum, unde notanter addit, διὰ τὸν Κύριον propter Dominum, qui scilicet Magistratum ordinavit, & à quo tùm Superiores, tùm inferiores Magistratus mittuntur. 2. Dicitur Magistratus humana creatura, non ratione primae originis, sed ratione causae instrumentalis, quia intervenit humana electio, nativitas, leges, consilia: ratione deinde subiecti, quia homines Magistratum gerunt. Quemadmodum enim Ministerium Ecclesiasticum non Angelis, sed hominibus commendatum est; ita quoque regimen politicum non per Angelos, sed per homines DEUS administrari voluit: similis phrasis extat in hoc ipso capite vers. 2. ubi per γάλα λογικὸν intelligitur λόγοςcap. 3. vers. 8. ubi per σκεῦος γυναικεῖον intelliguntur mulieves: ratione denique sinis, quia ad humanae societatis conservationem Magistratus à DEO institutus. 3. Hisce tribus rationibus superiùs expositis addi potest quarta, ratione obiecti, quòd Magistratus dicatur humana creatura, quia hominibus imperat, & est ordinata vivendi ratio inter homines.

2. Idem Anabaptistae ex eo, quod Christiani iubentur esse subditi omni humanae creaturae, colligunt, Christianum non posse bonâ conscientiâ Magistratum gerere, cum Aposlolus Christianos velit subesse, non praeesse. Resp. 1. Apostolus hoc loco describit officium subditorum, ex quo non potest colligi, quòd Magistratus non possit ab homine Christiano administrari, sed contrarium potiùs ex eo colligitur propter mutuam relationem. Si enim non pugnant cum professione Christiana officia subditorum, utique etiam non pugnant cum ea officia Magistratuum. Si DEO placet obedientia subditorum, utique etiam potestas Magistratûs DEO placet. 2. Si ex hoc loco colligi posset, Magistratûs officium non posse à Christiano geri, etiam ex illis dictis, quae officia auditorum describunt, posset colligi, Christianos non posse docendi officio fungi.

3. Cornelius à Lapide in comm. ex hoc loco colligit, non solùm Laicos, sed etiam Principes debere subiici Principibus Ecclesiasticis, i. e. Episcopis & Praelatis, quia Episcopi sint creaturae DEI, i. e. Praelati à DEO dati toti Ecclesiae, non solùm plebeiis, sed & Principibus. Resp. 1. Fatetur Cornelius, Petrum directè loqui de Principibus civilibus, iisque iubere subiici fideles, ne per Christum se ab eorum dominio exemtos putent. 2. Non refragamur, quò minùs ex hoc loco deducatur, non solùm Laicos, sed etiam Principes obedire debere praepositis suis, Hebr. 13. v. 17. sed haec obedientia in spiritualibus non impedit, quò minùs ipsimet Episcopi in politicis Magistratui sint subiecti. Subiectio enim ista non subvertit pietatem, inquit Chrysostomus homil. 23. in Epist. Rom.

4. Idem Cornelius â Lapide in h. l. sic scribit. Disce, signum & effectum verae fidei esse humilitatem, subiectionem, obedientiam subditorum erga Magistratus: infidelitatis vero & haeresis effectum esse superbiam, inobedientiam, rebellionem, uti vidimus & videmus factitari à Lutheranis &c. & magis à Calvinistis in Scotia, Anglia, Germania. Sanè Lutherus eorum omnium parens suâ rebellione & haeresi per suos discipulos centum millia rusticorum armavit contra Principes, bellumque rusticanum excitavit, quod tantas Germaniae clades edidit. Resp. 1. Calumnia est, quòd Lutherus sit Calvinistarum parens, fuit potiùs eorum acerrimus oppugnator. 1. Iohan. 2. v. 19. 2. Calumnia est, quòd Lutherani doceant rebellionem contra Magistratum. Contrarium testantur conciones, scripta, praxis ipsa. 3. Calumnia est, quòd Lutherus bellum rusti eorum excitaverit. Lutherus seditionem illam rusticorum Anno 1525. caeptam gravissimè improbavit. Nam ante publicationem postulatorum duodecim à rusticis divulgatorum scriptum edidit, quo subditos à seditione ad obedientiam revocavit, tom. 3. Ien. Germ. fol. 108. Sleidan. lib. 5. Comm. pag. 124. Post edita vero à rusticis postulata, idem Lutherus ad illos rusticorum articulos sine mora respondit, tom. 3. Ien. fol. 113. Sleidan. lib eod. & hortatus est amanter, ut ab armis recederent. paulo pòst aliud scriptum emisit, cuius summa est, ipsos Principes Catholicos, & praesertim Ecclesiasticos esse causam huius seditionis, quia Evangelii sinceram doctrinam impedituri, subditos oneribus intolerabilibus premant, eosque Principes ad poenitentiam hortatur. Sleidanus l. d. pag. 134. Postea emisit in lucem Epistolam ad Principes & rusticos simul, & utrosque hortatus est ad controversiam placidè dirimendam. Sleid. l. d. pag. 137. Denique alio evulgato scripto instigavit Magistratus, ut velut ad commune incendium restinguendum accurrerent tom. 3. Ien. Germ. fol. 122. 123. Wider die Ra uderische und Mo rderische Bauren. Sleid. pag. 130. cumque, illum libellum multi ut nimis acrem reprehenderent, Lutherus se defendit tom. 3. Ien. Germ. fol. 141. ubi nullis exhibendam esse docet misericordiam, nisi iis, qui admoniti deditionem fecerint. 4. Si haereticorum axioma est, suam sectam & haeresin omnibus modis & artibus, ac praesertim armis tutandam ac propagandam esse, ac consequenter Principi orthodoxo si obsistat, omnibus viribus obsistendum esse, ut hoc loco Cornelius à Lapide scribit, haeretici erunt Papae, qui subditos à iuramento fidelitatis absolvunt, & contra Magistratus armant, haeretici erunt Iesuitae, qui disertis verbis docent, Christianos non posse tolerare Regem haereticum, si ad haeresin subditos pertrahere conetur.

5. Estius in haec verba. Subditi estote omni humanae creaturae propter Dominum, sic commentatur. Haec intelligenda sunt de legitima potestate, quamvis ea fortè à Tyrannide & malis artibus initium duxerit. Resp. monuimus superiùs, duo esse Tyrannorum genera, quosdam occupatione, quosdam administratione. Quod attinet Tyrannos administratione tantùm tales, in illis potestas à potestatis abusu seu Tyrannide distinguenda est. Potestas ipsa est à DEO, ad quam etiam legitimis modis ac mediis sunt evecti, sed abusus potestatis sive Tyrannis ipsa non est à DEO, nec DEO probatur. Quod attinet Tyrannos occupatione, illorum potestas non est legitima, nec DEUS eam constituit, nec probat, interim tamen etiam hi Tyranni sunt à DEO, sc. permittente & iusto iudicio peccata subditorum puniente. Iud. 3. v. 8.cap. 4. v. 2.cap. 10. v. 7.1. Reg. 15. v. 27.cap. 16. v. 2.Os. 13. v. 11. Ab illis ergò, qui sunt merè subditi, non solùm legitimae potestati, sed etiam abutentibus legitimâ potestate parendum.

6. Idem Estius in h. l. sic commentatur. Subditi estote Regi tanquamὑπερέχοντι,in Republ. supremam potestatem habenti. Nam in his, quae ad Ecclesiae regimen, & qui illius regiminis finis, salutem animarum spectant, Christus suum habebat vicarium Petrum Apostolum, & habet nunc quoque eius successorem Romanum Pontificem Resp. latent in his semina indirectae potestatis, quam Pontifex in Imperatores, Reges & Principes sibi arrogat, de qua Bellarminus lib. 5. de R. P. cap. 7. sic disserit. Potestas civilis subiecta est potestati spirituali, quando utraque pars est eiusdem Reipubl. Christianae. Ergò potest Princeps spiritualis imperare Principibus temporalibus, & disponere de rebus temporalibus in ordine ad bonum spirituale, omnis enim superior imperare potest suo inferiori. Etpostea. Potest spiritualis Respubl. imperare temporali Reipubl. sibi subiectae, & cogere ad mutandam administrationem, & deponere Principes atque alios instituere, quando aliter non potest bonum suum spirituale tueri. Vi & vigore huius potestatis, quam Iesuitae Pontifici tribuunt, Pontifex aliquoties Imperatores sibi minùs aequos & commodos è solio deposuit, à iuramento fidelitatis eos absolvit, & in ipsorum locum pro lubitu alios substituit. Talem vero potestatem Petrus, cuius successor audire cupit Pontifex, nunquam sibi arrogavit, nunquam exercuit. Otto Frisingensis lib. 6. Chronic. cap. 35. Lego & relego Regum & Imperatorum res gestas, & nusquam invenio, quenquam eorum ante hunc Henricum Imperatorem, quem Hildebrandus deposuit, à summo Pontifice regno privatum.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. Verbum ὑποτάγητε nos admonet, DEUM creatorem & conservatorem genus humanum non reliquisse consusum, instar bestiarum, sed ordinem Magistratus instituisse, per, quem Politia sortitur suam τάξιν. Chrysost. homil. 23. in Epist. ad Rom. cap. 13. Quòd Magistratus sunt, quòd hi quidem imperant, isti verò parent, quòd non simpliciter ac temerè cuncta feruntur, nec populi fluctuum instar huc atque illuc circumaguntur, divinae sapientiae opus esse dico. Nazianz. orat. 3. de Theol. τὸ ἂναρχον ἂτακτον.

2. Eòdem nos remittit vocula κτίσεως: verbum enim κτίζειν usurpatur non solùm de primaeva creatione, in qua DEUS omnia, pulcherrimo ordine disposuit, sed etiam de aedificii extructione, in qua omnia aptè, & ad usus inhabitantium commodè ordinantur. Significatur igitur, quòd DEUS velut in mundi fabrica & in aedificio aptè disposito, singulos status in genere humano suo loco ordinatos ac dispositos esse voluerit.

3. Evangelium non tollit politias, sed ordinem in civili vita Divinitus institutum inviolatum relinquit.

4. πειθαρχία est εὐσεβείας filia, εὐτυχίας mater. Nec potest Deum verè & ex animo revereri, qui Magistratui recusat obedire, qui enim resistit potestati, DEI ordinationi resistit, ac sibi ipsi iudicium accersit. Rom. 13. v. 2.

5. Quatuor gravissimae causae ab Apostolo proponuntur, propter quas Magistratui obedientia praestanda. Prima, ut honoremus Deum, qui obedientiam illam praecepit. Secunda, ut evitemus poenas violatae iustitiae civilis. Tertia, ut à Magistratu consequamur laudem iustitiae, ac defensionem contra turbatores societatis humanae. Quarta, ut maledicorum calumnias retundamus, nec nomen Dei propter nos blasphemetur.

6. Non solùm aequo & iusto, sed etiam impio & duro Magistratui pareamus. Aug. lib. 5. de Civ. Dei c. 21. Qui Mario imperium dedit, ipse Caio Caesari; qui Augusto, ipse & Neroni; qui Vespasiano vel patri vel filio suavissimis Imperatoribus, ipse Apostatae Iuliano.

7. Quamvis vero dura Magistratus imperia sint ferenda, iniusta tamen & contra leges divinas pugnantia praecepta non sunt executioni danda. Act. 5. v. 29.Propter Dominum obediendum est Magistratui. Ergò Domino magis obediendum quàm Magistratui. Chrysost. hom. 71. in Matth. Tu cum audis reddenda Caesari, quae sua sunt, illa solùm dici non dubita, quae pietati ac religioni nihil officiunt, nam quod fidei aut virtuti obest, non Caesaris, sed Diaboli tributum est ac vectigal. Inde etiam quando Petrus praeceptum de subiectione Magistr atui praestanda repetit, timorem Dei honori Regis praeponit, sic enim honorandus Rex, ne contra Deum peccemus.

8. Non uni aut alteri tantùm formae regiminis subiectos esse convenit, sed cuivis, sive illa sit Monarchica, sive Aristocratica, sive Democratica, per βασιλὲα enim Petrus μοναρχίαν, per ἡγεμόνας Aristocratiam insinuat. Ignatius Epist. 7. ad Smyrnenses. Honorare oportet Regem, neque enim Rege quisquam praestantior, aut quisquam ei similis in rebus omnibus creatis.

9. Non est vera & perfecta obedientia, supremo tantùm Magistratui parere, inferioribus autem Magistratibus obedientiam denegare; coniungit enim Apostolus Reges & praesides.

In Magistratibus inferioribus Regem tanquam superiorem, in Rege DEUM ipsum intueriac revereri convenit.

10. Magistratûs officium est, improborum poenis & proborum praemiis civilem societatem tueri. Plato dicebat, praemiis & poenis Rempubl. contineri. Cicero ad Brutum laudat sententiam Solonis, qui rogatus. Quâ ratione optimè gubernaretur Respubl.? respondit. Si boni praemiis invitentur, mali poenis coërceantur. Chemnit. part. 2. Loc. comm. pag. 26. Quia Deus voluit esse gradus in Imperiis, ut sint aliqui Superiores Ordines privatis, qui sint pars consilii publici & gubernationis1. Petr. 2. v. 13.sive Regi tanquam praecellenti, sive Ducibus tanquam ab eo missis1. Tim. 2. v. 2.pro Regibus & omnibus qui in sublimitate constituti sunt. Illi igitur Superiores Ordines, quia ex officio debent consilia & operas conferre ad defensionem disciplinae, & communem salutem, non satisfaciunt suo officio tolerando iniustam saevitiam, sed debent improbare & suo loco resistere.

11. Ad praemia bonis & obedientibus civibus debita pertinet etiam defensio, propter quam Magistratus vocantur scuta terraePsal. 47. v. 10. Architas dixit, Magistratum esse instar arae, ad quam iniuriâ affecti confugiant.

12. Innocentia bonorum obstruit ora maledicorum.

13. Homines ignari Evangelii & salvificâ DEI cognitione destituti, à Spiritu sancto habentur stulti, vera enim sapientia in salutari DEI cognitione consistit. Recta intelligentia non est nisi in DEI notitia.

14. Ignorantia & stultitia sororio vinculo sibi invicem coniunguntur.

15. Verè pii praetextu libertatis spiritualis non indulgeant peccatis, nec libertatem spiritualem mutent in licentiam carnalem. Iohan. 8. v. 32.Rom. 6. v. 18.Gal. 5. v. 1. & 13.2. Petr. 2. v. 19. Beda in h. l. Libertatem suam in velamen malitiae vertunt, qui quò minùs humani famulatus iugo cohibentur, eo latiùs peccatorum dominio mancipantur, & cum vitiis impunè serviunt, libertatem vocant, nomine hoc suam tegentes culpam &c. Liberi rectè vocamur qui per Baptisma à peccatorum sumus nexibus absoluti. Qui à Daemoniaca servitute redemti, qui filii DEI effecti non tanto dono libertatis potiorem peccandi facultatem vel licentiam accepimus, quinimo si peccamus, mox libertate perditâ servi efficimur peccati. Et quisquis se ad hoc liberatum à Domino putat, utlicentiùs peccet, talis suam libertatem in velamen malitiae mutat.

16. Quinimò libertas spiritualis, per Christum nobis parta, debet esse incitamentum ad pietatis studium & omnis generis bona opera. Liberati enim sumus à maledicto legis, ab ira DEI, à servitute peccati, à captivitate Diaboli, à traditionibus hominum, non ut inposterum faciamus, quae carni nostrae allubescunt, sed ut DEO iuxta eius voluntatem in lege patefactam serviamus. Finis libertatis est, ut ad DEI servitium promtiores simus. Beda in h. l. Quasi liberi bona faciunt, qui quò maiore apud homines libertate utuntur, eò arctiùs imò liberius divino famulatui subiugantur. Gloss. interl. h. l. Quò maiore libertate utimini apud homines, eò liberius divino famulatui sitis subiugati.

17. Christianorum libertas est serva libertas, quia liberati sunt, ut DEO serviant; & libera servitus, quia non coactè sed sponte DEO & Magistratui obediunt.

18. Verè pii dona DEI in aliis reverenter agnoscunt, proinde sese invicem honore praeveniunt.Rom. 12. v. 10. in quem locum Lyranus sic commentatur. Quilibet deficit in alique bono, quod est in altero, & sic potest eum considerare ut meliorem se, & sic honorando praevenire.

19. Hic honor non consistit tantùm in gestibus, sed etiam in cordis affectu, ut Lutherus h. l. rectè monet: nec externam duntaxat reverentiam, sed omnis generis officia complectitur. Inde Ambrosius in cap. 12. Rom. quod Apostolus dixit, honore invicem praevenientes, sic exponit, mutuis obsequiis invicem praevenientes.

20. Eiusmodi honor mutuus amicitiam, benevolentiam & amorem proximi conservat. In libro Musar. 23. v. 1. mansuetus quidam interrogatus, cur ab omnibus amaretur, respondit. Nunquam vidi hominem, quem non honor avi & magis pium duxi, quàm ego sum.

21. Amoris proximo debiti sunt certi gradus. Ἒυνοιαν debemus omnibus, φιλαδελφίαν fidei domesticis. 2. Petri 1. v. 7. ministrate ὲν εὐσεβείᾳ τήν φιλαδελφίαν, ἐν δὲ τῆ φιλαδελφίᾳ τήν ἀγάπην.

22. Timor DEI non solùm intus in animo conclusus manet, sed etiam totam hominis vitam & omnia corporis membra ad Dei servitium, pietatem & honestatem componit. Inde timor Domini dicitur initium sapientiaePsal. 111. v. 10.Prov. 1. v. 7. h. e. veri cultus, quia vera sapientia est Deum rectè agnoscere & colere.

23. Timor Dei & honor Regis sive Caesaris hoc loco ab Apostolo coniunguntur, sicut etiam Christus Matth. 22. v. 21. tributum Dei & tributum Caesaris coniungit. Neque enim timor sive cultus Dei impedit honorem sive obsequium Caesaris, neque Caesari praestitum obsequium derogat quicquam timori divino.

24. Unus ergò non impediat imperium alterius. Deus animas & conscientias hominum sibi reservavit, corpora & fortunas hominum Regi subiecit. Animis hominum non ita imperatur, ut linguis; mentium Rex Deus est.

## 2:18
SERVANTS, BE SUBJECT IN ALL FEAR TO YOUR MASTERS, NOT ONLY TO THE GOOD AND MODEST, BUT ALSO TO THE FROWARD.

Connection. 1. To the special precept concerning the obedience to be rendered by subjects to the Magistrate, the Apostle adds another special precept concerning the obedience to be rendered by servants to their masters, and thus he passes from politics to economics.

2. If the political subjection of subjects toward the Magistrate is considered as a genus; the subjection of servants toward masters, and of wives toward husbands, as species of that, the Apostle can be said to descend from the genus to the species, from the thesis to the hypothesis. For from many families, in which husband and wife, parents and children, masters and servants exist, the Republic is constituted as a certain whole from its parts.

3. Bede gives this reason for the connection, that the Apostle has hitherto instructed the free, but now he instructs the servants. Although indeed subjects, as being subject to the Magistrate, are not simply free, yet with respect to servants subject to their masters, they can be considered free.

4. The occasion of the Apostolic exhortation is this. Many at the beginnings of the faith, says Jerome in chapter 6 of Ephesians, thought that gentile masters were to be despised by Christian servants, and under the pretext of Christian liberty they withdrew the services owed to their masters, or at least showed themselves less obedient. Therefore, lest the Christian religion be ill-spoken of among the heathens on that account, the Apostles exhort more often servants to perform the duties owed to their masters. Eph. 6. v. 5.Col. 3. v. 22.1. Tim. 6. v. 1.Tit. 2. v. 9. & in this place Peter.

5. Moreover, such services were harsh at that time, because masters had the right of life and death over their servants: this exhortation was therefore necessary, lest on account of the profession of the Christian religion, and the spiritual liberty obtained by Christ, they might rashly attempt to shake off that servile yoke, and thus give occasion for the divine name and doctrine to be blasphemed, 1. Tim. 6. v. 1.

Exposition. οἱ οἰκέται properly are domestics. But that the Apostle calls those to whom he writes οἰκέτας not δούλους, and those to whom he commands them to be subject δεσπότας, not κυρίους, some establish the cause of this thing to be that, because he writes especially to the Jews, to whom, because they were the people of GOD, to whom liberty was promised, it was troublesome to be called Servants, and to have Masters, and therefore the Apostle wished to diminish an odious and harsh matter by the gentleness of his words. But it is not likely that the Apostle wished to indulge that vain persuasion of the Jews concerning liberty, promised simply and absolutely to their people, whence also the Syrian rendered it by [consult facsimile image] which signifies servants of such a kind who are bound to harsher and viler services, to whom are opposed משרתים who are occupied in more liberal and honorable ministries. What of the fact that some establish that δούλους can be ἀπελευθέρους freedmen or those gifted with liberty, οἰκέτας but are slaves, as if affixed to the house or family of their masters, and therefore having their name from the house. Athenaeus lib. 6. from Chrysippus περὶ ὁμονοίας lib. 2. τοὺς ἀπελευθέρους indeed δούλους to be still, οἰκέτας but τούς μὴ τῆς κτήσεως ὰφειμὲνους, for, ὁ οἰκέτης δοῦλος ἐστι κτίσει κατατεταγμὲνος. Chrysippus therefore wishes δούλους to be servants or slaves, who are sometimes given the rod, or even sold, οἰκέτας but perpetual servants, who are never manumitted by him in whose ministry they are. The LXX οἰκέτης use for עבד Gen. 9. v. 25.cap. 27. v. 37.Cap. 44. v. 33. More correctly, therefore, it is said that the name οἰκέτων is placed generally in this place, so that freedmen along with slaves, servants of a harsher and more tolerable condition, may be understood here, all of whom Peter exhorts to subjection.

Ὑποτασσόμνυοι be subject, that is, be ye or let them be. It is the same word which Peter had used a little before v. 13. concerning the obedience of subjects toward the Magistrate. The Syrian rendered it thus: And those servants, who are among you, it is to be understood I now address. Be subject to your masters, Ἐν πάντι φόβῳ. By φόβον is not understood servile fear, which, as it ought to be absent from all Christians, so also from faithful servants, but fear joined with love, which we can call reverence, by which faithful servants solicitously take care, lest by acting beyond their duty they provoke their masters to anger. In that signification the noun φόβου. is used Acts 9. v. 31.2. Cor. 5. v. 11.Phil. 2. vers. 12. etc., and in the Pauline passage parallel to this one of ours Ephes. 6. v. 5. Servants, obey your carnal masters μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου.
