Coloss. 3. v. 22. the object of this fear is established as GOD Himself, who granted that power over servants to masters, and subjected servants to their dominion. Servants, obey in all things your carnal masters, fearing GOD. For these are subordinated in the duty of servants, that they ought to fear both GOD in their masters, and their masters on account of GOD. That he commands them to be subject in all fear, Lyranus explains that thus: that they ought to be subject with total or perfect fear, since total and perfect are the same. There is, however, he says, perfect fear, when one not only avoids the offense of GOD, but also of man on account of GOD, which exposition could be confirmed by a comparison of the parallel passage, Col. 3. v. 22. with this one of ours. It is answered more simply that the little word all is not taken here for discrete quantity, but continuous. Be subject with all fear, i.e., with much reverence and modesty, 2. Cor. 1. v. 3.Eph. 1. v. 3.James 1. v. 2.Jude v. 3. The Syrian omitted this προσδιορισμὸν, rendering it simply, in fear, οὐ μόνον τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς καὶ ἐπιεικέσιν, ἀλλὰ καί τοῖς σκολιοῖς. The Apostle amplifies the exhortation through a distribution between human masters and difficult ones, by which he meets the perverse opinion of certain servants, who thought they owed obedience only to human and accommodating masters, but not to morose and difficult ones. By τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς are not understood those who are good and holy before GOD, because even among Gentile masters there were some ἀγαθοί, who nevertheless were not participants in regeneration and renewal, but according to the common custom of speaking he calls good masters those who did not afflict servants unjustly, who did not press them with a lack of food and clothing, who did not rage against them even when undeserving with lashes and whips, but they showed themselves fair and modest. Hence ἐξηγητικῶς they are also called ἐπιεικεῖς, who do not cut everything to the quick, who do not show themselves too rigid, who do not demand what is commanded so exactly, but sometimes forgive certain things to their servants. The Syrian has the name [consult facsimile image] which signifies gentle and modest. Opposed to them are σκόλιοι, which the Vulgate rendered dyscoli. expressing the Greek word with another Greek word, which provided the unskilled an occasion for error. Bede in this place says: Dyscoli means undisciplined, with the name derived from Greek speech, because in Greek a school is called the place in which adolescents are accustomed to devote themselves to liberal studies and to be free to listen to masters, whence school is interpreted as leisure. Scholastics are those learned in Greek, dyscoli are unlearned and rustic. Hugh of Saint-Cher: dyscoli are unlearned, uneducated, because they have not been versed in schools. But it is derived neither from σκολιὸς nor δύσκολος ἀπὸ τῆς σχλῆς. Some out of ignorance understood dyscoli as dissolute or irregular, from which they wished to infer that the Pope and Bishops must be obeyed, even if they exercise grave Tyranny. Cornelius à Lapide says these things are falsely asserted, for the Pope and Bishops administer Ecclesiastical discipline, they do not exercise Tyranny. But experience itself testifies that the rule of the Pontiff over the Church is Tyrannical, since he casts snares upon the consciences of men, snatches away the reading of Scripture and the use of the Eucharistic chalice from the Laity, dislodges Kings from their throne, and burdens the Church with a multitude of Ceremonies. σκολιὸς properly signifies oblique, curved, Luke 3. v. 5. metaphorically him who is of depraved morals, of a corrupt and depraved mind, Acts 2. v. 40. Phil. 2. v. 15. ῤεῖα δε τ᾿ ἰθύνει σκολιὸν, says Hesiod in book 1. ἒργων, where its genuine meaning is gathered from the opposite word ἰθύνειν. The LXX use it for סורר, which signifies perverse and intractable, who is carried by his own will Ps. 77. v. 10. for עקש, which signifies depraved, crafty and tortuous, Deut. 32. v. 5. Prov. 2. vers. 15. which meanings agree with this place. Bede mentions, a certain ancient translation in Fulgentius reads 'more difficult' for dyscoli, which agrees more with the Greek name which the Apostle uses, than 'undisciplined', which pleases Bede. The Syrian has two words [consult facsimile image] The first [consult facsimile image] signifies austere, rigid, harsh, cruel, and pitiless,Genes. 49. v. 7.Exod. 32. v. 9. Posserius is formed from the root עשק he oppressed, he used force, he treated with any injury, which meanings all agree with this passage. Drusius in his praeterita, The Syrian has depraved, if only [consult facsimile image] signifies depraved, and not contentious, or certainly those oppressing through calumny. The Greek δύσκολος, which the Latin version uses, Athenaeus derives lib. 6. from κόλον, which τροφὴν he says signifies food; δύσκολος therefore it signifies him who is difficult in social life, who is of unpleasing manners, to whom everything, both words and deeds, moves the stomach. But the Greek σκολιοῖς, which the Apostle uses is more suitable. The Apostle therefore commands that servants ought to show obedience to their masters, whatever they may be, whether they are humane and agreeable, or cruel and intractable, hard and morose, who treat servants unjustly, impose upon them burdens heavier than is just, who show no humanity and benevolence to servants, who are rigid exactors of labor, sparing distributors of daily food, who do not sympathize with the infirmities of servants, but exercise a hard rule over them.

Latin:

SERVI, SUBDITI ESTOTE IN OMNI TIMORE DOMINIS, NON TANTUM BONIS & MODESTIS, SED ETIAM DISCOLIS.

Connexio. 1. Praecepto speciali de obedientia Magistratui à subditis praestanda, subiicit Apostolus aliud speciale praeceptum de obedientia heris à servis praestanda, sicque à politia transit ad oeconomiam.

2. Si politica subiectio subditorum erga Magistratum consideretur tanquam genus; subiectio servorum erga Dominos, & uxorum erga maritos, tanquam illius species, potest Apostolus dici à genere ad species, à thesi ad hypothesin descendere. Ex pluribus enim familiis, in quibus maritus & uxor, parentes & liberi, domini & servi, Respublica velut totum quoddam ex partibus constituitur.

3. Beda huiusmodi reddit connexionis rationem, quod Apostolus hactenus instruxerit liberos, iam vero instruat servos. Quamvis verò subditi, utpote Magistratui subiecti, non sint simpliciter liberi, tamen respectu servorum Dominis suis subiectorum, liberi censeri possunt.

4. Occasio exhortationis Apostolicae ea est. Multi inter initia fidei, inquit Hieronymus in cap. 6. Eph. putabant, gentiles dominos contemnendos à servis Christianis, ac sub praetextu Christianae libertatis debita dominis suis servitia subtrahebant, aut certe minùs obsequentes sese praestabant. Ne igitur propterea religio Christiana apud Ethnicos malè audiret, inde Apostoli saepius exhortantur servos ad debita heris suis obsequia praestanda. Eph. 6. v. 5.Col. 3. v. 22.1. Tim. 6. v. 1.Tit. 2. v. 9. & hoc loco Petrus.

5. Dura insuper tunc temporis erant eiusmodi servitia, quia domini ius vitae & necis in servos habebant: necessaria igitur erat haec exhortatio, ne ob religionis Christianae professionem, & spiritualem libertatem à Christo partam, iugum illud servile temerè excutere tentarent, sicque nominis divini & doctrinae blasphemandae occasionem darent, 1. Tim. 6. v. 1.

Expositio. οἱ οἰκέται propriè sunt domestici. Quòd autem Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit, vocat οἰκέτας non δούλους, ac illos, quibus eos subiici praecipit δεσπότας, non κυρίους, eius rei causam quidam statuunt eam, quòd ad Iudaeos potissimùm scribat, quibus propterea, quòd essent populus DEI, cui libertas promissa, molestum erat vocari Servos, & habere Dominos, ideoque rem odiosam ac duram lenitate verborum Apostolum minuere voluisse. Sed non est verisimile, Apostolum vanae illi Iudaeorum persuasioni de libertate, simpliciter & absolutè populo suo promissâ, indulgere voluisse, unde etiam Syrus reddidit per [consult facsimile image] quod servos eiusmodi significat, qui durioribus & vilioribus servitiis sunt obstricti, quibus opponuntur משרתים qui liberalioribus & honestioribus ministeriis occupantur. Quid quod quidam statuunt, δούλουςposse esseἀπελευθέρουςlibertos sive libertate donatos,οἰκέταςautem esse mancipia, herorum domui sive familiae quasi affixa, ac proinde à domo nomen habentes. Athenaeus lib. 6. ex Chrysippi περὶ ὁμονοίας lib. 2. τοὺς ἀπελευθέρους quidem δούλους adhuc esse, οἰκέτας autem τούς μὴ τῆς κτήσεως ὰφειμὲνους, nam, ὁ οἰκέτης δοῦλος ἐστι κτίσει κατατεταγμὲνος. Vult ergò Chrysippus, δούλους esse servos seu mancipia, quae aliquando rude donentur, aut etiam vendantur, οἰκέτας autem servos perpetuos, qui nunquam manumittantur ab eo, in cuius ministerio sunt. LXX. οἰκέτης utuntur pro עבדGen. 9. v. 25.cap. 27. v. 37.Cap. 44. v. 33. Rectiùs ergò dicitur, nomen οἰκέτων generaliter hoc loco poni, ut liberti cum mancipiis, servi durioris & tolerabilioris conditionis hîc intelligantur, quos omnes Petrus ad subiectionem hortetur.

Ὑποτασσόμνυοιsubditi sc. estote vel sint. Est idem verbum, quo Petrus paulo antè v. 13. de subditorum erga Magistratum obedientia fuerat usus. Syrus sic reddidit. Et illos servos, qui sunt inter vos, subintelligendum nunc alloquor. Subiecti estote dominis vestris,Ἐν πάντι φόβῳ. Per φόβον non intelligitur timor servilis, quem ut ab omnibus Christianis, ita quoque à fidelibus servis exulare oportet, sed timor cum amore coniunctus, quem vocare possumus reverentiam, quâ fideles servi solicitè cavent, ne praeter officium agendo heros suos ad iram provocent. In ea significatione usurpatur nomen φόβου.Actor. 9. v. 31.2. Cor. 5. v. 11.Phil. 2. vers. 12. &c. ac in loco Paulino huic nostro parallelo Ephes. 6. v. 5.Servi obedite dominis carnalibusμετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου.Coloss. 3. v. 22. obiectum huius timoris statuitur ipse DEUS, qui heris potestatem illam in servos concessit, & eorum dominio servos subiecit. Servi obedite per omnia dominis carnalibus timentes DEUM. Subordinata enim haec sunt in officio servorum, quòd & DEUM in heris suis, & heros suos propter DEUM timere debeant. Quod in omni timore subditos esse praecipit, illud Lyranus sic explicat, quòd toto seu perfecto timore subiecti esse debeant, cum totum & perfectum idem sint. Est autem, inquit, perfectus timor, quando quis non solùm cavet offensam DEI, sed etiam hominis propter DEUM, quae expositio ex collatione loci paralleli,Col. 3. v. 22.cum hoc nostro confirmari posset. Simpliciùs respondetur, voculam omnis hîc non sumi pro quantitate discreta, sed continua. Subiecti estote cum omni timore, i. e. cum multa reverentia & modestia, 2. Cor. 1. v. 3.Eph. 1. v. 3.Iacob. 1. v. 2.Iudae v. 3. Syrus hunc προσδιορισμὸν omisit, simpliciter reddens, in timore,οὐ μόνον τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς καὶ ἐπιεικέσιν, ἀλλὰ καί τοῖς σκολιοῖς. Amplificat Apostolus exhortationem per distributionem inter heros humanos, ac difficiles, quâ occurrit perversae quorundam servorum opinioni, qui humanis tantùm & commodis heris, non autem morosis ac difficilibus obedientiam se debere existimabant. Per τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς non intelliguntur illi, qui coram DEO boni & sancti, quia etiam inter Ethnicos heros erant quidam ἀγαθοί, qui tamen regenerationis & renovationis non fuêre participes, sed iuxta vulgatam loquendi consuetudinem bonos heros vocat eos, qui non affligebant servos iniustè, qui non premebant eos victus & vestitus inopiâ, qui non saeviebant adversus eos etiam immeritos verberibus & flagris, sed aequos & modestos se praebebant. Inde ἐξηγητικῶς iidem dicuntur ἐπιεικεῖς, qui non omnia ad vivum resecant, qui non nimiùm rigidos sese exhibent, qui non adeò exactè imperata exigunt, sed quaedam interdum servis condonant. Syrus habet nomen [consult facsimile image] quod lenem ac modestum significat. Illis opponuntur σκόλιοι, quod Vulgata reddidit dyscoli. Graecam vocem aliâ voce Graeca exprimens, quod imperitis errandi occasionem praebuit. Beda in h. l. Dyscolis indisciplinatis dicit, nomine ducto à Graeco eloquio, quia Graecè schola vocatur locus, in quo adolescentes liberalibus studiis operam dare, & audiendis mágistris vacare solent, unde schola vacatio interpretatur. Scholastici Graecè sunt eruditi, dyscoli indocti & agrestes. Hugo de S. Charo: dyscoli sunt indocti, ineruditi, quòd non sint versati in scholis. Sed nec σκολιὸς nec δύσκολος ἀπὸ τῆς σχλῆς deducitur. Quidam ex inscitia per dyscolos intellexerunt dissolutos vel irregulares, ex quo colligere voluerunt, Papae & Episcopis obediendum, etiam si gravem Tyrannidem exerceant. Cornelius à Lapide haec falsò asseri dicit, Papam enim & Episcopos disciplinam Ecclesiasticam administrare, non Tyrannidem exercere. At testatur ipsa experientia, imperium Pontificis in Ecclesiam esse Tyrannicum, cum laqueos iniiciat hominum conscientiis, Scripturae lectionem, & calicis Eucharistiae usum Laicis eripiat, Reges de solio deturbet, Ceremoniarum multitudine Ecclesiam oneret. σκολιὸς propriè significat obliquum, curvum, Luc. 3. v. 5. metaphoricè eum, qui est moribus pravis, animo corrupto & depravato, Act. 2. v. 40.Phil. 2. v. 15.ῤεῖα δε τ᾿ ἰθύνει σκολιὸν, inquit Hesiodus lib. 1. ἒργων, ubi ex verbo opposito ἰθύνειν genuina eius significatio eolligitur. LXX. utuntur pro סורר, quod significat perversum & intractabilem, qui pro arbitrio fertur Psal. 77. v. 10. pro עקש, quod significat pravum, versutum ac tortuosum,Deut. 32. v. 5.Prov. 2. vers. 15. quae significationes huic loco congruunt. Beda memorat, antiquam quandam translationem apud Fulgentium pro dyscolis legere difficilioribus, quod magis congruit Graeco nomini, quo Apostolus utitur, quàm indisciplinatis, quod Bedae placet. Syrus habet duas voces [consult facsimile image] Prius [consult facsimile image] significat austerum, rigidum, asperum, saevum ac immitem,Genes. 49. v. 7.Exod. 32. v. 9. Posserius formatur à rad. עשקoppressit, vim fecit, quavis iniuriâ affecit, quae significationes omnes huic loco congruunt. Drusius in praeterit. Syrus habet pravis, si modo[consult facsimile image]significat pravos, & non contentiosos, vel certè per calumniam opprimentes. Graecumδύσκολος,quo Latina versio utitur, deducit Athenaeus lib. 6. à κόλον,quodτροφὴνcibum significare dicit;δύσκολοςergò significat eum, qui difficilis in convictu, qui moribus est implacidis, cui omnia, tùm dicta, tùm facta stomachum movent. Sed Graecum σκολιοῖς, quod Apostolus usurpat, convenientius est. Praecipit ergò Apostolus, servos debere obedientiam praestare heris suis, qualescunque tandem illi sint, sive sint humani & commodi, sive saevi & intractabiles, duri ac morosi, qui iniquè tractant servos, onera iusto graviora eis imponunt, qui nihil humanitatis & benevolentiae servis exhibent, qui sunt rigidi laborum exactores, parci alimoniae quotidianae distributores, qui non condolent servorum infirmitatibus, sed durum in eos imperium exercent.

## 2:19
FOR THIS IS GRACE, IF FOR CONSCIENCE OF GOD ANYONE ENDURES SORROWS SUFFERING UNJUSTLY.

Connection. 1. Because he had made mention of hard and intractable masters, therefore he consoles the servants who were compelled to suffer such depraved and unjust masters, and refers them to the most ample, but gratuitous, remuneration of GOD.

2. He confirms the exhortation proposed in the verse immediately preceding with three arguments, the first of which, proposed in this little verse, is sought from the salutary consequence, because, namely, that tolerance of injuries, which faithful servants patiently endure when brought upon them by morose masters without merit, is pleasing to GOD, which He is also one day to reward most bountifully out of grace.

3. The arguments of the exhortation are accommodated to its latter part, that σκολιοῖς is to be obeyed by masters, because servants obey benign and humane masters with a more ready mind than hard and rigid ones. Some wish, on the occasion of servants afflicted by hard masters Peter passes to a general discourse, and exhorts all who suffer innocently in any way to tolerance. But the following verses show that Peter is still addressing servants specifically, though we do not deny that the doctrine itself is general.

Exposition of the text τοῦτο γὰρ χάρις. The Vulgate rendered it, for this is grace, so that this part might be connected to the preceding one. But in the Greek it is, For this is grace, namely that which is expressed in the following. By χάρον 1. Some understand κλέος praise or glory, for it immediately follows v. 20. ποῖον γὰρ κλέος 2. Some explain μετωνυμικῶς concerning the effect of grace, that is, a work proceeding from grace. But because such a work proceeding from grace is praiseworthy and worthy of praise, therefore these two expositions almost amount to the same thing.

3. Some explain it thus: This is grace, i.e., it conciliates grace for you before GOD, etc., just as Rom. 7. vers. 7. is the law sin? i.e., the cause of sin? But we can reconcile the grace of GOD to ourselves neither by the tolerance of injuries, nor by any work of ours; rather, it is necessary for the person to be first reconciled to GOD by faith and established in grace, before patience and other good works can please GOD. 4. Some explain grace as the reward to be given out of grace. This is grace, i.e., GOD will most bountifully reward this out of grace. Thus what Matth. 5. v. 46. is said: If you love those who love you, what reward have you? that is Luc. 6. v. 32. explained thus: If you love those who love you, what grace is it to you? 5. It is most simply said that the abstract is put for the concrete. This is grace, i.e., this is pleasing and acceptable to GOD, and this will be most bountifully rewarded out of grace, by which reasoning the two latter explanations can be joined. The Syriac rendered it: To them there is grace before GOD. Ἐι διὰ συνείδησιν θεοῦ ὑποφέρειτας λύπας πάσχων ἀδίκως. The opinions of interpreters vary as to what is understood by the conscience of GOD. This is certain, that it is not understood as the conscience which GOD has, but which man has before GOD, by which he takes care not to offend GOD. Therefore, by the conscience of GOD is understood in this place a good conscience before GOD, by which servants anxiously take care, lest by their disobedience, sedition, or rebellion against their masters they offend GOD; by τὰς λύπας are understood, by a certain species of metonymy, verbal and real injuries, which the wicked and morose inflict upon their servants yesterday, from which sickness of mind and sadness arises in them, whence the Syrian rendered it by [consult facsimile image] afflictions. Phil. 2. v. 27.

Latin:

HAEC EST ENIM GRATIA, SI PROPTER DEI CONSCIENTIAM SUSTINET QUIS TRISTITIAS PATIENS INIUSTE.

Connexio. 1. Quia mentionem fecerat herorum durorum & intractabilium, ideò consolatur servos, qui eiusmodi pravos & iniustos Dominos pati cogebantur, ac remittit illos ad amplissimam, sed gratuitam DEI remunerationem.

2. Confirmat exhortationem in versu proximè praecedente propositam tribus argumentis, quorum primum in hoc versiculo propositum, petitum est à consequente salutari, quia scilicet tolerantia illa iniuriarum, quas fideles servi à morosis dominis praeter meritum sibi illatas patienter sustinent, sit DEO grata, quam etiam ex gratia aliquando sit largissimè remuneraturus.

3. Argumenta exhortationis accommodata sunt ad partem eius posteriorem, quòd heris σκολιοῖς sit obediendum, quia benignis & humanis dominis promtiore animo parent servi, quàm duris ac rigidis. Quidam volunt, occasione servorum à duris heris afflictorum Petrum transire ad generalem sermonem, ac omnes, qui quomodolibet innocentes patiúntur ad tolerantiam exhortari. Sed sequentia ostendunt, Petrum adhuc in specie servos alloqui, ipsam tamen doctrinam generalem esse non negamus.

Expositio textus τοῦτο γὰρ χάρις. Vulgata reddidit, haec est enim gratia, ut sic pars isthaec annectatur praecedenti. Sed in Graeco est. Hoc enim est grantia, illud scilicet, quod in sequentibus exprimitur. Per χάρον 1. Quidam intelligunt κλέοςlaudem sive gloriam, statim enim sequiturv. 20.ποῖον γὰρ κλέος 2. Quidam exponunt μετωνυμικῶςde effectu gratiae h. e. opere ex gratia profecto. Quia vero tale opus ex gratia profectum est laudabile & laude dignum, ideò hae duae expositiones ferè eodem redeunt.

3. Quidam sic exponunt. Hoc est gratia i. e. conciliat vobis gratiam apud DEUM &c. sicutRom. 7. vers. 7.num lex peccatum est i. e. causa peccati? Sed nec iniuriarum tolerantiâ, nec ullo opere nostro gratiam DEI nobis conciliare possumus, verùm personam oportet priùs esse fide DEO reconciliatam & in gratia constituram, antequam patientia & reliqua bona opera DEO placeant. 4. Quidam gratiam exponunt de mercede ex gratia danda. Hoc est gratia i. e. hoc DEUS ex gratia largissimè remunerabitur. Sic quodMatth. 5. v. 46.dicitur. Si diligitis eos, qui vos diligunt, quam mercedem babetis? illudLuc. 6. v. 32.sic exponitur. Si diligitis eos, qui vos diligunt, quae vobis est gratia? 5. Simplicissimè dicitur, abstractum positum esse pro concreto. Hoc est gratia i. e. hoc est DEO gratum & acceptum, & hoc ex gratia largissimè remunerabitur, quâ ratione duae postremae explicationes coniungi possunt. Syrus reddidit. Illis est gratia coram DEO.Ἐι διὰ συνείδησιν θεοῦ ὑποφέρειτας λύπας πάσχων ἀδίκως. Quid per conscientiam DEI intelligatur, variant Interpretum sententiae. Certum hoc est, non intelligi conscientiam, quam DEUS habet, sed quam homo coram DEO habet, quâ cavet ne DEUM offendat. Ergò per conscientiam DEI intelligitur hoc loco bona coram DEO conscientia, quâ solicite cavent servi, ne suâ adversus heros inobedientia, seditione, rebellione DEUM offendant, per τὰς λύπας metonymiae quadam specie intelliguntur iniuriae verbales ac reales, quas heri iniqui ac morosi servis suis inferunt, ex quibus animi aegritudo ac tristitia in ipsis oritur, unde Syrus reddidit per [consult facsimile image] afflictiones. Phil. 2. v. 27.

## 2:20
FOR WHAT GLORY IS IT, IF YOU ENDURE WHEN YOU ARE SINNING AND BUFFETED; BUT IF YOU PATIENTLY ENDURE WHILE DOING GOOD, THIS IS GRACE BEFORE GOD.

Connection. The Apostle illustrates the first argument of the exhortation from the contrary. He opposes injuries and blows that are deserved to injuries inflicted without merit. He denies that the tolerance of the former brings praise and glory, but that the patient tolerance of the latter is pleasing to God, which therefore He also wishes to reward in His own time.

ποῖον γὰρ κλέος. Some Latin Codices also read in this place, as in the preceding verse and at the end of this little verse, grace. But the Greek Codices constantly read κλέος which signifies glory, in which way also the more emended Latin Codices have it. τὸ κλέος The Syrian rendered [consult facsimile image] which corresponds to the word δόξα Matth. 6. v. 13.

Luc. 2. v. 9. & 14. Moreover, κλέος signifies not simply praise, which for the Greeks is αἶνος but such praise as is made by many, whence glory is born. Eustathius on the Odyssey ψ. notes that κλέος signifies φήμην, not τιμήν. Rightly, therefore, Luther rendered it, Was ist das fur ein Ruhm? What honor, what illustrious thing, what great thing is it? Tertullian in Scorpiaco, chapter 12, How great is the glory? But the interrogation in this place corresponds to a negation. What is this glory? that is, none. Ἐι ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ κολαφιζόμενον ὑπομενεῖτε; The Vulgate rendered it, If you endure when sinning and buffeted. The Greek properly has, If when sinning or on account of sins you are struck with fists, you endure. κολαφίζεσθαι does not occur among the LXX in the O. T., in the N. Test. it is taken generally for blows and beatings Matth. 26. v. 67.Marc. 14. v. 65.1. Cor. 4. v. 11.2. Cor. 12. vers. 7. κόλαφος Eustathius derives from κόλον & ἁφᾶσθαι, so that it may be ὁ μεγάλην ἀφὴν ἒχων. between κόλαφον & ῥάπισμα they establish this difference, that a buffet is struck with a fist or a clenched hand, ῥάπισμα but with the palm or the hand extended, which blow they are accustomed to call a slap. By buffets, however, in this place συνεκδοχικῶς are understood all kinds of beatings, scourges, and lashes. The Syriac rendered it [consult facsimile image] which corresponds to the Hebrew צוקה θλίψις, anguish, afflictionMatth. 24. v. 9.Marc. 9. v. 17.cap. 13. v. 19. &c. from the root אלץ to bind and to reduce to straits. The sense is: What glory can you expect from that, if you endure lashes from your masters on account of your offenses. ἀλλ᾿ εἰ ἀγαθοποιοῦντες καὶ πάσχοντες ὑπομενεῖτε, τοῦτο χάρις παρὰ θεῷ The Vulgate rendered it, if doing well you endure patiently, this is grace before God. But the Greek words properly have it thus: If doing well and suffering you endure. That is, if you endure nonetheless, even if beyond your merit, nay even against your merit, and thus suffer on account of your good actions. In the same way Bede rendered it: If doing well and suffering you endure. So also some Latin Codices read, and the Syriac version supports it: When you do what is good and they afflict you and you tolerate it. The same reading is required by the antithesis of the preceding words. For he opposes those who, sinning and being buffeted, i.e., struck with blows on account of sins, endure; and those who, doing well and suffering, i.e., having suffered injuries on account of good deeds, endure. A parallel passage follows in cap. 3. v. 17.For it is better that doing well, if the will of GOD so ordains, you suffer, than doing evil. The Apostle repeats, however, what he had said above, τοῦτο χάρις adding παρά θεῷ to show that his discourse is not primarily about grace before men, but before God. For although the patient tolerance of injuries inflicted beyond merit sometimes procures grace even before men, that is not perpetual, nor do the truly pious anxiously seek grace before men, but they desire above all to approve their actions to GOD. The Syriac rendered it, then your praise will be multiplied before God. But in the Greek there is not κλέος, but χάρις and the Interpreter added the word for multiplying of his own.

Latin:

QUAE ENIM EST GLORIA, SI PECCANTES & COLAPHIZATI SUFFERTIS; SED SI BENEFACIENTES PATIENTER SUSTINETIS, HAEC EST GRATIA APUD DEUM.

Connexio. Illustrat Apostolus primum exhortationis argumentum à contrario. Iniuriis praeter meritum illatis opponit iniurias ac plagas promeritas. Harum tolerantiam negat laudem & gloriam afferre, illarum vero patientem tolerantiam esse Deo gratam, quam proinde etiam velit suo tempore remunerari.

ποῖον γὰρ κλέος. Quidam Codices Latini etiam hoc loco legunt, ut in versu praecedente & in fine huius versiculi, gratia. Sed Graeci Codd. constanter legunt κλέος quod gloriam significat, quo modo etiam emendatiores Codices Latini habent. τὸ κλέος Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image] quod respondet voci δόξαMatth. 6. v. 13.

Luc. 2. v. 9. & 14. Significat autem κλέος non simpliciter laudem, quae Graecis αἶνος sed eiusmodi laudem, quae fit à multis, unde gloria nascitur. Eustathius odys. ψ. annotat, κλέος significare. φήμην, non τιμήν. Rectèigitur Lutherus reddidit, Was ist das fur ein Ruhm? Quale decus, quid illustre, quid magnum est? Tertull. in Scorpiaco, cap. 12. Quanta est gloria? Interrogatio autemirespondet hoc loco negationi. Quae haec est gloria? id est, nulla.Ἐι ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ κολαφιζόμενον ὑπομενεῖτε; Vulgata reddidit. Sipeccantes & colaphizati suffertis. Graeca propriè habent. Si cum peccantes sive ob peccata colaphis caedimini, sufferatis.κολαφίζεσθαι apud LXX. in V. T. non occurrit, in N. Test. generaliter accipitur pro plagis ac percussionibus Matth. 26. v. 67.Marc. 14. v. 65.1. Cor. 4. v. 11.2. Cor. 12. vers. 7.κόλαφος deducit Eustathius à κόλον & ἁφᾶσθαι, ut sit ὁ μεγάλην ἀφὴν ἒχων. inter κόλαφον & ῥάπισμα hanc statuunt differentiam, quòd colaphus impingatur pugno sive manu compressâ,ῥάπισμα verò palmâ sive manu porrecta, quem ictum solent nominare alapam. Per colaphos autem hoc loco συνεκδοχικῶς intelliguntur omnis generis percussiones, flagra ac verbera. Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image] quod respondet Hebraeorum צוקה θλίψις,angustia, afflictioMatth. 24. v. 9.Marc. 9. v. 17.cap. 13. v. 19. &c. à rad. אלץconstringere & in angustiam redigere. Sensus est. Quam inde expectare potestis gloriam, si propter delicta vestra ab heris sustinetis verbera. ἀλλ᾿ εἰ ἀγαθοποιοῦντες καὶ πάσχοντες ὑπομενεῖτε, τοῦτο χάρις παρὰ θεῷ Vulgata reddidit, si benefacientes patienter sustinetis, haec est gratia apud Deum. Sed Graeca propriè sic habent. Si benefacientes & patientes sustinetis. h. e. si nihilo minus sustinetis, etiamsi praeter meritum, imò contra meritum vestrum, adeoque ob bonas vestras actiones patiamini. Eodem modo reddidit Beda. Si benefacientes & patientes sustinctis. Ita quoque legunt quidam Codices Latini & suffragatur versio Syriaca. Cùm facitis quod bonum est & affligunt vos ac toleratis. Eandem lectionem requirit antithesis verborum praecedentium. Opponit enim eos, qui peccantes & colaphizati i. e. ob peccata colaphis caesi sustinent; & eos, qui benefacientes & patientes i. e. ob bona facta iniurias passi sustinent. Parallelus locus sequitur in cap. 3. v. 17.Melius est enim ut benefacientes sivoluntas DEI ita ferat, patiamini, quàm male facientes. Repetit autem Apostolus, quod superius dixerat, τοῦτο χάρις addens παρά θεῷ ut ostendat, non de gratia apud homines, sed apud Deum sibi potissimùm sermonem esse. Quamvis enim patiens iniuriarum praeter meritum illatarum tolerantia etiam apud homines quandoque gratiam conciliet, illud tamen non est perpetuum, nec gratiam apud homines verè pii solicitè quaerunt, sed DEO actiones suas probare cumprimis cupiunt. Syrus reddidit, tunc multiplicabitur laus vestra apud Deum. Sed in Graeco non est κλέος, sed χάρις ac multiplicandi verbum Interpres de suo adiecit.

## 2:21
FOR UNTO THIS YOU ARE CALLED, BECAUSE CHRIST ALSO SUFFERED FOR US, LEAVING US AN EXAMPLE, THAT YOU SHOULD FOLLOW HIS STEPS.

Connection. 1. The Apostle submits two other arguments of exhortation, the former of which is drawn from the calling common to all Christians. All Christians are called to the tolerance of injuries, therefore it is fair that, mindful of their calling, they patiently sustain any injuries whatsoever; the latter is sought from the example of Christ. Christ, having suffered for us, left us an example, that we might follow his footsteps. Therefore, just as Christ patiently sustained injuries beyond, nay, contrary to the merit brought upon himself; so also we ought to tolerate injuries with an even mind.

2. In the former argument there is a tacit signification of the principal author, by whom adversities of every kind are sent upon the pious. GOD, by a salutary counsel, sends calamities upon the pious in this life, and permits injuries to be inflicted upon them beyond their merit, so that they may be means for faith to be tested and exercised. For if indeed the pious are divinely called to the tolerance of injuries, certainly those injuries also do not befall them without the permission of GOD; therefore, in patiently bearing these injuries, they ought to look to God, not to the men by whom they are inflicted. The pious experience calamities of a double kind in this life. Some are only evils of punishment, but others are at once evils of fault and evils of punishment. God is rightly said to send calamities of the former kind. Amos 3. v. 6. Shall there be evil in a city, which the Lord hath not done? God is said to send calamities of the latter kind, insofar as they are evils of punishment, but not insofar as they are evils of fault. 2. Sam. 16. v. 10. The Lord hath commanded, or as it is in the Hebrew, said to Semei, that he should curse David.

3. Bede establishes that the Apostle in v. 24 is no longer engaged in a special exhortation directed to servants, but is speaking in general about all the faithful to whom he writes. The ordinary Gloss begins the general discourse of the Apostle in this very v. 21. Since above, he says, he made a discourse specially to servants, now he admonishes generally, so that Masters also may call to memory what GOD and Lord sustained for them. Nay, he instructs the whole Church, what its author endured for its liberation. And indeed, the fruit of the Lord's passion and the example of virtues proposed in that passion is not to be restricted to servants, but pertains to all Christians whatsoever, nay, to all men, by reason of merit, acquisition, and example: meanwhile, the series of the text shows that the Apostle is still directly addressing servants, although those things which he brings forward are not to be restricted to servants alone, but should be accommodated to all Christians.

Exposition. Ἐὶς τοῦτο γαρ καὶ ὲκλήθητε. Some refer this to the preceding words. In this you were called, that doing good, and nevertheless affected by evils, you might patiently sustain. But some refer it to the following words. In this you were called, that you might be rendered conformable to Christ in passion. Rom. 8. v. 29. But the matter in both cases comes to the same thing, although the former exposition is more conformable to the text, as the little word καὶ shows, which is emphatic, less correctly omitted by the Vulgate interpreter. For in this you were also called. By that law you were called to Christ, and to the fellowship of the kingdom of Christ, that doing good, and nevertheless having suffered evils, you might patiently sustain. This your calling and profession requires, that in bearing evils patiently you might prove your obedience to GOD. ὃτι καὶ χριστὸς ἒπαθεν ὑπερ ἡμῶν, ὑμῖν ὑπο λιμπάνων ὑπογραμμὸν. The little word καὶ serves for emphasis. Christ himself also, our Lord and head, suffered for us. Therefore we ought not to shirk, so that we too, who are his servants and members, might not sustain passions in this world. The Apostle proposes Christ to servants as an example of patience, because Christ assumed the nature of a servant, and underwent the servile punishment of an ignominious death for our sake. Concerning the relative pronouns, a not mediocre variety of reading occurs. Most Greek Codices have the pronoun of the first person in both places. Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example. In the same way the Syrian reads, as does Luther in the German version. But most Latin Codices have the pronoun of the first person in the former member, and of the second person in the latter member. Christ suffered for Us, leaving you an example, in which way Bede also reads. Nor are there lacking some Greek and Latin Codices, in which the pronoun of the second person is held in both places. Christ suffered for you, leaving You an example. Oecumenius follows this reading from the Greeks, and Franciscus Lucas tries to prove the same to be genuine, as being more accommodated to the text, from the fact that Peter in this place addresses servants, admonishing them that they might bear with an equal mind if they receive blows from iniquitous masters, while they have done good, since this is their calling, and since CHRIST suffered for them, and left them an example of patience. Therefore since the preceding word ὲκλήθητε, and the following ἒπακολουθήσητε is of the person the second, therefore also the pronoun of the second person in both members is more conformable to the text. But since almost all the more approved Greek Codices read the pronoun of the first person in both places, therefore this reading is to be preferred to the others. Nor is the change of persons infrequent in the Apostolic Epistles, especially in κοινοποιήσει, which also has emphasis in this place. Christ suffered for each one of us, and left an example for each one of us, so that each one according to the reason of his calling might follow his footsteps. Therefore also you in a servile state ought not to refuse the measure of sufferings. In vain therefore does Estius seek emphasis in the pronoun for you. Christ suffered no less for you servants than for the free, since in Christ there is neither slave nor free, Galat. 3. v. 28.Coloss. 3. v. 11. For if we should even read in the first person, Christ suffered for us, nevertheless nothing is lost to that emphasis, because the first person through κοινοποίησιν here includes the second. In vain is the same Estius anxious about the occasion of changing the second person into the first, which he suspects to have been that, because it seemed to those not noticing the series of the discourse to be of an ungrateful and arrogant mind to say in the second person, Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example. And yet we deny that the second person was changed into the first, since that reading, which has the first person, is genuine, and thus the first person was rather changed into the second. John Huss observes that Peter does not express that Christ suffered, but simply says Χριστὸς ἒπαθεν, to intimate that Christ endured every kind of suffering for us, and because he presupposes as known that Christ had suffered. ὑπογραμμὸς is a form delineated and prescribed, according to the interpreter Budaeus. Hesychius renders it by τύπον καὶ μίμημα, in which way also ὑπογραμμὸν καί τύπον Damascenus joins it, speaking thus of Christ, τύπον ήμῖν ἑαυτὸν ἄριστον καὶ ὑπογραμμόν διδοὺς, It is used properly of a model, which teachers propose to disciples, and painters to novices, to which they may look in painting letters and images, about to exhibit a specimen of their art, which signification fits this place beautifully. 2. Macc. 2. v. 29. it is used a little differently τὸ ἐπιπορεύεσθαι τοῖς ὑπογραμμοῖς τῆς ἐπιτομῆς διαπονοῦντες, according to the given form, studying brevity. The Syrian renders [consult facsimile image] which is formed from the Greek τύπος by which word he also expressed the Greek ὐπόδειγμα John 13 v. 15.1. Cor. 10 v. 6. & 11.2. Thess. 3 v. 9. which corresponds to the noun ὑπογραμμὸς. But he rendered the noun ὑποδείγματος itself James 5 v. 10. by [consult facsimile image] likeness. In this place he notably added the pronoun [consult facsimile image] he left us this example, such an example. The sense therefore is that Christ in his passion proposed to us an example of the most beautiful virtues, but especially of patience, which we ought to imitate, whence the Apostle adds, ἵνα ἐπακολουθήοητε τοῖς ἲχνεσιν αὐτοῦ. The Syrian rendered, that you might go in his footsteps, that is, that you might keep his footsteps, and imitate his patience and his remaining virtues. Just as the former metaphor is from painters and writers, so this latter is taken from a guide of the way, whose footsteps he presses who, ignorant of the way, follows him, so that he may arrive at the proposed destination. Tertullian in Scorpiaco chapter 12 reads to follow.

Latin:

IN HOC ENIM VOCATI ESTIS, QUIA & CHRISTUS PASSUS EST PRO NOBIS, RELINQUENS NOBIS EXEMPLUM, UT SEQUAMINI VESTIGIA EIUS.

Connexio. 1. Subiicit Apostolus duo alia exhortationis argumenta, quorum prius ductum à vocatione omnibus Christianis communi. Omnes Christiani ad tolerantiam iniuriarum vocati sunt, ergò aequum est, ut vocationis suae memores, quasvis iniurias patienter sustineant, posterius petitum ab exemplo Christi. Christus pro nobis passus reliquit nobis exemplum, ut sequamur eius vestigia. Ergò ut Christus iniurias praeter, imò contra meritum sibi illatas patienter sustinuit; ita & nos iniurias aequo animo tolerare debemus.

2. Priori argumento inest tacita significatio principalis autoris, à quo omnis generis adversitates piis immittuntur. DEUS salutari consilio piis in hac vita calamitates immittit, ac iniurias praeter meritum ipsis inferri permittit, ut sint fidei probandae & exercendae media. Quod si enim pii ad iniuriarum tolerantiam divinitus sunt vocati, utique etiam iniuriae illae non sine DEI permissione ipsis obtingunt, proinde in hisce iniuriis patienter ferendis ad Deum, non ad homines à quibus inferuntur, respicere debent. Duplicis generis calamitates pii in hac vita experiuntur. Quaedam sunt tantùm mala poenae quaedam vero simul mala culpae & mala poenae. Prioris generis calamitates Deus rectè dicitur immittere. Amos 3. v. 6.Num erit malum in civitate, quod non faciat Dominus. Posterioris generis calamitates Deus immittere dicitur, quatenus sunt mala poenae, non autem quatenus sunt mala culpae. 2. Sam. 16. v. 10.Dominus praecepit vel ut in Hebraeo est, dixit Simei, ut malediceret Davidi.

3. Beda statuit, Apostolum in v. 24. non ampliùs versari in speciali exhoratione ad servos directa, sed in genere de omnibus fidelibus, ad quos scribit, loqui. Glossa ordinaria generalem Apostoli sermonem inchoat in hoc ipso v. 21. Cùm supra, inquit, ad servos specialiter fecerit sermonem, nunc generaliter admonet, ut etiam Domini in memoriam revocent, quid pro illis DEUS & Dominus sustinuerit. Imò totam Ecclesiam instruit, quid pro eius liberatione suus autor pertulit. Et sanè non restringendus est passionis Dominicae fructus ac exemplum virtutum in passione illa propositum ad servos, sed ad omnes omninò Christianos, imò ad omnes homines, ratione meriti, acquisitionis & exempli pertinet: interim series textus ostendit, directe Apostolum adhuc servos alloqui, quamvis ea, quae profert, non sint ad solos servos restringenda, sed ad omnes Christianos accommodanda.

Expositio. Ἐὶς τοῦτο γαρ καὶ ὲκλήθητε. Quidam hoc referunt ad praecedentia. In hoc vocati estis, ut benefacientes, & malis nihilominus affecti patienter sustineatis. Quidam vero ad sequentia. In hoc vocati estis, ut Christo conformes in passione reddamini.Rom. 8. v. 29. Sed res utrobique eodem redit, quamvis prior expositio textui magis sit conformis, ut ostendit vocula καὶ quae est emphatica, à vulgato interprete minùs rectè omissa. In hoc enim etiam vocati estis. Eâ lege ad Christum, & regni Christi consortium vocati estis, ut benè agentes, & mala nihilo minus perpessi patienter sustineatis. Hoc requirit vocatio & professio vestra, ut in malis patienter ferendis DEO vestram probetis obedientiam. ὃτι καὶ χριστὸς ἒπαθεν ὑπερ ἡμῶν, ὑμῖν ὑπο λιμπάνων ὑπογραμμὸν. Vocula καὶ inservit emphasi. Etiam Christus ipse, Dominus & caput nostrum, passus est pro nobis. Ergò non debemus subterfugere, quò minùs & nos, qui sumue ipsius servi ac membra, passiones in hoc mundo sustineamus. Christum Apostolus servis in exemplum patientiae proponit, quia Christus servi assumsit naturam, & servile mortis ignominiosae supplicium propter nos subiit. Circa pronomina relativa lectionis varietas occurrit non mediocris. Plerique Codices Graeci utrobique habent pronomen primae personae. Christus passus est pro nobis, relinquens nobis exemplum. Eodem modo legit Syrus, ut & Lutherus in versione Germanica. Plerique vero Latini Codices in priore membro habent pronomen primae, in posteriore membro secundae personae. Christus passus est pro Nobis, relinquens vobis exemplum, quo modo etiam legit Bèda. Nec desunt quidam Graeci & Latini Codices, in quibus utrobique habetur pronomen secundae personae. Christus passus est pro vobis, relinquens Vobis exemplum. Hanc lectionem ex Graecis sequitur Oecumenius, eandemque genuinam esse, utpote textui magis accommodatam, Franciscus Lucas probare conatur ex eo, quòd Petrus hoc loco servos alloquatur, admonens eos, ut aequo ferant animo, si ab iniquis dominis plagas referant, dum benefecerint, cum haec sit ipsorum vocatio, cumque CHRISTUS pro ipsis passus, exemplum patientiae ipsis reliquerit. Proinde cum praecedens verbumὲκλήθητε,ac sequensἒπακολουθήσητεsit personae secundae, ideò etiam pronomen secundae personae in utroque membro textui esse magis conforme. Sed cum probatiores Codices Graeci plerique omnes legant utrobique pronomen personae primae, ideò haec lectio caeteris praeferenda. Nec infrequens est personarum mutatio in Epistolis Apostolicis, praesertim in κοινοποιήσει, quae etiam h. l. habet emphasin. Christus pro quolibet nostrûm passus est, ac cuilibet nostrûm reliquit exemplum, ut quilibet pro ratione suae vocationis vestigia eius sequatur. Ergò etiam vos in statu servili non debetis passionum demensum recusare. Frustra igitur emphasin quaerit Estius in pronomine vobis. Etiam pro vobis servis Christus passus non minùs, quàm pro liberis, cum in Christo non sit servus nec liber, Galat. 3. v. 28.Coloss. 3. v. 11. Nam si vel maximè in prima persona legamus, Christus passus est pro nobis, emphasi tamen isti nihil decedit, quia persona prima per κοινοποίησιν hîc includit secundam. Frustra idem Estius solicitus est de occasione mutandae personae secundae in primam, quam suspicatur fuisse eam, quòd non advertentibus seriem orationis visum fuerit ingrati & arrogantis animi dicere in secunda persona, Christus passus est pro vobis, relinquens vobis exemplum. Atqui negamus, personam secundam, esse mutatam in primam, cum lectio illa, quae habet personam primam, sit genuina, sicque prima persona potiùs sit mutata in secundam. Iohannes Huss observat. Petrum non exprimere, quòd Christus passus sit, sed simpliciter dicereΧριστὸς ἒπαθεν,ut innuat, omne passionis genus Christum pro nobis tolerasse, ac quia tanquam notum praesupponat, quòd Christus passus fuerit.ὑπογραμμὸςest forma delineata ac praescripta, interprete Budaeo. Hesychius reddit per τύπον καὶ μίμημα, quo modo etiam ὑπογραμμὸν καί τύπονconiungit Damascenus, de Christo sic dicens,τύπον ήμῖν ἑαυτὸν ἄριστον καὶ ὑπογραμμόν διδοὺς, Usurpatur propriè de exemplari, quod praeceptores discipulis, pictores novitiis proponunt, ad quod in pingendis literis & imaginibus respiciant, specimen artis suae exhibituri, quae significatio huic loco pulchrè congruit. 2. Macc. 2. v. 29. paulo aliter usurpatur τὸ ἐπιπορεύεσθαι τοῖς ὑπογραμμοῖς τῆς ἐπιτομῆς διαπονοῦντες, fecundùm datam formam brevitati studentes. Syrus redd. [consult facsimile image] quod formatum ex Graeco τύπος quâ voce etiam expressit Graecum ὐπόδειγμαIohan. 13. v. 15.1. Cor. 10. v. 6. & 11.2.Thess. 3. Vers. 9. quod nomini ὑπογραμμὸς respondet. Ipsum autem ὑποδείγματος nomen Iacob. 5. v. 10. reddidit per [consult facsimile image]similitudinem. Hoc loco notanter addidit pronomen [consult facsimile image]reliquit nobis hoc exemplum, tale exemplum. Sensus igitur est, quòd Christus in passione sua proposuerit nobis exemplum pulcerrimarum virtutum, cumprimis vero patientiae, quod imitari debeamus, unde addit Apostolus, ἵνα ἐπακολουθήοητε τοῖς ἲχνεσιν αὐτοῦ. Syrus reddidit, ut vos in vestigiis eius iretis, h. e. ut vestigia eius teneretis, & patientiam, ac reliquas eius virtutes imitaremini. Sicut prior metaphora à pictoribus & scriptoribus, ita haec posterior petita est à viae duce, cuius vestigia premit, qui viae ignarus ipsum sequitur, ut ad propositum terminum perveniat. Tertullianus in Scorpiaco cap. 12. legit ad sequamini.

## 2:22
WHO DID NO SIN, NEITHER WAS GUILE FOUND IN HIS MOUTH.

Connection. 1. The example of patience proposed in Christ is illustrated by a comparison of dissimilars. Christ was never liable to any sin, and nevertheless patiently bore the injuries brought upon him beyond all merit. Therefore, much more ought you, who are not entirely innocent before GOD, but liable to various sins, patiently tolerate any injuries whatsoever.

2. Therefore he meets a tacit objection. There is no reason for you to pretend your innocence, for Christ did not sustain the punishment of evildoers, yet nevertheless he patiently bore the injuries brought upon him.

Exposition. Ὁς ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἐποίησε, οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῶ στόματι αὐτοῦ. A passage taken from Isa. 53 v. 9. because he did not do, or although he did not do חמס injury, violence, and in general iniquity, nor was guile in his mouth, to wit. The LXX rendered. ὅτι ἀνομίαν οὐκ ἐποίησεν, οὐδὲ δόλος ἐν τὡ στόματι αὐτοῦ In certain codices, added in place of a gloss, οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος, which is without doubt taken from this Petrine passage. Thus therefore Peter follows neither the Hebrew text nor the version of the LXX Interpreters. κατὰ πόθας but it expresses the sense, and indeed by a Hebrew idiom. For when he says, that guile was not found in the mouth of Christ, then he says the same thing that Isaiah says, that there was no guile in the mouth of Christ. For among the Hebrews, that which is, is said to be found, and that which is not, not to be found. Genes. 2. v. 20.cap. 16. vers. 26.Exod. 16. v. 24.2. Paral. 31. v. 1.Esa. 22. v. 3.Sir. 44. vers. 20. etc., which Hebraism the Apostles also imitate in the N. T. Phil. 2. v. 8.Apocal. 14. v. 5.cap. 20. v. 15. etc. In vain, therefore, does Cornelius à Lapide add, that guile was not found in the mouth of Christ by the Scribes and Pharisees, who were busy trying to catch him in his speech, so that they might kill him, Matth. 22. v. 15. By the name ἁμαρτίας the Apostle understands sins of every kind, committed by the external work itself; by the name δόλου sins committed by the mouth: he signifies, therefore, that the innocence of Christ is so great that he never sinned either by word or by deed, from which he leaves it to be understood and gathered that he never sinned even in thought, and thus is immune from all actual sins, and from original sin itself, the source of actual sins. The latter member, that guile was not found in the mouth of Christ, Salmeron adapts to the fact that Christ gave us an example of good doctrine. And indeed, from the negation, as in very many other sayings, so also in this place, the opposite affirmation is understood. Christ did not commit sin, but most perfectly fulfilled the law of GOD with good works. In the mouth of Christ guile was not found, but he brought forth truth, and glorified GOD with his words, and profited men. Meanwhile, the principal scope of the Apostle is to express the all-encompassing ἀναμαρτησίαν of Christ by this formula of speaking, that he never sinned in the least, neither in deeds nor in words.

Latin:

QUI PECCATUM NON FECIT, NEC INVENTUS EST DOLUS IN ORE EIUS.

Connexio. 1. Exemplum patientiae in Christo propositum, illustrat collatione dissimilium. Christus nulli unquam peccato fuit obnoxius, ac nihilominus iniurias praeter omne meritum sibi illatas patienter tulit. Ergò multò magis vobis, qui non prorsus innocentes estis coram DEO, sed variis peccatis obnoxii, quasvis iniurias patienter tolerare debetis.

2. Occurrit ergò tacitae obiectioni. Non est quòd innocentiam vestram praetendatis, nam nec Christus poenam malefactorum sustinuit, nihilo tamen minùs patienter iniurias sibi illatas pertulit.

Expositio. Ὁς ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἐποίησε, οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῶ στόματι αὐτοῦ. Locus desumtus ex Esa. 53. vers. 9.eò quod non fecerit, vel quamvis non feceritחמסiniuriam, violentiam, & in genere iniquitatem, nec dolus in ore eius, sc. fuerit. LXX. reddiderunt. ὅτι ἀνομίαν οὐκ ἐποίησεν, οὐδὲ δόλος ἐν τὡ στόματι αὐτοῦ In quibusdam, Codicibus glossematis loco adiectum, οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος, quod procul dubio ex hoc loco Petrino petitum. Sic ergò Petrus nec textum Hebraeum nec versionem LXX. Interpp. κατὰ πόθας sequitur, sed sensum exprimit, & quidem idiotismo Hebraeo. Quando enim dicit, non esse inventum dolum in ore Christi, tùm idem dicit, quod Esaias, non fuisse dolum in ore Christi. Hebraeis enim dicitur inveniri, quod est; non inveniri, quod non est. Genes. 2. v. 20.cap. 16. vers. 26.Exod. 16. v. 24.2. Paral. 31. v. 1.Esa. 22. v. 3.Sir. 44. vers. 20. &c. quem Hebraismum etiam Apostoli in N. T. imitantur. Phil. 2. v. 8.Apocal. 14. v. 5.cap. 20. v. 15. &c. Frustra ergò Cornelius à Lapide addit, non inventum esse dolum in ore Christi à Scribis & Pharisaeis, qui satagebant eum capere in sermone, ut possent occidere,Matth. 22. v. 15. Nomine ἁμαρτίας intelligit Apostolus omnis generis peccata, ipso opere externo commissa; nomine δόλου peccata ore commissa: significat ergò, tantam esse Christi innocentiam, ut nec verbo, nec facto unquam peccaverit, ex quo intelligendum ac colligendum relinquit, quòd nec cogitatu unquam peccaverit, adeoque ab omnibus actualibus, & ab ipso originali peccato actualium fonte immunis sit. Posterius membrum, quòd non fuerit in ore Christi dolus inventus, Salmeron eò accommodat, quòd Christus exemplum bonae doctrinae nobis dederit. Et sanè ex negatione, ut in aliis quamplurimis dictis, ita etiam hoc loco intelligitur opposita affirmatio. Christus non fecit peccatum, sed bonis operibus legem DEI perfectissmè implevit. In ore Christi non est inventus dolus, sed veritatem protulit, ac verbis suis DEUM glorificavit, hominibus vero prosuit. Interim principalis Apostoli scopus est, omnimodam Christi ἀναμαρτησίαν hac loquendi formulâ exprimere, quòd nec factis nec verbis unquam in minimo peccarit.

## 2:23
WHO WHEN HE WAS REVILED, DID NOT REVILE; WHEN HE SUFFERED, HE DID NOT THREATEN, BUT DELIVERED HIMSELF TO HIM WHO JUDGED HIM UNJUSTLY.

Connection. 1. The Apostle exaggerates the sufferings unjustly inflicted upon Christ by his enemies, distributing them into verbal and real injuries; he not only sustained curses, but also evil deeds. He not only suffered harsh words, but also harsher blows, and the hardest torments of the cross.

2. He also illustrates the patience of Christ, both by the negation of private vengeance, because he neither repaid curses with curses, nor suffering when he threatened those bringing evils, then by the affirmation of patient expectation of divine help. He seems to look to the Prophetic saying Esai. 53. v. 7. he opened not his mouth &c. from which chapter also the preceding verse of the Apostle is sought.

3. In the final words of this verse, he was delivering to him who judges justly, is contained a new, and therefore a fourth argument of exhortation, taken from the salutary outcome of sufferings. For the Apostle signifies that it will come to pass that, just as the heavenly Father finally snatched his Son from all straits, brought his innocence into the light, and after his passion crowned him with glory and honor; so also he himself, as a just judge, will assert the innocence of his own, who are unjustly afflicted, will reward their patience, and will indeed recall the impious oppressors and slanderers to their due punishments.

4. Moreover, he meets a tacit objection with these words. The servants could have said, is therefore all cruelty of masters to be borne and approved by silent consent? Peter answers that, by the example of Christ, vengeance is to be committed to GOD.

Exposition. Ὀς λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει λοιδορεῖν is to assail someone with insults and curses, to pursue with reproaches, to reproachfully object crimes to someone; among Isocrates συνωνύμως are called λοιδορεῖν τινα & βλασφημεῖν περὶ τινος and ἀντιθετικῶς are opposed, λοιδορεῖσθαι καὶ ἐγκωμιάζεσθαι. Among Plutarch in Apopht. they are synonyms λοιδορεῖν καὶ ὀνειδίζειν. Act. 23. v. 4. for λοιδορία is held, which Paul calls the high priest a whited wall, who sitting to judge according to the law, commands to strike the innocent against the law. The LXX use for רוב contended, litigated, disputed Ex. 17. v. 2. cap. 21. v. 18. Num. 20. v. 3. Deut. 33. v. 8. The Syrian has the verb [consult facsimile image] in Ethpael, by which elsewhere he expresses the Greek κακολογεῖν Matt. 15. v. 4. Act. 19. v. 9. Therefore, by the name λοιδορίας are understood all kinds of verbal injuries brought upon Christ, insults, calumnies, curses, just as by the name παθημάτων in the following words are understood all kinds of real injuries brought upon Christ, spittings, buffets, blows, scourges, and the very punishment of the cross, in which sense also λοιδορίαι and διωγμος are joined. Luc. c. 22. v. 65. he calls those λοιδορίας blasphemies because they were poured out not against a mere man, but against the Son of God himself.

Ἀντιλοιδορεῖν signifies to return curses for curses. Cyprian renders it throughout as to curse back. The Syriac and the Vulgate rendered it simply, he did not curse. πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει, when he suffered, he did not return threats. He not only did not return curses to those cursing, but he also returned no threats to those inflicting suffering. Those who, established in prison and chains, are inflamed by the flames of private vengeance, if they cannot even by the deed itself return evil for evil, nevertheless do not restrain themselves from threats, and what they cannot put into effect because of the present state of their condition, they threaten that they will do in the future time. But Christ in his passion neither returned evil for evil, nor did he ever threaten that he would return evils. The Syriac has the word [consult facsimile image] which not only signifies he threatened: but also he lay in wait, he opposed, so that the mind of Christ might be signified as clearly alien from every desire for vengeance. Prosper to Demetrias reads, to the one striking him he did not threaten. Apostolic Canon 28 at the beginning of the verse adds, when he was struck, he did not strike back. The Apostle, however, sends us back to the Evangelical History, especially of the Lord's passion, which testifies that Christ, having been affected by the most exquisite insults and curses, nevertheless never returned any curse, any insult, or any threats. Matth. 12. v. 23.cap. 26. v. 68.cap. 27. v. 42.Ioh. 8. v. 49.cap. 18. v. 30. etc. παρεδίδου δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως. The Vulgate not only added the relative pronoun himself, but also translated it in a clearly contrary manner, he delivered himself to the one judging him unjustly. And since the Latin Vulgate version was pronounced authentic at the Council of Trent, the Papists labor in various ways from that point to defend its truth in this place. The sense, they say, this version renders conveniently, namely that Christ delivered himself to Pilate the unjust judge to be judged, contradicting nothing nor murmuring. But although a convenient sense can be extracted, it is not yet proven from it that this reading is genuine, and that the original Greek Codex is corrupted. In the same way, they say, Didymus reads in this place, Paulinus Epist. 2. Gloss. ord. & interlinear. But those followed the reading placed in the Latin Codices, without inspecting the Greek Codex. The exposition of Didymus on the Canonical Epistles, which is held in vol. 9 of the Library of the Fathers, is subject to contradiction. The genuine The genuine reading, therefore, is this, but he committed it to him who judges justly. For 1. All Greek Codices read it so. 2. In that way all Greek Fathers cite it. 3. And the better ones among the Latins. August. tract. 21. in Ioh. He commended it to him, who judges justly. Fulgentius to Thrasimundus chapter 11. But he committed it to him who judges justly. 4. The Syrian rendered it paraphrastically thus. He committed his judgment or his cause to the judge of justice. 5. The Apostle seems to look back to the Prophetic passage Ierem. 11. v. 20. where after the Prophet had said, But I was like a gentle lamb, that is led to the slaughter (by which likeness also the patience of Christ is described Esai. 53. v. 7.) he adds, but you, O Lord of Hosts, who judge justly and test the reins and hearts, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you I have committed my cause, which is repeated cap. 20. v. 12. and likewise to that which David repeats so often in the Psalms. Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness. Judge my cause. Psal. 7. v. 9. Psal. 26. v. 1. Psal. 35. v. 24. from which Psalm Christ Ioh. 15. v. 25. cites verse 19, as if spoken about his own person. 6. Hence Estius confesses, that through the carelessness of scribes, it is read in Latin Codices unjustly instead of justly. The sense, however, is that Christ did nothing out of a desire for private vengeance, but committed his cause to God the just judge.

Latin:

QUI CUM MALEDICERETUR, NON MALEDICEBAT; CUM PATERETUR, NON COMMINABATUR, TRADEBAT AUTEM IUDICANTI SE INIUSTE.

Connexio. 1. Exaggerat Apostolus passiones Christo iniustè ab hostibus illatas, distribuens eas in iniurias verbales & reales, non solùm sustinuit maledicta, sed etiam malefacta. Non solùm, passus est dura verba, sed etiam duriora verbera, & durissima crucis tormenta.

2. Illustrat etiam Christi patientiam, tùm negatione vindictae privatae, quod nec maledictis reposuerit maledicta, nec passionem inferentibus mala fuerit comminatus, tùm affirmatione patientis èxpectationis auxilii divini. Videtur respicere ad dictum Propheticum Esai. 53. v. 7. non aperuit os suum &c. ex quo capite etiam praecedens Apostoli vers. petitus.

3. In postremis huius versiculi verbis, tradebat iudicanti iustè, continetur novum, adeoque quartum exhortationis argumentum, desumtum à salutari passionum eventu. Significat enim Apostolus futurum, ut quemadmodum Pater coelestis Filium suum ex omnibus angustiis tandem eripuit, innocentiam eius in lucem protulit & post passionem gloriâ & honore eum coronavit; ita quoque ipse tanquam iustus iudex innocentiam suorum, qui iniustè affliguntur, asserat, ipsorum patientiam remuneretur, impios vero oppressores & calumniatores ad debitas poenas revocet.

4. Occurrit insuper his verbis tacitae obiectioni. Potuissent servi dicere, an ergò omnis dominorum saevitia ferenda & tacito consensu approbanda? Respondet Petrus, exemplo Christi vindictam DEO committendam esse.

Expositio. Ὀς λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει λοιδορεῖν est convitiis ac maledictis aliquem incessere, probris insectari, probrosè alicui crimina obiicere, apud Isocratem συνωνύμως dicuntur λοιδορεῖν τινα & βλασφημεῖν περὶ τινος ac ἀντιθετικῶς opponuntur, λοιδορεῖσθαι καὶ ἐγκωμιάζεσθαι. Apud Plutarchum in Apopht. synonyma sunt λοιδορεῖν καὶ ὀνειδίζειν.Act. 23. v. 4. pro λοιδορία habetur, quod Paulus summum Sacerdotem vocat parietem dealbatam, qui sedens ad iudicandum secundum legem, contra legem innocentem percutere iubeat. LXX. utuntur pro רובcontendit, litigavit, disceptavitEx. 17. v. 2.cap. 21. v. 18.Num. 20. v. 3.Deut. 33. v. 8. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] in Ethpael, quo alibi exprimit Graecum κακολογεῖνMatt. 15. v. 4.Act. 19. v. 9. Intelliguntur ergò nomine λοιδορίας omnis generis iniuriae verbales Christo illatae, convitia, calumniae, maledicta, sicut nomine παθημάτων in verbis sequentibus intelliguntur omnis generis iniuriae realès Christo illatae, sputa, colaphi, verbera, flagella, & ipsum crucis supplicium, quo sensu etiam λοιδορίαι ac διωγμος coniunguntur. Luc. c. 22. v. 65. illas λοιδορίας vocat blasphemias quia non contra nudum hominem, sed ipsum Dei Filium effundebantur.

Ἀντιλοιδορεῖν significat maledicta maledictis regerere. Cyprianus passim reddit, remaledicere. Syrus & vulgata simplieiter reddiderunt, non maledicebat.πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει, cum pateretur, non regenerabat minas. Non solùm maledicentibus non regerebat maledicta, sed etiam inferentibus passionem nullas regessit minas. Qui in carcere & vinculis constituti privatae vindictae flammis accensi sunt, illi si vel maximè opere ipso non possint malum pro malo reddere, attamen à minis sibi minimè temperant, ac quod ob praesentem conditionis suae statum effectum dare nequeunt, futuro tempore se facturos minantur. Sed Christus in passione sua nec malum malo retulit, nec aliquando mala se relaturum comminatus est. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] quod non solùm significat comminatus est: sed etiam insidiatus est, adversatus est, ut ab omni vindictae cupiditate animus Christi planè alienus significetur. Prosper ad Demetriadem legit, percutienti se non comminabatur. Canon Apostolicus 28. in principio versiculi addit, cùm percuteretur, non repercutiebat. Remittit autem nos Apostolus ad Historiam Evangelicam, praesertim passionis Dominicae, quae testatur, Christum exquisitissimis convitiis & maledictis affectum, nullum tamen maledictum, convitium nullum, minas nullas unquam regessisse. Matth. 12. v. 23.cap. 26. v. 68.cap. 27. v. 42.Ioh. 8. v. 49.cap. 18. v. 30. &c. παρεδίδου δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως. Vulgata non solùm addidit pronomen relativum se, sed etiam modo planè contrario vertit, tradebat iudicanti se iniustè. Cumque vulgata versio Latina in Concilio Tridentino pronunciaaa sit authentica, inde Pontificii variis modis laborant, ut eius veritatem hoc loco tueantur. Sensum, inquiunt, haec versio reddit commodum, videlicet quòd Christus tradiderit se Pilato iniusto iudici iudicandum, nihil contradicens nec obmurmurans. At quamvis commodus erui possit sensus, nondum tamen ex eo evincitur, hanc lectionem esse genuinam, & Codicem Graecum originalem esse corruptum. Eodem modo, inquiunt, legunt Didymus in h. l. Paulinus Epist. 2. Glossordin. & interlinearis. Atqui secuti illi sunt lectionem in Codicibus Latinis positam, non inspecto Codice Graeco. Expositio Didymi in Epistolas Canonicas, quae habetur tom. 9. Biblioth. Patrum contradictioni est obnoxia Genuina Genuina igitur lectio haec est, tradebat autem iudicanti iustè. Nam 1. Ita legunt omnes Codices Graeci. 2. Eo modo allegant omnes Patres Graeci. 3. ac potiores ex Latinis. August. tract. 21. in Ioh. Commendabat illi, qui iustè iudicat. Fulgentius ad Thrasimundum cap. 11. Commendabat autem iudicanti iustè. 4. Syrus paraphrasticè sic reddidit. Tradebat iudicium suum vel causam suam iudici iustitiae. 5. Videtur Apostolus respicere ad locum Propheticum. Ierem. 11. v. 20. ubi postquam Propheta dixerat, Ego vero fui instar agni mansueti, qui ad lanienam ducitur (qua similitudine etiam Christi patientia describitur Esai. 53. v. 7.) sub iungit, tu autem Domine Zebaoth, qui iudicas iustè & probas renes & corda, videam ultionem tuam ex eis, in te enim devolvi causam meam, quod repetitur cap. 20. v. 12. itemque ad illud, quod David in Psalmis toties repetit. Iudica me Domine secundum iustitiam meam. Iudica causam meam.Psal. 7. v. 9.Psal. 26. v. 1.Psal. 35. v. 24. ex quo Psalmo Christus Ioh. 15. v. 25. versiculum 19. allegat, tanquam de sua persona dictum. 6. Inde Estius fatetur, librariorum incuriâ in Codicibus Latinis legi iniustè pro iustè. Sensus autem est, quòd Christus nihil ex privatae vindictae cupiditate egerit, sed causam suam Deo iusto iudici commendaverit.

## 2:24
WHO HIMSELF BORE OUR SINS IN HIS BODY UPON THE TREE, THAT WE MIGHT DIE TO SINS AND LIVE TO RIGHTEOUSNESS, BY WHOSE WOUND YOU HAVE BEEN HEALED.

Connection. 1. Because the Apostle had made mention of the passion of Christ, on this occasion he digresses to an exposition of the end for which Christ sustained it, which he established as twofold, principal and less principal. The principal end is the expiation of our sins, the less principal is the holy conversation of the faithful.

2. He specially adapts both this end as a salutary effect to the servants whom he addresses, saying, by whose wound you have been healed. He mentions the wound and weals by name, because servants were scourged by wicked masters, from which scourges they brought back weals. He warns them, therefore, that they should patiently tolerate weals, following the example of Christ who was unjustly scourged.

3. By the word healing he teaches that faithful servants both benefits that we have obtained from the passion of Christ, namely the remission of sins, and the restoration of nature corrupted by sin. Both benefits ought to be an incentive to them for a holy conversation, of which a not insignificant part is obedience toward masters, and the patient tolerance of injuries. For this reason, sins have been remitted to us on account of Christ, and our nature has been healed and renewed through Christ, so that henceforth we may send a message of farewell to sin and live for righteousness.

4. Such a connection can also be given. The Apostle had said in v. 22 that Christ was entirely devoid of every sin, both original and actual; now he shows the reason for which it was necessary that Christ our Mediator should be holy, innocent, undefiled, separate from sinners Hebr. 7. v. 26., namely so that he might be suitable to satisfy for the sins of others, and by his passion reconcile the whole human race to the heavenly Father.

5. The Apostle had said that Christ, having suffered for us, left us an example, that we should follow his footsteps. Lest anyone, therefore, should think that this is either the only or the principal end of the Lord's passion, he therefore adds, that Christ bore our sins in his body upon the tree. He teaches, therefore, that not a mere example of patience is proposed to us in the passion of Christ, but also that his passion is meritorious and satisfactory for our sins, and indeed that this is the power of the passion and death of Christ, that it might mortify our flesh, so that henceforth we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness.

6. The Apostle opposes the impatience of servants subjected to unjust masters, and the patience of Christ the Savior, whose faith they profess: he signifies that the former is in many ways harmful, not only to the servants themselves, but also to others, whom they harm by their example: but he says that the latter was in many ways salutary, not only to Christ himself, who through passion entered into glory, but also to the whole human race, for whose sins he satisfied, and especially to those who truly believe in Christ, in whom he mortified sin, so that henceforth they might live for righteousness.

7. He meets the complaints of the servants. Bruises and welts presuppose blows, lashes, contusions, etc.; therefore, this is what Peter wishes to say. There is no reason for you to complain about your blows, lashes, and scourges; Christ likewise endured such scourges, and indeed far harsher ones. Even the harshest servitude will not hinder your salvation, in Christ is the salvation laid up for you, to which the sufferings brought upon you without merit are promoting you, so far is it from being overturned by them.

Exposition ὁς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον, The Apostle looks back to chapter 53 of Isaiah, which he had also cited in the preceding verses. v. 4. Surely he hath borne our griefs הוא נשא and carried our sorrows, סבלם he hath borne them, v. 6. the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. v. 11. he shall bear their iniquities. הוא יסבל v. 12. he bare the sin of many, נשא where the LXX not only have the word Φέβει v. 4. ἀνοίσει v. 10. but also ἀνήνεγκεν v. 12. which Peter uses in this place. He also looks back to the saying of John the Baptist John 1. v. 29. Behold the Lamb of God, ὁ αἴρων bearing and taking away, taking upon himself, and lifting up the sin of the world. The little word αὐτὸς has great emphasis, whence the Prophet repeats it so often. Surely he hath borne our griefs הוא v. 4. והוא and he was wounded for our iniquities. v. 5. והוא and he was afflicted. v. 7. he shall bear their iniquities. הוא v. 11. והוא and he bare the sin of many. v. 12. The Prophet, and with him the Apostle, sends us back to the first Evangelical promise concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the serpent, to which is added the prophecy concerning the passion, and he shall lie in wait for his heel. Gen. 3. v. 15. I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed, הוא αὐτὸς it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel. It also signifies that Christ himself in his own person, and indeed alone, rendered full satisfaction for our sins, just as it is said Isa. 63. v. 3. I have trodden the winepress alone. ch. 43. v. 25. I, even I, הוא am he that blotteth out thy transgressions. LXX ἐγὼ εἰμὶ αὐτὸς. Heb. 1. v. 3. he made purification of our sins δι' έαυτοῦ, by himself; he did not offer an alien sacrifice, as the Priests of the Old Testament, but he himself in his own body bore our sins, he did not lay them upon the scapegoat, Lev. 16. v. 21. but he himself took them upon himself, so that he might present himself to the heavenly Father as a sacrifice for them. The word ἀνήνεγκεν formed from ἀναφέρομαι properly signifies to lift on high, to lift up, to raise up, so that ἀνήνεγκεν is the same as ἄνωσε ἤνεγκεν, Matt. 17. v. 1. Mark 9. v. 2. it is used of elevation onto a mountain, Luke 24. v. 51. of elevation into heaven. The Apostle therefore sends us back first to the sacrifices of the O.T. concerning which the word ἀναφέρειν is used Heb. 7. v. 27. James 2. v. 21. and by the LXX Interpreters

passim. For just as the guilt owed by the sinner in the O. T. was transferred onto the victim, which was offered in the sinner's place: so Christ took upon Himself our sins, and the curse owed to our sins, so that He might expiate our sins, and take away from us the curse owed to our sins. Hence Luther rightly rendered it. Christus hat unsere Su nde selbst geopffert. Secondly to the cross, on which Christ offered Himself to GOD the Father as a sacrifice for our sins, whence the Apostle also explicitly adds ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον. The cross of Christ was that sublime altar, onto which Christ ascended to offer Himself as a sacrifice, just as Isaac was led onto a high mountain to be offered as a burnt offering to GOD, Genes. 22. v. 2. and just as the sacrifices of the O. T. were placed upon the altar. Hence also the word ἀνήνεγκεν is used elsewhere by the Holy Spirit concerning this sacrifice of Christ offered on the altar of the cross for our sins. Hebr. 7. v. 27. εἁυτὸν ἀνενέγκας, cap. 9. vers. 28. Christ offered once εἰ τὸ ἑολλῶν ὲνεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας. Thirdly to the passage Esa. 53. v. 4. where for that which is in the Hebrew, truly He has borne our infirmities, the LXX have. He bears our sins for us. The Syrian attempted to express the emphasis of this word with two terms, [consult facsimile image] he bore all sins [consult facsimile image] and made them ascend with his body to the cross. [consult facsimile image] is for the Syrians, he carried, he bore, as a great burden and weight, since for the Hebrews שקל signifies, he weighed, he balanced. It is signified, therefore, that Christ took upon Himself our sins, as a most heavy burden and intolerable to a naked man, and that with, and under this burden of all our sins, or of the whole human race, He ascended the cross, which burden pressed Him so harshly that He cried out on the cross, My God, why have You forsaken me! [consult facsimile image] is the same as העולה he made to ascend, Marc. 9. v. 1. Hebr. 13. v. 20. from the root [consult facsimile image] he ascended, Ioh. 7. v. 8. Matth. 13. v. 2. It is signified, therefore, that Christ had not yet laid down the weight of our sins taken upon Himself when He ascended the wood of the cross, but that He carried our sins with Him onto the cross, and sustaining death on the cross, He provided the fullest satisfaction for them. Nor should it be omitted that the Apostle says that Christ bore τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, where the little word ἡμῶν is very emphatic. For it signifies not only that Christ ascended the cross not for his own sins, which he did not have, v. 22. but for our sins, but also by that change of the second person (which the Apostle had used in the preceding verses, v. 20. 21.) into the first, he insinuates that Christ suffered not only for the servants, whom he addresses particularly here, but also for the whole Church, nay, for the whole human race. Bede observes, that Peter includes himself, and asserts that Christ died on the altar of the cross for his sins also. Whereas above, he says, he had made his discourse specially to servants, now he admonishes generally, that even masters may call to memory what GOD and Lord endured for them. Nay, he instructs the whole Church, what its author endured for its liberation. For he does not say your sins, but with himself added, who, he says, himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree. The indefinite proposition, that Christ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν bore, the Syrian rightly explained by a universal, that he carried all our sins, because John 1. v. 29. it is said to have taken away the sin of the world, and 1. John 2. v. 2. it is said, a propitiation for the sins of the whole world. But that it is said he bore our sins in his body, is not to be taken exclusively, as if he bore the punishments due to our sins in his body alone, but by the body συνεκδοχικῶς is understood the whole human Nature of Christ, consisting of body and soul, because his most holy soul also labored, Isa. 53. v. 11. and Christ laid down his soul for sin, v. 10. and poured it out unto death, v. 12. but mention is made specially of the body, because that hung visibly on the cross, of which Peter speaks, and the pains which Christ endured in the body fall more into the eyes and senses. That by τὸ ξύλον is determinately understood that wood of the cross, to which the body of Christ was affixed, the added article shows, whence the Syrian rendered it by [consult facsimile image] which signifies crucifixion and cross, ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις απογινόμενοι τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσωμεν. The word ἀπογινόμενοι Ambrose rendered separated, made apart. But without doubt Peter wished by it to express the Pauline ἀποθάνοντνες, Rom. 6. v. 10. for as there the Apostle joins, to be dead to sin, and to live to GOD, which he afterwards v. 22. explains, to be freed from sin, and made a servant to GOD; so also Peter in this place joins, to be dead to sin, and to live to righteousness ἀπογάνεσθαι therefore here it is to be taken from the midst, To die, as if you were to say to be undone, in that sense in which this word is opposed to τῷ to be made, and τῷ to live, as the subject antithesis shows. The dative ἁμαρτίαις here expresses the thing from which something is taken away, for it is signified that we are dead to sins, i.e., exempted from their dominion and yoke, so that it may no longer rule and live in us, nor we live to it, but to righteousness, to which Christ has reformed us by his death. But when the Apostle says in this place that Christ therefore died for our sins on the altar of the cross, that we, being dead to sins, might live to righteousness, he signifies that Christ not only died on the cross to expiate our sins and obtain for us their forgiveness, which benefit pertains to justification and regeneration, but also that he might mortify sin in us and reform us to a life of righteousness and holy conversation, which benefit pertains to sanctification and renewal. He also repeats the principal proposition and proposes a tacit exhortation, that because we are dead to sins through Christ and in Christ, that is, freed from the guilt and dominion of sins, we should henceforth have no commerce with sin, but live to righteousness, that is, we should exercise the works of righteousness, and since the obedience of servants toward their masters and patience in enduring injuries is a certain part of that righteousness, he therefore exhorts them by this very thing to obedience and patience. οὗν τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἰάθητε. This is taken from Isa. 53. ver. 5. By his stripes we are healed, that is, his stripe was health to us. The LXX μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἡμεῖς ἰάθημεν Peter repeats the relative pronoun twice οὗ τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ, by a pleonasm customary to the Hebrews, and changes the first person into the second, because he applies the general sentence of the Prophet specifically to those to whom he writes. The interlinear Gloss ignorantly takes the little word of stripe concerning the envy of the Jews; by his stripe you are healed, it says, either by his flesh made livid in the passion, or because the Jews adjudged him to death for envy alone. For Peter does not treat here of the envy of the Jews, but of the wounds and blows which Christ sustained in his body. The Hebrew חבורה which the Prophet uses signifies a stripe, a sore, or an aposteme, in which blood or matter is collected, from the root חבר to be associated, to be collected. Gen. 4. v. 23. Exod. 21. v. 25. Ps. 38. v. 6. Isa. 1. v. 6.
