Lyranus in this place: Not rendering evil for evil in injurious deeds, nor evil word for curse in contentious words.

Λοιδορίαν The Vulgate rendered it by curse, it is more correctly translated reviling, since λοιδορεῖν is properly to pursue someone with revilings and reproaches, whether he be present or absent. Isocrates, in the encomium of Busiris, λοιδορεῖν τινα & βλασφημεῖν περί τινος joins them as synonyms, and in the same place λοιδορουμένους καί ἐγκωμιασμένους opposes them to one another. The Syriac has the noun [consult facsimile image] reviling, contumely, opprobrium. Parallel places to this Apostolic exhortation exist Prov. 24. v. 29.Do not say, as he has done to me, so I will do to him, I will repay each one according to his work.Prov. 20. v. 22.Do not say, I will repay evil for evil.Rom. 12. v. 17.Rendering to no one evil for evil.v. 19.not avenging yourselves.v. 21.Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.1. Thess. 5. v. 15. See that no one renders evil for evil to anyone.

τουναντίον δέ εὐλογοῦντες. The Vulgate rendered it blessing. To bless, however, in this place is to pray well, or to pray for all good things. This precept is opposed to the second member of the previous prohibition. If any pursue you with revilings and reproaches, you on the contrary pray well for them, by pouring out prayers to God for them, by praying for all the most auspicious things for them, and by making an honest mention of them before others. Parallel places exist Matth. 5. v. 44.Love your enemies, Do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.Luke 6. verse 27.Do good to those who hate you.verse 28.Bless those who curse you, and pray for those who slander you.Rom. 12. verse 14.Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.

Ἐιδόντες, ὃτι εἰς τοῦτο ἐκλήθητε, ἳνα εὐλογὶαν κληρονομήσητε The Vulgate, as also the Syriac, plainly omit the participle εἰδόντες. But it is emphatic. For Peter admonishes those to whom he writes that they should call to mind the end of their calling. Some refer that εἰς τοῦτο to the preceding things in this sense: To this you were called, that you might bless those who revile you, and thus patiently bear injuries brought upon you without merit. By this reasoning, that ἳνα, which follows will depend upon the participles ὰποδιδόντες, εὐλογοῦντες.. Some, however, join it with the following things by apposition: To this you were called, that you might obtain a blessing by inheritance. Thus, therefore, the sense will be: Because you were called to obtain a spiritual and heavenly blessing by right of inheritance, therefore know that you were also called to bless. Although both senses are convenient and conformable to the analogy of faith, since the pious, by the very fact that they were called to Christianity, were called to bless and do good, and since the promise of a blessing to be obtained by inheritance can and ought to be a most powerful stimulus to blessing, the latter sense nevertheless approaches more closely to the context. For Peter alludes to the words of Christ Matt. 25. verse 34.Come, you blessed of my Father, κληρονομήσατε the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. He therefore exhorts the pious to bless their neighbors even when they are cursing, with an argument taken from the end of the calling to inherit a blessing, so that the sense may be: Those who ought one day to inherit the heavenly kingdom, they are blessed and children of blessing, not only passively but also actively, receiving spiritual blessing from God through faith, and in turn blessing others out of charity.

For the word ἐκλήθητε a certain old book reads ἐκληρώθητε,, so that there is an allusion to the distribution of the land of Canaan made by lot, to which the word κληρονομεῖν also refers us. But all the remaining Greek and Latin codices have ἐκλήθητε you were called, in which way the Syriac also reads.

By εὐλογὶαν is understood directly and principally eternal life, to the inheritance of which the pious have been called through the Gospel, and which is the ultimate scope toward which the pious strive through faith and good works: meanwhile, nothing prevents the name εὐλογίας from being understood in a general sense as benefits of every kind, bodily and spiritual, earthly and heavenly, temporal and eternal, which are conferred upon believers in Christ out of grace in this life and the future one, just as the Apostle says Ephes. 1. vers. 3., Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in CHRIST. To this εὐλογίαν also pertains that which is promised by Christ Matth. 6. v. 15. to those who forgive injuries to their neighbor. If you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. Those things are called blessing by metonymy, because they are the effects of divine blessing. Gen. 33. v. 11. Jacob says to his brother Esau: Receive the blessing that I have brought to you, i.e., gifts from the divine blessing given to me. Therefore, the Apostle also calls those benefits divinely bestowed and to be bestowed upon the pious, especially eternal happiness and glory, εὐλογίαν, so that there may be an elegant antanaclasis in the participle εὐλογοῦντες and the word εὐλογίας.

Τό κληρονομεῖν seems to be placed both to express the manner by which we obtain heavenly benefits and eternal life, namely through gratuitous υἱοθεσίαν Iohan. 1. v. 12.Rom. 8. vers. 17. and to insinuate perpetuity, as if the Apostle had said that it would not be well for us for only a short time, but always and perpetually, if we bear injuries patiently and pray well for those who harm us, for those things which we obtain by inheritance, we possess perpetually.

Latin:

NON REDDENTES MALUM PRO MALO, NEC MALEDICTUM PRO MALEDICTO, SED E CONTRARIO BENEDICENTES, QUIA IN HOC VOCATI ESTIS, UT BENEDICTIONEM HEREDITATE POSSIDEATIS.

Connexio. 1. Sexta haec est virtus, ad quam Apostolus Christianos hortatur, videl. iniuriarum tolerantia & εὐλογία, quâ pro iniuriis & maledictis benedictionem verè pii reponunt.

2. Virtutes in vers. praecedente enumeratae, omnes pertinent ad Christianam & fraternam caritatem, illi vero extremè adversatur privatae vindictae cupiditas. Ne ergò pii adversariorum iniuriis & calumniis patiantur se ad vindictae cupiditatem impelli, requirit ab illis Apostolus patientiam, absque quâ caritas conservari minimè poterit.

3. Lyranus sic progreditur. Hîc consequenter Apostolus ordinat fideles in perpessione mali, in quo quis potest dupliciter deordinari, uno modo per audaciam vicem rependendo, alio modo per timorem in pusillanimitatem decidendo. Primum removet v. 10. secundum v. 13. Prima pars subdividitur in duas, quia primò monet vicem non rependere v. 10. secundo inducit ad hoc autoritatem Scripturae v. 11.

Textus dispositio: Primùm iniurias, quae piis à coelestis veritatis adversariis inferantur, distribuit Apostolus in duas species, quòd quaedam sint reales, quaedam verbales. Utrasque patienter à piis tolerandas esse praecipit. Secundò exhortationem suam amplificat antithesi & quadam exaggeratione. Pii non solùm non debent malum pro malo, nec male dictum pro male dicto reddere, sed insuper etiam illis, à quibus laesi sunt, benedicere. Tertiò subiicit duo exhortationis argumenta. Prius petitum est à DEI voluntate, DEUS ad hoc vos vocavit, ut in perferendis adversariorum iniuriis vestram probetis patientiam. Posterius à consequente salutari, quod est divinae benedictionis hereditas. Potest tamen utrumque argumentum commodè coniungi, ut dicatur ratio exhortationis petita ab insigni illo DEI beneficio, qui nos, cum adhuc essemus ipsius inimici, temporali & aeterna maledictione omninò digni, per Evangelium in regnum gratiae vocavit, ut non solùm à nobis maledictionem auferret, sed etiam coelestem benedictionem, adeoque omnium bonorum spiritualium & coelestium hereditatem in nos conferret. Eph. 1. v. 3.Gal. 3. v. 8. & seqq.

Textus expositio, Μὴ ὰποδιδόντες κακὸν αντὶ κακοῦ ἣ λοιδορίαν ἀντὶ λοιδορίας. Vivebant Christiani in medio infidelium, qui & factis & verbis ipsis erant molesti, praemonet igitur ipsos, ne ex vindictae cupiditate malefacta malefactis & convitia convitiis rependant. Glossa interlin. Non reddentes malum pro malo in actu, nec maledictum pro maledicto in verbis. Lyranus in h. l. Non reddentes malum pro malo in factis iniuriosis, nec male dictum pro maledicto in verbis contentiosis.

Λοιδορίαν Vulgata reddidit, per maledictum, rectiùs vertitur convitium, cum λοιδορεῖν propriè sit convitiis & probris aliquem insectari, sive praesens sit sive absens. Isocrat, in Busiridis encomio, λοιδορεῖν τινα & βλασφημεῖν περί τινος tanquam Synonyma coniungit, ibidemque λοιδορουμένους καί ἐγκωμιασμένους invicem opponit. Syrus habet nomen [consult facsimile image]convitium, contumelia, opprobrium. Loca huic Apostolicae exhortationi parallela extant Prov. 24. v. 29.Ne dicas, quomodo fecit mihi, sic faciam ei, rependam unicuique iuxta opus suum.Prov. 20. v. 22.Ne dicas, reddam malum pro malo.Rom. 12. v. 17.Nulli malum pro malo reddentes.v. 19.non vindicantes vosmetipsos.v. 21.Noli vinci à malo, sed vince in bono malum.1. Thess. 5. v. 15. Videte, ne quis malum pro malo alicui reddat.

τουναντίον δέ εὐλογοῦντες. Vulgata reddidit benedicentes. Benedicere autem hoc loco est benè precari, sive bona quaeque adprecari. Opponitur hoc praeceptum secundo membro superioris prohibitionis. Si qui convitiis & probris vos insectantur, vos è contrario eis bene precemini, pro ipsis ad Deum preces fundendo, faustissima quaeque ipsis adprecando, & honestam eorum mentionem apud alios faciendo. Loca parallela extant Matth. 5. v. 44.Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos, & orate pro persequentibus & calumniantibus vos.Luc. 6. vers. 27.Benefacite his qui oderunt vos.vers. 28.Benedicite devoventibus vos, & orate pro calumniantibus vos.Rom. 12. vers. 14.Benedicite persequentibus vos, benedicite & nolite maledicere.

Ἐιδόντες, ὃτι εἰς τοῦτο ἐκλήθητε, ἳνα εὐλογὶαν κληρονομήσητε Vulgata ut & Syrus participium εἰδόντες planè omittunt. Sed est emphaticum. Admonet enim Petrus eos, ad quos scribit, ut in memoriam sibi revocent finem suae vocationis. Quidam illud εἰς τοῦτο referunt ad praecedentia hoc sensu. In hoc vocati estis, ut benedicatis iis, qui vobis conviciantur, adeoque iniurias praeter meritum vobis illatas patienter feratis. Hac ratione illud ἳνα, quod sequitur, pendebit à participiis ὰποδιδόντες, εὐλογοῦντες. Quidam vero illud coniungunt cum sequentibus per appositionem, In hoc vocati estis, ut benedictionem hereditate consequamini. Sic ergò erit sensus. Quia vocati estis ad benedictionem spiritualem & coelestem hereditatis iure obtinendam, ideo sciatis, vos etiam vocatos esse ad benedicendum. Quamvis vero uterque sensus sit commodus & analogiae fidei conformis, cum pii eo ipso quando vocati sunt ad Christianismum, vocati sint ad benedicendum & benefaciendum, cumque promissio benedictionis per hereditatem obtinendae stimulus fortissimus esse possit ac debeat ad benedicendum, posterior tamen sensus magis accedit ad contextum. Alludit enim Petrus ad verba Christi Matth. 25. vers. 34.Venite benedicti Patris mei,κληρονομήσατεparatum vobis regnum à constitutione mundi. Hortatur igitur pios ad benedicendum proximis etiam maledicentibus, argumento ex fine vocationis ad benedictionem hereditandam desumto, ut sit sensus. Qui coeleste regnum aliquando hereditare debent, illi sunt benedicti ac filii benedictionis, non solùm passivè sed etiam activè, benedictionem spiritualem à Deo per fidem recipientes, & vicissim aliis ex caritate benedicentes.

Pro verbo ἐκλήθητε vetus quidam liber legit ἐκληρώθητε, ut alludatur ad distributionem terrae Canaan per sortem factam, ad quam etiam vox κληρονομεῖν nos remittit. Sed reliqui Codices omnes Graeci ac Latini habent ἐκλήθητεvocati estis, quo modo etiam legit Syrus.

Per εὐλογὶαν directè & principaliter intelligitur vita aeterna, ad cuius hereditatem pii per Evangelium vocati sunt, quaeque est ultimus scopus, ad quem pii per fidem & bona opera contendunt: interim nihil obstat, quò minùs εὐλογίας nomine in genere intelligantur omnis generis beneficia corporalia & spiritualia, terrena & coelestia, temporalia & aeterna, quae credentibus in Christum ex gratia in hac & futurâ vitâ conferuntur, sicut Apostolus Ephes. 1. vers. 3. dicit, Benedictus Deus & pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nos in omni benedictione spirituali in coelestibus in CHRISTO. Ad hanc εὐλογίαν pertinet etiam illa, quae à Christo Matth. 6. v. 15. condonantibus proximo iniurias promittitur. Si hominibus remiseritis delicta, etiam pater coelestis vobis remittet. Vocantur autem illa benedictio per metonymiam, quia sunt divinae benedictionis effectus. Gen. 33. v. 11. dicit Iacobus ad Esavum fratrem. Suscipe-benedictionem, quam attuli tibi i. e. munera ex benedictione divina mihi data. Ideo quoque Apostolus beneficia illa in pios divinitùs collata & conferenda, praesertim aeternam felicitatem & gloriam, vocat εὐλογίαν, ut sit elegans antanaclasis in participio εὐλογοῦντες & voce εὐλογίας.

Τό κληρονομεῖν positum videtur tùm ad exprimendum modum, quo beneficia coelestia & vitam aeternam consequimur, videlicet per gratuitam υἱοθεσίανIohan. 1. v. 12.Rom. 8. vers. 17. tùm ad insinuandam perpetuitatem, ac si dixisset Apostolus nobis non ad breve modò tempus benè fore, sed semper ac perpetuò, si iniurias patienter feramus, & illis, qui nos laedunt, benè precemur, quae enim per hereditatem consequimur, ea perpetuò possidemus.

## 3:10
FOR HE WHO WANTS TO LOVE LIFE AND SEE GOOD DAYS, LET HIM RESTRAIN HIS TONGUE FROM EVIL, AND HIS LIPS, LEST THEY SPEAK DECEIT.

Connection. 1. The Apostle confirms the argument of the exhortation proposed at the end of the preceding verse with the testimony of Scripture from Psal. 34., in which is contained the divine promise made to those who patiently tolerate injuries brought upon them, which, since it is of infallible truth, Therefore the pious can safely rely upon it with true confidence. Lyranus on this passage. Here the Apostle consequently introduces the authority of Scripture to the purpose.

2. The Apostle had said, not only that evil is not to be rendered for evil in deeds, but not even railing for railing in words; the Royal Psalmist exhorts us to that very thing in the cited saying, namely that we ought to restrain our tongue from evil.

3. The Apostle had said that we must pray well for those who harm us either by words or deeds, since we know that we are called to this, that we may obtain a blessing, i.e., that it may be well with us both in this life and in the future, that we may lead a peaceful life in this age with a good conscience, and that when the course of this life is finished we may attain the heavenly inheritance. But we cannot lead a peaceful and tranquil life in this age, and live peaceably with our neighbor, if everything is cut to the quick, but if injuries are muttered, which is what the Apostle confirms from the cited testimony of David.

4. A new argument for exhortation can also be established here, sought from the useful consequence. Those who patiently tolerate injuries and commit vengeance to God live much more tranquilly than those who strive to repel evil with evil, and to repay railings with railings.

5. Although the saying of the Psalmist is indeed alleged by the Apostle chiefly and principally to that end, that he may confirm that injuries brought on without merit are to be borne patiently, at the same time, however, he exhorts in general to the pursuit of justice and holiness, since that promise was made not only to those who patiently tolerate injuries, but in general to all who strive for justice and holiness.

Disposition. In this verse the Apostle teaches what vices of the tongue must be avoided by those who desire to lead a blessed life in this and the future age, namely: 1. That they ought not to be contumelious, indulging in the petulance of the tongue, and returning railings for railings. 2. That they ought not to be fraudulent and deceitful, bringing forth one thing with the tongue, but truly bearing another thing hidden in the heart. Lyranus disposes it thus. He who wishes to see good days. 1. Let him restrain his tongue from evil, so that he does not render a curse for a curse openly. 2. And let his lips not speak guile against one who is speaking evil to him by plotting evil in secret.

Exposition of the text. Ὁ γὰρ θέλων ζωτὴν ἀγαπᾷν &c. This testimony is taken from Psalm 34, verse 13, which in Hebrew word for word is as follows. What man is he that desireth lives (or who desires life, for חיים is plural only) loving days to see (or that he may see) good. verse 14 Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile. The LXX rendered it thus. τίς ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος ὁ θέλων ζωὴν, ἀγαπῶν ἡμέρας ἰδεῖν ἀγαθὰς, παῦσον τὴν γλώσσάν σου ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ χείλη σου τοῦ μὴ λαλῆσαι δὸλον. Peter brings it forward in this manner. ὁ γαρ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾷν, καὶ ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς, παυσάτω τὴν γλῶσσαν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ χείλη αὐτοῦ τοῦ μὴ λαλῆσαι δόλον. From this comparison it appears that between the Hebrew and the Greek, both of the Old and New Testament, there is no difference as to the sense, yet in the meantime Peter departs a little from the words of the Psalmist. 1. The Psalmist shapes the sentence by an interrogation. What man is he that desireth life? But Peter brings forth the same by a simple enunciation. He that desires life, let him restrain his tongue. 2. The Psalmist speaks in the second person, keep thy tongue from evil. Peter changes it into the third person. Let him restrain his tongue from evil. Therefore, what is said in the Psalm by apostrophe and by communication is here brought forth simply, and thus the scheme or figure of the sentence is changed. 3. Peter uses a certain transposition of words. The LXX, following the Hebrew text, or certainly not differing much from it, speak thus. τίς ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος ὁ θέλων ζωὴν, ἀγαπῶν ἡμὲρας ἰδεῖν ἀγαθὰς. But Peter changes the order, rendering the text thus. ὁ γαρ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾶν, καὶ ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς. The sense remains unchanged in both places.

Ὁ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾶν. He that desires to love life, i.e., he who both desires and loves life, or he who by loving loves, i.e., vehemently loves life. It is a Hebrew phrase, the emphasis of which is expressed in David by the word חפץ, which does not signify simply he willed, but he willed with desire, good pleasure, and delight, Gen. 34, v. 19 Psal. 147, v. 10 Is. 62, v. 4. The Syrian rendered it by [consult facsimile image] he had pleasure, it was well-pleasing. By the noun ζωὴν placed absolutely, is understood not just any life, but a blessed, tranquil, pleasant, and long-lived one, for which is required above all a good conscience. For he is said properly to live, who cheerfully and lives pleasantly, Job 21. v. 5. Why do the wicked live, i. e. act prosperously. Prov. 16. v. 15. In the joyfulness of the King's countenance is life, i. e. happiness and prosperity, he who has a good and tranquil conscience, which alone can render life pleasant. Nor is the discourse only about the life of this age, but also and especially about the blessed life in the future age, which alone is truly life, so that the sense may be: He who seeks to lead a tranquil life in this age, and to become an heir of eternal life at some time. Hence the interlinear gloss explains it thus: He who wishes to show that he has a blessing. John Huss: He who wishes for life, i. e. the blessed one, in which no one dies. Some think that this very thing is insinuated in David by the plural חיים he who wishes for lives, that is, a tranquil one in this, and a blessed one in the future age. But חיים is only a plural.

Καὶ ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς. By good days are understood tranquil and prosperous days, just as on the contrary evil days are full of hardship and calamitous. Gen. 47. v. 9. Some accept it only concerning eternal life, since in this life there are evil days. Clement of Alexandria: Good days are none but eternal ones. John Huss: He who wishes to see good days, namely in heavenly beatitude, where days are not interrupted by nights. Apoc. 21. v. 15. The days of eternal glory are called good, in distinction to the present life, which are evil, Eph. 5. v. 16. Days are also spoken of in the plural in the heavenly fatherland, not because of succession, which is none there, but because of infinite duration. But in both members the discourse is about a tranquil and blessed life, both in this and in the future age. The Hebrew in David properly has it thus: What man is he that desires days to see good, namely in them? i. e. Who desires a long life to that end, that he may enjoy many good things in it? Who seeks a long and happy life? The Syrian, having followed the Hebrew text, translates it thus: Who loves good days to see or to see.

Παυσάτω τὴν γλῶσσαν αὐτοῦ ἐπὸ κακοῦ let him cause to rest, or let him restrain his tongue from evil, i. e. let him temper himself from insults and calumnies, let him not disparage his neighbor with his tongue. In the Hebrew is placed the verb נצר, which signifies he guarded, preserved, fortified, and includes singular care. Deut. 32. v. 10. he guarded them as the apple of the eye. The Syrian has a cognate verb [consult facsimile image] he guarded with great zeal. Psalm

119. v. 22. καὶ χεὶλη αὐτοῦ. The Vulgate rendered it, and his lips, that is, let them be so ruled. But in the Greek there is a reciprocal pronoun, and his own lips, that is, let him restrain, so that the noun χείλη may be governed by the preceding verb παυσάτω, and not be in the Nominative case, but in the Genitive, as is evident from the Hebrew, Greek, and Syriac text.

Τοῦ μὴ λαλῆσαι δόλον, Namely ἕνεκα, that they speak no guile, that he may not bring forth one thing outwardly with his mouth, while he suppresses another inwardly in his heart. The Syriac has the verb [consult facsimile image] which signifies craftiness, the thought of evil in the heart. Thus, therefore, the Royal Psalmist, and Peter after him, prohibits two sins of the tongue. First, evil-speaking, which is an injury of the manifest tongue against a neighbor. Second, guileful speech, which is a hidden and occult injury. Under these species, however, συνεκδοχικῶς all other sins of the tongue ought to be understood as prohibited, and the contrary virtues as commanded, according to the customary Hebraism. But especially ἀντιθετικῶς is to be understood as commanded εὐλογία, to which, by the allegation of this Davidic saying, the Apostle especially wished to exhort those to whom he writes.

Latin:

QUI ENIM VULT VITAM DILIGERE & DIES VIDERE BONOS, COERCEAT LINGUAM SUAM A MALO, & LABIA EIUS, NE LOQUANTUR DOLUM.

Connexio. 1. Argumentum exhortationis in fine praecedentis versiculi propositum, confirmat Apostolus testimonio Scripturae ex Psal. 34. in quo continetur divina promissio illis facta, qui patienter iniurias sibi illatas tolerant, quae cum sit infallibilis veritatis, ideò pii verâ fiduciâ tutò illi inniti possunt. Lyranus ad hunc locum. Hîc consequenter inducit Apostolus ad propositum autoritatem Scripturae.

2. Dixerat Apostolus, non solùm non esse reddendum malum pro malo in factis, sed nec convitium pro convitio in dictis, ad illud ipsum nos hortatur Regius Psaltes in allato dicto, videlicet quòd linguam nostram à malo coërcere debeamus.

3. Dixerat Apostolus, benè precandum illis, qui vel verbis vel factis nos laedunt, cum sciamus nos in hoc vocatos, ut benedictionem consequamur i. e. ut & in hac & in futura vita nobis benè sit, ut bonâ conscientiâ pacatam in hoc seculo vitam agamus, & exacto huius vitae curriculo hereditatem coelestem adeamus. Pacatam autem & tranquillam in hoc seculo vitam traducere, & cum proximo pacificè vivere non possumus, si omnia ad vivum resecentur, sed si iniuriae mussitentur, id quod Apostolus ex citato Davidis testimonio confirmat.

4. Potest etiam hîc statui novum exhortationis argumentum, à consequente utili petitum. Qui iniurias patienter tolerant & vindictam Deo committunt, multò tranquilliùs vivunt, quàm qui malum malo propulsare, & convitia convitiis pensare satagunt.

5. Quamvis vero dictum Psalmographi praecipuè ac principaliter eo fine ab Apostolo allegetur, ut confirmet, iniurias praeter meritum illatas esse patienter ferendas, simul tamen in genere ad studium iustitiae & sanctitatis hortatur, cum promissio illa facta sit non solùm illis, qui patienter iniurias tolerant, sed in genere omnibus, qui iustitiae & sanctitati student.

Dispositio. Docet in hoc versiculo Apostolus, quae linguae vitia cavenda sint illis, qui beatam in hoc & futuro seculo vitam traducere cupiunt, videlicet. 1. Quòd non debeant esse contumeliosi, petulantiae linguae indulgentes, & convitia convitiis regerentes. 2. Quod non debeant esse fraudulenti ac dolosi, aliud quidem linguâ proferentes, aliud vero in corde absconditum gerentes. Lyranus sic disponit. Qui vult dies videre bonos. 1. Coërceat linguam à malo, ut non reddat maledictum pro maledicto in aperto. 2. Et labia eius non loquantur dolum contra maledicentem sibi machinando malum in occulto.

Textus expositio. Ὁ γὰρ θέλων ζωτὴν ἀγαπᾷν &c. Testimonium hoc petitum ex Psalm. 34. vers. 13. quod in Hebraeo ad verbum sic habet. Quis vir volens vitas (vel qui vult vitam,חיים enim est plurale tantùm) diligens dies ad videndum (vel ut videat) bonum.vers. 14.Custodi linguam tuam à malo, & labia tua à loquendo dolum. LXX. sic reddiderunt. τίς ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος ὁ θέλων ζωὴν, ἀγαπῶν ἡμέρας ἰδεῖν ἀγαθὰς, παῦσον τὴν γλώσσάν σου ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ χείλη σου τοῦ μὴ λαλῆσαι δὸλον. Petrus hoc modo adducit. ὁ γαρ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾷν, καὶ ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς, παυσάτω τὴν γλῶσσαν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ χείλη αὐτοῦ τοῦ μὴ λαλῆσαι δόλον. Ex hac collatione apparet, inter Hebraea & Graeca, tùm V. tùm N. Test. quoad sensum nihil esse discriminis, interim tamen Petrum à verbis Psaltis paululùm recedere. 1. Psalmographus sententiam figurat per interrogationem. Quis vir volens vitam? Sed Petrus per simplicem enunciationem eandem profert. Qui vult vitam, coërceat linguam. 2. Psalmographus loquitur in secunda persona, custodi linguam à malo. Petrus eam mutat in tertiam personam. Coërceat linguam à malo. Quòd ergò in Psalmo dicitur per apostrophen, & per communicationem, id hîc simpliciter profertur, & sic sententiae schema seu figura mutatur. 3. Petrus utitur quadam verborum transpositione. LXX. secuti textum Hebraeum, vel certè non multùm ab eo abludentes, sic loquuntur. τίς ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος ὁ θέλων ζωὴν, ἀγαπῶν ἡμὲρας ἰδεῖν ἀγαθὰς. Sed Petrus ordinem mutat, textum sic reddens. ὁ γαρ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾶν, καὶ ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς. Sensus utrobique manet invariatus.

Ὁ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾶν.Qui vult diligere vitam, i. e. qui vult & diligit vitam, sive qui diligendo diligit, i. e. vehementer diligit vitam. Phrasis est Hebraea, cuius emphasis apud Davidem exprimitur per verbum חפץ, quod non significat simpliciter voluit, sed cum desiderio, beneplacito & delectatione voluit,Gen. 34. v. 19.Psal. 147. v. 10.Es. 62. v. 4. Syrus reddidit per [consult facsimile image]voluptatem habuit, complacitum fuit. Per nomen ζωὴν absolutè positum, intelligitur non quaevis vita, sed beata, tranquilla, & iucunda, & longaeva, ad quam requiritur cumprimis bona conscientia. Is enim dicitur propriè vivere, qui hilariter & iucundè vivit, Iob. 21. v. 5.Quare impii vivunt, i. e. prosperè agunt. Prov. 16. v. 15.In hilaritate vultus Regis vita, i. e. felicitas & prosperit as, qui bonam & tranquillam habet conscientiam, quae sola vitam reddere potest iucundam. Nec de vita huius seculi tantùm sermo est, sed etiam ac praecipuè de beata in futuro seculo vita, quae sola verè est vita, ut sit sensus. Qui in hoc seculo vitam tranquillam ducere, & vitae aeternae aliquando heres fieri expetit. inde glossa interlin, sic explicat. Quivult ostendere, se benedictionem habere. Iohan. Huss. Qui vult vitam, sc. beatam, in qua nullus moritur. Quidam putant, hoc ipsum insinuari apud Davidem per pluraleחייםqui vult vitas, id est, tranquillam in hoc, & beatam infuturo seculo. Sed חיים est plurale tantùm.

Καὶ ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς. Per dies bonos intelliguntur dies tranquilli & prosperi, sicut contrà dies mali sunt aerumnosi & calamitosi. Genes. 47. vers. 9. Quidam accipiunt tantùm de aeterna vita, cùm in hac vita sint dies mali. Clemens Alexandrinus, dies boni non sunt nisi aeterni. Iohannes Huss. Qui vult videre dies bonos, scilicet in beatitudine coelesti, ubi dies noctibus non interrumpuntur.Apocal. 21. v. 15.Dicuntur dies aeternae gloriae boni, ad differentiam praesentis vitae, qui sunt mali,Ephes. 5. vers. 16.Dicuntur etiam dies pluraliter in patria coelesti, non propter successionem, quae ibi nulla, sed propter infinitam durationem. Sed in utroque membro agitur de tranquilla & beata vita, tùm in hoc, tùm in futuro seculo. Hebraea apud Davidem propriè sic habent. Quis vir diligens dies ad videndum bonum, scilicet in eis? h. e. Quis diligit eo fine vitam longaevam, ut in ea multis fruatur bonis? Quis vitam longaevam & felicem expetit? Syrus textum Hebr. secutus, sic vertit. Qui diligit dies bonos ad videndum sive videre.

Παυσάτω τὴν γλῶσσαν αὐτοῦ ἐπὸ κακοῦquiescere faciat, sive coërceat linguam suam à malo, i. e. temperet sibi à conviciis & calumniis, linguâ suâ proximo non detrahat. In Hebraeo ponitur verbum נצר, quod significat custodivit, praeservavit, munivit, ac singularem curam includit. Deut. 32. v. 10.custodivit eos sicut pupillam oculi. Syrus habet cognatum verbum [consult facsimile image]magno studio custodivit. Psal.

119. v. 22.καὶ χεὶλη αὐτοῦ. Vulg. reddidit, & labia eius, sc. sic regantur. Sed in Graeco est pronomen reciprocum, & labia sua, sc. coërceat, ut regatur nomen χείλη à verbo praecedente παυσάτω, nec sit casus Nominativi, sed Genitivi, ut patet ex textu Hebraeo, Graeco & Syro.

Τοῦ μὴ λαλῆσαι δόλον, Scil. ἕνεκα,ne loquantur dolum, ne aliud ore exteriùs proferat, aliud corde interiùs premat. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] quod significat astutiam, cogitationem mali in corde. Sic ergò duo linguae peccata Psaltes Regius, & ex eo Petrus prohibet. Primò maledicentiam, quae est manifestae linguae adversus proximum iniuria. Secundò Sermonem dolosum, quae est iniuria latens & occulta. Sub his autem speciebus συνεκδοχικῶς caetera omnia linguae peccata debent intelligi prohibita, & virtutes contrariae praeceptae, iuxta usitatum Hebraismum. Cumprimis vero ἀντιθετικῶς intelligenda praecipi εὐλογία, ad quam allegatione dicti huius Davidici specialiter Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit, exhortari voluit.

## 3:11
LET HIM DECLINE FROM EVIL, AND DO GOOD, LET HIM SEEK PEACE, AND FOLLOW IT.

Connection. 1. The Apostle continues the allegation of the Davidic saying from Psal. 34. and joins verse 15 to verse 14.

2. He had said that neither railing for railing, nor evil for evil, is to be rendered. After, therefore, he had confirmed the former exhortation from v. 14. Psal. 34. he confirms the latter exhortation from v. 15 of the same Psalm.

3. Thus, therefore, he descends from the vices of the tongue or mouth to the sins of the work, and warns that we should not inflict harm upon anyone, but should conduct ourselves as beneficent toward all.

4. B. Luther takes this member as ἐξηγητικὸν of the former. To decline from evil, he says, and to do good is to pass by curses with deaf ears, and to see injuries with blind eyes.

Disposition. Just as in the preceding verses ἀντιθετικῶς the Apostle had opposed to one another the virtue of speech, namely εὐλογιαν, and the vices of the same, namely κακολογίαν καὶ ψευδολογίαν:

Thus in this little verse ἀντιθετικῶς he opposes the evil and the good of a work to one another, when he commands to turn away from evil, but to pursue the good. Then he adds the general goal, to which the observation of the precepts handed down thus far must be directed, namely that we may be able to live peaceably with our neighbor in this life, and thus lead a tranquil and quiet life.

Exposition of the text. Ἐκκλινάτω ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ ποιησάτω ἀγαθὸν. In the same way the LXX rendered the Hebrew text of the Psalm, except that Peter changed the second person into the third. Ἔκκλινον ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ ποίησον ἀγαθὸν ἐκκλίνειν properly signifies to turn aside and decline from the way, Num. 22. v. 23. Jud. 14. v. 5. Isa. 9. v. 20. The Apostle therefore warns that we should turn away from the way of impiety and malice, and betake ourselves to the life of the divine commandments, so that we may walk in it. Job 31. v. 7. Ps. 119. v. 32. The phrase ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ κακοῦ or ἀπὸ κακῶν is most common among the LXX Interpreters Ps. 36. v. 25. Prov. 3. v. 7. chap. 14. v. 16. which Paul also uses Rom. 16. v. 17. (where, however, it is used of persons, here of things) to which ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ Κυρίου is opposed Soph. 16. ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ νόμου Ps. 119. v. 51. ἀπὸ ἐνταλμάτων Κυρίου Job 23. v. 11. to decline from the law of God, which is the rule of the royal road. In the Hebrew the verb סור receded, is held, in the Syriac version [consult facsimile image] passed over. Although in particular the Apostle here speaks properly of evil and good with respect to the neighbor, that we ought not to render evil for evil to the neighbor, but rather to compensate for evils with goods, and thus to love our very enemies in such a way that we not only pray well for those persecuting and slandering us, and pray for them, but also do good to those who hate us, Matt. 5. vers. 44. this precept can nevertheless be accepted generally without any absurdity, so that we are commanded to decline from every evil adverse to the first or second table of the Decalogue, and to do every good toward God, the neighbor, and ourselves. Let him decline from evil, that is, from all thoughts, words, and deeds fighting against the law; let him decline from the occasion of evil, from the conversation of evil men, from a wicked habit of life. Let him do good, that is, let him think, say, and do things conformable to the divine law, let him live σωφρόνως toward himself, δικαὶως toward the neighbor, εὐσεβῶς toward God. Tit. 2. v. 12. Let him decline from evil according to the will, And let him do good, i. e. let him work in act, says John Huss in his commentary on this passage, ζητησάτω εἰρήνειν καὶ διωξάτω αὐτὴν. the Vulgate rendered. Let him seek peace and follow it. But the Greek properly has: Let him seek peace and pursue it. ζητεῖν signifies to seek something with great zeal and solicitude. Matth. 2. v. 13. Cap. 6. v. 33. cap. 21. v. 46. Luc. 2. v. 45. In Hebrew the verb בקש is used, which likewise signifies diligent and studious care in seeking 2. Reg. 9. v. 23. all the earth sought the face of Solomon, i. e. was held by the desire of seeing him: and what is said 1. Paral. 21. v. 3. Why does this יבקש seek my Lord, for it is held 2. Sam. 24. v. 3. חפץ desires, requests. Therefore in the phrase to seek peace is a Hebraism for to strive with all one's might for peace Ierem. 29. v. 7. cap. 38. v. 4. τὸ διώκειν likewise includes the signification of study and zeal, to follow something with great study and zeal. Thus διώκειν δικαιοσύνην and νόμον δικαιοσύνης is to follow justice with great study and zeal. Rom. 9. v. 30. & 31. 1. Tim. 6. v. 11. διώκειν φιλοξενίαν is to follow hospitality with great study and zeal Rom. 12. v. 14. διώκειν τὸ ἀγαθὸν to follow good with great zeal 1. Thess. 5. v. 15. thence to this verb is added κατὰ ζὴλον Phil. 3. v. 6. and διώκειν καὶ ζηλοῦν are joined 1. Cor. 14. v. 1. In Hebrew the verb רדף is held, he pursued, he followed with care and study Ps. 38. v. 21. they were adversaries to me for the reason that I pursued good. Prov. 21. v. 21. Following justice and mercy, he shall find life Es. 51. v. 1. Hear me, you that follow justice, that seek the Lord. Hos. 6. v. 3. we shall pursue to know the Lord. The Syrian has the verb [consult facsimile image] let him run after it, or let him follow it. The sense therefore is that we ought to follow peace with the greatest study, that we ought to apply ourselves with all our strength to obtaining and retaining peace, which will then finally happen if we patiently tolerate injuries and keep silent, if we refrain from all vengeance, if we not only willingly forgive a neighbor who asks, but also, having been injured by a neighbor, we offer peace to him. The Interlinear Gloss on this passage: Let him seek peace, as a hidden thing, and pursue it as a fugitive thing. Parallel passages are Rom. 12. v. 18. If it be possible, as much as is in you, having peace with all men. cap. 14. vers. 19. ἄρα οὖν τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης διώκωμεν. Hebr. 12. vers. 14. εἰρήνην διώκετε μετὰ πάντων.

Latin:

DECLINET A MALO, & FACIAT BONUM, INQUIRAT PACEM, & SEQUATUR EAM.

Connexio. 1. Continuat Apostolus allegationem dicti Davidici ex Psal. 34. ac versum 15. versiculo 14. coniungit.

2. Dixerat nec convitium pro convitio, nec malum pro malo reddendum esse. Postquam igitur priorem exhortationem confirmaverat ex. v. 14. Psal. 34. posteriorem exhortationem confirmat ex eiusdem Psal. v. 15.

3. Sic ergò à vitiis linguae sive oris descendit ad peccata operis, ac monet, ne cuiquam damnum inferamus, sed erga omnes nos beneficos geramus.

4. B. Lutherus hoc membrum accipit ut ἐξηγητικὸν prioris. Declinare à malo, inquit, & facere bonum est surdis auribus maledicta praeterire, & coecis oculis iniurias videre.

Dispositio. Sicut in versibus praecedentibus ἀντιθετικῶς Apostolus sibi invicem opposuerat virtutem sermonis, videlicet εὐλογιαν, & eiusdem vitia, videl. κακολογίαν καὶ ψευδολογίαν:

ita in hoc versiculo ἀντιθετικῶς sibi invicem opponit malum & bonum operis, quando à malo declinare, bonum vero sectari praecipit. Deinde subiicit generalem scopum, ad quem observatio praeceptorum hactenus traditorum dirigenda, videlicet ut pacificè cum proximo in hac vita possimus conversari, sicque tranquillam & quietam vitam traducere.

Textus expositio. Ἐκκλινάτω ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ ποιησάτω ἀγαθὸν. Eodem modo LXX. reddiderunt textum Psalmi Hebraeum, nisi quòd Petrus secundam personam mutavit in tertiam. Ἔκκλινον ἀπὸ κακοῦ καὶ ποίησον ἀγαθὸν ἐκκλίνειν propriè significat à via deflectere ac declinare,Num. 22. v. 23.Iud. 14. v. 5.Esa. 9. v. 20. Monet igitur Apostolus, ut à via impietatis ac malitiae declinemus, & ad vitam mandatorum divinorum nos conferamus, ut in ea ingrediamur. Iob. 31. v. 7.Psal. 119. v. 32. Phrasis ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ κακοῦ vel ἀπὸ κακῶν usitatissima est apud LXX. Interpp. Psalm. 36. v. 25.Prov. 3. v. 7.cap. 14. v. 16. quâ etiam Paulus utitur Rom. 16. v. 17. (ubi tamen de personis, hîc de rebus usurpatur) cui opponitur ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ Κυρίου Soph. 16. ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ νόμουPsalm. 119. v. 51.ἀπὸ ἐνταλμάτων ΚυρίουIob. 23. v. 11. declinare à lege Dei, quae est regiae viae regula. In Hebraeo habetur verbum סורrecessit, in Syriaca versione [consult facsimile image]transivit. Quamvis vero in specie Apostolus hîc propriè loquatur de malo & bono respectu proximi, quòd non debeamus malum pro malo proximo reddete, sed potiùs mala bonis compensare, adeoque ipsos inimicos nostros eo modo diligere, ut non solùm beneprecemur persequentibus & calumniantibus nos, proque illis oremus, sed etiam benefaciamus illis, qui oderunt nos, Matth. 5. vers. 44. potest tamen sine ulla absurditate praeceptum hoc generaliter accipi, ut ab omni malo primae vel secundae Decalogi tabulae adverso declinare, & quodvis bonum erga Deum, proximum, & nos ipsos facere iubeamur. Declinet à malo, id est, ab omnibus cogitatis, dictis & factis cum lege pugnantibus; declinet à mali occasione, à malorum conversatione, ab improba vitae consuetudine. Faciat bonum, hoc est, cogitet, dicat & faciat conformia legi divinae, vivat σωφρόνως erga seipsum, δικαὶως erga proximum, εὐσεβῶς erga Deum. Tit. 2. v. 12.Declinet à malo secundùm voluntatem, & faciat bonum i. e. operetur in actu, inquit Iohan. Huss. in comm. huius loci, ζητησάτω εἰρήνειν καὶ διωξάτω αὐτὴν. Vulgata reddidit. Inquirat pacem & sequatur eam. Sed Graeca propriè habent. Quaerat pacem & persequatur eam.ζητεῖν significat magno studio & solicitudine aliquid quaerere.Matth. 2. v. 13.Cap. 6. v. 33.cap. 21. v. 46.Luc. 2. v. 45. In Hebraeo usurpatur verbum בקש quod itidem diligentem & studiosam in quaerendo curam significat 2. Reg. 9. v. 23.tota terra quaerebat faciem Salomonis i. e. tenebatur eius videndi desiderio: ac quod 1. Paral. 21. v. 3. dicitur. Quare hocיבקשquaeret Dominus meus, pro cohabetur2. Sam. 24. v. 3.חפץdesiderat, expetit. Ergò in phrasi quaerere pacem est Hebraismus pro summopere studere paci Ierem. 29. v. 7.cap. 38. v. 4.τὸ διώκειν itidem includit studii ac zeli significationem, magno studio ac zelo aliquid sectari. Sic διώκειν δικαιοσύνην ac νόμον δικαιοσύνης est magno studio ac zelo sectari iustitiam.Rom. 9. v. 30. & 31.1. Tim. 6. v. 11.διώκειν φιλοξενίαν est magno studio ac zelo sectari hospitalitatemRom. 12. v. 14.διώκειν τὸ ἀγαθὸνmagno zelo sectari bonum1. Thess. 5. v. 15. inde verbo huic additur κατὰ ζὴλονPhil. 3. v. 6. ac διώκειν καὶ ζηλοῦν coniunguntur 1. Cor. 14. v. 1. In Hebraeo habetur verbum רדףpersecutus est, curâ atque studio consectatus fuitPs. 38. v. 21.adversabantur mihi pro eo, quod persequebar bonum.Prov. 21. v. 21.Sequens iustitiam & misericordiam, inveniet vitamEs. 51. v. 1.Audite me sequentes iustitiam, quaerentes Dominum.Hos. 6. v. 3.persequemur ad cognoscendum Dominum. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image]currat post eam, sive sectetur eam. Sensus igitur est, quòd summo studio debeamus pacem sectari, quòd totis viribus debeamus incumbere paci consequendae ac retinendae, quod tùm demum fiet, si iniurias patienter toleremus ac mussitemus, si ab omni vindicta temperemus, si non solùm proximo deprecanti libenter condonemus, sed etiam laesi à proximo pacem ei offeramus. Glossa interlin. in h. l. Inquirat pacem, ut rem absconditam, & persequatur eam ut rem fugitivam. Loca parallela sunt Rom. 12. v. 18.Si fieri potest, quod ex vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habentes.cap. 14. vers. 19.ἄρα οὖν τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης διώκωμεν.Hebr. 12. vers. 14.εἰρήνην διώκετε μετὰ πάντων.

## 3:12
FOR THE EYES OF THE LORD ARE UPON THE RIGHTEOUS AND HIS EARS ARE OPEN UNTO THEIR PRAYERS: BUT THE FACE OF THE LORD IS AGAINST THEM THAT DO EVIL.

Connection. 1. The Apostle continues the citation of the Davidic saying, and joins verse 16, with the former part of verse 17, to verse 15.

2. Nor does he bring forward this verse 16 Psal. 34. merely on the occasion of the preceding ones, but also because this verse serves his purpose here as well. Bede in this place: Because Blessed Peter had forbidden us to render evil for evil, nay, had commanded us to bless those who curse us, he rightly confirms it with a Prophetic testimony, that by heavenly inspection both the good and the bad are always seen, so that we may remember both our patience, by which we tolerate the bad, and our benevolence, by which we wish good things for those who persecute us, is to be rewarded with an eternal prize, and our persecutors, if they are unwilling to repent, are to be punished with a worthy torment; but if they have repented, we also, for their salvation, which we were praying for from the Lord, shall receive from the Lord a crown of just congratulation.

3. The Apostle meets a tacit objection. If we patiently bear injuries brought upon us without merit, and do not manfully ward them off from ourselves, who will take care of us? Who will protect us in this perverse world? It is to be feared that by bearing an old injury we invite a new one. The Apostle answers. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous i. e. God mercifully looks upon and protects those who, justified by faith in Christ, strive for righteousness, a not insignificant part of which is patience or the tolerance of injuries.

4. Since the pious, while they tolerate injuries with an equal and patient mind, are meanwhile miserably afflicted, the Holy Spirit consoles them from the fatherly providence of God, because He looks with kind eyes upon the righteous who are afflicted without merit, and sees the machinations of the wicked with angry eyes and will require them in His own time. 2. Paral. 24. v. 22.

5. The Apostle obstructs the fountain from which the desire for vengeance, from which he had hitherto dissuaded, flows. For the fact that we who are injured are kindled with anger by our neighbor and burn with a desire for vengeance, is solely from this, that we do not believe or think that we are a care to God, and that God will be the avenger of injuries brought upon us, of which unless we are certain by firm faith, every exhortation to patience is in vain.

6. The Apostle shows the most secure remedy in all adversities and injuries, namely that we ought to flee to the Lord through prayers, and implore His protection and help, since he teaches that His ears are by no means closed, but open to our prayers.

7. He also shows who and what kind of people those are who pursue peace with their neighbor, namely the just and pious, who rest in the protection of GOD by true faith and commit their ways to Him, laying down before GOD the injuries brought upon them, as Tertullian speaks in his book on patience.

8. Finally, he confirms the truth of the promise brought forward in the preceding vers. 10.. He who shall keep his tongue from evil, and his lips, that they speak no guile; he who shall decline from evil and do good, shall obtain life and good days, i. e. a blessed life in this and the future age, temporal and eternal happiness: for he is just and dear to God, since those who are justified by faith and cultivate justice, God looks upon them with kind eyes, taking paternal care of them, and advancing them to happiness; nay, He even offers kind and easy ears to their prayers, He is prompt to hear and to grant what they ask, i. e. to give them the tranquil life which they desire, and the good days which they love.

Disposition. The Apostle opposes ἀντιθετικῶς the favor of God toward the just, and the wrath of God against the wicked. He describes the favor of God by kind eyes and open ears. He describes the wrath of God by an angry and averted face.

Exposition of the text. Ὃτι οἱ ὁφθαλμὸι Κυρίου ἐπὶ δικαίους. In the Hebrew text as also in the version of the LXX Interpreters, the connective particle ὅτι, is not added, which Peter added for the sake of σαφηνείας. The Syrian expressed it by [consult facsimile image]. The little word Eyes placed absolutely and by άνθρωποπάθειαν, just as ears and face attributed to God, are to be taken here as meaning mild and favoring eyes. For those whom we love and whom we favor, we cast our eyes upon them, we look upon them mildly and in a friendly manner, so that favor and love may shine forth from the eyes themselves.

Καὶ ὦτα αὐτοῦ εἰς δέησιν αὐτῶν. The Vulgate has rendered it: And his ears into their prayers. The Greek properly has: into their supplication. But one must understand are open and attentive. The Syriac expressed the sense: And his ears to hear them.

Πρόσωπον δέ Κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιοῦντας κακὰ. In the Hebrew is the word פנו in the construct state, the face of the Lord against those doing evil. Although the word פנים & πρόσωπον when used of God is of a middle signification, and is sometimes used in a good sense for favor, Num. 6. v. 25. The Lord make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you. v. 26. The Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace. Psal. 31. v. 17. Make thy face to shine upon thy servant. Psal. 80. v. 4. Cause thy face to shine and we shall be saved, etc. yet sometimes it is taken in a bad sense for anger and indignation Lev. 17. v. 10. I will set my face against the soul that eateth blood. c. 20. v. 5. I will set my face against that man and will cause him to be cut off, etc. Psal. 21. v. 10. Thou shalt make them as an oven of fire in the time of thy face, i. e. of thy anger. Psal. 68. v. 3. Let the sinners perish from the face of the Lord. Therefore it must be gathered from the circumstances whether the face of God is put for his favor or his indignation. Thus Psal. 21. v. 10. ἐξηγητικῶς is added, in thy nose he shall swallow them up. That in this place it is put for anger and indignation is evident both from the antithesis, the eyes of the Lord are upon the just, his face is upon those doing evil, and from the determination of the object, because God pursues the wicked not with love, but with hatred, and from the ἐξηγήσει added by the Psalmist, that he may cut off their memory from the earth, i. e. that he may punish and destroy them, and by total destruction blot out their memory from the minds of men, so that there is no one who speaks honorably of them: which ἐξήγησις is also added in this place in certain Greek codices. One must therefore understand, his face, namely, angry and averted, for anger, as also sadness, appears especially in the countenance, and shines forth from a grim and sullen face. 1. Sam. 1. v. 18. her face was no more to her, i. e. she was no longer sad. Luc. 24. v. 17. Why are you σκυθρωπὸι of a sad and sullen countenance? The Syriac has the noun [consult facsimile image] nostrils, nose, for in the nose anger appears from more vehement breathing. Iob. 40. v. 6. Psal. 6. v. 1. etc.

Latin:

QUIA OCULI DOMINI SUPER IUSTOS & AURES EIUS IN PRECES EORUM: VULTUS AUTEM DOMINI SUPER FACIENTES MALA.

Connexio. 1. Continuat Apostolus allegationem dicti Davidici, ac versum 16. cum parte priore vers. 17. versiculo 15. coniungit.

2. Nec tamen occasione duntaxat praecedentium hunc versiculum 16. Psal. 34. adducit, sed etiam quia instituto suo etiam hic versiculus inservit. Beda in h. l. Quia B. Petrus nos malum pro malo reddere vetuerat, imo maledicentibus benedicere iusserat, rectè Prophetico testimonio astruit, supernâ inspectione & bonos semper videri & malos, quatenus meminerimus, & nostram patientiam, quâ toleramus malos, & nostram benevolentiam, quâ persequentibus bona optamus, aeterno praemio remunerandam, & persecutores nostros, si poenitere noluerint, digno plectendos esse supplicio; Si vero poenituerint, nos quoque pro ipsorum salute, quam à Domino deprecabamur, à Domino coronam iustae congratulationis accepturos.

3. Occurrit Apostolus tacitae obiectioni. Si iniurias praeter meritum illatas patienter feramus, nec masculè eas à nobis depellamus, quis nostri curam aget? quis in hoc mundo perverso nos tuebitur? metuendum est, ne veterem iniuriam ferendo invitemus novam. Respondet Apostolus. Oculi Domini super iustos i. e. Deus illos clementer respicit ac tuetur, qui fide in Christum iustificati student iustitiae cuius pars non postrema est patientia sive iniuriarum tolerantia.

4. Quando quidem pii aequo ac patienti animo iniurias tolerantes ipsi interim miserè affliguntur, consolatur eos Spiritus Sanctus à paterna Dei providentia, quòd benignis oculis iustos praeter meritum afflictos intueatur, ac machinationes malorum oculis iratis videat & suo tempore requirat. 2. Paral. 24. v. 22.

5. Obstruit Apostolus fontem, ex quo cupiditas vindictae, à qua dehortatus fuerat hactenus, promanat. Quod enim laesi à proximo irâ accendimur & vindictae cupiditate flagramus, unicè ex eo est, quòd non credimus vel cogitamus, Deo nos curae esse, ac Deum fore iniuriarum nobis illatarum vindicem, de quo nisi firmâ fide certi simus, frustranea est omnis ad patientiam exhortatio.

6. Ostendit Apostolus rutissimum in omnibus adversis & iniuriis remedium, videlicet quòd per preces ad Dominum confugere, ipsiusque praesidium & auxilium implorare debeamus, quando aures eius ad preces nostras minimè clausas, sed apertas esse docet.

7. Ostendit etiam, qui & quales sint illi, qui pacem cum proximo sectantur, videlicet iusti & pii, qui verâ fide in DEI praesidio acquiescunt ac vias suas ipsi commendant, apud DEUM iniurias sibi illatas deponentes, ut loquitur Tertullianus lib. de patient.

8. Confirmat denique promissionis in praecedente vers. 10. adductae veritatem. Qui linguam suam custodierit à malo, & labia sua, ne loquantur dolum; qui declinaverit à malo & fecerit bonum, vitam & dies bonos i. e. beatam in hoc & futuro seculo vitam, temporalem & aeternam felicitatem consequetur: est enim iustus & Deo carus, siquidem qui ex fide iustificati sunt & iustitiam colunt, illos benignis oculis Deus intuetur, paternam eorum curam gerens, & ad felicitatem eos provehens; quin & benignas ac faciles aures praebet eorum precibus, promtus est ad exaudiendum & praestandum quod petunt i. e. ad dandum illis vitam tranquillam, quam volunt, & dies bonos, quos diligunt.

Dispositio. Opponit Apostolus ἀντιθετικῶς Dei favorem erga iustos, & Dei iram adversus malos. Favorem Dei describit per oculos benignos & aures apertas. Iram Dei describit per vultum iratum & aversum.

Textus expositio. Ὃτι οἱ ὁφθαλμὸι Κυρίου ἐπὶ δικαίους. In textu Hebraeo ut & in LXX. Interpp. versione non additur particula connexiva ὅτι, quam Petrus σαφηνείας causâ adiecit. Syrus eam expressit per [consult facsimile image]Oculorum vocula absolutè posita ac per άνθρωποπάθειαν aequè ac aures & vultus Deo attributa hîc accipienda de oculis blandis ac faventibus. Quos enim diligimus ac quibus favemus, in illos oculos coniicimus, eos blandè & amicè intuemur, ut ex ipsis oculis favor & amor eluceat.

Καὶ ὦτα αὐτοῦ εἰς δέησιν αὐτῶν. Vulgata reddidit. Et aures eius in preces eorum. Graeca propriè habent, in deprecationem eorum. Subintelligendum vero sunt apertae & intentae Syrus sensum expressit. Et aures eius ad audiendum eos.

Πρόσωπον δέ Κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιοῦντας κακὰ. In Hebreo est vox פנו in regimine, facies Domini in facientes mala. Quamvis vero vox פנים & πρόσωπον de Deo usurpata, sit significationis mediae, & quandoque in bonam partem pro favore usurpetur, Num. 6. v. 25.Lucere faciat Domini faciem suam ad te & misereatur tui.v. 26.Elevet Dominus faciem suam ad te & ponat tibi pacem.Psal. 31. v. 17.Lucere fac faciem tuam super servum tuumPsal. 80. v. 4.Illustra faciem tuam & servabimur &c. interdum tamen accipitur in malam partem pro ira & indignatione Lev. 17. v. 10.dabo faciem meam in animam comedentem sanguinem.c. 20. v. 5.ponam faciem meam contra virum illum & succidere faciam &c.Psal. 21. v. 10.pones eos ut clibanum ignis in tempore faciei i. e. irae tuae. Psal. 68. v. 3.pereant peccatores à facie Domini. Ex circumstantiis ergò colligendum, an facies Dei pro favore vel indignatione eius ponatur. Sic Psal. 21. v. 10.ἐξηγητικῶς subiicitur, naso tuo deglutiet eos. Hoc loco pro ira & indignatione poni, patet tùm ex antithesi, oculi Domini super iustos, facies eius super facientes mala, tùm ex determinatione obiecti, quia malos Deus non amore, sed odio prosequitur, tùm ex subiecta ἐξηγήσει apud Psalmographum, ut succidat è terra memoriam eorum. i. e. ut eos puniat atque perdat, ac totali excidio memoriam eorum ex animis hominum deleat, ut nemo sit, qui de eis honorificè loquatur: quae ἐξήγησις etiam h. l. in quibusdam Codd. Graecis additur. Subintelligendum ergò, facies eius scil. irata & aversa, nam ira uti etiam tristitia in vultu potissimùm apparet, & ex facie torva atque tetrica elucet. 1. Sam. 1. v. 18.facies eius non fuerunt ei ultra i. e. non ampliùs erat tristis. Luc. 24. v. 17.Quare estisσκυθρωπὸιvultu tristi ac tetrico? Syrus habet nomen [consult facsimile image]nares, nasus, in naso enim ira apparet ex vehementiori spiratione. Iob. 40. v. 6.Psal. 6. v. 1. &c.

## 3:13
AND WHO IS HE THAT WILL HARM YOU, IF YOU BE FOLLOWERS OF THAT WHICH IS GOOD?

Connection. 1. This is new, and therefore the third argument of the exhortation, likewise sought from the useful consequence. If you shall be emulators of good, that is, if you shall diligently strive for good works, among which the patient tolerance of injuries also has a place, it will come to pass that trouble will not easily be created for you by evil men.

2. He had said that the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears unto their prayer; from this he infers that the good are not afflicted by the evil, if they win them over by benefits, patience, kindness, and humility, the LORD, of course, bending their heart and rendering them more equitable.

3. He teaches that the innocence of life must be joined with patience, just as in cap. 4. seq. v. 15. an explanation is added. Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer.

4. He had promised the favor and protection of GOD to the placid and peaceful; he confirms that with an argument taken from common experience, which testifies that placid and peaceful men reconcile the minds of men to themselves, and thus by the benefit of GOD lead a peaceful and tranquil life.

5. The Apostle had brought forward the most benign promise of GOD from Psalm. 34. Who is the man who desires life &c. Now furthermore he shows that that promise pertains principally indeed to the future, yet in the meantime it can also be referred in its own way to the present age.

Exposition of the text. Καὶ τίς ὁ κακώσων ὑμᾶς; The Apostle uses an apostrophe and the figure of interrogation, so that his speech may more penetrate the minds of men.

Τίς ὁ κακώσων is placed for τίς ἐστιν ὁ κακώσων. Who then will there be, who may harm you? κακοῦν signifies to affect with evil, to inflict evil upon someone. Actor. 7. v. 6. it is used of the Egyptians afflicting the Israelites and pressing them with hard servitude. vers. 19. of Pharaoh, burdening the Israelite people with various loads. Cap. 12. vers. 1. of Herod persecuting the Church, cap. 18. v. 10. the Lord says to Paul, I am with you, and no one will be able to harm you. The LXX use it for דחק oppressed Iud. 2. vers. 18. for דכא crushed, humbled. Iob. 22. vers. 9. for ינה afflicted Exod. 22. v. 21. for לחץ constrained, compelled Ex. 23. v. 9.

for ענה he afflicted, he humbled,Gen. 15. v. 13.chap. 16. v. 6.Exod. 1. v. 11. etc. for רוע he treated harshly, he showed himself rough,Gen. 19. v. 9.Exod. 5. v. 22. etc. the Syrian rendered it by a circumlocution. Who is he, who may do evil to you?

Ἐὰν τοῦ άγαθοῦ μιμηταὶ γένησθε. By τόν ἀγαθὸν Primaticcius, Lorinus and others understand God, who is αὐταγαθὸν & the highest good. Thus therefore an argument taken from the example of God would be proposed in these words of the Apostle, who lets his sun rise upon the good and the bad, just as Christ also Matt. 5. v. 44. exhorts us, that we do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute and slander us, with an argument taken from the example of the heavenly Father, ver. 45. that you may be children of your Father, who is in heaven, who makes his Sun rise upon the good and the bad, and rains upon the just and the unjust. Some by τὸν ἀγαθὸν understand Christ, whom Justin Apol. 2. calls by an elegant paranomasia χρηστὸν. By this reasoning Peter would exhort us, that insisting upon the footsteps of Christ we might imitate his innocence and patience on the cross, just as Paul also says 1. Cor. 11. v. 1. Be μιμηταὶ imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. But τὸ ἀγαθὸν is more correctly taken concerning the good of virtue, or goodness, in which way the Syrian also renders it, concerning which good he had treated a little before v. 11., so that the sense may be: If by doing good, and by doing good to others, you shall expend strenuous effort, no one will be able or willing to harm you. Lyran. Hugo etc. A parallel passage exists 2. John ver. 11. Beloved, μὴ μιμοῦ τὸ κακὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, because for μιμηταὶ two Royal Codices have ζηλωταὶ. and the Syrian has the word [consult facsimile image] which signifies both, to emulate, and to imitate. August. serm. 107. de divers. cap. 6. reads lovers.

Latin:

ET QUIS EST, QUI VOBIS NOCEAT, SI BONI AEMULATORES FUERITIS?

Connexio. 1. Novum hoc est, adeoque tertium exhortationis argumentum, itidem à consequente utili petitum. Si fueritis boni aemulatores, id est, si bonis operibus, inter quae etiam patiens iniuriarum tolerantia locum habet, sedulò studueritis, futurum, ut non facilè à malis hominibus vobis molestia creetur.

2. Dixerat, oculos Domini esse super iustos, & aures eius ad deprecationem eorum, ex eo infert, bonos à malis non affligi, si illos beneficiis, patientiâ, comitate & humilitate demereantur, DOMINO scilicet cor eorum flectente, & aequiores eos reddente.

3. Cum patientia coniungendam esse docet vitae innocentiam, sicut in cap. 4. seq. v. 15. explicatio additur. Nemo vestrûm patiatur ut homicidia, aut fur, aut maleficus.

4. Promiserat placidis ac pacificis DEI favorem & praesidium, illud confirmat argumento à communi experientia sumpto, quae testatur, homines placidos, & pacificos animos hominum sibi conciliare, sicque DEI beneficio vitam pacatam & tranquillam ducere.

5. Adduxerat Apostolus benignissimam DEI promissionem ex Psalm. 34.Quis est homo, qui vult vitam &c. Iam porrò ostendit, promissionem illam principaliter quidem pertinere ad futurum, interim tamen suo modo etiam ad praesens seculum referri posse.

Textus expositio. Καὶ τίς ὁ κακώσων ὑμᾶς; Utitur Apostolus apostrophe & figurâ interrogationis, ut magis penetret hominum animos ipsius oratio.

Τίς ὁ κακώσων ponitur pro τίς ἐστιν ὁ κακώσων. Quis tandem erit, qui vobis noceat? κακοῦν significat malis afficere, malum alicui inferre.Actor. 7. v. 6. usurpatur de Aegyptiis Israëlitas affligentibus, ac durâ servitute prementibus. vers. 19. de Pharaone, variis oneribus populum Israëliticum gravante. Cap. 12. vers. 1. de Herode Ecclesiam persequente, cap. 18. v. 10. dicit Dominus ad Paulum. Ego sum tecum, & nullus poterit tibi nocere. LXX. utuntur pro דחקoppressitIud. 2. vers. 18. pro דכאcontudit, humiliavit.Iob. 22. vers. 9. pro ינהafflixitExod. 22. v. 21. pro לחץcoarctavit, compulitEx. 23. v. 9.

pro ענהafflixit, humiliavit,Genes. 15. v. 13.cap. 16. v. 6.Exod. 1. v. 11. &c. pro רועduriter tractavit, asperum sese praebuit,Genes. 19. v. 9.Exod. 5. v. 22. &c. Syrus per circumscriptionem reddidit. Quis est, qui faciat vobis malum?

Ἐὰν τοῦ άγαθοῦ μιμηταὶ γένησθε. Per τόν ἀγαθὸν Primaticcius, Lorinus & alii intelligunt Deum, qui estαὐταγαθὸν& summum bo num. Sic ergò proponeretur in his verbis Apostoli argumentum ab exemplo Dei petitum, qui sinit solem suum oriri super bonos & malos, sicut etiam Christus Matth. 5. v. 44. nos hortatur, ut benefaciamus his, qui oderunt nos, & oremus pro persequentibus & calumniantibus nos, argumento ab exemplo Patris coelestis petito, vers. 45.ut sitis filii Patris vestri, qui in coelis est, qui Solem suum oriri facit super bonos & malos, & pluit super iustos & iniustos. Quidam per τὸν ἀγαθὸν intelligunt Christum, quem Iustinus Apol. 2. eleganti paranomasia vocatχρηστὸν. Hac ratione Petrus nos exhortaretur, ut vestigiis Christi insistentes eius innocentiam & patientiam in cruce imitemur, sicut & Paulus dicit 1. Cor. 11. v. 1.Estoteμιμηταὶimitatores mei, sicut & ego Christi. Sed τὸ ἀγαθὸν rectiùs accipitur de bono virtutis, sive bonitate, quo modo etiam Syrus reddit, de quo bono paulo antè v. 11. egerat, ut sit sensus. Si benè agendo, & aliis benefaciendo strenuam operam impenderitis, nemo vobis nocere poterit vel volet. Lyran. Hugo &c. Locus parallelus extat 2. Iohan. vers. 11. Carissime,μὴ μιμοῦ τὸ κακὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, quia pro μιμηταὶ Regii duo Cod. habent ζηλωταὶ. & Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] quod utrumque significat, aemulari, & imitari. August. serm. 107. de divers. cap. 6. legit amatores.

## 3:14
BUT AND IF YOU SUFFER ANYTHING FOR JUSTICE' SAKE, BLESSED ARE YOU. AND FEAR NOT THEIR FEAR, AND BE NOT TROUBLED.

Connection. 1. By ἐπίπληξιν καὶ πρὸληψιν, he as it were corrects the prior sentence. If even in the greatest degree the wicked attempt to harm you, and consequently it happens that you are afflicted for justice' sake, nevertheless nothing will depart from your blessedness on that account.

2. Lyranus arranges the text thus: After the Apostle removed the first thing in which a man can be disordered in the suffering of evil, namely boldness in retaliating; now furthermore he removes the second, namely inordinate fear, through which a man falls into pusillanimity and is broken by inconstancy.

3. Just as in v. 10, 11, and 12 the Apostle brought forth some verses from Psal. 34. with the name of David suppressed: so with the name of Christ suppressed he cites His own sentiment from Matth. 5. v. 10. Blessed are they who suffer persecution for justice' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven? With the name of Isaiah also suppressed he cites his sentiment from cap. 8. v. 12. Fear not his fear (of the people) nor be afraid.

4. The Apostle adds a consolation for those who, although they seek peace and pursue good, are nevertheless exposed to the injuries, afflictions, and persecutions of wicked men, whom he consoles with the words of his Master, who pronounces them blessed.

5. The Apostle's speech rises. Persecutors not only cannot harm you, but they are even compelled, beyond their intention, to promote your salvation. Bede in h. l. says, Not only does he who inflicts evils upon those doing good do you no harm, but also when the enemy pursues you because of the good things which he execrates, he provides you with a cause for greater blessedness, when he exercises the powers of your patience. Gloss. interlin. in h. l. That which is inflicted by the wicked not only does not harm, but even profits, because it exercises patience.

Disposition of the text. There are two parts of the verse. The former contains παράκλησιν, the latter παραίνεσιν.

Exposition. Ἀλλ᾽ εἰ καὶ πάσχοιτε διὰ δικαιοσύνην. But even if it happens that you are afflicted for justice' sake. The Syrian rendered ἐλλειπτικῶς. And if (understand it happens) that you suffer. For ἀλλ᾿ εἰ καὶ two Royal Codices have εἰδὲ. But if you suffer. The Vulgate rendered, But and if you suffer anything. The interpreter added the little word anything of his own, for the Greek simply has, But if you even suffer.

Τὸ πάσχειν is placed absolutely, therefore it denotes any παθήματα brought about by evil men, whether they harm us by words or by deeds; whether they detract from our reputation, or practice the plundering of our goods, or inflict molestation upon the body. Meanwhile, because Peter repeats these things from the mouth of Christ Matth. 5. v. 10. therefore chiefly and principally afflictions are understood, which are inflicted by persecutors. For thus Christ speaks. Blessed οἱ δεδιωγμένοι, are they who suffer διωγμὸν persecution. The thing itself shows, however, that our Apostle has used this word absolutely several times. cap. 2. v. 19. v. πάσχων ἀδίκως, v. 20. πάσχοντες ὑπομενεῖτε. cap. 3. v. 17. Κρεῖττον ἀγαθοποιοῦντας πάσχειν. cap. 4. v. 1. ὁ παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ. v. 15. μηδεὶς πασχέτω ὡς φονεὺς cap. 5. v. 10. ὁ λίγον παθόντας. in which part he followed the style of the Evangelists and other Apostles, who likewise use this word placed absolutely concerning the passion of Christ. Luc. 22. v. 15. πρὸ τοῦ με παθεῖν. cap. 24. v. 26. οὐχὶ ταῦτα ἔδει παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν. v. 46. οὕτως ἔδει παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν. Act. 1. v. 3. μετὰ τὸ παθεῖν αὐτὸν. cap. 3. v. 18. παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν cap. 17. v. 3. τὸν χριστὸν ἔδει παθεῖν, Hebr. 2. v. 18. ἐν ᾧ πέπονθεν. c. 9. v. 26. πολλάκις πασθεῖν. &c. The Syrian has the word [consult facsimile image] or [consult facsimile image] he suffered. By τὴν δικαιοσύνην is understood not only the confession of heavenly truth, which is a certain part of Christian justice, of which Christ properly speaks Matth. 5. vers. 10. but in general the pursuit of piety, as appears from the preceding words of this place. If you do not render evil for evil, nor railing for railing, but on the contrary bless; if you decline from evil, and do good; if you seek peace, and pursue it; if you study justice, and be emulators of good, and nevertheless are afflicted with injuries by impious men. Gloss. interlin. in h. l. On account of holding or attaining justice. In this pursuit of piety and justice, however, the confession of faith stands out, to which it is clear the Apostle especially looks here, not only from the saying of Christ, which the Apostle alleges, but also from v. 15. seq. prepared always for a defense of the doctrine, and from cap. 4. v. 15. Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief &c. v. 16. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed. Some wish that to suffer on account of justice is the same as to suffer unjustly and without merit, so that this phrase signifies not only to be afflicted on account of the patronage of a good cause, but also to suffer unjustly, when one has lived innocently and holily in the fear of GOD. But the matter in both cases comes to the same thing.

Μακάριοι i.e. ἔστε, nevertheless you are blessed, your happiness will not be diminished on that account, which the Psalmist promises, nay rather you will be most blessed, certain indeed that you are being led through the way of affliction into the kingdom of heaven. Matth. 5. v. 10. Blessed are they who suffer on account of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Act. 14. v. 22. Through many tribulations it behooves we must enter into the kingdom of God.2. Tim. 2. v. 11.If we be dead with him, we shall also live with him.v. 12.If we suffer, we shall also reign with him.

Τὸν δέ φόβον αὐτῶν μὴ φοβηθῇτε. The passage is taken from Esai. 8. v. 12. where the LXX Interpreters speak thus in the very same words. τὸν δὲ φόβον αὐτοῦ οὐ μὴ φοβηθῆτε, οὐδὲ μὴ ταραχθῆτε. The Hebrew text is in the same manner. Fear ye not their fear, nor be afraid. But it is understood κατὰ according to the fear of this people do not fear, that is, do not fear with that fear with which this people trembles, who trusts in men and human protections and not in the Lord, and from this preposterous fear determines that a league must be entered into with the King of the Assyrians. Hence some think, that even with Peter the meaning of those words is entirely the same. Let not your fear be such as is wont to be theirs, understand of evil men or persecutors, who afflict you, that is, let it not be worldly and carnal, by which, fearing to lose temporal goods, they desert the confession of truth and the pursuit of justice and holiness. Or, do not fear preposterously that evil which they themselves fear and from that preposterous fear are rendered faint-hearted. But it is more correctly said that Peter adapts these Prophetic words to his own purpose, and leads them to a related meaning by a certain gentle deflection, so that the name of fear is not taken passively concerning the fear with which the wicked and persecutors fear preposterously, but actively concerning the fear which the wicked and persecutors haughtily strike into others, so that the sense may be: Do not fear their fear, that is, those formidable things which they threaten to you; their threats, by which they attempt to strike fear into you; or even the persecutors themselves, casting terror upon you by the threatening of losses and temporal punishments, which sense is gathered from the subject ἐξηγήσει, and be not troubled. The Syrian Interpreter also expressed the same. Do not fear from those who terrify you. There is therefore in the word fear a certain metonymy, by which the effect is put for the cause. Iob. 3. v. 25. the fear which I feared has come upon me, that is, the evil which I shall fear Ps. 64. v. 2.preserve my life from fear of the enemy that is, from the evils by whose threatening he attempts to strike fear into me Psal. 91. v. 5.Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by nightProv. 1. v. 26.I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh, that is, that evil which strikes fear into you. With this exposition agrees that by which some understand through their fear those things which are to be feared in persecutors, as are power, craftiness, spirit and powers of doing evil. For the sense comes to the same thing, that the pious ought not to be of a spirit too downcast and abject when they are afflicted by evil men or persecutors, but strong in the Lord and of a good spirit altogether, knowing that GOD stands on their side and wishes to defend them against hostile insults, just as it precedes in the Prophet. v. 10.Take counsel and it shall be dissipated, speak a word and it shall not stand, because here is Immanuel i. e. GOD with us. If however GOD is for us and with us, who is against us.Rom. 8. v. 31.

Μηδὲ ταραχθῆτε. ταράττεσθαι has the meaning of a more vehement perturbation, such as was that of Herod hearing of the new-born King, and fearing universal movements of the Republic, Matth. 2. v. 3. of the disciples thinking they saw a ghost Matth. 14. vers. 26.Marc. 6. v. 50.Luc. 24. v. 38. of Zechariah seeing an Angel Luc. 1. v. 12. The LXX use it for בהל which signifies he was struck with sudden terror, for it imports the speed of time with passion. Psal. 6. v. 2.Psal. 47. v. 5. &c. for בעת he was terrified at the sight of a thing, from which evil is feared.Esth. 7. v. 6. for געש he was shaken, he trembled.2. Reg. 22. v. 8.Ierem. 5. v. 22. for המה he was in a tumult, he murmuredPsal. 38. v. 9.Psal. 45. v. 6. &c. for זעף he was troubled with fear or with sadnessGen. 40. v. 6. for חול he was afraid, he trembledEsth. 4. v. 4.Psal. 54. v. 4. &c. for חלל he was vehemently dissolved, he was tormentedPsal. 108. v. 21. for חרד he was so moved by terror and fear, that it could be gathered from external signs.Gen. 42. v. 28.Iob. 37. v. 1. for ערץ he was dismayed and broken in spiritEsai. 8. v. 12. (from which place Peter brings the word ταράττεσθαι) for בעם he was struck with fear and was astonished,Gen. 41. v. 8.Psal. 76. v. 4. for רגש he was moved and disturbed by fear, for it is opposed to a quiet spirit, Deut. 2. v. 25.2. Reg. 18. v. 33. all of which meanings can be accommodated here. For the sense is that the pious ought not to be too much moved in spirit on account of the threats or injuries of evil men, but to maintain constancy of spirit even in adversities and dangers themselves. A parallel passage exists Ioh. 14. v. 1. & 27. μὴ ταρασσέσθω ὑμῶν ἡ καρδία.

Latin:

SED & SI QUID PATIMINI PROPTER IUSTITIAM, BEATI. TIMOREM AUTEM EORUM NE TIMUERITIS, & NON TURBEMINI.

Connexio. 1. Per ἐπίπληξιν καὶ πρὸληψιν, quasi corrigit priorem sencentiam. Si vel maximè mali conentur vobis nocere, ac proinde contingat, vos propter iustiriam affligi, nihil tamen propterea beatitudini vestrae decedet.

2. Lyranus textum sic ordinat: Postquam removit Apostolus primum, in quo potest homo in perpessione mali deordinari, videlicet audaciam in rependendo; iam porrò removet secundum, videlicet timorem inordinatum, per quem homo cadit in pusillanimitatem, & frangitur per inconstantiam.

3. Sicut in v. 10. 11. & 12. protulit Apostolus aliquot versiculos ex Psal. 34. suppresso nomine Davidis: ita suppresso nomine Christi citat ipsius sententiam ex Matth. 5. v. 10.Beati, qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum? Suppresso etiam nomine Esaiae citat eiusdem sententiam ex cap. 8. v. 12.Timorem eius (populi) ne timeatis, neque paveatis.

4. Subiungit Apostolus consolationem pro his, qui licet pacem quaerunt, & bonum sectantur, nihilo tamen minùs hominum improborum iniuriis, afflictionibus & persecutionibus sunt expositi, quos consolatur verbis Magistri sui, qui eos beatos pronunciat.

5. Assurgit Apostoli oratio. Persecutores non solùm vobis non possunt nocere, sed etiam coguntur praeter suam intentionem salutem vestram promovere. Beda in h. l. Non solùm, inquit, nihil vobis nocet, qui bonum facientibus mala irrogat, sed & cum vos propter bona, quae execratur, hostis insequitur, causam vobis maioris beatitudinis praestat, cum patientiae vestrae vires exercet. Gloss. interlin. in h. l. Non solùm non nocet, quod à malis irrogatur, sed etiam prodest, quia patientiam exercet.

Textus dispositio. Partes versiculi duae sunt. Prior continet παράκλησιν, posterior παραίνεσιν.

Expositio. Ἀλλ᾽ εἰ καὶ πάσχοιτε διὰ δικαιοσύνην. Sed enim etiamsi contingat vos affligi propter iustitiam. Syrus ἐλλειπτικῶς reddidit. Et si (subintellige contingat) ut patiamini. Pro ἀλλ᾿ εἰ καὶ Regii duo Codices habent, εἰδὲ.Siverò patiamini. Vulgata reddidit. Sed & si quid patimini. Voculam quid Interpres de suo addidit, Graeca enim simpliciter habent. Sed si etiam patiamini.

Τὸ πάσχειν absolutè ponitur, proinde quaevis παθήματα à malis hominibus illata denotat, sive illi nos laedant verbis sive factis; sive famae nostrae detrahant, sive bonorum nostrorum rapinam exerceant, sive corpori molestiam inferant. Interim quia Petrus repetit haec ex ore Christi Matth. 5. v. 10. ideò praecipuè ac principaliter intelliguntur afflictiones, quae à persecutoribus inferuntur. Sic enim Christus loquitur. Beatiοἱ δεδιωγμένοι,qui patiunturδιωγμὸνpersecutionem. Ostendit autem res ipsa, Apostolum nostrum aliquoties hoc verbum absolutè posuisse. cap. 2. v. 19. v. πάσχων ἀδίκως,v. 20.πάσχοντες ὑπομενεῖτε.cap. 3. v. 17.Κρεῖττον ἀγαθοποιοῦντας πάσχειν.cap. 4. v. 1.ὁ παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ.v. 15.μηδεὶς πασχέτω ὡς φονεὺςcap. 5. v. 10.ὁ λίγον παθόντας. quâ in parte secutus fuit stylum Evangelistarum & aliorum Apostolorum, qui de passione Christi itidem hoc verbo absolutè posito utuntur. Luc. 22. v. 15.πρὸ τοῦ με παθεῖν.cap. 24. v. 26.οὐχὶ ταῦτα ἔδει παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν.v. 46.οὕτως ἔδει παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸν.Act. 1. v. 3.μετὰ τὸ παθεῖν αὐτὸν.cap. 3. v. 18.παθεῖν τὸν χριστὸνcap. 17. v. 3.τὸν χριστὸν ἔδει παθεῖν,Hebr. 2. v. 18.ἐν ᾧ πέπονθεν.c. 9. v. 26.πολλάκις πασθεῖν. &c. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] sive [consult facsimile image]passus est. Per τὴν δικαιοσύνην intelligitur non solùm confessio veritatis coelestis, quae est iustitiae Christianae quaedam pars, de qua propriè Christus loquitur Matth. 5. vers. 10. sed in genere studium pietatis, ut apparet ex praecedentibus huius loci verbis. Si non reddatis malum pro malo, nec convitium pro convitio, sed contrà benedicatis; si declinetis à malo, & bonum faciatis; si pacem quaeratis, eamque per sequamini; si iustitiae studeatis, & boni sitis aemulatores, ac nihilominus ab impiis hominibus iniuriis afficiamini. Gloss. interlin. in h. l. Propter iustitiam tenendam vel assequendam. In hoc tamen pietatis & iustitiae studio eminet fidei confessio, ad quam Apostolum praecipuè hîc respicere, patet non solùm ex dicto Christi, quod Apostolus allegat, sed etiam ex v. 15. seq. parati semper ad defensionem doctrinae, & ex cap. 4. v. 15.Nemo vestrûm patiatur ut homicida, aut fur &c.v. 16.Si autem ut Christianus, non erubescat. Quidam volunt, propter iustitiam pati esse idem, quod iniustè ac praeter meritum pati, ut haec phrasis significet non modò ob bonae causae patrocinium affligi, sed etiam iniustè pati, cum quis innocenter & sanctè in timore DEI versatus. Sed res utrobique eòdem redit.

Μακάριοι sc. ἔστε,nihilo minùs beati estis, non propterea minuetur vobis felicitas, quam Psaltes promittit, imò quàm maximè beati eritis, certi scilicet vos per viam afflictionis deduci in regnum coelorum. Matth. 5. v. 10.Beati, qui patiuntur propter iustitiam, ipsorum enim est regnum coelorum.Act. 14. v. 22.Per multas tribulationes oportet nos intraere in regnum Dei.2. Tim. 2. v. 11.Si commortui sumus, etiam convivemus.v. 12.Si sustinebimus & conregnabimus.

Τὸν δέ φόβον αὐτῶν μὴ φοβηθῇτε. Locus desumtus est ex Esai. 8. v. 12. ubi LXX. Interpp. iisdem omninò verbis sic loquuntur. τὸν δὲ φόβον αὐτοῦ οὐ μὴ φοβηθῆτε, οὐδὲ μὴ ταραχθῆτε. Hebraeus textus eodem modo. Timorem eius non timebitis & non pavebitis. Subintelligitur autem κατὰsecundum timorem huius populi ne timeatis, h. e. non timeatis eo timore, quo hic populus trepidat, qui in hominibus & humanis praesidiis & non in Domino confidit, atque ex hoc praepostero timore foedus cum Rege Assyriorum ineundum esse statuit. Inde quidam censent, etiam apud Petrum eandem omnino esse verborum istorum sententiam.
