Vester timor non sit, qualis solet esse eorum, subintellige malorum hominum sive persecutorum, qui vos affligunt, h. e. non sit mundanus & carnalis, quo timentes amittere bona temporalia, deserunt veritatis confessionem & iustitiae ac sanctitatis studium. Vel, ne timeatis praeposterè illud malum, quod ipsi timent & ex praepostero illo timore redduntur pusillanimes. Sed rectiùs dicitur, Petrum haec verba Prophetica ad suum institutum accommodare, & ad cognatam significationem leni quadam deflexione deducere, ut timoris nomen non accipiatur passivè de timore, quo mali & persecutores praeposterè timent, sed activè de timore, quem mali, & persecutores fastuosè aliis incutiunt, ut sit sensus. Ne timeatis eorum timorem h. e. formidabilia illa, quae vobis minantur; minas eorum, quibus timorem vobis incutere conantur; vel etiam ipsos persecutores damnorum & suppliciorum temporalium comminatione terrorem vobis immittentes, qui sensus colligitur ex subiecta ἐξηγήσει, & non turbemini. Eundem etiam expressit Syrus Interpres. Ne timeatis ab illis, qui vos territant. Est ergo in voce timoris quaedam metonymia, quâ effectum ponitur pro causâ. Iob. 3. v. 25. timor, quem timebam, evenit mihi i. e. malum quod timebo Ps. 64. v. 2.à timore inimici custodi vitam meam i. e. à malis quorum comminatione timorem mihi incutere conatur Psal. 91. v. 5.Ne timeas à timore nocturnoProv. 1. v. 26.Etiam ego subsannabo vos, cum venerit timor vester, id est, malum illud, quod timorem vobis incutit. Cum hac expositione congruit ea, quâ quidam per timorem eorum intelligunt ea, quae in persecutoribus timenda, ut sunt potestas, calliditas, animus ac vires malefaciendi. Sensus enim eodem redit, quòd pii non debeant esse animo nimis demisso & abiecto, quando à malis hominibus vel persecutoribus affliguntur, sed fortes in Domino ac bono omnino animo, scientes DEUM ab ipsorum partibus stare, & contra hostiles insultus ipsos defendere velle, sicut apud Prophetam praecedit. v. 10.Inite consilium & dissipabitur, loquimini verbum, & non stabit, quia hîc Emanuel i. e. nobiscum DEUS. Si autem DEUS pro nobis & cum nobis, quis contra nos.Rom. 8. v. 31.

Μηδὲ ταραχθῆτε. ταράττεσθαι significationem habet vehementioris perturbationis, qualis erat Herodis audientis natum novum Regem, ac metuentis universales Reipubl. motus, Matth. 2. v. 3. discipulorum existimantium se spectrum videre Matth. 14. vers. 26.Marc. 6. v. 50.Luc. 24. v. 38. Zachariae videntis Angelum Luc. 1. v. 12. LXX. utuntur pro בהל quod significat subito terrore perculsus est, importat enim cum passione temporis celeritatem. Psal. 6. v. 2.Psal. 47. v. 5. &c. pro בעתterritus est ad conspectum rei, unde malum metuitur.Esth. 7. v. 6. pro געשconcussus est, contremuit.2. Reg. 22. v. 8.Ierem. 5. v. 22. pro המהtumultuatus est, murmuravitPsal. 38. v. 9.Psal. 45. v. 6. &c. pro זעףmetu seu tristitiâ turbatus estGen. 40. v. 6. pro חולformidavit, contremuitEsth. 4. v. 4.Psal. 54. v. 4. &c. pro חללvehementer dissolutus est, excruciatus estPsal. 108. v. 21. pro חרדita commotus fuit terrore & metu, ut ex signis exterioribus illud colligi possit.Gen. 42. v. 28.Iob. 37. v. 1. pro ערץconsternatus & animo fractus fuitEsai. 8. v. 12. (ex quo loco Petrus verbum ταράττεσθαι adducit) pro בעםtimore perculsus stupuit,Gen. 41. v. 8.Psal. 76. v. 4. pro רגשmetu fuit commotus & conturbatus, opponitur enim animi quieti, Deut. 2. v. 25.2. Reg. 18. v. 33. quae significationes omnes hûc accommodari possunt. Sensus enim est, quod pii non debeant nimiopere animo commoveri ob minas vel iniurias malorum hominum, sed animi constantiam in ipsis etiam adversis ac periculis tueri. Locus parallelus extat Ioh. 14. v. 1. & 27.μὴ ταρασσέσθω ὑμῶν ἡ καρδία.

## 3:15
BUT SANCTIFY THE LORD CHRIST IN YOUR HEARTS, ALWAYS READY TO A DEFENSE TO EVERY ONE THAT ASKETH YOU A REASON OF THAT HOPE WHICH IS IN YOU.

Connection. 1. The prior part of the verse pertains to the Prophetic saying Esa. 8. v. 13. whose citation Peter continues.

2. It contains, however, an exhortation to sanctifying God in our hearts, through true confidence, namely, opposed to the preceding dissuasion, that we should not fear too much from the threats and terrors of enemies.

3. Lyranus brings forward such a connection. After the Apostle had ordered those to whom he writes, toward their neighbor both in the conferring of good and in the suffering of evil, he furthermore orders them toward God. But a man is well ordered toward God through faith, and this in three things. The first is, that this faith be strengthened in his heart, and as to this, he says. But sanctify the Lord Christ, i. e. strengthen: for holy in one signification is the same as firm. In your hearts, i. e. by firmly adhering to him, because firm is he in himself. The second is, that this faith may be derived to others, and as to this, he adds, always prepared for a defense, etc. The third is, that on account of any adversities whatsoever a man may not be torn away from the faith, and as to this, it is added. For it is better, if the will of God should will it so, that you suffer doing good, etc.

4. The latter part of the verse explains the seventh virtue, to which the Apostle commonly exhorts all the faithful, which is constancy in the Christian faith, and the confession of it.

5. This confession of the Christian faith is a part of that sanctification, to which the Apostle had exhorted them in the former part of the verse. For among other things, for the sanctification of GOD or of the divine name, this also is required, that by words and deeds, and indeed by our whole conversation, we may act so that the name of GOD may be glorified. But by confession GOD is glorified.

6. He wishes patience, to which the Apostle had exhorted the faithful in the preceding parts in many ways, to shine even in persecutions, and therefore, because adversities are also and indeed especially intended against the pious on account of the confession of faith, he wishes that not even then should they be of a dejected spirit, but prepared to render an account of their faith.

7. Therefore this exhortation depends upon the preceding ones. For he demands from the faithful such tolerance and patience, that they may intrepidly answer the persecutors concerning their faith.

8. Luther shows such a connection. In persecution it is necessary for you to have hope; if a reason for the hope is demanded, it is necessary for you to have the word.

Disposition. The Apostle exhorts the faithful. 1. To the sanctification of GOD. 2. To rendering an account of the faith. By the former precept he informs the heart, by the latter the tongue of the faithful.

Exposition of the text. κύριον δὲ τὸν θεὸν ἁγιάσητε ἐκ ταῖς καρδίαισ ὑμῶν. For τὸν θεὸν some codices read χριστὸν, whence the vulgate rendered, But sanctify the Lord Christ; in which way the Syrian also has it. Sanctify [consult facsimile image] the Lord Messiah, and Clement of Alexandria in his commentary on this place, as also Fulgentius in book 2 to Thrasimund, chapter 14, indeed most of the older expositors. By which reasoning in this Petrine passage, joined with the Prophetic saying Isa. 8. verse 13. there would be an evident argument for establishing the divinity of Christ. For Isaiah says. The Lord God of hosts Sanctify him. Now indeed it belongs to the only true God to be the Lord of hosts. Wherefore, since Peter shows that Christ is that Lord of hosts whom we ought to sanctify, by that very fact it is immovably proven that Christ is the true God. But the more approved Greek codices read Κύριον δὲ τὸν θεὸν ἁγιάσητε, which corresponds to the Hebrew, Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself, as also the version of the LXX Interpreters, who likewise have τὸν Κύριον τῷν δυνάμεων αὐτὸν ἁγιάσατε, ἐν ταῖς καρδὶαις ὑμῶν. This is not added in the Hebrew text Isa. 8. v. 13. But Peter, for the sake of ἐξηγήσεως, and in order to accommodate the Prophetic saying more to his purpose, wished to subjoin it. For he shows in what manner he wishes God to be sanctified by them, namely, through the trust of their hearts, so that they may not be so dismayed and tremble at the threats of persecutors that they allow themselves to be cast down from the constancy of faith, or run to illicit means, but that they may place the trust of their heart in God, and rest in true faith in His promise of providing protection and help. In the Hebrew text it is added: He himself (the Lord of hosts) shall be your fear, and he himself your dread, which the LXX rendered thus: καὶ αὐτὸς ἒσται σου φόβος, κᾂν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ πεποιθὼς ᾖς, where mention is likewise made of πεποιθήσεως or of the trust and confidence which Peter in this place requires in the citation of the Prophetic saying.

Ἓτοιμοι δὲ ἀεὶ, namely ἒστε, be ready and prepared, namely, in your hearts, which ἀπὸ κοινοῦ is to be repeated from the preceding member.

Πρὸς ἀπολογίαν The Vulgate rendered it to satisfaction. Fulgentius, 1. to Thrasimund, chap. 1, renders it to answering. But in Greek it is properly to a defense, namely, of Christian doctrine, and indeed to a defense constant in speech and words, for that is what ἀπολογία. properly signifies Acts 22. verse 1. Paul, about to render an account of his faith and to purge himself from the attempted accusation of sedition, says ἀκούσατέ μου τῆς πρὸς ὑμᾶς νῦν ἀπολογίας. chap. 25. v. 16. Festus the Governor says: It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have license τῆς ἀπολογίας to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him περὶ τοῦ ἐγκλήματος. In the same way it is taken 1. Corinthians 9. v. 3. 2. Corinthians 7. v. 11. But the Apostolic sayings properly pertain here Philippians 1. verse 7. & 17. where it is called ἀπολογία τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, & 2. Timothy 4. v. 16. where Paul mentions his first apology before Caesar, in which he the Christian faith. he publicly professed, and defended himself against the accusations threatened by the Jews and Gentiles. The Syriac has [consult facsimile image] which is to say to the bringing forth of the Spirit, which among the Syrians is a periphrasis for an Apology. Acts 22. v. 1.Rom. 1. v. 20.ch. 2. v. 1. Preposterous fear closes mouths, lest they break forth into confession, but the confidence of the heart opens them, so that they may bring forth the Spirit into a free field, and publish a confession publicly. The ordinary Gloss brings forward as a parallel passage. Col. 4. v. 5.Walk in wisdom toward them that are without &c.v. 6.Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man; and it adds. Those existing without, i. e. not yet faithful wish to know something about the hope that is in you παντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντι ὑμᾶς λόγον περὶ τῆς ἐν ὑμῖν ὲλπίδος. To him that asketh of you or asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you. The Syriac λόγον rendered by [consult facsimile image] speech, in which way also some Latin Codices have it. But it is more correctly translated by reason, because the scope of Peter is that he wishes us to be prepared and ready to render a reason for our faith. Luther, regarding the sense, rendered it, Der Grund fordert. To the name ἐλπίδος the Syriac added also the name πίστεως, for thus he rendered the text, To everyone who shall ask of you a speech concerning the hope of faith. Some Latin Codices also read concerning that which is in you hope and faith; and Bede seems to have read it thus, as appears from his commentary. Whence Salmeron on this place annotates thus. In the Greek the word faith is lacking, but it is to be supplied. And yet the name πίστεως does not exist added in any Greek Codex, nor is it held in the commentaries of the Greek Fathers, nor in the more corrected Latin Codices. It would therefore be preposterous to correct the Greek text from Latin Codices, and those not sufficiently approved, and thus to prefer less pure streams to the fountains themselves. The Syriac as a paraphrast added this, wishing to explain the mind of the Apostle, for hope is placed here by a common phrase of Scripture for faith in God and Christ, which is the foundation of the hope of the heavenly inheritance promised to those believing in Christ: whence Cyril of Alexandria, citing this Petrine passage, sometimes mentions only faith, not hope, in Epist. to Anast. and others in vol. 2 of the Council of Ephesus, Appendix of the first ch. 6, sometimes he makes mention of hope alone vol. 5 of the Council of Ephesus

Gregory, part 2 of the Pastoral Care, last chapter, citing this Apostolic passage, does not add the word faith. Nor does any necessity compel us to establish that it was omitted from the Greek text, for the sense remains intact, which is as follows: Because unbelievers, but especially persecutors, boast that the hope which you have in GOD concerning glory and eternal happiness to be obtained through faith in CHRIST is empty, and on this account insult you, because for the sake of an uncertain hope you voluntarily expose yourselves to most certain dangers and various adversities, therefore I seriously exhort you that you always have in readiness a response by which you may demonstrate that your hope, or the faith of the hoped-for glory, is reasonable and rests upon an immovable foundation, on account of which you not undeservedly suffer such hard things in this life.

Μετὰ πραΰτητος καί φοβου. Two Royal Codices have ἀλλὰ μετὰ πραΰτητος,, just as certain Latin Codices also read, but with modesty. But the more approved Greek Codices read without the adversative particle μετὰ πραΰτητος,, which also does not exist in the Syriac. The Latin Codices join this προσδιορισμὸν (μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου) with the following verse: With modesty and fear, having a good conscience, which Salmero follows in his commentary. But the Greek Codices more correctly join it with the preceding, which the Syriac also does. Therefore, the Apostle requires two virtues, especially necessary in giving a confession of faith. The first is πραΰτης or πραότης, meekness or modesty, lest by untimely zeal and especially by a more bitter rejection and condemnation of some false dogma, we bring more detriment to the heavenly truth of the Church among adversaries than we promote the salvation of the pious. The account of faith must be rendered with an intrepid mind indeed, but yet with a Spirit of meekness and with placid words, so that enemies may not have anything which they can deservedly object against the confessors. The Syriac has the noun [consult facsimile image], which signifies both humility and meekness. 2. Corinth. 10. vers. 1. Galat. 5. vers. 23. Interlinear Gloss: Have not only doctrine, but also modesty in doctrine, which is the mother of all virtues. Ordinary Gloss from Bede: In the very knowledge of doctrine he warns that the quality of teaching be observed, so that humility, which is the mistress and mother of all virtues, and in speaking let it be spoken and shown by seeing. Lyranus. That defense ought to lack presumption and boasting, and be done in a due and honest manner. The latter is φόβος fear. Some understand it of the fear of God, lest the truth be dissembled for the favor of men or for fear of persecution, and by this reason God be offended, seeing that He demands an entire confession of doctrine. But others accept it of the fear of men, so that it may be referred to them πραΰτης & φόβος, in that sense. When questioned about the faith, you ought not to answer contentiously, arrogantly, and forwardly, but with meekness and reverence, especially if the confession of faith is to be given before a superior or Magistrate. Finally, some refer it to the confessor himself, in that sense, that one ought not, in giving a confession of faith, to rely on his own erudition, his own wisdom, his own strengths, but to approach the giving of the confession in fear and trembling. For there is no need of human strengths to give a confession intrepidly before enemies, but it is a singular gift of the Holy Spirit. Matth. 10. 19. When they deliver you up, do not think how or what you should speak, for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak v. 20. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. None of these expositions fights either with the analogy of faith or with the series of the text, therefore all can be joined. The Syriac has the noun [consult facsimile image] which Hebr. 12. verse is placed for εὐλαβεία reverence.

Latin:

DOMINUM AUTEM CHRISTUM SANCTIFICATE IN CORDIBUS VESTRIS, PARATI SEMPER AD SATISFACTIONEM OMNI, POSCENTI VOS RATIONEM DE EA, QUAE IN VOBIS EST SPE.

Connexio. 1. Prior pars versiculi pertinet ad dictum Propheticum Esa. 8. v. 13. cuius allegationem Petrus continuat.

2. Continet autem ea exhortationem ad Deum in cordibus nostris sanctificandum, per veram sc. fiduciam oppositam praecedenti dehortationi, ne à minis & terroribus hostium nimis timeamus.

3. Lyranus eiusmodi profert connexionem. Post quam ordinaverat Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit, ad proximum tùm in collatione boni, tùm in perpessione mali, ordinat porrò eos ad Deum. Ad Deum autem benè ordinatur homo per fidem, & hoc in tribus. Primum est, quod haec fides in eius corde firmetur, & quantum ad hoc, dicit. Dominum autem Christum sanctificate, i. e. firmate: sanctum enim in una significatione est idem, quod firmum. In cordibus vestris, i. e. firmiter sibi adhaerendo, quia firmus est in seipso. Secundum est, ut haec fides ad alios derivetur, & quantum ad hoc, subdit, parati semper ad satisfactionem &c. Tertium est, quod propter quaecunque adversa homo à fide non evellatur, & quantum ad hoc, subditur. Melius est enim benefacientes pati &c.

4. Posterior versiculi pars exponit septimam virtutem, ad quam Apostolus communiter omnes fideles hortatur, quae est constantia in fide Christiana, & eius confessione.

5. Haec fidei Christianae confessio est pars illius sanctificationis, ad quam in priore versiculi parte Apostolus eos fuerat exhortatus. Inter caetera enim ad sanctificationem DEI vel nominis divini etiam hoc requiritur, ut verbis & factis, adeoque totâ nostrâ conversatione id agamus, ut nomen DEI glorificetur. Per confessionem autem DEUS glorificatur.

6. Patientiam, ad quam in praecedentibus Apostolus multis fuerat fideles exhortatus, etiam in persecutionibus vult lucere, ac proinde, quia adversa etiam & quidem maximè ob fidei confessionem piis intentantur, vult, ne tùm quidem illos esse animo abiecto, sed ad rationem fidei suae reddendam paratos.

7. Pendet ergò haec exhortatio ex praecedentibus. Nam à fidelibus eam exigit tolerantiam ac patientiam, ut persecutoribus intrepidè de fide sua respondeant.

8. Lutherus eiusmodi connexionem monstrat. In persecutione oportet vos habere spem; si ratio spei exigitur, oportet vos habere verbum.

Dispositio. Exhortatur Apostolus fideles. 1. Ad DEI sanctificationem. 2. Ad red dendam fidei rationem. Priore praecepto informat cor, posteriore linguam fidelis.

Textus expositio. κύριον δὲ τὸν θεὸν ἁγιάσητε ἐκ ταῖς καρδίαισ ὑμῶν. Pro τὸν θεὸν quidam Codd. legunt χριστὸν, unde vulgata reddidit, Dominum autem Christum sanctificate; quo modo etiam habet Syrus. Sanctificate[consult facsimile image]Dominum Messiam, ac Clemens Alexandrinus in comm. h. l. ut & Fulgentius lib. 2. ad Thrasim. cap. 14. imò plerique enarratores antiquiores. quâ ratione in hoc loco Petrino, coniuncto cum dicto Prophetico Esa. 8. vers. 13. esset evidens argumentum pro astruenda Christi divinitate. Esaias enim dicit. Dominum Deum exercituum ipsum sanctificabitis. Iam vero soli vero Deo competit esse Dominum exercituum. Quare cum Petrus ostendat, Christum esse Dominum illum exercituum, quem sanctificare debemus, eo ipso immotè probatur, Christum esse verum Deum. Sed probatiores Graeci Codices legunt Κύριον δὲ τὸν θεὸν ἁγιάσητε, quod responder Hebraeo, Dominum exercituum ipsum sacrificate, ut & LXX. Interpp. versioni, qui itidem habent τὸν Κύριον τῷν δυνάμεων αὐτὸν ἁγιάσατε, ἐν ταῖς καρδὶαις ὑμῶν. Hoc non est additum in textu Hebraeo Esa. 8. v. 13. Petrus autem ἐξηγήσεως causâ, atque ut dictum Propheticum magis accommodaret ad suum propositum, subiicere voluit. Ostendit enim, quâ ratione Deum ab illis sanctificari velit, videlicet per cordium fiduciam, ne ita consternentur ac trepident ad persecutorum minas, ut à fidei constantia patiantur sese deiici, vel ad illicita media concurrant, sed ut fiduciam cordis in Deum collocent, & in promissione ipsius de praesidio & auxilio praestando verâ fide acquiescant. In textu Hebraeo additur. Ipse (Dominus exercituum) sit timor vester, & ipse pavor vester, quod LXX. sic reddiderunt, καὶ αὐτὸς ἒσται σου φόβος, κᾂν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ πεποιθὼς ᾖς, ubi itidem mentio fit πεποιθήσεως sive fiduciae & confidentiae, quam hoc loco Petrus in allegatione dicti Prophetici requirit.

Ἓτοιμοι δὲ ἀεὶ, scil. ἒστε,parati estote atque promti, videl. in cordibus vestris, quod ἀπὸ κοινοῦ ex praecedente membro repetendum.

Πρὸς ἀπολογίαν Vulgata reddidit ad satisfactionem. Fulgentius. 1. ad Thrasim. cap. 1. reddit ad respondendum. Sed in Graeco propriè est, ad defensionem, scil. doctrinae Christianae, & quidem ad defensionem sermone & verbis constantem, id enim propriè significat ἀπολογία.Actor. 22. vers. 1. Paulus fidei suae rationem redditurus, & ab intentata seditionis accusatione sese purgaturus dicit, ἀκούσατέ μου τῆς πρὸς ὑμᾶς νῦν ἀπολογίας.cap. 25. v. 16. dicit Festus Praeses. Non est consuetudo Romanis, gratis aliquem condemnare, prius quam is, qui accusatur, praesentes habeat accusatores, ac locumτῆς ἀπολογίαςsese defendendi accipiatπερὶ τοῦ ἐγκλήματος. Eodem modo accipitur 1. Corinth. 9. v. 3.2. Corinth. 7. v. 11. Propriè verò huc pertinent dicta Apostolica Philip. 1. vers. 7. & 17. ubi vocatur ἀπολογία τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, & 2. Timoth. 4. v. 16. ubi Paulus meminit primae suae apologiae coram Caesare, in qua fidem Christianam publicè fuit professus, & contra intentatas à Iudaeis & gentilibus accusationes sese defendit. Syrus habet [consult facsimile image] q. d. ad productionem Spiritus. quae apud Syros est periphrasis Apologiae. Actor. 22. v. 1.Rom. 1. v. 20.cap. 2. v. 1. Praeposterus timor concludit ora, ne in confessionem prorumpant, sed cordis fiducia ea aperit, ut Spiritum in liberum campum producant, & confessionem publicè edant. Glossa ordinaria tanquam locum parallelum adducit. Col. 4. v. 5.In sapientia ambulate ad eos, qui foris sunt &c.v. 6.Sermo vester sit semper in gratia, sale conditus, ut sciatis quomodo oporteat vos unicuique respondere; & addit. Foris existentes, i. e. nondum fideles volunt aliquid cognoscere de spe, quae in vobis estπαντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντι ὑμᾶς λόγον περὶ τῆς ἐν ὑμῖν ὲλπίδος.Petenti à vobis vel petenti vos rationem eius, quae in vobis est spei. Syrus λόγον reddidit per [consult facsimile image]sermonem, quo modo etiam quidam Codices Latini habent. Sed rectiùs vertitur per rationem, quia scopus Petri est, quòd ad fidei nostrae rationem reddendam paratos nos esse velit atque promtos. Lutherus sensum respiciens reddidit, Der Grund fordert. Ad nomen ἐλπίδος Syrus addidit etiam nomen πίστεως, sic enim textum reddidit, Apud omnem, qui à vobis quaeret sermonem de spe fidei. Quidam etiam Latini Codices legunt de ea, quae in vobis est spe & fide; ac Beda sic videtur legisse, ut apparet ex eius commentario. Unde Salmeron ad h. l. sic annotat. In Graeco deest verbum fides, sed supplendum est. Atqui nomen πίστεως in nullo Codice Graeco adiectum extat, nec in Graecorum Patrum commentariis, nec in castigatioribus Latinis Codicibus habetur. praeposterum igitur foret, ex Codicibus Latinis, iisque non satis probatis textum Graecum corrigere, adeoque rivulos minùs puros ipsis fontibus praeferre. Syrus ut paraphrastes, hoc addidit, mentem Apostoli volens explicare, spes enim vulgatâ Scripturae phrasi ponitur hîc pro fide in Deum & Christum, quae est fundamentum spei de coelesti hereditate credentibus in Christum promissa: unde Cyrillus Alexandrinus adducens hunc locum Petrinum, modò fidei duntaxat meminit, non spei, in Epist. ad Anast. & alios in tom. 2. Conc. Ephes. Append. primae c. 6. modò de spe sola mentionem facit tom. 5. Conc. Eph.

Gregorius part. 2. curae pastoralis cap. ult. hunc locum Apostolicum citans, fidei nomen non addit. Nec ulla nos cogit necessitas, ut ex textu Graeco illud omissum statuamus, sensus enim manet integer, qui sic habet. Quia infideles, praesertim vero persecutores spem, quam in DEO habetis de gloria & felicitate aeterna per fidem in CHRISTUM obtinenda, iactitant inanem esse, ac hoc nomine vobis insultant, quòd propter incertam spem certissimis periculis & variis adversis sponte vos obiiciatis, ideò seriò vos exhortor, ut semper in promtu habeatis responsionem, quâ spem vestram sive fidem speratae gloriae rationabilem esse, ac immoto niti fundamento demonstretis, propter quam haud immeritò tàm dura in hac vita patiamini.

Μετὰ πραΰτητος καί φοβου. Regii duo Codices habent, ἀλλὰ μετὰ πραΰτητος, sicut etiam quidam Codd. Latini legunt, sed cum modestia. Verùm probatiores Codices Graeci legunt sine particula adversativa μετὰ πραΰτητος, quae etiam non extat apud Syrum. Codices Latini hunc προσδιορισμὸν (μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου) coniungunt cum versu sequente. Cùm modestia & timore conscientiam habentes bonam, quos sequitur Salmero in commentario. Sed Graeci Codices rectiùs eum coniungunt cum praecedentibus, quod etiam facit Syrus. Requirit ergò Apostolus duas virtutes, in edenda fidei confessione apprimè necessarias. Prior est πραΰτης sive πραότηςmansuetudo sive modestia, ne zelo intempestivo & cumprimis acerbiore falsi alicuius dogmatis reiectione atque damnatione apud adversarios, coelestis veritatis Ecclesiae plus detrimenti afferamus, quàm salutem piorum promoveamus. Intrepido quidem animo, sed tamen cum Spiritu mansuetudinis ac verbis placidis fidei ratio reddenda, ut non habeant hostes, quod meritò possint confessoribus obiicere. Syrus habet nomen [consult facsimile image] quod & humilitatem & mansuetudinem significat. 2. Corinth. 10. vers. 1.Galat. 5. vers. 23. Gossa interlin. Non tantùm doctrinam, sed etiam in doctrina modestiam habeatis, quae est mater omnium virtutum. Gloss. ordin. ex Beda, In ipsa doctrinae scientia qualitatem docendi monet observari, ut humilitas, quae magistra est, materque omnium virtutum, & loquendo dicatur & videndo monstretur. Lyranus. Defensio ista debet carere praesumtione & iactantia, ac fieri modo debito & honesto. Posterior est φόβοςtimor. Quidam intelligunt de timore Dei, ne in gratiam hominum aut metu persecutionis veritas dissimuletur, & hac ratione Deus offendatur, quippe, qui integram doctrinae confessionem exigit. Quidam verò accipiunt de timore hominum, ut ad eosdem referaturπραΰτης & φόβος, sensu eo. Interrogati de fide non debetis contentiosè, arroganter & protervè respondere, sed cum mansuetudine & reverentia, maximè si apud superiorem vel Magistratum fidei confessio edenda. Quidam denique referunt ad ipsum confessorem, sensu eo, quòd non debeat quis in fidei confessione edenda suae eruditioni, suae Sapientiae, suis viribus considere, sed in timore ac tremore ad edendam confessionem accedere. Neque enim opus est virium humanarum, coram hostibus intrepidè confessionem edere, sed est singulare Spiritus sancti donum. Matth. 10. 19.Cùm tradent vos, nolite cogitare, quomodo aut quid loquamini, dabitur enim vobis in illa hora, quid loquaminiv. 20.Non enim vos estis, qui loquimini, sed Spiritus Patris vestri, qui loquitur in vobis. Nulla harum expositionum vel cum fidei analogia, vel cum serie textus pugnat, ideò omnes possunt coniungi. Syrus habet nomen [consult facsimile image] quod Hebr. 12. vers. ponitur pro εὐλαβείαreverentia.

## 3:15-18 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. What is understood by the sanctification of GOD? Resp. 1. Bede comments on this place thus. What is it to sanctify God in our hearts, but to contemplate His holiness, of how incomprehensible glory it is, with the inmost affection of the heart? 2. Fulgentius book 2 to Thrasimundus chapter 14. He sanctifies Christ, who thinks those things about Christ which are holy; which thought sanctifies the thinker, and by sanctifying preserves him. He confirms this from Cyprian, who declares that petition of the Lord's prayer, Hallowed be thy name, in such a way that the gift of divine sanctification may be conferred upon us, and that we who have been sanctified in Baptism may persevere in that which we have begun to be. In the same way Ambrose explains the Lord's prayer book 5 de Sacram. c. 4. What is hallowed be thy name? As if we desire that He be sanctified, who says, Be ye holy, because I am holy, as if something of sanctification might accrue to Him from our prayer? No; but let it be sanctified in us, so that His sanctification may be able to reach us. 3. Augustine book 2 de serm. Dom. in monte, Bernard sermon 6 quadrag. explain it thus. When we ask that the name of GOD be sanctified, then we ask this, that the name of GOD may become known to all, and may be sanctified by all. 4. All these things are indeed rightly said in their own place, meanwhile it is manifest, since GOD is sanctified in various ways, that Peter συνεκδοχικῶς understands a certain mode of sanctification here. Lyranus therefore seeks the explanation in the following words, and explains this sanctification of God as the well-establishing of faith in hearts, from which it may afterwards come to pass that we are able to satisfy those who object against it. Sanctify, he says, the Lord, i. e. establish, for holy in one meaning is the same as firm. 5. But from the preceding antithesis, do not fear their terror, nor be troubled; & from the added προσδιορισμῷ in your hearts, the explanation is more correctly gathered, since in the Hebrew text Isa. 8. v. 13. it is added, Sanctify the Lord of hosts, let him be your fear, & your dread. The sense therefore is this. Sanctify GOD in your hearts through true confidence in GOD's omnipotence, and his fatherly protection: rest with filial confidence in his goodness, being certainly persuaded that he both wills and is able to protect his sincere worshippers and the intrepid confessors of his name against the injuries of evil men. By this confidence of the heart GOD is sanctified. 1. Because he is acknowledged as upright and holy in his judgments, when by his just judgment he exposes us to the injuries and violence of evil men, even if we do not seem to have deserved this by more serious offenses. Psal. 119. v. 137. Luther in comm. on this passage: When I consider whatever is sent by GOD to be good & holy, then I sanctify him. 2. Because by this reason the praise of truth, wisdom & goodness is attributed to him, that he wills to keep his promises, and mercifully protect us, & can find a way of help.

Q. 2. Why does the Apostle add, sanctify the Lord in your hearts? Resp. 1. That he may lead us to the interior confidence of the heart, by which GOD is chiefly sanctified. 2. That he may show that external sanctification profits nothing without internal.

Q. 3. In what way ought we to be prepared to render an account of our faith? Resp. Bede on this passage: We ought to render an account to those demanding it concerning our hope & faith in two ways, so that we may both make known the just causes of our faith and hope to all, whether they ask faithfully or unfaithfully, & always keep the very profession of our faith and hope unblemished, even among the pressures of adversaries, showing through patience how reasonably we have learned that it must be kept, for whose love we fear neither to suffer adversities, nor to undergo death.

Q. 4. Why does Peter call the confession of faith an Apology? Resp. 1. Because at that time the name of Christians was infamous. It was called by the Gentiles & Jews a nefarious sect, & many crimes were objected against Christians, as we warned above in chapter 2. verse 12. 2. Because many things were objected against the very articles of the Christian faith by adversaries, to whom an apologetic response had to be opposed by the Confessors. Oecumenius in this place Since the Gentiles were saying that the hope of the Christians was vain, therefore Christians had to have prepared responses in readiness, suitable for refuting their calumnies.

Q. 5. Why does Chrysostom homily 34 on Matthew attribute this sentence, ready for a defense to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope &c., to Christ? Some here recognize ἁμάρτημα μνημονευτικὸν,, since in homily 16 on John he rightly attributes it to Peter. It is more conveniently answered that Chrysostom has regard for the principal cause, for through Peter Christ speaks to us Luke 10. v. 16. The Apostles in preaching were the mouth of Christ, in writing the hand of Christ. Likewise to the related sentence of Christ Matthew 10. v. 32. & 33.

Q. 6. Why does the Apostle require a good conscience and conversation for the confession of faith v. 16.? Resp. 1. because a good conscience provides confidence for speaking. Acts 23. v. 1. 2. The truth of confession rests on the foundation of the divine word, and life must also be conformed to the norm of the same; if both are a care and a concern to us, we shall have a good conscience. For in order that a good conscience may be had, it is necessary that we place the word of GOD as the foundation of our faith and actions. 3. If life does not correspond to the profession of faith, not only will there be no fruit, but also scandal and disadvantage will follow. Psalm 50. v. 16. To the wicked God said, why do you recite my statutes, and take my covenant through your mouth. 4. Paul likewise 1. Tim. 1. v. 5. a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith not feigned joins together, and expressly adds v. 6. those who wander from these, to be turned aside εἰς ματαιολογίαν of the same chapter v. 19. he again joins faith and a good conscience, and expressly adds, those who repel a good conscience, to make shipwreck concerning the faith.

Q. 7. Whether the confusion of the calumniators is signified to follow in this age or on the day of judgment? Bede in his commentary joins both explanations. Having, he says, a good conscience, so that those who mock in you the faith and hope of heavenly things, which they cannot see, may see your good works, and through these be confounded, which they cannot deny to be openly good. Or certainly it must be understood thus. Take care by doing good, so that those who disparage your good conversation, may be confounded when the time of future retribution arrives, seeing you crowned with Christ, but themselves condemned with the Devil. Truly the confusion of the calumniators will most certainly follow on the day of judgment, Sap. 5. vers. 2. meanwhile GOD also in this life brings the innocence of the pious into the light in various ways, and affects their calumniators with shame, as we showed above in the explanation of chapter 2, verse 12, question 6.

Q. 8. In what sense is the good conversation of the pious said to be in Christ? Resp. 1. because it is instituted according to the doctrine of Christ. Eph. 4. v. 17. This I say and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk, as the Gentiles also walk in the vanity of their mind, etc. v. 19. who have delivered themselves up to lasciviousness, etc. v. 20. But you have not so learned Christ. v. 21. If you have heard him, and have been taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus. 2. because this holy life is led in the Christian religion. 3. because it is conducted not only with Christ as teacher and author, but also with Christ as leader and director. The Spirit of Christ, which is given to those who believe in Christ, impels them to the pursuit of good works. 4. Just as Christ says of the good works of the pious, that they are done in God, Iohan. 3. v. 21. because they proceed from the Spirit of God, because they are done with God as witness, because they are done according to the norm of the divine command, because they are directed to the glory of God, and thus efficiently, finally, and objectively are done in God: so also Peter says that the holy conversation of the pious is instituted in Christ in almost the same respects.

Q. 9. Why is it better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil? Resp. 1. he who suffers for good deeds enjoys a peaceful conscience; he who suffers for evil deeds feels the bites of a gnawing conscience. 2. he who patiently tolerates punishment inflicted upon him for sins is not indeed deprived of the reward of his patience: meanwhile, far greater rewards will await those who patiently tolerate injuries and adversities brought upon them for the confession of faith or the pursuit of justice, and thus beyond merit, nay even against merit. 3. Those who suffer while doing good or for good deeds are more conformed to CHRIST, and to the holy men of God. Psalm. 44. vers. 22. Roman. 8. vers. 36. For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. Matth. 5. vers. 10. Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake, etc. v. 11. Blessed are you when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all that is evil against you, untruly, for my sake. vers. 12. Be glad and rejoice, etc. for so they persecuted the Prophets that were before you. 2. Cor. 4. v. 11. For we who live are always delivered unto death for Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh.1. Tim. 4. v. 10.For this we labor and are reviled, because we hope in the living God. From there also Peter, in place of confirmation, immediately adds: For Christ also suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, indeed, you are being conformed to his example, nay, to his image, if you endure sufferings while doing good or because of good deeds. 4. Bede proves the same thing by the examples of three persons who are said in the Scriptures to have been struck with blindness. So that the distance of the scourges in disparate merits may appear far different, let us see that Tobias, Saul, and Elymas were struck with one and the same trouble of blindness. But Tobias for this reason, that the virtue of his patience might shine forth more widely as an example to all.Tob. 2. v. 11. & seqq. Saul for this reason, that he might be changed from Saul the persecutor into Paul the Apostle.Actor. 9. v. 8.But Elymas, so that, paying the penalties worthy of his perfidy, he might also cease from the madness of those who were about to believe.Act. 13. v. 11.And if the option were given to me, I would rather, with such a father (Tobias), be subject to just blows, whether divine or human, than be drawn by the force of words from injustice to the pursuits of justice; and again, I would rather be drawn back from guilt by a scourge (with Paul) than be subjected to eternal vengeance for an incurable weight of sins (with Elymas). The Glossa ordinaria on this passage annotates thus: He who suffers justly imitates Christ. He who is corrected by scourges imitates the thief who, having recognized Christ on the cross, entered Paradise. He who is not corrected even by scourges imitates the thief on the left, who ascended the cross because of his sins, and after the cross went into the underworld.

Q. 10. Why does the Apostle add, if the will of God wills it? Resp. 1. to show that the wicked can bring nothing adverse or inconvenient to the pious, unless God permits and, as it were, loosens the rein for them. 2. to warn that the pious ought not to look to secondary causes, but to the first cause, and to receive whatever goods or evils, prosperous or adverse, befall them, as if from the hand of God, with a grateful and ready mind. Iob. 1. vers. 21.The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away.Sir. 11. vers. 14.Good and evil, life and death, poverty and riches are from God. 3. to teach that we ought not rashly to summon tribulations upon ourselves, or spontaneously expose ourselves to evils.

Q. 11. Why does the Apostle speak in a doubled manner, If the will of God wills it? Resp. 1. the will of God sometimes signifies the good pleasure of God. Ps. 30. vers. 6.Life is in his willvers. 8.in your will or according to his good pleasure you have established my mountain with strengthMalachiae 1. vers. 10.I have no will in you. He implies Therefore the Apostle, by the good and salutary counsel of God, signifies that the cross is sent to the pious. 2. It signifies that calamities are sent not only by God permitting, but also by God willing. For He does not permit unwillingly or forced, but willing. 3. The will of God is not something really distinct from His essence, but the will of God is God Himself willing. When therefore the Apostle says, if the will of God wills, the sense is, if God wills, if God by His good will determines that passions must be sent to you.

Q. 12. Why does the Apostle notably add that Christ suffered once? Resp. 1. To show the brevity of Christ's passion, which was immediately followed by eternal glory, in which lies an argument of exhortation to patience, as we showed above. 2. To show the perfection of the sacrifice offered by Christ in His passion and cross, in which part it is opposed to the legal sacrifices that had to be repeated daily. Hebr. 7. v. 27.cap. 9. vers. 12.25. & seqq. cap. 10. vers. 1. & seqq. 3. To teach that Christ will no longer be subject to passion and death, but as the victor of death reigns forever at the right hand of God. Roman. 6. vers. 9. & 10.

Q. 13. Why does he notably add that Christ suffered the just for the unjust? Resp. 1. So that the argument of exhortation may be the more effective. For thus the Apostle concludes from the greater to the less. If Christ, when He was most perfectly just, did not hesitate to suffer for the unjust, how much less should we refuse passions in this life, since we are not in all ways innocent. 2. To commend Christ's charity toward us and the heavenly Father's kindness. Rom. 5. vers. 8.God commends His charity toward us, because when we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.Gal. 2. v. 20.Christ loved me and delivered Himself for me.Apoc. 1. v. 5.Christ loved us and washed us from our sins in His blood. To explain the cause why Christ's passion could expiate our sins, namely because He Himself was most perfectly just and in the unity of person the Son of God. Hebr. 7. v. 27.Such it was fitting that we should have a High Priest, holy, innocent, undefiled &c.

Q. 14. By what reason is Christ said to have suffered for this purpose, that He might bring us to God? If the word προσάγειν is taken in the meaning of sacrificing, in three ways Christ in His passion and through His passion brought us to God, which we reviewed above in the exposition of the text. If the customary meaning of the word προσάγειν is retained; this bringing can to be brought. 1. to the past time. Christ therefore suffered, that He might bring us to God, i.e., that He might reconcile us to His heavenly Father, for it is evident from Rom. 5. v. 10.2. Cor. 5. v. 19.Eph. 2. vers. 16.Col. 1. vers. 20. that this reconciliation with the heavenly Father is the effect or fruit of the passion and death of Christ. The type in Exod. 19. v. 17. can be accommodated here: Moses as the Mediator of the O. T. in the promulgation of the law brought the Israelite people to meet God, as a Bride to the Bridegroom, as the Rabbis note on that passage: Christ, the Mediator of the N. T., brought us in His passion and through His passion to God, having become for us a Bridegroom of bloodExod. 4. v. 25. so that He might reconcile us to GOD, by whom we might be received as a beloved Bride. 2. to the present time. Christ therefore suffered, that He might bring us to God daily, that through Him as the divinely appointed Mediator we might have access in our prayers Rom. 5. v. 1. Being justified by faith we have peace with God through our Lord J. C. v. 2. through whom we have access by faith into this grace, in which we stand. Compare Ephes. 2. v. 18.c. 3. v. 12. For He alone is the way, through which we can approach God, no one comes to the Father, except through HimIoh. 14. v. 6. For that reason also Christ brings us daily, insofar as through His Holy Spirit He mortifies sin in us, and renders us near to God by the likeness of character and affections, which renewal and reformation of the divine image, however, is only begun in this life. 3. to the future time. Christ therefore suffered, that at some time on the day of judgment He might present us to His Father perfectly renewed and glorious, and might introduce us with Him into eternal life, to live with God forever in supreme happiness and glory. 1. Cor. 15. v. 24. when He shall have delivered the kingdom to God and the Father Ephes. 5. v. 26. Christ loved the Church and delivered Himself for it, v. 27. that He might sanctify it, cleansing it with the washing of water by the word. v. 28. that He might present it to Himself glorious, the Church not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing, but that it might be holy and immaculate. Peter seems to have looked back at this passage of Paul with the word προσάγειν. In this life Christ offers us to God as a sacrifice, while by His grace and Spirit He mortifies sin in us. In the future life He will offer us as a whole burnt offering, when sin will be utterly abolished, and we shall serve God perfectly renewed.

Q. 15. Why does Peter again make mention of the Lord's passion? Already before he had mentioned the passion of Christ several times in this Epistle.

cap. 1. 2. & 19.cap. 2. v. 21. & following, and furthermore he was about to make mention of him c. 4. v. 1. & 13. by which very thing he shows that he cannot be satisfied by the commemoration of the Lord's passion, whence he calls himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ cap. 5. v. 1. For the passion of Christ is not only the merit of our redemption, and the foundation of all life-giving consolation, but also the most perfect example of all Christian virtues, which we cannot perfectly express by our imitation in this life.

Q. 16. Whether by Spirit is understood the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Deity? Athanasius so determines, cited by Bede in the commentary on this place, who proves the divinity of the Holy Spirit from these words of Peter. Certainly this, he says, which is said, put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit, Athanasius, Pontiff of Alexandria, refers not to the spirit of man, which is better quickened when the flesh is mortified, the Prophet saying concerning the Lord, that he may quicken the spirit of the humble and quicken the heart of the contrite: but rather to the grace of the Holy Spirit, who bestows eternal life upon those who mortify their flesh. For he also uses this testimony against the Arians, who contradict the equality of the Holy Trinity, asserting that, by the undivided unity of operation, by which the Father quickens, the Son quickens, the Holy Spirit quickens; the Father, namely, and the Son; because it is written: For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them: even so the Son quickeneth whom he will. But the Holy Spirit, as is declared by this testimony, by which it is said concerning the Son, that he might bring us to God, being put to death indeed in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit. And therefore, of those whose operation is one, their substance or essence cannot be disparate. Resp. 1. From the work of quickening attributed to the Holy Spirit Rom. 8. vers. 11. the divinity of the Holy Spirit is rightly proved, and his equality with the Father and the Son. 2. However, in this place it is not a question of the quickening by which we are quickened through the Holy Spirit, either to spiritual life or to bodily life; but of the quickening by which Christ was quickened from the dead. 3. From this quickening and resuscitation the Holy Spirit cannot indeed be excluded, since he is of the same essence and power with the Father and the Son, and therefore, just as the Father raised Christ, as Christ raised himself, so also the Holy Spirit raised Christ, as can be gathered from Rom. 8. v. 11. 4. Meanwhile, the name Spirit in this place is not taken determinately for the third person of the Trinity, but indeterminately for the Deity and divine power, which is common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For here also the rule of Nazianzen holds place, oration 4 on Theology: That which acts is one in the three The Godhead common to the persons. 5. But if we wish to take the name of Spirit determinately, it must be taken rather of the divine Nature of the Son, as the antithesis shows. Christ was mortified in the flesh, i.e., according to his human Nature he suffered and died: but he was vivified in the Spirit, that is, by his own divine Nature he raised himself from the dead, by which determination, however, neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit are excluded, since they are of one and the same essence, equal power, and glory with the Son.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts.v. 15. But Ex. 31. v. 13.I am the Lord, who sanctify you. Resp. God sanctifies man in one way; man sanctifies God in another. God sanctifies man effectively, by making him holy; man sanctifies God objectively and relatively, by acknowledging and proclaiming him holy, by attributing to him the honor of holiness, by having faith in his promises as those of one who is truthful and holy.

2. Always prepared for a defense.v. 15. And yet 1. Cor. 12. v. 28.Are all teachers?Tit. 1. v. 9.It is required of the Bishop alone, that he be powerful, both to exhort in sound doctrine, and to refute those who contradict. Resp. Everyone, according to the measure of his calling and gifts, ought to render an account of his faith, and to answer those who ask concerning those things which pertain to the confession of faith. As in the natural life there are certain degrees and increments of bodily stature: so also in the spiritual life there are certain degrees and increments of the knowledge of Christ. Ephes. 4. v. 13. & 14. August. lib. 14. de Trin. cap. 1. With the knowledge by which faith is defended, very many of the faithful are not endowed, although they are endowed with faith itself in the highest degree. For it is one thing to know only what a man ought to believe for the sake of obtaining the blessed life, which is none other than eternal: but it is another thing to know how this same thing may both assist the pious and be defended against the impious, which the Apostle seems to call knowledge by a proper term. 1. Cor. 12. v. 8.

3. Prepared for a defense to everyone who asks for a reason. But Matth. 7. v. 6.Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine. Resp. The pious ought indeed to be prepared to render an account of their faith to everyone who asks, yet they should render an account of their faith in the act itself only if the glory of the divine name requires it, and fruit is hoped for from it, either in him to whom the answer is given, or in others. When they are questioned by those who are hardened and virulent blasphemers of the truth, then the rule of Christ has place. Do not give what is holy to dogs. Clement of Alexandria lib. 2. στρωματ. f. 156. We are forbidden to impart holy things to dogs, as long as the beasts remain. For it is not fitting that the divine and pure stream of living water should be poured out for those who, as far as their morals are concerned, are envious, disturbed, and even now unfaithful and shameless in their barking against the proposed question. Hence Paul Col. 4. v. 5. commands, that the pious should walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time, and v. 6. that their speech should always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that they may know how they ought to answer each one; upon which words Chrysostom in Homily 11 on the Epistle to the Colossians comments thus: Therefore it is added, toward those who are outside, so that we may learn that we do not have need of as much caution against our own members as against strangers. For there is no equality even between enemies and foes, and between friends.

4. Be always ready for a defense to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you. v. 15. But Matth. 10. v. 19. Marc. 13. v. 11. Luc. 12. v. 11. When they lead you to the governors, do not premeditate how or what you should speak, for it will be given to you in that hour. Resp. Christ forbids excessive anxiety joined with diffidence and pusillanimity; Peter requires due preparation, joined with confidence in divine aid. Oecumenius, from Chrysostom in Homily 34 on Matthew, answers, The Lord in the Gospel spoke about Martyrdom, but Peter about doctrine, yet outside the case of Martyrdom. But the command of both Peter and Christ is general, looking not only to the time of Martyrdom, but also of confession. Certainly Peter v. 14. preceding had expressly made mention of persecutors, and in this very place he says explicitly: Be always ready. Therefore also in the time of Martyrdom.

5. It is better, if it is the will of God, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil vers. 17. But he sins more gravely who, beyond, nay against merit, inflicts injuries upon another. Resp. The Apostle speaks about him who suffers, not him who inflicts the passion. He who inflicts injury upon one doing good beyond merit harms himself far more.

6. Christ died for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God. But Heb. 9. v. 14. Christ through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God. Iohan. 17. v. 19. I sanctify myself for them. Resp. Christ, by offering himself as a sacrifice to the heavenly Father, also offered to God those who believe in him as sanctified, and reconciled them to his heavenly Father. Therefore, as he himself was put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, so also it behooves the pious to be put to death in the flesh: but to be made alive in the Spirit, that they may be a pleasing sacrifice to God. Rom. 6. v. 4. cap. 12. v. 1.

7. Christ put to death in the flesh, made alive by the Spirit. And yet not only the quickening, but also the offering in death was made through the Spirit.Hebr. 9. v. 14. Response: it is one thing to die, another to die for the sins of the whole world, or which is the same thing, to offer oneself as a sacrifice for the sins of the whole world. The former is a property of human Nature, in respect of which Christ is rightly said to be put to death in the flesh. But the latter is an action θεανδρικὴ, and such a ἀποτέλεσμα, to which the ἐνέργεια of both Natures concurs, in respect of which Christ is said to have offered himself to GOD through the eternal Spirit.

Ἒλενχος. 1. The Apostle commands the pious to be always ready to give an account of their faith. Therefore the Elcesaites err, who, as Origen reports in Psalm 82, and from him Eusebius in book 6 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 37, said it was indifferent whether one confesses or denies, and that he who understands, in necessities will deny with his mouth, not with his heart.

2. Be always ready for a defense. Therefore the Jesuits err, when in the Ratisbon Colloquy they were long evasive in disclosing their opinion concerning the judge of controversies. And when this Apostolic passage was opposed to them, they answered, that an account of faith must indeed be given, but when it is necessary: and that it is necessary when the Magistrate has demanded it, as is evident from the Relation of Tanner. In almost the same way Perkins in book 2 of the cases of conscience, chapter 13, question 1, writes that the sense of the Apostle's saying is this, that an account of faith is to be given only then, when they are examined by those who are established in authority, such as Princes. But the words of the Apostle are most clear, that an account of faith is to be given to anyone who asks, provided he acts seriously in a competent place and time. For that one should answer every tempter and explorer, which Perkins objects, or that it should be done by one sleeping, or taking food, as Tanner trifles, is not necessary, which anyone understands.

3. Even the Laity, as they are called, ought to be ready to give an account of their faith. For the command of Peter is general, pertaining not only to the Ministers of the Church, but also to the hearers. Therefore the Papists err, who keep the Laity from the reading of Scripture and the judging of controversies, and command them to be content with only an implicit faith. Salmero excepts in volume 16, Disputation 5, on 1. Petr. 1. that this command does not apply to all, but to some, even to the Laity by the gift of OF GOD, who know how to respond to questions proposed concerning the faith. Otherwise, it pertains to Bishops, Preachers, & Priests. Resp. Although there are degrees of divine knowledge, and a discernment of Spirits, just as the word of knowledge, by which the faith is defended against heretics, is a peculiar gift of the Holy Spirit 1. Corinth. 12. v. 8. & 10., nevertheless, in their own way and measure, it also behooves hearers to beware of False Prophets, and therefore to know them by their fruits.Matth. 7. v. 15. & 16.to observe those who cause dissensions & scandals contrary to the doctrine which they have learned, and to turn away from them,Roman. 16. v. 17.to test all things, to hold fast to that which is good,1. Thess. 5. vers. 21.to test the Spirits whether they are from GOD,1. Iohan. 4. v. 1. by the example of the Beroeans praised by the Holy Spirit, who daily searched the Scriptures, whether these things were so, which were announced to them by Paul & Barnabas.Actor. 17. v. 11. 2. That in the primitive Church almost all were preachers, because they had received the grace of the Holy Spirit, and the gift of tongues,Actor. 2.& were dispersed through diverse places, so that they might scatter & propagate that faith to others. Resp. In the primitive Church the distinction between preachers & hearers was not abolished, but in it likewise that Apostolic saying had a place 1. Corinth. 12. v. 29. Are all Teachers?Ephes. 4. v. 11. He placed some Pastors & Teachers. Although indeed the pious in the primitive Church were made participants in the extraordinary manner of the peculiar gifts of the Holy Spirit, Actor. 10. vers. 44. & 46. which today do not have a place in all Christians, nevertheless the general calling of all Christians requires this, that through ordinary means, namely through the studious hearing of the word, reading, meditation, and pious prayers, they acquire for themselves a knowledge of the fundamental articles of faith, and defend it according to the manner of their calling, and according to the measure of the Spirit given to them from the word of God. 3. That these words are to be referred only to those who can perform what is commanded, as when John 1. Epist. 4. says, test the Spirits, if they are from GOD, he does not address everyone. That which is said, test all things, hold fast to that which is good, tends to the same end.1. Thess. 5. Resp. Nay, indeed, these precepts are general, which pertain to all Christians, since both Epistles are inscribed to all the faithful of Christ. Therefore, all ought to strive with pious zeal so that they may be able to perform this. We can prove this from the Canon law itself. c. Oves caus. 2. q. 7. from Pope Eusebius. The sheep, who are committed to their shepherd, ought not to rebuke him, unless he has deviated from the right faith. c. Sicuti caus. & quaest. iisdem. Clerics are deservedly by the Laity sometimes they are rebuked. c. Nolite caus. 11. q. 3. from Chrysostom. Just as the Priest is a debtor, that he may freely preach the truth which he has heard from God: so the Layman is a debtor, that he may confidently defend the truth which he has indeed heard from the Priests, proven in the Scriptures. But if the sheep ought to rebuke a Pastor who is deviating from the right faith, it is certainly necessary that they be knowledgeable of Scripture, so that they may be able to pass judgment on the doctrine of the Pastor. If the Layman ought to confidently defend the truth which he has heard proven in the Scriptures, he certainly ought to pay attention to whether what the Priest preaches is proven in the Scriptures. Cornelius à Lapide objects. Peter demands a response, not a disputation, and that it is to be given to infidels at the origin of the Church, not to heretics now that the faith has been confirmed by the consensus of all ages. I reply, indeed rather ὰπολογίαν Peter requires, which has no place where the foundation of the faith is not yet known. He also commands the pious to be always ready for an apology to everyone who asks. Therefore also to a heretic and in this our age.

4. The Apostle says, it is better to suffer for doing good, if the will of God should will it, than for doing evilv. 17. Therefore they err, who of their own accord summon tribulations upon themselves, as once the Circumcellions and Donatists, today the Anabaptists and superstitious Monks.

5. The Apostle says, Christ has sufferedv. 18. The name of Christ is the name of a person. Therefore it is false, what the Calvinists establish, that the passion of Christ is the passion of the flesh alone. Orthod. cons. p. 18. & 122. For although in the first kind of communication of idioms the passions and actions, which are attributed to Christ in the Scriptures, are distinguished by the diversity of the Natures, of which the person of Christ consists Rom. 1. v. 3. & 4.cap. 9. v. 5.1. Tim. 3. v. 16.1. Petr. 4. v. 1. nevertheless on account of the unity of the person, both divine and human things are truly and properly predicated of Christ. Athanasius in Cyril in Apol. Just as we say the body is the Lord's own, so also the passions of the body are said to be his own, even if they do not happen according to his divinity, otherwise the body would be of one, and the passions would be said to be of another. If however the flesh of the Word is flesh, it is necessary that the passions of the flesh also be said to be of him, whose flesh it is. Vigil. lib. 2. against Eutych. Theodoret, Dial. 3. What are proper to the Natures, become common to the person.

6. Christ is said to have suffered once. Therefore it is false, that Origen is said to have held, as it is in the 5th Synod and Nicephorus reports l. 17. Hist. Eccl. c. 27. that Christ would suffer again and more often in the air for the Demons, Jerome to Avitus concerning Origen writes thus: At the end he brought in, that And it is sacrilege to have thought that, for the salvation of demons, Christ would suffer even in the air and in the heavenly places.

7. Christ suffered once, that is, he does not have the necessity daily, just as the priests of the Old Testament, first to offer sacrifices for their own sins, then for those of the people, for this he did once by offering himself, Hebr. 7. v. 27. through his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption Hebr. 9. v. 12. once in the consummation of the ages he appeared for the destruction of sin by his sacrifice. v. 26. By one oblation he has perfected forever those who are sanctified. Hebr. 10. v. 14. Therefore there is no need that he be offered again in the Mass. For in that very thing the sacrifice of Christ is opposed to the Levitical sacrifices, because those were repeated daily, but Christ was offered once. Ambrose, book 10 on Luke, proves from this apostolic passage that the fruit of the death of Christ is perpetual. Christ, he says, died once indeed for the sin of the people, but he is to redeem the sins of the people daily. Lorinus excepts in this passage: Christ offered himself once by a bloody oblation on the cross, and the day before he suffered, bloodlessly, by instituting the Sacrament of the Eucharist and leaving to the Church a visible sacrifice. We offer the same victim daily through a bloodless sacrifice, because the Church cannot consist without a true priesthood and sacrifice, and it was fitting that a memory of the bloody one be made daily, and furthermore, through the said oblation of the victim or bloodless sacrifice, the fruit of the bloody one, which was the universal and sufficient cause of the salvation of all and of the remission of sins, comes to us more and more and is applied, and has efficiency. Resp. 1. The distinction between the bloody and bloodless sacrifice of Christ is destitute of the foundation of Scripture. 2. Indeed, it fights with Scripture, since it asserts only one external and properly so-called sacrifice, offered by Christ on the cross, and celebrates only the efficacy of that true sacrifice offered on the cross and the intercession of Christ for us. If the bloodless sacrifice of Christ in the first Supper was propitiatory for the sins of the world, what need was there for a bloody sacrifice on the cross? Where there is remission of sins, there is no longer an oblation for sin. Hebr. 10. v. 18. Furthermore, Scripture holds against those who have a bloodless and yet real oblation for sins, because it denies that remission is made without the shedding of blood. Heb. 9. v. 12 14. and 22. and also, with remission having been obtained through Christ, it denies that there is any longer a place for an oblation for sin. Hebr. 10. v. 18. 3. That the Church cannot consist without an external and visible sacrifice being repeated daily is false. The sacrifice of Christ offered on the cross is sufficient in the New Testament, by which He imposed an end to all external sacrifices of the Old Testament. 4. We concede that a memorial of the bloody sacrifice is made in the Church. But the commemoration of a sacrifice is not immediately a visible and external sacrifice. 5. The fruit of the bloody sacrifice is applied to us through the Word and the Sacraments, which are the means divinely instituted, but not through some other external and visible sacrifice.

8. Christ suffered once for sins, that is, He perfectly satisfied for all the sins of the whole world and for all the punishments of sins. Therefore our satisfaction is not required, which the Papists nevertheless demand. They indeed object, that Christ satisfies for the guilt and eternal punishment, we for temporal punishments, and also that the satisfaction of Christ is applied to us through our satisfaction. But all these things contain a begging of the question and are mutually opposed to each other.

9. The fruit of the passion of Christ is not only an example, but also a satisfaction for sins and the merit of redemption. For it is said that He suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, so that with the expiation of sins having been made, He might reconcile us to GOD. Therefore the Photinians err, who stubbornly deny that satisfaction provided by the passion of Christ. They object, that Christ is said to have died for our sins. But that He could not have died in the place or stead of our sins. Therefore when He is said to have died for us, it is understood that He died not in our place, but only for our sake. Resp. The meaning of the particle For is not entirely the same in these propositions, Christ died for us, and, Christ died for our sins. In the former, the preposition For is added to a person, and is explained τὸ ὑπὲρ, by τὸ ἀντὶ, which properly denotes the stead of another and substitution. Matt. 20. v. 28.Mark 10. v. 45. In the latter, it is added to a thing, and is explained by περὶ & ὑπέρ. Christ died for us, so that He might place Himself in our stead, so that by receiving the punishments of our sins into Himself He might redeem us: He died for our sins, so that He might expiate and take them away.

10. From the fact that Christ is said to have suffered for sins, so that He might bring us to God, Augustine in book 1 of On the Merit and Remission of Sins, chapter 7, and Epistle 99 against the Pelagians, proves that infants do not attain salvation without Baptism and Christ. We admit that the latter statement is general, but to the former we add a limitation, namely that the case of necessity is to be excepted as extraordinary.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Lorinus comments on v. 1 thus: That he commands by the mode of 'sanctify', indicates the freedom of the will, just as the form of the petition, 'Hallowed be thy name', and of others expressed impersonally, indicates our cooperation with divine grace. Resp. It is a question here of the reborn, who are so moved by the Holy Spirit that they themselves also act. They cooperate with grace, however, not by natural powers, but by new powers granted by the Holy Spirit.

2. From the fact that Peter says, be ready for a defense to everyone who asks for a reason, Salmero gathers that a reason is also to be sought in matters of faith. That is true, he says, that Blessed Peter in Clement, book 1 of the Recognitions, handed down that it is best not only to apprehend by faith the mysteries which are contained in the Scriptures, but also to have some reason to confirm them. These are the words of Peter: Do not think that we say that these things are to be received by faith alone, but by bringing forward a reason. For it is not safe to entrust these things to bare faith without reason, since truth certainly does not lack reason. And therefore, he who has received these things fortified by reason can never lose it; but he who receives them without assertions, by the assent of simple speech, can neither keep them safely, nor, if they are true, is he certain, because he who believes easily, also easily withdraws: but he who has sought the reason of those things which he has believed and received, as if bound by certain chains of reason itself, can never be torn away or separated from those things which he has believed. And therefore, the more inclined one is in seeking a reason, the firmer he will be in preserving the faith. Resp. 1. Sixtus Senensis in book 2 of the Bibliotheca under the word Clemens, Baronius in the year 44, no. 42, in the year 51, no. 53, in the year 102, no. 21, Iohan. Driedo concerning Ecclesiastical Dogmas and Scripture, part 5, book 4, chapter 5, p. 602, Bellarmine in book 2 concerning the Roman Pontiff, c. 2, Pererius in Genesis, book 2, q. 1, etc., deservedly reject the books of the Recognitions. Hence Lorinus, in this place, about to adduce the same saying of Clement, premises: Clement of Rome, if indeed it is not rather someone else, in book 1 of the Recognitions introduces Peter speaking. 2. By reason in matters of faith is understood either the confirmation of the articles of faith from the Scriptures, or the proof of the same from the principles of reason. In the former signification we concede that it is useful, nay even necessary, to have reasons for the faith in readiness. 3. That which is deservedly opposed to the Papists, who commend a coal-heaver's and implicit faith. 4. In the latter signification, with the name of reason accepted, we deny that those things which are of mere and pure faith can be proven from reason, since faith is above reason. Alphonius de Castro, book 5 against heresies, under the word GOD, heresy 5. Since the mystery of the Trinity and unity is so deep that it surpasses human and angelic intellect, here it is necessary to take our intellect captive under the obedience of faith. Wherefore it is superfluous, nay ridiculous, to treat this with reasons and arguments, but only with the testimonies of the Scriptures. And afterwards. The more we strive to investigate this mystery by reason alone, the less we know, and for this very reason we make God fly away from us. 5. Let Salmero hear himself in vol. 2, tract. 2, p. 5, where he discourses thus concerning the mystery of the Trinity. If there is anything that seems to us contrary to natural reason, and yet is proposed for belief, we ought to take pains that we take our intellect captive under the obedience of Christ. For just as sense is to be subjected to reason, and as it were forced captive into its assent: so our intellect ought to yield and obey the superior light of faith, as to a more certain and greater one. vol. 15, Disput. 10, on chap. 11 of Hebrews. It is not necessary that you examine those things which are of faith, and which are not seen, by the meager judgment and small light of human reason, etc. For the animal man cannot spiritually perceive those things which are spiritually examined, that is, which ought to be examined by spiritual light, and not by the light of reason. For just as brute animals, while they consider themselves, cannot grasp those things which are of man and of reason, because they are destitute of that which is superior to them: in that manner man, however sagacious and acute, is not able to perceive and conjecture those things which are of faith, and of which it itself is the argument or demonstration. 6. But let him also hear his own associate Bellarmine, lib. 2, de Sacram., chap. 11, § Adhaec. We are indeed bound to give an account of the hope that is in us 1. Petr. 3. but we are bound to do that from the principles of faith, not from Metaphysics. For 5. Augustine, lib. 3, de peccat. merit. & remis, chap. 4. I, he says, speaking of arguments against the manner of the transmission of original sin, even if I am not able to solve the arguments of these men, I see nevertheless that one must adhere to the divine letters. And in Epist. 29, to Jerome, he says that when he is asked how the sin of Adam is propagated to his descendants, he is accustomed to answer: I confess that I am ignorant of this, as of many other things.

3. Lorinus on v. 15 annotates thus. To compose an apology of the faith, only those who are well learned can and also ought to do, since it is a crime for just anyone to dispute about matters of faith with adversaries, as Jacobus Simancas elegantly shows, citing many de Cathol. Instit. tit. 20. Resp. We concede that to compose a fundamental apology of the faith against heretics or infidels belongs to the office of It pertains to a Doctor of the Church Tit. 1. v. 9. in the meantime to publish such an apology as Peter requires in this place, it pertains to all Christians altogether, whence Lorinus himself immediately adds. John commands all, that they test the Spirits 1. Epist. 4. vers. 1. (observe this against Salmeron, who denies the same thing) & yet Paul writes that the discernment of Spirits is a certain peculiar gift,1. Cor. 12. v. 10.Each one according to his measure ought to test the Spirits & render an account, but some do both more by office and more perfectly.

4. Estius on the same verse annotates thus. This is not to be accepted as if Peter wishes that all Christians are Theologians, who might know how to discourse about the dogmas of faith, either by teaching or by responding. There are certain general reasons, by which any Christian whatsoever could somehow defend himself against pagans, and satisfy those asking, such as that the Christian religion was foretold by the Prophets, that it was confirmed by innumerable miracles by Christ and his Apostles, that it teaches justice, innocence, and beneficence even to the love of enemies &c. I respond: it is not sufficient to hold certain general reasons by which the Christian religion is defended, but it is also necessary that each one hold the fundamental articles of faith, and be able to render an account of them. For the Savior commands, that to this end everyone search the ScripturesIohan. 5. v. 39. by the example of the Beroeans, who consulted the Scriptures concerning each of the dogmas proposed by Paul and Barnabas,Actor. 17. vers. 11. Paul commands, that the word of GOD may dwell in us richly in all wisdomColoss. 3. v. 16.that all things be tested, and from all things that which is good be held.1. Thess. 5. v. 21. whence he also gives thanks to GOD, that the Corinthians were made rich in all things in Christ in all word and all knowledge1. Corint. 1. v. 5. and David pronounces blessed those who meditate in the law of the Lord day & nightPsalm. 1. v. 2. What of the fact that Estius himself, convinced by the force of truth, adds. Although it is also vehemently expedient that certain more special reasons or arguments be in readiness for the faithful to respond, according to what they are capable of.

5. The same Estius ibid. writes thus. In this way also today there are by no means lacking reasons & general arguments as certain principles, with which it is necessary that the faithful be instructed against heretics attacking our Catholic faith, or wishing to dispute about it. Namely, that the Church of Christ is one, and that it is visible and manifest; continued from the Apostles even to you by the succession of Bishops, in which there have been so many saints in various times as Martyrs and Confessors, by whose blood, doctrine, and miracles the Catholic faith has long since been signed and sanctioned. That we should listen to that Church, because it is the pillar and foundation of truth, Scripture itself refers us, which he proves from1 John 4:1 and 6. In almost the same way Cornelius à Lapide in this place Laymen asked by heretics why they believe, for example, that Christ is present in the Eucharist, should answer, because the Church, which is the pillar and foundation of truth, believes and has believed it in every age. Resp. 1. We concede that the Church is one and visible, but it is nowhere promised that the visible Church will be perpetually immune from every error whatsoever. 2. God can preserve the Catholic Church of the elect, which is invisible, even if the visible Church is for a time involved in certain errors. 3. The Roman Church has received no promise of an absolute privilege of not erring. 4. Nor is local and personal, but doctrinal succession commended to us. 5. The truly Catholic faith, confirmed by the blood, doctrine, and miracles of the Martyrs and Confessors, is proposed to us in the Scriptures. 6. We are commanded to listen to the Church as a mother, insofar as and as long as she listens to the voice of the heavenly Father. Our faith is not ultimately resolved, nor ought it to be resolved, into the Church, but into the word of God. 7. Those who wish to test the spirits must listen to the Apostles, says John. But we cannot listen to the Apostles except in their writings, just as the brothers of the rich glutton could not listen to the Prophets except in their writings. Luke 16:29 In what respect and sense the Church is called the pillar and foundation of truth, was explained in its own place. art. on the Church § 116.

6. Lorinus on this place annotates thus: The study of theologians is very praiseworthy and meritorious in devising reasons for the faith which they hold tenaciously, he gathers from this place Blessed Thomas 2. 2. q. 2. last art. so that in the same faith, toward which they are greatly affected, and which they would nevertheless follow if other reasons were lacking because of the divine revelation sufficiently proposed to them by the Church, they themselves may be more confirmed, and may take more pleasure in it. Resp. those reasons cannot confirm faith more than divine revelation, which is firmer than any demonstration. Basil in Psalm 115 vol. 1. p. 300. Faith is one for all, which ought to be the leader of all the words of God. Faith, I say, not demonstration. Faith draws the mind to consent above every reason of sciences or disciplines. Faith, finally, not geometric or necessary proofs relies, but is instilled into souls by the operations of the Holy Spirit. The mystery of theology seeks a building from faith, not at all proven by reasons. Chrysostom, Homily 4 on 1 Corinthians, col. 347.
