Some wish, that respect is had to the Levitical ablutions, of which Paul Hebr. 9. vers. 13. says, that they sanctified the defiled πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα. 3. It could also be thought that the Apostle is looking to those frequent washings which the Pharisees and Jews used by the tradition of the elders, Matth. 15. v. 2. Marc. 7. v. 3. & 4. in which they trusted so much that for that reason they rejected the Baptism of John. Luc. 7. v. 30. Thomas Anglicus on this passage thinks that respect is had to the Baptism of John, which was only in water. But the Baptism of John was just as much an efficacious Sacrament of regeneration as the Baptism of the Apostles. 4. It is answered most simply, that the Apostle is looking to the common washing away of the filth of the flesh, which is in a bath or a foot-washing. For he teaches that Baptism was not instituted for the external washing of the body, but for the internal cleansing of the heart, which consists in regeneration and renewal, Eph. 5. v. 27.Tit. 3. v. 5.

Q. 10. What is ἐπερώτημα τῆς ἀγαθῆς. συνειδὴσεως? Resp. 1. ἐπερώτημα properly signifies an interrogation. Some therefore by the interrogation of a good conscience understand as it were by a consequence, the antecedent, namely the remission of sins, from whose confidence a good conscience is born, relying on which the believer boldly interrogates concerning His favor toward himself, reconciled to him through the death of Christ, and confirmed by His resurrection. To this can be referred the fact that interrogation among the Hebrews is sometimes used in vehement asseveration Gen. 13. v. 8.Ezech. 22. v. 2. It is signified, therefore, that a conscience cleansed from the stain of sin through Baptism can asseverate, and before GOD, that it is pure and good. 2. Akin to this exposition is that by which through this ὲπερώτημα of a good conscience some think it is signified that this is the effect of Baptism, that the conscience, cleansed from sins by this washing of water in the word, now interrogates God i. e. invokes Him, saying Abba Father.Rom. 8. v. 15. 3. Oecumenius by ἐπερώτημα understands a pledge and earnest, because Baptism is a witness to our conscience, that we are in the grace of GOD on account of Christ; and it seals the covenant of grace and the promise of salvation, so that the baptized may confidently address GOD in their prayers. Of this place is that observation, that the LXX use the word ἐπερωτᾷν, when the Israelites in the O. T. are said to inquire of the mouth of the Lord sitting upon the Cherubim, so that they might be made certain, how GOD in such a case was affected toward them. Baptism therefore is an interrogation, by which it is transacted between God and the sinner concerning a good conscience toward God on account of Christ, that is, how God is affected toward the baptized, what the conscience ought to promise itself concerning the grace of God. To this interrogation the History of the Baptism of Christ shows the answer. D. Chemnic. in Harmon. cap. 17. pag. 16. 4. Some translate by stipulation, in that sense, that Baptism is a certain solemn convention, confederation and mutual obligation, by which GOD offers, applies and seals His grace to man, and in turn the conscience, made more certain of the grace of God, stipulates that it believes the remission of sins, and binds itself to obedience to God. To this looks B. Luther, When ἐπερώτημα renders it as covenant. Lyranus refers it to the questions which are proposed to the godparents in Baptism, to which they respond in the name of the baptized. The interrogation of a good conscience. For it is asked of the one being baptized: Do you believe in God, and he responds, I believe, through himself, if he is an adult, or through godparents, if he is a little child. For a stipulation is a conception of words, by which he who is questioned responds that he will give or do what he is asked, such as it is in Baptism, when it is said to the one being baptized, Do you believe, Do you renounce, etc. Actor. 8. v. 37. Nicetas notes in 3. on the 40th oration of Nazianzenus. In the number of which is also Baptism, which indeed, as Peter's words use, is not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the interrogation of a good conscience toward God. For being questioned in Baptism, how our conscience stands toward God, and what faith we have in Him, we respond that we are joined to His side, and, to say it in one word, we profess the Symbols of faith. But these expositions are not opposed, but subordinated, and can be joined with the best reasoning. 6. The Syrian Interpreter went a little further from the Greek text, because he rendered it, confessing: God in a pure conscience. 7. Some understand simply a well-conscious mind, as one who through internal interrogation, having made an examination of himself, finds nothing in himself which would render him unworthy of the fruit of Baptism. But it is manifest that the Apostle is speaking about the effect of Baptism. 8. Suarez. P. 3. q. 62. Disp. 7. sect. 1. judges that here it is only signified with what disposition one must approach Baptism, namely, that we may ask and desire to be cleansed through Baptism, not the body, but the conscience. But the Apostle is not speaking about the disposition of those being baptized, but about the effect of Baptism.

Q. 11. Why does the Apostle add εἰς θεὸν? Resp. 1. Because the conscience has business with GOD, and indeed with GOD alone. GOD alone sees and knows whether the conscience is good. 2. The whole matter in Baptism is transacted before GOD i.e. with GOD as witness. 3. Lyranus in h. l. Faith formed by charity (effective through charity) makes a good conscience tending toward God. 4. Luther rendered it, with GOD, because the covenant of grace is entered into in Baptism between God and the baptized.

Q. 12. Why does the Apostle add δι' ἀναστάσεως Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ; We warned above that some join this προσδιορισμὸν with the word σώζει, so that the intermediate words, οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου, ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς θεὸν, are included in a parenthesis, as is done in the Lyons edition. But how Baptism:

That we are said to be saved by the resurrection of Christ, they explain in various ways. 1. Some proceed thus. The resurrection of Christ exhibits to us a certain form of rising again to righteousness and newness of life, to which we are regenerated and renewed in Baptism, so that just as Christ rose from the dead, so we also might walk in newness of life, Rom. 6. v. 4. But this is a secondary fruit of the Lord's resurrection. 2. Christ rose again for our justification Rom. 4. v. ult. but we are baptized into the death (and resurrection) of Christ Rom. 6. v. 3. Therefore the fruit of righteousness and salvation obtained for us through the death and resurrection of Christ is communicated to us in Baptism and through Baptism; hence also Peter says, that we have been regenerated into a living hope through the resurrection of Christ, 1. Epist. 1. v. 3. Bede in this place: Just as He himself rising from the dead ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God: so also he signified that for us through Baptism the way of salvation and the entrance to the heavenly kingdom lies open. Hugo and Thomas: He who is reborn by Baptism, at the same time in a certain way rises again, having been dead and as it were buried and suffocated in sins, which are remitted to him. 3. By the resurrection of Christ συνεκδοχικῶς the passion and death of Christ are also denoted, since the end of the passion and death was the resurrection. It is said therefore Baptism saves us through the resurrection of Christ, because the power of Baptism regenerating and renewing us descends from the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ. 4. Some explain it thus. Baptism saves us through the resurrection of Christ i. e. by the virtue of Christ the Mediator, who died for our sins and rose again for our justification. But more correctly this προσδιορισμὸς is referred to what immediately precedes, namely to the interrogation of a good conscience, because the resurrection of Christ confirms our confidence concerning the remission of sins, from which a good conscience arises, which testifies that Christ is the victor over sin, the Devil, death, and hell. For in the same sense as the Apostle said above, that God according to his mercy has regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Christ, 1. Epist. 1. v. 3. in the same sense he says in this place, that the interrogation of a good conscience is made through the resurrection of Christ i. e. that a good conscience relies upon the resurrection of Christ, inasmuch as it is a public testimony that for our sins it has been fully satisfied, that we have been perfectly reconciled to God, that death has been swallowed up in victory, and that all things which pertained to meriting our salvation have been perfectly consummated.

Q. 11. According to which Nature is Christ at the right hand of God? Resp. According to the divine, He is the very right hand of God; according to the human, He is placed at the right hand of God in time. The Apostle joins the departure into the heavens and the sitting at the right hand of God. Now, indeed, according to the human Nature, Christ has departed into heaven. Therefore, according to the same, He sits at the right hand of God. Beda in h. l. There is no doubt for anyone that the Angels and all the virtues and powers of the heavenly fatherland were always subject to the Son of God, whom they praise, tremble before, and adore as one God without beginning with the Father and the Holy Spirit. But blessed Peter judged it necessary to admonish that the assumed humanity was so sublimated by rising again into such glory that it is preferred with an incomparable peak to every power of Angelic dignity. According to which the Psalmist also, when he said to the Father concerning Him: You have made him a little less than the Angels, immediately added, You have crowned him with glory and honor, and have set him over the works of your hands, you have subjected all things under his feet.

Q. 12. Why does he say by name that Angels, powers, and virtues are subject to Christ? This is not to be taken exclusively or restrictively, as if of all creatures only the Angels, and of all Angels only these three orders were subject to Christ, but cumulatively and extensively, that not only the Angels, but all creatures whatsoever were subject to Christ in the placement at the right hand of God. Psal. 8. v. 7.1. Cor. 15. v. 27.Ephes. 1. v. 20. & 21.Hebr. 2. v. 8. because he who says the greater includes the lesser; and he who is the Lord of the Angels, he is also the Lord of the inferior creatures.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Christ in Spirit πορευθεὶς preached in the times of Noahv. 19. But Matth. 4. v. 17.From then Jesus began to preach. Resp. 1. Peter speaks of Λόγῳ ἀσάρκῳ, Matthew of ἐνσάρκῳ. 2. one must distinguish between preaching mediated through Noah, and immediate; Peter speaks of the former, Matthew of the latter.

2. The antediluvian men were incredulousv. 19.& yet that vast building of the ark was prepared,v. 20. Resp. 1. although they denied faith to the Divine threats denounced through Moses, yet for the sake of gain they hired out their labors to Noah for constructing the ark. 2. August. lib. 15. de C. D. c. ult. says, the space of one hundred years consumed in it compensated for the fewness of the builders.

3. Baptism saves us.v. 21.But in God alone is the efficacy of saving.Esa. 43. v. 3. Resp. one must distinguish between the principal cause of salvation, and the instrumental cause. God does not save us immediately, but mediately through the Word and Sacraments, which are the means on the part of God; and through faith, which is the means on the part of us.

4. Christ is at the right hand of God, with angels subjected to him,v. 22. But even in the state of humiliation the angels served,Matt. 4. v. 11. Resp. That subjection, as far as it pertains to the power given to Christ as man, was made at the first moment of the incarnation, which he exercised when he wished, and where he wished: but he was introduced into the plenary use of that power after he ascended into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of the heavenly Father.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Christ preached in the Spirit during the antediluvian times through Noah. v. 19. Therefore he is not only true man, but also in the unity of his person true God, nor did he begin the start of his existence at his birth from the virgin, but he existed before Mary, before Moses, before AbrahamJohn 8. v. 58. indeed before the beginning of the world, and thus from eternity. This is to be opposed to the Photinians, who deny the Deity and eternity of Christ.

2. The patience of God in the times of Noah awaited the conversion of men. From this Peter infers this consequence 2. Epist. 2. v. 9. The Lord does not delay the promise, as some think there is delay, but acts patiently for our sake, not wishing any to perish, but all to return to repentance. This is to be opposed to the architects of the absolute decree of reprobation, against whom we conclude thus. Those whose conversion God patiently awaits, he does not wish to perish by some absolute hatred. But God patiently awaits the conversion even of those who proceed securely in their sins. Therefore

3. In the ark of Noah there were only eight souls, within the compass of whom the whole visible Church on earth was contained. Therefore amplitude and multitude is not a proper and perpetual mark of the Church. against Bellarmine lib. 4. de Eccles. cap. 7. Rightly Salmero tom. 12. comment. in Act. Apost. tract. 9. upon the words. There was however a crowd of men of almost one hundred and twenty. You see how small a number the Church then consisted of, which nevertheless was soon to be propagated into all parts and nations of the world. For the truth of the Church of God does not consist in a multitude, as the primitive [Church] teaches &c.

4. Noah with his family was shut up in the ark for a whole year, exposed to the storms of winds and the whirlpools of waves, but preserved by divine kindness and power in the flood. Therefore temporal happiness is not a mark of the Church, but divine preservation in persecutions. Against Bellarmine, book 4 on the Church, chapter 18, where he establishes temporal happiness as the fifteenth mark of the Church, who nevertheless in the same book, chapter 6, §. Iam vero &c., discourses thus from this Apostolic passage: It is evident that the Church has grown from persecutions. For just as the waters of the flood overwhelmed and cast down the palaces of Kings, but lifted up the ark of Noah ever more and more: so persecutions easily destroy temporal kingdoms, but they not only do not destroy the kingdom of Christ, which is the Church, but even illuminate it &c.

5. Just as all men placed outside the ark perished in the flood, but only those who had entered the ark by divine command were preserved: so in the Church alone can we be preserved against the flood of divine wrath; outside of it there is nothing but death and destruction, to which the verse of Nazianzen pertains, Ζητῶ Νῶε Κιβωτὸν, ὅπως μύρον αἴνον ἀλύζω. Cyprian on the simplicity of prelates, p. 164: If he could escape who was outside the ark of Noah, then he who is outside the Church will also escape. This must be opposed to all those who create a hope of salvation for the more sound Gentiles outside the Church.

6. Baptism saves us, says the Apostle. Therefore the efficacy of Baptism also extends into the future. Peter, after having received Baptism, had fallen into the most grievous sin of denial, yet nonetheless he sought the consolation and certainty of his salvation from Baptism. No one is saved to whom past, present, and future sins are not remitted. But believers are saved through Baptism. Therefore, for believers, past, present, and future sins are remitted through Baptism. Hence also the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures speaks of the efficacy of Baptism in words of past, present, and future time, Tit. 3. v. 5. Galat. 3. v. 27. Ephes. 5. v. 26. Marc. 16. vers. 16. in order to show that the efficacy of Baptism is not to be restricted to that moment of time in which we are baptized, but extends through the whole of life. This must be opposed to the Papists, who deny that the efficacy of Baptism extends into the future. Bellarm. book on Baptism, cap. 18. Lorinus excepts, Peter is not comparing Baptism with sins, but the time of Christ with the time of Noah, so that just as under Noah the flood saved eight through the ark, so now the Baptism of Christ saves believers. Then, that some are saved and cleansed daily through Baptism, but immediately from past sins, although mediately also from future ones, insofar as through By the baptismal character, a right is given to the Sacrament of penance. Resp. 1. Peter not only compares the time of Christ with the time of Noah, but also denotes the perpetual efficacy of Baptism in the New Testament, because for those who have received this Sacrament, it is a perpetual means of salvation, just as John 1, v. 29 Christ is called the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, because the power of the passion of Christ lasts perpetually. 2. We concede that Baptism does not cleanse immediately from past, or present, or future sins, but through the mediation of faith, which is kindled, increased, and confirmed in this Sacrament, which confirmation of faith can be sought throughout the whole life from Baptism. 3. Baptism saves for this reason, because through it we are received into the covenant of grace. And yet that covenant lasts through the whole life, and even if we should fall from it most greatly through sins, nevertheless through penance access to it is open to us again.

7. Baptism is not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, says the Apostle. Therefore the analogy of the Calvinists has no place, that just as exterior Baptism washes away the filth of the body, so interior Baptism of the Spirit takes away the filth of the soul; and that the interior washing of sins through the blood of Christ is only signified by the external washing in Baptism.

8. Baptism is the interrogation of a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Christ, and thus, accepted by faith, it is profitable, from which faith a good conscience arises. It is false, therefore, what the Papists teach, that Baptism is profitable by the work performed. August. tract. 80. in John. Whence comes such great power of water, that it touches the body and washes the heart, unless by the word acting? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed. For even in the word itself, one thing is the passing sound, another is the remaining power. This is the word of faith, which we preach, says the Apostle, etc. Whence we read in the Acts of the Apostles: Cleansing their hearts by faith. And in his Epistle, Blessed Peter. So also you, he says, Baptism saves, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the interrogation of a good conscience, etc. serm. 30. de verb. Dom. Then what does it show you? That Baptism, which is applied once, cleanses through faith. Faith, however, is within, not without. Whence it is said and read in the Acts of the Apostles, cleansing their hearts by faith. And the Apostle Peter speaks in his Epistle. So, he says, he gave us a likeness of the ark of Noah, in which way eight souls were saved through water, and he added: So also you in a similar form Baptism will save, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the interrogation of a good conscience toward God. Basil on the Holy Spirit chap. 15.

Ἐι τις ἔστιν ἐν τῷ ὕδατι χάρις, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς φύσεως ἔστι τοῦ ὕδατος, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ πνέυματος παρουσίας. οὐ γὰρ ἔστι τὸ βάπτισμα ρὕπου σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις, ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς θεόν. Salmero, disp. 6, on 1 Peter, annotates this Apostolic passage thus: Augustine, book 19, against Faustus, chapter 12, and tractate 80 on John, wills that, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, is the correction of that which preceded, namely that Baptism saves us, so that the sense may be: What I said, that Baptism saves, I did not say as if that external washing saves us by itself, because in the ceremonies of Baptism, being asked whether we believe in Christ, and renounce Satan and his pomps, we answer with a good conscience that we believe and renounce; this is what saves through repentance and faith, not that exterior ablution. Whence the same Augustine in sermon 3 on the words of the Lord compares him who is baptized without faith and repentance to him who washes the external part of a dish, leaving the internal, in which food is received, filthy. And at the end of the book on the perfection of righteousness, he hands down that sacraments received without the internal fortification of faith and repentance are similar to precepts and examples, which without the Spirit make one worse and kill. Estius annotates on this place thus: Such effects are ascribed (regenerating, renewing, saving) to the sacraments not as causes effective by themselves and by their nature, but as certain signs and instruments instituted by Christ for our sanctification. Peter explains what he says, that Baptism saves us, using a certain rhetorical correction, by which he teaches that in the very sacrament of Baptism, one should not look so much at the external ablution, which by itself is only valid for taking away the filth of the body, as at the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, etc. Therefore, the doctrine of the Apostle Peter in this place is that internal faith, expressed by an exterior profession while one is being baptized, is that which saves us in Baptism, not that he removes this effect from the external ceremony of ablution, but that he teaches what is primary. For Scripture is accustomed to speak thus when it commends one thing over another, Hos. 6. 1 Sam. 15., so in this place faith is not commended in such a way that water is repudiated, for he had already said that Baptism saves us, but he shows which is more important for salvation. For if you separate each from the other, faith will be able to save without Baptism, but Baptism will not without faith. Nor does faith have its power from Baptism, but Baptism from faith, at least as a disposition necessary in itself for the effect of Baptism.

9. Peter describes Baptism in such a way that it is the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, where by ἐπερώτημα Oecumenius understands a pledge and an earnest, as we warned above, because Baptism is a witness of our conscience, that we are in the grace of God on account of Christ, who rose again for our justification. Therefore Baptism seals the covenant of grace and the promise of salvation, which must be opposed to the Papists who deny that the end of the Sacraments is that they are seals of divine promises. Bellarm. lib. 1. de Sacram. cap. 14. See the discussed exceptions of Bellarmine in the article on the Sacraments §. 88. Lorinus objects, that Peter does not say that a pact is sealed by Baptism, but that we are saved or justified by Baptism, whence that testimony of a good conscience arises, just as those who were in the ark of Noah were saved through the waters, not by testifying or sealing promises, but by actually lifting the ark on high by the waters. Resp. We attribute both effects to the Sacraments, that they are efficacious means of salvation, and that they are seals of divine promises; this latter effect is not to be opposed to the former, since Peter joins both, by reason of the former he says that Baptism saves us, by reason of the latter, that it is ἐπερώτημα of a good conscience toward God. Cornelius à Lapide falsely attributes to us here the opinion, that we maintain that faith alone justifies, but that the Sacraments are only signs, protestations, and sealings of justifying faith. But we have no commerce with this opinion of Calvin.

10. Baptism is the interrogation of a good conscience toward God. Lorinus explains that thus, that the Apostle μετωνυμικῶς describes Baptism by its effect. For it so washes away sins, that if the mind of the baptized (who has not approached Baptism feignedly, but seriously) examines and interrogates itself before God, being in no way conscious of a grave stain, then as much as the weakness of human judgment allows, it can answer and render to God that very testimony which the Holy Spirit gives in the heart, that he is by adoption a son of God, Rom. 8. v. 4. Gal. 4. v. 5. Therefore a baptized and believing man can be certain of the grace of God, which, however, the Papists deny.

II. The sitting of Christ at the right hand of God is described in this place, as also Ps. 8. v. 7. 1. Cor. 15. v. 27. Eph. 1. v. 20. & 21. Hebr. 2. v. 8. by the subjection of Angels and all creatures. Therefore Christ is not at the right hand of God in the category of position, as if the right hand of God were a place circumscribed in heaven, nor in the category of passion, as if he were enclosed there, but in the category of action, because He governs all things in heaven and on earth most presently and most powerfully. This must be opposed to the Calvinists, who define the sitting at the right hand of God through the communication of some finite glory and power, and who assert that Christ sits at the right hand of God in one place only. Calvin in chapter 21 of Matthew, verse 44. The sitting at the right hand is taken metaphorically for the second or next rank, which He obtains as the vicar of God. Piscator in the analysis of Luke 22, verse 69. From this time the Son of man shall be, sitting at the right hand of the power of God, i.e., I shall shortly begin to reign in heaven as the one next to God.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Certain of the ancient heretics wished to gather from this Apostolic passage that the spirits of the impious were converted by the preaching of Christ descending to the underworld and were liberated from the underworld. Philastrius in the heresy concerning the descent of Christ to the underworld, which is 121. There are other heretics who say that the Lord descended into the underworld and preached to all after death even there, so that those confessing there might be saved. Augustine on heresies, no. 79. Another heresy, that the unbelievers believed when Christ descended to the underworld, and it thinks all were liberated from there. Bede mentions this error, and ascribes it without naming him to Hilary, who in Psal. 118. seems to establish it. Someone, he says, interpreted this passage in such a way that that consolation, concerning which the Lord says to the Apostles, Many prophets and righteous men desire to see what you see; and to hear what you hear and did not hear: concerning which also the Psalmist, my eyes have failed for thy word, saying, when wilt thou comfort me, the saints resting in the underworld desired, that this, when the Lord descended into the underworld, even to those who were in prison and were once unbelieving in the days of Noah, consolation or exhortation was preached. To them the words of Hilary, d. 1, respond exactly, differing thus. The Prophet knows that this exhortation ( Psal. 118. When wilt thou comfort me, or as he reads, when wilt thou exhort me?) the saints resting in the underworld desire. He knows, with Peter testifying, that when the Lord descended into the underworld, even to those who were in prison, and had once been unbelieving in the days of Noah, an exhortation had been preached. Similar things occur in Jerome in the questions upon Genesis to that chapter 6. My spirit shall not remain in man, for which he says, I read in the Hebrew, My spirit shall not judge these men forever, because they are flesh. But he explains it thus. Because the condition in man is fragile, I will not keep them for eternal torments, but here I will restore to them what they deserve. Therefore it sounds not of the severity, but of the clemency of God, while the sinner here for his crime he is visited. Which words of Jerome, Eucherius, writing on Genesis, inserted into his own commentary. Although indeed some attempt to recall the words of Hilary, Jerome, and Eucherius to a good sense, nevertheless those of Clement of Alexandria in book 6 of the Stromata are too manifest to receive any convenient explanation. For he teaches from Hermes or the Shepherd, not only those who had lived according to the law, not perfectly, but also those who had lived according to Philosophy in the worship of idols, were to be saved. And so after death it was preached to the former by Christ, but to the latter by the Apostles, and that they were converted to the hearing of that preaching and consequently saved. Gregory of Nazianzus in oration 42, Epiphanius in heresy 46, Augustine in Epistle 99 to Evodius, Bede in his commentary on this place, the Apostolic [constitutions], and Gregory the Great in book 6, Epistle 179, refute this error, and indeed deservedly, for to those who remain impenitent and unbelieving until death, no hope of salvation is left. If we admit this opinion, says Augustine, by which it can be thought that men who did not believe while they lived can believe in Christ among the dead, who could bear it? What absurdities will follow, and what things contrary to the faith? First, lest we seem to grieve in vain for those who departed from the body without that grace, and in vain to take care and urgently exhort that men receive it before they die, lest they be punished with eternal death, or if only those believe uselessly and fruitlessly among the dead who, when the Gospel was announced to them, were unwilling to believe here, but it will profit those to believe who did not despise here what they were unable to hear at all, another more absurd thing follows, that the Gospel should not be preached here, since all are certainly going to die, and they ought to come to the dead without any guilt of despising the Gospel, so that it might profit them when they have believed there, which is a sentiment of impious vanity. Moved by these difficulties, Augustine determined that that preaching of Christ, of which Peter speaks, was made not in hell, but in the times of Noah.

2. Salmero, insisting on the footsteps of Clement of Alexandria, comments thus on this place. With the remaining senses excluded, we assert that Christ, after his Spirit was sent forth on the cross, came to the spirits who were held confined in the prison of hell, and evangelized or preached to them, and preached that a resurrection from the dead would be theirs, which was not only to show himself by deed to be God and the Savior of the world, as Oecumenius on this place, Ambrose, and Thomas explain, but also to have acted with words, and all the good who had believed, that not only those who were born from the seed of Abraham and had conceived the hope of their salvation concerning the future Messiah were comforted, but also those who were from the Gentiles, and who had led an approved life not without the grace and help of GOD, who, while they lived among the living, cultivated holiness and virtue in such a way that if Christ had come at that time, or had foretold to them through some Prophet that He would come for their salvation, they would have immediately believed. Yet these, even if believing those two articles which Nature proclaims in the hearts of each, namely that God exists and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him, were not devoid of faith, are nevertheless called unbelievers and infidels if they are compared to Evangelical men, who have such a distinct and clear knowledge of the articles of faith. Wherefore, since they cannot properly be called infidels and absolutely unbelievers with that implicit faith, for neither were they compelled to believe what they had never heard, nor did God compel them to believe. For which reason, when those who were already dead were receiving eternal salvation, and He was rendering their weak and feeble faith more enlightened and confirmed, Christ came immediately after death to the underworld, and supplied what was lacking to their faith, so that they might know the Redeemer and Mediator, through whom they might obtain salvation. But 1. that preaching of Christ, of which Peter speaks, was not immediate, made in hell, but mediate, made through Noah in antediluvian times. 2. If it be accepted even in the greatest degree concerning the preaching made in hell, that would nevertheless not be verbal, but real. 3. Those who depart from this life without faith in Christ the Mediator never aspire to the future glory of eternal life. 4. In order for someone to be numbered among the assembly of believers, that general and confused knowledge is not sufficient, that GOD exists, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him, Hebr. 11. v. 6. but a distinct knowledge of Christ the Mediator is required, not to be expected after this life, but to be acquired in this life, Ioh. 17. v. 3. 5. Salmero, on the occasion of this exposition, slips into that most absurd opinion, by which he establishes that Plato the Gentile was saved without the knowledge and faith of Christ. From this, he says, sense we elicit that many perhaps are saved before God, whom many who are not very wise in divine counsels hold as lost and damned. Which, so that I may make it plain by some example, Anastasius of Antioch, who flourished at the time of the VI. Synod, in the book which he inscribed ὁδηγὸς, i. e. Itinerary, recounts that Christ, descending to the underworld, preached to the Spirits detained there, and complains that a certain one of the Scholastics condemned Plato the unbeliever, and cursed him, who nevertheless through a dream to him he appeared, and that he was among the first who had believed in Christ at the descent of Christ into the underworld. And Anastasius adds. But when you hear these things, do not think that there is always repentance in the underworld. For this happened once, when Christ descended into the underworld to visit those who were living in the age. To this dream of Salmeron we oppose the dissertation of Bellarmine, book 4 on Christ, chapter 16. In the descent of Christ into the underworld, no soul of those damned to hell was freed. Wherefore that narrative, which Nicetas says is circulated in the Histories of the Fathers, must be numbered among fables, in his commentary on the 2nd oration of Gregory Nazianzen on Easter. For he says that to a certain Christian, who was attacking the memory of Plato with curses as an impious and damned man, Plato appeared in his sleep and said. I do not deny that I was a sinner, but when Christ descended into the underworld, no one approached the faith before me. This is a fable, etc. Pererius refutes the same fable about Plato in chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Romans, question 18.

3. Cajetan comments on this place thus. Christ, descending into the underworld, preached even fruitfully to those who had been incredulous in the time of Noah, since they had trusted in the goodness of GOD. Gagnaeus replies in his notes on this place. Why to these more than to others? And who indicated to him that, besides Noah and a few others admitted into the ark, they had believed? Fruitful preaching of the word has no place except in this life. Lorinus rises up against Cajetan on this place thus. How did they believe in God, who did not believe Noah preaching in the name of GOD? And what did it profit to have awaited the patience of GOD while not repenting?

4. Bellarmine, book 4 on Christ, chapter 13. Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, and other Papists in their commentaries on this place prove the Limbo of the Fathers from these words of Peter. I say, says Bellarmine, d. 1. §. To the second, etc. the preaching of Christ in the underworld was not to convert the infidels, but was only for the announcement of great joy to the pious souls, to whom he announced that the redemption was completed, so that they might understand that they were now to be freed from there, and in their own time would also receive their bodies. But. 1. the Limbo of the Fathers is a dogma not only ἄγραφον, but also ἀντίγραφον, as is demonstrated in its place. 2. in Limbo there were only the pious and faithful according to the hypothesis of the Papists. But Peter says in this place, that Christ preached to the Spirits ἀπειθήσασι πότε. If you say, that they were indeed before the flood of the deluge ἀπειθεῖς, as the adverb indicates πότε but afterwards, with the deluge already flooding, they did penance, I answer first From Lorinus, That they are sometimes called unbelievers does not follow that they were believers afterwards, as can be shown by similar examples concerning such adverbs as until, etc. Then I answer from Estius, that that repentance was indeed true, but imperfect, and therefore according to the hypothesis they descended not into the limbo, but into purgatory. 3. When flesh and Spirit are opposed in the person of Christ, Spirit signifies divinity, flesh humanity. Rom. 1. v. 3. & 4. 1. Tim. 3. v. 16. manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, where by Spirit some interpreters understand Christ's Deity, some the Holy Spirit, which expositions are subordinate. Therefore, by Spirit also in this place, not Christ's soul, as Bellarmine, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, etc. wish, but Christ's Deity or divine power is understood. 4. It cannot be conveniently said of the soul of Christ that it was ζωοποιηθεῖσα,, which argument Augustine urges in Epistle 99 to Evodius. They object indeed, that to be vivified in the Scriptures often signifies the same as not to be killed. But the opposite to be mortified shows that the text must be accepted concerning true and real vivification, that is, the restoration of lost life. Add that in this signification only those are said to be vivified, i.e., preserved in life, which can die, and for which danger hangs from death, which cannot be said of the soul. 5. The Apostle does not mention any liberation, or translocation into eternal life, but only preaching. 6. Augustine in the same place urges this, that the Apostle does not make mention of the holy Fathers, but of those who in the times of Noah were sometimes unbelievers. There would be no cause for specially naming those who were in the times of Noah while the ark was being prepared, if indeed by that liberation which the Papists assert, nothing peculiarly accrued to them. For by their hypothesis, all the rest numbered from Adam up to those times were waiting equally with them. Bellarmine objects, that those who were in the days of Noah were expressly named because there was a greater doubt concerning them, whether they were saved or not, since they were punished by God and submerged by the waters of the flood. I answer: if some of them performed true and serious repentance even at the end of life, they are to be numbered among the believers, and placed in heaven, not however in hell. 7. In the Greek text it is not held that those spirits to whom Christ preached were in prison, and from it have now been liberated by Christ, but it is said simply, τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι, to those who are in prison, where you will more correctly understand the present than the past. 8. Gagnaeus to this exposition concerning the limbo he does not assent, for he denies that he can see how from this passage it is gathered that this descent of Christ was fruitful. Andradius lib. 2. Defens. Trident. p. 121. trusts that he has demonstrated that this passage of Peter does not in the least pertain to the descent of Christ into the limbo of the Fathers. Lorinus refutes Salmeron, Fevardentius, Catharinus, Sà, Bellarmine, Suarez & Valencia, who establish that Peter means this, that their souls, which repented at the time of the flood, received the joyful news of their redemption from Christ: which opinion he says rests solely on a pious judgment concerning the repentance of some before they were submerged by the waters. He himself on the contrary establishes, that Peter speaks of the damned who perished in the flood. And yet the exposition concerning limbo presupposes that some, and indeed those of whom Peter speaks, had performed repentance at the time of the flooding flood.

5. Certain Papists interpret the Apostolic passage concerning purgatory, and assert from it that the souls of those who had first indeed been incredulous, but afterwards truly at the time of the flooding flood had performed repentance, were liberated in Christ's descent to the underworld. Francisc. Turrianus lib. 4. pro Epist. Pontif. cap. 12. Christ preached in the descent to the underworld not where the damned were, because they are incapable of redemption etc. But where souls were paying the remaining debt of temporal punishment. Salmero in h. l. Some of the Catholics interpret this passage concerning the prison of purgatory. Firstly because he says: To those who had been incredulous at one time, namely at the time when the ark was being built: Afterwards however, with such a great abundance of waters arriving, they believed and performed repentance. Secondly because it is said that Christ preached to the spirits of the dead, and because it was not to be preached to the incredulous and obstinate, in whom he would have made no fruit, therefore he preached to those already believing in purgatory. Thirdly, purgatory was a certain prison, in which souls were expiated, and a lake, from which they were led out, in which there was no water of consolation. Zach. 9. Estius ad h. l. That opinion, which establishes that only good spirits are understood, to whom was preached and granted liberation from the infernal places, seems to have more probability than the others, yet in such a way that the whole is understood in part; that is, that what is said to have been preached to the spirits, who had been formerly incredulous, is extended to all spirits capable of salvation placed in the underworld, when Christ arrived there, as much those who were then in the bosom of Abraham, whose receptacle theologians call the limbo of the Fathers, as those who were still detained by purgatorial punishments, among whom were those formerly incredulous, not all, but some, For it is very credible etc. many of those, who the preaching They had despised or neglected Noah as he announced destruction to sinners, which Peter here calls having been incredulous, and upon the flood coming and inundating, they had conceived true, but imperfect, repentance out of fear, whose spirits were therefore thrust into prison in the underworld and held in it, until they were liberated when Christ descended to the same places. Resp. 1. Salmero rejects this exposition. For he notes in the margin: The third sense which is refuted. And after he had brought forward the foundation of this exposition, he adds: But what need was there for these to be preached to, who had already believed? And a little later he adds: These senses therefore being excluded, we assert that Christ, after his spirit was sent forth on the cross, came to the spirits who were held enclosed in the prison of hell. Lorinus refutes the same opinion in h. l. Whence, he says, can we know that those who were in the days of Noah had departed with such a debt and had been just and had performed penance? He also does not render a reason why it was preached to these rather, nor does he show what the preaching was, since they had believed while they lived before it was necessary to believe, etc. It is improbable that those souls had been in purgatory for so long: it is likewise uncertain whether Christ then led any souls out of purgatory. Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. It seems little credible that the souls which went to purgatory at the time of the flood had paid penalties in it until Christ for 2928 years; for so many precisely flowed from the flood until the death of Christ. 2. Bellarmine, book 4 de Christo, chapter 16, § Quartum &c., to the question, Whether besides the souls of the just, which were in the bosom of Abraham, any others were also liberated in Christ's descent to the underworld, he responds in this way: No souls of the damned were liberated to Gehenna, etc. The reason is the same concerning the souls of infants who departed with original sin, for it is not credible that any of them were saved, etc. Concerning the souls of purgatory, there is a greater doubt. For it seems to be gathered from that Eccles. 24. I will enlighten all who hope in the Lord, that all pious souls were then beatified. Furthermore, Augustine, Epist. 99 to Evod. and book 12 de Genesi, chapter 33, openly says that some were released by Christ from the pains of the underworld, and he explains that he is not speaking of the holy souls which were in the bosom of Abraham, nor of the impious souls, which he considered most absurd to have been converted when Christ descended to the underworld: therefore it remains that he speaks of the souls which were still paying purgatorial penalties. Likewise Gregory, book 13 moral. chapter 20, says all the elect were liberated. But B. Thomas part. 3. q. 52. art. 8. teaches that the souls of purgatory were not liberated simply from the descent of Christ to the underworld.

For Christ did not confer anything upon anyone, except what He had merited by His passion, but the passion of Christ does not have a temporal effect, but an eternal one. For it is always equally efficacious. Therefore, Christ would not have liberated then except those who had such a disposition as those have who are liberated now. Blessed Thomas adds, however, that it could have happened in two ways that some were liberated then. First, if they had completed the time of their purgation. Second, if out of a peculiar devotion to the passion of Christ they had merited in this life that they should be liberated then when Christ descended into that place. And in this way Saint Augustine ought to be explained, who says that those were liberated whom the Lord knew were to be liberated. Regarding the passage of Ecclesiasticus and Gregory, it could be said that Christ liberated all the elect when He descended to the underworld, but not all at once, for He liberated some immediately, others afterwards, namely when their purgation was finished; but yet He granted this to all, that they should not remain in limbo awaiting beatitude. Although it would not be an error if someone were to say that many others, or even all, were then liberated from purgatory by special grace, because the Lord is not bound by the Sacraments or our merits. This dissertation of Bellarmine shows that the things which are disputed concerning the liberation of souls from purgatory in Christ's descent to the underworld are doubtful and uncertain. 3. The arguments which prove that this is not about limbo, most of them also prove that this is not about purgatory. 4. Even if it were most strongly maintained that some who had previously been unbelievers performed penance at the time of the flooding deluge, it is not yet proven that Peter is speaking about them in this place. For if he were speaking about those who performed penance before the end of their life, he would not call them ἀπειθεῖς. 5. That those who perform a true but imperfect penance, i.e., who have not yet fully satisfied for the temporal punishments of their sins, descend to purgatory, that is shown to be false in its own place. Concerning the penitent thief, Bellarmine, book 1 on purgatory, chapter 12, writes thus: A most harsh death endured with a most patient mind and a confession so admirable, at that time when the Apostles themselves were denying Christ, could justly be imputed as full satisfaction. And yet the same could be said about the penitents drowned in the deluge according to the hypothesis of the Papists, since their death also was most harsh and most bitter. 6. Hence also Bellarmine, book 4 on Christ, chapter 13, seems to place those who performed penance at the time of the flooding deluge not in purgatory, but in the limbo of the Fathers. For thus he writes, I say that Christ preached in hell to all the good Spirits, but that they were expressed by name Those who were incredulous in the days of Noah, because there was greater doubt concerning them, whether they were saved or not, since they were punished by God and submerged by the waters of the flood. Therefore, Peter indicates here that there were some among those incredulous ones who even at the end of their life performed penance, and although they perished as to the body, nevertheless as to the soul they were saved. And afterwards. I say that the preaching of Christ in hell was not for the sake of converting the infidels, but was only for the announcement of great joy to the pious souls, to whom he announced that the redemption was complete, so that they might understand that they were now to be liberated from there and in their own time would also receive their bodies back.

6. The Papists commonly gather from this place that Christ descended to the underworld according to his soul only. But 1. this opinion rests upon a false hypothesis, that by Spirit in this place is understood the soul of Christ. We have shown the contrary above. 2. If the Apostolic passage is to be accepted concerning the descent of Christ to the underworld, it confirms our opinion rather. For Peter says that Christ, having been made alive in the Spirit, went now to the spirits in prison. These things cannot be explained concerning the soul or the divinity alone, since both live by themselves and are immortal, and do not need any vivification; it follows therefore that that vivification must be understood concerning the humanity of Christ, which alone was made alive or raised up by the Spirit, whence the whole Christ, both God and man, is proven to have descended to the underworld.

7. Estius annotates thus on this place. Although for some of those spirits (whom Christ liberated from purgatory in his descent to the underworld) perhaps some punishments still remained to be paid, Christ could nevertheless entirely forgive whatever remainder of this debt there was, which it becomes probable even from this place that he did, so that by this means of the power of conferring Indulgences, which he was about to leave to his Church, he might consecrate certain first-fruits, as it were, by his descent to the underworld. Resp. 1. The hypothesis of this conjecture is false, namely that Christ preached to the spirits established in the prison of purgatory. 2. Thomas, p. 3, q. 52, art. 8, argues that only those were liberated from purgatory in the descent of Christ to the underworld who had completed the time of their purgation. 3. That forgiveness of punishments still to be paid would have been an extraordinary benefit, and therefore the conferring of Indulgences cannot be proven from it. Bellarmine, in the same place: It would not be an error if someone were to say that many others, or all, were then liberated from purgatory by special grace, because the Lord is not bound to the Sacraments or our merits.

8. Sixtus Senensis in book 6 of his Bibliotheca, annotation 312, weighs that which Chrysostom, homily 2 on Colossians, gathers from this Apostolic passage, μακροθυμίαν that it is attributed to God, but not ὑπομονὴν. The words of Chrysostom are as follows: We are long-suffering toward those whom we can avenge, but patient toward those whom we cannot avenge. Therefore, patience is indeed never attributed to God, but long-suffering very often. To this observation of Chrysostom, which is in conformity with our Apostolic passage, Sixtus objects this, that very many testimonies of Divine Scripture seem to him to cry out against it, which call God patient, and commend His patience, Psalm 85. You, O Lord God, are patient. Psalm 144. The Lord is patient and very merciful. Ecclesiastes 8. A sinner does evil a hundred times and is awaited by God through patience. Romans 9. God endured in much patience the vessels of wrath. 1 Peter 3. They awaited the patience of God in the days of Noah. I respond: 1. In the Greek text of these passages, the word μακροθυμία, is held, not ὑπομονὴ.. Therefore, these passages are so far from overturning Chrysostom's observation that they rather establish it. 2. The Greek noun μακροθυμίας the Vulgate interpreter sometimes translates as long-suffering, sometimes as patience, but this translation does not remove the genuine meaning of the words. 3. Having regard for the Vulgate version, Sixtus Senensis rightly adds: It must be known that the word patience signifies two things in the Holy Scriptures, namely, the virtue by which adversities are bravely tolerated, ὑπομονὴν called , which is not ascribed to God, in whom there is no calamity to be tolerated; and a certain expectation, μακροθυμίαν called by the Greeks, by which those who err are accustomed to be awaited for a long time for repentance, which is properly attributed to God. Augustine, embracing both meanings of patience in his book On Patience, said: The patience of God is preached, not in this, that He suffers some evil, but in this, that He awaits the wicked so that they may be converted.

9. Lorinus on this passage: Heretics abuse the likeness of the ark of Noah, in which those who were inside were made safe from the flood, to prove that only the predestined are within the Church. The comparison is valid only in this, that there is no salvation outside the Church, but within it for those who are not only in number, but also in merit, having the interrogation of a good conscience toward God. I respond: 1. We do not deny that in the external society of the Church, hypocrites are mixed with the saints in this life. 2. But we say that only believers and the reborn belong to the internal society of the Church, and are true and living members of the Church. 3. Thomas in this place: As the ark was made of smoothed and hewn wood: so the Church consists of saints afflicted through straits and tribulations. 4. In the ark itself was the wicked Ham, so in the visible Church there are hypocrites:

10. Salmero on this verse annotates thus: Just as GOD could have saved by Himself without the ark, yet He did not wish to, so that Noah himself might be rendered a human co-worker of his own salvation: so neither did He decree to save us unless we cooperate with our salvation, and keep ourselves within the ark, and are free for the frequenting of the Sacraments and the study of good works. Response. 1. The Apostle institutes a comparison not between the ark and our works, but between the ark and Baptism, which is not our work, but a Sacrament of regeneration and our salvation divinely instituted. 2. Comparisons are not to be pressed against the analogy of faith, but to be conformed according to it. 3. That God did not decree to save us unless we cooperate with our salvation can be taken in a double way, either in the sense that we ought to use the means of salvation, namely the hearing of the word and the Sacraments λήψει; that we ought to work out our salvation with fear and trembling Phil. 2. v. 12., solicitously taking care lest by sins against conscience we squander the grace of GOD and eternal salvation; that we ought to insist upon the way of the divine commandments, to proceed strenuously in it, and to contend for the prize of salvation, observing the will of GOD in all the institutions of our life with solicitous zeal, and omitting no occasion of doing good things. Or that we ought to trust in our works as merits of eternal salvation, and to work well with the confidence of salvation to be obtained through our merits. We accept the former sense, we repudiate the latter. The word ἐργάζεσθαι Ioh. 6. v. 27.Apoc. 18. v. 18. is used concerning the expenditure of labor, not concerning the merit or efficiency of the work, and σωτηρίαν κατεργάζεσθαι is taken in the same way in which the Greeks say ἐργάζεσθαι γῆν Gen. 2. ἐργάζεσθαι θάλασσαν Apoc. 18. not to work the earth, but to occupy oneself in those things which pertain to the earth. Therefore, the truly pious τὴν ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίαν κατεργάζουσι then, when they strenuously exercise the due offices of piety, by hearing the word, by using the Sacraments, by praying devoutly, by fighting against sin and the flesh, by persevering in faith, by bringing forth the true fruits of faith, lest the flesh receive dominion, and they fall away again from their salvation.

18. Chamierus tom. 4. panstrat. lib. 2. cap. 5. §. 9. writes thus. We have from Peter that Baptism is ἀντίτυπον of the ark, i. e. another type of the same thing, namely, of Salvation. lib. 3. cap. 1. §. 6. Peter said the ark was of Baptism ἀντίτυπον, not as we often hear among the Fathers that bread and wine are ἀντίτυπα of the body and blood of Christ, that is, that they are images of the things immediately signified, but in that both the ark and Baptism were signs of the same thing; namely, of salvation conferred upon the Church through Christ, by which reasoning among the Greek Grammarians ἀντίστοιχα are clemena, whose sound is the same, although the time is different. We do not believe that Circumcision was instituted to signify our Baptism, in which sense figures are accustomed to be named, but that it might designate the same grace as Baptism, that is, the remission of sins. Piscator in b. l. The Apostle passes from the old type of spiritual preservation to a new type of the same preservation corresponding directly to that old type, which he therefore calls ἀντίτυπον, through which he says we are saved from eternal death. Resp. 1. The little word ἀντὶ in composition is sometimes used for that which is in the place of another, as ἀντίχειρ a thumb, which fills the place of a hand, ἀντιστρατηγὸς, which is in the place of a Leader &c. sometimes for that which is against, as ἀντίπαλος signifies a rival in a struggle, ἀντίδοτον a contrary remedy, ἀντίφρασις a contrary locution &c. When therefore Peter calls Baptism the ἀντίτυπον of the ark, he does not use the little word ἀντι in the former signification, as if Baptism as a new type had succeeded that old one, but in the latter signification, because Baptism is opposed to that old type, as a thing shadowed forth by the same, whence Tossanus himself rendered it Begenbild Paraeus in comm. Hebr. 9. v. 24. p. 456. In the common speech of the Church ἀντίτυπα we call things signified by types. Thus we call the Ceremonies of the law types of Christ and of spiritual things. But Christ is the ἀντίτυπον signified: Nor is this signification foreign to Scripture. For thus Peter calls our Baptism the ἀντίτυπον of the flood, i. e. Signified by the water of the flood. Aretius in 1. Petr. 3. v. 21. The flood, insofar as it saved Noah with his own, is a figure of Baptism. Nassonius part. 4. Anatom. cap. 8. p. 88. Die Lauffe deren Gegenbild etwa die Su ndfluth war/machet uns selig. 2. Ambrosius Catharinus rightly warns that in this comparison opposition is joined with similarity, and that this is indicated by the preposition ἀντὶ, which composes the word antitype. For as those eight were saved in the ark through water, lest by touching they were overwhelmed: so we in the contrary manner are saved through the contact of water and immersion, receiving Baptism which is in the ark, i. e. in the Church. 3. We have warned above that the little word ἀντιτύπου is used only twice in the N. T., but in a different meaning. Hebr. 9. v. 24. it signifies a figure pre-signifying something by its own image, but in this place it signifies the truth itself, responding to the type by a certain likeness or analogy.

12. Bellarmine lib. 1. de Sacram. cap. 9. §. Unde &c. The Greek Fathers everywhere call the Sacraments ἀντίτυπα, which word signifies a thing so similar to another, that it seems to contend with it as it were in form, as if a painted image expresses the thing so well and as it were to the life, that it seems not an image, but the thing itself. For thus Nazianzen takes this word in orat. 2. on Easter, where he calls the paschal night, because of the infinite multitude of burning candles by which it was illuminated, the antitype of the celestial firmament, where the infinite lights of the stars are seen. Thus also before Gregory, St. Peter in the first Epistle cap. 3. calls our Baptism the antitype with respect to the ark of Noah, where our Interpreter rightly translates it of similar form. Resp. 1. Peter calls Baptism ἀντίτυπον of the ark in a far different sense than that in which Nazianzen calls the paschal night the antitype of the celestial firmament. Nazianzen uses this little word in that meaning rather, in which Paul Hebr. 9. v. 24. uses it, than that in which Peter uses it in this place. 2. This description of ἁντιτύπου is not general. For Paul in the said place calls the holy things made by hands of the O. T. ἀντίτυπα of the celestial and true things, which nevertheless no one would say have contended with the celestial things, for they were σκιὰ, Hebr. 8. v. 5.cap. 10. v. 1. 3. Bellarmine contradicts himself. For he calls the Sacraments ἀντίτυπα, which word he says signifies a thing so similar to another, that it seems to contend with it as it were in form, as if a painted image expresses the thing so well and as it were to the life, that it seems not an image, but the thing itself. The same man, however, in the same book and chapter, §. Huius &c., refers the Sacraments to signs of the third kind, which he describes thus. Some signs have themselves in a middle way. For they indeed have some analogy with the thing, but so indeterminate and confused, that they are more apt for signifying, than they signify in act, unless they are determined by something, in which way an image of a man not made to the likeness of any particular man, signifies no one in particular, and yet can signify anyone, if it is determined by the written name of someone, or by the added clothing, or by another sign of a particular man. Of this third kind, he says, are all the Sacraments.

13. Calvin comments on this passage thus: We must leave to both Christ and the Holy Spirit their honor, so that no part of salvation is transferred to the sign. Ibid. when Peter, having made mention of Baptism, immediately excepts it, he sufficiently shows that for some, Baptism is merely literal, and therefore the external sign is worth nothing in itself. Aretius on this passage: Lest we attribute too much to the element of water in this Sacrament, he explains himself, indeed that external water does not suffice for the cleansing of our souls, but as it washes away the filth of the body: so the merit of Christ purges the souls, and Baptism is the Sacrament of this purging. Piscator on this passage: Lest anyone think that Baptism provides this of itself and by the work performed, he warns by way of correction that salvation, strictly speaking, depends on the remission of sins obtained through the death of Christ, and thus he implies that Baptism saves us insofar as it testifies to that remission of sins. In the Scholia, Baptism saves us, as the Apostle teaches, not by the power of that external washing by which the filth of the body is put away, but by the power of the Holy Spirit, confirming in the hearts of the elect the faith of the remission of sins, obtained through the death of Christ and testified to by His resurrection, and thus effecting in them a good conscience. Tossanus on this passage: By Baptism, believers are admonished and confirmed that they are cleansed by the Spirit and blood of Christ and preserved from eternal death. Chamier, vol. 4, panstrat. book 2, chap. 8, §. 1: If the signs of the Sacraments effected that which they signify by some power inherent in them. Therefore, in Baptism, the washing away of the filth of the flesh would save the baptized. But this is absurd. Therefore, that is also. The consequence is clear, because in Baptism the external sign is the washing of the body. For it is agreed that Sacraments are not only elements, but rites, i.e., elements used in a certain way, which mode in Baptism is the washing of the body. Therefore, either this power must be in the external washing, or it is not in the visible sign at all. The assumption is established from the explicit words of Peter, in which there is a twofold force. The former, when salvation is denied to be from the washing of filth, which is the very thing posited in the argument. The latter, when that salvation is ascribed to the interrogation of a good conscience, which is indeed opposed to the external washing. Resp. 1. We explicitly reject the Papist hypothesis, that Sacraments are profitable by the work performed. 2. Yet it does not follow from that, that Sacraments are only signs and seals, for a third is given, namely, that they are efficacious means of grace and salvation. 3. We therefore concede that Sacraments are signs and seals, but we deny that they are only signs σημαντικὰ and sealing seals, since they are means παραδοτικὰ and efficacious instruments. 4. whence Peter he joins both effects of the Sacraments, when he says, that Baptism saves, and that it is the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, which among other things also embraces a stipulation and a pledge, as Oecumenius warns. 5. We invert the argument of the adversaries. Baptism is not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the interrogation of a good conscience, i.e., the putting away of the filth of the soul, because through Baptism occurs the remission of sins, from which arises a good and tranquil conscience. Therefore Baptism is not a bare sign σημαντικόν, but a medium παραδοτικὸν. 6. Hence Calvin himself writes thus on this passage. Fanatical men, such as Swencofeld, wrongly distort this testimony, while they derogate all power and efficacy from the Sacraments. But Peter did not wish to teach that the institution of Christ is empty and inefficacious, but only to exclude hypocrites from the hope of salvation, who, as far as in them lies, deprave Baptism. 7. Honor is not derogated from Christ or the Holy Spirit, when the Sacraments are established as efficacious media of salvation, for one must distinguish between the principal cause and the instrumental or organic one. 8. Nor from the fact that Baptism is for some only literal, i.e., that it does not actually confer heavenly benefits, can it be inferred that it is not an efficacious medium, because the consequence from the removal of the second act to the removal of the first act is not valid. 9. We do not say that the efficacy of Baptism inheres in the water by itself as some physical quality, but we say that Baptism is a Sacrament of the New Testament divinely instituted, so that through it as a salutary and efficacious medium heavenly goods may be offered to men, and conferred and sealed to believers.

14. Piscator on this passage gathers from the words of Peter, that there is a twofold Baptism, interior and exterior, and that the exterior is merely a testimony of salvation obtained through Christ. I answer. Eph. 4. v. 5. the Apostle says there is one Baptism. We can most strongly refute the distinction between interior and exterior Baptism, taken in the Calvinian sense, from this text. For it relies on this analogy, that just as exterior Baptism washes away the filth of the body, so interior Baptism or the Spirit washes away the filth of the soul. But Peter denies that Baptism is the putting away of the filth of the flesh. Therefore he denies that Baptism was instituted because of that significative analogy. We do not deny that the actions of Christ and the baptizing Minister are distinct, but we deny that they are to be torn apart and separated, and that in this sense interior Baptism is to be separated from exterior.

15. The Anabaptists gather a twofold argument from this passage, by which they attack infant baptism. 1. Baptism is the putting away of the filth of the soul, that is, of sins. But infants are destitute of such filth. Therefore. I answer: the principle is begged, for it is most firmly demonstrated in its own place that infants are born with original sin. What is clearer than the Apostolic sayings Rom. 5. v. 12.Eph. 2. v. 3? 2. Baptism is the stipulation of a good conscience and a covenant with God. But a covenant ought to be entered into between those who have knowledge, conscience, and intelligence. Wherefore, since infants do not understand the heads of the covenant which God enters into with us in Baptism, they are not to be baptized. I answer: 1. Circumcision was the covenant of God Gen. 17. v. 10. and yet infants were circumcised on the eighth day by God's command. 2. God enters into a covenant with irrational creatures Gen. 9. v. 10., how much more can He enter into a covenant with infants, although they are destitute of the use of reason. 3. The stipulation which is made in Baptism proceeds not so much from man as from God. It is God who is primarily stipulating there that He is propitious to the baptized, where although an open stipulation is not provided in turn by the infant, yet because the pacts are reciprocal, it suffices that a tacit stipulation be made. 4. Furthermore, in place of the infants, godparents pledge and testify from the mouth of Christ that the baptized infant believes. Wherefore, since such covenants are sometimes entered into among men, in which parents pledge in place of infants and commit them to the heads of the covenant, how much more will God be able to enter into a covenant with infants, whose mouth and Advocate, Christ, grants them faith and the kingdom of heaven Matth. 19. v. 14.Marc. 10. v. 14.Luc. 18. 16.

16. That Baptism is called the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, Cajetan explains that of an adult already baptized, whose true zeal and consequent effect from Baptism, if he wishes to cooperate, is that he may seek the application of a good conscience toward God. I answer: The Apostle speaks generally about the effect of Baptism, not only about that which it has in adults, but also in infants. From the consequent, however, he understands the antecedent, teaching that through Baptism the filth of the soul is washed away, so that the goodness and tranquility of conscience may have a place in man.

17. Salmero annotates thus on this passage: Those who are well conscious of themselves and embrace an inculpable life dare to be interrogated and examined with a good conscience in the judgment and tribunal of God, and thus Baptism is called a good interrogation toward God, by that trope by which the name of the effect is attributed to the efficient cause. Gagnaeus on this passage: A stipulation of this kind, by which they believe in God and of Satan The one to be baptized professes to send a message, it saves him. Resp. 1. Although the pious are not conscious of more serious sins in themselves, yet in this good conscience they do not seek their own righteousness before God, but solely in Christ. 1. Cor. 4. v. 4. 2. Baptism itself is called the stipulation of a good conscience, insofar as it is received by faith and confers the remission of sins, which is followed by the peace and tranquility of conscience. 3. Faith, which we profess in the external stipulation, saves us, because it embraces the benefits of Christ offered in Baptism. 4. What the Apostle attributes to Baptism as a means on the part of God is not to be attributed to the external work of our stipulation, but to faith, which is the means on our part.

18. Estius annotates on this passage thus. The Apostle does not say that Baptism is the interrogation of a good conscience, but since in Baptism well received there are two things, the exterior washing, and the interrogation of a good conscience, he declares which parts are to be attributed as more important for salvation, namely the interrogation of a good conscience. Resp. 1. The words of the Apostle are manifest, Baptism saves us, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, where τὸ ἐπερώτημα is joined with the word τὸ βάπτισμα by the figure of apposition. 2. The Apostle denies that the putting away of the filth of the flesh happens in Baptism, and opposes to it the putting away of the filth of the soul, which μετωνυμικῶς describes by the interrogation of a good conscience, which is the effect of that. 3. If in Baptism well received there must be two things, the exterior washing and the interrogation of a good conscience, Baptism could not be administered by the sprinkling of water, but the one to be baptized would have to be led away to a bath, so that the filth of the body might be washed away.

19. Lorinus comments on this passage thus. Augustine argues in the book on faith and works chapter 15 from this passage, that it is not enough for salvation that one believes, otherwise it would seem to have been said in vain by Peter concerning the interrogation of a good conscience, if indeed, he says, even those having the worst consciences, full of all flagrant crimes and wicked deeds, and not changed by repentance for those evils, nevertheless Baptism makes them safe on account of the foundation, namely of faith, which is placed in that Baptism. Resp. Augustine disputes against those who thought the Apostolic passage 1. Cor. 3. was to be understood thus, that those seem to build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, who add good works to the faith which is in Christ: but those wood, hay, stubble, who, while they have the same faith, work badly. Therefore, in the name of faith, which he denies is sufficient for salvation, and He proves the same thing from this passage, he understands historical faith, or a bare profession of life, or as he himself speaks, faith which is dead without works, but not living and justifying faith, which exerts itself through works, nor can it consist with sins against conscience. Iac. 2. 18.

20. The same person annotates thus on this place. This passage (Baptism saves us through the resurrection of Christ) is of no use to heretics to prove that faith is the cause of justification by itself. For Peter does not say that Baptism saves through faith in the resurrection, and if we were to interpret him thus, we ought to understand it of living faith, as the Carthusian understands it: but through the resurrection that is because the baptized person represents the resurrection of Christ, by emerging from the waters, and because Baptism makes us righteous, so that we may walk in newness of life, in the way that Christ began to live a new life through the resurrection, Rom. 6. v. 5. which he took from Bellarm. l. 2. de Sacram. C. 9. Resp. 1. We warned above, that this προσδιορισμὸν, through the resurrection of Christ, is more correctly referred to the closer, namely to ἐπερώτημα ἀγαθῆς συνειδήσεως, than to the more remote, namely to the word σώζειν. 2. If it should even be referred to the word σώζειν, it still does not prove that justification consists in renewal. For the Apostle would say that Baptism saves us through the resurrection of Christ in a far different sense than that which Bellarmine and Lorinus intend. By the name resurrection συνεκδοχικῶς the passion and death of Christ are also understood. Therefore Baptism is said to save us through the resurrection of Christ, because all the power and efficacy of Baptism, as also of the remaining Sacraments, descends from the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ. 3. Those benefits obtained for us by the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ and offered in Baptism are received only by faith, therefore faith and indeed faith alone is the cause of justification, because it alone has the power of apprehending Christ and his merit. 4. That faith, however, is not dead but living and efficacious. 5. Renewal and newness of life, the type of which is proposed in the resurrection of Christ, is not the form of our justification before God, but a consequence. And although renewal is likewise an effect of Baptism Tit. 3. v. 5. it does not yet follow from that, that justification formally consists in our renewal before God.

21. Estius comments thus on v. 22. Christ is said to be at the right hand of God, because Christ, after God, obtains supreme power, glory, and dignity in the kingdom of God, as second from God. Piscator on this place. At the right hand of God i. e. in that place, which is at the right hand of God. It is an anthropopathy that is a metaphor from the custom of men that is of Kings or Princes, who at they are accustomed to place at their right hand those whom they wish to be most honored, and to whom they wish the honor next to themselves to be attributed. And afterwards. The sitting at the right hand of God is dominion over all creatures; for this dominion it is not necessary that the body of Christ be everywhere. Resp. Scripture has not left it to us to divine what is to be understood by the sitting at the right hand of God, but has explained it quite clearly and perspicuously. For if Ps. 110. v. 2. is compared with the Apostolic passage 1. Cor. 15. v. 25. and 27., it will be manifest that what is for David to sit at the right hand of God, that is for the Apostle the same as to reign and to have all things subjected. If Mark 16. v. 19. is compared with the Apostolic passage Eph. 4. v. 10., it will be manifest that to sit at the right hand of God and to fill all things with his presence, to wit, of majesty is ἰσοδυναμοῦντα.. Peter himself in this place describes the exaltation to the right hand of God by the subjection of the Angels, and thus of all creatures, as is gathered from the parallel passages. Ps. 8. v. 7.1. Cor. 15. v. 27.Heb. 2. v. 8. The right hand of God itself is described to us in the sacred writings thus, that it is not some corporeal, circumscribed, finite place, but the infinite power of God and his most present majesty in heaven and on earth, that most present and most powerful dominion by which God preserves and governs all things.Exod. 15. v. 6.Ps. 18. v. 36.Ps. 44. v. 4.Ps. 63. v. 9.Ps. 77. v. 11.Ps. 108. v. 7.Ps. 118. v. 16.Ps. 139. v. 7. & seqq. Is. 48. v. 13. whence it is called the right hand of powerMatt. 26. v. 64.Luke 22. v. 69. the right hand of majestyHeb. 1. v. 3. throne μεγαλωσύνης Heb. 8. v. 1. the right hand of the throne of GodHeb. 12. v. 2. throne δόξης Matt. 25. v. 31. Therefore also the placing at the right hand of God is to be explained in such a way that by it is not understood a placing in a certain circumscribed place of heaven, but a participation in divine power, majesty, and dominion in heaven and on earth. And because that dominion is divine, therefore Christ exercises it not absent but present, filling all things in all, as the Apostle speaks Eph. 4. v. 10., consequently also when he will come to judgment in the clouds of heaven, he will nonetheless sit at the right hand of the power of God,Matt. 24. v. 30.C. 25. v. 31.C. 26. 64. Basil on the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius f. 206. The word of the right hand does not signify some lower place, but only equality, in that the right hand is not taken corporally concerning God, for to that same manner perhaps something left could also be in God.

20. The same Piscator writes thus on this place. Christ then sat at the right hand of God, when he went into heaven. Therefore they teach falsely, who say that he sat at the right hand of God in the womb of his mother,Acts 2. v. 32.Rom. 8. v. 34.Eph. 1. v. 20.Heb. 1. v. 3. Resp. 1.
