Most refer that pronoun ᾧ to the noun ὕδατος immediately preceding, so that the sense may be, to which, namely, to the water, Baptism, being conformable and similar, makes us safe. For just as the water of the flood saved Noah with his family by lifting up the ark: so Baptism saves us by lifting us from earth into heaven. But because this effect of the water is clearly accidental, for the water of the flood rather destroyed and extinguished than saved, therefore that pronoun ᾧ is more correctly referred to the whole sentence immediately preceding concerning the eight souls saved in the ark, in that sense that Baptism corresponds as ἀντίτυπον to this preservation as a type of spiritual preservation, in which way the Syrian also accepted the text, rendering it thus: According to which type you also have been made safe.

The little word ἀντιτύπου is used twice in the N. Testament but in a different signification. Hebr. 9. vers. 24. it signifies a figure pre-signifying something by its own image, when the Apostle says, τὰ ἅγια χειροποίητα to have been ἀντίτυπα τῶν ἀληθινῶν, where it is placed simply for τύπῳ Roman. 5. vers. 14.1. Cor. 10. v. 11.Hebr. 8. v. 5. in which sense the pious ancients call bread and wine in the Eucharist ἀντὶτυπα of the body and blood of Christ. Gregor. Nazianz. in his oration on the passover, calls the paschal night burning with infinite candles the antitype of the celestial firmament, in which are the stars. In this place, however, it signifies the truth itself, corresponding to the type and figure by a certain likeness or analogy. Thus the preservation of Noah in the ark at the time of the flood was τύπος; the preservation of the faithful to eternal salvation through Baptism is ἀντίτυπον, through that prefigured type in which sense Epiphanius and Cyril of Jerusalem call the Sacraments of the N. T. ἀντίτυπα of the old, because the Sacraments of the N. T. are prefigured by the Sacraments of the O. T.

For ἡμᾶς in the first person some Greek Codices read ὑμᾶς in the second person. Just as also some Latin Codices have, makes safe, as the Syrian, according to which type you also have been made safe. Bede in his commentary in the same way, makes you safe. But the true and

The genuine reading is ἡμας, because Peter numbers himself among the number of those for whom Baptism is a means of preservation unto eternal life, whence also in the Vulgate version in the following verse it is said in the first person, that we might be made heirs of eternal life, which however are not held in the Greek text. Τὸ σώζειν in this place is taken in another signification than the compound διὰσώζειν in the preceding verse. For here it signifies spiritual and eternal salvation, but there temporal salvation, which was a figure of that. The Syrian rendered it by [consult facsimile image] living, you are saved. Moreover, there is here in the Greek a transposition, for instead of that which the text has ᾧ ἀντίτυπον καὶ ἡμᾶς νῦν σώζει βάπτισμα, the collocation of words would be more natural and clear as this, ᾧ ἀντίτνπον βάπτισμς και ἡμᾶς νῦν σώζει. An example of a similar transposition occurs in the 2nd Epistle Petr. 1. vers. 19. ᾧ καλῶς ποιεῖτε προσέχοντες for ᾧ προσέχοντες ὡς λύχνῳ etc. καλῶς ποιεῖτε. Cyprian in Epistle 74 and Firmilian in Epistle 75 among the works of Cyprian read in the future tense He will save. But in the Greek is a verb of the present tense σώζει he saves, in which way also Idacius reads against Varimadus and the Vulgate version.

Οὐ σαρκὸσ ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου. Again in these words occurs a transposition familiar to our Apostle, for it should have been said, οὐκ ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου σαρκὸς. The little word ἀπόθεσις is joined by apposition to the word βάπτισμα: for it is signified that Baptism was neither instituted by God for that end, nor is to be used by us, that we might wash away the filth of the flesh or body, but for an end far other and more sublime, which the following antithesis expresses, ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς θεὸν, The Greek Scholia on this place annotate thus, ἐπερώτημα τουτέστιν ἀῤῥαβὼν, ἐνέχυρον, ἀπόδειξις, an earnest, pledge, and demonstration of a good conscience. Luther rendered it by covenant, because in covenants the contracting parties question one another, concerning which more will be said in the questions. Moreover, the Apostle signifies the antecedent by the consequent. Because also by Baptism not the filth of the flesh, but of the soul is washed away, thence it happens that the conscience, having been made more certain of the grace of GOD, is rendered peaceful and tranquil. εἰς θεὸν The same Greek Scholia teach to be taken κατὰ θεὸν, in God, or to God. The Syrian, by referring this whole place to the baptized persons themselves ἐξηγητικῶς rendered it thus. You have been made safe through Not the washing away of the filth of the flesh by baptism, but the confession of GOD in a pure conscience.

Δι' ἀναστάσεως Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Some refer this προσδιορισμὸν to what is more remote, and join it with the word σώζει, in this sense, that baptism saves us through the resurrection of Christ, since the foundation and meritorious cause of the salvation conferred upon us in baptism is the resurrection of Christ, by which, synecdochically, the passion and death of Christ is understood. In this sense the Syrian interpreter also rendered it, for he inserted the copulative O You have been saved through baptism and the resurrection of Christ. But it is more elegantly referred to what is nearer, and is joined with the immediately preceding noun ἐπερώτημα, with the participle γινόμενον, understood, in this sense, that that interrogation of a good conscience before God is made through the resurrection of Christ, inasmuch as it is the foundation of faith, which apprehends the promise concerning the remission of sins and the grace of GOD offered in Christ. 1. Cor. 15. v. 17. If Christ has not risen, your faith is vain, for you are still in your sins. Therefore, by the contrary sense: If Christ has risen, our faith is firm, and we are no longer in our sins.

Latin:

QUOD & NOS NUNC FIMILIS FORMAE SALVOS FACIT BAPTISMA NON CARNIS DEPOSITIO SORDIUM, SED CONSCIENTIAE BONAE INTERROGATIO IN DEUM PER RESURRECTIONEM CHRISTI.

Connexio. 1. Mentione factâ in versu praeced. aquarum diluvii & Noahi cum familia sua in arca divinitùs servati, transit à typo & antitypum, videlicet ad conservationem spiritualem, cuius medium est Baptismus, quia conservatio Noae in arca tempore diluvii fuit typus spiritualis conservationis credentium à diluvio irae divinae.

2. Lyranus profert hanc connexionem. Infert Apostolus ex praedictis corollarium. Dixerat enim, paucos per aquam fuisse salvatos in diluvio, in quantum arca elevavit eos à terra, ideò dicit, quod simili modo aqua baptismatis salvat spititualiter, quia per gratiam ibi datam elevat mentes à terrenis de fideriis ad petendum coelestia.

3. Applicat Apostolus allatum ex Historia diluvii exemplum ad suum institutum. Quemadmodum Noah cum sua familiâ tempore diluvii in arca servatus fuit, impiis per aquas diluvii extinctis ac deletis: sic aqua Baptismi correspondens aquae diluvii veterem hominem extinguit, novum ad vitam aeternam conservat.

4. Qui versum 19. praecedentem de Christi ad inferos descensu accipiunt, sic connectunt textum, ut statuant hîc describi alterum mortis CHRISTI effectum. Ut enim impii ex ea consecuti sunt confirmationem iustae suae damnationis: Ita pii confirmationem suae salutis Illi in descensu CHRISTI ad inferos, hi in resurrectione CHRISTI.

5. Dixerat Apostolus v. 18. Christum esse passum, mortificatum carne, vivificatum Spiritu, i. e. ex mortuis refuscitatum, ut nos adduceret Deo: iam ostendit, fructum passionis, mortis & resurrectionis Christi esse non solùm reconciliationem cum Deo, sed etiam bonae conscientiae stipulationem.

Dispositio. De Baptismo spiritualis conservationis & aeternae salutis medio tria praedicat Apostolus. 1. quòd sit antitypon conservationis in arca tempore diluvii, quia per mirabilem illam Noahi & familiae ipsrus in arca conservationem praefigurata fuit spiritualis conservatio piorum per Baptismum ad vitam aeternam. 2. quòd salutaris eius vis & effieacia non consistat in ablutione fordium carnis, sed in ablutione sordium animae, i. e. in remissione peccatorum, quam describit à consequente, quae est tranquillitas conscientiae in Deo acquiescentis. 3. quòd omnis vis Baptismi descendat ex Christi resurrectione, i. e. ex sanctissimo ipsius merito per passionem, mortem & resurrectionem parto. Potest tamen hoc tertium membrum referri ad secundum, sensu eo, quòd fiduciae nostrae ac tranquillae conscientiae fulcrum sit Christi resurrectio, quippe quae est evidens argumentum perfectae satisfactionis pro peccatis nostris à Christo praestitae & remissionis peccatorum per Christum nobis partae, nisi enim Christus, utpote sponsor noster, pro peccatorum nostrorum debitis plenè & perfectè solvisset, ex carcere sepulchri dimissus minimè fuisset.

Textus expositio ᾧ ἀντίτυπον καὶ ὑμᾶς νῦν σώζει βάπτισμα. Quidam Codices legunt ὁ καὶ ἡμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σώζει βάπτισμα, sed prior lectio, quae Complutensi editioni congruit, est genuina, unde Gagnaeus ad h. l. sic annotat. Crederem in Graeco esse mendum & proὁlegendumᾧ. Sed in vulgata versione Latina potiùs agnoscendum erat mendum, quippe quae legit ὃ, textum sic reddens. Quod & nos nunc similis formae salvos facit Baptisma. Quidam lectionem illam, quae habet ὃ, dicunt esse magis sinceram, eamque explicant hoc modo ὃ scil. ὕδωρ,quae aqua in re illo typo seu figura significata, h. e. ipsum eius antitypon, quod est Baptisma, nunc tempore N. T. nos salvos facit salute spirituali, quemadmodum illa servabat ab interitu corporali. Sed quilibet videt, hoc esse coactum. Sicut & illud, quod Carthusianus putat, supplendum verbum dico, hoc modo. Quod dico, quia Baptisma similis forme nos salvat. Pronomen illud ᾧ plerique referunt ad nomen ὕδατος proximè praecedens, ut sit sensus, cui scil. aquae conforme ac simile Baptisma nos salvos facit. Ut enim Aqua diluvii Noahum cum familia servavit, arcam elevando: sic Baptismus nos salvat, è terra in coelum nos elevando. Sed quia hic aquae effectus est planè accidentarius, aqua enim diluvii potiùs perdidit & extinxit quàm servavit, ideò pronomen illud ᾧ rectiùs refertur ad totam sententiam proximè praecedentem de servatis in arca octo animabus, sensu eo, quod isti conservationi tanquam typo spiritualis conservationis Baptismus velut ἀντίτυπον respondeat, quo modo etiam Syrus accepit textum, sic reddens. Secundùm quem typum vos quoque salvi facti estis.

Vocula ἀντιτύπου bis usurpatur in N. Testam. sed in diversa significatione. Hebr. 9. vers. 24. significat figuram imagine suâ aliquid praesignantem, quando Apostolus dicit, τὰ ἅγια χειροποίητα fuisse ἀντίτυπα τῶν ἀληθινῶν, ubi simpliciter ponitur pro τύπῳRoman. 5. vers. 14.1. Cor. 10. v. 11.Hebr. 8. v. 5. quo sensu pii veteres panem & vinum in Eucharistia vocant ἀντὶτυπαcorporis & sanguinis Christi. Gregor. Nazianz. orat. de pascha, noctem paschalem infinitis cereis ardentem vocat antitypum firmamenti coelestis, in quo sunt stellae. Hoc autem loco significat ipsam veritatem, similitudine seu analogiâ quadam typo ac figurae respondentem. Sic conservatio Noahi in arca tempore diluvii fuit τύπος; conservatio fidelium ad salutem aeternam per Baptismum est ἀντίτυπον, per typum illum praefiguratum quo sensu Epiphanius & Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Sacramenta N. T. vocant ἀντίτυπαveterum, quia Sacramenta N. T. sunt per Sacramenta V. T. praefigurata.

Pro ἡμᾶς persona prima quidam Codd. Graeci legunt ὑμᾶς in secunda persona. Sicut etiam quidam Codices Latini habent, salvos facit, ut Syrus, secundum quem typum vos quoque salvi facti estis. Beda in comment. eodem modo, salvos vos facit. Sed vera &

genuina lectio est ἡμας, quia Petrus seipsum eorum numero annumerat, quibus Baptismus est medium conservationis ad vitam aeternam, unde etiam in versione vulgata in versu seq. in prima persona dicitur, ut vitae aeternae beredes efficeremur, quae tamen non habentur in textu Graeco. Τὸ σώζειν hoc loco in alia significatione accipitur, quàm compositum διὰσώζειν in versu praecedente. Hîc enim significat salutem spiritualem & aeternam, ibi vero salutem temporalem, quae illius fuit figura. Syrus reddidit per [consult facsimile image]viventes, salvi vos estis. Est autem hîc in Graeco traiectio, pro eo enim, quod textus habet ᾧ ἀντίτυπον καὶ ἡμᾶς νῦν σώζει βάπτισμα, collocatio verborum magis naturalis & perspicua esset haec, ᾧ ἀντίτνπον βάπτισμς και ἡμᾶς νῦν σώζει. Similis traiectionis exemplum occurrit 2. Epist. Petr. 1. vers. 19.ᾧ καλῶς ποιεῖτε προσέχοντες pro ᾧ προσέχοντες ὡς λύχνῳ &c. καλῶς ποιεῖτε. Cyprianus Epist. 74. & Firmilianus Epist. 75. apud Cypr. legunt in tempore futuro Salvos faciet. Sed in Graeco est verbum praesentis temporis σώζει salvat, quo modo etiam legit Idacius contra Varimadum & vulg. versio.

Οὐ σαρκὸσ ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου. Denuò in his verbis occurrit traiectio Apostolo nostro familiaris, dicendum enim erat, οὐκ ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου σαρκὸς. Vocula ἀπόθεσις per appositionem coniungitur voci βάπτισμα: significatur enim, Baptismum nec eo fine à Deo institutum, nec à nobis usurpandum esse, ut sordes carnis sive corporis abluamus, sed fine longè alio ac sublimiore, quem sequens antithesis exprimit, ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς θεὸν, Graeca Scholia ad h. l. sic annotant, ἐπερώτημα τουτέστιν ἀῤῥαβὼν, ἐνέχυρον, ἀπόδειξις,bonae conscientiae arrbabo, pignus & demonstratio. Lutherus reddidit per foedus, quia in foederibus paciscentes sese mutuò interrogant, quâ de re in quaestionibus plura dicentur. Significat autem Apostolus ex consequente antecedens. Quia etiam per Baptismum non carnis, sed animae sordes abluuntur, inde fit, ut conscientia de gratia DEI certior facta reddatur pacata & tranquilla. εἰς θεὸν eadem Scholia Graeca docent sumiκατὰ θεὸν,in Deum, vel ad Deum. Syrus totum hunc locum ad personas baptizatas eum referendo ἐξηγητικῶς sic reddidit. Salvi facti estis per Baptismum non corpore abluti à sordibus, sed confitentes DEUM in conscientia pura.

Δι' ἀναστάσεως Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Quidam hunc προσδιορισμὸν referunt ad remotius, & coniungunt eum cum verbo σώζει, sensu eo, quòd Baptismus nos salvet per resurrectionem Christi, cum fundamentum & causa meritoria salutis nobis in Baptismo collatae sit resurrectio Christi, per quam synecdochieè intelligitur passio & mors Christi. Hoc sensu etiam Syrus interpres reddidit, nam interposuit copulativam O Salvi facti estis per Baptismum & resurrectionem Christi. Sed concinniùs refertur ad propinquius, & coniungitur cum proximè praecedente nomine ἐπερώτημα, subintellecto participio γινόμενον, sensu eo, quòd interrogatio illa bonae conscientiae apud Deum fiat per resurrectionem Christi, quippe quae est fidei, promissionem de remissione peccatorum ac DEI gratia in Christo oblata apprehendentis, fundamentum. 1. Cor. 15. v. 17.Si Christus non resurrexit, vana est fides vestra, adhuc enim estis in peccatis vestris. Ergò à contrario sensu. Si Christus resurrexit, firma est fides nostra, & non sumus ampliùs in peccatis nostris.

## 3:22
WHO IS AT THE RIGHT HAND OF GOD, SWALLOWING UP DEATH, SO THAT WE MIGHT BE MADE HEIRS OF ETERNAL LIFE, HAVING GONE INTO HEAVEN, WITH ANGELS AND AUTHORITIES AND POWERS MADE SUBJECT TO HIM.

Connection. 1. The Apostle had said that the fulcrum of faith and a peaceful conscience is the resurrection of Christ, inasmuch as he was raised for our justification, Rom. 4. v. 25. to this fulcrum he adds also another, namely, the session of Christ at the right hand of GOD, and his exaltation above the Angels, nay, all creatures in heaven and on earth. Moreover, this exaltation of Christ is the fulcrum of our faith in a twofold way. First, because it is an argument of the singular love with which the heavenly Father embraces Christ raised from the dead, and therefore it is also an indication of the perfect satisfaction rendered for our sins. For unless Christ had fully satisfied for our sins, and had perfectly reconciled the human race to his Father, the heavenly Father would never have raised him to such sublimity. Secondly, because through the placing of Christ at the right hand of God we are confirmed that in him there is enough power and protection to save us.

2. Therefore the Apostle consoles the pious, because since Christ is their head not only as God, being the very right hand and power of God, but also as man raised from the dead, and having departed into heaven, has been placed at the right hand, and powerfully reigns at the very right hand of God, and has all things in heaven and on earth subjected to himself, therefore they can and ought to firmly conclude that they will be sufficiently safe under that most powerful guardian and protector of their salvation.

3. Those who interpret this concerning the descent of Christ to the underworld v. 19. say, that a third effect of the death of Christ is described here, which pertains to the person of Christ himself, that through passion and death he entered into his glory Luc. 24. v. 26. and through the passion of death he was crowned with glory and honor. Hebr. 2. v. 9.

4. Not only to console the pious, but also to strike terror into the impious who do not do penance, he makes mention of the exaltation of Christ to the right hand of GOD, through which all things are subjected to his dominion, so that he may signify that he is able to protect and save whom he wills; and is able to prostrate and damn whom he wills.

5. Beda brings forward this connection. Just as Christ rising from the dead ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of GOD: so also he signifies that we too, through Baptism, seek the way of salvation and the entrance to the heavenly kingdom.

Disposition of the text. He explains the session of Christ at the right hand of God. 1. The antecedent, which is the departure or ascension of Christ into heaven. 2. The consequent, which is the subjection of Angels and all creatures.

Exposition of the text. ὁς ἐστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θεοῦ, πορευθεὶς εἰς οὐρανὸν. A certain transposition occurs here also, for the discourse is to be ordered thus, ὃς πορευθεὶς εἰς οὐρανὸν ἐστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θεοῦ, so that Peter says this, which the article of faith in the Apostolic Creed holds. He ascended into heaven, he sits at the right hand of GOD. The Syrian expressed the same order, who rendered the text thus. Who was taken up into heaven, and is at the right hand of GOD. After the words is at the right hand of GOD follows in the vulgate version, swallowing up death, that we might be made heirs of eternal life. Beda has and explains the same in his commentary on this place, noting thus. He well says, swallowing up death. For what we swallow, we act so that it may never appear in our bodies. And the Lord swallowed up death, which rising from the dead he so thoroughly consumed, that nothing against it could prevail any further through the touch of any corruption, and while the appearance of the true body remained, every stain of former frailty was entirely absent. Which very thing is promised to be for us also in the end, the Apostle saying, when he was speaking about our resurrection. Then shall come to pass the saying that is written. Death is swallowed up in victory. Well swallowed up, for when we also shall have been made partakers of eternal life, thus indeed the power of the immortal body will take away every vice of past corruption, just as the flame of fire is accustomed to consume with the power of its heat a drop of water cast into it. Fulgentius has the same things in his book on faith to Peter, chapter 2. The Ordinary Gloss, Lyranus, etc., on this passage. And yet 1. Nothing of these exists in the Greek Codices. Catharinus indeed says, it is held in the Greek books of the new edition. But Lorinus replies, that he has not yet found them. 2. Nor in the Syriac version. 3. Nor in the commentaries of the Greek Interpreters. 4. Rufinus does not seem to have acknowledged it, while in the exposition of the Creed on the article, he ascended into heaven etc. he cites these words of Peter speaking about Christ. Who is at the right hand of GOD sitting in the heavens. For he said sitting in the heavens, for that which follows here, having gone into heaven, with the intermediate words, which are not held in the Greek, being omitted. 5. These words are inserted less conveniently after that, who is at the right hand of GOD, unless the present is taken as placed in the place of the past, swallowing up death i.e. death having been swallowed up.

Ὑποταγέντων αὐτῷ Ἀγγέλων καὶ ἐξουσιῶν καὶ δυνάμεων. The Vulgate rendered, Angels being subject to him. But in the Greek it is not, ὑποτόξας ἑαυτῷ τοὺς Ἀγγέλους, but ὑποταγέντων αὐτῷ Ἀγγέλων, Angels being subject to him, or when the Angels were subject to him. In the same way the Syrian. And the Angels are subjected, or are subject to him, namely by the heavenly Father, to whom also in other places of Scripture parallel to this one of ours this subjection is attributed, 1. Cor. 15. v. 27.Hebr. 2. v. 8. from Psal. 8. v. 7. He subjected all things under his feet, namely the heavenly Father. v. 24. Eph. 1. v. 20. GOD wrought the operation of the power of his virtue in Christ, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places v. 21. Above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this world, but also in the future. v. 22. And he subjected all things under his feet. From which passage it is understood at the same time, under the names of the three orders of Angels, which are expressed here in explicit words, that Peter also wished the rest to be included, such as Archangels, principalities, dominions, thrones etc. indeed all creatures.

For since Angels are the most noble and most powerful creatures, therefore by the subjection of the Angels, through a certain species of synecdoche, the subjection of all creatures is signified. Hebr. 2. v. 8. In that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing not subjected to him. Lyranus in h. l. Here three orders of Angels are expressed, one from the lower Hierarchy, when it is said, Angel: and two from the middle, there: And powers and virtues, and through these all others are understood, over whom Christ the man is set.

Latin:

QUI EST IN DEXTRA DEI DEGLUTIENS MORTEM, UT VITA AETERNAE HEREDES EFFICEREMUR, PROFECTUS IN COELUM SUBIECTIS SIBI ANGELIS & POTESTATIBUS & VIRTUTIBUS.

Connexio. 1. Dixerat Apostolus, fulcrum fidei & pacatae conscientiae esse resurrectionem Christi, utpote propter iustificationem nostram resuscitati, Rom. 4. v. 25. huic fulcro addit etiam alterum, videlicet sessionem Christi ad dextram DEI, & exaltationem eius supra Angelos, imò universas creaturas in coelo & terra. Duplici autem modo haec exaltatio Christi est fidei nostrae fulcrum. Primò, quia est argumentum singularis amoris, quo Pater coelestis Christum ex mortuis resuscitatum complectitur, proinde etiam est indicium perfectae satisfactionis pro peccatis nostris praestitae. Nisi enim Christus pro peccatis nostris planè satisfecisset, ac genus humanum Patri suo perfectè reconciliasset, nunquam Pater coelestis in tantam sublimitatem eum extulisset. Secundò, quia per collocationem Christi ad dextram Dei confirmamur, quòd in ipso satis potentiae & praesidii sit ad nos servandos.

2. Consolatur ergò Apostolus pios, quòd cum Christus caput ipsorum non solùm ut Deus sit ipsa Dei dextra & virtus, sed etiam ut homo à mortuis resuscitatus, & in coelum profectus ad dextram collocatus sit, & in ipsa Dei dextra potenter regnet, ac omnia in coelo & terra sibi subiecta habeat, ideò sub illo salutis suae custode & protectore potentissimo se satis tutos fore firmiter statuere possunt ac debent.

3. Qui de descensu Christi ad inferos v. 19. accipiunt, dicunt, tertium bîc describi effectum mortis Christi, qui ad personam ipsius Christi pertineaet, quòd per passionem & mortem intraverit in gloriam suamLuc. 24. v. 26.ac per passionem mortis sit gloria & honore coronatus.Hebr. 2. v. 9.

4. Non solùm ut pios consoletur, sed etiam ut impiis non agentibus poenitentiam terrorem incutiat, mentionem facit exaltationis Christi ad dextram DEI, per quam omnia ipsius dominio subiecta, ut significet, ipsum posse, quos vult, tueri ac salvare; & posse, quos vult, prosternere ac damnare.

5. Beda profert hanc connexionem. Sicut Christus resurgens à mortuis ascendit in coelum, & sedet à dextris DEI: sic etiam & nobis per Baptisma viam salutis ac regni coelestis introitum paetere significat.

Textus dispositio. Sessionis Christi ad dextram Dei exponit. 1. Antecedens, quod est Christi in coelum profectio sive ascensio. 2. Consequens, quod est subiectio Angelorum & omnium creaturarum.

Expositio textus. ὁς ἐστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θεοῦ, πορευθεὶς εἰς οὐρανὸν. Occurrit & hîc quaedam traiectio, sic enim sermo ordinandus, ὃς πορευθεὶς εἰς οὐρανὸν ἐστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θεοῦ, ut hoc dicat Petrus, quod habet fidei articulus in Symbolo Apostolico. Adscendit ad coelos, sedet ad dextram DEI. Eundem ordinem expressit Syrus, qui textum sic reddidit. Qui sublatus est in coelum, & est ad DEI dextram. Post verba est in dextra DEI sequitur in versione vulgata, deglutiens mortem, ut vitae aeternae beredes efficeremur. Eadem habet & exponit Beda in comm. ad hunc locum sic annotans. Benè ait, deglutiens mortem. Quod enim deglutimus, agimus, ut in corporibus nostris assumtum nunquam pareat (appareat) Et deglutivit mortem Dominus, quam resurgens à mortuis ita funditùs consumsit, ut nihil contra se ultra per attactum alicuius corruptionis valeret, ac manente specie veri corporis abesset prorsus labes omnis prista fragilitatis. Quod ipsum & nobis in fine promittitur futurum, dicente Apostolo, cum de nostra resurrectione loqueretur. Tunc fiet sermo, qui scriptus est. Absorpta est mors in victoria. Benè ab sorpta, quis cùm & nos vitae aeternae participes fuerimus effecti, ita nimirum virtus corporis immortalis omne praeteritae corruptionis vitium tollet, quomodo solet flamma ignis immissam sibi aquae guttam ardoris sui consumere virtute. Eadem etiam habent Fulgentius lib. de fide ad Petrum cap. 2. Glossa ordinaria, Lyranus &c. in h. l. Atqui 1. Nihil horum extat in Graecis Codicibus. Catharinus quidem dicit, haberi in Graecis libris novae editionis. Sed Lorinus respondet, se eos nondum reperisse. 2. Nec in versione Syriaca. 3. Nec in commentariis Interpretum Graecorum. 4. Ruffinus non videtur agnovisse, dum in expositione Symboli ad articulum, ascendit ad coelos &c. citat haec verba Petri dicentis de Christo. Qui est in dextra DEI sedens in coelis. Nam sedens in coelis dixit, pro eo quod hîc sequitur, profectus in coelum, mediis, quae in Graeco non habentur, omissis. 5. Inseruntur haec verba minùs commodè post illud, qui est à dextra DEI, nisi praesens accipiatur loco praeteriti positum, deglutiens mortem i. e. absorpta morte.

Ὑποταγέντων αὐτῷ Ἀγγέλων καὶ ἐξουσιῶν καὶ δυνάμεων. Vulgata reddidit, subiectis sibi Angelis. Sed in Graeco non est, ὑποτόξας ἑαυτῷ τοὺς Ἀγγέλους, sed ὑποταγέντων αὐτῷ Ἀγγέλων, subiectis ei Angelis, sive cum ei subiecti essent Angeli. Eodem modo Syrus. Et subiiciuntur, sive subiecti ei sunt Angeli, scilicet â Patre coelesti, cui etiam in aliis Scripturae locis huic nostro parallelis haec subiectio tribuitur, 1. Cor. 15. v. 27.Hebr. 2. v. 8. ex Psal. 8. v. 7.Omnia subiecitpedibus eius, scil. Pater coelestis. v. 24. Eph. 1. v. 20.DEUS operationem potentiae virtutis suae operatus est in Christo, suscitans illum à mortuis & constituens ad dextram suam in coelestibusv. 21.Supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & virtutem, & dominationem, & omne, quod nominatur non solùm, in hoc seculo, sed etiam in futuro.v. 22.Et omnia subiecit sub pedibus eius. Ex quo loco simul intelligitur, sub nominibus trium ordinum Angelicorum, qui hîc disertis verbis exprimuntur, Petrum etiam reliquos voluisse comprehensos, ut Archangelos, principatus, dominationes, thronos &c. imò omnes creaturas.

cùm enim Angeli sint nobilissimae & potentissimae creaturae, ideò ex subiectione Angelorum per speciem quandam synecdoches significatur subiectio omnium creaturarum. Hebr. 2. v. 8.In eo, quod subiecit ei omnia, nihil dimisit non subiectum ei. Lyranus in h. l. Hic Angelorum tres ordines exprimuntur, unus de inferiori Hierarchia, cum dicitur, Angelus: & duo de media, ibi: Et potestatibus & virtutibus, & per hos omnes alii intelliguntur, quibus Christus homo praefilitur.

## 4:1
FORASMUCH THEN AS CHRIST HATH SUFFERED FOR US IN THE FLESH, ARM YOURSELVES LIKEWISE WITH THE SAME MIND: FOR HE THAT HATH SUFFERED IN THE FLESH HATH CEASED FROM SIN.

CHAPTER IV.

Connection. 1. Those who accept the Apostolic exhortation concerning the showing of patience under the cross, bring forward a connection of this kind, that after παρέκβασιν, comprised in the last four verses of the preceding chapter, the Apostle returns to the argument brought forward immediately before that digression, namely, to the example of Christ who suffered for us, which he had begun to explain in v. 18, and that he may again console those placed under the cross, and exhort them to patience. Bede in this place: After he had established the example of the Lord's resurrection and of our washing, which takes place in Baptism, from the Sacrament of the ark and the flood, he returns to that which he had begun to say, so that, imitating the work of our Redeemer, we may patiently tolerate the wickedness of evil men among the good things which we do.

2. But it is more elegant to accept the Apostolic exhortation concerning the mortification of the flesh or of depraved desires in the flesh, by which reasoning the connection can be such.

1. The Apostle had exhorted Christians in the chapter immediately preceding, that they should patiently bear afflictions, especially those which befall them on account of the profession of the Christian faith, now he proceeds further, warning that adversities are to be tolerated in such a way that we may use the cross divinely sent for the mortification of the flesh.

2. He had proposed the passion of Christ to the faithful in the preceding chapter as a gift, when he said, Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God.v. 18.Now he proposes it as a type and example, which we should follow in the mortification of the flesh. Luther in this place.

3. Scripture commends to us a double type and likeness of the death of Christ. First, that we may be conformed to him in patiently bearing reproaches and miseries. Second, that through the mortification of the flesh we may be spiritually crucified with Christ, and through the vivification of the Spirit we may spiritually rise again with him.Rom. 6. Vers. 3. & 4.Phil. 3. vers. 10. The Apostle had dealt with the former in the preceding chapter and was about to deal with it again in the latter part of this chapter, he begins to deal with the latter in this place.

4. He had said v. 18. that Christ was mortified in the flesh and vivified in the Spirit, from that he infers the present exhortation to the mortification of the flesh or of the old man, and the vivification of the Spirit or of the new man, having taken the argument not only from the example, but also from the virtue of the death of Christ. For the passion, and death, and resurrection of Christ is not only the example of our spiritual death and resurrection, but also the efficient cause of the same, because Christ by his passion, death, and resurrection merited for us not only the remission of sins, but also the gift of the Holy Spirit, who mortifies the flesh in us and renews our nature.

5. He continues the exhortation to holiness and innocence of life chap. 1. vers. 15. and following chap. 2. vers. 11. and following chap. 3. vers. 11. and following, which had begun to be proposed, opening the fountain of our sanctification, namely the passion and death of Christ, by whose force and virtue we die to sin, so that it may no longer rule over us.

6. In chap. preceding v. 21. he had explained the two principal ends of Baptism, namely, first that it saves us, i.e., offers to us the grace of God and the remission of sins, and confers them upon believers. Secondly, that it is the stipulation of a good conscience toward God, i.e., that it seals the spiritual benefits conferred upon us. Now he passes to the secondary end of Baptism, which consists in this, that it signifies the daily mortification of sin, that the old man ought continually to be submerged and extinguished in us through mortification and repentance with all sins and depraved concupiscences, and again daily to emerge and rise again as a new man, who may live in holiness and justice before God forever. Rom. 6. v. 4. 5. & 6.Col. 2. v. 12. Thus, therefore, not only in the death of Christ, but also in Baptism we have an example, nay, the cause of spiritual mortification and vivification.

Disposition. 1. From the passion and death of Christ he draws an argument, by which he exhorts the faithful that, by mortifying the concupiscences of the flesh, they may conform themselves to the passion of Christ. 2. He explains the salutary fruit of that mortification, which is the cessation from sins.

Exposition of the text. Χριστοῦ οὺν παθόντος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν σαρκὶ. The Vulgate version rendered it. Christ therefore having suffered in the flesh. But it omitted that ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, which is in all Greek Codices, which the Syrian paraphrast expressed [consult facsimile image] which Jerome also reads in book 1 against Jovinian, which finally corresponds to v. 18. C. preceding 3. Christ suffered δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων. The particle οὐν shows that this Apostolic exhortation is deduced by way of inference from in the same verse, 18, in which mention had been made of the passion of Christ, and the end of the same expressed, namely our being brought to God. Προσδιορισμὸν that Christ suffered σαρκὶ in the flesh, as Jerome reads in book 1 against Jovinian, the Vulgate has not unsuitably rendered in the flesh, for σαρκὶ is placed for ἐν σαρκὶ, or κα τὰ σάρκα according to the flesh, through the flesh, as Augustine rendered it, citing this passage in his book on faith and works, chapter 10. For as he had said above in chapter 3, verse 18, concerning Christ, that he was θανατωθεὶς σαρκὶ, so in this place he says, he παθόντα σαρκὶ. But in both places by the name of flesh is understood the whole and entire human nature of Christ, consisting of body and soul John 1, v. 141 Tim. 3, 16 pure and clean from every stain of sin.

καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν αὐτὴν, ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθαι. Jerome in the said book reads, be armed with the same conversation. But in the Greek it is ἐννοιαν, therefore these things are to be accepted as said by way of interpretation. Fulgentius in book 3 to Theos, chapter 9, reads, with the same knowledge. The Vulgate: And you be armed with the same thought. Oecumenius understands κατὰ, just as the Syrian also rendered be armed according to the same thought. The sense is that they ought to put on a similar thought as if it were certain weapons, or what is the same, that they ought to fortify themselves with a similar thought as if with a certain shield and buckler. Luther Wapnet euch mit dem selbigen Sinn. In commentary harnischt euch/leget solchen Sinn an als einen harnisch. Τὰ ὅπλα are called weapons in general, in particular this word is used for shield and buckler, whence the LXX rendered the Hebrew מגן with it, which signifies shield, buckler, with which a man fortifies himself in time of war, 3 Kings 10, v. 17chap. 14, v. 28Psal. 34, v. 2 etc. Also צנה which likewise signifies buckler and shield 1 Kings 17, v. 7Psal. 5, v. 15Psal. 90, v. 5 etc. which signification fits this place. Hence ὁπλέζεσθαι to be clothed with weapons, to be fortified with shield and buckler, (Eustathius teaches that ὁπλίζειν is sometimes the same as ἑτοιμάζειν, παρασκευάζειν to prepare, to instruct, etc. which signification could likewise have a place here. But it is more suitable to retain the customary signification of arming and fortifying in this place.) But it is also used actively for ὁπλίζειν, in which way it can also be accepted in this place, put on the same thought as if it were a certain spiritual armor. But what is that ἔννοια, with which the Apostle commands the faithful to arm and fortify themselves? Some establish that the discourse is solely about patience in the cross, so that the sense may be:

Since Christ demonstrated singular patience in his passion, he teaches you also who have given your name to Christ, nay, have been grafted into him through Baptism, to be affected in the same way, to be armed and instructed with the same mind, thought, and purpose for patiently bearing the cross sent by God. But it appears from what follows that the discourse here is chiefly about the mortification of the flesh, of which, however, we by no means deny that patience in bearing the cross is a part. The sense, therefore, is this. Because Christ suffered in the flesh for you, you ought therefore to conceive a firm purpose of mind, that you may wish to die and be crucified spiritually with him through the mortification of the flesh. Rom. 6. v. 2. & seqq. Just as he suffered and died in the flesh, so also you ought to die to sin, and crucify the flesh with its desires Gal. 5. vers. 24. this thought, this affection will be for you like a most firm shield and fortification against sin.

ὅτι παθὼν ἐν σαρκί πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας. The Vulgate rendered it, because he who has suffered in the flesh, has ceased from sins. But in the Greek it is singular. He has rested from sin, in which way also Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian, cites this saying. The Syrian rendered it paraphrastically. He ceases from all sins. Augustine, on faith and works, chapter 19, has ceased to sin. But what indeed is it to suffer in the flesh and who is that παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ; Some determine that the Apostle is speaking about Christ himself, of whom he had said a little before, that he himself suffered in the flesh. But we shall refute this exposition in its proper place. Bede seems to take it specifically concerning a Martyr, who has suffered on account of the confession of Christ. Whoever of the saints, he says, has subjected his body to the violence of persecutors for Martyrdom, there is no doubt that, as far as is possible for human Nature, he has abstained from sins until the end of his life. For what could he think about the perpetration of sin, what about carnal desires, what could he revolve in his mind except the will of God, who, whether fixed to wood, or surrounded by the blows of stones, or subjected to the bites of beasts, or placed upon the flames of fires, or pierced by the scourges of scorpions, or affected by any other kind of punishments, was compelled to desire only this, when, the struggle finished, he might receive the crown of life? Therefore, blessed Peter desires us to imitate the mind of such men always, when he commands us to be armed with the same thought against the wickedness of the depraved and against the delights of vices, by the proposed example of the Lord's passion, wishing it to be understood that even we, resting in the peace of the Church, if we put on the habit of one suffering, easily With the Lord helping, we avoid the falls of all sins, and we subject all the desires of the divine will to His commands. To this exposition of Bede, the Syriac version could be accommodated, which has it thus: He who dies in his body. But the Apostle speaks in general about any pious person, as the circumstances of the text show. Therefore, some concerning the afflictions of the body, which the Apostle 1. Cor. 7. v. 28. calls the tribulation of the flesh, accept this passage, so that the sense may be: Those who through passions and afflictions are rendered conformable to Christ crucified, they are restrained by tribulations as if by a certain bridle, lest they satisfy the desires of corrupt Nature, because the cross is προφυλακτικὸν of sin, to which our flesh is prone. Some think the faithful are compared to those who, on account of their crimes, have been subjected to capital punishment, and therefore can no longer commit those crimes; and that the Apostle uses this comparison because he considers the faithful in Christ, who for their sins endured the ignominious punishment of the cross, which is just as if they themselves had endured that punishment. But it is manifest from the consequences that by τό to suffer in the flesh in this place is understood the mortification of the flesh, through which the pious are rendered conformable to the passion of Christ. Therefore, the past tense παθὼν is put for the present, so that the sense may be: He who is conformed in that way to the likeness of the passion and death of Christ, which He sustained in the flesh, so that he himself also suffers in the flesh, i.e., mortifies and crucifies his flesh with depraved affections and concupiscences, he ceases from sin, since it pertains to the actions of the carnal life. He who crucifies the flesh with its concupiscences in Christ and with Christ, he ceases to sin. There is, therefore, in the word flesh an elegant ἀντανακλάσις. For in the former part of the verse it is taken substantially, for the human Nature of Christ, utterly devoid of all sin and stain: but in this latter part of the verse it is taken accidentally, for carnal concupiscence, for the viciousness of Nature, which we draw from Adam, and the remnants of which are still surviving in the pious even after regeneration, which they ought to purge and mortify through the Spirit. Moreover, the Apostle preferred to say παθῶν ἐν σαρκὶ rather than ἀποθανὼν as Paul speaks in a parallel passage Rom. 6. v. 2. because he wished to recall us to Christ the archetype and to teach that through the mortification of our flesh we are rendered conformable to the passion of Christ. Some accept the little word ὅτι causally or ratiocinatively, so that it may be the reason for the exhortation from the definition and effect of mortification. But it is more correctly taken expositorily, for the Apostle explains that thought by which he wishes us to be armed, namely that it is fitting for us, as members of Christ, to die spiritually in Christ and with Christ, that our old man ought to be crucified with Him, so that thus the kingdom of sin may be abolished in us; that therefore, because we have died and been crucified with Christ, we ought to have no more business with sin, so that it may still dominate and reign in us.

Latin:

CHRISTO IGITUR PASSO IN CARNE, & VOS EADEM COGITATIONE ARMAMINI, QUIA QUI PASSUS EST IN CARNE, DESIIT A PECCATIS.

CAPUT IV.

Connexio. 1. Qui exhortationem Apostolicam de praestanda in cruce patientia accipiunt, eiusmodi proferunt connexionem, quod post παρέκβασιν, ultimis quatuor versiculis praeced. cap. comprehensam, redeat Apostolus ad argumentum proximè ante illam digressionem allatum, videl. ad exemplum Christi pro nobis passi, quod v. 18. explicare coeperat, eodemque constitutos sub cruce denuo consoletur, & ad patientiam exhortetur. Beda in h. l. Post quam exemplum resurrectionis Dominicae & ablutionis nostrae, quae fit in Baptismo, de arcae ac diluvii Sacramento astruxerat, revertitur ad hoc, quod dicere coeperat, ut imitantes opus Redemtoris nostri inter bona, quae facimus, patienter malorum nequitiam toleremus.

2. Sed concinniùs est, exhortationem Apostolicam de mortificatione carnis sive pravarum concupiscentiarum in carne accipere, quâ ratione connexio potest esse talis.

1. Hortatus fuerat Apostolus Christianos in cap. proximè praecedente, ut exemplo Christi afflictiones, praesertim eas, quae ob fidei Christianae prosessionem ipsis obtingunt, patienter ferrent, iam longiùs progreditur, monens, adversa sic toleranda, ut cruce divinitùs immissà ad mortificationem carnis utamur.

2. Christi passionem proposuerat fidelibus cap. praeced. ut donum, quandó dixit, Christum semel pro peccatis passum, iustum pro iniustis, ut nos offerret Deo.v. 18.iam proponit eam ut typum & exemplum, quod in mortificatione carnis sequamur. Luth. in h. l.

3. Duplicem typum ac similitudinem mortis Christi Scriptura nobis commendat. Primò ut illi configuremur in probris & aerumnis patienter ferendis. Secundò ut per mortificationem carnis spiritualiter cum Christo crucifigamur, & per vivificationem Spiritus spiritualiter cum ipso resurgamus.Rom. 6. Vers. 3. & 4.Phil. 3. vers. 10. De priore egerat Apostolus in cap. praeced. & in posteriore huius capitis parte denuò acturus erat, de posteriore hoc loco agere incipit.

4. Dixerat v. 18.Christum mortificatum esse carne & vivificatum Spiritu, ex eo infert praesentem exhortationem ad mortificationem carnis sive veteris hominis, & vivificationem Spiritus sive novi hominis, sumto argumento non solùm ab exemplo, sed etiam à virtute mortis Christi. Christi enim passio, & mors, & resurrectio non solúm est spiritualis nostrae mortis & resurrectionis exemplum, sed eiusdem etiam causa efficiens, quia Christus suâ passione, morte & resurrectione non solùm peccatorum remissionem, sed etiam donationem Spiritus sancti nobis promeruit, qui carnem in nobis mortificat, & Naturam nostram renovat.

5. Exhortationem ad vitae sanctitatem & innocentiam cap. 1. vers. 15. & seqq. cap. 2. vers. 11. & seqq. cap. 3. vers. 11. & seqq. proponi coeptam continuat, aperiens fontem nostrae sanctificationis, videlicet passionem & mortem Christi, cuius vi & virtute peccato morimur, ut illud non ampliùs nobis dominetur.

6. In cap. praeced. v. 21. exposuerat duos principales Baptismi fines, videl. primò quòd nos salvet i. e. gratiam Dei & remissionem peccatorum nobis offerat, & credentibus conferat. Secundò quòd sit stipulatio bonae conscientiae erga Deum, i. e. quòd spiritualia beneficia nobis collata obsignet. Iam transit ad secundarium Baptismi finem, qui in eo consistit, quod significat quotidianam peccati mortificationem, quòd vetus homo debeat subinde per mortificationem ac poenitentiam in nobis submergi, & extingui cum omnibus peccatis, & pravis concupiscentiis, ac rursus quotidie emergere ac resurgere novus homo, qui in sanctitate & iustitia coram Deo vivat in aeternum. Rom. 6. v. 4. 5. & 6.Col. 2. v. 12. Sic ergò non solùm in morte Christi, sed etiam in Baptismo habemus exemplar, imò causam spiritualis mortificationis & vivificationis.

Dispositio. 1. Ex passione & morte Christi ducit argumentum, quo fideles exhortatur, ut mortificando concupiscentias carnis Christi passioni sese conforment 2. Exponit salutarem mortificationis illius fructum, qui est cessatio à peccatis.

Textus expositio. Χριστοῦ οὺν παθόντος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν σαρκὶ. Vulgata versio reddidit. Christo igitur passo in carne. Sed omisit illud ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, quod est in omnibus Graecis Codicibus, quod paraphrastes Syrus expressit [consult facsimile image] quod legit etiam Hieronymus lib. 1. contra Iovinian. quod denique respondet v. 18. C. praeced. 3.Christus passus estδίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων. Particula οὐν ostendit, hanc exhortationè Apostolicam per modum illationis deduci ex eodem versu, 18. in quo passionis Christi facta fuerat mentio, eiusdemque finis expressus, videlicet adductio nostra ad Deum. Προσδιορισμὸν quod Christus passus sit σαρκὶcarne, ut legit Hieron. lib. 1. contra Iovin. vulgata haud inconcinnè reddidit in carne, nam σαρκὶ positum pro ἐν σαρκὶ, vel κα τὰ σάρκαsecundum carnem, per carnem ut reddidit Augustinus, locum hunc citans lib. de fid. & oper. cap. 10. Ut enim superiùs cap. 3. v. 18. de Christo dixerat, quod fueritθανατωθεὶς σαρκὶ, ita hoc loco dicit, eum παθόντα σαρκὶ. Utrobique autem carnis nomine intelligitur tota & integra humana Christi Natura, corpore & animâ constans Ioh. 1. v. 14.1. Tim. 3. 16. ab omni peccati labe pura atque munda.

καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν αὐτὴν, ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθαι. Hieronymus d. l. legit, eadem conversatione armamini. Sed in Graeco est ἐννοιαν, ideò haec per interpretationem dicta sunt accipienda. Fulgentius lib. 3. ad Theos. cap. 9. legit, eadem scientiâ. Vulg. Et vos eadem cogitatione armamini. Oecumenius subintelligit κατὰ, sicut & Syrus reddidit iuxta eandem cogitationem armemini. Sensus est, quod similem cogitationem velut arma quaedam induere, vel quod idem est, simili cogitatione velut clypeo quodam & scuto sese munire debeant. Luth. Wapnet euch mit dem selbigen Sinn. In comm. harnischt euch/leget solchen Sinn an als einen harnisch.Τὰ ὅπλα in genere dicuntur arma, in specie usurpatur haec vox pro clypeo ac scuto, unde LXX. eâ reddiderunt Hebraeum מגן quod significat clypeum, scutum, quo homo tempore belli sese circummunit, 3. Reg. 10. v. 17.cap. 14. v. 28.Psal. 34. v. 2. &c. Item צנה quod itidem significat scutum ac clypeum1. Reg. 17. v. 7.Psal. 5. v. 15.Psal. 90. v. 5. &c. quae significatio huic loco congruit. Inde ὁπλέζεσθαιarmis indui, scuto & clypeo muniri, (Eustathius docet, ὁπλίζειν quandoque esse idem quod ἑτοιμάζειν, παρασκευάζεινpraeparare, instruere &c. quae significatio itidem hîc posset habere locum. Sed concinniùs est, usitatam significationem armandi ac muniendi, h. l. retinere.) Sed usurpatur etiam activè pro ὁπλίζειν, quo modo etiam hoc loco accipi potest, induite eandem cogitationem velut spiritualem quandam armaturam. Quae verò est illaἔννοια,quâ Apostolus fideles sese armare ac munire praecipit? Quidam statuunt de patientia in cruce unicè sermonem esse, ut sit sensus.

Cùm Christus in sua passione singularem patientiam demonstraverit, vos etiam qui Christo nomen dedistis, imó per Baptismum ipsi insiti estis, docet eodem modo affectos esse, eadem mente, cogitatione & proposito ad crucem divinitùs immissam patienter ferendam armatos & instructos esse. Sed ex sequentibus apparet, de mortificatione carnis praecipuè hîc sermonem esse, cuius tamen partem esse patientiam in cruce ferenda minimè inficias imus. Sensus igitur hic est. Quia Christus pro vobis carne passus, ideò firmum animi propositum debetis concipere, quod per mortificationem carnis spiritualiter cum ipso mori & crucifigi velitis.Rom. 6. v. 2. & seqq. Sicut ille carne passus est, & mortuus, ita & vos debetis mori peccato, & crucifigere carnem cum suis concupi scentiisGal. 5. vers. 24. haec cogitatio, hic affectus erit vobis instar firmissimi scuti ac munimenti contra peccatum.

ὅτι παθὼν ἐν σαρκί πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας. Vulgata reddidit, quia qui passus est in carne, desiit à peccatis. Sed in Graeco est singularis. Quievit à peccato, quo modo etiam Hieron. lib. 1. contra Iovin. hoc dictum adducit. Syrus paraphrasticè reddidit. Desinit ab omnibus peccatis. Aug. de fid. & operibus cap. 19. desiit peccare. Quid vero est in carne pati & quis est illeπαθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ; Quidam de ipso Christo Apostolum loqui statuunt, de quo paulo ante dixerat, ipsum esse carne passum. Sed hanc expositionem suo loco refellemus. Beda videtur specialiter accipere de Martyre, propter Christi confessionem passo. Quisquis sanctorum, inquit, corpus suum ad Martyrium persecutorum violentiae subdidit, nulli dubium, quin usque ad vitae suae terminum, quantum humanae Naturae possibile est, sese à peccatis abstinuerit. Quid enim de peccati perpetratione, quid de carnalibus desideriis cogitare, quid nisi voluntatem Dei potuit animo versare, qui vel ligno affixus, vel lapidum ictibus circumdatus, vel bestiarum morsibus subactus, vel ignium flammis superpositus, vel scorpionum flagris perfossus, vel alio quolibet poenarum genere affectus, hoc tantummodo desiderare cogebatur, qùando finito certamine coronam vitae perciperet? Talium ergò mentem nos B. Petrus cupit semper imitari, cum proposito Dominicae passionis exemplo nos eadem cogitatione contra nequitiam pravorum, contraque vitiorum oblectamenta praecipit armari, volens intelligi, quod etiam nos in pace Ecclesiae quiescentes, si habitum patientis induimus, facilè adiuvante Domino lapsus vitamus peccatorum omnium, cunctaque desideria divinae voluntaris subiugamus imperiis. Ad hanc Bedae expofitionem accommodari posset versio Syriaca, quae sic habet. Qui moritur in corpore suo. Sed loquitur Apostolus in genere de quovis pio, ut ostendunt textus cirucumstantiae. Quidam igitur de affictionibus corporis, quas Apostolus1. Cor. 7. v. 28.vocat tribulationem carnis, hunc locum accipiunt, ut sit sensus. Qui per passiones & afflictiones Christo crucifixo conformes redduntur, illi tribulationibus tanquam freno quodam coërcentur, ne desideriis corruptae Naturae satis faciant, quia crux estπροφυλακτικὸνpeccati, ad quod caro nostra proclivis. Quidam putant, fideles comparari iis, qui propter scelera sua capitali supplicio affecti sunt, ac proinde scelera illa non ampliùs committere possunt; ideò vero Apostolum hac comparatione uti, quia considerat fideles in Christo, qui propter illorum peccata ignominio sum crucis supplicium pertulit, quod perinde est ac si ipsimet supplicium illud pertulissent. Sed ex consequentibus manifestum est, per τόpati in carne hoc loco intelligi mortificationem carnis, per quam passioni Christi pii conformes redduntur. Praeteritum ergò παθὼν ponitur pro praesenti, ut sit sensus. Qui eo modo conformatur similitudini passionis & mortis Christi, quam in carne sustinuit, ut ipse quoque in carne patiatur i. e. carnem suam mortificet & crucifigat cum pravis affectibus & concupiscentiis, is desinit à peccato, quippe quod ad vitae carnalis actiones pertinet. Qui carnem cum concupiscentiis suis in Christo & cum Christo crucifigit, ille peccare desinit. Est ergò in voce carnis elegans ἀντανακλάσις. In priore enim versiculi parte sumitur substantialiter, pro Naturâ Christi humana, omnis peccati & labis penitus experte: sed in hac posteriore versiculi parte sumitur accidentaliter, pro carnali concupiscentia, pro vitiositate Naturae, quam ex Adamo trahimus, & cuius reliquiae etiam post regenerationem in piis adhuc superstites sunt, quas per Spiritum debent expurgare & mortificare. Maluit autem Apostolus dicere παθῶν ἐν σαρκὶ quàm ἀποθανὼν ut in loco parallelo loquitur Paulus Rom. 6. v. 2. quia voluit nos ad Christum archetypum revocare ac docere, quod per mortificationem nostrae carnis passioni Christi conformes reddamur. Voculam ὅτι quidam accipiunt causaliter vel ratiocinativè, ut sit ratio exhortationis à definitione & effectu mortificationis. Sed rectiùs accipitur expositivè, exponit enim Apostolus illam cogitationem, quâ nos vult armari, videlicet quod nobis utpote Christi membris conveniat in Christo & cum Christo spiritualiter mori, quod vetus noster homo cum ipso debeat crucifigi, ut sic regnum peccati in nobis aboleatur; quòd propterea, quia sumus Christo commortui & crucifixi, nihil ampliùs cum, peccato nobis debeat esse negotii, ut in nobis adhuc dominetur & regnet.

## 4:1-5 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. In what sense is Christ said to have suffered in the flesh? 1. Some wish the sense to be that, that Christ in the days of his flesh Heb. 5. v. 7. i.e., while he lived in this mortal life, suffered, but that the soul separated from the body suffered nothing, which explanation is consistent with the analogy of faith. 2. Some wish, that the Apostle uses the name of flesh for this reason, because most of the pains of Christ, such as blows, scourges, spittle, thorns, nails, etc., were in the flesh. 3. Some judge, that regard is had to this, that the sensible cause of the passion is from the flesh, although the sensation happens by the work of the soul. 4. It is answered most simply, that by the name of flesh is understood synecdochically the whole humanity, a phrase used in the Scriptures John 1. v. 14. 1. Tim. 3. v. 16.

Q. 2. Why does the Apostle use the word ὁπλίσασθε; Resp. 1. to intimate, that the whole life of man, especially of a Christian, is a warfare, Job 14. v. 1. and that a pious man ought to stand in a perpetual battle line against the Devil, the world, and the flesh. 2. To insinuate, that Christ by his passion and death, as if with a certain most strong armor, fought against the Prince of this world, and brought back a glorious triumph from him, whence the pious ancients compare the cross of Christ to a sword, by which the head of the infernal dragon was crushed, Rev. 5. v. 6. Christ then shows seven horns, when he appears as if slain, because he exerted his power and strength especially in his passion and cross. Leo serm. 10. de past. Those nails, which pierced the hands and feet of the Lord, fixed the Devil with perpetual wounds and the punishment of the holy members was the killing of the hostile powers. 3. To teach, that faith in Christ and a devoted meditation on the passion of Christ is our spiritual panoply, by which we can fortify ourselves against all temptations and persecutions. 1. Cor. 2. v. 2. I judged myself to know nothing except Christ crucified. Eph. 6. v. 16. taking above all the shield of faith. Heb. 12. v. 3. Consider him who endured such contradiction against himself, lest you be wearied, fainting in your minds. 4. To show that the pious with a strong and as it were hardened mind ought to tolerate adverse things patiently and mortify the flesh, so that they may seem as if armed for the enduring of afflictions and the mortification of the flesh. 5. That he may teach that the pious ought to be prepared to receive any darts of a more sinister fortune and to fight against the concupiscences of the flesh, just as a soldier fortified with his arms is prepared for battle. Hugo notes that by the word arming it is signified that the thought of the passion is not undertaken to delight the mind, but to impugn vices, and because it is not granted to all to suffer, that we may at least be prepared.

Q. 3. What is understood by the name of Sin, when the Apostle says: He who has suffered in the flesh, has ceased from sin? Resp. To cease from sin is the same for Peter as it is for Paul to die to sin Rom. 6. v. 2., which he explains thus v. 6.: That we should no longer serve sin. He speaks, therefore, of the dominion of sin, that the reborn ought not to permit the dominion of depraved concupiscences still remaining in the flesh, but to mortify it, which is what Paul Gal. 5. v. 24. calls to crucify the flesh with its vices and concupiscences. Some establish that by the name of sin placed absolutely, mortal sins committed against conscience are understood. But the matter returns to the same thing, for he who dies to sin and mortifies the concupiscences of the flesh, he abstains from sins against conscience.

Q. 4. Whether this Apostolic passage is parallel to the Pauline passage Rom. 6. v. 7. He who is dead, is justified from sin? Resp. 1. Some explain the Pauline passage concerning natural death, in which there is a plenary liberation of man from sins and from every other servitude. For in death the soul is separated from the body, and thus the dead cease from the actions of this life and consequently from sinning. 2. Some accept it concerning civil death, thinking that the Apostle alluded to the sentences of capital judgments, by which those condemned to death do not sin further. 3. Most simply, according to the series of the context, it is accepted concerning Spiritual death. He who is dead, viz. to sin v. 2. and 11. who has been buried together with Christ through Baptism into death v. 4. who has been made σύμφυτος made in the likeness of his death v. 5. whose flesh or old man has been crucified together with Christ v. 6. who has spiritually died with Christ v. 8. this one is justified from sin, i.e., he is liberated and absolved from sin, not only by reason of guilt, but also by reason of dominion, so that he is no longer subject to the servitude of sin. Basilius in orat. de Bapt. Christi tom. 1. p. 460. Justified from sin i.e. he is absolved, he is liberated, he is cleansed from every sin, not only as to works and words, but as to the very of thoughts is committed to the affections. Thus, therefore, the Petrine passage is clearly parallel to this Pauline passage. For what Paul says, who has died, namely to sin, Peter expresses thus: who has suffered in the flesh, namely with Christ who suffered in the flesh. What Paul says, he has been justified from sin, that Peter expresses thus: he has ceased from sin.

Q. 5. What is it to live for the desires of men? Resp. To live for the desires of men signifies to conform oneself in life to the desires or will of carnal men, to set before oneself the desires of carnal men as the norm of life and actions, to be in a certain way driven and led in life by the desires of men, in order to establish one's life according to their example. For that by the word ἀνθρώπων placed absolutely, carnal men not yet regenerated by the Holy Spirit are to be understood, is clear: 1. From the opposition, because the will of God is opposed to those desires of men, to which the will of regenerated men, as such, is conformed. 2. From the subject exposition in the following verse: the time past is sufficient to have wrought the will of the Gentiles. 3. From the collation of parallel passages. Matt. 16. ver. 23.1. Cor. 3. v. 3.Coloss. 2. v. 8.Tit. 1. v. 14. Jerome, in book 1 against Jovinian, expressing the sense, rendered it: to live in the desires of men.

Q. 6. How does the Apostle draw an argument for exhortation from the former state of life? Resp. 1. Because renewal is joined to the regeneration of the pious by an indissoluble bond and requires a new life and new morals. Therefore, those who still follow the former manner of living show by that very fact that they are not yet renewed and consequently not regenerated. 2. It is fair that for that singular divine grace, which drew them from the mire of sins, they should show themselves grateful, not only in words, but also in life and deeds themselves. 3. Because they had consecrated the greater and better part of their life to the Devil through crimes in paganism, it was altogether fair that they should consecrate the remaining part of it to God.

Q. 7. Whether he addresses those converted from paganism, or indeed from Judaism? Some gather from this passage that Peter writes these things to those converted from the Jews, whom he reproaches because they had accommodated themselves to the will and morals of the Gentiles, from whom God had separated them. But it is more correctly gathered from this passage that the Apostle writes these things chiefly to those converted from the Gentiles, as is gathered from the parallel passage Eph. 4. v. 17. & following. Because almost all Gentiles before their conversion to Christ followed the manner of living customary to the Gentiles, to which we do not deny that some of the Jews conformed themselves before their conversion to Christ: meanwhile, some of them, by the example of Paul while still established in Pharisaism, pursued an external honesty of life according to the norm of the divine law. Act. 26. v. 5.Phil. 3. v. 6.

Q. 8. Why does the Apostle enumerate these vices specifically? Resp. Nefarious lusts reigned among the Gentiles, Rom. 1. v. 24. & 26.Eph. 4. v. 19. which were not judged to be sins, just as that man says in the Comedian. It is no disgrace for a young man to fornicate. The Apostle lashes those with the name ἀσελγείων καὶ ἐπιθυμίων.. But because intemperance of food and drink, & luxurious banquets provide fuel for lusts, therefore he joins to them οὶνοφλυγίας, κώμους & πότους.. Finally, because idolatry is also accustomed to arise from luxury, and spiritual fornication is usually joined with bodily [fornication] for the most part, Exod. 32. v. 6.1. Corinth. 10. v. 7. therefore the Apostle joins idolatries with the aforementioned vices, just as Paul also Rom. 1. v. 24. & 25. had joined the same. It could be referred here that the Gentiles, among other gods, also worshipped Victua, who might procure food, and Potua, who might procure drink, as witnessed by Arnobius in book 3 against the Gentiles. Educus, or Edulina, Edusa, Edua, who might minister food; and Potina or Potica and Potua, who might minister drink, as witnessed by Aug. in book 4 of the City of God, chapter 11, and book 6, chapter 9, about whom Ludov. Vives [writes] in his commentary on that place.

Q. 9. What kind of admiration does the Apostle understand? Bede takes that admiration in a good sense, for thus he comments in this place. Because, he says, you have crucified your flesh with its vices and concupiscences, it happens indeed that even if they blaspheme you because of their own perfidy, as being separated from their company, they nevertheless see in your conversation always the works of justice and piety, which they deservedly admire, and for which they rightly praise the faith, and venerate the Christian [faith]. But it is manifest from the word ξενίζονται & the annexed participle βλασφημοῦντες, that admiration is taken here in a bad sense.

Q. 10. Who is ὁ ἑτοίμως ἔχων κρῖναι; Some take it concerning God, with this name οὐσιωδῶς accepted, just as it applies equally to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For it is said of God that He is about to judge His peopleDeut. 32. v. 36.that He has prepared His throne for judgmentPs. 9. v. 8.that He is about to come to judge the earthPs. 82. v. 8.Ps. 98. v. 9. etc. But some [take it] concerning Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgmentJohn 5. v. 22.and has given him power to execute judgment, because he is the Son of manv. 27.who is ordained judge of the living and the deadActs 10. v. 42. etc. But these expositions are not contrary, but subordinate, as is evident from the Apostolic passage Acts 17. v. 31.GOD has appointed a day, in which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he has ordained. The power of executing judgment belongs to all three persons of the Deity κατ᾿ αὐτοκρατορίαν & κατ᾿ εὐδοκίαν on account of ὁμοουσίαν. For just as there is one and equal essence of the three persons of the divinity, so also there is one and the same power; meanwhile, however, κατ᾿ οἰκονομίαν is attributed peculiarly in the Scriptures to Christ θεανθρώπῳ divinely ordained judge of the dead and the living. For he will visibly and immediately administer this judgment in the assumed human Nature. Judgment is attributed to the whole Trinity, as regards judicial power, dominion, authority, and decree. It is assigned peculiarly to the Son as regards the visible and external exercise.

Q. 11. Who are to be understood by the name of the living and the dead who are to be judged? Isidore, book 1, Epistle 222, thinks it can be explained in a triple way, that Christ is called the judge of the dead and the living. 1. That it will be that soul and body come into judgment together, and neither be separated from the other, but just as they had a common union in this life, so they may also undergo the future judgment. 2. The living, that is, those who have followed a life eternal and pleasing to GOD, are to be distinguished from the dead, that is, those who, dead in sins, have buried the talent given to them in sloth just as in a sepulcher, and that immortal rewards are to be paid to the former, but punishments to the latter. 3. That those are to be judged who will have been left alive, as well as those who before them exchanged life with death. John Huss explains it thus. The living in grace to blessedness, the dead in guilt to damnation. Benedictus Arias Montanus interprets the living as those still in that flesh of Adam, the dead in Christ. Some take the living of those who now live and are to live, the dead of those who have long since died, but will then be resurrected into life. Most simply, by the living are understood those whom the coming judge will find alive; by the dead, those who had already been dead before, whom he will recall from the sepulchers into life, and will judge together with the living, and thus all men, Acts 10. v. 42.2. Tim. 4. v. 1. They are called dead by reason of the term from which, i.e., those who had been dead, but then those who have been resurrected will stand by. Jerome in chapter 26 of Matthew Sometimes in Scripture, with the thing changed, the original name remains.

Q. 12. Why does he make mention of the dead? Resp. 1. so that he may show that Christ will be the universal judge of all men whatsoever, because all men are distributed into these two classes. In the same sense it is said that God will judge the pious and the impious, the just and the unjust, the faithful and the unbelievers Eccl. 3. v. 17.Wis. 5. v. 1. the great and the small. Rev. 20. v. 12. 2. so that we may not think that we suffer any loss if, when we are dying, our slanderers and persecutors remain as survivors, because they will not on that account escape the hand of GOD the judge.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Christ is said to have suffered in the flesh v. 1. But the soul of Christ also laboredIsa. 53. v. 11.and he himself testifies that his soul is sorrowful even unto death.Matt. 26. v. 38. Resp. By the name of flesh, the whole humanity of Christ is understood synecdochically, and thus not only the sensitive soul, but also the rational one. For Christ not only endured the most grievous torments in his most holy body and thus in all its members, but also in his most holy soul he felt the wrath of GOD owed to the sins of the whole human race.

2. Since Christ has suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought, that you also may suffer in the flesh v. 1. But in Christ there was and is nothing vicious; how therefore does he make us conformable to Christ, in that we suffer in the flesh? Resp. The word flesh is taken in one way when it is used of Christ, namely, of the very substance of the flesh, and that pure and clean; it is taken in another way when it is used of us, namely, of the vicious qualities of corrupt Nature; meanwhile, the conformity is in suffering and death, insofar as through the spiritual mortification of the flesh we are spiritually conformed to the passion and death of ChristRom. 6. v. 2.

3. The passion of Christ is proposed in this place as an exemplary cause of spiritual mortification. But the passion and death of Christ is not only an example of our mortification, but also its cause, for it is the power of the death of Christ that we should die to sin, and the Spirit of Christ makes it so that his death is effective for mortifying the flesh in us. Resp. The inclusion of one is not the exclusion of the other. When Christ is proposed to us as an example, the merit and the gift are not also denied in a different respect.

4. He who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin. v. 1. But in this life we are not entirely immune and free from every sin. Resp. He is not speaking of the sense and consent of sin; nor of the vice of the flesh adhering to the reborn, but of its dominion Roman. 6. v. 12. Consider yourselves to be dead to sin v. 12. Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its lusts. August. tract. 61. in Ioh. He does not say, let it not be, but let it not reign. For as long as you live, it is necessary for sin to be in your members, at least let its kingdom be taken away, and let not that be done, which it commands.

5. One must not live for the desires of men v. 2. But Paul says of himself 1. Corinth. 10. v. 33. I please all men in all things. Resp. Peter speaks of those desires of men which are contrary to the divine will, Paul of those which are conformable to the divine law, whence he immediately adds, not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved. And Rom. 15. v. 2. he hands down this rule. Let each one of you please his neighbor for good unto edification. Concerning the former kind of human desires the same Apostle says Galat. 1. v. 10. If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ 1. Thessal. 2. v. 4. Not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts. We ought to please all, not by serving their vicious affections, nor by conforming ourselves to their impious customs, but by sympathizing with their infirmities, and promoting their salvation. Augustine in chapter 1 to the Galatians, tom. 4, near the end. He who pleases men, not seeking his own glory from them; but God's, so that they may be saved, no longer pleases men, but God, or certainly when he pleases both God and men at the same time, he does not in any way please men. For it is one thing to please men, another to please both God and men. Likewise, he who pleases men on account of the truth, it is not he himself who pleases them, but the truth.

6. It is enough to have spent the past time of life in fulfilling the will of the Gentiles. v. 3. But no time at all should have been given to fulfilling the will of the Gentiles, and whatever is given to it is not enough; but too much. Resp. The Apostle by no means intends this, that we ought to be filled even to satiety by fulfilling the will of the Gentiles i. e. by committing sins, but he mitigates the bitterness of the reproach, and wishes the memory of the past life to be a goad for us to spend the remaining time of life in piety and honesty according to the admonition of Christ Iohan. 5. vers. 14. Behold you have been made whole, sin no more. chapter 8.

v. 11.Go and sin no more. Lyranus in this place: By that which he says, it is enough, an approval of the past life is not to be understood, but rather a reprobation, so that the sense may be: It ought to suffice for the penitent that in the past time he lived carnally.

7. It is enough for the past time of life to have wrought the will of the Gentiles. But a man immersed in sins, especially in lusts, never says, it is enough.Prov. 30. v. 16. John Huss proposes this ἐναντιοφανείαν in his commentary on this place, writing thus: On the contrary, he says, the pleasure of the flesh never says, it is enough, according to that Prov. 30. There are three things that are never satisfied, and a fourth which never says, it is enough. The grave, the barren womb, and the earth that is not satisfied with water; and the fire never says, it is enough. Where by the grave, pride; by the earth, avarice; by the barren womb, luxury; by the fire, carnal concupiscence are designated. For those are never satisfied, and if one hungers in one, he thirsts in another, which is included in carnal concupiscence. Therefore it seems that the past time is not enough to have wrought the will of the Gentiles. He answers, however, in this way: Although the avaricious as such (i.e., as such) and the luxurious as such, never say, it is enough, yet a man, when he has known the justice of God, will say: that time is enough for me, so that I may no longer live thus. Peter speaks therefore of the judgment of a man reborn and converted, not of the judgment of a man still immersed in sins.

8. The past time is enough for you. But not all those to whom the Apostle writes had committed those graver sins.1. Cor. 6. v. 11. ταῦτα τίνες ἦτι. Resp. 1. There is in this locution a Synecdoche used in the Scriptures, by which the denomination is made from the greater part, and those things which apply to most are predicated of the whole group. 2. By Nature all were prone to such vices, and the seed of those sins lies hidden in all, even if it does not bring forth equal fruits in all. 3. Those who were preserved from those graver crimes should acknowledge themselves to be bound to give greater thanks to GOD, August. lib. 2. Confess. cap. 7. I attribute it to your grace and to your mercy, that you have melted my sins like ice, I attribute to your grace whatever evils I did not do. For what could I not have done, who even loved a gratuitous crime?

9. Peter says that those to whom he writes, before their conversion to Christ, had walked in abominable idolatries verse 3. But this Epistle was written primarily to the Jews placed in the dispersion, who from idolatry they abhorred most gravely 1. Epist. 1. v. 1. Resp. 1. Calvin establishes that by idolatries he understands superstitions, to which the Jews were even most addicted. 2. Some respond, the Jews, intermixed with the Gentiles, when they were exiles and needy, had mingled themselves in the banquets of the Gentiles, to which they were invited, in which sacrificial meats were set before them, and perhaps even had taken part in their sacred rites, which, since Paul teaches that they are to be imputed to idolatry 1. Cor. 10. v. 20. therefore Peter taxes them by the name of idolatries. 3. It is answered most simply that this Epistle was written to a Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles, and therefore certain things in it are so arranged that some pertain especially to the Jews, while others pertain especially to the Gentiles, in which latter class this taxation of idolatries also falls. 4. Nor can it be denied that in the later times of the Israelite Church, especially after the destruction of Jerusalem and the dispersion of the Jews among the Gentiles, they began to be contaminated by the idolatry of the Gentiles.

10. Christ will judge the living i. e. those whom He will find living when He comes to judgment, and the dead, that is, those who were dead before His coming to judgment. But those whom Christ, coming to judgment, will find living, will be changed, which change will be analogous to death. 1. Cor. 15. v. 51. Resp. 1. They are called living by reason of the term from which, when Christ will come to judgment, then they will be living, and soon in a moment they will be changed. 2. That change will indeed be analogous to death, yet it will not be death, hence it is opposed to death in the Apostolic saying. We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed. For in that change the soul will not depart from the dwelling of the body, but the soul and body will be clothed with the robe of immortality and glory, having put off the tunic of flesh. v. 53. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, etc.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. There are two distinct Natures in Christ; the divine, which is entirely ἀπαθὴς; and the human, in which and according to which He sustained passion and death. For lest anyone should introduce a confusion of Natures and properties, the Apostle used the particle διοριστοκῇ or a distinctive one, Christ suffered σαρκὶ. This is to be opposed to Eutyches, who confuses the Natures and their properties in Christ. Bede on this passage: It is to be noted that the Apostle, speaking distinctly, says, Christ therefore having suffered in the flesh. Because as Ambrose says, His flesh suffered, the divinity however was free from death, He granted His body to the passion by the law of human Nature. But can divinity truly die, when the soul cannot?Math. 10.They cannot kill the soul. If therefore the soul cannot be killed, how can divinity? If he knew that the divinity of Christ had been passible, it would have sufficed for him to say, Christ therefore having suffered, nor would he have added, in the flesh. But because he knew that in one and the same Christ there was both a passible Nature before death and an impassible divine substance remaining forever. Fulgentius lib. 3. ad Thrasim. c. 9. Therefore he confesses that Christ suffered in the flesh, whose divinity he knew to remain altogether impassible.

2. As in Christ the Nature διττοτης: so also the person ἑνότης must be asserted. For one and the same Christ is He who suffered in the flesh, and remained impassible in divinity. Athanasius in his sermon on the incarnation teaches, that the same one ought to be said to be that which suffered, and that which did not suffer. For it is not that there is another besides the Word of God Himself, who received passion and death, but that the same impassible and incorporeal One sustained the generation of the flesh and performed all those things, so that He might have what He could offer for us. Gelasius lib. de duab. Natur.
