Peter said that Christ suffered in the flesh, not in the Deity, although the Deity Itself makes everything that the flesh has suffered its own, just as the Son of man also has as His own everything that is of God. And under one person, one and the same is deservedly said to suffer whatever the God-man suffers, not by infirmity and passible condition, but by dignity making the injury of the passion His own; suffering by union but sympathizing without passibility, just as one and the same One works the virtues, whatever the Man-God works. This must be opposed to Nestorius, who tears apart the unity of the person in Christ.

3. The name of Christ is the name of a person. Χριστὸς τὸ συναμφότερον νοεῖ ται. Athanas. orat. 5. contra Arian. p. 321. Damasc. lib. 3. orth. sid. cap. 3. τό χριστὸς ὁνομα ὑποστασεως λεγομεν, οὐ μονοτρόπως μέν, ἀλλὰ τῶν δύο φυσεων ὑπαρχον σημαιτικὸν, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ἒχρισεν, χρίων μὲνώς θεὸς, ὅς ἐχρισὲ τὸ σῶμα τῆ θεότιτι αὐτοῦ, χριόμειος δὲ ώς ἄνθρωπος, αὐτὸς γαρ ἐστι τοῦ το κακεῖνο. Because therefore Christ is said to have suffered, from that it is rightly inferred that God also is rightly said to have suffered. For although the divine Nature does not suffer in itself, nor die: yet the Son of God Himself is said to suffer and die, as truly and really as He was truly made a participant of the flesh, in which He sustained passion and death. Hebr. 2. vers. 14. Hence the author of life is said to have been killed Acts 3.

v. 15.God is said to have acquired the Church with his own blood.c. 20. v. 21.we are said to be reconciled to God through the death of his Son.Rom. 5. vers. 10.The Lord of glory is said to have been crucified.1. Cor. 2. v. 8. Cyril in Apology from Athanasius. Just as we say the body is the Lord's own, so also the passions of the body are said to be his own, even if they do not happen according to his divinity, otherwise the body would be of one, and the passions would be said to be of another, but if the flesh of the Word is flesh, it is necessary that the passions of the flesh be called those of him whose flesh it also is. Leo. Epistle 10 to Flavian. We say the Son of God suffered and died, not in the property of the divine Nature, but in the infirmity of the assumed human Nature. Vigilius book against Eutyches. Although God did not suffer in the property of the Nature (divine) yet he suffered in the union of the person (in the human Nature, which he assumed into the unity of the person, so that for that reason the passion is rightly attributed to God himself.) This must be opposed to the Calvinists, who resolve the Petrine proposition, Christ suffered in the flesh, thus. Only the human Nature in Christ suffered. Anhald. Apol. p. 246. The human Nature of Christ alone died, not the Deity, not the whole person. Herborn. in rudim. book 2. p. 100. Christ the man died for us, that is, that human Nature of Christ alone, which is considered not by itself in a separate hypostasis, but in that one person of Christ, died. Danaeus against Chemn. P. 24. And yet those distinct particles ἐν, κατὰ etc. are not χωριστικαὶ καὶ διαμεριστικαὶ, by the use of which Natures are separated and divided, so that the human is restricted only to humanity and the divine only to divinity, so that the Natures are παντάπασι ἀκοινώνητοι πρός ἑαυτὰς, as Samosatenus feigned, but they are διακριτικαὶ of Natures and natural properties; they are διοριστικαὶ, for they show according to which Nature such things are predicated of the person; and they are ἐνδεικτικαὶ τοῦ καθ᾿ αὐτὸ ἀιτίου, showing the primary and per se cause, for which reason human affections are attributed to God and divine actions to man.

4. The passion of Christ is not only an example, but also a merit and ἀντίλυτρον. for Christ is said to have suffered for us. This must be opposed to the Photinians, who deny the satisfaction of Christ.

5. The Apostle opposes the desires of men and the will of God, by that very fact showing that the whole Nature of man is thoroughly corrupted and depraved through sin, and that its desires, affections, motions, longings etc. are repugnant to the divine will. Estius in h. l.

Man without God is entirely carnal, and executes not the will of God, but of the flesh. Lorinus in this place: Man taken simply is taken in the worse part and signifies the carnal, whence to walk according to man and to be carnal is the same. 1 Cor. 3 v. 3 to be born also of bloods and what is the same of the will of the flesh and of man, and to be born of God are opposed John 1 v. 13 as well as the commandments of God and of men, or traditions and doctrines Matt. 15 vers. 9 Coloss. 2 v. 8 Tit. 1 v. 14 and to savor the things that are of God, and the things that are of men Matt. 16 v. 23 It is false, therefore, what the Scholastics teach, that man can from pure naturals love God above all things, that naturals have remained intact in man after the fall, that man can merit the infusion of grace from congruity, that there are still given some powers of free will in conversion etc. which opinions the Papists have long since made their own.

6. The Apostle gravely warns the reborn, that they should not suffer themselves to be entangled again in the mire of their former sins, from which they have emerged, nor spend the time of life that still remains on the desires of men. Certainly, therefore, the reborn can recede from the study and race of piety, loosen the reins to the concupiscences of the flesh, and thus fall away from faith, the grace of God, the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and eternal salvation. For if this were ἐκ τῷν ἀδυνάτων, to what end would there be need for such Apostolic admonitions? This must be opposed to the Anabaptists and Calvinists who deny that the truly reborn can again fall away from faith and the grace of God. Aug. Cons. art. 12.

7. The Gentiles of old used to wonder and be offended, seeing that those converted to CHRIST did not run with them into the same confusion of luxury. Indeed, they were offended by the fewness of the Christians, who were following a new, as they called it, religion and a peculiar kind of life, and they urged the concurrence, and thus the multitude of men, still embracing Gentile rites and Gentile customs. In the same way, even today, the Papists are offended by the fewness of those who embrace the Evangelical doctrine, which they call new, and do not run together with them to the Mass rites, to the adoration of images, to the kissing of the Pope's feet, to the filth of forced celibacy, etc.

8. Christ will judge the living and the dead, and thus all men. It is false, therefore, what the Papists establish, that some of the faithful, namely those who have vowed voluntary poverty, are not to be judged, but when you will be judges with Christ. Salmero vol. 4. tract. 25. q. 563. Costerus in postill. Sunday 2. Adv. p. 19. and that infidels outside the Church, who lacked faith, are not to be judged by a judgment of discussion. Thomas in Supplement q. 89. art. 7. & others from the Scholastics. 4. sent. dist. 47. whom Peter Martyr followed from the Calvinists, in explanation of the Apostles' Creed class. 2. Theological Topics cap. 17. p. 432. writes thus. I maintain that infidels have no need of examination, as those who on account of their infidelity are already condemned. Compare the article on the Final Judgment §. 50.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Cornelius à Lapide on v. 1. comments thus. Christ suffered only in this life, while he was in mortal flesh, but not after death, when he descended to the underworld, as Calvin blasphemes, saying that Christ endured the punishments of the damned, so that he might take our damnation upon himself and pay for it. Response 1. It is not a peculiar and proper opinion of Calvin that Christ felt the pains of hell, but we maintain the same thing with him. 2. And we prove this from the fact that Christ complains that he was forsaken by God and not heard Psalm 22. v. 2.5. 6. 7.Matthew 27. v. 46. that he is said to have been made a curse for us, that he might deliver us from the curse of the law,Galatians 3. v. 13. that he truly took our sins upon himself, with which, not yet expiated, the wrath and judgment of God are joined in an inseparable bond Isaiah 53. v. 6.8.10. that deaths in the plural number are attributed to Christ Isaiah 53. v. 9. that in the very onset of his passion, being placed in ἀγωνὶᾳ he began to ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι, ἀδημονεῖν καὶ λυπεῖσθαι, so that he said, his soul was περίλυπον even unto death, and he emitted a bloody sweat dripping drop by drop to the groundMatthew 26. v. 37. 38. &c. 3. But he did not feel these pains after death, but before death in the garden of olives, therefore the contrary cannot be proven from this passage of Peter. 4. Nor is his real descent into the underworld, which followed after death, removed or denied by this metaphorical descent of Christ into the underworld.

2. Lorinus on v. 1. annotates thus. To suffer in the flesh, or by the flesh, signifies that Christ suffered only while he lived in this mortal life, but nothing then either of his divinity, or of his soul, when it was separated from the body; although while he lived, the higher part of his soul also had its own pains, yet with the beatific vision safe, in which even the higher part was joined, there followed, although it did not overflow into the lower part, delight. In which matter Melchior Cano, denying that regarding delight book 12. Topics

chap. 13. I do not approve, namely, that it was hindered at least on the cross, while saving the true definition of beatitude. Henry judges that opinion of Canus quodlibet. 8. q. 7. to be contrary to the faith: Suarez. part. 3. tom. 1. Disp. 38. d. 3. false and rash and against all Theologians. Resp. 1. The opinion of Canus manifestly supports ours, that Christ truly endured infernal pains in his passion. Just as, he says, throughout his whole life the Lord as it were suppressed the glory of his soul, lest it should flow into the body: so at least on the cross he restrained the joy which by its own Nature would proceed from the clear knowledge of GOD. I confess that joy is necessarily born in the will from GOD being seen, not otherwise than light from the Sun, heat from fire. But the Sun sometimes withdrew its rays and fire was also contained so that it might not heat. Wherefore it ought to seem strange to no one, if in the redemption of men, to be fulfilled through the pains of one man, all pleasure was repressed, which the reason of Nature demonstrates would otherwise proceed from the vision of GOD. And afterwards. Christ not only saw, but also enjoyed, although abandoned by GOD, he did not rejoice, being utterly destitute of all consolation. But to feel the greatest sadness, not only in the sensitive appetite, but also in the rational or will, without any consolation and joy, is nothing other than to endure truly infernal pains. 2. Nor is this the sole and private opinion of Canus, but many of the Papists have thought so. Bartholomaeus Medina on Thom. p. 3. q. 46. art. 6. There is a kind of punishment, which the damned suffer in hell, who lack all consolation. Our Redeemer deigned to endure something similar to this, who renounced all consolation and remedy of comfort from himself in his passion. Ludovicus à Ponte on chap. 8. Cant. p. 537. Christ for love of you endured not only death, but most bitter pains of the cross like unto hell. Maldonatus on chap. 26. Matth. By a certain dispensation it came about, that while Christ was blessed, he admitted sadness even into the higher part of the soul. For just as he could restrain his beatitude, lest it should flow down into the body, so that he could suffer: so he could suppress it and in a certain way hide it, so that for a time it would yield to sadness, which was to be one part of his passion. Compare Sanctius on chap. 2. Acts. on the words, Having loosed the pains of hell, and Salmeron tract. 13. on Acts. 3. When Peter says absolutely, that Christ suffered, he includes all tortures, pains, anguishes etc. which Christ endured not only in his body, but also in his most holy soul, and not only in the lower, but also in the higher part of the soul, as they say, or faculty. Therefore, by the name of passion he does not exclude infernal pains, but includes them.

3. Lorinus and Cornelius à Lapide apply the words of the Apostle, arm yourselves with the same thought, to the Sacrament of Confirmation. The sacrament of confirmation, says Lorinus, by which we are made soldiers of Christ, is called a seal, especially from the signing of the cross on the forehead, by Pope Cornelius in Euseb. lib. 6. Hist. cap. 35. and Ambrose lib. 3. de Sacrament. cap. 2. By the symbol of this thing, says Cornelius à Lapide, we are signed by the Bishop on the forehead in the Sacrament of Confirmation, and by it we are as it were enlisted and strengthened as soldiers and champions of Christ to contend for the faith of Christ even unto death and Martyrdom. Resp. 1. Neither Peter in this place, nor the Apostles anywhere in Scripture, hand down anything concerning the Sacrament of Confirmation. 2. The sign of the cross was used by the ancients in the very administration of Baptism, not for the sake of any spiritual efficacy, but for the sake of pious admonition and signification. Betuleius in his notes to Lactant, lib. 4. div. Instit. cap. 27. The ancients had the sign of the cross as a badge and Symbol, by which they wished to testify to the profession of the crucified Christ among the gentiles and the Jews. 3. The Papists in the administration of this Sacrament form the figure of the cross on the forehead only with oil mixed with balsam. But Cornelius à Lapide himself admits that formerly other members of the body were also anointed with chrism. The ancients, he says, in Confirmation did not only anoint and sign with the cross the forehead, in which modesty resides, for the sake of fearlessly professing the faith and the cross, but also other members. The Greeks still observe this, who anoint the forehead, eyes, and back in the form of a Cross. The Ethiopians, however, as their Ritual or order of Baptism has it, anoint not only the eyes, forehead, and back in the form of a cross, but also the nostrils, lips, chest, stomach, shins, knees, and feet, so that they may signify (note well, so that they may signify, therefore this is done only for the sake of signification) that all members, all senses, and all actions of a Christian must be sealed. 4. The ancients say that the grace of the Holy Spirit given in Baptism and faith in Christ crucified is that seal by which we are strengthened for spiritual combat. Ambros. l. 4. de Spiritu S. c. 6. We are signed with the Spirit, so that we may be able to hold His splendor and image and grace, which is indeed a spiritual seal.

4. Erasmus refers the words of the Apostle ὁ παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ to Christ, for he renders it, who suffered. Salmero brings forward the same exposition, and he by no means rejects it. The third, he says, doubt we resolve by a double reason. First indeed, that we may understand it of Christ, who did not cease from any of His own sins, but from ours, which nevertheless in His body upon the tree he carried to be expiated, not wishing to take them upon himself further, so that we die again, for whom it was enough to die once for all sins. It follows, but by the will of God, that he lives the remaining time in the flesh. For Christ, raised in new flesh, living in this world for forty days, was present with us. And it signifies the time of our life from Baptism even unto death, teaching the spiritual life which we ought to live. He adds, however. Another open and suitable sense, by which this argument is more easily solved, is that we refer it to the man grafted into Christ and baptized, etc. Lorinus comments on this place thus. The whole speech has an ambiguity, which the Carthusian saw, so that it can be understood either of Christ or of the imitation of Christ. But the first way, which pleases Titelmann and Salmeron, whom the same rightly postpones, is handed down everywhere by the others, not only by expositors, but also by Jerome in book 1 against Jovinian and Augustine in the book on faith and works chapter 10, homily 20 from the fifty homilies, and in the Syriac edition, Christ did not cease from sins, as if he ever sinned, but because he always abstained, or rather because he ceased to be sin for us2. Cor. 5. v. 21.and to be called, that is a bloody sacrifice for sin, and because he died, he died to sin onceRom. 6. v. 10. Socinus likewise joins both expositions. For thus he writes in Epistle 3 to Schmalz, p. 518. Insofar as those words, he suffered in the flesh, are referred to Christ, they signify his death and the passion of the cross, so that the sense is that he was freed through the passion of the cross from those things which are accustomed to be the punishments of sins. But insofar as it is referred to us, it signifies that we cease from sinning through the killing or rejection of carnal desires. I reply 1. In the Greek it is the perfect παθὼν therefore it is rendered less correctly as he was suffering. 2. Christ did not cease from sins, because he never began to sin. If they except, that Christ ceased from sins, which he had taken upon himself to be expiated. I reply that this is a very harsh catachresis. He is properly said to cease from sin who, having sinned until now, sins no more. If they except, that Christ is said to have ceased from sins, who is freed from the punishments of sins, I reply that this also is forced, for one must not pass from the propriety of the letter to a metonymy unless necessity itself compels us. If they except that Christ is said to have ceased from sin, because he abolished sin, I reply: If there were the force of abolishing in the word πέπαυται, it would be constructed with the accusative. For thus the Greeks speak, πάυω τὴν δυστυχὶαν I take away unhappiness; πάυω βοηθείαν I take away help; πάυω νόσον, I take away disease. But when is constructed with the genitive, then it properly signifies to cease, as πάυομαι τῆς μαχῆς, I withdraw myself from the fight; πάυομαι τῆς ἀρχῆς I lay down the Magistracy; πάυομαι ἁμαρτίας I cease from sin, which properly befits a sinner. 4. Nor can it be attributed to Christ sufficiently conveniently, what follows v. 2. that he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh to the desires of men, but to the will of God. For Christ never lived for the desires of men, nor did he live in the flesh after he once died to sin, but through his resurrection he entered into a spiritual and heavenly life; the days of his flesh were finished in death itself. Hebr. 5. v. 7. 2. Cor. 5. v. 16.

5. Salmero on v. 1. comments thus. It was enough for Christ to die once for all sins, because as Paul said Hebr. 10. If we sin willfully after having received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, namely, to purge away all such sins, as he does in Baptism, but the new sinner himself satisfies God through penance, if he wishes to reconcile himself to Him. For he who has returned into grace can make satisfaction for a sin committed. Resp. 1. Nowhere in the whole Scripture does this distinction occur, that Christ made satisfaction for our sins committed before Baptism; but that we ourselves must make satisfaction for sins committed after Baptism through penance, but Scripture always speaks generally. Ioh. 1. v. 29. Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Ioh. 1. v. 7. The blood of Jesus Christ the Son of GOD cleanses us from all sins. cap. 2. v. 2. He is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world. Bellarmine is entirely correct in lib. 3. de poenit. cap. 4. §. Altera solutio. Scripture everywhere, when it speaks absolutely about sins, is accustomed to and ought to be understood as referring to all sins; and if it were permitted to explain it as referring to some, not all, most absurd opinions would be found in the divine writings. We subsume. When Scripture speaks about the satisfaction provided by Christ for our sins, it speaks indefinitely and absolutely, as is evident, Esai. 53. v. 5. 1. Petr. 2. v. 24. etc. Therefore it must be accepted concerning all sins. 2. Sin is an infinite evil, because it is committed against an infinite good. Therefore, for satisfaction for sin, an infinite power, efficacy, and dignity is required, which has no place in the works or sufferings of the reborn. Bellarm. lib. 2. de Iustif. cap. 5. God does not accept as true satisfaction for sin anything except infinite justice, since sin is an infinite offense.

4. Bellarmine in the same place adds. That some justice may be infinite, that is, of infinite price and value, etc., it is enough that it be the justice of an infinite person, such as is Christ GOD and man. Therefore the obedience, passion, and death of the Son of God, although in itself and essentially it was created and finite, yet by reason of the person obeying, suffering, and dying, it was infinite, and by the true rigor of justice it was a propitiation for the sins of the whole world. But if the satisfaction of Christ is of infinite price and value, it is certainly sufficient for all sins whatsoever. Item. If for infinite justice and satisfaction it is required that it be the justice and satisfaction of an infinite person, it follows that no man can satisfy for sins, since no man is infinite. 4. The Apostolic saying Hebr. 10. does not speak of any actual sins committed after Baptism, but of a certain kind of sin, namely, of the sin against the Holy Spirit.

6. Lorinus on verse 3 notes thus. The error of the heretics of this time must be avoided, that concupiscence itself, and all its motions, are sins. James from concupiscence i. e. from the power of desiring teaches that we are drawn away and enticed by suggestion, and delight, when it has conceived through some imperfect consent, then it brings forth sin: but if sin has been consummated through full consent, it generates death etc. Augustine frequently testifies that concupiscence, however much it may burn, boil, or tumult in the flesh, is not sin before GOD, until the consent of the will has been added, yet it is called sin, because it is from original sin and inclines to sinning, but by the commandment, thou shalt not covet, the depraved consent of the will is forbidden. lib. 6. contra Iulian. cap. 5. & 7. lib. 2. de nupt. & concup. cap. 23. 25. 26. lib. 1. contra duas Epist. Pelag. cap. 13. & alibi. Resp. 1. We concede that by ἐπιθυμίας in the Apostolic text in this place are understood depraved concupiscences, to which the consent of the will is added, for he speaks of actual mortal sins, which do not consist with faith and the grace of God. From that, however, it cannot be inferred that depraved concupiscence, to which the consent of the will has not yet been added, is not sin, but this only follows, that it is not an actual, mortal sin, casting out faith and the grace of GOD. 2. Depraved concupiscence, to which consent has not yet been added, is not only called sin, which the Papists concede, but the definition of sin 1. Ioh. 3. v. 4. handed down also agrees with it, since it is ἀνομία, Rom. 7. v. 7. And likewise the properties and effects of sin as is demonstrated in its own place. 3. James speaks of concupiscence in general, not restricted to the faithful, but considered most generally. But if, therefore, it could be proven from the passage of James that concupiscence is not a sin, it would follow that concupiscence is not a sin not only in the regenerate, but also in the unregenerate. 4. The Apostle distinguishes the degrees of sins and, concerning actual mortal sin, asks from where it arises; he answers, however, that it arises from depraved concupiscence, not from God. Although, therefore, depraved concupiscence habitually inherent in the regenerate and the first movements of concupiscence, which are resisted through the Spirit, are not actual mortal sins, it cannot be inferred from that, however, that they are in no way sins, for from the negation of one species to the negation of the genus the consequence is not valid. 5. Therefore, the major proposition in the argument of Lorinus must be restricted in this way. That which begets sin is not sin, namely that very thing which begets it. Concupiscence begets sin, namely actual mortal sin, reigning in man and wounding the conscience. Therefore it is not sin, namely such a one. Unless this restriction is added, original sin itself could be denied. 6. Augustine calls depraved concupiscence not only the cause and punishment of sin, but also sin. What is clearer than that classic passage in book 6 against Julian, chapter 3: Just as blindness of heart, which God alone removes, is illuminated, and is a sin, by which one does not believe in God, and a punishment of sin, by which the proud heart is punished with worthy retribution, and a cause of sin, when something is committed by the error of a blind heart: so the concupiscence of the flesh, against which the good Spirit lusts, is also a sin, because there is in it disobedience against the dominion of the mind, and it is a punishment of sin, because it has been rendered to the merits of the disobedient, and it is a cause of sin by the failure of the one consenting or the contagion of the one being born.

7. Gregorius de Valentia, book 2 on Idolatry, chapter 7, page 718, from that which Peter says, ἐν ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις in illicit cults of idols, gathers that there is some licit cult of idols and images, thence in Disputation 6, question 2, on idolatry, point 1, he defines Idolatry as that which is a cult by which divine honor is attributed to some creature as to God. He explains this definition in point 3 thus: that he confers divine honors upon a creature as to God, who pursues it with divine cult in such a way that, as much as is in him, he wishes to reconcile to it such an opinion as in truth belongs only to the majesty of GOD: from which he gathers in point 6,

That Roman Catholics are not idolaters, since they honor images in such a way that they nevertheless by no means apply divine honor to a creature as to God. Resp. 1. The little word illicit is not διακριτικὴ distinctive, by which illicit idolatry is distinguished from licit, but it is ὁριστικὴ & ἐξηγητικὴ circumscriptive, by which all idolatry is established as illicit. 2. Estius rightly warns that ἀθεμίτοις should be properly translated in the nefarious cults of idols. Through this version, the inference of Gregory vanishes into smoke. For who, from that, if someone were to call fornications nefarious or abominable, would want to collect that there is some licit fornication? 3. That appendix of the Gregorian definition is clearly superfluous. Whenever divine honor is exhibited to any creature, by that very fact that creature is raised into the place of GOD, and is held as GOD, since divine honor is nothing other than that which is owed to GOD, and consequently, by such honor being offered, divinity itself is truly attributed, or certainly is understood to be attributed by an immovable consequence. 4. Gregory's definition behaves just as if someone were to want to define adultery as intercourse with another who is not a spouse as if with a spouse, and consequently that she is not an adulteress who has intercourse with him whom she does not hold as a spouse, but only she who prostitutes herself to another as if to a spouse.

8. Piscator on v. 4 annotates thus: The use of this admonition today is against the blasphemy of those who, when they see us disapprove and rebuke those drinking bouts and dances in weddings and other banquets or solemnities, say that the Zwinglian or Calvinistic Spirit is a melancholic Spirit, by which they doubtless imply a Diabolical one. Resp. 1. We do not tax the Calvinists on the grounds that they disapprove of lascivious, shameless, libidinous, etc., drinking bouts and dances, for we disapprove of them just as much as they do. 2. But we disapprove of this, that they assert that all social dances whatsoever are vicious, illicit, profane, and unworthy of a Christian in their entire genus. Marloratus on chapter 14 of Matthew. Aretius at place 169 of John. Münster in the tract Von dem ungottseligen Tantz. 3. We establish that, with certain conditions applied, not only solitary dances but also social ones are granted especially to the youthful age, namely if moderation is kept in them, and they are not too frequent, if they are done in the presence of honest persons, if they are instituted only for the sake of delight, and not out of any levity, or for the sake of exciting, nourishing, or increasing lust. 4. That which we call the Calvinistic spirit is melancholic, this is so not so much on account of the prohibition of dances, as on account of the assertion of the absolute decree of reprobation.

9. Lorinus on the same verse comments thus. Almost all the heretics of our time, and furthermore not very chaste Catholics, think and declare that continence is either impossible for men, or is by no means kept by those who profess it. They measure, that is, others by their own lust. Resp. 1. There exist public complaints of the whole world and of the Papist writers themselves concerning the fruits of forced priestly and monastic celibacy. Georgius Cassander in his consultation, article 23. We see that by this decree concerning priestly celibacy, chastity and continence in the clergy are not confirmed to such a degree, that through it a window seems to be opened to every kind of lust and wickedness. And afterwards. The matter has now come to such a point, that you would scarcely find one in a hundred who abstains from all commerce with women. The legate of Albert, Duke of Bavaria, in an oration delivered at the Council of Trent, among other things brought forth these words. Our clergy indulges in gluttony and lusts, and as if it wishes in contempt of GOD and men to be recognized openly as covered in every kind of vice, rather than to be noticed as amended in the slightest thing, so that the other vices of the clergy, which it has in common with the people, may be passed over in silence, but certainly that lust, too free and notorious, on account of which it is now especially held to be infamous, is judged to be most alien to the common people and the provoked populace. 2. Bellarmine, book on the Clergy, chapter 21, to the argument that the celibacy of the clergy (forced upon persons less suited for it) produces prodigious lusts, fills the world with concubines and the Church with scandals, among other things answers thus. We do not admit that there are so many (note, so many) concubinary and impure men among ecclesiastics as the heretics say, who, measuring all others by themselves, think that no one is chaste. Certainly there are very many who celebrate daily and of whom no evil suspicion is heard (note, no suspicion is heard) 3. We do not only not disapprove of spontaneous celibacy in persons suited and divinely instructed with the gift of continence, but we even commend it. Therefore we do not simply say that it is impossible, or by no means kept by those who profess it.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. The passion and death of Christ principally and primarily is merit and gift, secondarily and less principally it is an example, by which we are admonished concerning the mortification of sins and affections. Rom. 6. v. 2. & following Col. 2. v. 12.cap. 3. v. 3. & 5.

2. Therefore, by many names the passion and death of Christ are ὁρμητήρια for the hatred of sin and the study of a holy life. Christ suffered for us, i. e. for our sins. Our sins were the cause of that most bitter passion and death for Christ. It is therefore just that we should hold sins in hatred and desist from them, since they drew such great torments upon Christ. Christ suffered for us, so that by having rendered satisfaction for our sins, He might avert from us the wrath of God due to our sins, and reconcile us to Himself. With the grace of God reconciled, the Holy Spirit is given, who mortifies sin in us and takes away the dominion from sin. Christ suffered for us in the flesh. Therefore we also ought to suffer in the flesh, i. e. to mortify the flesh and desist from sin. As in Christ suffering the flesh was dead; so in us the vices of the flesh ought to be mortified.

3. Every kind of death indeed could have been a type of our flesh to be mortified, but especially that which was perfected in Christ by crucifixion exhibits the most beautiful type of that spiritual mortification. For he who is crucified, the power of moving his members at will is taken away from him.Rom. 6. v. 10.Our old man is crucified together with him.Gal. 2. v. 19.I am crucified with Christ to the crossv. 20.And I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me.cap. 6. v. 14.By Christ the world is crucified to me, and I to the world. Bernard, sermon 6, on the pilgrim dead and crucified. Not only dead to the world, but also crucified, which is an ignominious kind of death. I to it, and likewise it to me. All things which the world loves are a cross to me, the delight of the flesh, honors, riches, the vain praises of men. But those things which the world deems a cross, to them I am affixed, to them I adhere, them I embrace with my whole affection.

4. Nor indeed is the passion and death of Christ proposed only as an example of spiritual mortification, but also as its efficient cause, insofar as the death and resurrection of Christ is effective in the reborn for the mortification of the flesh and newness of life Rom. 6. v. 4. The mortification of the flesh proceeds from the virtue of the death of Christ, which is offered to us in Baptism, and is conferred through faith.

5. The whole life of a Christian on this earth is a certain spiritual warfareIob. 7. v. 1. in which against the allurements of the flesh, the snares of the Devil and the snares of the world must be fought; for this matter it is fitting that we be equipped with a strong and unbroken spirit.

6. The memory of the passion of Christ, joined with true faith in Christ crucified, is the greatest strength and fortification of the pious against so many insults of enemies. Hebr. 12. v. 3. Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, losing heart in your minds. In the Greek it is ἀναλογίσασθε, seriously weigh and consider the analogy or proportion which is between that contradiction which Christ endured for your sake from sinners, and that persecution which you endure.

7. For if indeed we apply to ourselves by faith the benefits and merit of Christ who suffered for us, from that we obtain the strength of the Spirit, so that we not only bear the cross with an undaunted spirit, but also mortify the flesh with its concupiscences. Gal. 5. v. 27. Those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its passions and affections. Through these works, says Luther in his commentary on this place, faith becomes stronger, if the body is restrained, so that it does not become wanton.

8. The sign and effect of the mortified flesh is the cessation from sins, if one lives no longer for the desires of men, but for the will of GOD. Just as in Nature the corruption of one thing is the generation of another, so if the old man dies in us, the new one lives. Rom. 6. v. 5. 6. &c.

9. There are two parts of our sanctification. The flight and hatred of sin, to which human desires impel us: and the pursuit of the good work required of us in the divine law. Ephes. 4. v. 22. & 23. Col. 3. v. 9.& 10. 1. Petr. 3. v. 11.

10. The will of God revealed in the word is the rule of a holy life, Rom. 12. v. 2. for Peter defines the cessation from sin as when a man conforms his own will to the divine will, by that very fact implying that nothing is right, holy, composed, and pleasing to God in life which departs from this rule.

11. Every time of life is lost which is not consecrated to the service of God and the fulfilling of his will. August. in Manuali. He loses what he lives, who does not love God; he who cares to live, not for you O Lord, is nothing and is for nothing; he who refuses to live for you is dead; he who does not have a taste for you is foolish.

12. When the Apostle commands that the whole remaining time of life is to be conformed to the divine will, he teaches that one must persevere in the pursuit of piety and holiness. Gregory in Ps. 32. Nothing is good which we begin, unless we complete it with a persevering end. Bernard on the passion of the Lord c. 14. The virtue of a good work is perseverance. To this alone is the crown of righteousness rendered. For what does it profit to be good, to be wise, to be powerful, if one has not persevered until the end? The last letter of the Hebrew alphabet is Thau. This Ezech. 9. v. 6. is a sign of liberation and life. Do not kill anyone upon whom you shall see the Thau. He who desires to be liberated from eternal death and to obtain immortal life, let him pursue faith and the study of piety until the very end of life.

13. A most sharp stimulus for walking in the way of the Lord and running well is to recall to one's mind that one has wandered outside the way for a great part of one's life.

14. The connection of the Apostolic argument is most firm. Before conversion we securely indulged in sins. Therefore after conversion we ought to desist from sins. For the effects of contrary efficient causes are contrary. The darkness of ignorance draws with itself the darkness of sins; the saving light θεογνωσίας brings with itself the works of light, Rom. 6. v. 19. As you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity: so now yield your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification. c. 13. v. 11. Knowing the time, that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. 1. Cor. 6. v. 11. And such were some of you, but you are washed &c. 1. Thess. 5. v. 6. You are all the children of light and the children of the day v. 6. therefore let us not sleep, as others. 2. Petr. 2. v. 20. For if fleeing &c.

15. It is useful to recall to our memory more often the former kind of life which we followed before conversion, so that the magnitude of the benefit granted to us in conversion may appear more, and the shame struck by the recollection of shameful deeds may move us more to their detestation.

16. There are three degrees of actual sins, The first is to approach sin; the second to walk and progress in it; the third to sit in it, and to surrender oneself entirely to it. Ps. 1. v. 1. The sins of the wicked are ropes Prov. 5. v. 22. because they add consent to an iniquitous thought; to consent, a work; to a work, a habit; to a habit, necessity; to necessity, an excuse; to an excuse, a defense; to a defense, impenitence; to impenitence, desperation.

17. The pious walk in the way of the divine commandments: the impious in the way of sins; the former always ascend more and more, the latter always descend more and more. Prov. 18. v. 3. according to the vulgate translation. When the wicked man has come into the depth of sins, he contemns.

18. The sins which the Apostle recounts in this place are mortal in their own kind, thence they are placed in their catalogue, on account of which the gentiles are excluded from the kingdom of God.

19. Even the internal desires of sin joined with the consent of the will, although they are prohibited from going out into an external work, pertain to the life of the gentiles, and from the very light of Nature, are recognized to be damnable. Cic. lib. 1. of duties. Well did Pericles, when he had the poet Sophocles as a colleague in the Praetorship, and they had met concerning a common duty and by chance a beautiful boy passed by, and Sophocles had said, O what a beautiful boy? Pericles replied. But indeed, Sophocles, it befits a praetor to have not only hands, but also eyes that are continent. Philemon says, that a good man, whom God loves, ought to look at or covet nothing of another's, not a preeminent woman, not a house, not a possession, not a boy or a maidservant, not horses or oxen, or anything of beasts of burden, not a thread of a needle.

20. The vices of gluttony supply fuel to lusts, thence the Apostle joins ἀσελγείας, οἰνοφλυγίας, κώμους and πότους. c. Belly dist. 35. from Jerome. The belly boiling with wine quickly foams into lust. distinct. 14. in the beginning likewise from Jerome. The belly and the genitals are neighbors to themselves, so that from the proximity of the members the confederacy of vices may be understood. Hence Nabuzardan, Prince of the cooks, is read to have destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, because the belly, where a multitude of cooks serves, reduces the buildings of virtues to the ground. Camerarius part. 1. Succisiv. cap. 94. Prudent antiquity was of the persuasion that the sign of the Virgin avoids the vine.

21. Idolatry is spiritual adultery, which therefore God can no more bear in a man than a husband can adultery in a wife. Sap. 14. v. 27. ἡ τῶν ἀνωνύμων εἰδώλων θρησκεία παντὸς ἀρχὴ κακοῦ καὶ αιτία καὶ πέρας ἐστιν. But there is a double species of idolatry. The former is from the manner of worship, when the true God is worshipped not divinely, that is, not in that way in which He commanded Himself to be worshipped in His word. The latter is from the object, when that which is not the true God is worshipped religiously.

22. Those who stick in the mire of sins judge and desire all to be contaminated by the same. Ecclesiastes 10. v. 3. Even if a fool walks foolishly in the way, he esteems all to be fools.

23. Those who run together in the stadium of vices will obtain the same punishments for their impiety. Esai. 5. v. 18. Woe to you that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope. Those who run together in the stadium of virtues will obtain the same rewards for their piety. 1. Cor. 9. v. 24. They that run in the race, all run indeed, but one receiveth the prize, so run that you may obtain.

24. The judgment of the world, as being blinded and unclean, is perverse concerning the holy conversation of the pious; they hold them for a mockery and a laughingstock, indeed for περικαθάρμασι and περιψήμασι. 1. Cor. 4. v. 13. when nevertheless they are lights shining in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation. Matth. 5. v. 14. Phil. 2. v. 15.

25. When therefore we see that the world, that is, worldly men, are offended by our manners composed to honesty and gravity, we ought not on that account to be greatly moved, or even persuaded, to enter upon the same path of vices with them. Rom. 12. v. 2. Be not conformed to this world, but be reformed in the newness of your sense.

26. Worldly men are not only offended by the conversation of the pious, but they also begin to hate and slander them; nor do they stop at hatred of the person, but they proceed to blasphemy of religion itself, as if its professors were compelled to follow a life abhorrent from common humanity. But let us oppose the favor of God to this hatred of the world, and let us consider it better to sustain reproaches in this life than the torments of eternal fire in the judgment.

27. Ἐν τῇ ἀσωτία ἀνάχησις, In luxury there is confusion. Prov. 23. v. 29. Who hath woe? whose father hath woe? who hath contentions? who falls into pits? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes? Surely they that pass their time in wine, and study to drink off their cups. Ambros. de Elia & ieiunio cap. 16. Drunkenness is the fuel of lust, the incentive of insanity, the poison of foolishness. Through it men lose their voice, change their color, their eyes burn, they pant with their mouth, they snort with their nostrils, they blaze with fury.

28. That just judgment, which Christ will exercise at the consummation of the world, can and ought to animate us to sustain all the insults of enemies, and to despise their revilings. He himself will bring our innocence into the light, he himself will assert our cause, he himself will justly condemn those who in this life unjustly and rashly condemn us.

29. To this just judge, they would be compelled to render an account and to stand before his tribunal, whether they wish it or not, even the impious, in whatever degree of sublimity they may have been established in this age.

30. On this decisive day and universal assembly, the living and the dead, and thus all men, shall be judged. Acts 10. verse 42.2. Tim. 4. verse 1. Maximus of Turin, homily on the exposition of the Creed: The living and the dead are reported to be judged, so that it may be believed that there is care for all men before God.

31. The meditation of this judgment should excite in us a serious fear of God. Gregory, book 14 of the Morals, chapter 30: The terror of the judge can be avoided only before the judgment, while he is not seen, but is appeased by prayers. But when he shall have sat in that tremendous examination, he can both be seen and can no longer be appeased, because he will render all the deeds of the wicked, which he long endured in silence, at once in his wrath. Augustine, in Soliloquies, chapter 14: A great necessity has been placed upon us to do all things justly and rightly before the eyes of the judge who sees all things.

32. Because he himself is prepared to judge, let us be prepared to be judged Matt. 25. verse 10.And you be ready.Luke 12. verse 35.Let your loins be girded, etc. Ephrem on the beatitude of the soul, chapter 3: As the harvest of the age has arrived to be reaped, and the angels, girded and prepared, hold sickles in their hands, awaiting the command of the Lord. Augustine, Epistle 3: Let the last day always be before your eyes, and when we have risen at dawn, let us not trust that we shall reach the evening, and when we have laid down our limbs in our bed, let us not trust in the arrival of the light.

Latin:

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quo sensu Christus dicatur carne passus? 1. Quidam volunt, sensum esse eum, quòd Christus in diebus carnisHebr. 5. v. 7.h. e. dum in hac vita mortali egit, passus fuerit, animam verò à corpore separatam nihil fuisse passam, quae explicatio fidei analogiae congrua. 2. Quidam volunt, Apostolum ideò uti carnis nomine, quia plerique dolores Christi, ut verbera, flagella, sputa, spinae, clavi &c. fuerunt in carne. 3. Quidam censent, respectum eò haberi, quòd causa sensibilis passionis sit à carne, licet sensatio fiat animae operá. 4. Simplicissimè respondetur, carnis nomine Synecdochicè intelligi totam humanitatem, phrasi in Scripturis usitata Ioh. 1. v. 14.1. Tim. 3. v. 6.

Q. 2. Quare Apostolus utatur verboὁπλίσασθε; Resp. 1. ut innuat, totam hominis, praesertim Christiani, vitam esse militiam,Iob. 14. v. 1. ac pium in perpetua acie contra Diabolum, mundum & carnem stare oportere. 2. Ut insinuet, Christum passione & morte sua, velut armaturâ quadam fortissima contra Principem huius mundi pugnasse, ac gloriosum ex ipso triumphum retulisse, unde pii veteres crucem Christi conferunt gladio, quo caput infernalis draconis fuerit contritum, Apoc. 5. v. 6. Christus septem cornua tunc ostentat, cum tanquam occisus apparet, quia vim & fortitudinem suam praecipuè in passione & cruce exeruit. Leo serm. 10. de past. Clavi illi, qui manus pedesque Domini transfoderunt, perpetuis Diabolum fixêre vulneribus & sanctorum poena membrorum inimicarum fuit interfectio potestatum. 3. Ut doceat, fidem in Christum & devotam passionis Christi meditationem esse spiritualem nostram panoplian, quâ contra omnes tentationes ac persecutiones nos munire possumus. 1. Cor. 2. v. 2. Iudicavi me nihil scire praeter Christum crucifixum. Eph. 6. v. 16. ante omnia sumentes scutum fidei. Hebr. 12. v. 3.Recogitate eum, qui talem sustinuit adversus semetipsum contradictionem, ut ne fatigemini, animis vestris deficientes. 4. Ut ostendat, pios forti & quasi obfirmato animo ad res adversas patienter tolerandas & carnem mortificandam esse debere, ut quasi armati ad afflictonum perpessionem & carnis mortificationem videantur. 5. Ut doceat, pios paratos esse debere ad excipienda quaevis fortunae sinisterioris tela & ad pugnandum contra carnis concupiscentias, sicut miles armis suis munitus ad pugnam est paratus. Hugo notat, verbo armandi significari, cogitationem passionis non suscipi ad oblectandum animum, sed ad impugnandum vitia, & quia non omnibus conceditur pati, ut simus saltem parati.

Q. 3. Quid nomine Peccati intelligatur, quando Apostolus dicit. Qui passus est in carne, desiit à peccato? Resp. Desistere à peccato Petro idem est, quod Paulo mori peccatoRom. 6. v. 2. id quod v. 6. sic explicat, Ulterius non servire peccato. Loquitur igitur de peccati dominio, quòd pravae concupiscentiae in carne adhuc residuae renati non debeant dominium permittere, sed eam mortificare, id quod Paulus Gal. 5. v. 24. vocat carnem cum vitiis, & concupiscentiis suis crucifigere. Quidam statuunt, peccati nomine absolutè posito intelligi mortalia peccata, contra conscientiam admissa. Sed res eòdem redit, qui enim moritur peccato & concupiscentias carnis mortificat, ille à peccatis contra conscientiam abstinet.

Q. 4. An hic locus Apostolicus sit parallelus loco PaulinoRom. 6. v. 7.Qui mortuus est, iustificatus est à peccato? Resp. 1. Quidam locum Paulinum exponunt de morte naturali, in qua sit plenaria hominis liberatio à peccatis & ab omni alia servitute. In morte enim anima à corpore separatur, sicque mortui ab actionibus huius vitae & consequenter à peccando cessant. 2. Quidam accipiunt de morte civili, existimantes, Apostolum allusisse ad iudiciorum capitalium sententias, quibus condemnati ad mortem ulteriùs non delinquunt. 3. Simplicissimè iuxta seriem contextûs accipitur de morte Spirituali. Qui mortuus est, sc. peccato v. 2. & 11.qui consepultus cum Christo per Baptismum in mortemv. 4.qui factusσύμφυτοςfactus similitudini mortis eiusv. 5.cuius caro sive vetus homo simul cum Christo crucifixusv. 6.qui cum Christo spiritualiter mortuusv. 8.hic iustificatus est à peccato i. e. liberatus & absolutus est à peccato, non solùm ratione reatûs, sed etiam ratione dominii, ut non ampliùs subiectus sit servituti peccati. Basilius in orat. de Bapt. Christi tom. 1. p. 460. Iustificatus est à peccato i. e. absolutus est, liberatus est, ab omni peccato repurgatus est, non solùm quod operibus ac verbis, sed quod & ipsis cogitationum affectibus sit commissum. Sic ergò locus Petrinus loco isti Paulino est planè parallelus. Quod enim Paulus dicit, qui mortuus est, scil. peccato, id Petrus sic exprimit. Qui passus est in carne scil. cum Christo in carne passo. Quod Paulus dicit, iustificatus est à peccato, illud Petrus sic exprimit, desiit à peccato.

Q. 5. Quid sit desideriis hominum vivere? Resp. desideriis hominum vivere significat, carnalium hominum desideriis sive voluntati in vita sese conformare, desideria hominum carnalium normam vitae & actionum sibi praestituere, desideriis hominum quodammodo agi ac duci in vitâ, ad eorum exemplar instituendâ. Per vocem enim ἀνθρώπων absolutè positam intelligi homines carnales nondum per Spiritum sanctum regenitos, patet 1. Ex oppositione, quia desideriis illis hominum opponitur voluntas Dei, cui voluntas hominum renatorum, quà talium, est conformis. 2. Ex subiecta expositione in versu seq. sufficit praeteritum tempus ad voluntatem gentium consummandam. 3. Ex locorum parallelorum collatione. Matth. 16. vers. 23.1. Cor. 3. v. 3.Coloss. 2. v. 8.Tit. 1. v. 14. Hieronymus lib. 1. contra Iovin. sensum exprimens reddidit, vivere in desideriis hominum.

Q. 6. Quomodo ex pristino vitae statu argumentum exhortationis Apostolus ducat? Resp. 1. Quia renovatio regenerationi piorum nexu indissolubuli coniuncta novam vitam ac novos mores requirit. Ergò qui pristinum vivendi morem adhuc sectantur, eo ipso ostendunt, se nondum renovatos ac proinde nec regenitos esse. 2. Aequum est, ut pro singulari illa divina gratia, quae ex peccatorum coeno ipsos traxit, sese gratos praestent, non verbis solùm, sed ipsà quoque vita & factis. 3. Quia maiorem & potiorem vitae partem Diabolo per flagitia in gentilismo consecraverant, aequum omninò erat, ut reliquam eius partem Deo consecrarent.

Q. 7. An conversos ex gentilismo, an vero Iudaismo alloquatur? Quidam ex hoc loco colligunt, quòd Petrus ad conversos ex Iudaeis haec scribat, quibus exprobret, quòd gentilium voluntati ac moribus sese accommodassent, à quibus eos Deus segregaverat. Sed rectiùs ex hoc loco colligitur, Apostolum ad conversos ex gentilibus haec potissimùm scribere, ut colligitur ex loco parallelo Eph. 4. v. 17. & seqq. Quia gentiles plerique omnes ante suam ad Christum conversionem vivendi morem gentibus usitatum sectabantur, quibus quosdam ex Iudaeis ante suam ad Christum conversionem sese conformasse, non imus inficias: interim quidam eorum exemplo Pauli in Pharisaismo adhuc constituti, externam vitae honestatem iuxta normam legis divinae sactabantur. Act. 26. v. 5.Phil. 3. v. 6.

Q. 8. Quare Apostolus in specie haec vitia enumeret? Resp. regnabant apud gentes nefandae libidines, Rom. 1. v. 24. & 26.Eph. 4. v. 19. quae non iudicabantur esse peccata, sicut ille apud Comicum dicit. Non est flagitium adolescentem scortari. Illas perstringit Apostolus nomine ἀσελγείων καὶ ἐπιθυμίων. Quia vero intemperantia cibi ac potus, & convivia luxuriosa fomentum suppeditant libidinibus, ideò coniungit illis οὶνοφλυγίας, κώμους & πότους. Denique quia ex luxuria etiam solet oriri idololatria, ac scortatio spiritualis cum corporali ut plurimùm solet esse coniuncta, Exod. 32. v. 6.1. Corinth. 10. v. 7. ideò cum praedictis vitiis idololatrias Apostolus coniungit, sicut etiam Paulus Rom. 1. v. 24. & 25. eadem coniunxerat. Posset huc referri, quòd gentiles inter alias Deas etiam colerent Victuam, quae victum, & Potuam, quae potum procuret, teste Arnobio lib. 3. contra gentil. Educum, sive Edulinam, Edusam, Eduam, quae escam ministret; ac Potinam sive Poticam & Potuam, quae potionem ministret, teste Aug. lib. 4. de Civ. DEI cap. 11. & 34. lib. 6. cap. 9. de quibus Ludov. Vives in comm. illius loc.

Q. 9. Quodnam admirationis genus Apostolus intelligat? Beda admirationem illam accipit in partem bonam, sic enim in h. l. commentatur. Quia carnem, inquit, vestram crucifixistis cum vitiis & concupiscentiis, evenit profectò, ut etsi propter suam perfidiam vos blasphement, utpote segregatos ab eorum consortio, in vestra tamen conversatione semper opera iustitiae & pietatis videant, quae meritò admirentur, & pro quibus fidem iure laudent, & venerentur Christianam. Sed manifestum est ex verbo ξενίζονται & annexo participio βλασφημοῦντες, admirationem hîc in malam partem accipi.

Q. 10. Quisnam sitὁ ἑτοίμως ἔχων κρῖναι;Quidam accipiunt de Deo, nomine isthocοὐσιωδῶςaccepto, prout Patri, Filio ac Spiritui sancto aequaliter competit. De Deo enim dicitur, quòd sit iudicaturus populum suumDeut. 32. v. 36.quòd solium suum paraverit ad iudiciumPs. 9. v. 8.quòd venturus sit iudicare terramPs. 82. v. 8.Ps. 98. v. 9. &c. Quidam vero de Christo, cui Pater omne iudicium deditIoh. 5. v. 22.eique dedit potestatem faciendi iudicium, quia Filius hominis estv. 27.qui constitutus est iudex vivorum & mortuorumActor. 10. v. 42. &c. Sed hae expositiones non sunt contrariae, sed subordinatae, ut constat ex loco Apostolico Act. 17. v. 31.Statuit DEUS diem, in quo iudicaturus est orbem terrarum in iustitia per virum, in quo decrevit. Potestas faciendi iudicii competit omnibus tribus Deitatis personis κατ᾿ αὐτοκρατορίαν & κατ᾿ εὐδοκίαν propter ὁμοουσίαν. Ut enim trium divinitatis personarum est una & aequalis essentia, ita quoque una eademque potentia; interim tamen κατ᾿ οἰκονομίαν Christo θεανθρώπῳ iudici mortuorum, ac vivorum divinitùs constituto, peculiariter in Scripturis tribuitur. Is enim iudicium hoc in assumta Natura humana visibiliter & immediatè administrabit. Toti Trinitati tribuitur iudicium, quoad potestatem iudiciariam, dominium, autoritatem & decretum. Filio peculiariter assignatur quoad visibile & externum exercitium.

Q. 11. Quinam nomine vivorum & mortuorum iudicandorum intelligantur? Isidorus lib. 1. Epist. 222. triplici modo exponi posse censet, quòd Christus mortuorum ac vivorum iudex dicitur. 1. Fore ut anima & corpus simul in iudicium veniant, nec alterum ab altero seiungatur, verum quemadmodum in hac vita communem coniunctionem habuerunt, sic etiam futurum iudicium subeant. 2. Vivos, h. e. qui vitam aeternam & DEO gratam sectati sunt, à mortuis h. e. qui peccatis immortui datum sibi talentum in socordia perinde ut in sepulchro defoderunt, esse discernendos, illisque, immortales mercedes, his vero poenas persolvendas. 3. Iudicandos esse tùm eos, qui vivi relicti fuerint, tùm eos, qui ante ipsos vitam cum morte commutarunt. Ioh. Huss sic exponit. Vivos in gratia ad beatitudinem, mortuos in culpa ad damnationem. Benedictus Arias Montanus vivos interpretatur adhuc in carne illa Adami mortuos in Christo. Quidam vivos accipiunt de illis, qui iam vivunt & victuri sunt, mortuos de illis, qui iamdum mortui sunt, sed tunc in vitam resuscitabuntur. Simplicissimè per vivos intelliguntur, quos iudex veniens reperiet vivos; per mortuos, qui iam ante fuerint mortui, quos ex sepulchris in vitam revocabit, atque unà cum vivis, adeoque omnes homines iudicabit, Act. 10. v. 42.2. Tim. 4. v. 1. Dicuntur mortui ratione termini à quo i. e. qui fuerant mortui, sed tunc resuscitati adstabunt. Hieron. in c. 26. Matth. Aliquando in Scriptum mutatâ re pristinum nomen manet.

Q. 12. Quare mortuorum mentionem facit? Resp. 1. ut ostendat, Christum fore iudicem Universalem omnium omninò hominum, quia in has duas classes omnes homines distribuuntur. Eodem sensu dicitur Deus iudicaturus pium & impium, iustos & iniustos, fideles & incredulos Eccl. 3. v. 17.Sap. 5. v. 1. magnos & pusillos. Apocal. 20. vers. 12. 2. ne putemus, nos damni quidpiam pati, si morientibus nobis calumniatores ac persecutores nostri maneant superstites, quia non propterea manum DEI iudicis effugient.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Christus dicitur passus carne v. 1. Atqui etiam anima Christi laboravitEsa. 53. vers. 11.ac ipsemet testatur, animam suam esse tristem usque ad mortem.Matth. 26. v. 38. Resp. Carnis nomine synecdochicè intelligitur tota Christi humanitas, adeoque anima non solùm sensitiva, sed etiam rationalis. Christus enim non solùm in sanctissimo suo corpore adeoque in omnibus eius membris gravissimos cruciatos pertulit, sed etiam in sanctissima sua anima iram DEI peccatis totius humani generis debitam persensit.

2. Christo passo in carne & vos eadem cogitatione armemini, ut ipsi quoque in carne patiamini v. 1. Atqui in Christo nihil fuit nec est vitiosum, quomodo igitur Christo conformes nos facit, quod in carne patimur? Resp. aliter accipitur vox carnis, quando de Christo usurpatur, videlicet de ipsa carnis substantia, eademque pura & munda, aliter, quando de nobis usurpatur, videlicet de vitiosis corruptae Naturae qualitatibus, interim conformitas est in passione & morte, quatenus per spiritualem carnis mortificationem passioni & morti Christi spiritualiter conformamurRom. 6. v. 2.

3. Christi passio proponitur hoc loco ut causa exemplaris mortificationis spiritualis. Atqui passio & mors Christi non solùm est exemplar mortificationis nostrae, sed etiam eiusdem causa, est enim virtus mortis Christi, ut peccato moriamur, ac Spiritus Christi facit, ut mors eius ad carnem in nobis mortificandam sit efficax. Resp. inclusio unius non est exclusio alterius. Quando Christus nobis proponitur ut exemplum, non negatur etiam diverso respectu meritum ac donum.

4. Qui in carne passus est, desiit à peccato. v. 1. Atqui in hac vita non sumus ab omni peccato prorsus immunes ac liberi. Resp. non loquitur de peccati sensu & consensu; nec de adhaerente renatis carnis vitio, sed de eiusdem dominio Roman. 6. v. 12.Existimate, vos mortuos esse peccatov. 12.Non ergò regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore, ut oboediatis concupiscentiis eius. August. tract. 61. in Ioh. Non ait, non sit, sed non regnet. Quamdiu enim vivis, peccatum necesse est esse in membris tuis, saltem illi regnum auferatur, nec fiat, quod iubet.

5. Non est vivendum desideriis hominumv. 2.At Paulus de seipso dicit1. Corinth. 10. v. 33.ego per omnia omnibus placeo. Resp. Petrus loquitur de illis hominum desideriis, quae sunt voluntati divinae contraria, Paulus de illis, quae legi divinae conformia, unde statim addit, non quaerens, quod mihi utile est, sed quod multis, ut salvi fiant. Et Rom. 15. v. 2. tradit hanc regulam. Unusquisque vestrûm proximo suo placeat in bonum ad aedificationem. De priore desideriorum humanorum genere idem Apostolus dicit Galat. 1. v. 10.Si adhuc hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem1. Thessal. 2. v. 4.Nos quasi hominibus placentes, sed Deo, qui probat corda nostra. Omnibus placere debemus, non vitiosis eorum affectibus serviendo, nec impiis eorum moribus nos conformando, sed infirmitatibus compatiendo, & salutem eorum promovendo. Augustinus in cap. 1. ad Galat. tom. 4. circa fin. Qui placet hominibus, non ab ipsis suam gloriam quaerens; sed Dei, ut salvi fiant, non iam hominibus, sed Deo placet, aut certè iam cum & Deo placet simul & hominibus, non utique, hominibus placet. Aliud est enim placere hominibus, aliud & Deo & hominibus. Item qui hominibus propter veritatem placet, non ipse illis, sed veritas placet.

6. Sufficit, praeterito vitae tempore voluntatem gentium consummasse.v. 3.At nullum omninò tempus dandum fuerat consummandae gentium voluntati, & quicquid ei datur, non satis est; sed nimium. Resp. nequaquam hoc vult Apostolus, quod ad satietatem usque debeamus expleri consummanda gentium voluntate i. e. peccatis perpetrandis, sed mitigat exprobrationis acrimoniam, ac memoriam vitae praeteritae vult nobis stimulum esse debere ad reliquum vitae tempus in pietate & honestate transigendum iuxta monitum Christi Iohan. 5. vers. 14.Ecce sanus factus es, noli amplius peccare. cap. 8.

v. 11.Vade & noli amplius peccare. Lyranus in h. l. Per hoc quod dicit, sufficit, non intelligenda est approbatio vitae praeteritae, sed magis reprobatio, ut sit sensus. Debet poenitenti sufficere, quod praeterito tempore vixit carnaliter.

7. Sufficit praeterito vitae tempore voluntatem gentium consummasse. Atqui homo immersus peccatis, praesertim libidinibus, nunquam dicit, sufficit.Prov. 30. v. 16. Proponit hanc ἐναντιοφανείαν Iohannes Huss. in comm. h. l. sic scribens. Contrà, inquit, voluptas carnis nunquam sufficit, iuxta illudProv. 30.Tria sunt insaturabilia & quartum, quod nunquam dicit, sufficit. Infernus, matrix conclusa & terra, quae non satiatur aqua; ignis vero nunquam dicit, sufficit. Ubi per infernum superbia; per terram, avaritia; per matricem conclusam luxuria; per ignem carnalis concupiscentia designantur. Illa enim nunquam satiantur, ac si quis in uno esurit, in alio sitit, quod in carnali concupiscentia includitur. Ergò videtur, quod non sufficit praeteritum tempus ad voluntatem gentium consummandam. Respondet autem hoc modo. Quamvis avarus ut huius (i. e. quâ talis) & luxoriosus ut huius, nunquam dicit, sufficit, tamen homo, dum cognoverit Dei iustitiam, dicet: sufficit mihi illud tempus, ut ulterius non sic vivam. Loquitur ergò Petrus de iudicio hominis renati & conversi, non de iudicio hominis adhuc peccatis immersi.

8. Sufficit vobis praeteritum tempus. At non omnes illi, ad quos scribit Apostolus, graviora illa peccata perpetraverant.1. Cor. 6. v. 11.ταῦτα τίνες ἦτι. Resp. 1. est in hac locutione Synecdoche Scripturis usitata, quâ denominatio sit à parte maiore, ac quae plerisque competunt, de toto coetu praedicantur. 2. Per Naturam omnes ad eiusmodi vitia fuere propensi, ac semen illorum peccatorum latet in omnibus, etiamsi non proferat in omnibus aequales fructus. 3. Qui à gravioribus illis sceleribus praeservati, ad maiores gratias DEO agendas agnoscant se esse obstrictos, August. lib. 2. Confess. cap. 7. Gratiae tuae deputo & misericordiae tuae, quòd peccata mea tanqum glaciem solvisti, gratiae tuae deputo & quaecunque non feci mala. Quid enim non facere potui, qui etiam gratuitum facinus amavi?

9. Petrus eos, ad quos scribit, ante conversionem ad Christum dicit ambulasse in nefariis idolorum cultibus vers. 3. At haec Epistola potissimùm scripta ad Iudaeos in dispersione positos, qui ab idololatriae gravissimè abhorruerunt 1. Epist. 1. v. 1. Resp. 1. Calvinus statuit, per idololatrias intelligit superstitiones, quibus Iudaei vel maximè erant dediti. 2. Quidam respondent, Iudaeos intermixtos gentilibus, cum exules & inopes essent, conviviis gentilium, ad quae invitabantur, in quibus imolatitiae carnes apponebantur, sese miscuisse, ac fortè etiam Sacris eorum interfuisse, quae cum ad idololatriam imputari doceat Paulus1. Cor. 10. v. 20.ideo Petrum nomine idololatrias ea taxare. 3. Simplicissimè respondetur, Epistolam hanc scriptam esse ad Ecclesiam ex Iudaeis & gentibus collectam, ac proinde quaedam in ea ita comparata esse, ut potissimùm ad Iudaeos; quaedam vero ut potissimùm ad gentiles spectent, in qua classe posteriore etiam haec idololatrias taxatio. 4. Nec potest negari, posterioribus Ecclesiae Israeliticae temporibus, praesertim post excidium Hierosolymitanum & Iudaeorum dispersionem inter gentes eos idololatria gentilium contaminari coepisse.

10. Christus iudicabit vivos i. e. quos veniens ad iudicium inveniet vivos & mortuos. id est, qui ante ipsius ad iudicium adventum fuere mortui. At qui illi, quos Christus ad iudicium veniens inveniet vivos, immutabuntur, quae mutatio erit morti analoga.1. Cor. 15. v. 51. Resp. 1. dicuntur vivi ratione termini à quo, quando Christus ad iudicium veniet, tunc erunt vivi, mox in momento immutabuntur. 2. immutatio illa erit quidem morti analoga, non tamen mors erit, inde morti opponitur in dicto Apostolico. Non omnes quidem obdormiemus, omnes autem immutabimur. Neque enim in illa immutatione anima è corporis domicilio egredietur, sed anima & corpus stolâ immortalitatis & gloriae exutâ carnis tunicâ induentur. v. 53. Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem &c.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Duae sunt in Christo distinctae Naturae; divina, quae prorsus ἀπαθὴς; & humana, in qua & iuxta quam passionem & mortem sustinuit. Ne quis enim confusionem Naturarum & proprietatum introduceret, usus est Apostolus particula διοριστοκῇ sive distinctiva, Christus passus est σαρκὶ. Opponendum hoc Eutychi, Naturas & earum proprietates in Christo confundenti. Beda in h. l. Notandum, quòd Apostolus distinctè loquens ait, Christo igitur passo in carne. Quia sicut Ambrosius ait, Caro eius est passa, divinitas autem mortis libera, passioni corpus Naturae humanae lege concessit An vero mori divinitas potest, cum anima non possit.Math. 10.Animam occidere non possunt. Si ergò anima occidi non potest, quomodo divinitas potest? Si sciret, Christi divinitatem fuisse passibilem, suffecisset, ut diceret, Christo igitur passo, nec addidisset, in carne. Sed quia noverat, in uno eodemque Christo & passibilem ante mortem fuisse Naturam & impassibilem semper divinam manere substantiam. Fulgentius lib. 3. ad Thrasim. c. 9. Propterea Christum fatetur passum in carne, cuius divinitatem noverat prorsus impassibilem permanere.

2. Ut in Christo Naturam διττοτης: ita quoque personae ἑνότης asserenda. Unus enim atque idem Christus est, qui passus carne, impassibilis permansit in divinitate. Athanasius serm. de incarn. docet, eundem dici debere, quod passus est, & quod non est passus. Non enim alium esse praeter ipsum Dei Verbum, quod passionem & mortem recepit, sed idem illud impassibile & incorporeum carnis generationem sustinuisse & iis omnibus perfunctum esse, ut haberet quod offerret pro nobis. Gelasius lib. de duab. Natur. Carne passum dixit Petrus Christum, non Deitate, cum tamen ipsa Deitas totum faciat, quicquid caro perpessa est, sicut & Filius hominis suum habet totum, quicquid est Dei. & sub una persona meritò unus atque item dicitur pati, quicquid ut Deus homo patitur, non infirmitate & conditione passibili, sed dignitate suam faciens passionis iniuriam; adunatione patiens sed sine passibilitate compatiens, sicut unus idemque virtutes operatur, quicquid ut homo Deus operaetur. Opponendum hoc Nestorio, personae unitatem in Christo divellenti.

3. Nomen Christi est nomen personae. Χριστὸς τὸ συναμφότερον νοεῖ ται. Athanas. orat. 5. contra Arian. p. 321. Damasc. lib. 3. orth. sid. cap. 3. τό χριστὸς ὁνομα ὑποστασεως λεγομεν, οὐ μονοτρόπως μέν, ἀλλὰ τῶν δύο φυσεων ὑπαρχον σημαιτικὸν, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ἒχρισεν, χρίων μὲνώς θεὸς, ὅς ἐχρισὲ τὸ σῶμα τῆ θεότιτι αὐτοῦ, χριόμειος δὲ ώς ἄνθρωπος, αὐτὸς γαρ ἐστι τοῦ το κακεῖνο. Quia ergò Christus dicitur passus, ex eo rectè infertur, quòd etiam Deus rectè dicatur passus. Quamvis enim divina Natura in se non patiatur, nec moriatur: ipse tamen Filius Dei pati & mori dicitur, tàm verè & realiter, quàm verè carnis particeps factus, in qua passionem & mortem sustinuit. Hebr. 2. vers. 14. Inde autor vitae dicitur interfectus Actor. 3.

v. 15.Deus proprio suo sanguine dicitur acquisivisse Ecclesiamc. 20. v. 21.reconciliati dicimur Deo per mortem Filii eiusRom. 5. vers. 10.Dominus gloriae dicitur crucifixus1. Cor. 2. v. 8. Cyrillus in Apolog. ex Athanasio. Sicut proprium Domini esse dicimus corpus, ita & corporis passiones propriae eius dicuntur, etiamsi non contingant secundùm divinitatem eius, alioqui alterius esset corpus, alterius dicerentur passiones, Si autem caro Verbi caro est, necessarium, passiones carnis dici eius, cuius & caro est. Leo. Epist. 10. ad Flavian. Filium Dei dicimus passum & mortuum, non in Naturae divinae proprietate, sed in assumta Naturae humanae infirmitate. Vigilius lib. contra Eutych. Quamvis Deus non sit passus in proprietate Naturae (divinae) tamen passus est in unione personae (in Natura humana, quam in personae unitatem assumsit, ut propterea ipsi Deo rectè tribuatur passio.) Opponendum hoc Calvinianis, qui propositionem Petrinam, Christus passus est carne, sic resolvunt. Sola humana Natura in Christo est passa. Anhald. Apol. p. 246. Humana Natura Christi tantùm mortua est, non Deitas, non tota persona. Herborn. in rudim. lib. 2. p. 100. Christus homo mortuus est pro nobis, id est, Natura tantùm illa Christi humana, quae non per se in separata hypostasi, sed in ipsa una Christi persona consideratur, mortua est. Danaeus contra Chemn. P. 24. Atqui particulae illae distinctae ἐν, κατὰ &c. non sunt χωριστικαὶ καὶ διαμεριστικαὶ, quarum usu Naturae separentur ac dividantur, ut humana tantùm ad humanitatem & divina solùm ad divinitatem restringantur, ut Naturae sint παντάπασι ἀκοινώνητοι πρός ἑαυτὰς, ut Samosatenus finxit, sed sunt διακριτικαὶ Naturarum ac naturalium proprietatum; sunt διοριστικαὶ, ostendunt enim, secundùm quam Naturam talia de persona praedicentur; & sunt ἐνδεικτικαὶ τοῦ καθ᾿ αὐτὸ ἀιτίου, monstrantes causam primam & per se, quamobrem humanae affectiones tribuantur Deo & divinae actiones homini.

4. Christi passio non solùm est exemplum, sed etiam meritum & ἀντίλυτρον. Christus enim dicitur passus pro nobis. Opponendum hoc Photinianis, satisfactionem Christi negantibus.

5. Opponit Apostolus desideria hominum & voluntatem Dei, eo ipso ostendens, totam hominis Naturam per peccatum penitùs corruptam ac depravatam, eiusdemque cupiditates, affectus, motus, desideria &c. voluntati divinae repugnare. Estius in h. l.

Homo sine Deo totus carnalis, nec Dei, sed carnis voluntatem exequitur. Lorinus in h. l. Homo simpliciter sumtus in deteriorem sumitur partem & carnalem significat, unde secundùm hominem ambulare & carnalem esse, idem est.1. Cor. 3. v. 3.nasci quoque ex sanguinibus & quod idem est ex voluntate carnis & viri, atque ex Deo nasci opponuntur Iohan. 1. v. 13. nec non mandata Dei & hominum, vel traditiones ac doctrinae Matth. 15. vers. 9.Coloss. 2. v. 8.Tit. 1. v. 14. & sapere quae DEI sunt, & quae hominumMatth. 16. v. 23. Falsum ergò est, quod Scholastici docent, posse hominem ex puris naturalibus Deum super omnia diligere, naturalia in homine post lapsum mansisse integra, posse hominem ex congruo mereri infusionem gratiae, dari adhuc aliquas liberi arbitrii vires in coversione &c. quas opiniones Pontificii iampridem suas fecêre.

6. Graviter monet Apostolus renatos, ne peccatorum pristinorum coeno, ex quo emersi, iterum se involvi patiantur, neve desideriis hominum, quod adhuc tempus vitae reliquum, impendant. Utique ergò renati possunt à studio ac stadio pietatis recedere, concupiscentiis carnis frena laxare, sicque fide, gratiâ Dei, inhabitatione Spiritus S. & salute aeternâ excidere. Quod si enim hoc esse ἐκ τῷν ἀδυνάτων, quorsum opus foret admonitionibus huiusmodi Apostolicis? Opponendum hoc Anabaptistis & Calvinianis negantibus, verè renatos posse iterum fide & gratia Dei excidere. Aug. Cons. art. 12.

7. Admirabantur & offendebantur olim gentiles videntes, conversos ad CHRISTUM non concurrere cum ipsis in eandem luxuriae confusionem. Nimirum paucitate Christianorum, novam, ut vocabant, religionem & peculiare vitae genus sectantium, offendebantur, ac urgebant concursum, adeoque multitudinem hominum, sacra gentili & mores gentiles adhuc amplectentium. Eodem modo adhuc hodie Pontificii offenduntur paucitate eorum, qui doctrinam Evangelicam, quam vocant, novam amplectuntur, nec unà cum illis ad sacra Missatica, ad imaginum adorationem, ad pedes Papae osculandos, ad coacti caelibatûs sordes &c. concurrunt.

8. Christus iudicabit vivos & mortuos, adeoque omnes homines. Falsum igitur est, quod Pontificii statuunt, quosdam ex fidelibus eos sc. qui paupertatem voluntariam voverunt, non esse iudicandos, sed cum Christo iudices futuros. Salmero tom. 4. tract. 25. q. 563. Costerus in postill. Domin. 2. Adv. p. 19. ac infideles extra Ecclesiam, qui fide caruerunt, non esse iudicio discussionis iudicandos. Thomas in Supplem. q. 89. art. 7. & alii ex Scholasticis. 4. sent. dist. 47. quos secutus ex Calvinianis Petrus Martyr, in explic. Symb. Apost. class. 2. Loc. Theol. cap. 17. p. 432. sic scribit. Statuo infideles nullo opus esse examine, ut qui propter suam infidelitatem iam condemnati sunt. Confer artic. de Extr. Iudic. §. 50.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Cornelius à Lapide ad v. 1. sic commentatur. Christus passus tantùm in haec vita, dum esset in carne mortali, non vero post mortem, cum descendit ad inferos, uti blasphemat Calvinus, dicens Christum damnat orum poenas pertulisse, ut nostram damnationem in se susciperet & lueret. Resp. 1. non est peculiaris & propria Calvini opinio, Christum dolores infernales sensisse, sed idem cum ipso statuimus. 2. Idque probamus ex eo, quòd Christus conqueritur, se à Deo derelictum & non exaudiri Psalm. 22. v. 2.5. 6. 7.Matth. 27. v. 46. quod dicitur pro nobis factus maledictum, ut nos à maledictione legis liberaret,Gal. 3. v. 13. quòd verè in se susceperit peccata nostra, cum quibus nondum expiatis ira & iudicium Dei individuo nexu coniuncta Esa. 53. v. 6.8.10. quòd mortes in numero plurali Christo tribuuntur Esai. 5. vers. 9. quod in ipso passionis aggressu in ἀγωνὶᾳ constitutus coeperit ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι, ἀδημονεῖν καὶ λυπεῖσθαι, adeò ut diceret, animam suam esseπερίλυπονusque ad mortem, ac sanguineum sudorem guttatim in terram destillantem emitteretMatth. 26. v. 37. 38. &c. 3. hosce verò dolores non sensit post mortem, sed ante mortem in horto oliveti, ideò contrarium ex hoc loco Petri non potest probari. 4. nec per hunc metaphoricum Christi ad inferos descensum tollitur vel negatur realis eiusdem ad inferos descensus, post mortem subsecutus.

2. Lorinus ad v. 1. sic annotat. Pati in carne, vel carne, significat, Christum duntaxat passum, dum in hac mortali vita vixit, nihil autem neque tunc divinitatem ipsius, neque animam, quando à corpore separata est; quamvis dum viveret, pars animae quoque superior suos habuerit dolores, salvâ tamen visione beatificâ, in qua etiam coniuncta fuerit consequens in parte superiore, licet non redundaret in inferiorem, delectatio. Quà in re Melchiorem Canum, id de delectatione negantem lib. 12. Locor.

cap. 13. non probo, scilicet saltem in cruce impeditam, salvâ verâ beatitudinis ratione. Illam Cani sententiam Henricus quodlibet. 8. q. 7. censet fidei contrariam: Suarez. part. 3. tom. 1. Disp. 38. d. 3. falsam & temerariam atque contra omnes Theologos. Resp. 1. Cani sententia manifestè suffragatur nostrae, quòd Christus dolores verè infernales in passione sustinuerit. Sicut, inquit, per totam vitam Dominus gloriam animae quasi premebat, ne in corpus efflueret: sic saltem in cruce retinuit gaudium, quod suapte Natura ex clara DEI notitia prodiret. Gaudium fateor ex DEO viso in voluntate necessariò nasci, non secus atque ex Sole lumen, calorem ex igne. Sed retraxit aliquando Sol radios suos & ne calefaceret, comprehensus est etiam ignis. Quare nihil mirum videri cuipiam debet, si in hominum redemtione, per hominis unius dolores explenda, voluptas omnis reprimeretur, quam aliàs ex visione DEI proficisci, Naturae ratio demonstrat. Et postea. Christus non solùm videbat, sed etiam fruebatur, quamvis derelictus à DEO, omnigs penitus solatio destitutus non gaudebat. Atqui summam non solùm in appetitu sensitivo, sed etiam rationali sive voluntate sentire tristitiam sine ullo solatio & gaudio, nihil aliud est, quàm dolores verè infernales sustinere. 2. Neque haec sola & privata est Cani opinio, sed multi ex Pontificiis ita senserunt. Bartholomaeus Medina in Thom. p. 3. q. 46. art. 6. Est genus poenarum, quod patiuntur damnati in inferno, qui omni solatio carent. Quiddam huic simile Redemtor noster sustinere dignatus est, qui omne à se solatium & consolationis remedium in passione abdicavit. Ludovicus à Ponte in cap. 8. Cant. p. 537. Christus amore tui non solùm mortem, sed acerbissimos instar inferni crucis dolores pertulit. Maldonatus in cap. 26. Matth. Dispensatione quadam factum fuit, ut cum Christus beatus esset, tristitiam etiam in superiorem animae partem admiserit. Nam sicut beatitudinem suam cohibere potuit, ne deflueret in corpus, ut pati posset: ita premere eam potuit & quodammodo occultare, ut ad tempus tristitiae cederet, quae una passionis suae pars futura erat. Confer Sanctium in cap. 2. Actor. super verba, Solutis doloribus inferni, ac Salmeronem tract. 13. in Acta. 3. Quando Petrus absolutè dicit, Christum esse passum, complectitur omnes cruciatus, dolores, angores &c. quos Christus non solùm in suo corpore, sed etiam in sanctissima sua anima, nec solùm in inferiore, sed etiam superiore animae parte, ut loquuntur, sive facultate sustinuit. Passionis ergò nomine dolores infernales non excludit, sed includit.

3. Lorinus & Cornelius à Lapide verba Apostoli, eadem cogitatione armemini, applicant ad Sacramentum Confirmationis. Sa cramentum confirmationis, inquit Lorinus, quo creamur Christi milites à crucis consignatione potissimùm in fronte vocatur signaculum à Cornelio Papa apud Euseb. lib. 6. Hist. cap. 35. & Ambrosio lib. 3. de Sacrament. cap. 2. Huius rei Symbolo, inquit Cornelius à Lap. in Confirmationis Sacramento ab Episcopo in fronte signamur, eogs quasi milites & pugiles Christi auctoramur & raboramur ad certandum pro fide Christi usque ad mortem & Martyrium. Resp. 1. de Sacramento Confirmationis nec Petrus hoc loco, nec Apostoli uspiam in Scriptura quidquam tradunt. 2. Crucis signum in ipsa Baptismi administratione fuit à veteribus adhibitum non spiritualis cuiusdam efficaciae, sed piae admonitionis & significationis causâ. Betuleius in notis ad Lactant, lib. 4. div. Instit. cap. 27. Veteres signum cruois habuerunt pro insigni & Symbolo, quo testatam Christi crucifixi professionem inter gentes, iudaeosque volebant. 3. Pontificii in administratione huius Sacramenti ex oleo cum balsamo mixto figuram crucis in fronte duntaxat formant. Sed fatetur ipse Cornelius à Lap. olim etiam alia corporis membra fuisse chrismate uncta.
