Sed ex Rom. 1. v. 27. apparet, rectiùs verti exardescere per insanam scil. libidinem, Pro luxuria in Graeco non est ἀσέλγεια, quod in versu praeced. Vulgatus Interpres per luxuriam reddidit, sed ἀσωτία, quod propriè significat luxum, sive profusionem. Syrus retinuit nomen Graecum & addidit, in pristinaἀσωτία. Nec in Graeco est σύγχυσιν confusionem, ut vulg. reddidit, sed ἀνάχυσιν, quod propriè significat refusionem, per quam denotari putant, quòd Christiani non refundunt, i. e. non respondent illecebris, provocationibus & solicitationibus inhonestis: Posset etiam cogitari, quòd hac voce exprimatur fervor libidinis & intemperantiae, metaphorâ ductâ à mari exundanti & effundenti aquas ultra alveum. Quidam transtulerunt per profusionem. Graeca Scholia exponunt per σύγχυσιν.Confusionem, quando res diversi generis inter se sine ordine commiscentur & confunduntur,Act. 19. v. 29. quae expositio ingluviei luxuriosorum & congeriei flagitiorum in gentilibus pulchrè congruit. Hesychius & Suidas ἀνάχυσιν inter caetera significare dicunt animi βλακείαν καὶ ἔκλυσιν viriumque exolutionem, mollitiem, quae significatio pulchrè huic loco congruit. ἀσωτία enim animi & corporis vires tandem dissolvit. βλασφημοῦντες. Vulg. blasphemantes. Quidam accipiunt de conviciis & probris, quibus gentiles conversos ad fidem Christianam hoc nomine insectabantur, quòd more vivendi pristino immutato ab omni humanitate & communi societate videantur alieni.βλασφημεῖνenim dicitur, quasiβλάπτειν τὴν φημὴν,famam alterius laedere, in qua significatione accipiturRoman. 3. v. 8.1. Corinth. 4. v. 13. Sed verisimile est, maledicos illos non substitisse in personis Christianorum, sed ipsam quoque religionem Christianam calumniatos fuisse, ac si in ea & cum ea nemo possit hilaritatem exercere & aliorum exemplo vivere, atque hac ratione Deum ipsum religionis Christianae autorem blasphemasse, in qua significatione verbum βλασφημεῖν accipitur Matth. 9. v. 3.cap. 26. v. 65.Rom. 2. v. 24. &c. Syrus perspicuitatis causâ textum sic ordinat. Et ecce nunc obstupescunt & blasphemant vos in eo, quòd non exardescitis cum ipsis in eadem crapula pristina.

## 4:5
WHO SHALL RENDER AN ACCOUNT TO HIM, WHO IS READY TO JUDGE THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.

Connection. 1. The Apostle amplifies the impiety of the Gentiles by the indication of the punishment which they will one day sustain on account of their contempt of the Gospel and the blasphemies cast against the Christian religion.

2. He admonishes the faithful, lest they be broken in spirit on account of the insults of the infidels, but that they should commend their cause to GOD, the just judge and avenger.

3. He consoles the pious against the blasphemies of the impious, from the future judgment of God. Beda in h. l. Therefore care less, grieve less, if while doing good you are blasphemed by the reprobate, because even if you are silent, God, who is indeed a just judge, will not be silent nor restrained, who will restore to them their due rewards for their blasphemy and to you for your patience.

4. A new reason for exhortation, by which he brandishes a grave threat against the blaspheming Gentiles, so that he may both deter them from the impurity of life and those blasphemies, and add a spur to the pious in the straight course of a holy life. A most grave punishment hangs over those who speak evil and are contemners of a holy life. Therefore, one must strive by all means for the holiness of life. God will bring all things into judgment, whether they be good or evil, and will affect the good with rewards and the evil with punishments. Therefore, one must renounce impiety and pursue the study of piety.

Exposition of the text. Οἵ ἀποδώσουσι λόγον. The metaphor is taken from stewards, who are compelled to render an account of their dispensation to the fathers of families and their masters. Matth. 18. v. 23.cap. 25. v. 19.Luc. 16. vers. 2. τῷ ἑτοίμως ἔχοντι κρῖναι ζῶντας καὶ νεκροὺς Vulg. To him who is ready to judge. In Greek who has in readiness, to whom it is most ready to judge &c.Actor. 21. vers. 13. ἑτοίμως ἔχω δεθῆναι I will suffer myself to be bound with a most ready mind.2. Corinth. 12. v. 14. ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ἡμᾶς. The LXX ἔτοιμον εἶναι & ἑτοίμως ἔχειν use for עתיד, which the Syrian also uses in this place, which not only signifies to be ready, prepared and intent, but also to be imminent, to be at handDeut. 32. vers. 35.Esth. 3. vers. 14.cap. 8. vers. 13.Dan. 3. v. 15. which signification agrees beautifully with this place, for immediately it follows, but the end of all things approachesv. 7. because the consummation of the world will be immediately joined with the final judgment. And for this reason, the passage Iac. 5. vers. 9. is parallel to this place, Behold the judge stands before the door.

John Huss warns, that this judge is said to be prepared to judge, in contrast to the judges of this age, whom it behooves first to hear witnesses, to investigate the case, to examine the accused, before he judges: but this judge is prepared to deliver a sentence, not awaiting a long production of witnesses. He will judge, however, not only the living, but also the dead, having first been recalled to life, and thus all men. A parallel passage is held Acts 10. v. 42. he is appointed Judge of the living and the dead.

Latin:

QUI REDDENT RATIONEM EI, QUI PARATUS EST IUDICARE VIVOS & MORTUOS.

Connexio. 1. Amplificat Apostolus impietatem gentium indicatione poenae, quam olim sustinebunt ob contemtum Evangelii & blasphemias in religionem Christianam coniectas.

2. Admonet fideles, ne ob infidelium convitia animis frangantur, sed DEO iusto iudici ac vindici causam suam commendent.

3. Consolatur pios contra blasphemias impiorum, à futuro Dei iudicio. Beda in h. l. Ideo minùs curate, minùs dolete, si benefacientes blasphemamini à reprobis, quia etsi vos tacueritis, non tamen tacebit neque compescetur Deus iudex utique iustus, qui & illis blasphemiae suae & patientiae vestrae vobis praemia digna restituet.

4. Nova exhortationis ratio, qua gravem in blasphemantes gentiles vibrat comminationem, ut & eos â vitae impuritate & blasphemiis illis deterreat, & piis in recto vitae sanctae cursu calcar addat. Maledicis vitae sanctae contemtoribus gravissima impendet poena. Ergò vitae sanctitati modis omnibus studendum. Omnia in iudicium Deus adducet, sive bona fuerint sive mala, ac bona praemiis, mala poenis afficiet. Ergò impietati renunciandum, pietatis studium sectandum.

Textus expositio. Οἵ ἀποδώσουσι λόγον. Metaphora sumta est ab oeconomis, qui patribus familias ac dominis suis rationem dispensationis suae reddere coguntur. Matth. 18. v. 23.cap. 25. v. 19.Luc. 16. vers. 2.τῷ ἑτοίμως ἔχοντι κρῖναι ζῶντας καὶ νεκροὺς Vulg. Ei qui paratus est iudicare. Graecè qui in promtu habet, cui promtissimum est iudicare &c.Actor. 21. vers. 13.ἑτοίμως ἔχω δεθῆναιanimo promtissimo patiar me ligari.2. Corinth. 12. v. 14.ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ἡμᾶς. LXX. ἔτοιμον εἶναι & ἑτοίμως ἔχειν utuntur pro עתיד, quo etiam Syrus hoc loco utitur, quod non solùm significat promtum, paratum & intentum esse, sed etiam imminere, inproximo esseDeut. 32. vers. 35.Esth. 3. vers. 14.cap. 8. vers. 13.Dan. 3. v. 15. quae significatio huic loco pulchrè congruit, statim enim sequitur, omnium autem finis appropinquatv. 7. quia mundi consummatio cum extremo iudicio immediatè erit coniuncta. Et hac ratione huic loco parallelus est locus Iac. 5. vers. 9.Ecce iudex ante ianuam assistit.

Iohannes Huss. monet, hunc iudicem dici paratum iudicare, ad differentiam iudicum huius seculi, quos oportet priùs testes audire, causam cognoscere, reum examinare, antequam iudicet: hic vero iudex ad sententiam ferendam paratus est, non expectando longam testium productionem. Iudicabit autem non vivos, sed etiam mortuos, in vitam priùs revocatos, adeoque omnes homines. Locus parallelus habetur Act. 10. v. 42.constitutus est Iudex vivorum & mortuorum.

## 4:6
FOR FOR THIS CAUSE WAS THE GOSPEL PREACHED ALSO TO THEM THAT ARE DEAD, THAT THEY MIGHT BE JUDGED ACCORDING TO MEN IN THE FLESH, BUT LIVE ACCORDING TO GOD IN THE SPIRIT.

Connection. Those who interpret this passage concerning the descent of Christ to the underworld, hand down such a connection. So that you may understand that not only the living, but also the dead are to be judged by Christ, the Gospel was preached by him not only to the living in the days of his flesh, but also to the dead, when after death he descended to the places of the dead, to hell.

Those who explain it concerning the preaching done in the times of Noah, hand down this reason for the connection: Because remembering the future judgment he had made mention of the dead, on that occasion he repeats the history concerning those dead who were punished by the flood, and thus by the example of that judgment he confirms the proposition set forth by an argument from parity, and at the same time he warns to what end that corporal punishment was profitable for some. But because this Apostolic passage is more correctly understood concerning the spiritually dead, therefore another reason for the connection must be shown. 1. The Apostle had said that the Gentiles, who were wantonly blaspheming the Christian religion and its confessors, would render an account to Christ who is to judge the living and the dead. The Apostle adds, etc., for this reason also the Gospel of God was preached by command to the impious Gentiles, who were spiritually dead and knew nothing of Christ, so that they might be saved and live to God spiritually, even if they are punished in the flesh by the Lord in this life after the manner of men on account of preceding enormous sins. 1. Cor. 5. v. 5.

2. By that very thing, however, the Apostle hints that they would not have anything which they could plead as an excuse, since the Gospel had been preached to them also, which nevertheless they were unwilling to receive by faith, whence they are condemned by the just judgment of God, while the rest who embraced it by faith are freed from the judgment of condemnation.

3. A new reason for the exhortation is added, taken from the end of the Evangelical preaching, which is our regeneration and salvation, which however has no place without the mortification of the flesh. We shall add other expositions, and the reasons for the connection taken from them, in q. 1.

Disposition. The Apostle explains the Evangelical preaching. 1. The object, which is men spiritually dead in sins. 2. The end, and that a double one ἀντιθετικῶς opposed to each other, that they might indeed be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit.

Exposition. Ἐὶς τοῦτο γὰρ. The Vulgate rendered for this. But in the Greek it is not διὰ τοῦτο, but εἰς τοῦτο to this, which phrase hints that the causality signified by it is not to be referred to the preceding part of the discourse, but to the following. Ioh. 18. v. 37. εἰς τοῦτο to this I was born, καὶ εἰς τοῦτο & to this I came into the world, that I might bear witness to the truth, Rom. 14. v. 9. εἰς τοῦτο for to this Christ both died and rose again, that he might have dominion both over the dead and the living. The Syrian has [consult facsimile image] for this reason. καὶ νεκροῖς εὐηγτελίσθη. The Gospel was preached even to the dead. For this verb is placed impersonally, so that the sense may be, the preaching of the Gospel was done to them. The Syrian has the verb [consult facsimile image] from the root [consult facsimile image] he announced joyful and pleasing things. In Hithpael, he received a good and joyful message.

῝Ινα κριθῶσι μὲν κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπους σαρκὶ, ζῶσι δὲ κατὰ θεὸν πνεύματι. Vulg. that they might be judged indeed according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit. The little word ἵνα looks back to the preceding causal εἰς τοῦτο. For the Gospel was preached also to the dead, and that in this, that is, to this end, that they might be judged. The verb κριθῶσι placed in the aorist has not the signification of future time, but rather of past. He speaks therefore of a judgment which had already been done, or which could and ought to have been done. To the little words σαρκὶ in Greek is not added the preposition ἐν σαρκὶ, which however the Latin Interpreter, as also the Syrian, expressed. To the little words πνεύματι likewise in Greek is not added the preposition ἐν πνεύματι, which however in certain Latin Codices and in the Syriac paraphrase is expressed. But what is understood by to be judged according to men in the flesh and by to live according to God in the Spirit, will be explained below in q. 3. τὸ τὸ

Latin:

PROPTER HOC ENIM & MORTUIS EVANGELIZATUM EST, UT IUDICENTUR QUIDEM SECUNDUM HOMINES IN CARNE, VIVANT AUTEM SECUNDUM DEUM SPIRITU.

Connexio. Qui de descensu Christi ad inferos locum hunc accipiunt, tradunt eiusmodi connexionem. Ut intelligatis non solùm vivos, sed etiam mortuos à Christo iudicandos, non vivis tantùm ab ipso in diebus carnis praedicatum est Evangelium, sed etiam mortuis, quando post mortem ad loca mortuorum ad infernum se. descendit.

Qui de praedicatione facta temporibus Noae exponunt, tradunt hancce connexionis rationem. Quia iudicium futurum comremorans mentionem fecerat mortuorum, eâ occasione repetit Historiam de illis mortuis, qui puniti fuerunt diluvio, atque ita illius iudicii exemplo sententia propositam per rationem à pari confirmat, simulque monet, ad quid poena illa corporalis nonnullis profuerit. Sed quia de spiritualiter mortuis locus hic Apostolicus rectiùs accipitur, ideò alia connexionis monstranda est ratio. 1. Dixerat Apostolus gentiles religionem Christianam eiusdemque confessores protervè blasphemantes reddituros rationem Christo vivos & mortuos iudicaturo. Subiungit Apostolus &c. propterea etiam impiis gentibus, quae erant spiritualiter mortuae, neque quidquam de Christo noverant, Evangelium Dei mandato esse praedicatum, ut salventur & vivant Deo spiritualiter, etiamsi more humano à Domino in hac vita castigentur in carne propter antegressa enormia delicta. 1. Cor. 5. v. 5.

2. Eo ipso autem innuit Apostolus eos non habituros, quod obtendere possint, cum ipsis quoque Evangelium fuerit praedicatum, quod tamen fide recipere noluerunt, unde iusto Dei iudicio damnentur, reliquis qui fide illud amplexi sunt, à iudicio damnationis liberatis.

3. Subiungitur nova exhortationis ratio desumta à fine praedicationis Evangelicae, qui est nostra regeneratio & salvatio, quae tamen absque carnis mortificatione non habet locum. Alias expositiones, & ex iis desumtas connexionis rationes subiungemus q. 1.

Dispositio. Exponit Apostolus praedicationis Evangelicae. 1. obiectum, quod sunt homines spiritualiter in peccatis mortui. 2. finem eundemque duplicem ἀντιθετικῶς sibi invicem oppositum, ut iudicentur quidem secundùm homines in carne, vivant autem secundùm Deum Spiritu.

Expositio. Ἐὶς τοῦτο γὰρ. Vulgata reddidit propter hoc. Sed in Graeco non est διὰ τοῦτο, sed εἰς τοῦτοad hoc, quae phrasis innuit causalitatem eâdem significatam non ad praecedentem orationis partem, sed ad sequentem referendam esse. Ioh. 18. v. 37.εἰς τοῦτοad hoc natus sum,καὶ εἰς τοῦτο& ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhiberem veritati,Rom. 14. v. 9.εἰς τοῦτοad hoc enim Christus & mortuus est & resurrexit, ut & mortuis & viventibus dominaretur. Syrus habet [consult facsimile image]propter hoc.καὶ νεκροῖς εὐηγτελίσθη. Etiam mortuis evangelizatum sive Evangelium praedicatum est. Verbum enim hoc ponitur impersonaliter, ut sit sensus, Evangelii praedicatio ipsis facta. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] à rad. [consult facsimile image] annunciavit laeta & grata. In Hithpaël, bonum ac laetum nuncium accepit.

῝Ινα κριθῶσι μὲν κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπους σαρκὶ, ζῶσι δὲ κατὰ θεὸν πνεύματι. Vulg. ut iudicentur quidem secundùm homines in carne, vivant autem secundùm Deum Spiritu. Vocula ἵνα respicit praecedens causale εἰς τοῦτο. Nam & mortuis evangelizatum est, idque in hoc, id est, in hunc finem, ut iudicarentur. Verbum κριθῶσι positum in aoristo non futuri temporis, sed potiùs praeteriti significationem habet. Loquitur ergò de iudicio, quod iam factum, vel quod fieri poterat & debebat. Voculae σαρκὶ in Graeco non additur praepositio ἐν σαρκὶ, quam tamen Latinus Interpres, uti etiam Syrus expressit. Voculae πνεύματι itidem in Graeco non additur praepositio ἐν πνεύματι, quae tamen in quibusdam Codicibus Latinis & in Syriaca paraphrasi exprimitur. Quid autem per τὸiudicari secundùm homines carne ac per τὸvivere secundùm Deum Spiritu intelligatur, explicabitur inferiùs q. 3.

## 4:6-7 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place 1. Who are to be understood by the dead in this place? Resp. Some accept of the dead, naturally, some of the dead spiritually such. Those who explain the Apostolic place concerning the dead naturally such, some of them take the name of the dead indefinitely for any dead persons, before this writing of Peter, or even before the coming of Christ deceased; But some definitely and determinately concerning a certain kind of dead. Those who take the name of the dead indefinitely concerning any dead persons whatsoever, they establish that the sense is this, that the Gospel is not only preached to men still living in the flesh, but also was preached to those who are already dead, so that they too might be converted from sins to God and might escape the sentence of condemnatory judgment. Therefore, they hand down a connection of this kind. 1. The Apostle meets a tacit objection. For someone could think, how will not only the living, but also the dead be judged, since they have already perished? The Apostle answers that the dead are to be judged no less than those who now live, since the Gospel was announced also to the dead, namely to those who are indeed already dead, but formerly lived. For just as the dead, who have indeed already perished, will be judged when they are restored to life: so the Gospel was preached to the dead, who have indeed already perished, but formerly lived. 2. Such a reason for the connection can also be given. It could be objected that those who died before the coming of Christ into these lands would have an excuse in judgment, because they did not hear the preaching of the Gospel. Peter denies this, and teaches that the Gospel was preached also to the dead, since the doctrine concerning the Messiah sounded perpetually in the Church not only in the New, but also in the Old Testament. 3. But this connection can also be given, so that it may be said, the Apostle wished to teach by these words that death is no obstacle to Christ being nonetheless our avenger and liberator. For however much liberation may not happen in this life, but we are compelled to struggle even to blood and death for the truth of the Gospel Hebr. 12. v. 4. nevertheless our hope of redemption will not be empty or void on that account, because the power of this our liberator extends even to the dead. This exposition concerning the dead taken naturally and indefinitely contains nothing at all contrary to the analogy of faith, and therefore we leave it in its place and judge that it can be entirely tolerated. Those who take the passage concerning the dead taken naturally and definitely, that is, concerning a certain kind of dead, some of them. 1. expound it concerning those dead, whose souls at the time when Christ descended into hell, were established in hell. They think that this passage is parallel to that which preceded in cap. 3. v. 19., in which also coming he preached to the spirits who were in prison. But they in turn depart into two classes. Some wish that Christ in his descent to the underworld preached the Gospel to the souls of the damned, so that some of them he might convert and transfer with himself into the heavenly kingdom. But we have refuted this opinion above, inasmuch as it fights with the analogy of faith. Some, however, maintain that Christ in his descent into hell did not so much by words as by the thing itself proclaim his victory to the spirits of the damned and manifest to them the just cause of their damnation, because they were unwilling to embrace by faith the Gospel that was preached to them also while they were among the living. This exposition indeed contains nothing fighting with the analogy of faith, meanwhile it is less conformable to the text. For 1. The Apostle does not express that that preaching was done by Christ in his own person among the dead. 2. The word of evangelizing is always taken in a good sense, nor can the contrary be demonstrated by any example, therefore in this place it cannot be taken for a declaration of damnation. 3. Nor is it yet proven that 1. Petr. 3. v. 19. must necessarily be taken concerning Christ's descent into hell. 4. And even if it were most strongly treated there concerning this descent, it is not yet demonstrated that this place of ours is altogether parallel to that.

2. Some therefore by the name of the dead take the spirits of the blessed in heaven, which exposition is directly opposed to the former. They urge the force of the word εὐηγγελίσθη, so that the sense may be, that the Gospel was preached by Christ to the pious even after death, because the redemption was already perfected, which preaching they say was done in the ascension to the heavens. But this exposition labors under the difficulty that it can hardly be said of the spirits of the blessed that they are to be judged according to men in the flesh; just as it can hardly be said of the spirits of the damned that they are to live according to God in the Spirit, and therefore the following words of the Apostle do not fit either exposition sufficiently aptly.

3. Some expound concerning the limbo of the Fathers.

4. Some concerning purgatory, from both of which Christ liberated souls in his descent into hell, and by this reason evangelized to them, i.e., brought the good news concerning liberation from limbo and purgatory, fire. But we showed in the preceding chapter that these expositions fight with the analogy of faith.

5. Some take it concerning those dead who lived in the times of Noah, to whom Christ at that time, when they still lived on earth, evangelized through Noah, of whom some, doing penance when the flood was inundating, were judged according to men in the flesh, i.e., their bodies perished in the flood, but meanwhile they live according to the Spirit To God, that is, their souls were translated into heavenly glory and happiness after death, so that by this reasoning the present passage is parallel to that which preceded in c. 3. v. 19. But this parallelism has not yet been proven. For there, mention is made expressly of those who lived in the times of Noah, but here it is simply said, that the Gospel was preached to the dead. Meanwhile, regarding this exposition, the same judgment holds as for that by which the name of the dead is taken indefinitely for those naturally dead, namely, that it does not conflict with the analogy of faith.

6. This exposition of Johannes Hesselius of Louvain and Pererius, 1. 9. in Genes. Disp. 30. n. 91., was fought against, by which they understand by the dead those about to die, or those near to death, who are situated on the border of death. Matth. 9. v. 18. my daughter is just now dead, i. e. is in extremis, as is explained Marc. 5. v. 23. Luc. 8. v. 42. Thus 2. Cor. 11. v. 23. in deaths often, i. e. in dangers of death. 1. Cor. 15. v. 31. I die daily, i. e. I am established in dangers of death. In the same sense some accept v. 29. of the same chapter. What do they do who are baptized for the dead? They therefore maintain, that Peter proves by a similar argument from the preaching which is done to those about to die, that the dead are to be judged, just as Paul proves the resurrection from the Baptism of the dying dead. Estius refutes this exposition of Hesselius with three arguments. 1. because it does not agree with the passage of the preceding chapter v. 19. 2. The Apostle does not say, it is preached, but it was preached. 3. in the verse immediately preceding, the dead are understood properly. Therefore also in this place. But it would be easy for Hesselius to respond to these arguments. That, however, is deservedly urged, that no reason appears why we should wish to accept the Apostolic text concerning those about to die rather than the dead. For that which Peter is said to prove by a similar argument, that the dead are to be judged from the preaching which is done to those about to die, just as Paul proves the resurrection of the dead from the Baptism of the dying, 1. Cor. 15. v. 29. is a light conjecture.

7. Most simply, therefore, by the dead, to whom the Apostle asserts the Gospel was preached, are understood those spiritually dead in sins, especially the Gentiles, blaspheming the Christian religion, and proceeding securely in sins, to whom, just as to the faithful Jews, Christ wished the Gospel to be preached, so that an approach to salvation might be opened to them also; and so that they could have no excuse in judgment. Augustine, Epist. 99. to Evodius. It is possible that he called the infidels dead, that is, dead in soul, of whom it is said. Let the dead, that they may bury their own dead. But the living who believe in him, not hearing in vain. Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you, of whom the Lord himself also says. The hour will come, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and they who have heard, shall live. Therefore also this which follows: For this cause also was the gospel preached to the dead &c. does not compel one to understand it as being among the dead in the underworld. For therefore in this life was it preached to the dead, that is, to the unfaithful and the wicked, so that when they have believed, they may indeed be judged according to men in the flesh, that is, in diverse tribulations and in the very death of the flesh, whence the same Apostle says in another place, that it is time for judgment to begin at the house of the Lord, but that they may live according to God in the Spirit, because they also had been mortified in him, when they were held by the death of infidelity and impiety. Bede on this passage: So great is the care of God, so great the love, so great the desire to mortify us in the flesh, but to vivify us in the spirit, that he commanded the word of faith to be preached even to those who are involved in greater crimes and are rightly to be named among the dead, namely, in luxuries, desires, drunkenness, gluttony, carnal drinking, and illicit cults of idols, so that even they, being judged, i. e. having spurned and cast off carnal desires, may live spiritually, together with those whom he found living innocently by the grace of the Gospel, they may await eternal life. Luther on this passage: The Apostle says concerning the dead, that they are judged in the flesh. Now truly the naturally dead do not have flesh, therefore it is understood of men living on earth. The dead are therefore understood as the unfaithful, who are judged in the flesh, but live in the Spirit, when they are reborn. In almost the same way Vatablus explains it, taking the dead as those to whom the gospel had not yet been preached, so that before they were held as if dead, afterwards as if living in the Spirit, because they were endowed with charity and abstaining from sins. This exposition: 1. agrees with the scope and context, as the reason for the connection handed down above shows. 2. agrees with the phrase of Scripture, in which the name of the dead is attributed to those who are alienated from the life of God, i. e. who are spiritually dead. Luke 9. v. 60.John 5. v. 25.1. Tim. 5. v. 6. &c. 3. agrees with the purpose of the preaching, which the Apostle assigns in this place, as will appear from q. 3. Salmero, vol. 16. Disp. 7. p. 93. urges against this passage, that the living are distinguished from the dead in the words of the Apostle. And if by the dead were understood the spiritually dead, they could not be distinguished from the living. Resp. Augustine in v. 5. likewise understands the spiritually dead by the dead, by which reasoning the nerve of the argument is cut. But because we showed above in v. 5. that it is understood naturally We therefore answer differently regarding the dead, namely that such an antanaclasis and diverse signification of the same word is not infrequent in the Scriptures, a fact which could be demonstrated by many examples. Primarily, the passage John 5, verse 25 & verse 28 pertains to this, where likewise the naturally dead are joined with the spiritually dead.

8. Arias Montanus likewise understands by the name of the dead the spiritually dead, but he explains it of that blessed death, by which the pious die to sin Rom. 6, v. 2 not of that unhappy death, by which the impious are said to be dead in sins Eph. 2, v. 1 Col. 2, v. 13 so that the sense is, that the message would be brought to those dead in Christ spiritually, that although they were considered similar to other men, as far as external hope pertains, yet in the Spirit of God they referred to the son J. C., who being found in fashion as a man Phil. 2, v. 7 yet the man was the son of God. In the same way Alcasar in Apoc. 20 ann. 18, It was evangelized to the dead by the Apostles, i. e. to the faithful, who are dead to sin & the world, so that they may patiently bear being judged in the flesh, i. e. condemned, tortured & killed for Christ, knowing that in the tribunal of God their cause is to be adjudged to them, and they are to be gifted with the reward of eternal life, so that, namely, they may live before God in an immortal, most joyful & most blessed Spirit.

Q. 2. What is signified by the word to evangelize? Resp. The Gospel 1. is taken properly & specifically for the doctrine concerning the gratuitous remission of sins through faith in Christ, whether still to be exhibited or already exhibited. Isa. 61, v. 1 Matt. 11, v. 5 Mark 1, v. 15 Romans 1, v. 16 &c. 2. Akin to this signification is that by which it is used concerning the public proclamation of the exhibited Messiah and the solemn promulgation of the N. T. Mark 1, v. 1 Rom. 1, v. 2, 3 γενικως is taken for the whole ministry of the N. T., which embraces not only the doctrine of grace, but also of the law. Mark 16, v. 15 where, however, it must be noted that it is not inconvenient to posit a Synecdoche in those pronouncements which express the whole teaching ministry by the name of the Gospel, so that the whole may be understood from the more worthy & better part. Therefore, some take the word to evangelize in the first signification, namely those who explain this passage concerning the faithful in the O. T. dead before the coming of Christ. The same is maintained by those who take it concerning the preaching done in the times of Noah. But because we have already shown before that the Apostle is primarily dealing with the calling of the Gentiles who were spiritually dead and immersed in more grievous sins, which took place in the N. T., therefore it is more fitting that the voice of the Gospel be taken in the second signification here, which includes the first and third together, because with that public proclamation of the exhibited Messiah, the doctrine of both the Law and the Gospel, properly so called, was joined. As for the fact that some explain the word of evangelizing as the manifestation of damnation, and others as the preaching of liberation from limbo or purgatory, that is entirely foreign to the use of this word in the Scriptures.

Q. 3. What is to be understood by Τὸ being judged according to men in the flesh, and by Τὸ living according to God in the Spirit? Resp. This judgment can be understood either in a good or in a bad sense. And likewise either as past, or present, or future. Life also can be understood either of the soul alone, or of the whole man; from this, various interpretations arise. 1. Those who take this passage concerning the preaching done in the times of Noah, establish that it is taught by the Apostle in these words, for what purpose bodily punishment profited some who were destroyed in the flood, namely, that through it the preaching of the Gospel, which they had heard from Noah and had kept heard in their heart, might be rendered effective, namely, that in the flesh indeed, i.e., in the body they were judged and punished, to wit, by the waters of the flood, and that according to men, i.e., as far as the knowledge of men is concerned, who could discern, and still can, in them a manifest example of divine judgment against the despisers of the word: yet they lived according to God in the Spirit, i.e., they obtained eternal life and salvation through repentance and faith, by which they believed the Gospel previously preached to them, and that according to God, i.e., by the grace of the merciful God, and with Him alone being conscious, since He alone is καρδιογνώστης, and knows who are His 2. Tim. 2. v. 21. This exposition is confirmed by the fact that flesh and Spirit seem to be opposed to each other in this way 1. Cor. 5. v. 5. I have judged him who has done this, to deliver him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the Spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus; that 1. Cor. 11. v. 31. & 32. the word judging is taken concerning bodily punishments; finally, that salvation is attributed to souls elsewhere in this Epistle κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν. cap. 1. v. 9. According to this exposition, the former member (that they might be judged according to men in the flesh) would not be placed as the final cause of the preached Gospel, but would have to be explained by an adversative conjunction in this way. The Gospel was preached even to the dead, to wit, in the times of Noah, so that although they were judged, i.e., punished in the flesh or body, when they were miserably destroyed in the flood, and indeed according to men, i.e., publicly, in the knowledge of men: yet they might live happily and blessedly on account of Christ, in the Gospel preached and finally apprehended by true faith, in the Spirit, that is, in the soul, which God, having freed it from the prison of the body, made a participant of heavenly glory, while the flesh suffers temporal corruption, which spiritual and heavenly life belongs to them according to God, that is, before God, although the world may not know or believe that they live before God. 2. This exposition can have a place, even if the little word of the dead is not taken determinately for those who once lived in the times of Noah, but generally for any who died before the coming of Christ: for from the beginning of the world the Gospel was preached to men, so that even if they are punished in the flesh after the human manner on account of sins, they nevertheless live and are saved in the Spirit before God. 3. Moreover, this exposition also has a place, even if the little word of the dead is taken concerning the spiritually dead. For God caused the Gospel to be announced by the Apostles to the Gentiles, who were spiritually dead, for this reason, that they might be saved in the Spirit according to God, even if they are judged in the flesh on account of preceding sins in this life, that is, are subject to tribulations and to death itself. Thus Augustine explains in Epistle 99 to Evodius. None of these expositions conflicts with the analogy of faith. 4. Some explain it concerning the perverse and preposterous judgment of the Pharisees, in this sense. Even to the dead that is, to the most grievous sinners, infamous on account of their public and notorious crimes, it was evangelized, namely, by John the Baptist, Christ, and the Apostles. For it is known from the Evangelical history that John preached the Gospel even to publicans, and thus to notorious sinnersLuke 3. v. 12.that publicans and sinners approached Christ, that they might hear himLuke 15. v. 1.that Christ said to the Chief Priests and Pharisees to their face, publicans and harlots go before you into the kingdom of God.Matthew 21. verse 31.that he said to the sinful woman, your sins are forgiven youLuke 7. Verse 48.that he absolved the adulteressJohn 8. v. 10.But therefore it was evangelized even to those infamous sinners, so that according to men that is, the Pharisees, (who justified themselves before menLuke 16. verse 15.and who trusted in themselves that they were just and despised othersc. 18. v. 8.) judging according to the flesh,John 8. v. 15.judging according to the facec. 7. v. 24.and looking only at external things, judged and condemned according to the flesh that is, carnally, they might live in the Spirit according to God that is, renewed in the Spirit, they might be rendered participants of eternal life. 5. Conformable to this is the exposition of Lyranus. To the dead, that is, to the infidels it was preachedMatthew 8. v. 22.so that the believers might be condemned according to men, that is, by men living carnally, but they might live according to God. From conversion to the faith these two things follow, but the first occasionally, the second from the intention of those evangelizing the faith. Neither of these expositions fights with the analogy of faith. John Huss, in this place, that they might indeed be judged i. e. that believers might be condemned by men living carnally, but they might live a spiritual life according to God. 6. Those who maintain that Christ in his descent into hell freed certain ones from hell, or purgatory, or certainly limbo, and take the words of the Apostle concerning this liberation, bring forward such an exposition. Even to the dead established in hell or purgatory or limbo it was evangelized, namely by Christ descending into hell, so that to those who lived according to man in the flesh, that is, lived carnally, it might be for condemnation; but to those who lived according to God in the Spirit, that is, led a spiritual life, it might be ready for glory, honor, and liberation. But Scripture knows nothing at all about the liberation of certain ones from hell or purgatory or limbo. 7. Those who take the Apostolic passage concerning the preaching made to the spirits of the blessed at the ascension of Christ above all the heavens, assert that the Apostle means this, that they are indeed to be set before the tribunal of Christ, because they are men, and yet they will not come into judgment, but will pass from death to life: whence they are said to be about to live in spirit according to God or the Spirit of God, because they see God even up to the judgment. Closely approaching this is that which some maintain is the sense of the Apostolic saying. Although according to the reason of the world the dead suffer destruction in their flesh, and are held to be condemned as to the external man, they nevertheless do not cease to live before God, and that in spirit, because Christ has vivified them by his Spirit. The Spirit is life, therefore it absorbs what is left of death in us. Rom. 8. v. 10. 8. Conformable to this exposition is that by which it is said that the Gospel was preached to the dead before the judgment of Christ to this end, that even if they are condemned to death before the Lord has arrived, they may nevertheless live in spirit before God by the virtue of the Gospel which they received by faith in this life, being about to receive their flesh when the Lord arrives to judge. Lorinus in almost the same way. So that just as the nature of men composed of flesh demands, they may be judged publicly and openly when they have resumed their flesh in the general resurrection, but they may live a life in a certain way spiritual, with the flesh itself spiritualized, if I may so speak. But anyone sees that both expositions are forced. 9. Most simply, therefore, by τὸ to be judged according to men in the flesh is understood the condemnation and abolition of the old man, that is, of the carnal conversation, according to men walking in carnal concupiscences; through τὸ to live according to God in the Spirit, a spiritual life according to the new man conformed to the divine will. Thus Bede explains in his commentary that they might be judged, that is, having spurned carnal desires, they might live spiritually. John Huss on this passage: That they might be judged, namely, in the present by themselves, that is, through the mortification of the flesh concerning their human deeds, which they committed while living carnally in the flesh, but that they might live a spiritual life, which is according to God. For to be judged, or to be condemned in the flesh, to suffer in the flesh, not to be in the flesh, to be dead to sin, are ἰσοδυναμοῦντα; to the Apostles, just as also on the contrary, to live in the Spirit, not to live according to the desires of men, but according to the will of God, to walk in newness of life, to live together with Christ, to live to God in Christ, they declare to be entirely the same in the Apostolic School. Therefore the Apostle expresses the end of the preached Gospel; which already from the beginning of the world; but especially in the New Testament through the Apostles, for the same reason the Gospel had been preached to the Gentiles who were spiritually dead, for which reason it is still announced in the Church, so that with the flesh of sin abolished and the old man mortified, a new and holy life conformed to the divine will might be begun in men by the Holy Spirit; so that the sinful flesh might perish more, so that sin might be mortified and abolished: which sin, since it clings to the nature of men, and is intimately fixed in it Heb. 12. v. 1., therefore the Apostle adds, according to man; but that they might live according to God in the Spirit, that is, that they might lead a holy life conformed to the will of God under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. In this sense the word to be judged is taken 1. Cor. 11. v. 31. If we would judge ourselves, in true repentance through the mortification of the flesh, we would not be judged, that is, punished by the Lord, and sin is said to be condemned in the flesh, when sin is mortified in the flesh of the reborn man, so that it may no longer reign Rom. 8. v. 3. for he who is condemned, together with life loses all power and dominion. 10. Those also approve this exposition who, if not indeed the end, yet establish that the sum of the Gospel, preached even to the dead, is explained by these words, and they take the Apostolic passage concerning the preaching before the coming of Christ in the Old Testament. Peter had said, they say, that the Gospel had been announced also in previous centuries, he wished therefore to subjoin the sum of that Gospel, partly so that he might teach that one and the same Gospel had always existed, partly so that he might return to his purpose. For those things concerning the judging of the living and the dead He said, not indeed rashly nor inappropriately, but yet παρὲγγως (by way of digression) he said, when he had happened upon the mention of the impious. He had, however, begun to discourse concerning sanctification, of which he had said there were two parts, namely, to have suffered in the flesh or to die to sin, and to live to the will of God. This very thing, therefore, is what he now says, had been announced also in previous ages. But it is more consistent with the text to take these words concerning the end of the preached Gospel, as the particle ἵνα, shows, corresponding to the preceding phrase εἰς τοῦτο.

Q. 4. Whether the vigilance and sobriety, to which the Apostle exhorts, pertain to the soul or to the body? Resp. The Apostle requires principally the vigilance and sobriety of the mind, less principally also the vigilance and sobriety of the body, namely, moderation in food, drink, and other bodily things, for without that, the vigilance and sobriety of the mind have no place. Bede in h. l. We are well commanded to watch in prayers, so that when we stand for prayer, neither the carnal and secular thought of man may approach, nor at that time may the mind think of anything except that alone which it prays. For the enemy frequently steals in and, subtly deceiving, so empties our prayers that we have one thing in our heart, and we utter another in our voice, since not the sound of the voice but the sense of the soul ought to pray to God with sincere intention.

Q. 5. Why does the Apostle require the sobriety and vigilance of the body? Resp. 1. On account of prayers, which without them have no place. Luc. 2. v. 34.Take heed, lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting v. 36.Watch therefore at all times, praying. Oecum. in h. l. The prayer and outpouring of petitions is of the sober i. e. of the vigilant and not of those who are lulled to sleep and oppressed by the drunkenness of worldly things. 2. On account of charity, to which he exhorts in the following verse. For unless the flesh is tamed through temperance and abstinence, charity toward one's neighbor cannot have a place. 3. Without a doubt the Apostle remembers his own fall in the garden, that, oppressed by sorrow and sleep, he did not watch in prayer, on account of which he had heard from the Master Matth. 26. v. 4.So, can you not watch one hour with me? v. 41.Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation.

Q. 6. Why does he exhort so solicitously to prayers? Resp. 1. In pious prayers consists the best preparation for judgment, concerning which the Apostle had dealt in the preceding. Luc. 21. v. 36.Watch therefore, praying at all times, that you may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of man. 2. Through prayers the soul is turned away from earthly and worldly things and lifted up to God, which is necessary for those who do not wish to perish with the perishing world, concerning which consummation of the world the Apostle had just spoken. 3. The spiritual strength of the Christian man depends solely upon God, to be obtained from Him through pious prayers. When, therefore, we are weak in ourselves, we must ask the Lord that He may strengthen and confirm us. 4. The increase of virtues, to which the Apostle exhorts in the following, is obtained solely through prayers. The Apostle therefore wishes that the faithful should always and vigilantly pray, so that God may preserve them in faith and piety, rule them by His Spirit, and continually increase His gifts in them.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Even to the dead was the Gospel preached. But God is not the God of the dead, but of the livingMatt. 22. v. 32.how therefore did He command the Gospel to be preached to the dead? Resp. 1. If the Apostle's statement is taken concerning those dead corporally (which exposition we have said is not to be disapproved), one must respond to the statement of Christ in the same way as to the Apostolic passage compared with it Rom. 14. v. 9. where Christ is said to be Lord of the living and the dead, namely, that Christ accommodates His response to the opinion of the Sadducees, who thought that man, like the brutes, is extinguished in both soul and body at once, and is never to be recalled to life. 2. But because we have said that the words of the Apostle are to be taken concerning those dead spiritually, it must be responded that God is indeed not the God of those spiritually dead in sins, i.e., He does not embrace them with special love, nor forgive their sins, nor make them partakers of eternal life, as long as they are and remain such (for that this phrase embraces this is shown in its place); meanwhile, however, He pursues them with general love, and seriously desires their salvation also, and therefore He also takes care that the Gospel be preached to them, so that when they have embraced it with faith, He may be able to embrace them with special love, forgive their sins, and make them partakers of eternal life.

2. The end of all things approaches. And yet more than one thousand five hundred years have flowed by since that time. Resp. 1. The time intermediate between the first and second coming of CHRIST, lasting from the promulgation of the Gospel until the end of the world, is called the last, because no further illustrious and universal manifestation of God is to be expected in this age. 1. Cor. 10. v. 11.The ends of the ages have come upon us.

Hebr. 1. v. 1.God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.1. Ioh. 2. v. 18.Little children, it is the last time. Certainly, from the time that Christ once appeared in His first coming, nothing else is left for the faithful than that they should always have their minds intent upon His second coming. 2. The Apostles therefore spoke of the second coming of Christ and the consummation of the age as if it were immediately impending, because, while they knew that they were living in the last time of the world, they were nevertheless ignorant of the day and hour of the coming of the Lord and the end of the world Marc. 13. v. 32.; therefore they spoke of it in such a way as those who were prepared at every moment to receive their Lord with joy. 3. The Apostle himself answers cap. 3. poster. Epist. v. 8. (from Psalm. 90. v. 4.) But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.v. 9.The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, &c. Certainly, in comparison with eternity, all time that will eventually end is short. 2. Corinth. 4. v. 17. & 18. 4. For every man, when he dies, the day of his judgment comes. For each person will be presented to the judge such as he is found in death. Therefore, even if the end of the macrocosm is greatly delayed, the end of the microcosm is always near. Aug. Epist. 80. Then that day will come to each one, when the day comes for him to depart from here, such as he is to be judged on that day. 5. B. Luther answers thus. Not as much time remains until the day of judgment as has already elapsed. 6. The pious ancients count seven ages of the world, of which they establish the first from Adam to Noah and the flood; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to Moses; the fourth from Moses to David; the fifth from David to the Babylonian captivity; the sixth from the Babylonian captivity to Christ; the seventh from Christ to the end of the world. Wherefore, since the Apostle wrote these things in the seventh age of the world, he could deservedly say, the end of all things is at hand.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. The Gospel was preached by the will of God even to the Gentiles, who were spiritually dead and immersed in the mire of the most grievous crimes, so that they might live in the Spirit according to GOD. Therefore, GOD has not reprobated any man to eternal damnation by some absolute hatred. For to those to whom GOD offers the benefits of Christ in the word of the Gospel, to them He also offers His grace and eternal life. But even to the Gentiles spiritually in sin dead, He offers the benefits of Christ. Therefore, He also offers His grace and eternal life, and consequently He did not reprobate them by some absolute decree. This must be opposed to the Calvinists, the architects of absolute reprobation, whom the Papists also support in part.

2. The end of the preached Gospel is the mortification of the flesh and the renewal of the Spirit, or the vivification of the new man. Therefore, it is a calumny by which the Papists weigh down the Evangelical doctrine, as if it granted a license to sin and undermined the pursuit of good works. Rom. 3. v. 8. The Cologne theologians in the Censura p. 176 assert, that the Evangelicals by their doctrine loosen the reins to all impiety, and give the opportunity to wicked men to commit any crimes whatsoever, so that they may draw more into their opinion. Iustus Baronius in Pseudoiubil. Luther spread among the common people such a kind of doctrine concerning justification by faith alone without works, by which, as if at an Epicurean trumpet, all were called away from holiness to license and profanity and flocked together.

5. Peter did not wish to define in what year and day the consummation of the age and the final judgment immediately joined to it is to be expected, but he says in a general and indeterminate way, the end of all things has drawn near. This must be opposed to the rashness of those who have dared to define a certain day of the final judgment. August. lib. 18. de civ. DEI cap. 53. having brought forward the words of Christ Act. 1. v. 7. It is not for you to know the times &c. he adds. In vain do we attempt to compute and define the years that remain for this age, since we hear from the mouth of Truth that to know this is not for us. And afterwards. He loosens the fingers of all who calculate concerning this matter, and commands them to be quiet, He who says: It is not for you to know the times. Durandus lib. 4. sent. dist. 47. q. 1. The time of judgment cannot be known to anyone with certainty, since it depends on the mere will of GOD, concerning the expression of which Scripture says nothing. Compare the article concerning the Final judgment § 78.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Some have long since wished to gather from this Apostolic passage that Christ descended to the underworld for this reason, that by the preaching of the Gospel He might free certain damned ones from hell. Irenaeus lib. 4. adv. haeres. cap. 45. p. 281. from the tradition of a certain Elder, who heard these things from those who had seen the Apostles, writes, that Christ descended into those things which are under the earth, evangelizing and to them His coming being the remission of sins for those who believe in Him. Clemens Alexandr.

Book 6 of the Stromata: It is said that Christ descended to the underworld, so that He might preach the Gospel to the damned minds, and bring the hope of salvation to those who believe. Oecumenius in his commentary on this passage: Just as when He came into the world, He came for the justification of those who were prepared to know Him, and for the condemnation of those who wished to be ignorant: so also to those who were in the underworld. For to those who had lived according to the flesh in the human manner, He came for judgment, but to those who had lived according to the Spirit, that is, according to a spiritual and honest life, for glory and salvation. Salmero in his commentary on verse 19 of the preceding chapter approaches this opinion most closely, whence he also cites and approves the words of Oecumenius in his commentary on this passage, and prefers his exposition to all others. And yet 1. This exposition fights against the analogy of faith, which teaches that there is no redemption from the underworld. 2. It implies a contradiction, that some were damned in the underworld to eternal punishments, and yet were afterwards saved. For eternal damnation includes the certainty of a punishment that is never to be ended. 3. Hence Philastrius in his book on heresies in the chapter on the descent into the underworld, and Augustine in his book on heresies to Quodvultdeus, chapter 79, say that it is a heresy if anyone asserts that any impious persons were converted and saved in the underworld while Christ was preaching. 4. This opinion took its origin from the heresy of the Marcionites, of whom Irenaeus writes in book 1 against heresies, chapter 29, page 83: Marcion taught that Cain and those who are like him, and the Sodomites and the Egyptians and those like them, and all the nations altogether, who walked in every mixture of wickedness (you hear the words of our Apostolic passage most wickedly twisted to this heresy) were saved by the Lord when He had descended into the underworld, and they had run to Him, and He had taken them into His kingdom. But Abel and Enoch, and Noah, and the remaining just men, and those who are with the Patriarch Abraham with all the Prophets and those who pleased God, did not participate in the salvation which was in Marcion, the serpent proclaimed. For because they knew, he says, their GOD always tempting them, and suspected that He was then tempting Him, they did not run to Jesus, nor did they believe His announcement, and for that reason he said that their souls remained in the underworld. 5. The end of Christ's descent into the underworld is not the preaching of the Gospel for the conversion and liberation of some, but the demonstration of a glorious victory, brought back from the Devil, death, and the underworld. 6. Oecumenius takes the words of Peter distributively, as if some are to be judged in the flesh according to men, but others are to live in the Spirit according to GOD, when nevertheless Peter predicates both of the same dead.

Thence 7. Estius refutes this exposition of Salmeron while suppressing his name. As for, he says, the spirits of the dead who are damned and reprobate, the gospel was no more to be preached to them by Christ having gone to the underworld than to the demons, whose companions they had become. Cornel. à Lap. refutes the exposition of Oecumenius, which Salmero prefers to all others, with the same argument which we brought forward a little earlier. Oecumenius, he says, posits two orders, one of those to be saved, another of those to be damned, and consequently makes them different from those who were vivified, whereas St. Peter seems to make them the same. For this is what those particles indeed and but signify, which are accustomed to be opposed to one another in the same subject.

2. Cornelius à Lapide takes this passage concerning the liberation of souls from limbo. Christ, he says, in order to show that he would judge the dead just as the living, descended to the dead Fathers dwelling in limbo, who in this life lived piously, chastely, and holily according to the Spirit, not according to the flesh, and to them he evangelized, i.e., he brought the joyful message of blessedness, namely by adjudging them to heaven and the blessed life, and by granting it to them in reality as if he were judge, so that although they are judged and esteemed according to men, i.e., to be dead by worldly men, τὸ (for it is clear that dead must be repeated here, from the antithesis which follows, but they may live) that is, to have perished completely in the flesh, and therefore to have been miserable and superstitious, or foolish, because while they lived, they spurned the pleasures of the flesh, and mortified and crucified it with its vices and concupiscences, so that they might assimilate themselves to Christ who later suffered and was crucified, yet the same ones live according to God, i.e., before God and by the gift of God in the Spirit of grace and heavenly glory.

3. Estius explains it concerning the liberation of souls from purgatory. For he compares this passage with v. 19. c. of the preceding and maintains, that it deals only with those who were established in the prison of purgatory, who had been incredulous in the days of Noah, and concerning others whose cause was similar, when they were detained in that prison. To them he says that Christ, in his descent to the underworld, preached the Gospel, so that although they were judged, i.e., punished in the flesh or body, when the waters of the flood suffocated them, they might nevertheless live happily and blessedly through the redemption of Christ, in the Spirit, i.e., in the soul, which Christ, by announcing the Gospel to them, made a participant of his glory. Fevardentius explains it in almost the same way. Resp. 1. Both the limbo of the Fathers and purgatory are dogmas ἀγραφα. 2. The Apostle does not say that that preaching was done immediately by Christ, but he speaks indeterminately and impersonally, ὲυηγγελίσθη. 3. Nor does he say, that the gospel was preached among the dead. 4. This passage is difficult and obscure, subject to various interpretations. Lorinus brings forward ten explanations, and finally adds, I agree with Ambrosius Catharinus, who ingenuously professes his own ignorance in the understanding of this passage. How, therefore, will the dogma of purgatory or of limbo be able to be proven from this passage, unless other clear sayings of Scripture support it? 5. Not even the Papists themselves agree in the explanation of this passage. We have just seen the exposition of Salmeron. Pererius, in his book on Genesis, Disp. 30, n. 91, understands by the dead those about to die, to whom the gospel is preached in this life. Vatablus understands of those who, before the Gospel was preached to them, were held as if dead. Arias Montanus of those who are spiritually dead in sin. All of them wish for this preaching of the Gospel to have been done in this life. Iacobus Andradius Paiva, in book 2 of the Defense of the Council of Trent, says that it was likewise preached to the dead, that is, to those who had long since been dead, because this doctrine is not new, so that they might be judged according to men in the flesh by pronouncing sentence against the sins which cling in the very flesh of man and are worthy of extreme punishment, by which persuasion of mind they are accustomed to be deterred, so that they might voluntarily submit themselves to be cultivated by the Spirit of GOD. 6. Moreover, Estius, who embraces the exposition concerning purgatory, refutes the exposition concerning limbo. For thus he argues in his commentary on this passage: What the Apostle said in the previous chapter, that Christ preached to the spirits who were in prison, is the same as that which he says here, that it was evangelized to the dead, except that some think this part can be extended to more, namely to all the dead who were capable of the fruits of the Gospel preached to them, whether they had already been received into the bosom of Abraham, fully purged, or were still subject to purgatorial punishments, whereas in the former opinion express mention had been made only of those spirits who were in prison, etc. But I rather judge it to be the mind of the Apostle that it is treated here only of those of whom he had treated before, that is, of the spirits established in the prison of purgatory, who had been incredulous in the days of Noah, and of others whose cause for being detained in that prison was similar. 7. Conversely, however, Lorinus repudiates this exposition concerning purgatory in his commentary on this passage, arguing thus: By what reason purgatory is proven from this, and all the souls of the just led out from there, as Fevardentius asserts, I do not indeed grasp. 8. But neither do those who explain this passage concerning the limbo of the Fathers agree among themselves. For thus writes Cornelius à Lapide in his commentary on this passage, exposit. 5. Others explain in this way, Christ descending to the dead Fathers detained in limbo evangelized and announced to them that they might be judged, in Greek κριθῶσι in the future, that is, that they are to be judged, and indeed on the day of judgment, according to men, that is, insofar as men, now revived, shall exist again in the flesh, for in it they are to rise again and go to judgment, but he announced to them equally that they who are to be judged are to be made alive in heaven by the Spirit of grace and eternal glory. But this exposition does not sufficiently explain the antithesis, which is in being judged in the flesh and being made alive in the Spirit; again between τὸ according to men and according to God; but it subjects and subordinates men to God, flesh to Spirit, and judgment to vivification. Therefore, he prefers the seventh exposition, which was expressed by his own words a little before. Compare those things which were said in the preceding chapter, v. 19.

4. Lorinus on v. 7 notes thus. Hugo well observed in his commentary on this place that men before the coming of Christ fled from death and desired life, because the dead lacked the vision of God, and at the same time were deprived of the opportunity of accumulating merits, [but] now the just desire to be dissolved, because they can immediately be with Christ. I reply 1. This opinion also rests upon the hypothesis concerning limbo, which is unknown to the Scriptures. 2. The pious of the O. T. just as the pious of the N. T. did not flee from death, but by faith in the promised Messiah overcame its terrors and sought the blessed ἀνάλυσιν. Gen. 49. v. 18. Jacob, about to die, says: I wait for thy salvation, O Lord. 2. Sam. 23. v. 1. These are the last words of David: The man who was raised up concerning Christ, the God of Jacob, said, etc. 1. Reg. 19. v. 4. Elijah prays: It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my soul, for I am no better than my fathers. 3. Bellarmine, in his book on the blessedness of the saints, c. 3, refutes that opinion, that the souls of holy men are kept until the day of the last judgment in certain hidden receptacles, where they do not see God, nor can they be called blessed, except in hope, not only by the sayings of the N. T. but also of the O. T. Eccl. 11. It is easy before GOD in the day of death to reward everyone according to his ways. He indeed adds: that Ecclesiasticus understood that a remuneration is rendered, such as could be had according to the diversity of times, and because heaven was not yet opened then, but now it has been opened by Christ, it follows from his opinion that on the day of death, and then, rest was accustomed to be given to the just, [but] now true happiness. But in this appendix the principle is begged. Christ is called the lamb slain from the foundation of the world Apoc. 13. vers. 8. therefore his passion and death were profitable before he was, consequently also by the virtue of the passion and death of Christ heaven was opened to the pious in the O. T. as well. 4. Concerning the souls of the pious of the O. T. the Holy Spirit speaks thus, that they are gathered in the bundle of the living 1. 25. v. 29. that they are in the hand of God, and torment shall not touch them Sap. 3. v. 2. and it is said concerning the soul of Lazarus before the passion and death of Christ, having been freed from the prison of the body, that it was carried by Angels into Abraham's bosom and soothed by consolation Luc. 16. vers. 22. it is said concerning the soul of the converted thief who died before Christ's descent into hell, Luc. 23. v. 43. that it was taken into Paradise. Concerning the saints of the O. T. it is said Hebr. 11. v. 10. that by faith they expected a city having foundations, whose builder and maker is God. v. 16. that they sought a heavenly country. and therefore their souls were not thrust down into some floor of hell after death, but were commended into the hands of GOD Psal. 31. v. 6. they returned to God, who gave them Eccl. 12. v. 7. The examples of the Patriarchs and Prophets of the O. T. also testify that their souls after the death of the body were not thrust down into some bosom of hell, but were carried up into heaven. Enoch was translated into Paradise Gen. 5. v. 24. Sir. 44. v. 16. according to the vulg. transl. cap. 49. v. 16. ἀνελήφθη ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς. Therefore he was not thrust down under the earth. Abraham the father of all believers Rom. 4. vers. 11. saw the day of the Messiah and was glad Ioh. 8. v. 56. and before the death of Christ was in that ποῦ to which the soul of Lazarus was carried Luc. 16. v. 22. where he received consolation. v. 25. which ποῦ is most distant and separated from hell v. 25. & 26. Elijah was carried up in a fiery chariot into heaven, but was not cast down into hell. 2. Reg. 2. v. 11. Sir. 48. v. 9. 1. Macc. 2. v. 58. etc. 5. Lorinus himself rejects the reason by which Hugo previously attempts to establish the member of his assertion. It does not seem, he says, a suitable proof of the former member, nor so true, that those ancients, who feared death, were accustomed to use that, The Lord liveth 2. Reg. 2. v. 6. and elsewhere throughout and therefore the Jews acclaimed to their King, Let the King live 1. Reg. 1. v. 9. and wished to those for whom they prayed well, that they might see children and children's children even unto the third and fourth generation Tob. 9. v. 11. But indeed the reasons by which the Jesuits attempt to prove the same thing are not of greater weight than that of Hugo. The opinion therefore collapses, deprived of suitable supports of proof.

5. Franciscus Turrianus lib. 2. de dogm. charact. determines that by prayers h. l. is understood the reception of the Eucharist, on account of which one must abstain from conjugal intercourse, which he proves from this, because the Syrian rendered, be chaste. Resp. 1. In the Greek it is σωφρονήσα τε, which means sobriety, temperance, modesty, prudence, but not properly chastity signifies. 2. This σωφροσύνη can also have a place in the very marriage of the pious, as the Apostle testifies 1. Timoth. 2. v. 15. ἡ γὰρ κοίτη ἀμίαιτος Hebr. 13. v. 4. hence Paphnutius in the Council of Nicaea said, that chastity is intercourse with one's own wife. 3. Lorinus rejects this exposition of Turrianus. It does not agree, he says, with the word vigil, and it seems a more general precept, and τὸ εἰς τὰς προσευχὰς denotes not only the perseverance of nocturnal prayer, but also that one must be vigilant by giving effort at such a time, as being more apt for prayers. 4. Estius in his commentary on 1. Cor. 7. v. 5. after he had said, that Paul in the place cited and Peter 1. Epist. 3. vers. 7. warn the faithful not to be so occupied with the conjugal work that they are hindered by this from receiving the Eucharist on appointed days, he adds. It is to be noted, that the Apostle does not permit the use of the marriage bed to be interrupted for the sake of prayer if one party requests it, but only by consent. But if anyone has been joined to his wife only for the sake of rendering the debt, he is not prohibited from communicating on the same day with the other faithful. Which thing Gregory also grants to him who is joined to his spouse solely for the desire of procreating offspring etc.

6. Lorinus in his commentary on this place reports us among the condemners of vigils, and opposes to us this Apostolic passage. Watch in prayers. I respond 1. The Apostle speaks primarily and principally of spiritual vigilance. 2. Secondarily he also requires a moderation of sleep necessary for serious prayers. 3. We do not simply disapprove of nocturnal vigils, undertaken for the sake of the ardor of prayers: for we know that David rose in the middle of the night to praise the Lord. Psalm. 119. v. 62. and preached that it is good to trust in the Lord, and to sing to the name of the Most High, to announce in the morning his mercy, and his truth through the night Psal. 92. v. 2. & 3. and to admonish the servants standing in the house of the Lord, that in the nights they lift up their hands in the sanctuary Ps. 134. 2. we know that Christ spent the night in prayer, Luc. 6. 12. and promised being heard to those who cry to God day and night Luc. 18. 7. but this we reprehend in the Papal vigils, that they foist them upon people under the opinion of necessity, worship, and merit, and that they are solicitous not so much about spiritual vigilance in prayers and the study of piety, as about bodily vigils. 4. Those vigils, on account of which Jerome so sharply attacks Vigilantius, and judges him to be called Dormitantius rather, have long since been antiquated in the Church, Erasmus notes in his annotations to that book of Jerome against Vigilantius.

7. The Euchites wished to gather from this Apostolic passage and others parallel to it, that every time of life is to be attributed to the recitation of prayers. I respond: to watch in prayers, ἀδιαλείπτως to pray,1. Thess. 5. v. 17. to pray always and not to faintLuc. 18. v. 1. to pray at all timesEph. 6. v. 18. to be instant in prayer, and to watch in the sameCol. 4. v. 2. does not signify that one should consecrate oneself entirely to the continuous and uninterrupted recitation of prayers, and always continue the external act of praying itself, which even hypocrites and heathens can do, Matth. 6. v. 7. but these phrases require: 1. Devotion of the mind, which ought always to be directed toward GOD, lest on account of diffidence in adversities we murmur against GOD, but patiently comply with Him, commending our whole selves to Him, and humbly awaiting His help; hence the Apostle notably adds Eph. 6. v. 18. that we ought to pray at all times in the Spirit. 2. Assiduous zeal in prayers, so that we may begin all our works with prayers, and end in them. Hence Augustine, in De haeresibus ad Quodvultdeum, chapter 57, teaches that the words of Christ and the Apostles are to be accepted thus, that no day should be passed without prayer. The Euchites, he says, pray so much that to those who hear this about them, it seems incredible. For when the Lord said, it behooves one to pray always, and not to faint; and the Apostle, pray without ceasing, which is most often understood thus, that certain times of praying are not to be omitted on any day, these people do this so excessively that they are judged from this to be numbered among the heretics. 3. These precepts of Christ and the Apostles can also be understood concerning continuous sighs, with which the pious groan to GOD at almost every moment, since they understand that they are in need of His grace, help, and protection at every moment of time. Augustine in Psalm. 37. He who desires the good without ceasing, and directs his desire to GOD, because your continuous desire is your continuous voice; if you do not wish to cease praying, do not cease to desire. 4. But this is also required, that Christians should perpetually abstain from those things which can impede prayer, and should institute their life in such a way that they are always prepared for prayers pleasing to GOD, if a sudden occasion should demand them. Augustine, Epistle 121 to Proba, chapter 9: What the Apostle says, pray without ceasing, what is it other than to desire the blessed life, which is none other than the eternal one, without ceasing from Him who alone can give it. Therefore, let us always desire this from the Lord GOD, and let us pray always. But for that reason, from other cares and businesses, by which the desire itself in a certain way grows tepid, at certain hours to the business of praying we recall the being, admonishing ourselves with the words of prayer to intend toward that which we desire, lest what had begun to grow lukewarm should grow cold entirely, and be extinguished completely, unless it is inflamed more frequently. 5. These precepts are also opposed to the superstitious observation of certain hours. For as in every place, so also at every time we ought to lift up pure hands to God in prayers, 1. Tim. 2. v. 8. so that without distinction of times and places, as being already abolished in the N. T., we may pour out our prayers before God. Ioh. 4. v. 21.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. An example of ineffable divine kindness is proposed to us in the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of Christ through the preaching of the Gospel. They were alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that was in them Eph. 4. v. 18. they were without Christ, having no hope, and without God in the world Eph. 2. v. 12. But God from death to life through the Gospel, which is the word of life Phil. 2. v. 16. called them. This benefit is deservedly attributed to ὑπερβάλλοντι πλούτῳ τῆς χάριτος θεοῦ. Eph. 2. v. 7.

2. Because Christ is constituted judge of the dead and the living, i. e., of all men, therefore before that extreme judgment He called all men, not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles, through the Gospel to His kingdom, so that no one, namely, might be able to put forward an excuse of ignorance. Act. 17. v. 30. God announces to all men, that all everywhere should repent, v. 31. in that He has appointed a day, in which He is to judge the world in righteousness by the man in whom He has appointed.

3. The end of the preached Gospel is the mortification of the flesh and the renewal of the Spirit. Let us by no means, therefore, abuse the doctrine of the Gospel for carnal security, so that we may securely indulge in the concupiscences of the flesh, but rather let us mortify them through the Spirit. Gal. 5. v. 27. They who are Christ's, crucify their flesh with the passions and concupiscences.

4. As this world with all things that are in it had a certain beginning, so also it will have a certain end. Gen. 8. v. 22. All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest &c. shall not cease, upon which words the blessed Luther comments thus: It is not without reason that he says, all the days of the earth; for he indicates that these days of the earth will at some time cease and other days of heaven will follow. Therefore, while the days of the earth stand, the earth will stand and these cycles of times will remain, but when these days of the earth cease, all things will cease, and the days of heaven will follow, i. e., eternal days, which will be a Sabbath from a Sabbath, Psalm. 102. vers. 27. Esai. 34. v. 4. cap. 51. v. 6. Matth. 13. v. 39. Luc. 21. v. 33.

1. Cor. 7. v. 31. &c. 2. Petr. 3. v. 7. & following. Basilius homil. 1. hexaem. Those who ἀπὸ χρόνου have begun, it is necessary that all things ἐν χρόνῳ end and be consumed. If they have a temporal beginning, do not doubt about the end.

5. But if the world is not stable, firm, and perpetual, but flowing, unstable, momentary, and transitory, therefore let us not use it as a perpetual thing, but as a flowing one, in passing and in the course of the journey, let us not cling to it with inordinate love, nor set our heart upon those flowing and momentary things. 1. Cor. 7. v. 29. & following. 1. Iohan. 2. v. 15. & 17. August. tract. 40. in Ioh. Use the world, just as a traveler in an inn (in a lodging) uses a table, a cup, a pitcher, about to leave, not about to remain. Gregorius part. 3. curae pastoralis admon. 28. The fashion of this world passes away, says the Apostle, as if he were saying openly: Do not constantly love the world, when even it itself, which you love, cannot stand; you fix your heart in vain as if remaining, while it itself, which you love, flees. The same homil. 36. in Evang. Let us so hold those things which are of this world, that nevertheless we are not held by them; let the temporal thing be in use, the eternal in desire; let the temporal thing be on the journey, let the eternal be desired in the arrival. How the consideration of the end of the world ought to recall us from the greedy acquisition of riches, and from the delay of repentance, and on the contrary excite us to the sincere fear of God, to the love of heavenly things, to the fervor of beneficence, to the ardor of a blessed emigration, &c., was set forth in the article on the consummation of the age §. 103. 104. 105.

6. As the world is not to be loved inordinately, because it will have an end: so also for the same reason it is not to be feared preposterously. Whatever adversities happen to the pious in the world, they will have an end with the world.

7. If that end of the world was near in the time in which Peter wrote, much more is it in the near future today, which meditation ought much more to recall us from the inordinate love of the world, and its preposterous fear. Cyprianus ad Demetrian. sect. 3. The world itself now speaks and testifies to its own setting by the proof of failing things &c. You ought to know that the world has already grown old, not standing with those strengths with which it stood before, nor prevailing with that vigor and robustness with which it prevailed previously. serm. 4. demoral.
