Exposition of the text. Πρὸ πάντων δὲ τὴν εἰς ἑαυτοῦς ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ ἔχοντες. The Vulgate rendered it. Before all things, however, having mutual love among yourselves continuous. But the Greek words have properly, in yourselves, in which way also the more correct Latin Codices read, and the Syrian also rendered it. Before all things let love be prompt [consult facsimile image] [consult facsimile image] of one toward another be to you. Augustine in the book on grace and free will, chapter 17, reads among you, in which way also Erasmus translates. From this it can be judged what is to be determined concerning the emphasis which some urge in this place. Having charity among yourselves, not outside yourselves; in the heart, not only in outward signs; and because of that which is internal in you, that is, because of the image of God and other spiritual gifts, not because of temporal ones; finally, that each one may love another as himself. Naturally, they follow the Vulgate version, since in the Greek it is εἰς ἑαυτοὺς.. The Vulgate rendered the little word ἐκτεκῆ as continuous; Oecumenius, extended in length and persevering and lasting; Erasmus, vehement. The Syrian [consult facsimile image] sharp, penetrating, intense. Luth. Burning/ Hebr. 4. v. 12. The little word ἐκτονὴς is used also intensively. Act. 12. v. 5. προσευχὴ ᾖν ἐκτενὴς γινομένη. Vulg. Prayer was made without ceasing by the Church for Peter. Erasmus rendered it, assiduous. The Syrian [consult facsimile image] constant, persevering, continuous, because Col. 4. vers. 2. the Greek ωροσκαρτερεῖτε τῇ προσεοχῇ is rendered by [consult facsimile image] Luc. 22. vers. 4. it is said of Christ ἐν ἀγωνίᾳ being in an agony, he prayed ἐκτενέστερον he prayed more intensely, more vehemently. The Vulgate more prolixly. The Syrian [consult facsimile image] from the root [consult facsimile image] Luc. 23. vers. 23. ἐπέκειντο they were instant with loud voices, this the Syrian rendered [consult facsimile image] pressing, urging. 1. Petr. 1. vers. 22. there is a passage parallel to this one of ours, ἀλλήλους ἀγαπήσατε ἐκτενῶς. where the Vulgate rendered it more intensely. Luth. Bru nsrig. The Syrian from a perfect heart. Compare what has been said above regarding that parallel passage. From all of which it becomes manifest that by charity ἐν τενῆ is understood 1. serious, ardent, intense, and vehement charity. 2. continuous, lasting, and persevering charity, both of which are required for true charity, so that the sense may be: Love your neighbor not with bare words or tongue, but in work and truth 1. Ioh. 3. vers. 18. love not coldly or tepidly, but ardently; love not for a time, but continuously and perseveringly; cherish and preserve charity with mutual duties, lest it be interrupted by any dissensions; let this fire always burn in your hearts, lest it ever be extinguished. Cant. 8. vers. 7. many waters cannot extinguish charity, nor can rivers overwhelm it. Rom. 12. vers. 10. τῇ φιλαδεολφίᾳ εἰς ἀλλήλους φιλόστοργοι, which pertains to the intensive study of charity. Hebr. 13. vers. 1. ἡ φιλαδιλφία μενὲτω, which pertains to the extensive study of charity. The little word ἐκτενὴς. embraces both.

Ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη καλύψει πλῆθος άμαρτιῶν. The passage is taken from Prov. 10. vers. 12. which in Hebrew stands thus. Hatred will stir up contentions, and charity will cover all transgressions. The LXX rendered it in this way μῖσος ἐγείρει νῖκος (Symm. & Theodot. from the Hebrew μάχας) πάντας δὲ τοὺς μὴ φιλονεικοῦντας καλύψει φιλία.). From which it appears that the Apostle in this place followed not the version of the LXX Interpreters, but the Hebrew text. For the future καλύψει in some Greek Codices annotated by Robert Stephanus, namely in two Royal ones and just as many others, the present καλύπτει, is held, in which way also some Greek Codices read Prover. 10. vers. 22. and the Vulgate Interpreter in this place, which version does not differ from the Hebrew text, for it is most customary among the Hebrews for past tenses to be placed for present ones, just as these do not differ, that Salmeron says, all transgressions are covered by charity, but Peter τὸ πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν a multitude of sins is covered by charity, for the sense is the same in both places, namely that charity covers all the faults of a neighbor, however many and various they may be. This κάλυψις embraces 1. the dissimulation of injuries brought by a neighbor, because true charity connives at the injuries of a neighbor, and for the sake of peace dissimulates them. 2. the extenuation and excuse of the blemishes and errors of a neighbor, because true charity does not exaggerate the errors of a neighbor, but rather extenuates them. 3. fraternal condonation, because true charity willingly and promptly remits offenses to a neighbor who asks for it. Parallel passages exist 1. Corinth. 13. vers. 7. ἡ ἀγάπη πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστέυει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει. Iacob. 5. vers. 20. He who shall have caused a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, shall save his soul from death καὶ καλύψει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν, although there κάλυψις ἁμαρτιῶν is taken a little differently than in this place, as we shall see later. Bernard, sermon 23 on the Canticles, and before him Clement of Alexandria, book 6 of the Stromata, chapter 6, seems to take this Apostolic passage not concerning our charity, but concerning the charity of CHRIST, since he writes, blessedness, that the Lord may not impute sin to us, is made upon the elect by GOD through J. C. O. L. for charity covers, he says, sin a multitude of sins. But it is manifest from the circumstances of the text that the Apostle is speaking of our charity, since he exhorts to it so seriously. Ambrose, sermon 16 on Psal. 118., indicates another way in which charity covers a multitude of sins, namely, by preventing them from being committed. See, he says, how much it covers, how much it corrects. If the law makes one immaculate, charity rightly covers a multitude of sins, because charity is the fullness of the law. But it is manifest from the circumstances that the discourse here is not about our own sins, but about the sins of our neighbor.

Latin:

ANTE OMNIA AUTEM MUTUAM IN VOSMETIPSOS CARITATEM CONTINUAM HABENTES, QUIA CARITAS OPERIT MULTITUDINEM PECCATORUM.

Connexio. 1. Postquam Apostolus ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam cos, ad quos scribit, fuerat exhortatus, iam porrò ad caritatem mutuam ac fraternam eos exhortatur, quae est altera virtus, cuius studium piis maximè debet esse commendatum.

2. Docuerat hactenus, in vers. proximè praeced. quomodo abnegatis carnalibus desideriis erga nos ipsos nos gerere debeamus, videlicet σωφρόνως per sobrietatem; Itemque quomodo erga Deum nos gerere debeamus, videlicet εὐσεβῶς per pias & serias preces, iam porrò ostendit, quomodo erga proximum nos gerere debeamus, videlicet δικαίωςTit. 2. vers. 12. pars enim δικαιοσύνης proximo debitae est caritas Rom. 13. vers. 8. Nemini quicquam debeatis, nisi ut invicem diligatis. Lyranus in h. l. Postquam ordinaverat Apostolus fideles respectu suiper concupi scentiarum repressionem, consequenter revertitur ad ordinanadum fideles respectu proximi, talis enim reversio maximè fit in moralibus propter connexionem virtutum. Ordinat autem eos. 1. in communicatione bonorum. 2. in perpessione malorum.

3. Ut ad orationem & pietatem erga Deum requiritur tùm mentis vigilantia, tùm corporis sobrietas: ita officiorum, quae proximis debemus, fundamentum est caritas, quae errata fratrum tegit & est effectrix atque nutrix officiorum mutuorum.

Dispositio. Partes huius versiculi duae sunt. 1. ad caritatem fraternam exhortatio. 2. Exhortationis pondus ac ratio, desumta à salutari caritatis fructu, quem probat verbis Salomonis Prov. 10. v. 12. In exhortatione describit caritatis 1. subiectum, quinam debeant caritatem exercere, omnes scil. Christiani, cum praeceptum caritatis sit universale. 2. obiectum, quibus caritatis & misericordiae opera praestanda, videlicet fratribus. 3. modum, qualis debeat esse caritas, videl. ἐκτενὴς.

Textus expositio. Πρὸ πάντων δὲ τὴν εἰς ἑαυτοῦς ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ ἔχοντες. Vulgata reddidit. Ante omnia autem mutuam in vobis metipsis caritatem continuam habentes. Sed Graeca propria habent, in vos metipsos, quo modo etiam correctiores Codices Latini legunt, ac Syrus etiam reddidit. Ante omnia caritas promta[consult facsimile image][consult facsimile image] unius erga alium sit vobis. Augustinus lib. de grat. & lib. arbit. cap. 17. legit inter vos, quo modo etiam vertit Erasmus. Exeo iudicari potest, quid statuendum de emphasi, quam quidam hoc loco urgent. Caritatem habentes intravos, non extravos; in corde, non tantùm in signis exterioribus; atque propter id quod in vobis est internum, h. e. propter imaginem Dei & alia dona spiritualia, non propter temporalia; denique ut quivis alium diligat sicut seipsum Nimirum sequuntur illi versionem vulgatam, cum in Graeco sit εἰς ἑαυτοὺς. Voculam ἐκτεκῆ vulgata reddidit continuam; Oecumenius, in longum protensam & per severatem ac durantem; Erasmus vehementemSyrus[consult facsimile image]acutam, penetrantem, intentam. Luth. Brùnstig/ Hebr. 4. v. 12. Vocula ἐκτονὴς usurpatur tùm intensivè. Act. 12. v. 5.προσευχὴ ᾖν ἐκτενὴς γινομένη. Vulg. Oratio fiebat sine intermissione ab Ecclesia pro Petro. Erasmus reddidit, assidua. Syrus [consult facsimile image]iugis, perseverans, continua, quia Col. 4. vers. 2. Graecum ωροσκαρτερεῖτε τῇ προσεοχῇ redditur per [consult facsimile image]Luc. 22. vers. 4. de Christo ἐν ἀγωνίᾳconstituto dicitur, orabatἐκτενέστερονorabat intentiùs, vehementiùs. Vulgata prolixiùs. Syrus [consult facsimile image] à rad. [consult facsimile image]Luc. 23. vers. 23.ἐπέκειντοinstabant vocibus magnis, id Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image]instantes, urgentes.1. Petr. 1. vers. 22. habetur locus huic nostro parallelus, ἀλλήλους ἀγαπήσατε ἐκτενῶς. ubi vulgata reddidit intentiùs. Luth. Bru nsrig. Syrus ex corde perfecto. Confer quae dicta sunt superiùs ad locum illum parallelum. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum evadit, per caritatemἐν τενῆ intelligi 1. caritatem seriam, ardentem, intensam ac vehementem. 2. caritatem continuam, durantem ac perseverantem, quorum utrumque ad veram caritatem requiritur, ut sit sensus. Diligite proximum non nudis verbis vel linguâ, sed opere & veritate 1. Ioh. 3. vers. 18.diligite non frigidè vel tepidè, sed ardenter; diligite non ad tempus, sed continuè & perseveranter; fovete & conservate caritatem mutuis officiis, ne ullis dissidiis interrumpatur; semper hic ignis in cordibus vestris ardeat, ne unquam extinguatur.Cant. 8. vers. 7.aquae multae non possunt extinguere caritatem, nec flumina eam obruere.Rom. 12. vers. 10.τῇ φιλαδεολφίᾳ εἰς ἀλλήλους φιλόστοργοι, quod spectat ad studium caritatis intensivum. Hebr. 13. vers. 1.ἡ φιλαδιλφία μενὲτω, quod spectat ad studium caritatis extensivum. Utrumque complectitur vocula ἐκτενὴς.

Ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη καλύψει πλῆθος άμαρτιῶν. Locus desumtus est ex Prov. 10. vers. 12. qui in Hebraeo sic habet. Odium suscitabit contentiones, & omnes praevaricationes operiet caritas. LXX. reddiderunt hoc modo μῖσος ἐγείρει νῖκος (Symm. & Theodot. ex Hebr. μάχας) πάντας δὲ τοὺς μὴ φιλονεικοῦντας καλύψει φιλία. Ex quo apparet, Apostolum hoc loco non versionem LXX. Interpp. sed textum Hebraeum fuisse secutum. Pro futuro καλύψει in aliquot Codicibus Graecis à Roberto Stephano annotatis, duobus sc. Regiis totidemque aliis, habetur praesens καλύπτει, quo modo etiam legunt quidam Codd. Graeci Prover. 10. vers. 22. ac vulgatus Interpres hoc loco quae versio non discrepat ab Hebraeo textu, est enim apud Hebraeos usitatissimum praeterita poni pro praesentibus, sicut nec haec discrepant, quod Salmeron dicit, omnes praevaricationes tegi à caritate, Petrus autem τὸ πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶνmultitudinem peccatorum à caritate tegi, sensus enim utrobique idem, videlicet caritatem operire omnia proximi delicta, quamvis multa sint ac varia. Complectitur haec κάλυψις 1. iniuriarum à proximio illatarum dissimulationem, quia vera caritas ad iniurias proximi connivet, easque pacis causa dissimulat. 2. naevorum & erratorum proximi extenuationem & excusationem, quia vera caritas errata proximi non exaggerat, sed potiùs extenuat. 3. fraternam condonationem, quia vera caritas proximo deprecanti libenter ac promtè remittit offensas. Loca parallela extant 1. Corinth. 13. vers. 7.ἡ ἀγάπη πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστέυει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει.Iacob. 5. vers. 20.Qui converti fecerit peceatorem ab errore viae suae, salvabit animam eius à morteκαὶ καλύψει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν, quamvis ibi κάλυψις ἁμαρτιῶν paulo aliter accipiatur quàm hoc loco, ut postea videbimus. Bernhard. serm. 23. in Cant. & ante eum Clemens Alexandr. lib. stromat. cap. 6. hunc locum Apostolicum videtur accipere non de nostra, sed de CHRISTI caritate, siquidem scribit, beatitudinem, ut non imputet nobis Dominus peccatum factam super electos à DEO per I. C. D. N. operit enim, inquit, caritat multitudinem peccatorum. Sed ex circumstantiis textus manifestum, de nostra caritate Apostolum loqui, cum ad eam tàm seriò hortetur. Ambros. serm. 16. in Psal. 118. indicat alium modum, quo caritas operiat multitudinem peccatorum, sc, impediendo, ne committantur. Vide, inquit, quanta operiat, quanta corrigat. Si lex immaculatum facit, rectè caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum, quia plenitudo legis caritas est. Sed ex circumstantiis manifestum, non de nostris, sed de proximi delictis hîc sermonem esse.

## 4:8-11 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place 1. Why does the Apostle commend mutual charity to the faithful before all things? I respond. Some wish it to be a manner of speaking accustomed to be used in serious exhortations.Iacobi 5. v. 12. but it is said more correctly, that both Peter in this place, and Paul in the parallel passage Col. 3. v. 14. ἐπὶ πᾶσι δὲ τού τοις τὴν ἀγάπην (ἐνδύσασθε ) add this προσδιορισμὸν to the precept of charity. 1. because charity stands in such a relation to other virtues, as the most excellent virtue. 1. Cor. 12. v. 21.Be zealous for the better charisms, and I show you a still more excellent way ch. 13. v. 2.If I should have prophecy, and should know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I should have all faith, so that I should remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.v. 13.and now there remain faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity, where the Apostle speaks properly of the faith of miracles, as is evident from v. 2. But if indeed we wish to apply this also to justifying faith, it must be said that charity is preferred to faith for a threefold reason. First, because faith exerts itself by receiving, charity by giving, but it is more blessed to give than to receive Acts 20. v. 35. Secondly, justice is twofold; imputed, which is obtained by faith in Christ; and inherent, which consists of faith, hope, charity, and good works, which however is not perfect in this life; in this kind of justice, charity has the better parts. Thirdly, the Apostle properly looks to this, that charity, with faith and hope ceasing, is to endure in eternal life. For faith will pass into open knowledge and the revealed sight of the present thing, by which reason it will change its species and Nature, which does not befit charity, because although it becomes greater and more vehement, yet it retains the same substance. Chrysost. Theodor. & Anselm in this place. 2. The Apostle himself adds in place of a reason why he wishes us to study charity above all things, because charity covers a multitude of sins. 3. By which reason also Paul ἀιτιολογικῶς subjects to the precept of charity that it is the bond of perfection Col. 3. v. 14. where it is not signified that we are rendered perfect by charity to stand in the judgment of God, but it is taught that individual believers are perfected through charity as members of one mystical body, so that nothing is lacking to any, but necessary things are supplied to individuals from mutual fellowship with the other members. 4. As without faith a person cannot please God Heb. 11. v. 6. so no good work pleases Him without charity. 1. Cor. 13. v. 1. & 2.

Q. 2. Why is the precept of hospitality so often inculcated by the Apostles? Resp. 1. Christians at that time were daily subject to persecutions and exiles, and because of the Christian religion were hated by the world, therefore there was the greatest need for hospitality among them. There were not at that time public inns, such as are established today, but good men received pilgrims into hospitality without price. 3. Hospitality in itself contains all the offices of mercy, whence also Christ in judgment will commend the faithful for this virtue. Matt. 25. v. 35.

Q. 3. What is the sense of the Apostolic precept, if any man speak, as the oracles of God? Resp. 1. Some take it concerning the form and manner of preaching.

If anyone preaches the word of God, in interpreting Scripture in the Church, or in bringing forth doctrine from Scripture, let him speak as the oracles of God that is, in such a way as it befits to pronounce the oracles of God, with singular reverence and devotion applied, let him treat the oracles of God reverently and holily, considering that it is not his own word which he dispenses, but God's, and that he performs the role of Christ and an embassy for Christ.2. Cor. 5. v. 20. 2. But it is more correctly understood concerning the matter of preaching, as is evident from the parallel passage Rom. 12. vers. 6. He who performs the office of teaching in the Church, let him not bring forth his own dreams or the inventions of men, but the pure and sincere word of God, let him speak from the mouth of Christ himself, inasmuch as he performs his embassy in the Church. Bede on this passage: If anyone speaks, as the words of God, fearing evidently, lest he either say or command anything beyond the will of God, or beyond what is evidently commanded in the holy Scriptures, and be found as a false witness of God, or sacrilegious, or introducing something alien to the doctrine of the Lord, or certainly leaving behind and passing over any of those things which are pleasing to God, when he himself most manifestly commands the preachers of truth concerning those whom they have imbued, saying: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. And for those things which he himself commanded, not others; and these not in part, but all he orders to be delivered to his hearers to be observed. which words are in part translated into the Canon law c. si is qui prae est caus. 11. q. 3. He who presides, if he says or commands anything beyond the will, or beyond what is evidently commanded in the holy Scriptures, let him be held as a false witness of God or sacrilegious. Ordinary Gloss on this passage: If anyone has the knowledge of speaking, let him not impute it to himself, but to God; let him fear, lest he teach beyond the will of God, or the authority of the holy Scriptures, or beyond the utility of the brethren, nor let him be silent about what must be taught. 3. With this exposition agrees that by which this Apostolic precept concerning the fidelity to be applied in the office of teaching is understood. If anyone speaks, as the oracles of God, that is, let him administer his office with such fidelity, lest he retail the word of God 2. Cor. 2. v. 16. by corrupting it with human dreams, just as wine is accustomed to be adulterated by retailers with water mixed in Esai. 1. vers. 22. or by seeking his own gain from the treatment of the word, and for his own private advantage distorting it into a foreign sense. He who speaks i. e. preaches the word of God in the Church, let him not think that he spends anything from his own pockets, but from the goods of Christ; therefore he does injury to God, whose word it is, if he sells it as his own, by demanding some price. Matth. 10. v. 8.

Q. 4. What are those oracles of God, which ought to sound uniquely in the Church? Resp. Although God manifested His oracles to men not only in the O. but also in the N. T. through the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles, and His own beloved Son Christ Jesus by the preaching of a living voice, yet after He took care to have them reduced into the Canonical Scriptures of the O. and N. T., today they are found nowhere except in those sacred Scriptures, whence they are said to have been entrusted to the Israelite people τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ of old Rom. 3. v. 2., namely, because Moses and the Prophets were commanded to write down the principal and necessary heads of divinely revealed doctrine, and to commend these books to the Levites and the Israelite Church, so that they might be placed at the side of the ark. Deut. 31. vers. 24.Ioh. 24. v. 26.Esai. 8. v. 1.cap. 30. v. 8.Ierem. 30. v. 2. They are called oracles of God, not only by reason of the object, because they are discourses about God and divine things, not about worldly and earthly things; but also and principally by reason of the principal efficient cause, because they are the words of God speaking, discourses which God spoke through the Prophets and Apostles, and of God as the author and giver of those discourses. Psal. 68. v. 12. The Lord shall give the word, to the evangelists with a great army. which exposition is confirmed from the following member. If any man minister, as of the ability, which God supplieth.

Q. 5. Why did the Apostle wish to bring forward these two species of divine gifts λαλίαν καὶ διακονόαν; Resp. because there is more excellence in them and they are illustrious above the rest. For the office of teaching in the Church is a distribution of singular and extraordinary divine grace, which office not only the Angels, but even the whole Most Holy Trinity has not blushed to perform. The Father cries from heaven. This is my beloved Son, hear him Matth. 3. v. 17. c. 17. v. 5. The Son immediately after the fall brought forth the protevangelium concerning the seed of the woman about to crush the head of the serpent Gen. 3. v. 15. and in assumed flesh performed the office of teaching for over three years; to the Holy Spirit is peculiarly attributed the divine power, which exerts itself through the Ecclesiastical Ministry, whence it is called the ministration of the Spirit 2. Cor. 3. v. 6.

Q. 6. Why does the Apostle add this προσδιορισμὸν through Christ Jesus? Resp. 1. because Christ is the head of the Church Eph. 1. vers. 22. and through His Holy Spirit distributes those gifts in the Church. cap. 4. v. 8. ascending on high &c. he gave gifts to men v. 11. he himself gave some indeed Apostles, others however Prophets etc. 2. because through the merit of Christ we have, not only that we may do good things, but also that we may direct the good things which we do to the glory of God. 3. because on account of Christ our obedience, although imperfect, is pleasing to GOD. 4. because neither prayers nor acts of thanksgiving are pleasing to GOD, unless they are made in the name of Christ, that is, unless they proceed from faith resting solely upon the merit of CHRIST the Mediator. John 16. verse 23.If you shall ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you.Heb. 13. v. 15.Through him let us offer the sacrifice of praise always to God. There is no one pleasing to God unless Christ is that altar.

Q. 7. Why does the Apostle add this δοξολογίαν; Resp. He had said that God is to be glorified by us in all things through Christ, and having made this mention of the ultimate end of all our actions, he breaks forth into this δοξολογίαν, so that he may move us to the glorification of God by his own example, since it ought to be done both by words and by works.

Q. 8. Does the relative ᾧ refer to God, or indeed to Christ? Resp. Mention of both God and Christ had been made in the preceding. Some therefore refer to God, whom he had said was to be glorified in all things.Matt. 5. v. 16. but some prefer to refer to Christ, through whom he had said God was to be glorified, of whomRev. 1. v. 6.it is said, he made us Kings and Priests to God and his father, to him be glory and power for ever and ever, Amen.chap. 5. v. 12.The Lamb, who was slain, is worthy to receive power and riches, and wisdom and strength, and honor and glory and blessing. But it is the same, whether it is referred to God or to Christ. For God cannot be honored, except in Christ and through Christ John 5. v. 23.chap. 14. v. 6.

Q. 9. Why does the Apostle add the particle of assertion ἒστι & not rather of wishing ἒστω; Resp. In such δοξολογίαις, which are very frequent in the Apostolic Epistles, nowhere else is the particle ἒστι, added, but the particle ἒστω is understood, let it be, since these δοξολογίαι are by the common opinion of interpreters wishes. But Peter peculiarly added here the verb of assertion ἒστι, because by wishing he had already said before, that God may be honored in all things through Christ. We willingly meanwhile confess, that nothing absurd is to be thought, if even in the remaining δοξολογίαις the verb ἒστι is understood.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Above all things having mutual charity among yourselves.v. 8.And yet not only brothers and companions in the faith, but also enemies and persecutors are to be loved.Matth. 5. v. 44.Luc. 6. v. 27. Resp. The Apostle in this place by the example of Christ and the rest of the Apostles particularly exhorts to φιλαδελφίαν Ioh. 13. v. 34.A new commandment I give unto you, that you love ἀλλήλους. cap. 15. vers. 12.This is my commandment, that you love ἀλλήλους, as I have loved you.Roman. 12. v. 10. τῆ φιλαδελφία εἰς ἀλλήλους φιλόστοργοι. Hebr. 13. vers. 1. ἡ φιλαδελφία μενέτω; meanwhile he does not deny that common charity extends itself even to enemies. 2. Petr. 1. v. 7.Minister in piety τὴν φιλαδελφίαν τὴν ἀγάπὴν.

2. Charity covereth all sins. v. 8. But Matth. 18. v. 15.If thy brother shall offend against thee, go, and rebuke him between thee and him alone.v. 16.And if he will not hear thee, take with thee one or two morev. 17.And if he will not hear them, tell the Church. Resp. both are of charity, to cover and hide the infirmities and blemishes of one's neighbor ὑπεριδεῖν,; and to rebuke one's neighbor on account of sins. But when the infirmities of a neighbor are to be covered, and conversely, when a neighbor is to be rebuked on account of sins, Christian prudence, the genuine sister of charity, will teach. One must distinguish between private persons and those established in public office; between lighter blemishes and graver sins; between offenses against us and sins committed against God. The Apostolic precept is therefore to be understood with the discipline of justice preserved, which charity does not hinder, but moderates and directs. August. explaining the passage Matth. 18. vers. 5.Charity itself, he says, demands that those things which are sinned more secretly be corrected secretly. Where the evil happens, there let it die. For if you alone know it, and you wish to argue before all, you are not a corrector, but a betrayer. Anselm, book on beatitude, The sins of a neighbor are never to be uncovered, unless for the utility of those sinning or of others.

3. Hospitality one to anotherv. 9.But the poor cannot be hospitable toward the rich. Resp. the Apostle does not demand a reciprocity of benefit, which the poor cannot provide, and which the rich do not at all need, but he requires this, 1. that others toward others, namely the rich toward the poor, those having their own homes toward exiles, hospitality may exercise. 2. And lest anyone require more from others than he himself is prepared to provide.

4. Let him speak as the oracles of God.v. 11.But the words which a Minister ought to bring forth are truly the oracles of God. Response: the particle ὡς corresponding to the Hebrew כ is not of likeness, but of truth, Ioh. 1. v. 14. nor is it placed for the sake of diminishing, as if it were sufficient to profess that the word which is delivered is the word of God, and it were free to bring forth any doctrine whatsoever under the pretext that it was revealed by God, but it performs the office of demonstrating and limiting, in the sense that Ministers of the Church ought to deliver nothing except the oracles of God and doctrine consistent with the word of God set forth in the sacred Scriptures.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. The Apostle exhorts the faithful that they should have ἐκτενῆ charity, persevering and extended for a long time. v. 8. Therefore, the faithful can fall away from charity in this life, just as they can from faith. Hence it is written to the Angel of the Ephesian Church Apoc. 2. v. 4. I have against you that you have left your first charity.v. 5.Be mindful therefore from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works; if not, I come to you quickly, and I will move your candlestick out of its place, unless you do penance; which exhortation would be in no way necessary if the faithful could not fall away from charity. It is indeed said 1. Cor. 13. v. 8. that charity never falls away, but Chrysostom in his commentary on that place distinguishes in this way: Charity never falls away, but we sometimes fall away from it. The Apostle teaches there that charity, persevering in the pious even unto the end of life, will have a place even in eternal life, when prophecies, tongues, and knowledge shall cease: from that, however, it does not at all follow that charity once possessed cannot be lost in this life. Ambrose on that place: Charity never falls away, because it is profitable both in the present and remains with God for eternity. It is indeed said Cant. 8. v. 7. that many waters cannot extinguish charity, but this is not to be accepted absolutely, that charity cannot be lost if someone should want to cast it away perversely and indulge the concupiscences of his flesh, but reduplicatively, that while charity remains, all tribulations signified by the name of waters are easily tolerated. This is to be opposed to the Calvinists, who deny that those once reborn can fall away from faith and charity.

2. Solomon says, charity covers all offenses. Peter says, charity covers a multitude of sins, from which it is gathered, many in the Scriptures is sometimes used for all,Rom. 5. v. 12.19.chap. 4. v. 4.17. & 20.Dan. 12. v. 2. This is to be opposed to the Calvinists, who from the fact that Christ is said to have laid down his life for many,Matt. 26. v. 28. conclude that Christ did not die for all.

3. Nothing should sound in the Church except the oracles of GOD. v. 11. This is to be opposed to the Papists, who mix human traditions, fictitious miracles, lying Legends of the saints, and the dreams of human reason, like chaff and rubbish, with the pure wheat of the divine word. Dante Alighieri of Florence, around the year of Christ 1300, in his writings, especially in Canto 29, complained that the preaching of the word of GOD had been interrupted in the Roman Church, and instead of it, most vain fables were preached by the Monks, and faith was given to their trifles, and thus the sheep of Christ were fed not with the true food of the Gospel, but with wind. Jean Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, in a sermon on the 2nd Sunday after Easter, held in the Council of Reims before the Pope and Bishops in the year 1408, part 2, f. 238, among other things has this. There are few sermons among so many that are delivered to the people by the Vicars of the Bishops, many in number, I say, but most rare in the praise of perfection. Why? Because the word of GOD is adulterated and corrupted, while either gain is considered piety, or while the evil seeds of errors are mixed in, or useless and sterile tares of frivolous narrations are sown over them. Vincent Ferrer of Valencia, Doctor of Theology of the Order of Preachers, in his little work written around the year 1455, in which he compares the state of the Church, by which it degenerated from its primitive integrity, with the statue of Daniel, in which silver succeeded gold, bronze succeeded silver, and iron succeeded bronze, discourses among other things thus. The best color of gold has been changed, i.e., the Evangelical word, which paints souls with various colors, that is, with virtues, has been changed, because the understanding of the sacred page now has a Philosophical or Poetic color, so that all preachers, except a few, do not preach the Gospel or the Bible, but Tully or Aristotle. In the Grievances of the Empire of the year 1523, exhibited to the Papal Legate, the Estates and Princes of the Empire, art. 21, complain that hired Pastors offer to the simple common people of Christ, instead of the most limpid fountain of the Gospel, turbid, worn-out, and rubble-filled cisterns, while they publicly teach to the people of Christ in the sermon the so-called Legends of the Saints, which are not even received by the Church and are more similar to pagan fables than to Christian and Evangelical doctrine. Michael Neander in the preface to his Catechism, p. 52, writes thus concerning the state of the Church under the Papacy. There were teachers who fables They adapted Ovidian stories, Livian histories, the maxims of Aristotle, Theophrastus, Porphyry, the physicians, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, physical and medical disputations, to Christ, to Mary, and to the disciples of Christ. Examples in the Lumine animae, Roman History, and the Moralitates of Thomas Waleys on Ovid's Metamorphoses. Estius himself seems to criticize this abuse, which has prevailed publicly in the Roman Church, when he comments thus on this passage: If anyone has received from GOD the grace of speech, and is called to such a duty in the Church, let him speak as the words of GOD, of whom he is a minister in that function; let him bring forth nothing that is not consistent with the word of GOD, let him not teach the inventions of men, let him not relate false miracles, let him not treat useless questions. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: The Apostle commands that the teacher and preacher should speak words not his own, but GOD's, i.e., let him teach things that are true, holy, and worthy of GOD, namely, those things which Christ taught in the Gospel, and which GOD inspires in him, not those which the human or worldly spirit suggests.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. The Apostle commends charity to the faithful above all things; therefore, charity is the greatest virtue. But the greatest virtue justifies most. Therefore, not faith, but charity justifies most. Thus do the Papists conclude from this passage and 1. Cor. 13. v. ult.. Resp. 1. Charity is the greatest virtue not absolutely and simply, but with respect to the ministering gifts, or graces freely given, as is gathered from 1. Corinth. 12. v. ult., and with respect to its duration in eternal life, as is evident from 1. Cor. 13. v. ult.. 2. That the greatest virtue justifies most is true neither legally nor evangelically. Speaking legally, the greatest virtue does not suffice for justification before GOD, but the perfect fulfillment of the whole law is required, and thus a chorus of all virtues in the highest and perfect degree. Speaking evangelically, it is not the greatest virtue that justifies, but faith in Christ, which alone obtains the power of apprehending the righteousness of Christ's obedience. 3. The Apostle is not here engaged in the doctrine of justification before GOD, but in an exhortation to the pursuit of piety and Christian virtues, through which we deal with our neighbor, among which we willingly concede that charity is preeminent. However, when we have to do with GOD in the court of justification, we cannot rely on our charity, since it is both imperfect and contaminated by the blemishes of sins.

2. From the fact that charity is said to cover a multitude of sins, the Papists conclude, through charity the remission of sins and therefore also to obtain justification before God for us. Salmero on this passage: Charity grants the forgiveness of all sins, whence it will be said to those who are to be condemned: You have not redeemed your sins with alms. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: Charity covers all offenses, one's own and another's: one's own, therefore, because charity toward one's neighbor arises from the charity of GOD, which abolishes all sins and sanctifies man. And thus can be understood that which Prov. 10. v. 12. which Peter cites here. Just as hatred stirs up the angers of men and of God: so charity reconciles the friendship of God and of men, and covers and hides all sins: hatred offends God and men, charity reconciles us who are hateful or offended and hostile to God and men. Lorinus on this passage: Fraternal charity has the greatest importance for forgiving sins. And afterwards: Charity covers a multitude of sins, because they are remitted through an act of it dispositively and through a habit, if it does not differ from grace formally, by restoring the garment of that same grace which sin had despoiled. ibid. Three things are signified to be covered by charity: one's own sins, and punishments, and those things which others commit against us, indeed, what can be added in the fourth place, the punishments which we could exact from them. ibid. Observe then against the heretics of our age, that faith does not suffice for remitting sins, then that after these have been remitted, the guilt of temporal punishment can remain, then that sins are remitted by charity if it is actual, as the final disposition; if habitual or formally, assuming it does not differ from habitual grace, or concomitantly principally, because after grace it is the most noble gift. To this he adapts the saying of Christ Matth. 6. v. 12. If you forgive your neighbor, God will also forgive you. Luc. 7. v. 48. Her many sins are forgiven, because she has loved much; as also Iacobi cap. 5. v. 20. He who has caused a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, will save his soul from death, and will cover a multitude of sins, namely his own, as the Syrian adds. Resp. 1. The Apostolic passage is taken from the passage Prov. 10. vers. 12. which in its entirety reads thus: Hatred will stir up contentions and charity will cover over all transgressions, where the opposition manifestly shows that it is not a question in these words of the remission of sins in the judgment of GOD, before whom only CHRIST is our ἱλαστήριον Rom. 3. vers. 25. whose blood alone cleanses us from all sins 1. Ioh. 1. v. 7. on account of whom by grace GOD covers and forgives sins Psal. 32. vers. 1. but of the fraternal forgiveness of offenses among men, for the effects of hatred and charity are opposed. Hatred carefully observes the blemishes of one's neighbor, them traduces, stigmatizes, and persecutes, but charity covers, forgives, and excuses them, as much as can be done with a safe conscience and regard for duty. 1. Cor. 13. v. 7.Gal. 6. v. 2. etc. Lyranus on chapter 10 of Proverbs: As hatred through anger manifests the defects of others, so charity conceals them, unless as much as fraternal correction requires. Blessed Luther on 1. Petr. 4.: The merit of Christ apprehended by faith covers sins before GOD, but charity covers the sins of one's neighbor. Just as GOD with His charity covers our sins, so with our charity we ought to cover the sins of our neighbor. Therefore the Apostle is not speaking about the covering of our sins before GOD, but the uncovering of the sins of our neighbor before us, lest they come into our sight. 2. This exposition, as being not only conformable to the analogy of faith, but also extracted from the very bowels of the text, not even the Papists themselves can repudiate. Estius on this passage comments thus: That fraternal charity is signified, that is, that by which one's neighbor is loved, is evident from the preceding part, and no less from the antithesis which the wise man makes between hatred and charity. For he does not refer hatred to men and charity to GOD, but both to men. The same opinion of the Wise Man shows that the discourse is about the offenses of neighbors, and not of him whose charity is commended. For what the wise man says is such: Just as hatred stirs up quarrels and dissensions with others whom one holds in hatred: so charity, on the contrary, not only does not sow or stir up quarrels and dissensions, but also composes and settles those that have been stirred up, and covers offenses and injuries, which are wont to be the causes of quarrels, by tolerating, dissimulating, and excusing; finally, whatever is a sin in itself, it forgives, and intercedes and obtains that God may forgive. Lorinus in his commentary on this passage, after he had said that the more common exposition of the Enarrators, as also of Tertullian in Scorpiacus, chapter 6, Ambrose on the flight from the world, chapter 12, and sermon 16 on Psalm 118, Augustine book 2 against Cresconius, chapter 12, tractate 1 on chapter 1 of 1 John, Clement of Alexandria book 2, Stromata, chapter 6, Ephrem on penance, Bernard sermon 4 on the dedication, Chrysologus sermon 94, Prosper to Demetrias, Peter of Blois in his book on the confession of the Sacrament, take this passage in such a way that charity covers one's own sins and their punishments, he adds: Now he has interpreted this passage concerning the charity by which we cover, dissimulate, excuse, and forgive the sins of others, which are, namely, against us, or by which we extenuate the defects and imperfections of others. Chrysostom homily 4 on the Acts. of the Apostle: (Charity, he says, covers a multitude of sins: but enmities suspect even those things which are not.) Bernard Epistle 7: Charity, he says, is prior covers a multitude of sins, but enmity suspects even those things which are not. That sentence of Solomon is confirmed, from where these things seem to be transcribed. Hatred stirs up strife, and love covers all transgressions. From there it can further follow that love, with which we pursue others, covers their sins in this way, so that he who is provoked is converted and cries out by our dutiful love, according to that. If your enemy is hungry, etc.Prov. 25. vers. 21.Rom. 12. v. 20.It seems that the Council of Ilerda also used the present passage in this way c. 7. namely concerning love, to which he who is litigating and has sworn not to have peace with him ought to return, etc. Augustine uses the present passage concerning the excusing of the same sins or light errors of others lib. 1. de Baptismo cap. 17. &c. Ambrose indicates in sermon 16 on Psalm 118 a third way by which love covers a multitude of sins, namely by preventing them from being committed, etc. From these expositions I judge the second (which takes this passage concerning the sins of a neighbor) to be most congruent to the purpose, namely concerning love, as it respects others and easily forgives the sins of others: for immediately before Peter had dealt with mutual love, and suddenly he renders a reason, because love covers a multitude of sins. Paul commands us to put on this garment under the name of bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, patience, etc.Col. 3. v. 12.And afterwards. Sins are said to be covered by love, because he who is endowed with love elevates and excuses the errors of others, just as each person does for himself and his own deeds. Cornelius à Lapide in this place warns, that the little word פשעים which SolomonProv. 10. v. 12.uses, properly signifies injuries, transgressions, and offenses, by which others offend one another and provoke to anger. Certainly, therefore, it is properly a matter here of the covering of the sins of a neighbor, therefore he adds: that this is the genuine sense, is clear 1. From the antecedents and consequents, which all look to mutual love 2. From Prov. 10. v. 12. which passage St. Peter cites here. 3. Nor can the first exposition concerning the covering of our own sins before GOD through love be proven from the cited sayings. For Matth. 6. v. 12. it is not a matter of the meritorious cause of remission (for if the condoning of injuries were the cause and merit of the remission of our sins, then remission would no longer be gratuitous, but a certain debt of reward for our merit, and reconciliation with GOD and the remission of our sins would become uncertain) but then it is a matter of the sign of remission before GOD (for if we remit offenses to our brothers, from that we can be certain of the remission of sins before GOD, since that remission is a work of love, love is a fruit of faith, faith in Christ seeks and finds. Those who have true charity and from charity forgive offenses to their neighbor, are already justified by faith, and their sins are covered before GOD.) then concerning the quality of the object, to whom GOD wills to remit sins. The promise concerning the remission of sins is indeed plainly gratuitous, meanwhile, however, it is not made to the impenitent, the implacable, and the secure, but to those who acknowledge their sins, embrace Christ by faith, and working well from faith, forgive injuries to their neighbor; then concerning the removal of the impediment to obtaining remission, for when we remit to our neighbor, then the obstacle is removed, which hinders very many, so that they might less obtain the remission of their sins. 4. Luke 7. verse 48. likewise it is not a matter of the merit of obtaining the remission of sins from GOD, but of the consequent and fruit of the same already obtained, as is evident from v. 42. where Christ teaches that sins, those spiritual debts, are remitted to us freely, since we are not able to pay; from v. 50. where it is attributed to faith, that through it this woman was saved and obtained peace of conscience, from the scope of the parable, which consists in this, that it may be shown that that debtor loves more, to whom more is remitted, from the words immediately following, but to whom little is remitted, he also loves less, where the remission of sins itself is said to precede love, therefore it cannot be its effect. Rightly therefore Lyranus warns, that the particle ὅτι is to be understood not causally, but consecutively, and Didacus Stella taught that it should be rendered. Her sins are forgiven, many, therefore she loved much. 5. James 5. v. 20. likewise it is a matter of the sins of the neighbor. He who shall have caused a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, shall save his soul from death, and shall cover a multitude of sins i.e. he shall cause that GOD cover the sins of that one already converted, however great and many they may be. Micah 7. verse 19. which exposition is confirmed from the member immediately preceding. For the sins of him are said to be covered, whose soul is said to be saved from death. Lyranus in this place If any of you shall have wandered from the truth of faith or of morals, and someone shall have converted him, from infidelity to faith, or from vices to virtues, he shall save his soul from death, namely of guilt and of hell, and he covers a multitude of sins, so that they may not be seen by GOD to be punished with eternal punishment, and thus he shall be received by him into glory. The Syriac text can be rendered equally; he shall save his soul and shall cover a multitude of his sins, and he shall save his own soul and shall cover a multitude of his own sins, as appears from this very of the chapter v. 11.14. 15. & 19. from there Lorinus himself a little later reviews the passage of James among those which speak about the covering of the sins of a neighbor. 6. But, says Estius, if charity, that is, a man through charity covers the faults of another, how much more through the same charity will he obtain and merit before GOD that He might cover and forgive his own sins, and that according to the covenant of the Lord's Prayer. Resp. there is no συνέχεια in this argument. For charity covers the sins of a neighbor, not by meriting for him the remission of sins, but by dissimulating injuries brought by a neighbor, by extenuating and excusing the errors of a neighbor, by forgiving offenses to one who asks fraternally, etc., from which by no color of truth can it be inferred that charity merits the forgiveness of one's own sins; indeed this conclusion fights with the analogy of faith, which testifies that the remission of sins comes to us freely through faith in Christ, as the whole Scripture witnesses.

3. The same Lorinus gathers from this place, that it is not necessary by necessity of means for justification that one explicitly and formally elicit an act of penance or contrition, but it suffices if it is contained by virtue in an act of love of GOD above all things, even when one remembers sins. Cornel. à Lapide in this place: An act of love of GOD above all things extrudes every mortal sin, and justifies the sinner, even if he does not elicit pain and contrition for them on account of actual forgetfulness, as Theologians teach everywhere. Resp. 1. It is evident from what has been said that this is not about the remission of one's own sins, or justification before GOD, but about the forgiveness of the sins of a neighbor. 2. Nor is this directly about the love of GOD, but about the love of a neighbor. 3. From every man to be justified, penance is required, since faith, by which we are justified before GOD, is the soul of penance, nor does it have a place except in a contrite heart. GOD does not pour the oil of mercy except into a contrite vessel. 4. In that assertion, that it is not necessary by necessity of means for justification that one explicitly and formally elicit an act of penance or contrition, not even the Scholastics themselves agree, whence Lorinus adds: The contrary opinion is of Major. 4. distinct. 14. q. 1. & Soto dist. 15. q. 1. & 2. &c. de Nat. & gratia cap. 16.

4. From the fact that χάρις and χάρισμα are taken in this place by the Apostle and elsewhere in the Scriptures, as ἰσοδυναμοῦντα, the Papists gather, that by grace in the article of Justification is understood an infused habit of justice. Bellarmin. lib. 2. de Iustific. cap. 3. lib. 1. de grat. & lib.

arbitr. cap. 3. Resp. none of us denies that in certain sayings of Scripture, to which this place of ours from the Apostle must also be referred, the word grace is used for gifts given out of grace; therefore, there is no question between us and the Papists concerning that, but this is in question, what is the proper and genuine meaning of the word grace in the article of justification, and consequently what is that grace of GOD by which we are justified and saved, where we say that grace signifies the favor and mercy of GOD, and not an infused habit of righteousness, which we prove by most evident arguments. 1. Because this justifying grace in the sayings of Scripture dealing with our justification before GOD ἐξηγητικῶς is explained by the gratuitous clemency, favor, love, mercy, φιλανθρωπίαν, kindness, etc. of GOD John 3. v. 16.Titus 3. v. 4.Heb. 4. v. 16.1. John 4. v. 9. 10. etc. The Apostolic passage Eph. 2. v. 4. 5.7. & 8. is especially evident. 2. Justifying grace is opposed to our virtues, works, and merits. Rom. 11. v. 6. But grace habitually inherent in us is not opposed to them. 3. Justifying grace is said to have been given to us in Christ before eternal times 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. But a quality inherent in us, since it did not exist from the outside, cannot be said to have been given to us before eternal times.

5. From the fact that the Apostle says, If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of GOD, the Photinians gather, that the power of teaching has been given to anyone in the Church, and that there is no need for a peculiar calling. Socinus in the treatise on the Church, page 14. Racovian Catechism, chapter 2. p. 344. etc. Resp. The Apostolic saying must be limited by other places of Scripture, which teach that a calling to the public Ministry of teaching is necessary, in this way: If anyone has been called and has received gifts, so that he may teach publicly in the Church. Thus Rom. 12. v. 8. ὁ προϊστάμενος, He who rules, who has been called to presidency, let him rule with diligence, i.e., let him preside.

Observations. 1. The pursuit of charity ought to be commended to the faithful above all things, for to it all divine precepts are referred, says Augustine in Enchiridion, chapter 121. As it is the sum of all precepts, so also it is the sum of all virtues; without it, other virtues profit nothing. The fruit is not good which does not rise from the root of charity, Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 14.

2. Let charity not be cold or remiss, but vehement and ardent, for it is compared to fire Cant. 8. v. 6. Luther on chapter 26 of Exodus: Our charity ought to be twice-dyed scarlet, which can tolerate hatreds and detractions.

3. Charity ought to be continuous, persevering, lasting even until the end of life. Just as Christ, that living mirror of true love, loved his own until the end, Ioh. 13. v. 2. so also the true lover always loves, and never ceases to love. The sacred fire by the command of God always burned on the altar of the tabernacle Lev. 6. v. 12. so also the fire of charity ought always to burn on the altar of the faithful heart. Bede in this place: He adds continuous well, because we are able to love always, but we are unable to watch always in prayers, the fragility of the flesh standing in the way. We are by no means able to insist always upon these virtues which he subjoins, that is, hospitality, doctrine, the administration of graces, whether common or special toward neighbors, and other things of this kind, because these, indeed, must necessarily be done both through the office of the body and through opportune times. But charity itself, by whose instinct these things are done outwardly, because it presides over the inner man, can always be held there, although it cannot always be shown in public.

4. Charity is to be exercised toward all, and thus even toward enemies themselves, but especially toward brothers and partners in the faith. Gal. 6. v. 10. Let us work good toward all, but especially toward those of the household of faith. 2. Petr. 1. v. 7. Minister ἐν τῆ φιλαδελφία τὴν ἀγάπτην. Just as GOD embraces the whole human race with general love, but the Church and his beloved sons with special love: so our charity likewise has its own degrees.

5. Just as the charity of GOD covers our offenses: so let our charity cover the offenses of the neighbor. Charity bears all things, endures all things 1. Cor. 13. v. 7. where in the Greek is held the little word στέγει, in which is a metaphor from beams supporting an imposed burden, or from a palm tree, which does not succumb to the burden, but rather is raised up like an arch. Gal. 6. v. 2. Bear one another's burdens, i. e. tolerate with a gentle spirit the flaws and infirmities of others, which can be a burden to you, so you will fulfill the law of Christ, that is, the command of Christ concerning mutual charity. Ioh. 13. v. 34. Augustine, sermon 2 on Ps. 21. The seamless tunic of Christ is charity, and the unity of the Church woven from above, i. e. from heaven by the Father and the Holy Spirit.

6. Just as GOD out of charity covers our sins, by remitting them to us on account of Christ, and taking away their punishments Psalm. 85. v. 3. you have forgiven the iniquity of your people, you have covered all their sins, just as on the contrary when he punishes sins, he is said to manifest and uncover them. Psal. 90. v. 8. you have set our iniquities in your sight. Thren. 4. v. 22.

He will visit your iniquity, he will reveal your sins: so also we ought to forgive the offenses of our neighbor out of charity Matt. 18. v. 35. and not rigidly call them back to account.

7. Caesarius of Arles, homily 9 on almsgiving, in the words it is fitting that the ease of covering, of loving, and of forgiving one's neighbor be insinuated. For nothing is easier than to cover oneself or one's neighbor with a garment. It can also be thought that by the word covering regard is had to the deed of Shem and Japheth, the sons of Noah, who placed a cloak upon their shoulders, and walking backward covered the nakedness of their father Gen. 9. v. 23. from which they obtained a blessing from their parent. v. 26. & 27. Constantine the Great in the Council of Nicaea used to say, that if by chance he had seen with his own eyes a Bishop violating another's marriage bed, he would cover the wicked deed with his imperial cloak, lest by chance that sight might harm any of those who saw it. Theodoret, book 1, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 11.

8. If we cover the sins of our neighbor, God will also cover our sins. Matt. 6. v. 14.Mark 11. v. 28. Abbot Pastor in The Lives of the Fathers, book 5, booklet 9, number 6, At whatever hour we cover the sin of our brother, God will also cover ours; and at whatever hour we shall have betrayed the faults of our brothers, God will likewise betray ours.

9. There are three duties of hospitality. First, the friendly invitation and reception of strangers. Second, humane treatment and the refreshing of those exhausted by the weariness of the journey. Third, a peaceful dismissal with a favorable blessing. Gen. 18. v. 2. & seqq.

10. To exercise this virtue we ought to be moved by 1. the divine command. Isa. 58. v. 7.Rom. 12. vers. 13.Heb. 13. v. 1. Do not forget hospitality, for indeed its forgetfulness quickly creeps upon us. 2. the binding together of the members in the mystical body of Christ through the bond of charity. 1. Cor. 12. v. 26. 27. All the truly pious are bound to cherish and refresh the members of Christ. 3. the common condition of the pious in this life: No one can promise himself a certain lodging until the very end of life. It can happen to anyone, what has happened to one. 4. the consideration of the examples set forth in the Saints, such as in Abraham. Gen. 18. v. 2. in Lot Gen. 19. v. 2. in the hostess of Elijah, the widow of Zarephath 1. Kings 17. v. 11. in the hostess of Elisha 2. Kings 4. v. 8. in the disciples of Christ Luke 24. vers. 29. in Gaius. 3. John v. 5. 5. the abundance of rewards. Ps. 41. v. 2. Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy, in the evil day the Lord will deliver him.

Matth. 10. v. 40.He who receives you, receives me, and he who receives me, receives him who sent me.vers. 41.He who receives a Prophet in the name of a Prophet, shall receive the reward of a Prophet. c. 25. v. 35.I was a stranger, and you took me in.2. Tim. 1. v. 16.May the Lord grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me. Abraham [received] the Son of God himself. Gen. 18. v. 2. Lot received the Angels into his hospitality unknowingly. Gen. 19. v. 2. But where the Son of God and the holy Angels are, there is every blessing. Hebr. 13. v. 2. Through hospitality some have received Angels into their hospitality unknowingly. To Abraham practicing hospitality a son is promised. Aug. serm. 68. de temp. Because hospitality cannot be fruitless before God, he immediately received the price of the reward. A son is given to the old man, posterity is given to the despairing one. Lot is freed from the fire of Sodom by the benefit of his guests, whence Alcuin, the tutor of Charlemagne, comments thus on the passage of Hebr. 13 from August. d. l. The Angels entered a hospitable house; fire entered houses closed to guests. It is a great thing to receive an Angel, but a greater thing to receive a poor Christian, in whom Christ dwells through faith, accompanied by many thousands of Angels. Rahab with her own is kept safe in the destruction of Jericho, because she had treated the guests piously.Ios. 6. v. 23.Hebr. 11. v. 31.Elias raised from the dead the son of the woman who had received him into her hospitality.1. Reg. 17. v. 23.The Shunammite likewise received the reward of her hospitality. For Elisha the guest obtained a son for her by his prayers.2. Reg. 4. v. 16.And afterwards miraculously recalled him when dead to life.v. 35.The disciples of Emmaus are led through their hospitality to the recognition of Christ.Luc. 24. v. 30. Ambrose in cap. 13. Hebr. Pious hospitality has a double reward of human grace and divine remuneration. Aug. serm. 32. de verb. Dom. secundùm Lucam. Recognize hospitality, through which one has arrived at the Lord. Receive the guest, of whom you also are a companion on the way, because we are all pilgrims. He is a Christian who recognizes himself to be a pilgrim both in his own house and in his own country. lib. 2. qq. Evang. q. 51. Hold onto hospitality, if you wish to recognize the Savior: what infidelity had taken from the disciples, hospitality restored. 6. The gravity of punishments. Matth. 25. v. 43.I was a stranger, and you did not take me in, depart from me.Iac. 2. v. 13.Judgment without mercy will be to him who has not shown mercy. Ambrose. Let us beware, lest if we are hard and negligent in receiving guests, the hospitality of the saints be denied to us also after the course of this life. Gregor. homil. 23. in Evang. Receive Christ at your tables, so that you may be able to be received by him to eternal banquets, offer now to the pilgrim Christ hospitality, so that He may not be ignorant of you in judgment as if you were strangers, but may receive you as His own into the kingdom.

11. Hospitality is to be exercised especially toward brothers who have been cast into exile on account of the confession of the Gospel.

12. Moreover, it ought to be exercised without murmuring and impatience, lest we murmur against our guests if some expense must be incurred for their sake, or if they are a burden to us for too long.

13. This precept is to be extended also to other works of charity. Rom. 12. v. 8. He who shows mercy, with cheerfulness 2. Cor. 9. vers. 7. not out of sadness, or necessity: for God loves a cheerful giver. August. conc. 1. in Ps. 105. Charity is not dispensed from the purse, but especially from the heart and the will, in which it has its seat. If the purse does not have what it may give, the heart and the will do.

14. The Apostle calls the diverse functions in the Church and the virtues necessary for the administration of those functions χαρίσματα,, just as Paul also does Rom. 12. v. 6. 1. Cor. 12. v. 4., who also Eph. 4. v. 8. calls the same δόματα gifts, namely because they come to men out of the mere grace and kindness of God.

15. With whatever gift or virtue each one excels, he ought to exercise it diligently and turn it to the common use of the Church. For this reason they are called ministering gifts, because we ought to use them for the ministry and benefit of others.

16. For by this law God distributes His gifts, which are various, to individuals, so that each one may not claim for himself alone what he has received, nor hide the talent he has received in the ground Matth. 25. v. 25. Luc. 19. v. 21., but as a steward of another's good, may spend it on others. Gregory, Homil. 7. in Ezech., explains Peter's words thus: Humbly expend the good upon your neighbors, because you know that what you have is not from yourselves. The same, lib. 28. moral. cap. 6. (al. 11.) Then the multiform grace of God is well dispensed, when the gift received is believed to belong also to him who does not have it, when it is thought to have been given to oneself for the sake of him upon whom it is expended.

17. For this reason God distributes His gifts variously, and does not give everything to one, but gives to individuals their own, so that no one may be displeased with himself if he seems to have attained less; nor attribute too much to himself if he excels in extraordinary gifts. But that variety of gifts is also a bond for maintaining concord in human society.

18. Just as we have received charisms from God, so also the same toward our neighbor let us administer. We received these things freely from God. Therefore, let us also administer them freely. Matth. 10. v. 8. God did not seek His own advantage in the bestowing of them, nor let us seek our own advantage in their administration. God bestows His gifts even upon the unworthy and the ungrateful, nor let the unworthiness or ingratitude of men deter us from their administration. God distributes His gifts not sparingly, but πλουσίως and abundantly 1. Tim. 6. v. 17. so let us also be liberal in the administration of gifts.

19. We are all stewards of the heavenly householder Luc. 16. v. 1. not only in respect of interior and spiritual goods, but also in respect of external and corporal goods, to which this Apostolic passage can likewise be extended. In a steward, however, prudence and faithfulness are required. Luc. 12. v. 42.1. Cor. 4. v. 2. and besides these also charity, uniquely seeking the salvation of the neighbor in the administration of gifts, as Peter hints in this place, when he joins the administration of gifts with the commandment of charity.

20. Since, therefore, we are stewards of the gifts granted to us by God, let us prepare ourselves to render an account, which will be demanded of us on the day of judgment. Luc. 16. v. 1. To whom much is given, from him much will be sought, and to whom they have entrusted much, they will ask more from him. Luc. 12. v. 48.

21. The multiform grace or variety of gifts in the Church, the bride of Christ, is described in mystical words by David and Solomon in their spiritual Epithalamia as follows. Psal. 45. v. 10. The queen stands at your right hand in gold of Ophir (The Vulgate adds, clothed in variety) v. 14. All glorious is the daughter of the King within, clothed in gold-woven garments. v. 15. She shall be brought to the King in embroidered garments. Cant. 1. v. 11. We will make thee chains of gold with silver studs. cap. 4. v. 9. Thou hast ravished my heart with one of thy necklaces.

22. In the House of God, which is the Church 1. Tim. 3. v. 15. let nothing else sound forth but the word of God. In the city of God, let men live not by human, but by divine laws. Hence the Prophets repeat so often. The word of the Lord came to me Ierem. 1. v. 2. Thus says the Lord of hosts Ierem. 5. v. 9. Hear the word of the Lord Esa. 1. v. 10. The mouth of the Lord has spoken v. 20. cap. 58. v. 14. and God Himself says, that He puts words in the mouth of the Prophets Esa. 51. v. 16. Ierem. 1. v. 9. Ezech. 3. v. 10.

23. Whoever, therefore, performs the office of teaching in the Church, not let him act by his own judgment, let him not lord it over the faith of the hearers 2. Corinth. 1. v. 24. but let him be certain that God speaks and acts through him, and let him not think that Scripture is ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως 2. Petr. 1. v. 30. but let him conform the prophecy to the analogy of faith Rom. 12. v. 6. Luther in this place.

23. Let them depart from the Church, who turn silver into dross, and mix wine with water Esa. 1. v. 22. καπηλέυοντες τόν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ 2. Cor. 2. v. 16. mixing the leaven of human traditions into the purity of the word, δολοῦντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ 2. Cor. 4. v. 2. just as tavern-keepers adulterate wine mixed with water for the sake of profit. The prophet who has a dream, let him tell the dream, and he who has my word, let him speak my word truly. What is the chaff to the wheat, says the Lord. Ier. 23. v. 28.

24. Because a Minister of the Church, as an Ambassador of God, ought to bring forth nothing but the oracles of GOD, it is understood from this that he ought to be sparing in citing the sayings of the gentiles and profane Histories in a sermon. The Gospel is the power of GOD unto salvation to every one that believeth Rom. 1. vers. 16. the word of God is the word of eternal life Ioh. 6. v. 68. we do not have such a promise concerning the sayings of the gentiles and profane Histories.

25. The word of God is to be handled with the greatest reverence and modesty in view of the divine majesty, from which it has proceeded. 2. Corinth. 2. v. 16. As of God, in the sight of God, we speak in Christ. Gregory, part 3 of the pastoral care, ch. 25. He speaks of God in the sight of God, who understands the word of preaching both because he has received it from God and seeks to please God through it, not men. ibid. Who do not have the words which they bring forth from their own, why do they swell as if from their own?

26. Whoever has been entrusted with any office in the Church or even in the Polity, let him not act timidly and languidly, but with the greatest zeal, faithfully and with as much strength as he can Rom. 12. v. 8. He that exhorteth, in exhortation; he that ruleth, with diligence v. 11. Not slothful in business. And because no one's effort is ever happy and useful, if God does not give counsel and help, therefore let him solicitously seek divine illumination, government, and direction through earnest prayers.

27. As in all our actions, so also in the administration of an Ecclesiastical office, let us have the glory of God as the sole and highest goal set before us. 1. Cor. 10. v. 31. Do all to the glory of God; on which passage Theodoret is commended thus. Beautifully he comprehends all things, both to sit, and to walk, and to discourse, and to show mercy and to teach, that the glory of God is the one scope of all things. For because all that we are, can do, act, and have, is from God, because by divine gift we are all that we are, therefore we ought deservedly to refer all our studies, actions, and all our endeavors solely to his glory.

28. But then is GOD truly glorified in the works of our office, when we attempt nothing whatsoever in reliance upon our own powers, but implore divine grace and the help of the Holy Spirit, when we do not seek the glory of erudition or eloquence in treating the word of God, 1 Cor. 1 v. 17. when we turn all our study from sincere love toward the salvation of our neighbor, when we attribute to God the whole of whatever good and salutary thing we do in our office. 1 Cor. 15 v. 10. 2 Cor. 3 v. 5. etc. Bede in this place God is honored in our acts, when we attribute everything that we do well and according to his will not to our own merits, but to grace; on the other hand, however, we attribute the evils which we commit only to our own malice or ignorance.

29. Because God cannot be truly glorified unless the works of our office are performed with faith shining before them, therefore in every office of our calling a word is required upon which faith may lean, so that the conscience may be certain that these works please God. Rom. 14 v. last Heb. 11 v. 6.

30. As we cannot please GOD except in CHRIST; so also GOD cannot be glorified by us, except in CHRIST and through CHRIST. Just as all benefits descend to us from GOD through CHRIST, so also in humble thanksgiving all things must be referred to the glory of GOD through Christ. Bernard, sermon 13 on the Song of Songs Let the rivers of graces return to the place from whence they go forth, that they may flow again; let the heavenly flood be sent back to its source, that it may be poured out more abundantly upon the earth.

Latin:

Quaeritur h. l. 1. Quare Apostolus ante omnia earitatem mutuam fidelibus commendet? Respond. Quidam volunt, esse modum loquendi in seriis exhortationibus adhiberi solitum.Iacobi 5. v. 12. sed rectiùs dicitur, & Petrum hoc loco, & Paulum in loco parallelo Col. 3. v. 14.ἐπὶ πᾶσι δὲ τού τοις τὴν ἀγάπην (ἐνδύσασθε) hunc προσδιορισμὸν caritatis praecepto addere. 1. quia caritas eo modo sese ad alias virtutes habet, ut virtus excellentissima. 1. Cor. 12. v. 21.Aemulemini charismata meliora, & adhuc excellentiorem viam vobis demonstro cap. 13. v. 2.Si habuero Prophetiam, & noverim mysteria omnia & omnem scientiam, & si habuero omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam, caritatem autem non habeam, nihil sum.v. 13.nunc autem manet fides, spes, caritas, tria haec; maior autem his est caritas, ubi propriè de fide miraculorum loquitur Apostolus, ut constat ex v. 2. Quod si verò etiam ad fidem iustificantem haec applicare velimus, dicendum triplici nomine caritatem fidei praeferri. Primò, quia fides exerit se accipiendo, caritas dando, beatius autem est dare quàm accipere Actor. 20. v. 35. Secundò, duplex est iustitia; imputata, quae fide in Christum obtinetur; & inhaerens, quae constat fide, spe, caritate & bonis operibus, quae tamen in hac vita non est perfecta; in hoc iustitiae genere caritas habet potiores partes. Tertiò propriè eò Apostolus respicit, quòd caritas fide & spe cessante sit duratura in vita aeterna. Fides enim transibit in apertam notitiam & rei praesentis aspectum revelatum, quâ ratione mutabit speciem ac Naturam, quod caritati non convenit, quia licet fiat maior & vehementior, tamen eandem substantiam retinet. Chrysost. Theodor. & Anshelmus in h. l. 2. Apostolusipse rationis loco adiicit, quare ante omnia caritati nos studere velit, quia caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum. 3. Quâ ratione etiam Paulus ἀιτιολογικῶς praecepto caritatis subiicit, quòd eadem sit vinculum perfectionis Col. 3. v. 14. ubi non significatur, nos caritate perfectos reddi ad consistendum in Dei iudicio, sed docetur, singulos fideles perfici per caritatem tanquam membra unius corporis mystici, ut nulli quicquam desit, sed singulis necessaria suppetant ex mutuo cum caeteris membris consortio. 4. ut sine fide persona non potest Deo placere Hebr. 11. v. 6. ita nullum opus bonum ipsi placet sine caritate. 1. Cor. 13. v. 1. & 2.

Q. 2. Quare praeceptum hospitalitatis toties ab Apostolis inculcecetur? Resp. 1. Christiani tune temporis persecutionibus & exiliis quotidie erant obnoxii, ac propter religionem Christianam mundo exosi, ideò vel maximè hospitalitate inter ipsos erat opus. Non erant tunc temporis hospitia publica, qualia hodie instituta, sed viri boni sine precio peregrinos hospitio excipiebant. 3. hospitalitas in se continet omnia misericordiae officia, unde etiam Christus in iudicio ab hac virtute fideles commendabit. Matth. 25. v. 35.

Q. 3. Quis sensus praecepti Apostolici, si quis loquitur, tanquam iloquia Dei? Resp. 1. Quidam accipiunt de forma & modo praedicationis.

Si quis praedicat verbum Dei, in Ecclesia interpretando Scriptoram, aut doctrinam proferendo ex Scriptura, loquatur ut eloquid Dei h. e. ita ut decet pronunciare eloquia Dei, adhibita scil. singulari reverentiâ & devotione, reverenter & sanctè tractet eloquia Dei, reputans non suum esse verbum, quod dispensat, sed Dei, seque personâ Christi at legatione pro Christo fungi.2. Cor. 5. v. 20. 2. Sed rectiùs accipitur de materia praedicationis, ut constat ex loco parallelo Rom. 12. vers. 6. Qui docendi officio in Ecclesia fungitur, non proferat sua somnia vel hominum commenta, sed purum & sincerum Dei verbum, loquatur ex ipsius Christi ore, quippe cuius legatione in Ecclesia fungitur. Beda in h. l. Si quis loquitur, quasi sermones Dei, timens videlicet, ne praeter voluntatem Dei, vel praeter quod in Scripturis sanctis evidenter praecipitur, vel dicat aliquid vel imperet, & inveniatur tanquam falsus testis Dei, aut sacrilegus, vel introducens aliquid alienum à doctrina Domini, vel certè subrelinquens & praeteriens aliquid eorum, quae Deo placita sunt, cum ipse manifestissimè praedicatoribus veritatis de his, quos imbuerint, praecipiat, dicens. Docentes eos servare omnia, quacunque mandavi vobis. Et ea enim, quae ipsa mandavit non alia; & haec non ex parte, sed omnia suis auditoribus observanda tradere iubet. quae verba ex parte sunt translata in ius Canonicum c. si is qui prae est caus. 11. q. 3. Is qui praeest, si praeter voluntatem, vel praeter quod in sanctis Scripturis evidenter praecipitur, vel dicit aliquid vel imperat, tanquam falsus testis Dei aut sacrilegus habeatur. Glossa ordin. in h. l. Si quis habet scientiam loquendi, non sibi, sed Deo imputet; timeat, ne praeter voluntatem Dei, vel autoritatem sanctarum Scripturarum, vel praeter utilitatem fratrum doceat, nec quod docendum est, taceat. 3. Cum hac expositione congruit ea, quâ praeceptum hoc Apostolicum de fidelitate in officio docendi adhibenda accipitur. Si quis loquitur, tanquam eloquia Dei h. e. tali fidelitate officium suum administret, ne verbum Dei cauponetur 2. Cor. 2. v. 16. humanis somniis illud corrumpendo, sicut vinum admixtâ aquâ à cauponibus solet adulterari Esai. 1. vers. 22. aut lucrum suum ex verbi tractatione quaerendo, & ob privatum commodum suum illud in peregrinum sensum detorquendo. Qui loquitur i. e. verbum Dei in Ecclesia praedicat, non putet, quod ex suis loculis quippiam expendat, sed ex bonis Christi; iniuriam ergò Deo facit, cuius est verbum, si ut suum vendit, precium aliquod exigendo. Matth. 10. v. 8.

Q. 4. Quaenam sint eloquia illa Dei, quae in Ecclesia unicè sonate debent? Resp. Quamvis Deus non solùm in v. sed etiam in N. T. per Patriarchas, Prophetas & Apostolos, ac ipsum dilectum Filium suum Christum Iesum vivae vocis praedicatione eloquia sua hominibus manifestaverit, tamen postquam ea in Canonicas v. & N. T. Scripturas redigi curavit, hodie ea nuspiam nisi in Scripturis illis sacris inveniuntur, unde populo Israelitico illa τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ olim concredita fuisse dicuntur Rom. 3. v. 2. nimirum, quia Moses ac Prophetae iussi erant praecipua & necessaria doctrinae divinitùs revelatae capita conscribere, & libros hosce Levitis atque Ecclesiae Israëliticae commendare, ut in latere arcae ponerentur. Deut. 31. vers. 24.Ioh. 24. v. 26.Esai. 8. v. 1.cap. 30. v. 8.Ierem. 30. v. 2. Dicuntur illa eloquia Dei, non solùm ratione obiecti, quia sunt sermones de Deo & rebus divinis, non de rebus mundanis & terrenis; sed etiam ac praecipuè ratione causae efficientis principalis, quia sunt Dei loquentis verba, sermones quos Deus per Prophetas & Apostolos locutus est, ac Dei ut autoris ac donantis illos sermones. Psal. 68. v. 12.Dominus dabit verbum, Evangelistas magno exercitu. quae expositio confirmatur ex membro sequente. Si quis ministrat, tanquam ex virtute, quam Deus suppeditat.

Q. 5. Quare Apostolus duas hasce charismatum divinorum species adducere volueritλαλίαν καὶ διακονόαν; Resp. quia in illis plus est praestantiae atque illae prae caeteris sunt illustres. Docendi enim munus in Ecclesia est singularis & eximiae gratiae divinae distributio, quo munere non solùm Angeli, sed etiam tota Sacrosancta Trinitas fungi haud erubuit. Pater de coelo clamat. Hic est Filius meus dilectus, hunc auditeMatth. 3. v. 17.c. 17. v. 5. Filius statim post lapsum protulit protevangelium de semine mulieris contrituro caput serpentis Gen. 3. v. 15. ac in assumta carne ultra triennium docendi officio functus est; Spiritui S. peculiariter tribuitur divina virtus, quae se per Ministerium Ecclesiasticum exerit, unde vocatur Ministerium Spiritûs2. Cor. 3. v. 6.

Q. 6. Quare addat Apostolus huncπροσδιορισμὸνper Christum Iesum? Resp. 1. quia Christus est Ecclesiae caputEph. 1. vers. 22.ac per Spiritum suum sanctum distribuit charismata illa in Ecclesia.cap. 4. v. 8.ascendens in altum &c. dona dedit hominibusv. 11.ipse dedit quosdam quidem Apostolos, quosdam autem Prophetas &c. 2. quia per Christi meritum habemus, non solùm ut bona agamus, sed etiam ut bona, quae agimus, ad Dei gloriam dirigamus. 3. quia propter Christum nostra obedientia, licet imperfecta, est DEO grata. 4. quia nec preces nec gratiarum actiones sunt DEO gratae, nisi in Christi nomine fiant, h. e. nisi procedant ex fide in CHRISTI Mediatoris merito unicè recumbente. Iohan. 16. vers. 23.Si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis.Hebr. 13. v. 15.Per ipsum offeramus hostiam laudis semper Deo. Nulla est grata Deo nisi Christus lilius ara.

Q. 7. Quare Apostolus addat hancδοξολογίαν; Resp. dixerat in omnibus glorificandum â nobis esse Deum per Christum, factâ isthac ultimi finis omnium nostrarum actionum mentione, in hanc δοξολογίαν erumpit, ut suo ad glorificationem Dei nos permoveat exemplo, quippe quae & verbis & operibus fieri debet.
