Cursed, however, is he who does the work of the Lord committed to him negligently Jerem. 48. vers. 10. 4. Those who τὰ ἀλλότρια περεργάζουσι, are overly anxious censors of the sins of others, but neglecters of their own, see sharply in the observation of the vices of others, but are blind and connive in their own, which vice is most especially opposed to charity. 5. Αλλοτριοεπίσκοποι those desire to dominate others and correct those who are not subject to their power, whence they bring upon themselves unnecessary dangers. 6. That monstrous πολυπραγμοσόνης καὶ ἀλλοτριοεπισκοπῆς cacoethes leads certain ones to such a point that they explore the secrets of others, open the letters of others without the master knowing, and vex the servants of others with torments, so that they may shake out some secret.

Q. 11. Whether these words, it is time that judgment should begin from the house of the Lord, are taken from a certain place of the O. T.? Calvin in his commentary determines, Peter did not note any certain place, but took this from the common and perpetual doctrine of Scripture, so that the sense is: That this has been customary for the Lord for a long time now, that He should show the first examples of chastisements among His own people, all the Prophets are witnesses. But it is more correctly said that the Apostle is looking primarily to the following O. T. sayings. Isaiah 10. v. 12. And it shall be, When the Lord has completed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, I will visit upon the fruit of the magnificent heart of the King of Assyria.Jer. 25. v. 15.The Lord God of Israel says to the Prophet: Take the cup of the wine of this fury from my hand, and you shall give it to all the nations to whom I shall send you.v. 17.And I took the cup from the hand of the Lord, and I gave it to all the nations to whom the Lord sent me.v. 18.Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its Kings and its princes (in the first place) that I might make them a solitude, a desolation.v. 19.To Pharaoh the King of Egypt and his servants and his Princes etc.v. 29.Thus says the Lord: You shall surely drink, for behold, in the city which is called by my name, I begin to afflict, and shall you be innocent and immune? You shall not be immune.v. 30.The Lord shall roar from on high, and from his holy habitation he shall give his voice etc.v. 31.for the Lord has a judgment with the nations.c. 49. v. 12.Thus says the Lord to the Edomites: Behold, those for whom there was no judgment to drink the cup, drinking they shall drink, and shall you be left as if innocent? You shall not be innocent, but drinking you shall drink.Ezech. 9. v. 6.the Lord says to the men having the vessels of slaughter in their hand: Begin from my sanctuary, where by sanctuary is mystically signified the Church of the saints or of the faithful cap. 21. v. 4.For the reason that I shall kill in you the just and the impious, therefore my sword shall go out of its sheath against all flesh from the South even to the North.

Q. 12. In what sense does the Apostle say that it is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord? Resp. Some think the Apostle is looking back to the predictions of CHRIST, noted in the Evangelical History.Luke 21. vers. 21.Before all these things they will lay their hands upon you and will persecute you, delivering you to the Synagogues and prisons, dragging you to Kings and governors for my name's sake.John 16. vers. 2.The hour will come that everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God. Lyranus in this place: In the primitive Church many passed through Martyrdom, just as the Savior had predicted.John 16. Some wish that regard is had to the prophecies of the Prophets, so that the sense is that what the Prophets affirm of their own age, in the kingdom of Christ, propagated at this time throughout the whole world through the Universal preaching of the Gospel, most especially applies, namely, that the beginning of correction should be made from the Church. Some wish that regard is had to the sermons of the Apostles concerning the imminent final judgment, in this sense: After it began to be preached to the whole world by the Apostles that the final judgment was imminent, God willed to begin this judgment in a certain manner from in his own house and family, by afflicting his elect and his own household, they might impiously understand how hard and intolerable a judgment they should expect.2. Thess. 1. v. 4.we glory in all your persecutions and tribulations, which you endurev. 5.as an example of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer, etc. This Pauline passage Augustine, in book 22 against Faustus, chapter 20, compares with this Petrine one. Pressures, he says, and persecutions of the righteous, Paul says are an example of the righteous judgment of God, which sentiment is more broadly manifested by the Apostle Peter, where he says, it is time that judgment begin at the house of the Lord, etc. By a like reason also Gregory, in book 5 of the Morals, chapter 9, compares this Apostolic passage with 2. Thess. 1. v. 4. and adds, While you who do such upright things endure so many hard things, what else do you give but examples of the righteous judgment of God? Because from your punishment it must be gathered how he strikes those with whom he is angry, if he allows those in whom he rejoices to be so afflicted, or how he is going to strike those to whom he shows righteous judgment, if he even so tortures you, whom he cherishes while piously rebuking you? It is most simply answered that the Apostle is looking to the whole course of this age and life which the pious lead in these lands. According to the ordination of God, in this age and in this life, the pious are compelled to endure persecutions, so that God may be able to spare them in the future day of judgment.

Q. 13. Whether Peter derived this sentiment, If the righteous is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear, from a certain passage of the O. T.? Calvin thinks that the Apostle in these words did not wish to adduce any certain passage of the O. T., but a worn and familiar sentiment. But it is more correctly said that the saying Prov. 11. v. 31. is cited, which in the version of the LXX Interpreters is read in the same words that occur in this place in Peter. Bede, in his commentary on this place, says, It is to be noted that blessed Peter assumed this sentiment from the Proverbs of Solomon according to the old edition only, for which in ours, which descends from the fountain of Hebrew truth, it is written: If the righteous in the earth receives, how much more the ungodly and the sinner? But here it is further asked, how the version of the LXX Interpreters, which Peter follows here, can be reconciled with the Hebrew fountains. Truly the Chaldean paraphrast and certain Rabbis, R. Abraham and R. Levi, in the former member understand the reception of the tribulation of rewards for works of righteousness, by which reasoning the Greek version and the Apostolic allegation will scarcely be able to be reconciled with the fountains. But in truth the context clearly shows that Solomon is not speaking of the retribution of rewards or goods, but of the retribution of adversities or evils in both members, for he argues from the lesser to the greater. Behold, it shall be repaid to the righteous on earth, how much more to the ungodly and the sinner? But this argument would be little effective if the discourse were about the retribution of goods for the works of justice, because it seems no less equitable for the reward of justice to be repaid to the righteous than the reward of injustice to the ungodly. Bede in this place agrees that the Hebrew text of Solomon says this openly. Such is the fragility of mortal life, that not even the righteous, who are to be crowned in heaven, pass through it without tribulation on account of the innumerable stain of vitiated Nature, how much more do those who are exiles from heavenly grace await the certain outcome of their perpetual damnation? Draconites in his commentary on this place: That it is repaid to the righteous on earth means that the Church is therefore temporally subject to the cross on account of the sin inherent in the flesh, so that it may live perpetually after this death. If therefore the Church, repenting and heir of eternal life, is afflicted on account of the sin inherent in the flesh, how much more will the ungodly, sinning contumaciously and dying in their sins, if not here, as the pious, yet in the other life be tormented more harshly and perpetually.

Q. 14. In what respect does the Apostle assert that the righteous is scarcely saved? John Huss in his commentary on this place towards the end brings forward seven causes. 1. on account of the unworthiness of our merits, Rom. 8. Our sufferings are not worthy of the future glory, because our justices are as a menstruous cloth Es. 65. Therefore the Lord says well Luc. 17. When you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants. 2. on account of the contrariety of body and soul. Gal. 5. The flesh lusts against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh. 3. on account of the heaviness and corruption of the flesh. Sap. 9. The body, which is corrupted, weighs down the man. 4. on account of the narrowness of the way Matth. 7. Narrow is the way, which leads to life. 5. on account of the difficulty of good works, because virtue consists about difficult things. 6. on account of the imperfection of our justice. Es. 65. Our justices as a menstruous cloth. Gregory: Our justice, brought to the examination of divine justice, is injustice and is filthy in the sight of the Judge, which shines in the consideration of the worker. 7. on account of the strictness of the Judge. Ps. 142. Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified. But we showed above that Peter looks principally to the tribulations of this life, through which the righteous enter into the kingdom of heaven Act. 14. v. 22. as the whole context shows.

Q. 15. Whether one is understood as ungodly, another as a sinner? Didymus of Alexandria raises this question in his commentary on this passage. He answers, however, that the ungodly is he who is entirely outside the Lord: the sinner is he whom God contains, but he despises Him, while he transgresses His laws. If indeed sometimes in the text the same person is found to be both sinner and ungodly, he will nevertheless have a difference in meaning. It is possible, however, for him who sins to be also ungodly at once, when through contempt he acts ungodly against God. These are his words, with which that which some understand by ἀσεβῆ as infidel, and by ἁμαρτωλὸν as bad Christian, almost agrees. Others explain the ungodly as him who sins against God; the sinner as him who sins against his neighbor. But because both are opposed to the just, and because by חוטא not just any sinner is understood, but he who sins securely, contumaciously, and against his conscience, who is a sinner not out of infirmity, but out of malice and impiety, therefore it is more correctly said that these appellations in this place are synonymous. Gen. 13. v. 14. The Sodomites were very wicked and sinners before God exceedingly.

Q. 16. Why in the exhortation to commend souls to God does he call Him the creator? Resp. David Psal. 31. v. 6. calls Him, to whom he commends his Spirit, the Lord God of truth, reminding Him of the truthful promise, to which Peter also refers us with the little word πιστῷ, Christ Luc. 23. v. 56. calls Him, to whom He commends His Spirit, Father. And indeed we can, by the example of Christ, call the Lord our God, into whose hand we deposit our souls, our Father, because on account of Christ and in Christ He has received us into His beloved sons Ioh. 20. v. 17. Eph. 1. 6. meanwhile it pleased Peter to call Him, to whom we ought to commend our souls, the creator 1. so that he might show that we ought to depend entirely upon the will of God in the cross, since we are the creatures of God. For the being of a creature depends entirely upon the creator, since preservation is nothing other than the continuation of being. 2. so that he might intimate that God will not reject His work, but will promptly receive into His hands the souls which He created. Sap. 11. v. 25. You hate nothing of those things which You have made, for You did not establish or make anything while hating it. And the Apostle seems to look back to the passage Eccl. 12. v. 7. The spirit returns to God, who gave it. 3. At the same time he also wished to insinuate the distinction between the sonship of Christ and our own. Christ according to His divine Nature is the son of God by generation and Nature, we by adoption and grace. grace. Hilarius lib. 3. de Trinit. p. 26. & lib. 12. p. 255. Many are sons to us, but this one is not such a Son. For this one is the true and proper and only-begotten Son, by origin, not by adoption; by truth, not by naming; by birth, not by creation.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. The fervor of the cross is sent upon the pious εἰς πειρασμὸν. v. 12.And yet it is already known to God beforehand, what is in manIoh. 2. v. 25.nor does He have need of any testing or exploration. Resp. that exploration does not regard God tempting, but men being tempted: for to them therefore temptation is sent by God through the cross, so that they may become better known both to themselves and to others. Indeed Gen. 22. v. 12. the Son of God says, after He had tempted Abraham. Now I have known, that you fear God. But He speaks in a human manner concerning practical and experimental knowledge, because He had indeed already perceived the mind of Abraham most perfectly beforehand, but now He beholds it after the manner of men from the work itself. Aug. 1. 4. de Gen. ad liter. c. 9. explains it concerning the manifestation made to others. Now I have known, i. e. now I have caused, that it should be known. in Psal. 78.Now I have known, i. e. now I have caused to be known. For everyone is unknown to himself before the interrogation of temptation, but Abraham, having been tested, was made known to himself. By this reason the word ידע placed in Kal would be through הודיע in Hiphil.

2. The Spirit of the Lord rests upon you.v. 14.But this is attributed as if it were proper to ChristEs. 11. v. 2. Resp. if by Τὸ נחה to rest is understood. 1. The visible descent of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove upon Christ. 2. The inseparable dwelling in Him and upon Him. 3. The giving of the Holy Spirit without measure, then that rest of the Holy Spirit belongs to Christ alone, Matt. 3. v. 16.Marc. 1. v. 10.Luc. 3. v. 22.Ioh. 1. v. 32.cap. 3. v. 34. But if by Τὸ to rest is understood the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and the communication of His gifts, then that rest is common to the faithful as members of the mystical body with Christ the head.

3. Let none of you suffer, as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoerv. 15.And yet even evildoers performing serious repentance, and patiently tolerating deserved punishments from faith, are blessed. Resp. patience in punishments, brought on by crimes, also has its own praise and rewards, meanwhile patience in evils brought on beyond merit for the sake of Christ's name, obtains greater praise and more ample rewards. Patience in deserved punishments is joined with shame and blushing, but concerning him, who suffers as a Christian, the Apostle says in the following verse, let him not be ashamed.

4. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this namevers. 16.And yet persecutors also sometimes arrogate to themselves the name of Christian and the title of the true Church. Resp. The Apostle speaks of a Christian, who is such not μέχρι τοῦ λέγειν μόνον, but also κατὰ τὸ εἶναι. B. Luther on this passage persecution is to be endured from the impious, even if they nevertheless are reckoned by the name of Christ, so that it is now permitted to no one to endure persecution as a Christian, but rather as an enemy of Christ, with the persecutors boasting themselves to be true Christians, and asserting the same things as we do, namely that he is blessed who suffers as a Christian or for the name of Christ. Here no one except the Spirit discerns true Christians from false ones. Certainly, to those false boastings of the persecutors must be opposed the definition of a true Christian, which Justin hands down in Apol. 2. pro Christ. p. 49. ὅ ἂν μὴ εὑρίσκονται (πιστεύοντες καὶ) βιοῦντες ὡς ἐδίδαξε (ὁ Χριστὸς) γνωριζέσθωσαν μὴ ὄντες χριστιανοὶ, καὶ λέγωσιν διὰ γλώττης τὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδάγματα.

5. It is time that judgment should begin at the house of God.v. 17.And yet the afflictions of the pious are not τιμωρίαι, but δοκιμασὶαι and μαρτύρια. Resp. Although the truly pious do not suffer on account of certain enormous crimes, in respect to which the afflictions of certain penitents are called τιμωρίαι, yet they still carry around the remnants of the flesh, and sometimes they themselves are also overtaken by some fall Galat. 6. v. 1. in this respect their afflictions can be called κρίματα and τιμὼρίαι. Thus therefore one and the same affliction in a different respect can have the nature of δοκιμασίας, τιμωρίας & μαρτυρίου. Δοκιμασία it is, insofar as it is sent for the testing of faith and patience; τιμωρία, insofar as for our sins before God, before whom no one is innocentExod. 34. v. 7.we have deserved it.Matth. 7. v. 9.I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned,Ierem. 30. v. 11.I will chastise you in judgment, that you may not seem innocent to yourself. Μαρτύριον, insofar as it is inflicted by persecutors on account of the confession of the Gospel.

6. What shall be the end of them that do not believe the Gospel of God?v. 17.ButRom. 2. v. 16.God shall judge the secrets of men according to my Gospel. Resp. Paul's Gospel is by reason of ministry and preaching, the Gospel of God by reason of first origin and revelation. Item by reason of the matter, because the true and saving knowledge of God is handed down in it, and by reason of the final cause, because as it is from God, so also when received by faith it leads us to God. Hence Paul himself calls it the Gospel of GodRom. 1. v. 1.cap. 15. v. 16.1. Thess. 2. v. 8.and the Gospel of the Son of God Jesus Christ.Roman. 1. v. 9.cap. 15. v. 19.1. Cor. 9. v. 12. etc.

7. The righteous is scarcely savedv. 18. But 2. Tim. 1. v. 12. I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit against that day. To God nothing is impossible, except what he does not will, nay, nothing at all is difficult for him, which he wills. Resp. John Huss says, that that difficulty is understood in three ways. First, that it may be referred to God himself who saves. Second, that it may be referred to the judgment, by means of which salvation is made. Third, that it may be referred to the man himself who is to be saved, and according to each one of these ways the righteous is scarcely, i. e. saved with difficulty. He says the first is evident from this, because God in the salvation of man presupposes something, namely free will, which although God could change for the better, he cannot however force it while liberty remains, for the reason that coercion is repugnant to liberty. Therefore it is necessary for man to will to be saved, otherwise God does not save him, because according to Blessed Augustine: He who made you without you, will not justify you without you. But in other acts God presupposes nothing, and especially in creation, the reason for which is the power of the creator. Likewise to justify the ungodly has resistance, because injustice is repugnant to God himself. But it did not have this in creation, in which there was no resistance, and hence Augustine says: That it is a greater thing to make a godly man out of an ungodly one, than to create heaven and earth. He says the second is evident from this, because many things seem to be just among us, which in the sight of God are unjust. Whence Augustine, treating this word, says: You ask perhaps, why the righteous can scarcely be saved in the judgment of God? and he answers, solving the question: And why is it, except because it is certain that the justice of God is so great, that sometimes those things which seem to men to be just by our judgment, are found to be unjust by the judgment of God. He says the third is evident from this, because no mere man could be saved of himself, for the reason that all are born children of wrath. Therefore it is difficult for anyone to be saved of himself, because if he is saved, this is through the mercy of God, which wills us to possess the perpetual kingdom through many struggles and tribulations. This last point properly agrees with the Apostolic text, inasmuch as he establishes the cause of this difficulty in the tribulations which the godly are compelled to sustain in this life. When therefore Peter says, the righteous is scarcely saved, he has no respect to divine power, but to human infirmity.

8. Those who suffer according to the will of God, let them commend their souls to a faithful creator.v. 19.But those who ought to commend not only their souls, but also their bodies to God. For God guards all the bones of the pious, and not one of them shall be broken.Psal. 34. v. 21. Resp. The words of the Apostle are not to be taken exclusively, but ἐξοχικῶς, that the pious ought to have special care about commending their souls to God, just as Christ says Matth. 10. v. 28.Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the souls. Although indeed God sometimes permits that persecutors of the pious cast their bodies to be torn apart by beasts, or reduce them to dust by fires, nevertheless nothing departs from this heavenly guardianship or the assertion of David. For 1. God, as a faithful depositary, has the souls of the Martyrs commended to him in his hand, and torment does not touch them. Sap. 3. v. 1. 2. He will also at some time raise the very bodies of the Martyrs from the dust of the earth, and indeed as perfect and whole as if not even one little bone of them had ever been harmed. 3. He will again unite those resurrected bodies to the souls deposited in his hands, and thus on the day of judgment he will restore the deposit committed to his faith to the pious, whole in all parts and numbers, nay, far more perfect and glorious than he received it when commended to him. 4. This also can be referred to the faithfulness of this depositary, that in the midst of the death of holy confessors and Martyrs he strengthens their minds, so that they may endure the tortures of the body not only with a strong, but also with a joyful mind, and, certain of the resurrection, may spontaneously deposit their souls into the hands of God.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. The pious ought not to marvel and be stunned in the heat of tribulations, as if something strange were happening to them. v. 12. Therefore calamities and persecutions are an inseparable companion of the pious in this life, nay, as Chrysostom speaks in homily 25 on 1 Cor. They are the characters of the Gospel (and of the true Church that has embraced the doctrine of the Gospel). This must be opposed to Bellarmine, who counts temporal happiness among the marks of the true Church, book 4 de Eccles. cap. 18.

2. Let none of you suffer as a murderer.v. 15. Therefore the thief on the cross converted to Christ cannot properly be called a Martyr, as the Jesuits wished in the Colloq. Ratisbon. sess. 1. p. 46. he confesses to receive what is worthy of their deedsLuke 23. v. 41. therefore the glory of Martyrdom, strictly speaking, cannot be attributed to him. The ancients say by a certain rhetorical figure, that the thief filled up the measure of a Martyr, because he believed in Christ at the time when those who were to be Martyrs had failed. But those oratorical flourishes do not bring it about that Martyrdom, strictly so called, can be attributed to this thief; for the distinction remains between τιμωρίαν & μαρτύριον. The cross of this thief is τιμωρία, which he had justly deserved for more serious crimes, therefore it is by no means μαρτύριον, which is the death of the saints, endured not because of external crimes, but because of the confession of Christ. Hence Lorinus comments on this passage thus: The thief, who was on the right of Christ on the cross, cannot be considered a Martyr so strictly, although Augustine in book 1 de anim. & eius orig. cap. 9 calls him so, also according to the opinion of Cyprian. Those Fathers seem to assert that the laurel of Martyrdom was granted to him by a certain singular privilege. Cyprian certainly says more than once that he was baptized by his own blood, and that by a contrite heart his punishment was changed into Martyrdom. Epist. 73. serm. de Coena & serm. de pass. Jerome says in Epist. 58 that Christ made the punishment of homicide for the thief a Martyrdom. Emissenus speaks in the same manner in his homily on the thief. It was a certain Martyrdom, a testimony of the innocence of Christ. But he was not killed because of it, unless perhaps, which I cannot divine, he was heard speaking such things to his blaspheming companion, and therefore was finally killed with his legs broken. Cornel. à Lapide on this passage: what Cyprian in Epist 73. & Jerome in Epist. 58. say, that Christ made the punishment of homicide for the converted thief a Martyrdom, understand it as a testimony, suppose a protestation of faith in Christ; indeed Christ brought it about that the thief, crucified for his crimes, should believe in Christ on the cross itself, and publicly protest his faith, and thus become a Martyr i. e. a witness of Christ and should obtain the reward of glory worthy of such a testimony.

3. Peter in this place counts it among the most serious crimes, for which the Magistrate inflicts deserved punishments upon transgressors. It is therefore false, what Alciatus asserts at the beginning of comm. de verb. signif. & in lib. 225, that theft is not prohibited by Nature. By way of argument he brings forward that, because it is prohibited in the Decalogue, and because it was permitted to the Egyptians of old, and was praised by the Lacedaemonians, provided they were not caught in this crime. But the former argument can be reduced to an absurdity, for it would follow that adultery and homicide are also not prohibited by Nature, since both in the Decalogue it is prohibited. Nay rather, the Decalogue contains the solemn promulgation and repetition of the law of Nature. The latter argument shows that the Gentiles sinned against the law of Nature, as in other things, so also in this part: but it does not prove that theft is not prohibited by Natural law.

4. Peter numbers himself among the household of God. For after he had said, it is time that judgment begin at the house of God, he adds, If however from us, namely the faithful and the household. Therefore he knew that he believed, because none belong to the household of God except the truly faithful; and he knew that he was in grace before God, because the heavenly Householder embraces his household and beloved children with special love. This must be opposed to Bellarmine, who in book 3 of Justification, chapter 9, argues, that no one is certain by faith that he has living faith, and to all Papists, who deny that the reborn in this life can or ought to be certain of the grace of God.

5. From the fact that the righteous is scarcely saved, it is said, Bede refutes the Pelagians at verse 18, annotating thus: The Pelagians do not want to believe that in one man the whole mass of the human race is corrupted and wholly condemned, from which vice and condemnation the grace of Christ alone heals and frees. For why shall the righteous scarcely be saved? Is it a labor for God to free the righteous? Far be it: but that it may be shown that Nature was deservedly condemned, not even the Almighty himself wishes to free it easily from so great an evil, on account of which both sins are prone and righteousness is laborious, except to those who love, but charity, which makes those who love, is from God. He follows in this part Augustine, who in book 2 of the merits and remission of sins, chapter 19, and book 4 against Julian, chapter 3, and elsewhere argues against the Pelagians, that it is said the righteous is scarcely saved, so that we may understand the necessity of grace, and may diligently implore this, and may cooperate with it with the great effort of our will (renewed through the Holy Spirit) although free, and may studiously retain humility, and not think that to be our own which is God's, which error, he says, is much contrary to religion and piety.

6. Estius at the same verse 18 annotates thus: Why is the righteous scarcely saved, unless because he is scarcely righteous, that is, because he has imperfect righteousness, since he fails in many things, and the very works of righteousness which he does, for the most part have something of filth mixed in, either from an impure intention, or from another circumstance. These things must be opposed to the remaining Papists, who defend the perfection of works, and that confidence can be placed in works asserting. Bellarm. lib. 4. de Iustificat. cap. 10. & lib. 5. de Iustificat. cap. 7.

7. That which the Apostle says, the righteous shall scarcely be saved, is deservedly opposed to the Calvinists, who maintain, those once reborn cannot again fall away from faith, the grace of God, and the hope of eternal life. Zanch. in Miscel. f. 65. The Holy Spirit once given to someone remains with him forever. Keckerm. in Syst. Theol. lib. 3. cap. 7. p. 434. Saving faith once kindled in the elect can never be completely extinguished or fail. But by this reasoning it would clearly follow that ἀδύνατον, the righteous is not saved, so far is it from being correctly said that he is scarcely saved. But that it is most truly said by Peter that the righteous is scarcely saved is testified by the parable of the seed which falls upon the rock, which because it does not have depth of earth, when the sun has risen it immediately withers away Matth. 13. vers. 5. & 6. by which part of the parable are rebuked πρόσκαιροι, those who when tribulation and persecution arise because of the word are immediately offended, vers. 21. The exhortations of Christ also testify, Apoc, 2. vers. 20. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. cap. 3. vers. 11. Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown.

8. From the fact that the pious are commanded in persecutions to commit their souls into the hands of God, it can be gathered that the soul is immortal. Eccl. 12. vers. 7. The dust returns to the earth, from whence it was, and the Spirit returns to God, who gave it. For because souls are commended and also ought to be commended, as excellent deposits into the hands of God the creator, thence the souls of the righteous even after their death are in the hand of God Sap. 3. v. 1. they are bound in the bundle of the living with God 1. Sam. 25. vers. 29. and that faithful depositary will unite them in turn to the bodies on the day of resurrection. These things are to be opposed to the Anabaptists and Photinians, who deny the immortality of souls, as was shown in the article on Death §. 149.

9. Peter teaches that souls are to be commended to God, as to their faithful creator. This is to be opposed to the Papists, who in the Psalter of Mary address the B. Virgin thus. Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my Spirit. And lest anyone object that it is a private writing, it is to be noted that it has been commended by the public authority of several Popes, and in previous years was reprinted several times at Ingolstadt with singular commendation.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Cornel. à Lapide on v. 12. The heretics are foolish, who either ignorantly or maliciously twist these things against pilgrimages to the thresholds of the Holy Apostles, to Compostella to St. James, to Jerusalem to the Holy places, as if Peter here forbids traveling there. Resp. Cornelius names no one, nor can he name anyone, who among our own has used this argument.

2. Franciscus Turrianus on the dogmas of character πύρωσιν explains that which the Apostle speaks of v. 12. as the heat of lust, so that the sense may be, let not the Religious, especially novices, marvel in the fire of the temptation of lust, and if they feel themselves πυροῦσθαι or to be burning, as the Apostle speaks 1. Cor. 7. v. 9. But it is highly absurd to take this passage concerning the fire of lust, since the scope and the whole context show that the Apostle is dealing here with the fire of the cross and tribulation.

3. The Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 8, from the fact that the pious are said to share in the sufferings of Christ, gathers their own satisfactions. It befits, they say, the divine clemency, that sins should not be forgiven us without any satisfaction. And afterwards. While we suffer by making satisfaction for sins, we are made conformable to Christ Jesus, who made satisfaction for our sins, from whom all our sufficiency is. They follow Thomas in this part, who in p. 3. q. 49. art. 3. to the question, Why is a satisfactory penalty enjoined upon the penitent, answers thus. In order that we may obtain the effect of the passion of Christ, it is necessary that we be configured to him. But we are configured to him in Baptism Sacramentally, in penance through some penalty or suffering, which we sustain in ourselves, which nevertheless, being much less, suffices, than would be condign to the sin, with the satisfaction of Christ cooperating. Resp. 1. Peter speaks of sufferings divinely sent, not of satisfactions voluntarily assumed or imposed by a Priest. 2. We share in the sufferings of Christ on the cross, not insofar as they are meritorious and satisfactory, for that belongs to them on account of the infinity of his person, but insofar as we tolerate sufferings with an even mind for the confession of truth to the glory of God by the example of Christ. 3. Insofar as Christ suffered in his own body, personally united to himself, to expiate our sins, to that extent he says his sufferings are finished and complete, but insofar as the members of the mystical body of Christ are configured to their head through sufferings, by taking up their cross, and following Christ, to that extent they are said ἀνταναπληροῦν τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν θλίψεων τοῦ Χριστοῦ Col. 1. v. 24. 4. That communion with the sufferings of Christ is exemplary, not instrumental; we communicate with the sufferings of Christ instrumentally through faith.

4. Lorinus on v. 14 comments thus. Rest implies the governance of the Holy Spirit, so that those in whom it is, are led by Him, as a rider governs a horse Rom. 8. v. 14. or as the Carthusian suggests, it signifies an inherent quality, which formally justifies and strengthens. Resp. 1. The gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit is not the form of justification, but a consequence, for it is necessary that a man be first reconciled to God by faith in Christ, and receive the remission of sins, before the Holy Spirit dwells in him graciously. Gal. 4. v. 6. Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying Abba Father. 2. The Holy Spirit, dwelling in a man already reborn, kindles new and spiritual motions in his heart, and confers upon him various gifts, which we do not deny to be inherent qualities. But our justification does not consist in them, but in the gratuitous remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ.

5. Estius on v. 16 annotates thus. Nowhere is this name (χριστιανὸς) read except Act. 11. v. 26. & cap. 26. v. 28. it seems to have been imposed by outsiders, not assumed by the faithful, who called themselves brothers. Resp. Nay, truly this Apostolic passage of ours testifies that Christians were so named by the Apostles in honor of Christ, whose doctrine they embraced, and whom they invoked as the true Son of God, separating themselves from Jews and Gentiles as much by the profession of the name as by religion. 1. Cor. 1. v. 12. Each one of you says, I indeed am of Paul, and I of Apollo, and I of Cephas, and I of Christ, on which words Estius comments thus. Caietanus thinks that even those saying this are rebuked by Paul, because they established CHRIST as the head of one faction. But the constant opinion of other interpreters, both Greek and Latin, is that Paul brought this forward as if it were well and Christianly said, and grieved that not all said this same thing. For this was a voice of unity, not of schism. For Christ was the head of all. And those things which are written in c. 3, especially that final one, confirm this sense. But you are of Christ. Justin Apol. 2. for the Christians p. 46. ταῦτα πάντα προεῖπε ὁ ἡμέτερος διδάσκαλος καὶ Ἀπόστολος ὢν Ιησοῦς Χριστὸς, ἀφ' οὗ καὶ τὸ χριστιανοὶ ἐπονομάζεσθαι ἔσχήκαμεν. Outsiders or infidels called Christians Galileans, as is evident from Theodoret, book 3 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 8, and they were changing the name of Christians into Chrestians.

6. From the fact that the afflictions of the pious are called κρίματα,, the Papists gather that after the guilt has been remitted, a debt of punishment remains, for which satisfaction must be made either in this life or in purgatory. Resp. 1. They are called κρίματα, because they are public indications of divine judgment against sins and public examples, by which others are impelled to a hatred of sin. 2. Meanwhile, they are not punishments properly and accurately so called, since they do not proceed from GOD as angry, but as reconciled, nor are they the beginnings of eternal torments, but fatherly chastisements. Chrysostom, homily 28 on 1 Corinthians: When we are rebuked by the Lord, it is more of an admonition than a condemnation, of medicine than of punishment, of correction than of penalty. Augustine, book 2 on the merit and remission of sins, chapter 34: Before remission those are punishments of sins, but after remission they are struggles and exercises of the righteous. 3. From this, some distinguish between the punishment of penalty and the punishment of chastisement or probation. They call that the punishment of penalty which is properly to be called a punishment and is owed for sins committed. That is remitted together with the sins. The punishment of chastisement or probation, which is properly to be called a cross and calamity, is left to be sustained by the pious in this life even after reconciliation. 4. It is false, however, that after the guilt is remitted, some debt of punishment always remains still to be paid, since GOD very often takes those calamities away entirely. It is also false that we can make satisfaction for that debt of punishment, since satisfaction for guilt and punishment belongs uniquely to Christ alone.

7. What the Apostle asserts, the righteous is scarcely saved, some refer to the difficulty of the salvation of the righteous on the very day of judgment, as if there the righteous, either all or some, were to be in danger regarding their salvation. Resp. The Apostle does not designate a future time, but the present; nor does he preach the rigor of GOD, but teaches that very many adversities, many struggles, and arduous dangers must be overcome by the righteous before he arrives at the prefixed goal of salvation. Estius opposes to this exposition the saying Sap. 5. v. 1. Then the righteous shall stand in great constancy against those who have afflicted them. And likewise that Apocal. 2. v. 10. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. Lorinus discourses thus concerning this exposition: Jerome proves from this passage, book 2 against Pelagius, that the righteous is he who is scarcely saved on the day of judgment, would be saved easily, if he had nothing of stain in himself, etc. Bernard likewise posits in his book on the inner house, that the discourse here is about the just man being scarcely saved on the very day of judgment, etc. That the just man is scarcely saved even in the judgment itself, says Didymus in his commentary on this place, because although he is conscious of no sin, he is anxious as to how his judgment may be transacted, etc. But these things and things similar to these are said by way of exaggeration, just as also concerning the holy Angels in Augustine, sermon 130 on the times, and others, nor is there any doubt that the particular sentence already pronounced for each one at death renders him certain and establishes him in a perpetual state. Therefore, that the just man is scarcely saved in the judgment, if we speak of the Universal one, is that such great difficulty has preceded, which will then be openly known to all, so that just as Christ said Matthew 24, v. 24 that the elect would be led into error, if it were possible, on account of the force of the persecution, it would have been little lacking but that they would have made a loss of salvation. Lorinus most rightly says these things.

8. But the same man less rightly attempts to undermine the certainty of grace and justification from the same Apostolic place. The just, he says, who are saved, are called elect and few, Matthew 20, v. 16 and are compared with the few, as with eight souls in the ark, 1 Peter 3, verse 20 with the two who entered the land of promise, Numbers 14, v. 35 with a brand snatched from the fire. Amos 4, verse 11 Zechariah 3, v. 2 It is therefore further away that we ought to persuade ourselves that we are just by divine faith, as the heretics wish; or to remove every doubt from the soul, as Catharinus does. We read that every most holy man was seized by divine fear at the same time, and Augustine said woe to even a praiseworthy life, if GOD examines it with mercy removed. book 9, Confessions, chapter 13. Response 1. The fewness of those to be saved does not undermine the certainty of grace and justification, otherwise no man could be certain of his own salvation, not even through special revelation, which the Papists do not admit. Friedrich Myconius in the book whose title is The Dream, reports concerning his parent, that under the middle of the darkness of the Papacy he said that the blood of Christ is a sufficient price for sins and that this faith is necessary for every Christian, that if only three men were to be saved through the blood of Christ, yet he ought to establish most certainly that he is one of those three and that it is an insult to the blood of Christ to doubt about this matter. Wolff, volume 2, memorabilia, p. 1. D. Probus in his oration on the life of Friedrich Myconius E. ii. 2. The certainty of grace and justification does not exclude filial fear, but diffidence, doubt, and desperation. And conversely, filial fear does not exclude certainty of grace and justification, but carnal security. 3. The foundation of this certainty is not inherent or actual justice, concerning which Augustine rightly said: Woe to the life of men, even that which is praiseworthy, if GOD should examine it with mercy removed, but the promise of grace and the remission of sins received through faith for Christ's sake, or which is the same thing, the justice of Christ imputed through faith. Andreas Fricius, book 4, On the Amendment of the Republic, chapter 11: It must necessarily be done that all who wish to be certain of the remission of sins, of their adoption as sons of GOD, and of the gift of eternal life, should rest in that justice of Christ, which is perfect.

9. Estius comments on the same verse 18 thus: Those to whom the Gospel has not been preached are indeed impious and sinners, yet not guilty of unbelief. I reply: nay, truly those sayings of Scripture Mark 16. v. 16. He who has not believed shall be condemned, John 3. v. 18. He who does not believe is already judged, v. 36. he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of GOD remains upon him, are general, and they convict as guilty of unbelief not only those to whom the Gospel was actually preached, but also those who, through the fault of their ancestors, lost this treasure, while in the meantime, through the light of Nature, through the report of the Church, and through other means, they could have been invited to the Church and heard the Gospel preached therein. Therefore, one must distinguish between privative and positive unbelief. Those to whom the Gospel has not been actually preached are likewise guilty of unbelief, if not of positive, which is the stubborn contempt of the preached Gospel, yet of privative, which is the ignorance of Christ and the Gospel.

10. Salmero writes thus on verse 19: Those who are struggling with adversities are taught by the Apostle both by prayers and by good works to merit GOD. I reply: we read in the Apostle that those who are struggling with adversities ought to commend their souls to GOD through prayers and persevere in the pursuit of good works: but that they can or ought to merit GOD for themselves through prayers and good works, we do not read in the Apostle, but Salmero added that of his own. Let him therefore fear that woe which is pronounced against those who add Apoc. 22. v. 18. A man can merit a man for himself, but before GOD, to whom we owe both ourselves and all our things, there is no place for merit properly so called.

11. Lorinus annotates on the same verse thus: The commending of souls He argues that spirits in the hands of God are not material, nor from the transmission of seed, for they are commended to the creator, by whom alone they were created and to whom they return. Resp. with the words of Bellarmine, book 4, on the state of sin, chapter 11: that the passage of Genesis chapter 2 indeed effectively demonstrates that the soul of the first man was not drawn from matter, but created by GOD from nothing, but it does not compel us to judge the same concerning the remaining souls, since it can be answered: Just as GOD formed the body of the first man from the slime of the earth, but the remaining bodies not by Himself from the slime of the earth, but through generation from the bodies of parents: so the soul of the first man was properly and from nothing created by GOD, but now the remaining ones are propagated from that first one. (That this answer is most true is evident even from this, that God forms the animated Eve from the animated rib of Adam, but does not inspire a soul into her anew. Gen. 2. vers. 22.) Bellarmine continues: The remaining passages (in which GOD is called the creator of souls, to which this passage of ours also pertains) indeed prove that GOD is the founder of all souls, yet they do not indicate the manner in which they were founded by GOD, whether through creation from nothing, or through propagation from the soul of the first man. (That this answer is most true is evidently clear from the fact that Scripture uses the same phrase concerning the formation of the body. Iob. 10. vers. 9.As clay you formed me, as milk you milked me, and as cheese you coagulated me.cap. 31. vers. 15.Did He not make me in the womb?Ierem. 1. vers. 4.before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.Actor. 17. vers. 25.God gives to all life and inspiration.)

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. The sweetness of divine love tempers the bitterness of the cross. That which comes from a friendly hand cannot be ungrateful.

2. The Gospel is the word of consolation, therefore it exerts its power in the cross; it is the word of life, therefore it exerts its power in death.

3. The cross is compared with the fervor or heat of fire. Just as the potter by the benefit of fire forms vessels for honor from vile clay: So GOD by the benefit of the cross promotes our salvation, and hardens the softness of our flesh, so that we may be rendered vessels of honor,2. Timoth. 2. vers. 20.As fire tests gold: so calamity tests the just man. What the file is to iron, what the furnace is to gold and the flail to grain, this is tribulation to the just man. Esai 48. vers. 10.Behold I will refine you, but not as silver, I will make you chosen in the furnace of affliction.Dan. 11. v. 35.that they may be refined and chosen and made white,Sap. 3. v. 6.as gold in the furnace he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust he hath received them.Eccl. 27. v. 6.The furnace trieth the potter's vessels, and the trial of affliction just men. This can be declared by the typical example of the Israelites in the brazen furnace of Egypt and of the three companions of Daniel burning in the Babylonian furnace. Ephrem, sermon on patience: Man knows how much he heats the furnace for vessels; how much more is it fitting for God to explore the soul of the just with how many temptations.1. Cor. 10. vers. 13.

4. The sun hath discolored me, says the Spouse of Christ Cant. 1. v. 6. Without the fervor and heat of the Sun, nothing of those things which are born from the earth can grow: thus through the cross the increase of the inner man is promoted. A tree planted by the running waters is not at all harmed by the heat of the Sun: thus if the heat of tribulation should come even in the greatest degree, the just man does not fear, because he is like a tree planted by the running watersPsal. 1. v. 3.Ierem. 17. v. 8.

5. The end of afflictions is the proving and testing of our faith. The fire of persecutions and afflictions is kindled by God so ordaining, that our faith and patience may be rendered more illustrious.1. Petr. 1. v. 7.being now a little grieved in divers temptations, that the trial of your faith may be found much more precious than gold which is tried by the fire. It is of probation, not of reprobation, says Bernard in the nativity of Mary, col. 216.

6. God tempts no one to evil, ὁ θεὸς ἀπείραστός ἐστι κακῶν Iacob. 1. v. 13. but He tempts the faithful to good; hence Augustine, Epistle 146, book 6 of the City of God, chapter 32, sermon 11 on the words of the Lord, distinguishes between the temptation of seduction and of probation.

7. Bede in h. l.: It is very ancient and frequent for the elect of God to tolerate the adversities of the present life for eternal salvation. I am not better than my fathers, said Elias1. Reg. 19. v. 4. Indeed, it ought not to seem new, strange, and unusual to the faithful of Christ, that which was decreed from eternity Rom. 8. v. 29., that which was so often foretold in the Scriptures Matth. 10. v. 17.Luc. 21. v. 12.Iohan. 15. v. 20cap. 16. v. 32.Act. 14. v. 22.2. Tim. 3. v. 11., that which was prefigured in Christ the head Matth. 16. v. 2.Luc. 9. v. 23.Ioh. 15. v. 20., that which has been customary for all the pious from the very beginning of the world 2. Tim. 3. v. 11.2. Cor. 1. v. 8.Matth. 23. v. 34. etc., that which is necessary for the mortification of the old man for all who are to be saved 2. Cor. 4. v. 10.

8. Therefore, the pious ought to prepare themselves for bearing the cross by long meditation. 1. Thess. 3. v. 3. Let no one be moved in tribulations, for you yourselves know that we are appointed for this. v. 4. For when we were with you, we foretold to you that we would suffer tribulation. Jerome, Epist. You are mistaken if you think that a Christian ever does not suffer persecution. Salvian, book 3, on providence. What is it to be wondered at if we endure all evils, we who serve as soldiers to tolerate all things?

9. The affliction of the pious in this life is a communion with the passions of Christ. Christ on the cross, and you in the light? Christ in insults, and you in banquets? Christ on the gallows and you in Paradise? To wish to live among roses under a thorny head is the sign of a mind too delicate. Cyprian, on the praise of martyrdom. You are adorned with martyrdom as with the blood of Christ, your companion.

10. Because of this communion with the passions of Christ, the pious are said not so much to bear their own cross as the cross of Christ. Matth. 11. v. 28. Take my yoke upon you. 2. Cor. 4. v. 10. Always carrying about in our body the mortification of Jesus. Gal. 2. v. 20. I am nailed to the cross with Christ. Gal. 6. v. 17. I bear the marks of Jesus in my body. Hebr. 13. vers. 13. Let us go forth to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.

11. And conversely, Christ, as the head of the mystical body, is said to suffer in his members because of the same communion of passions. Act. 9. v. 4. Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? When the foot of the body is trodden upon, the tongue of the head cries out. Why do you tread upon me? Col. 1. v. 24. ἀνταναπληρῶ τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν θλίψεων τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν τῇ σαρκίμου. Paulinus in his Epistle to Aper. From the beginning of the ages Christ suffers in all his own, etc. Slain in Abel by his brother, mocked in Noah by his son, a pilgrim in Abraham, offered in Isaac, a servant in Jacob, sold in Joseph, exposed and put to flight in Moses, stoned and sawed asunder in the Prophets, tossed about on land and sea in the Apostles, and frequently killed in the many and various tortures of the blessed Martyrs. He himself also suffers reproaches in you, and this world hates him in you, but thanks be to him, because he conquers when he is judged and triumphs in us. But because Christ himself suffers in us, therefore he also supplies us with the strength for suffering, and finally triumphs in us over all passions.

12. John Huss, in this place, warns that we ought to communicate in the passions of Christ in four ways. 1. By meditating cordially on his passion 2. of boasting in him.Gal. 6. v. 14. 3. of rejoicing in the sufferings brought upon one for ChristAct. 5. v. 41. 4. of expecting the reward from him.

13. It is honorable and glorious to be conformed to Christ as to the head, and as soldiers to the Leader, through afflictions brought upon one for the confession of the Gospel.

14. Because we communicate in the sufferings of Christ on the cross, therefore we ought also to communicate with him in patience. Abimelech said to his soldiers Iud. 9. v. 48.What you have seen me do, do quickly. Christ still says the same to his spiritual soldiers, What you have seen me do on the cross, do you also the same.

15. We ought to bear the cross not only patiently, but also joyfully. To tolerate the cross patiently is praiseworthy, better willingly; best, joyfully. Rom. 12. v. 12.Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation.Iacob. 1. v. 2.Count it all joy, when you shall fall into various temptations. Tiburtius, walking on burning coals, said that he was walking on roses. Theodorus, by the order of the Emperor Julian, was publicly hung on a wooden beam, and his back was lashed with thongs, and his sides were pierced with claws, and indeed for an entire day, which he endured not only with a strong, but also with a joyful mind. Some later asked him, whether he had felt any torture, when he was sustaining such cruel and bitter torments? to whom he replied: that at the beginning he had felt not much, afterwards there appeared someone who would frequently wipe away the sweat flowing from his face with a soft and cool cloth, and would urge him to be of a strong mind, as he was. Wherefore, when the executioners ceased, he had perceived not delight, but sadness. For at the same time his refresher also departed. Theodoret. lib. 3. Hist. cap. 11.

16. That joy in the cross is worked by the effective and interior consolation of the Holy Spirit, as also by the sincerity and constancy of faith, explored and discovered through the cross. Rom 5. v. 3.We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience. vers. 4. and patience probation, and probation hope.Iacob. 1. v. 2.Count it all joy, if you shall fall into various temptationsv. 3.knowing that the probation of your faith works patience.

17. But especially that joy is brought about by the immovable certainty of hope concerning the communication of glory, which will follow the communication with the sufferings of Christ. For if we are κοινωνοὶ ποθημάτων. we shall also be κοινωνοὶ τῆς δόξης. Luc. 22. v. 28.You are they who have continued with me in my temptations.v. 29.And I dispose to you a kingdom, as my Father has disposed to me my father.Rom. 8. v. 17.Joint heirs with Christ, if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.2. Cor. 1. v. 7.As ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation.2. Tim. 2. v. 11.It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him.vers. 12.If we suffer, we shall also reign with him.Apoc. 1. v. 9.I John, your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ. Luther in this place: The suffering is bodily, the joy is spiritual, which begins on the cross, and lasts into eternity.

18. The day of judgment will be the day of ἀποκαλύψεως. For then the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven, then his glory also shall be revealed. Then the truly pious and elect shall be revealed, then their life and glory hidden in Christ shall be revealed.Col. 3. v. 3. & 4.

19. The children of GOD are exercised in this world chiefly in two ways, by reproaches and by torments. Reproaches touch the heart, torments touch the body. Sap. 2. v. 19.Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness.1. Timoth. 4. v. 10. κοπιῶμεν καὶ ὀνειδιζόμεθα.

20. In the primitive Church, Christians were held in such hatred by the Gentiles on account of the name of Christ, that they were called to court and demanded for punishment for the name of Christians alone. Jerome, in his work on Ecclesiastical writers, recounts in the life of Apollonius the edict of Nero promulgated against the Christians in the year of Christ 70. Whoever confesses himself a Christian, he, as one convicted of being an enemy of the human race, is punished with death without any further defense of himself. This was predicted by Christ. Matth. 24. v. 9.Luc. 21. v. 17.Ye shall be hated of all nations for my name's sake.

21. When we patiently bear the reproaches of the world for the name of Christ, this turns to our glory and promotes our blessedness. That patience is an indication that the Spirit of GOD dwells graciously within us.

22. The Spirit of GOD dwells in the pious in such a way that he rests in them as if in his own proper temple and house. He arms them with patience, so that they may tolerate any hardships with a joyful mind.

23. The blasphemies of persecutors, by which they attempt to defame the name of Christ, redound upon the Holy Spirit himself. For because the Holy Spirit glorifies Christ through the preaching of the Gospel Ioh. 10. v. 14., therefore whoever treats the Gospel and its confessors with insults, treats the Holy Spirit himself with insult. Hebr. 10. v. 29.

24. By the afflictions of the pious patiently tolerated, the Spirit is glorified. holy, both because they patiently bear those injuries and afflictions for the sake of the Holy Spirit, so that they may obey His will and command, by which He enjoins the confession of heavenly truth, and because through the same afflictions patiently endured, testimony of the truth is given to the Gospel, which is the doctrine of the Holy Spirit. Tertullian to the Martyrs, chapter 3. You are about to enter a good contest, in which the judge of the contest is the living GOD, the trainer is the Holy Spirit, the crown is eternity, the prize is the citizenship of angelic substance for ever and ever.

25. Augustine replies to the Donatists and Circumcellions, who, because they cast themselves from cliffs, seemed to themselves similar to Martyrs, in book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 47. Finally understand that it is not the punishment but the cause that makes a Martyr of Christ. book 9, Epistle to Parmenianus, chapter 7. Justice is not certain from the passion, but the passion is glorious from justice. Discourse 2 on Ps. 34. The punishment is similar for the good and the bad. Therefore, it is not the punishment that makes Martyrs, but the cause. For if the punishment made Martyrs, all mines would be full of Martyrs, all chains would drag Martyrs, all who were struck by the sword would be crowned. Therefore, let the cause be distinguished. Epistle 107 to Festus. It is not the punishment that makes a Martyr, but the cause. book 2 against the Epistle of Gaudentius, chapter 12. These things would be rightly said by you seeking the glory of Martyrs, if you had the cause of Martyrs. This saying of Augustine, taken from Cyprian, is often cited by Luther, volume 2, Wittenberg, f. 223, volume 8, Jena, fol. 178, and elsewhere throughout, which is to be opposed to all who falsely glory in Martyrdom. Just as formerly the Messalians, because they underwent death for idols, called themselves Martyrians, according to Epiphanius, heresy 80, p. 110.

26. Although Martyrdom has no place in those who undergo the punishment of death for crimes committed against the laws, they ought not therefore to despair, but in true repentance and patience let them acknowledge that they are receiving what is worthy of their deeds Luc. 23. v. 41. and, by the example of the converted thief, let them implore with serious groans the mercy of GOD promised in Christ, certain in faith of the remission of sins and eternal punishment.

27. To murderers, thieves, and criminals are joined άλλοτριοεπίσκοποι, let us therefore diligently beware, lest having gone beyond the limits of our duty we involve ourselves in the affairs of others, mindful of that saying of Funccius.

Learn by my example to perform the duty commanded, And flee like the plague τὴν πολυπραγμοσύνην.

28. Bernard on the manner of living well, chapter 54. Foolish men, while they wish to rebuke the errors of others, demonstrate their own. A man is ignorant of his own sins, which he ought to have wept over, for as long as he curiously seeks out the vices of others: but when a man returns to himself and considers himself well, he does not seek what he might rebuke in others, because he finds many things in himself which he should mourn.

29. As a Christian suffers, who suffers as an innocent; therefore the mark of a true Christian is the integrity of faith and the innocence of life.

30. Sufferings endured for the name of Christ are precious pearls before GOD. Therefore, a Christian ought to be no more ashamed of them than a maiden is of pearls and gems.

31. Calamities are not only to be endured patiently, but thanks are also to be given to GOD for them Acts 5. v. 41. Lactantius book 5 on justice, chapter 23. When we are vexed and pressed, then most of all we ought to give thanks to the most indulgent Father, because He does not suffer our corruption to proceed further, but amends us with blows and stripes, from which we understand that we are a care to GOD, with whom, because we sin, He is angry. Chrysostom homily 5 on Job. He who is inflamed with the love of Christ would choose rather to be bound for Christ than to inhabit the heavens, and he will hold this more glorious than to sit upon twelve thrones, as long as it is the will of GOD that he should suffer.

32. The house of GOD is the Church and any truly pious person John 14. v. 23.Ephes. 2. v. 20.1. Tim 3. v. 15.Hebr. 3. v. 6. the house of the Devil is the Church of the malignant and any impious person. Luke 11. v. 24.

33. The judgment of GOD begins at the house of GOD, just as a father first of all chastises his own children. Levit. 10. v. 3.I will be sanctified in those who approach me, and I will be glorified in the sight of all the people, because subjects praise and follow with greater reverence that Prince who begins judgment from his own house. Zech. 9. v. 6.Begin at my Sanctuary etc. Amos 3. v. 2.You only have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities. Naturally, the heavenly head of the household purges his house especially. Oecumenius in this place cites the saying of Basil. It is provided by nature that we are indignant against those who are most familiar to us when they sin against us, and there are no others more familiar to GOD than the faithful, who fill and build the house of GOD, i.e., the Church.

34. The judgment of GOD begins with the pious, as being the household of GOD, but is fulfilled in the impious, who are aliens from the family of GOD. Psal. 75. v. 9.A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine, and he shall pour out from it, yet the dregs thereof all the impious of the earth shall drain and drink.Esa. 32. v. 13.Upon the ground of my people briers and thorns shall ascend, how much more upon all the houses of joy of the exulting city.Ierem. 25. v. 29.Behold in the city, in which my name is invoked, I shall begin to afflict, and shall you as innocent be immune? You shall not be immune.cap. 49. v. 12.Behold they to whom there was no judgment to drink the cup, drinking shall drink, and yet shall you be left as innocent? You shall not be innocent, but drinking you shall drink.Ezech. 21. v. 4.For this, that I have killed in you (my people) the just and the impious, therefore my sword shall go forth from its sheath against all flesh.

35. The sufferings of the pious are called κρίματα, because by the just judgment of GOD, they are sent partly on account of preceding sins, partly on account of the remnants of sin still clinging in the flesh, furthermore also with a benevolent and paternal mind, lest on account of their sins they be condemned with the impious in this world. 1. Corinth. 11. v. 32.When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.Hebr. 12. v. 6.Whom the Lord loves, he chastises: he scourges however every son, whom he receives. Although indeed they are κρίματα, yet they are not sent for κατάκριμα, but for παιδείαν.

36. Beda in h. l. There are two judgments of GOD, insinuated through the Scriptures. One hidden, the other manifest. The hidden judgment is the punishment, by which now each one of men is either exercised for purification, or admonished for conversion, or if he has despised the calling and discipline of GOD, he is blinded for damnation. The manifest judgment, however, is that by which the Lord is to come to judge the living and the dead. Now however it is said to be the time, in which judgment begins from the house of the Lord, that is, from the Church, which through the exercise of present afflictions is prepared for future joys. Gloss. ordin. ad h. l. Double is the judgment of GOD in the Scriptures, one which is the hidden judgment of temporal affliction, the other indeed the manifest, which is of eternal retribution. The first is as it were a preliminary judgment, so that vengeance and retribution may be made.

37. There is a great difference between the cross of the pious, and of the impious. The cross of the pious is the chastisement of a benevolent father, the cross of the impious is the punishment of a severe judge. They differ also in time and place. The pious are chastised first, and that in this life: the impious in this life seem blessed, and live in delights even to the very end, but afterwards are afflicted with eternal punishments. August. in Psal. 93. If the sons are scourged, what ought the most wicked servants to hope for? How then will the wicked be with you, when you do not even spare your own faithful ones, so that you may exercise and instruct them?

38. Bede in h. l. Hence is gathered the strict judge, with how great strictness he will strike there those whom he rejects, if he thus tortures here those whom he loves. For if the sons are scourged, what ought the most wicked servants to hope for? And a little before. The reprobate lead a transitory life so much the more secure now and without any lash of vengeance, by how much nothing but vengeance remains for them in the future. 2. Thess. 1. vers. 5. You sustain tribulations and persecutions as an example of the just judgment of GOD, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of GOD, for which you also suffer. vers. 6. Since it is just with GOD to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, etc.

39. The sons of God, instructed and chastised by the scourges of persecutions and tribulations in this life, will receive the paternal inheritance at the end: but the end and as it were the inheritance of the impious will be in eternal torments. Sap. 5. v. 18

40. Since the Gospel is the Gospel of GOD, i.e., having proceeded from God, may it instruct us about God and lead us to God, therefore it is to be held in price by us and accepted with true faith.

41. The just man is scarcely saved, because the course of the just in this world is as it were a dangerous navigation among many reefs, infested by many storms and tempests. Therefore, to lead the ship unharmed to the port is difficult.

42. Bede in Psal. 32. Otherwise the Lord scourges a servant, that he may expel him; otherwise a son, whom he may receive into the inheritance.

43. If the pious are not without scourges in this world, the impious cannot doubt of the destruction that is to follow. Because it goes badly for the good in this life, from that it is gathered that it will go worst for the impious in the day of judgment and the other age, for that is what the judgment and justice of GOD requires.

44. Therefore let us not pray for evils upon persecutors out of a desire for vengeance, nor out of impatience let us envy them their brief happiness in this world, because eternal torments are prepared for them.

45. Persecutions of the Church and tribulations are sent upon the pious not by the will of men, but by the will of GOD. We are not tortured when the Tyrant wills it; but we are corrected when GOD has approved it.

46. Let us therefore submit ourselves to the divine will in adversities, so that with Christ and according to the prescription of Christ at the time of the impending passion we may be able to say: Thy will be doneMatth. 6. v. 10.cap. 26. v. 42. Leo serm. 7. de passion. This voice of the head is the salvation of the whole body; this voice has instructed all the faithful, has inflamed all Confessors, has crowned all Martyrs. For who could overcome the hatreds of the world, who the whirlwinds of temptations, who the terrors of persecutors, unless Christ, suffering in all, said to the Father: Thy will be done! Let all the sons of the Church, redeemed at a great price, justified freely &c., therefore learn this voice.

47. God is faithful, therefore in the cross according to his promise he will be present to us with consolation and help. God is faithful, therefore he will not suffer us to be tempted above our strength. 1. Cor. 10. v. 13. God is faithful, therefore let us commend our souls into his hands by the example of David Ps. 31. v. 6. and of Christ Luc. 23. v. 46. and of Stephen Act. 7. v. 59..

48. God, who permits persecutions to be stirred up, nay, who sends them upon us, is the faithful creator of our souls, therefore he both can and will preserve us in persecutions. Therefore he will not reject those commended to him, but will receive them into his fatherly hands 2. Paral. 24. v. 22. Therefore he will be their guardian, even when bodies are extinguished, and he will faithfully keep this excellent deposit commended to his faith, lest it perish. Therefore no one will be able to snatch them out of his hands.Ioh. 10. v. 29.2. Tim. 1. v. 12. God is powerful to guard the deposit entrusted to you.

49. Before we commend our souls into the hands of God, we must first pray for transgressors by the example of Christ and Stephen. Luc. 23. v. 34.Act. 7. v. 59. For God does not receive the deposit of souls from sinners, but from the just; nor from those who die in hatred and dissensions, but who die in charity, who have first commended themselves to God through faith.

50. We must not be deterred by the hatreds and persecutions of the world from the pursuit of good works. Gal. 6. v. 9. Doing good, let us not fail. Patience and beneficence in a true Christian must be joined by a most sweet συζυγίᾳ. From the thorns of tribulations and the roses of virtues a most beautiful crown is fashioned.

Summary of the chapter, and its division. The parts of this chapter are two. 1. The continuation of the exhortation. 2. The conclusion of the whole Epistle. The exhortation is. 1. Special. 2. General. The special is directed. 1. To the Presbyters from v. 1 up to 5 exclusively. 2. To the younger men v. 5. The general is to all to whom he writes, from v. 5 up to 12 exclusively.

The conclusion of the Epistle consists of. 1. Ἀνακεφαλαιώσει that is, a brief repetition of the principal chapters treated in this Epistle, and the commendation of the same. v. 12. 2. Ἀσπασμοῖς salutations, in which at the same time the place is set forth where this Epistle was written, v. 13. 3. Προτροπῇ to the kiss of charity, v. 14. 4. εὐχῇ a pious wish, in the same verse.

Latin:

Quaeritur h. l. 1. Quare Apostolus exhortaturus ad patientiam, praemittat,ἀγαπητὸι; Resp. 1. Oecumenius hanc tradit rationem. Ex ipso nomine significat, eos non propterea, quia asslictiones ipsis contingunt, odio à DEO baberi, sed valde ei caros esse, vehementerque amari.Prov. 3. v. 12.Hebr. 12. v. 6.Apoc. 3. v. 19. 2. Praemiserat v. 8. exhortationem ad mutuam caritatem: suo igitur exemplo ostendit, se eâdem eos, ad quos scribit, sincerè complecti.

Q. 2. Quare denuò ad patientiam hortetur? Resp. διὰ τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην1. Corinth. 7. v. 26. Conversi ad Christianisium, cumprimis ex Iudaismo, partim gentis, partim religionis nomine, gentilibus erant exosi, quando & à contribulibus suis odio habebantur 1. Thessal. 2. vers. 14. contra isthaec odia & persecutiones ex odiis illatas patientiâ ipsorum animi erant armandi ac muniendi.

Q. 3. Quare addat,πύρωσινillam afflictionem fieri adπειρασμὸν; Resp. ad mitigandum ustionis dolorem, quidem Cogitate, non ad vestrum exitium vel condemnationem, sed ad tentationem ac probationem hanc crucis ustionem vobis obtingere, ac proinde fine salutari vobis immitti. Respicite ad exemplum Abrahae patris vestri, quem DEUS itidem tentavit Genes. 22. vers. 1. non autem ad malum, sed ad bonum. Iacobi 1. vers. 13.

Q. 4. Quid perἀποκάλυψιν τῆς δόξης Χριστοῦintelligatur? Resp. Apostolus hoc insinuat, quòd quamvis Christus ad dextram Patris coelestis, quae est dextra virtutis & gloriae, collocatus, in se gloriosus sit, tamen in membris corporis sui mystici communicationem illam gloriae nondum ostendat, sed quòd in die extremi iudicii, quando venturus est in gloria Patris suiMatth. 16. vers. 27.cum virtute & gloria multacap. 24. vers. 30.in gloria suacap. 25. vers. 31. demum coram Angelis & hominibus gloriam suam publicè manifestaturus sit. Revelatur quidem gloria Christi beatis animabus sanctorum, ex corporis ergastulo solutis, sed plena, perfecta & universalis revelatio sequetur in die iudicii, quando animae beatorum corporibus vicissim unitae Salvatorem suum videbunt in gloria, & cum ipso atque in ipso triumphabunt contra omnes hostes in resuscitatis corporibus glorificatae. Col. 3. v. 4.Cùm Christus apparuerit vita vestra, tune & vos apparebitis cum ipso in gloria.1. Ioh. 3. v. 2.cùm apparuerit, similes ei erimus. Inde Glossa interlin. dicit, tunc demum illam revelationem gloriae Christi secuturam, quando omne velamen auferetur, quod fiet in die iudicii.Esai. 25. vers. 7.Et absorbebit Deus in monte isto superficiem operimenti, quo operti sunt omnes populi & velum, qui velatae sunt omnes gentes.v. 8.absorbebit mortem in sempiternum, & auferet Dominus lachrymam ab omni facie &c.

Q. 5. Quomodo ex probrorum & calamitatum, praeter meritum illatarum, tolerantiae colligi potest, Spiritum Dei requiescere super eum, qui patienter illa sustinet? Resp. quia homo carnalis pronus est ad probra non ferenda, sed regerenda; quando igitur probra & maledicta ob nomen Christi illata patienter tolerantur, argumento hoc est, eiusmodi hominem esse per Spiritum sanctum regenitum, ac proinde etiam Spiritus sancti templum. Hac ratione glorificatur Deus in corpore & Spiritu renatorum 1. Corinth. 6. v. 20. Spiritus sanctus est Spiritus lenitatis & mansuetudinis,Gal. 6. v. 1. ac μακροθυμία & πρᾳότης sunt fructus Spiritus Galat. 5. v. 22. qui ergò probra ob Christi nomen patienter tolerant, eo ipso ostendunt, quòd Spiritus Christi in ipsis habitet.

Q. 6. Quâ occasione Petrus hortetur eos, ad quos scripsit, ne quis eorum patiatur ut fur, aut homicida? Resp. Quidam persecutores videri voluerunt Christianis non simpliciter, propterea quod Christiani essent, sed propter maleficia persecutiones inferre, inde confictis criminibus ac maleficiis Christianos onerabant, tum ne crudeles & iniusti ipsimet haberentur, tum ne Christiani gloriam Martyrii apud suos consequerentur. Sic de Nerone memoratur, quòd crimen incendii urbis Romae à se excitati in Chrisrianos contulerit. Petrus igitur Christianos graviter hortatur, ne quis eorum vel homicidium, vel furtum, vel aliud flagitium, in quod leges civiles poenas statuerunt, committat, ne unius crimen in reliquos Christianos à persecutoribus diffundatur.

Q. 7. Quare in specie homicidii mentionem faciat? Resp. quia Christianis crimen infanticidii ac coenae Thyesteae à gentilibus obiiciebatur, uti memorant Minutius in Octavio, Tertullianus in Apologet. c. 9. Iustinus in orat. ad Antonin, Pium, Athenagoras in Apol. pro Christian.

Q. 8. Quare furti? Resp. quia Martyres quidam cum hoc infami hominum genere supplicium extremum pati compulsi sunt, ut socii in poena viderentur etiam socii in culpa, quo fine etiam Iudaei Christum inter duos latrones ad locum supplicii educebant.

Eusebius lib. 6. Hist. Eccles. cap. 40. ex Epistola Dionysii Episcopi Alexandrini ad Fabium Episcopum Antiochenum de certaminibus eorum, qui sub Decio Imp. Alexandriae Martyrium pertulerunt. Nemesion quidam Aegyptius defertur quasi latronum contubernalis quâ calumniâ tanquam alienissimâ apud Centurionem repurgatus, de Christianismo accusatur, & hoc nomine vinctus ad praesidem venit. Iniquissimus autem iudex duplo hunc acerbiùs quàm latrones torturis ac flagris adflictatum inter latrones comburit, & beatum, honoratumque Christi exemplo reddit.

Q. 9. Quis proprièἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος; Resp. Vulgata reddidit, alienorum appetitor. Versionem illam defendit Estius, ad h. l. sic annotans. Sola curiositas rerum alienarum non est inter crimina, quae legibus publicis castigari solent, de quibus hîc loquitur Apostolus. Intelligitur igitur alienorum appetitor, scil. cum effectu, h. e. cupidè rebus alienis inhians & tollens ubi potest. Quia vero obiici poterat, iam antè sub nomine furti huius criminis factam esse mentionem, subiicit Estius, differt hoc crimen à furto, quia non est simplex furtum, sed furtum vel rapacitas cum fraudulentia coniuncta. Diceretur ergò alienorum appetitor ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος, quia qui aliquid appetit, illud impectat. Sed rectiùs accipitur de πολυπραγμοσόνῃ, quâ quis fines alieni officii invadit, ea curare satagit, quae ad se nihil attinent, in aliorum vocationem sese ingerit sine legitima vocatione, omnia reformare studet, cum tamen ea nec intelligat, nec facere iussus sit. Hanc explicationem probat. 1. Ipsa vocis compositio. Quid enim aliud est ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος, quàm ἀλλοτρίων ἐπίσκοπος, vel ἀλλότριος ἐπίσκοπος,qui alienam procurationem sibi sumit, ut Budaeus vertit apud Areopagitam. 2. Veterum expositio. Tertullianus in Scorpiaco cap. 12. reddidit, alieni speculator. Cyprianus lib. 4. Epist. 6. & Augustinus in expos. Epistolae ad Romanos inchoata, curas alienas agens. 3. Temporis & loci circumstantia. Scribit. Apostolus ad illos Christianos, qui in medio Iudaeorum & gentilium vivebant.
