But all the remaining Codices read ὁ συμπρεσβύτερος,, just as the Syrian also rendered it [consult facsimile image], I the elder, your companion. First, in this little word is contained the argument of the exhortation, drawn from his own person. But in the explanation a diversity occurs. Some think that regard is had to age. Gloss. interlin. Show favor to senile age. Thus, therefore, the sense would be. Because senile counsel is sober and mature, and because this reverence is wont to be deferred to old men, that place be given to their precepts, therefore it is equitable that you Presbyters show yourselves obedient to me prescribing salutary precepts. Paul uses a similar argument in the Epistle to Philemon v. 9. Διὰ τὴν ἀγάπην μᾶλλον παρακαλῶ τοιοῦτος ὢν ὡς Παῦλος πρεσβύτης. But because the preceding name Presbyter is used concerning the office, as we showed a little before, therefore also the name fellow-presbyter is more rightly offered to the office, so that the force of the argument is this. Because I am established with you in the same Ecclesiastical office, because I am equal to you in the dignity of the office, therefore it is equitable that you leave place for my exhortation. He therefore conciliates authority for himself by this title, hinting that he warns the Presbyters by a certain right of his own, since he is one from the number of them.

Καὶ μάρτυς τῶν τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθημάτων. Luther rendered it, Ein Zeuge der leiden die in Christo sind. It seems therefore that he accepted this concerning the passions which are still in the mystical body of Christ, to which pertains that which some interpret the passions of Christ, not which Christ suffered in his own body, but which Peter suffered for Christ, so that as a witness of the afflictions of Christ, he is a witness afflicted for Christ. But the Greek simply has, witness of the passions of Christ, where they can be understood sufferings, not those which still are, but those which once were in the personal and proper body of Christ, which in the plural are called παθήματα, as he had also done chap. 1. vers. 11. & chap. 4. v. 13. because Christ sustained sufferings of a various and diverse kind in his most holy soul and body. Moreover, another argument of exhortation is contained in these words. But in the application likewise a certain diversity occurs. For some wish that Peter therefore calls himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ, because through the word of the cross 1. Cor. 1. v. 18. i. e. through the preaching of the Gospel concerning Christ crucified he was bearing witness concerning the sufferings of Christ, inasmuch as he himself together with the remaining Apostles had been an eyewitness of them. Acts 10. v. 39. & 40. According to this hypothesis the connection of the argument would be such. Because I am a witness αὐτό πτης of the sufferings of Christ, and with these eyes of mine I have beheld how hard and heavy things he suffered, and consequently at how dear a price he redeemed the Church committed to your faith Acts 20. v. 28. therefore it is fair that you Presbyters should leave room for my exhortation, and solicitously provide for the Lord's flock, in which manner this Apostolic passage would be clearly parallel with the Pauline exhortation Acts 20. v. 28.. But because the Apostle immediately adds that he is not only a witness of the sufferings of Christ, but also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed, therefore it is more rightly established that Peter does not call himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ only because he preached the sufferings of Christ, i. e. death and the cross, by word, but also because he was bearing witness to the doctrine concerning Christ crucified by the work itself, i. e. by sustaining various sufferings on account of Christ and his word, and thus was as it were representing the sufferings of Christ in his own person. Thus Matt. 10. v. 17. when Christ had predicted to the Apostles, they will deliver you up to councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues v. 18. and you will be led before governors and kings for my sake, he adds, for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles, or against them, i. e. so that seeing your παῤῥησίαν and constancy they may be convinced of the truth of the Gospel, nor be able to bring forward anything in the final judgment by which they might excuse themselves. Hence Bede joins both explanations. Therefore clearly a witness, he says, because he stood present while he was suffering, and beheld all things as they were being done: or certainly because he himself also suffered prison, chains, and stripes on account of the name of Christ, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. The connection and nerve of the Apostolic argument therefore is this. Because in the office of teaching, which I have in common with you, I tolerate various afflictions, persecutions, and insults on account of Christ, therefore it is fair that room be given to my admonition. For from those you can easily gather that I am dealing with a most serious matter, and that I am a faithful minister of Christ, since I have given proof of my faith through the endurance of the cross.

Ὁ καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι δόξης κοινωνός. The Vulgate rendered it, and of that which in the future is to be revealed, a partaker of the glory. But Erasmus rightly warns, that “in the future” is redundant. For the Greek τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι is properly, which shall be revealed, or which is to be revealed. The Syrian rendered it, which is prepared to be revealed, i. e., which is to be revealed. A still greater fault of the Vulgate version is that it rendered κοινωνὸν as partaker. For “partaker” is not taken passively for him who is a consort and participant, which the Greek κοινωνὸς properly signifies, but actively for him who makes others partakers. But it would be very absurd to establish that Peter wished to ascribe to himself the power and dignity by which he could make others partakers of heavenly glory. We know indeed that Paul writes to Timothy 1. Epist. 4. vers. 16. Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee. But it is manifest that the Apostle is speaking there of the efficacy of the Ministry, so that the sense is, you will be a saving instrument, through whose doctrine and ministry GOD will effectively work in hearts Acts 26. vers. 18. Romans 11. vers. 14. 1. Corinthians 9. vers. 12. James 5. vers. 20. But Peter is by no means dealing with this efficacy of the Evangelical ministry in this place, but rather with κοινωνίᾳ the glory, which κοινωνίαν παθημάτων will follow at some time. Lyranus, in order to soften this fault of the Vulgate version, explains partaker as preacher of glory, without doubt looking back to the exposition just brought forward. But anyone sees that this is forced, whence Estius freely confesses the fault of the Vulgate version in this place. Partaker, he says, is not properly said of one who becomes a consort, but of one who makes others consorts, which Peter did not wish to ascribe to himself. This is the third argument of the exhortation, likewise taken from the person of Peter. But in the application, a diversity occurs again. For some wish glory in this place to be understood as that glory of Christ which had been revealed to him, as also to James and John, in the transfiguration, which was a certain type of the glory to be communicated to the elect in a certain degree on the day of judgment, concerning which the 2nd Epistle cap. 1. vers. 16. & 17. the Apostle speaks thus. ἔποπται we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, for he received from God the Father honor and glory &c. Related to this exposition is that which is of Hugo, Dionysius etc., by which glory is taken for that glory of Christ, which shone forth in his own resurrection and ascension. Bede joins both expositions. Then, he says, he was a partaker of glory, when he beheld the heavenly glory of his countenance on the Holy Mount with John and James, or when he saw the power of his resurrection and ascension with the other disciples who were present. In the same way the interlinear Gloss, Hugo, the Carthusian, etc., expound it. According to this opinion, a verb of past tense must be supplied or understood, I was a partaker of glory. But it is more likely that the Apostle is speaking of the glory to be revealed on the day of judgment, in which way Oecumenius expounds this passage. For it is expressly said τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι δόξης κοινωνὸς, which is a periphrasis of the glory to be revealed at the last coming of Christ to judgment. Rom. 8. v. 18. For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy προς τὴν μέλλουσαν δόξαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι εἰς ἡμᾶς, and our Apostle has used a similar phrase in chap. 1. vers. 5. concerning the salvation of believers. You are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation εἰς σωτηρίαν ἑτόιμην ἀποκαλυφθῆναι ἐν καιρῷ ἔσχάτῳ, which passage is clearly parallel to this one of ours. The Apostolic saying Coloss. 3. vers. 3. can also be referred to here: Your life (and glory) is hid with Christ in God v. 4. When Christ, who is your life, shall appear, then shall you also appear with him in glory. The antithesis between the sufferings of Christ, i.e., those which the pious endure through Christ in this life, and the glory of the future age, confirms the same exposition, which manifestly shows that the Apostle is dealing in this place with the glory to be revealed on the day of judgment. 2. Cor. 4. v. 17. For that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation works for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. 2. Timoth. 4. vers. 7. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. vers. 8. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness. Apocal. 1. vers. 9. I John, your brother and companion in tribulation and in the kingdom, The sinew of the argument therefore is such. The reward of my heavenly glory in the office of faithfulness will be common to me with you, if you yourselves also apply due diligence in your office. Therefore it is fair that a place be left by you for my admonition.

Latin:

SENIORES ERGO QUI IN VOBIS SUNT, OBSECRO, CONSENIOR & TESTIS CHRISTI PASSIONUM, & EIUS, QUAE IN FUTURO REVELANDA EST, GLORIAE COMMUNICATOR.

Connexio. 1. Postquam à v. 8. capitis 3. usque ad finem cap. 4. praecedentis in genere omnes eos, ad quos scribit, Apostolus fuerat exhortatus ad vitae sanctitatem, Christianam caritatem & cumprimis ad afflictionum tolerantiam ac patientiam, redit ad exhortationem specialem, sive ad locos personales & hypotheticos, quales etiam tractaverat secundo ac tertio capitibus. Ut ergò ibi primùm subditos cap. 1. v. 13. Secundò servos cap. eiusd. v. 18. Tertiò uxores cap. 3. v. 1. Quartò maritos cap. eiusd. v. 7. sui admonuerat officii. iam porrò Presbyteros & iuniores compellat, eosdemque itidem de muneris sui debito informat. Sic ergò à statu politico & oeconomico transit Apostolus ad statum Ecclesiasticum.

2. Dixerat Apostolus cap. proximè praeced. v. 11. Si quis loquitur, ut eloquia Dei. Si quis ministrat, tanquam ex virtute, quam suppeditat Deus, quae praecepta directè & propriè pertinent ad eos qui in ministerio Ecclesiastico constituti sunt, hanc ergò exhortationem uberiùs hoc loco declarat.

CAPUT V.

3. Sub finem praecedentis capitis eos, qui patiuntur secundùm Dei voluntatem, exhortatus fuerat, ut animas suas Deo fideli earum conditori in bonis operibus commendent. Quia vero salutare hoc monitum non nisi ex ministerii Ecclesiastici informatione sciri, ac non nisi ex eiusdem seriâ inculcatione in praxin deduci potest, ideò Apostolus iam porrò eos, qui Ministerio Ecclesiastico funguntur, sui officii admonet.

Textus dispositio. Exhortaturus eos, qui docendi officio in Ecclesia funguntur ad sedulam gregis sibi commissi curam, tria praemittit exhortationis argumenta, quae omnia & singula è persona exhortantis sunt deducta. Primò se vocat sympresbyterum. Secundò passionum Christi testem. Tertiò gloriae coelestis suo tempore revelandae consortem. Quae concludendi vis insit singulis argumentis, postea apparebit.

Expositio. Πρεσβυτέρους τοὺς ἐν ὑμῖν παρακαλῶ. Regius & alius Codex addunt particulam illativam οὖν, quam etiam habet Syrus Interpres [consult facsimile image] ut & vulgata translatio. Seniores ergò obsecro, quâ ratione connexio huius exhortationis cum praecedentibus expressè insinuaretur, sed reliqui Codices omnes simpliciter legunt, πρεσβυτέρους τοῦς ἐν ὑμῖν. Lorinus ex ignorantia supina existimavit voculam [consult facsimile image] in textu Syriaco significare autem, cum particula [consult facsimile image] in textu Syriaco ponatur pro οὖν,[consult facsimile image] ac pronomen relativum ego coniungatur cum verbo [consult facsimile image]peto, obsecro. Tremellius reddidit autem. Sed [consult facsimile image] absolutè positum est coniunctio adversativa Matth. 1. v. 12.18. &c. quando autem coniungitur cum [consult facsimile image] est illativa & connexiva respondens Graeco οὖνMatth. 7. vers. 20.cap. 12. v. 12. &c. Intelligit autem Apostolus per Presbyteros eos, quos Spiritus sanctus gregi praeposuit Episcopos pascere Ecclesiam DEIAct. 20. v. 28.qui laborant in verbo & doctrina.1. Timoth. 5. v. 17. qui sunt Ecclesiae doctores, & morum gubernatores, unde Hieronymus in Epistola 85. ad Evagrium rectè monet, Presbyterum hoc loco, quemadmodum & in Actis Apostolicis & in Epistolis Paulinis non esse nomen aetatis, sed officii & dignitatis, id quod evidenter colligitur ex praecepto pascendi, in versu seq. Presbyteris hisce dato, unde etiam Beda secutus Hieronymum, Presbyteros hosce vocat Ecclesiae Pastores. Sicut, inquit, Dominus Beato Petro totius gregis eius, hoc est, Ecclesiae curam habere iussit, ita ipse Petrus sequentibus Ecclesiae pastoribus iure mandat, ut eum quisque, qui secum est, gregem DEI solicita gubernatione tutetur. Addit autemτοὺς ἐν ὑμῖν,ut significet, se determinatè & in specie compellare illos Presbyteros, qui in Ecclesiis Ponti, Galatiae, Cappadociae, Asiae & Bithyniae docendi munere tùm temporis fungebantur,1. Petr. 1. vers. 1.ipsum interim praeceptum generale est, pertinens ad omnium temporum & locorum Presbyteros. Hugo monet, Apostolum hâc loquendi formulâ Presbyteros humilitatis monere voluisse, cum non dicat, Presbyteros, qui super vos sunt, sed qui in vobis, seu inter vos sunt. Sed hoc subtilius, quàm verius, statim enim in v. seq. Apostolus eâdem loquendi formulâ de grege Presbyteris hisce commisso utitur. ac si vel maximè κυριότης ac primatus Monarchicae potestatis Presbyteris meritò denegetur, tamen ἐξοχὴ ac primatus honoris ipsis denegari nequit, ac proinde non possunt nec debent Pastores gregi omnimodè exaequari.

Παρακαλῶ Vulgata reddidit obsecro, id quod Iohannes Hussus exponit: ob sacra vel per omnia sacra oro. Syrus itidem reddidit per [consult facsimile image]petens, obsecransMatth. 8. vers. 5.Rom. 12. vers. 5. Glossa interlinearis ex eo deducit hanc doctrinam, quod Seniores sint obsecrandi.1. Tim. 5. vers. 1.Seniorem ne increpaveris, sed obsecra ut Patrem, iuniores ut fratres. Et sanè verbum παρακαλῶ quandoque obsecrandi significationem obtinet, Matth. 8. vers. 5.31. & 34.cap. 14. vers. 36.cap. 18. vers. 29. & 32. &c. interim tamen saepius, praesertium in Actis & Epistolis Apostolicis significationem etiam exhortandi habet Actor. 2. vers. 40.capitis 11. vers. 23.cap. 14. vers. 27.

Roman. 15. vers. 30.cap. 16. vers. 17. quo modo etiam à Petro usurpatur in hac ipsa Epistola cap. 2. vers. 11.cap. 5. vers. 12. unde Lutherus eam hoc loco in versione Germanica secutus fuit LXX. itidem utuntur pro סית quod significat extimulare, suadereDeuter. 13. vers. 6. Interim potest utraque significatio, ut in cap. 2. vers. 11. ita quoque hoc loco coniungi. Hortor, & si fas est, oro atque obsecro.

ὁ συμπρεσβύτερος. Hieronymus Epist. 85. reddidit, compresbyter. Complutensis Codex pro ὁ substituit ὡςtanquam sympresbyter. Sed reliqui Codices omnes legunt ὁ συμπρεσβύτερος, sicut & Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image]ego senior, vester socius. Primum in hac vocula continetur exhortationis argumentum, à persona sua ductum. Sed in explicatione occurrit diversitas. Quidam existimant, respectum haberi ad aetatem. Gloss. interlin. Senili aetati confavete. Sic ergò foret sensus. Quia consilium senile est sobrium & maturum, & quia senibus haec deferri solet reverentia, ut eorum praeceptis locus detur, ideò aquum est, vos Presbyteros mihi salutaria praecepta praescribenti obsequentes vos praebere. Simili argumento utitur Paulus in Epistola ad Philemonem v. 9.Διὰ τὴν ἀγάπην μᾶλλον παρακαλῶ τοιοῦτος ὢν ὡς Παῦλος πρεσβύτης. Sed quia nomen praecedens Presbyteri de officio usurpatur, ut paulo antè ostendimus, ideò etiam sympresbyteri nomen rectiùs ad officium offertur, ut argumenti vis sit ista. Quia in eodem officio Ecclesiastico vobiscum constitutus sum, quia officii dignitate vobis par sum, ideò aequum est, vos meae exhortationi locum relinquere. Conciliat ergò sibi hoc titulo autoritatem, innuens, se iure quodam suo Presbyteros monere, cum sit unus ex ipsorum numero.

Καὶ μάρτυς τῶν τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθημάτων. Lutherus reddidit, Ein Zeuge der leiden die in Christo sind. Videtur igitur hoc accepisse de passionibus, quae adhuc sunt in mystico Christi corpore, quò pertinet, quod quidam passiones Christi interpretantur, non quas Christus in proprio suo corpore paessus, sed quas Petrus pro Christo passus, ut testis afflictionum Christi, sit testis pro Christo afflictus. Sed Graeca simpliciter habent, testis Christi paessionum, ubi possunt intelligi passiones, non quae adhuc sunt, sed quae olim fuerint in personali & proprio Christi corpore, quae in plurali vocantur παθήματα, uti etiam fecerat cap. 1. vers. 11. & cap. 4. v. 13. quia Christus varii & diversi generis passiones in sanctissima sua anima & corpore sustinuit. Continetur autem in his verbis alterum exhortationis argumentum. Sed in applicatione itidem quaedam diversitas occurrit. Quidam enim volunt, Petrum ideò vocare seipsum testem passionum Christi, quia per verbum crucis1. Cor. 1. v. 18. h. e. per praedicationem Evangelii de Christo crucifixo de Christi passionibus testimonium ferebat, quippe quarum ipse unà cum reliquis Apostolis oculatus testis fuerat.Act. 10. v. 39. & 40. Iuxta hanc hypothesin nexus argumenti esset talis. Quia sum testisαὐτό πτηςpassionum Christi, & oculis hisce meis conspexi, quàm dura & gravia fuerit passus, ac proinde quàm caro precio Ecclesiam fidei vestrae commissam redemeritAct. 20. v. 28.ideò aequum est, vos Presbyteros exhortationi meae locum relinquere, & gregi Dominico solicitè providere, quâ ratione hic locus Apostolicus cum exhortatione PaulinaActor. 20. v. 28.esset planè parallelus. Sed quia statim addit Apostolus, se non solùm passionum Christi esse testem, sed etiam gloriae revelandae consortem, ideò rectiùs statuitur, Petrum non ideò solûm se vocare passionum Christi testem, quòd Christi passiones, h. e. mortem & crucem verbo praedicaret, sed etiam quia doctrinae de Christo crucifixo opere ipso, h. e. varias passiones propter Christum & eius verbum sustinendo testimonium praebebat, adeoque passiones Christi in sua persona quasi repraesentabat. Sic Matth. 10. v. 17. cum Christus praedixisset Apostolis, tradent vos in Concilia, & in Synagogis suis flagellabunt vosv. 18.& ad Praesides & Reges ducemini propter me, subiungit, in testimonium illis & gentibus, sive contra illos, i. e. ut videntes vestram παῤῥησίαν & constantiam de veritate Evangelii convincantur, nec possint in iudicio extremo quidquam afferre, quo se excusent. Inde Beda utramque explicationem coniungit. Ideò videlicet testis, inquit, quòd praesens illo patiente astitit, & cuncta, ut gerebantur, aspexit: vel certè quia & ipse propter nomen Christi carcerem, vincula ac verbera passus est, ut in Apostolorum actibus legimus. Nexus ergò ac nervus argumenti Apostolici hic est. Quia in officio docendi, quod vobiscum commune habeo, varias propter Christum afflictiones, persecutiones & contumelias tolero, ideò aequum est, admonitioni meae locum dari. Ex illis enim facilè colligere potestis, me rem maximè seriam agere, & fidum, Christi ministrum esse, cum per crucis tolerantiam fidei meae experimentum dederim.

Ὁ καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι δόξης κοινωνός. Vulgata reddidit, & eius, quae in futuro revelanda est, gloriae communicator. Sed Erasmus rectè monet, illud in futuro redundare. Graecum enim τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι propriè est, quae revelabitur, seu quae futura est revelari. Syrus reddidit, quae parata est revelari, i. e. quae revelanda. Maius adhuc vulgatae versionis vitium est, quod κοινωνὸν reddidit communicatorem. Communicator enim non sumitur passivè pro eo, qui consors est & particeps, quod Graecum κοινωνὸς propriè significat, sed activè pro eo, qui consortes alios facit. perquam vero absurdum foret statuere, quòd Petrus sibi adscribere voluerit potestatem & dignitatem eam, quâ possit alios coelestis gloriae consortes facere. Novimus quidem, Paulum ad Timotheum scribere 1. Epist. 4. vers. 16.Attende tibi & doctrinae, permane in illis, haec enim faciens, & teipsum salvum facies, & eos, qui te audiunt. Sed manifestum est, Apostolum ibi loqui de efficacia Ministerii, ut sit sensus, eris salutare organum, per cuius doctrinam & ministerium DEUS efficaciter in cordibus operabitur Actor. 26. vers. 18.Roman. 11. vers. 14.1. Corinth. 9. vers. 12.Iacob. 5. vers. 20. Sed de hac ministerii Evangelici efficacia Petrus hoc loco minimè agit, verùm de κοινωνίᾳ gloriae, quae κοινωνίαν παθημάτων aliquando sequetur. Lyranus ut hoc vulgatae versionis vitium emolliret, communicatorem exponit per praedicatorem gloriae, dubio procul respiciens ad expositionem modò allatam. Sed quilibet videt hoc esse coactum, unde Estius vitium vulgatae versionis h. l. liberè profitetur. Communicator, inquit, propriè non dicitur, qui fit consors, sed qui consortes alios facit, quod Petrus sibi adscribere non voluit. Tertium hoc est exhortationis argumentum, itidem à persona Petri sumtum. Sed in applicatione denuò occurrit diversitas. Quidam enim volunt, per gloriam hoc loco intelligi eam Christi gloriam, quae in transfiguratione ipsi, ut etiam Iacobo & Iohanni fuerat revelata, quae typas quidam fuit gloriae in die iudicii electis certo gradu communicandae, de quae Epist. 2. cap. 1. vers. 16. & 17.Apostolus sic loquitur.ἔποπταιinspectores facti sumus illius magnificentiae, accipiens enim à Deo Patre honorem & gloriam &c. Huic expositioni cognata est ea, quae est Hugonis, Dionysri &c. quâ gloria accipitur pro ea Christi gloria, quae in ipsius resurrectione & ascensione reluxit. Beda utramque expositionem coniungit. Tunc, inquit, fuit gloriae consors, cum in monte Sancto gloriam vultus eius coelestem cum Iohanne & Iacabo conspexit, sive cum resurrectionis & ascensionis eius potentiam cum caeteris, qui affuêre, discipulis vidit. Eodem modo exponit Glossa interl. Hugo, Carthusianus &c. Secundùm hanc sententiam supplendum vel subintelligendum praeteriti temporis verbum, consors fui gloriae. Sed verisimilius est, Apostolum loqui de gloria in die iudicii revelanda, quo modo hunc locum exponit Oecumenius. Expressè enim dicitur τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι δόξης κοινωνὸς, quae est periphrasis gloriae in novissimo Christi ad iudicium adventu revelandae. Rom. 8. v. 18.Existimo enim, quòd non sint condignae passiones huius temporisπρος τὴν μέλλουσαν δόξαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι εἰς ἡμᾶς, ac simili phrasi in cap. 1. vers. 5. de salute credentium Apostolus noster usus est. Custodimini in virtute Dei per fidem ad salutemεἰς σωτηρίαν ἑτόιμην ἀποκαλυφθῆναι ἐν καιρῷ ἔσχάτῳ, qui locus huic nostro planè parallelus. Potest etiam huc referri dictum Apostolicum Coloss. 3. vers. 3.Vita (& gloria vestra) abscondita est cum Christo in Deo v. 4.Cùm autem Christus apparuerit vita vestra, tunc & vos cum ipso apparebitis in gloria. Eandem expositionem confirmat antithesis inter passiones Christi i. e. quas per Christum pii in hac vita tolerant & gloriam futuri seculi, quae manifestè ostendit, de gloria in die iudicii revelanda Apostolum hoc loco agere. 2. Cor. 4. v. 17.Id quod in praesenti est momentaneum & leve tribulationis nostrae supra modum in sublimitate aeternum pondus gloriae operatur.2. Timoth. 4. vers. 7.Bonum certamen certavi, cursum consummavi, fidem servavi.vers. 8.In reliquo reposita est mihi corona iustitiae.Apocal. 1. vers. 9.Ego Iohannes frater vester & particeps in tribulatione & regno, Nervus igitur argumenti talis est. Gloriae coelestis meae in officio fidelitatis merces mihi vobiscum communes erit, si ipsimet quoque debitam in officio diligentiam adhibueritis. Ergò aequum est, admonitioni meae locum à vobis relinqui.

## 5:1-5 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. Who are understood by Presbyters? Although the name πρεσβυτέρων is sometimes understood simply regarding age in the sacred Scriptures Luke 15. v. 25.John 8. v. 9.Acts 2. v. 17.1. Tim. 5. v. 1. etc., to which are opposed νεώτεροι or νεανίσκοι, in which signification our Apostle uses this name in this very chapter v. 5.: nevertheless, from the word of feeding in v. 2. it is manifest that the name Presbyter in this place is a name of office and dignity, by which the overseers of the Churches were formerly called. Therefore, the Latin Interpreter would have done better if he had retained the name Presbyter from the Greek, as Jerome did in Epistle 85 to Evagrius. And since it can be gathered from 1. Tim. 5. v. 17. that there were twofold Presbyters in the Church, or two orders of Presbyters. For some labored in the word and doctrine, i.e., they were pastors and teachers of the Church, but some were only ἡγούμενοι, who together with the teachers governed the Church, and had care of doctrine and discipline, it is manifest that Peter is dealing in this place with the former order of Presbyters.

Q. 2. Why are the Teachers of the Church called Presbyters? Resp. 1. Because they ought to excel others either in age or in senile prudence. 2. Because they were for the most part chosen from the Elders, just as those who preside over the Republic are called Senators, for the reason that the Senate is for the most part gathered from the Elders, whence the Senate has its mild name from the Elders, and In Homer, Iliad, β γέροντες the same are said, who ἀριστῆες. Job 12. v. 12. In the aged is wisdom, and in much time is prudence. Yet it was not constituted of old men alone πρεσβυτερεῖον, but younger men were also sometimes co-opted into it, as the example of Timothy shows, of whom the Apostle says, 1. Tim. 4. vers. 12. Let no one despise your youth: meanwhile the whole College was called a Presbytery with respect to the more powerful part.

Q. 3. Whether simple Presbyters, who are not at the same time Bishops, are also included under this name? Estius denies it, for he comments on this passage thus. Insofar as the name of Presbyter is general even by the usage of the Apostles, so that it embraces all who are of the Priestly order, as Philipp. 1. 1. Tim. 3. & 5. Tit. 1. yet principally this term suits only Bishops, Peter, as those who alone properly and in a full sense are pastors of the Lord's flock, not called to a part of the work, as parish priests are, but having absolute and unlimited power, as far as divine law pertains, of exercising the pastoral office in their own flock, to whom therefore it pertains not only to preach the word of God, and to administer the Sacraments, which both parish priests do, but truly also to set laws, and to punish transgressors, and to cast out the contumacious from the Church through excommunication, whence also in the canons and among the ancients they alone are called Pastors. But also Paul Eph. 4. understood only Bishops when naming pastors and teachers. But it is more correctly said that the name of Presbyters is a common name for all ministers of the word. 1. Estius himself admits that by the usage of the Apostles this name embraces all who are of the Priestly order, as is evident Act. 14. v. 23. cap. 15. v. 2. & seqq. cap. 20. v. 17. 1. Tim. 5. v. 17. Tit. 1. v. 5. Iac. 5. v. 14. &c. 2. We are compelled by no necessity to depart from this customary meaning, since those things which the Apostle prescribes to the Presbyters in this place pertain to all ministers of the Church. 3. They are indeed commanded ἐπισκοπεῖν, but from that it cannot be proven that only Bishops placed over the inspection of other Doctors of the Church are understood here, since they are commanded ἐπισκοπεῖν to the Lord's flock, which is common to all Pastors. 4. To set laws, to punish transgressors, to excommunicate the contumacious &c. does not pertain to Bishops alone, but to the whole Presbytery, indeed to the whole Church, whose consent must be added Act. 15. v. 22. 1. Cor. 5. v. 4. therefore we by no means grant absolute and unlimited power to the Bishops of the Church. 5. And the name of pastors and teachers is general, pertaining to all ministers of the Church, whence Hieron.

In his commentary on this passage, and Augustine in Epistle 59 to Paulinus, note that while the Apostle distinguished the kinds of offices in other places, here he joined two. For he did not say, some pastors, some teachers, but others pastors and teachers, because whoever are pastors, the same ought also to be teachers. Cornelius à Lapide, departing from Estius, says, that Elders are understood here both by age, and by dignity and Priesthood, whether it be lesser and common, or greater, such as the Episcopate.

Q. 4. Why does the Apostle admonish the Presbyters of their duty only in the last place? Resp. 1. Because their order is more excellent than the remaining orders and ages, therefore, as if ascending by degrees after various admonitions, delivered to subjects, servants, wives, and husbands established in the economic and political order, he addresses the Presbyters, who bear the care of souls, and are established in the Ecclesiastical order. 2. As the safety of a kingdom consists in the King, the safety of the sheep in the Shepherd, the health of the members in the head: so the safety of the Churches consists in the Overseers or Presbyters. Just as seeing a tree, withered with pale leaves, you understand that it has some fault around the root: so when you see an undisciplined people, without doubt know that its Priesthood is not holy, says Chrysostom on the symbol. Deservedly, therefore, the Apostle deferred the exhortation to the Presbyters to the last place, since the safety of the remaining Orders depends upon them. 3. Since Presbyters instruct others in life and morals, they seemed to need fewer admonitions than the remaining Orders.

Q. 5. For what purpose does the Apostle call himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ? Resp. 1. That he may thereby procure greater authority and faith for his exhortation. For because he has proven himself a faithful minister of Christ by this tolerance of sufferings, therefore it is just that room be left for his admonition, which has proceeded from a faithful heart. 2. By that commemoration of his own sufferings, by which sufferings he bears witness to the sufferings of Christ, he admonishes the Presbyters not to cease from their office for fear of persecutions and afflictions, or to dissimulate the truth; but to confess Christ freely and intrepidly, and by no means to fear to sustain sufferings, or even death itself, for the truth, for which purpose he also immediately raises them up with himself into the same hope of future glory.

Q. 6. Why does he command the Presbyters not to provide for the flock by compulsion, but voluntarily and with a ready mind? Resp. 1. He wishes to prevent the office they make their own, though unwilling, that which is proper to those who perpetually complain about the troubles of pastoral care. 2. Because as in other kinds of life, so much more in the Ecclesiastical office, forced services do not please GOD. 3. True Pastors are distinguished from hirelings by this reason, that the former perform their duty with a ready and liberal mind, but the latter do not do so unless unwillingly.

Q. 7. Whether it pertains to the pastors, or to the flock, that the pasturing ought not to be done ἀναγκαστῶς; Resp. Some refer it to the flock, in the sense that such commands ought not to be given to the sheep, and that they should be ruled in such a way that they do not appear to execute them unwillingly and forced, but willingly and eagerly. Nazianzen in Apolog. seems to have followed this sense, confirming from this Apostolic passage that subjects are not to be restrained by force, but to be enticed by persuasion. For what is expressed by force and necessity, he says, besides being Tyrannical and not at all praiseworthy, is not even firm and stable. For that to which force is applied is accustomed, not unlike a plant bent by force by the hands, as soon as it has been released, to return to itself again: but that which proceeds from free will is accustomed to be both most equitable and most firm, inasmuch as it is bound and preserved by the bonds of benevolence. Next he cites this Apostolic passage and adds. And therefore our law and our legislator have sanctioned this most of all, that the flock be pastured not forcedly, but spontaneously and with a willing mind. But the context shows that it pertains properly to the pastors. 1. Because the Apostle here deals directly with the office of pastors. 2. Ἐπισκοποῦντες pertains properly to Pastors or Bishops. 3. What follows, μὴ αἰσχροκερδῶς, ἀλλὰ προθύμως, μηδὲ κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων, likewise pertains uniquely to Pastors. Meanwhile, the doctrine of Nazianzen, which he deduces not inappropriately from this passage, is deservedly opposed to the Papal manner of conversion and Ecclesiastical government, by which they do not entice subjects by persuasion, but force them by violence.

Q. 8. Whether the Ministry or the office of pasturing ought to be committed to anyone unwilling? Resp. Sometimes even pious and holy men, most suitable for the Ecclesiastical Ministry, refuse to undertake it, since it is a thing to be trembled at even by Angelic shoulders. Thus Moses, called to the office of leading the people out of Egypt, opposed the exception of eloquence, Exod. 4. vers. 10. Jeremiah, called to the Prophetic office, opposed the exception of age, Ierem. 1. vers. 6. Many Claudius Espensaeus reviews examples of this refusal in book 3 of his digressions on the First Epistle of Paul to Timothy. That for the most part he is not worthy of the Ministry, unless he has been ordained against his will, it is said in law Si quenquam, 31. C. de Episcopis. But those who refuse out of modesty must be persuaded not to have greater regard for private rest than for public advantage, and not to bring upon themselves the punishment of Jonah by stubbornly resisting a divine calling. Jon. 1. vers. 3. Peraldus the Bishop in his summa of virtues cap. 12. Those who can be suitable for the office of Preacher and choose to live only for themselves, although they do so with a good intention, namely that they may serve GOD with a purer conscience, nevertheless it seems much to be feared, because that servant who hid his talent in a napkin is called by the Lord a wicked servant, and as Gregory says, those who are endowed with knowledge and virtue and seek the retreat of contemplation are guilty of as many souls as they could have benefited by preaching. But if nevertheless someone continues to refuse the offered Ministry, it is rightly gathered from this Apostolic passage that it should not be conferred upon him against his will and reluctantly, but that another suitable person should be looked for. Gregory writes of himself in book 4, Epist. 35, that he never wished to force anyone to accept a Bishopric, Ambrose in Psalm. 118. octon. 14. from the Davidic words, Approve the voluntary offerings of my mouth. The Lord approves of waiting for the Lord with voluntary ministers, and that the reward of this entire devotion is fuller, which he proves by the example of Isaiah, whom he says was filled with a richer grace of the Spirit as a voluntary instrument because he had said: Behold I, send me. Esai. 6. vers. 8. Luther on this passage. Those who perform the office under compulsion do not provide useful work for the Church. Compare, artic. de Minist. § 188.

Q. 9. What is understood by filthy lucre prohibited to Pastors? Primasius in his commentary on chapter 3 of the first to Timothy says, Filthy lucre is to seek earthly wealth from heavenly Sacraments. Sedulius, in almost the same way; to pursue earthly things from heavenly mysteries. But from a comparison of this saying with parallel passages 1. Tim. 3. v. 3. & 8. Tit. 1. v. 7. it is understood that by the desire for filthy lucre, avarice is generally understood.

Q. 10. Why does the Apostle wish the desire for filthy lucre to be absent from Presbyters? Resp. 1. Because where the desire for gain reigns, Pastors they easily become mercenaries, nay, wolves. Luth. in h. l. 2. Those who are given to avarice for a handful of barley flatter their hearers, and sew pillows, upon which sinners may sleep sweetly. Ezech. 13. v. 18. & 19. 3. Because the root of all evils is φυλαργυρία. 1. Tim. 6. v. 10. since the avaricious man has no concern from where and for what cause he receives, intent only on increasing his wealth. Guillandus in h. l. The Apostle wishes avarice, the root of all evils, to be especially alien to a Bishop. For there is nothing that more hinders the Episcopal function and dishonors the name of Bishop than the corruption of gifts.

Q. 11. Who are understood by τοὺς κλήρους in v. 3. ? Resp. Some understand those deputed to Ecclesiastical Ministries, namely Presbyters and Deacons, over whom Bishops are set, in which sense dominion over other Presbyters would be forbidden to Bishops. Whence from this place they desire to prove that Ministers of the Church are called Clerics, for the reason that they belong peculiarly to the inheritance of the Lord. Jerome in his Epistle to Nepotianus. Bishops should know that they are Priests, not Lords, let them honor Clerics as Clerics, so that honor may also be deferred to them by Clerics as Bishops. That saying of the Orator Domitius is well known. Why should I hold you as a Prince, when you do not hold me as a Senator? Afterwards he brings forward this Apostolic place, μήδε κατακυριέυοντες τῶν κλήρων. Salmero in h. l. Feed with gentleness and modesty, not as exercising dominion or principality over the Clergy &c. By the Clergy he understands the sacred assembly, inscribed to the Ministry of the altar. But by τοὺς κλήρους are more correctly understood the portions of the Lord's flock, which have fallen to individual Bishops to be fed. 1. Because Peter speaks here of Presbyters in general i. e. of all ministers of the Church, not of Bishops in species, as we showed above. 2. Τοὺς κλήρους Peter himself explains by τὸ πόιμνιον both in the preceding verse 7, and in the following words of this verse, where the Apostle opposes to dominion over the Clergy the becoming τύπον of the flock. 3. The Syrian rendered τοὺς κλήρους by the flock. 4. The word κλήρου or κλήρων is nowhere in the N. Test. attributed peculiarly to the Ministers of the Church. 5. It would follow from this exposition that Bishops ought not indeed to lord it over Presbyters because of the Apostolic interdict, yet they could well exercise proud dominion over the flock committed to them, for thus the Papists explain the word κατακυριέυειν. 6. Nay, it is contained in in the word τῶν κλήρων there is a certain silent reason why they ought not to feed their flock in such a way that they exercise a certain lordship over it, namely because it is κλῆρος the lot and inheritance of the Lord. 7. That exposition, by which the little word τῶν κλήρων is extended to the whole flock attributed to each Bishop, is approved by Cyril in his book on Isaiah, oration 3, and Bede in this place. Some reckon Oecumenius among those who by τοὺς κλήρους understand Presbyters or the Ecclesiastical Senate. But he explains it by ἱερὸν σύστημα a sacred assembly, which can conveniently be understood as the Lord's flock. 8. Many of the Papists themselves embrace this exposition, not only Erasmus, whom Bellarmine calls a Semi-Catholic, and Vatablus, to whom they likewise do not attribute much, but also Cajetan, Gagnaeus, Titelmannus, Emanuel à Sa in this place, Jansenius in Psal. 67. etc. Estius proves this exposition with many arguments. Cleros, he says, many of the Latins interpret as Clerics, that is, those deputed to Ecclesiastical Ministries etc. Nevertheless, it is far more probable that by Cleros are understood the portions of the Lord's flock which have fallen by lot to individual Bishops to be fed and ruled, according to that which Cyprian says, that the Church is one, of which individual Bishops hold individual portions in solidum etc. Certainly, that the whole flock is understood here by the name of Clerus is sufficiently argued by the adversative which Peter makes, not lording it over the Cleros, but being examples of the flock, as if Clerus and flock were the same. Wherefore also the Syrian Interpreter wrote flock for Cleros, not as lords of the flock etc. Finally, it is not customary to call them Cleros in the plural, but Clerus as a collective noun. Therefore, we do not hesitate to prefer this understanding, by which the word Cleros is extended to the whole flock attributed to each Bishop, over the former.

Q. 12. Why does the Apostle propose to faithful Presbyters the hope of a most ample reward in heaven? Resp. He does this by the example of Christ Matth. 24. v. 45.cap. 25. v. 21. in order to show that faithful Ministers must look not to the rewards of this age, but to those of the heavenly life, and therefore, lest a longer expectation beget languor, he simultaneously proclaims the amplitude of the heavenly reward, which will most bountifully compensate for that delay, whatever it may be.

Q. 13. Who are understood by τοὺς νεωτέρους in v. 5.? 1. Some wish that by them are understood the hearers, committed to the care and faith of the Presbyters, to whom obedience toward their pastors and leaders is prescribed, That this passage of ours from the Apostle may be parallel to the Pauline preceptHebr. 13. v. 17.Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls. 1. Because this precept given to the younger corresponds to the precept given to the Presbyters in the preceding words, so that therefore there by πρεσβυτέρους are understood the Bishops or Pastors of the Church, who are commanded to feed the flock committed to them: so in turn by τοὺς νεωτέρους are seen to be understood the hearers, belonging to the Lord's flock. 2. The term ὁμοίως, favors this exposition, by which the reciprocal duty of Presbyters and the younger seems to be insinuated. 3. The same is proved from the word ὑποτάγητε. For although the younger in age ought to show reverence to the elders Lev. 19. v. 32., they do not properly owe them obedience, unless they are subject to them for some reason other than age. 4. Luc. 22. vers. 26. the name νεωτέρου is opposed to μείζοι, just as the name διακονοῦντος τῷ ἡγουμένῳ. 5. Bede seems to indicate this sense, who comments thus on this place. After he taught the Elders how they should preside, it was fitting that he should also instruct the younger to obey their fatherly provision. But there was no need to say more to them, but he only gives the precept of subjection, because indeed he had commanded the Elders that they should be an example to the subjects &c. 2. Salmero by τοὺς νεωτέρους understands simple Presbyters subject to Bishops, hence he comments on this place. There was a doubt not to be despised, to whom these adolescents are to be referred, whether to the grades lower than the Episcopate, as are the seven sacred orders, or to those who are younger in age. The former opinion pleases me more, just as it also pleases the Presbyter Bede, to which some things move me. First because he says, likewise you who are younger, so that he speaks of those who are under the pastors already mentioned. Secondly because he said, not lording it over the Clergy, whom he now shows these adolescents to be. Thirdly because just as he calls Bishops Elders, or Presbyters: so he calls the lower grades younger, which by the Greek word νεωτέρους he denotes, and it is opposed to those whom he called πρεσβυτέρους i. e. simple Presbyters, Deacons and Subdeacons. The word be subject also serves this understanding, that is, be subject to others, or subordinate ὑποτασσόμενοι in the Ecclesiastical Ministry &c. Therefore under the name of the younger he comprehends every function pertaining to the lower grades, as if he were describing the proper duties of individual orders and grades. Cornel. à Lapide on this place principally by adolescents are accepted the Clerics of the lower of orders such as Deacons, Lectors, Exorcists, this truly above all befits those subject to Presbyters, i. e. Priests. For just as a little before the command was for presbyters not to lord it over the Clergy, i. e. the minor and younger Clerics, so in turn he warns these, that they should not grow insolent against the Presbyters, but submit themselves to them. Thus Cajetan, Salmeron, Arias & others. 3. But the name νεωτέρων is more correctly understood of those who are younger in age. For although the name of Presbyters in v. 1 is a name of office, yet because that College of Presbyters was constituted principally from those who are Elders in age, therefore the Apostle passes from a related meaning to a related one in a manner customary in the Scriptures, and after he had dealt with those who are Presbyters by office and dignity, he proceeds to treat of those who are Presbyters by age. By the name of subjection he does not require any servile obedience from the younger, nor does he attribute any absolute lordship to the elders, but he demands the reverence and obedience owed to senile age, for ὑποτάττεσθαι is properly to be subordinated.

Q. 14. Why does he wish the younger to be subject to the elders? Resp. because the old are strong in authority, counsel, and prudence; he requires, therefore, that the younger be ruled by the counsels of the elders, and that they follow them with due reverence.

Q. 15. Why does he require only subjection from them? Bede answers in this way. There was no need to say more to them, but only to give the precept of subjection, because, of course, he had commanded the Elders that they should be a pattern to the subjects, and it was sufficient for the younger to look to the examples of the elders acting well, and to imitate these devoutly. But these things proceed from that hypothesis, that the name of Presbyters in v. 1 and 5 is used in the same meaning. It must be answered, therefore, that this is done because humility is the mother of all the remaining virtues. For he who judges himself inferior to another, reveres him, complies with his counsels, and accommodates himself to his manners.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Pastors are called Presbyters or Elders. O. T. But even younger men can be chosen for the Ministry1. Timoth. 4. v. 12. Resp. 1. The Ecclesiastical Senate is called the Presbytery, not because it consists only of, but because it consists principally of elders. 2. Ministers of the Church ought to be πρεσβύτεροι, if not in age, yet in senile prudence. The younger, therefore, are by no means absolutely and simply from They are excluded from the Ecclesiastical Ministry. Ambrose on Acholius, Truly that old age is venerable, which is not whitened by gray hairs, but by merits. For that is a reverend grayness, which is the grayness of the soul shining in gray thoughts and works. For what is truly the age of old age, if not an immaculate life, which is propagated not by days or months, but by ages, whose duration is without end, whose longevity is without weakness. Bernard in Epist. to Theobald. We see many of the younger ones surpassing the old in morals, anticipating the times of the ancients in merits, and compensating for what is lacking in age with virtues. Confer tract. on Minist. § 185.

2. Peter calls himself a fellow-presbyterv. 1.But he was an Apostle of Jesus Christ1. Epist. 1. v. 1.But an Apostle is the highest degree of Ecclesiastical Ministry.1. Corinth. 12. v. 28.Eph. 4. v. 13. Resp. The name of Presbyter is general, pertaining to all Ministers of the Church, and the Apostleship differs from the remaining Ecclesiastical Ministries not in species, but only in degree. Peter therefore calls himself one of the Presbyters, considering more what he had in common with all the rest, for the sake of insinuating humility, modesty, and fraternal friendship, than because anything peculiar had been given to him and the remaining Co-apostles over the rest of the pastors.

3. Feed τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον the flock committed to youv. 1. But τὸ ποίμνιον that is τοῦ θεοῦ ποίμνιον, in the same verse Acts 20. v. 28. Resp. The flock is of GOD and of Christ as the supreme Shepherd Eccl. 12. v. 11.Ezech. 34. v. 23.chap. 37. v. 24.Zachar. 13. v. 7.John 10. v. 11.Hebr. 13. v. 20. & as Peter himself v. 4. declares, as the Prince of shepherds. Also as the head of a household Matt. 10. v. 25. The flock of the Presbyters is as of subordinate and less principal Pastors. Jerem. 3. v. 15.chap. 23. v. 4.Ephes. 4. v. 11. Also as of stewards in the house of GOD, which is the Church 1. Tim. 3. v. 15. divinely appointed 1. Corinth. 4. v. 1.

4. Feed the flock of GOD μὴ ἀναγκαστῶς. v. 2.Therefore those are to be admitted who thrust themselves in without a calling, and pretend to teach by the free impulse of the Holy Spirit. Resp. Peter does not speak of αὐτοκλήτοις those running, since they are not sent divinely. Jerem. 23. v. 21. but of those who have been legitimately called to the Ministry Hebr. 5. v. 4. whence he notably says, feed the flock which is among you, i. e. the flock committed to you, namely through a legitimate calling. Isaiah indeed offers himself spontaneously, but he had heard first from GOD. Whom shall I send, and who will go to usEsa. 6. v. 8.and before his lips had been cleansed by the touch of a burning coal taken from the altarv. 7. Whatever the case may be, this Prophetic example is extraordinary.

5. Feed the flock of GOD μὴ ἀναγκαστῶς v. 2. But1. Cor. 9. v. 16.Necessity is laid upon me. Resp. The Apostle understands the necessity of his office and of his own calling, but not the necessity of coercion. For he immediately adds, v. 17. For if ἑκὼν I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if ἀκὼν against my will, a dispensation is committed to me, that is, the dispensation of preaching the Gospel is nonetheless entrusted to me, and therefore unless I faithfully perform it, I shall not have a reward, but a punishment.

6. Not for filthy lucre's sakev. 2.And yet all gain is filthy. Resp. The adjective αἰσχρὸν in this place is not added διακριτικῶς distinctively, as if it distinguishes dishonest gain from honest, but διοριστικῶς definitively, so that it may show that all gain which is sought from Ecclesiastical Ministry is filthy. It is called filthy lucre, however, not because it comes from a filthy thing, for he is speaking about Ecclesiastical functions, but because it is sought with a greedy mind and a desire for filthy lucre.

7. Likewise, you younger, submit yourselves unto the elderv. 5.And yetEsa. 65. vers. 20.There shall be no more thence an infant of days, nor an old man that hath not filled his days: for the child shall die an hundred years old; but the sinner being an hundred years old shall be accursed. Where impious old men, destitute of wisdom, are censured, to whom many years are still lacking, if one is to judge of years and age by piety and prudence, to whom also honor is not to be deferred.Psalm. 15. v. 5. Resp. The Apostle speaks of such old men who are old not only in age, but also in prudence. Iob. 12. v. 12.With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding.Sirac. 25. v. 6.How comely is the judgment of gray hairs and for elders to know counsel.v. 7.Much wisdom is the glory of old men, and the thought and counsel of the honorable!v. 8.Much experience is the crown of old men, and the fear of God is their glory.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. The Apostle calls the ministers of the Church πρεσβυτέρους, because they ought to excel either in age or certainly in senile prudence. Therefore, a grave sin is committed in the Papacy, in which, as Erasmus reports and experience attests, those who are still immature in age are more often chosen for Ecclesiastical benefices, even those with a cure, as they say, that is, those which have the care of souls joined to them. Johannes Hoffmeister in Harm. Fabricii. I shall speak with the Apology. How great is the evil, that in ordaining priests they do not choose suitable men. What of the market of Priesthoods. Also in dangerous dispensations, is there no vice! From the stables of horses, from the kitchen, Priests are snatched, who have not even in a dream thought about what a Priest is, men who are unworthy of the profession. These things they say, and truly. Afterwards. But now, as Nazianzen says, the thrones belong not to the more worthy, but to the more powerful. We make men holy in a single day, and we command those to be wise who are endowed with no wisdom, and who bring nothing to the rank except the desire for it. This fights against the Nature of the Ecclesiastical Ministry, which is ἔργον 1. Tim. 3. v. 1. it fights against the canons, which forbid anyone younger than thirty years to be chosen for the Presbyterate c. si quis dist. 78. from Boniface; c. Presbyter dist. ead. from the Council of Neocaesarea, c. cum in cunctis extra de electione & electi potest. from the Lateran Council. Although indeed a certain general rule cannot be handed down concerning the age of those to be chosen for the Ministry, nor can the number of years be precisely defined, since the statute concerning waiting for the 30th year before anyone is applied to sacred ministries Num. 4. vers. 3. is Levitical, and therefore by reason of the species it does not bind us in the N. T. at all; since Christ and John the Baptist by their own example Luc. 3. v. 23. did not wish to prescribe a certain rule, and to determine a certain number of years in choosing for the Ministry; since the Apostle in the form, according to which Bishops and Deacons are to be chosen 1. Tim. 3.Tit. 1. makes no mention of a certain age: it is certain, however, that ἱκανότητα must be regarded in the election to the ministry, which cannot have a place in boys. c. Pueri caus. 1. q. 1. Boys should by no means be admitted to sacred orders, lest they fall the more dangerously, the more quickly they hasten to ascend to higher things. Salmero in h. l. Disp. 8. p. 98. It was rightly instituted in the Church that no one should be promoted to the Episcopate who was younger than thirty years, and those completed at that. Let those, therefore, to whom it pertains to make these promotions consider how Bishops who are boys in age and morals can be accepted as elders, when they are destitute of the gravity of morals and age, which is indeed otherwise a great and most serious inconvenience.

2. Peter calls those who perform the Ecclesiastical Ministry Presbyters. v. 1. Therefore the same are Presbyters and Bishops. The argument is confirmed from the fact that he says the duties of Presbyters are ἐπισκοπεῖν v. 2. from which Bishops are named Actor. 20. vers. 28. It is false, therefore, what the Papists teach, that Bishops as regards power of jurisdiction are by divine right superior to Presbyters. Erasmus in his commentary on this place: He calls Presbyters Bishops, for the crowd of Priests had not yet grown, but as many as there were Presbyters, so many were Bishops. Salmero on this place: Jerome in his Epistle to Evagrius teaches, and from chapter 20 of the Acts it is shown, that the Apostle Paul calls those whom he had a little before called elders by birth that is Presbyters, soon after calls them Bishops, when he says; Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as Bishops to rule the Church of God. And whom Paul in the Epistle to Timothy calls a Bishop, in that to Titus he calls a Presbyter, and a little later in the same place he calls him a Bishop, whom he had called a Presbyter.

3. Peter holds Presbyters and Bishops in the same place. Therefore the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy is not of divine right, contrary to what the Papists teach. The argument is confirmed by the fact that Peter, in prescribing the duties of his office to the Presbyters, makes no mention of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, which he would certainly not have omitted if it descended from divine right. We have here again Salmero confessing, who comments thus on this place, page 103: It was asked why Peter does not mention the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, which has so many degrees of Bishops, Archbishops, Patriarchs, etc. This was done because it consists of Ecclesiastical and Canonical institution. But if they were enumerated here, they could be thought from this to exist by divine right, which would be false, even if we read in Clement in the Epistle to James, or in Anacletus in the first Epistle, that those degrees were instituted by the order and command of the Lord.

4. Peter calls himself συμπρεσβύτερον v. 1. Therefore he did not conduct himself as Christ's vicar on earth, the visible head and Monarch of the Church. For if he had been endowed with Monarchical power, and had said that he was endowed with it, the exhortation would have been more effective. This must be opposed to the Papists who inculcate the Monarchical power of Peter not so much for the sake of Peter, as for the sake of the Roman Pontiff. Salmero objects on this place to v. 4. 1. That Peter has supreme power in the Church over all Pastors, that was already sufficiently expressed in the Gospels, where he is instituted as Pastor of the sheep John 21. 2. and strengthener of his brethren Luke 22. 3. and the keys of the kingdom of heaven are promised to him Matthew 16. 4. in which the eminent power of Peter is signified, so that there was no need for it to be repeated here; especially since the whole Church and the Apostles regarded Peter as their primary that all might be subject to the head after Christ and might venerably obey him. Resp. That all these things contain a mere begging of the question is shown in its own place. The care of feeding the sheep committed to Peter by Christ is in turn committed by Peter to the Presbyters in this place. στήριξιν Paul also attributes to himself the title of brother Rom. 1. v. 11. the same is attributed to Timothy 1. Thess. 3. v. 2., the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to all the Apostles, indeed to all the ministers of the Church. Matth. 18. v. 18.Ioh. 20. v. 23. But Salmeron contradicts himself. For he says, because it had already been sufficiently expressed in the Gospels that Peter has supreme power in the Church over all Pastors, therefore there was no need for that to be repeated in this place, and yet he himself tries with great effort to evince the Monarchical power of Peter from this place, as we shall see later in ἐκδικήσει. 2. He objects, that Peter, when he calls himself one of the Elders, considered more what he had in common with all the rest, for the sake of indicating humility, and modesty, and mutual friendship, than to urge here supremely what was proper and singular to him above all others, i. e. to be the Pastor of the Universal Church and the Vicar of Christ. In the same way Estius in h. l. Who does not understand that Peter spoke thus for the sake of modesty, as one who knew that his exhortation to the Bishops would be more effective if he addressed them as brothers and partners, than if as subjects. And afterwards. But if the objection of Calvin were worth anything, it would follow that neither Peter nor Paul had any power of government over the common people of the faithful. For in their Epistles they call everyone brothers. Calvin ought to have remembered that the Lord Savior himself spoke of his Apostles in this way Matth. 28. Go, announce to my brothers. Resp. The argument against the Monarchical primacy of Peter is taken not only from this place, but from the whole of Scripture in this way. Peter neither in this place, nor anywhere else calls himself the Monarch of the Church, nor is this title attributed to him by Christ or the other Apostles. Therefore he was not the Monarch of the Church. Furthermore, the argument is not taken from the name alone, but also from the thing itself joined to the name. Peter neither in this place nor anywhere else conducts himself as a Monarch, but rather says that he is παρακαλεῖν ὡς συμπρεσβύτερον. Therefore he was not the Monarch of the Church. Although, therefore, we willingly concede that Peter for the sake of modesty calls himself a fellow-elder, when he could have called himself an Apostle, yet the reason for the Apostleship and Monarchical power is different. He could have truly called himself an Apostle, just as he also calls himself 1. Epist. 1. v. 1. 2. Epist. 1. v. 1. because he had been called to the Apostleship by Christ, but he neither calls himself a Monarch nor could he call himself he could have, because monarchical power was not given to him by Christ. Furthermore, to be a fellow-presbyter and an Apostle do not conflict with one another, for each is a name of a ministry, the former ordinary, the latter extraordinary. But to be a fellow-presbyter and a monarch cannot consist together.

5. Peter calls himself συμπρεσβύτερον,, not a monarch; nor does he compel by commanding, but exhorts by beseeching. Therefore, the Roman Pontiff is not the true successor of Peter, since he conducts himself as a monarch of the Church, and arrogates to himself absolute power over the Church: hence he calls himself Bishop of Bishops, Spouse of the Universal Church, etc. No one can confer more right upon another than he himself has. Since, therefore, Peter was not the monarch of the Church, the Pontiff could not have received monarchical power from Peter. Lorinus objects in this place: The Pontiffs are accustomed in letters and decrees to call bishops brothers and co-bishops, etc., and many proofs of such modesty exist in many places, and then truly in the title of servant of servants. Leo I displays remarkable humility in his first and second sermon on the anniversary day of his assumption, and among other things names his fellow-priests. Estius in the same way: The Roman Bishop, successor and imitator of Peter, has been accustomed to call other bishops brothers in his letters and rescripts to them, sometimes co-bishops and fellow-priests, but never sons. I reply: The Pontiff calls himself in words a brother of bishops, nay, a servant of servants, but in reality he conducts himself as their master and monarch. He attributes to himself the power of confirming and deposing bishops throughout the whole world; of enacting laws throughout the whole Church; of dispensing throughout the whole Church; of judging the whole Church, etc. He asserts that he can be judged by no one, he attributes to himself supreme and infallible judgment in controversies of faith, nay, he even arrogates to himself the power of deposing Emperors, Kings, and Princes from their throne, some of which things are so constituted that Peter never arrogated them to himself, and some indeed he taught were not proper to him alone, but were common with the other Apostles.

6. Three faults of the Vulgate version in this first verse are noted by Erasmus, Estius, and others. Bartholomaeus Petrus, who added certain small additions to the annotations of Estius, comments thus on this place: Our interpreter would have done better, both in this place, and Act. 15. and in the beginnings of the second and third Epistles of blessed John, if he had translated the Greek he should have retained the name of Presbyter and Conpresbyter, which ought to have been done, since by that name not old age, but an Ecclesiastical rank, as is designated here, even Laurentius himself (Valla) diligently warned, in the annotations to chapter 15. of Acts & at the beginning of the second Epistle of blessed John, with Desiderius himself also approving (Erasmus) annotations in chapter 20. of Acts & in this passage of blessed Peter. Erasmus on this passage. He would have spoken more correctly as Presbyters and Conpresbyter. And Jerome translates it thus, although here too he is somewhat offended by the Greek name added to the Latin conjunction. And I do not know whether anyone will tolerate Sympresbyter. And afterwards. There was no need for these words, in the future. Estius on this passage. One is not properly called a Communicator who becomes a sharer, but one who makes others sharers, which Peter certainly did not wish to ascribe to himself. Therefore the decree of the Council of Trent is erroneous, that the Vulgate version ought to be held as authentic, from which it should be permitted to no one under any pretext to depart, session 4.

7. Peter calls himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ, not only verbal, because he preached Christ crucified1. Cor. 1. v. 23. but also real, because he provided testimony to the doctrine concerning Christ crucified by enduring various sufferings. The Pope with his Prelates does not preach Christ crucified, much less does he represent the sufferings of Christ in his own person, but he delights most sweetly, and is an enemy of the cross of Christ Phil. 3. v. 18. both because he mocks and persecutes the doctrine concerning righteousness to be sought solely in Christ crucified through faith, and because he turns away from the cross, the inseparable companion of the Gospel. Therefore the Pope is not the true successor of Peter.

8. Peter calls himself a partaker of the glory that is to be revealed in the day of judgment. Therefore he was certain of his salvation. The same certainty (although not in the same degree) is in all the faithful, since they have the same spirit of faith. Rom. 8. v. 38. I am certain &c. 2. Cor. 4. v. 13. But having the same Spirit of faith &c. v. 14. Knowing that he who raised up Jesus will also raise us up with Jesus and will set us with you. Salmero excepts on this passage that Peter said this either because he certainly knew his election, and foreknew that Christ had prayed that his faith would not fail.Luke 22. or because Jesus Christ had revealed to him the death by which he was to glorify him.John last. In the same way Lorinus on this passage If Peter knew (that he was in grace or of the number of the elect) he received it through revelation, as Marcus de la Camera answers in the questions of the Council of Scriptural places, question 193.

In almost the same way also Estius on this passage: That you call yourself a partaker of that glory, whether he says it from a special revelation, namely that which he mentions 2. Epist. chap. 1. or whether these words are only of good and Christian hope, it is not clear, and perhaps it appears more that that revelation was made to Peter later, when he began to approach martyrdom. I answer: 1. It appears from these that the Papists do not agree on this question. For some attribute this certainty to a peculiar revelation, but others say it is only the certainty of good and Christian hope. If the former, this certainty is proper and peculiar to Peter; if the latter, it is common to him with the rest of the truly believing. 2. Lorinus in the words immediately preceding writes thus: The discourse concerning his future happiness did not seem so accommodated to the exhortation of others to feed the flock, but from that foretaste of happiness which he had already had, and had been in a certain way glorified, which Catharinus does not well deny, refuting this exposition, he wishes them also to argue that it will be, which he adds a little later v. 4. that when the Prince of shepherds shall appear, they may receive the unfading crown of glory. But if from that foretaste of happiness which Peter had already had, he wishes the Presbyters also to argue that it will be that they too shall be partakers of his happiness, then certainly that certainty was common to him with the faithful Presbyters, and therefore did not rely on a peculiar revelation. 3. 2 Peter 1. v. 10. he exhorts all, and requires of all, that they make their calling and election sure. Therefore this certainty does not arise from a peculiar revelation, but is common to all truly believing. 4. Paul, treating of the certainty of salvation, manifestly joins himself with others. Rom. 8. v. 39. I am certain that neither life, nor death can separate us. 5. That certainty of good and Christian faith is called by Bellarmine, lib. 3. de Iustific. cap. 9., only a conjectural certainty, and not one of faith, although the Apostle 2 Cor. 4. v. 13. & v. 14. pronounces that we are certain of this matter from the Spirit of faith or from faith.

9. Peter was certain of his salvation, and yet he was not on that account carried away in spirit, but out of humility and modesty called himself συμπρεσβύτερον. It is therefore false what the Papists say, that the certainty of salvation brings with it spiritual pride. Hosius de autorit. Script. s. 218. Do not think, Brentius, that without cause GOD, just as the day of the final judgment, so also our justification and the attainment of grace, did not wish to be most certain to us, for the weaker ones.

For that certainty would be a certain occasion of pride. For if anyone is persuaded that he is in favor with some King or Prince, however much he may know how to command the affections of his mind, he can nevertheless hardly escape being puffed up in spirit. Is it likely that any common person, if he could know for certain that he is in favor with God, could guard himself against this crime of elation? Bellarm. lib. 3. de Iustif. c. 8. It is not expedient that men should ordinarily have certainty of their grace, because this certainty begets pride, but ignorance begets and preserves humility. And yet if the certainty of grace and salvation of itself and by itself begat pride, it would always and in all people beget it. Lorinus on v. 5. cap. 5. of this Epistle 1, Paul did not lack humility when he writes that he cannot be separated from the love of GOD Rom. 8. v. 39. The persuasion of one's own righteousness exalts a man, but trust in imputed righteousness makes him humble.

10. As many as are established in the Ecclesiastical Ministry are commanded to feed the flock of the Lord. But the Pontiff does not feed the flock, but wages wars, walks about pompously, overflows with luxury, administers an earthly kingdom, and is a Bishop in name only.

Pontiffs now aid wars, the rest are trifles,

sings Marcellus Paling. Julius 2, the Roman Pontiff, waged so many wars that within seven years two hundred thousand men were killed in them. When the same man was once leading an army against an enemy, and was preceding it on the Tiber bridge, he threw his keys into the Tiber, adding these words.

Since the keys of Peter accomplish nothing for battles, perhaps the sword of Paul will be of help.

Arnold. Ferron. in Annal. Gall. Hence Ulrich von Hutten wrote an epigram of this kind against Julius 2.

He, the successor in the long line of his Peter, does such great things with a new custom and zeal. For he neither prays for the people, nor, left to peace, does he teach the sacred rites and the faith, which Peter would do. But he stirs up wars, bears arms, and rejoices in blood; clearly he has preferred Paul to Peter. Paul has a sword, but he does not strike, he kills: but this evil man has brought destruction to many. Dire offspring, produced from a poisonous birth, is it on this condition that you follow Christ, on this condition that you follow the Father?

Bellarm. lib. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap. 15. §. ultimo. Although most Popes do not preach, yet they exercise many other pastoral acts, while they bind, loose, dispense, judge controversies, create Bishops, and what they do not do by preaching themselves, they do through others. lib. 3. de P. R. cap. 24. §. Adde. Popes are not bound to preach and administer the Sacraments by themselves, if they are hindered by any just cause, but it is enough if they take care that all these things are performed through others. For a response to Bellarmine's exposition, that the Pope teaches through others, see in tract. de Minist. §. 267.

II. Papal Bishops likewise do not feed the flock with the word of preaching, but administer political rule, wage war, hunt, and do anything rather than feed. Therefore they do not obey Peter's admonition, nor are they true Bishops, but merely titular ones. When William of Honstein was elected Bishop of Strasbourg, Geiler of Kaysersberg said in a sermon. In one hundred years it has neither been seen nor heard that any of the Bishops have exercised spiritual matters. They have visited not souls but purses, and this indeed every year. In the grievances of the German nation in the year 1523, offered to the Legate of Pope Adrian at the Diet of Nuremberg, the Estates of the Empire, both Papal and Lutheran, speak thus. gravam. 21. But a heavier burden arises from this for the Germans, that since they can neither possess nor govern these benefices and Parish Churches in their own person, which nevertheless the office of Pastor would primarily demand of them, namely that they should offer themselves as an excellent example to their parochial subjects in integrity and innocence of morals, so that the Pastors themselves might feed their sheep as the sheep of Christ with solid doctrine, sincere and drawn from the pure fountains of the Gospel, as far as it pertains to the salvation of the souls of the sheep, neither of these is cared for by those substitute Pastors. The author of Oneris Ecclesiae cap. 20. §. 2. Exquisite doctrine is required in Bishops, so that by teaching and preaching they may be able to preside over and benefit others. Alas, who among the Bishops today preaches, or cares for the souls committed to him? Claude d'Espence on 1 Tim. lib. 2. digress. cap. 2. How many of the greater or lesser prelates seem to have their people taught? Certainly among our own Bishops, who were a certain part at Trent, where the duty of preaching was imposed upon Prelates as their primary office Sess. 24. cap. 4. no one teaches by himself. Are we playing in a serious matter? Or rather are we mocking those demanding reformation with the appearance of decrees? I know of those from among them, who are generous toward that servitude of teaching, namely, they stubbornly deny that they are bound. Our business is with those who shout more than anyone else about Councils, Fathers, and the Church, and yet cast aside the function most proper and necessary to them, which is doctrine.

12. Presbyters are commanded to feed the flock of Christ, from which they are also called Pastors Ephes. 4. v. 11. but it does not command them to offer any unbloody Mass-sacrifice, whence they are nowhere called Priests by a special and proper title. Therefore, the Papist Mass-priests, occupied in daily Masses and meanwhile neglecting the duty of teaching, do not obey the Apostle's warning, nor are they true Presbyters. Estius objects. 1. Christ himself then most performed the office of Pastor, when, offering himself on the altar of the cross, he laid down his life for his sheep. Resp. In this part, the reason for Christ and other pastors is disparate. Christ was sent into this world to perform not only the parts of the Prophetic office, but also the Priestly, but to Pastors the parts of sacrificing are nowhere attributed. Christ alone could offer himself as a sacrifice ἱλαστικὸν. the remaining Pastors, laying down their lives for the sheep, offer a sacrifice εὐχαριστικόν. Christ alone could lay down his life for redeeming the sheep; the remaining pastors lay down their lives for the sheep in confirming and preserving them in the truth of the faith. 2. By the same argument, prayer could be excluded from the office of a Pastor. For if to sacrifice for the sheep is not to feed, therefore neither will to pray for them be to feed. Resp. Our negative argument is deduced not only from this passage, but from other places of Scripture taken together in this way. Neither in this Petrine passage, nor anywhere else in the whole of Scripture, are Presbyters commanded to sacrifice. But there is another reason for prayer, which is entrusted to Pastors by both the words and examples of Scripture, as was shown in the treatise on the Ministry §. 274. Indeed, Peter himself in this chapter shines before the Presbyters with his own example v. 10.

13. Presbyters, who are the same as Bishops, are commanded to feed the flock of the Lord, and indeed ἐπισκοποῦντες. Therefore, the residence of Bishops (as they call it) is of divine law: For how can Bishops feed the flock committed to them, and provide for the same, if they are not present to their flock? Hence, in the Council of Trent, very many bitterly defended that residence is of divine law, as is evident from the History of Petrus Suavis Polanus. Maldonatus Summ. q. 10. art. 3. 5. 6. They noted Jerome on chapter 4. of Ephesians & Augustine Epistle 57. for this reason Paul did not distinguish between Pastors and Teachers, because every Pastor ought to teach, and the name of Pastor signifies a personal action, just like the name Physician. Therefore, just as no one can heal through another, so no one can feed his sheep through another. Nor is the common response of any value, that it is sufficient to labor through a Vicar, because according to the same rule it would be sufficient to eat through a Vicar, because it is written. He who does not labor, let him not eat. There are many testimonies in the Holy Scriptures concerning divine law, as keep watch in the custody of the tabernacle. But no one can keep watch unless he is present. Christ also describes the Pastor by his own marks among others, that he knows his sheep and they hear his voice. But neither can he know them unless he is present; nor can they hear him unless he is present. Estius on this passage proves the same from the words ἐν ἡμῖν. It is to be noted, he says, just as the flock is said to be in the Pastor, so conversely according to Scripture the Pastor is in the flock, as Acts 20. Paul exhorting the Pastors thus. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as Bishops to rule the Church of God. Just as Ecclesiasticus also commands chapter 32. v. 1. Have they made thee ruler? be thou in them. By which reciprocal speech it is signified that the union of the Pastor and the flock ought to be most intimate, so that neither the sheep may wander from their Pastor, nor the Pastor be separated from his sheep either in mind or in body. Therefore, from such Scriptures, the perpetual residence of Pastors among their sheep is best established as necessary by divine law. Salmero objects on this passage, p. 100. It is indeed necessary for all Pastors and commanded by divine law that they feed in general, whether they be present or absent.
