But to feed by themselves by assisting the flock and exhibiting continuous presence, which is to reside, is Ecclesiastical or Canon law etc. Wherefore, not to reside without a proven and legitimate cause, and not to assist one's sheep, is a deadly sin, especially if on account of his absence the sheep perish etc. Resp. 1. we repeat the words of Maldonado, the name of Pastor signifies a personal action. 2. what indeed are the legitimate causes of absence among the Papists? to attend the political councils of Magnates, to administer political government, to set out for Rome to receive the pallium and to kiss the feet of the Pontiff. 3. If residence is deduced from a divine precept, as Estius asserts, then certainly it will not only be of Canon and Ecclesiastical law, but also of divine.

14. Peter τὸ to feed all Presbyters with the duty of teaching prescribes for those serving in the Church. It is therefore false, what Bellarmine in book 1 on the Roman Pontiff c. 12. attempts to prove from the mandate of feeding given to Peter, that Bishops in their own Dioceses, and the Roman Pontiff in the whole Church, are true Ecclesiastical Princes, who can by their own authority, even without the consent of the people or the council of Presbyters, enact laws which bind in conscience. And yet Bellarmine will not attribute such power νομοθετικὴν to all Presbyters.

15. Feed, τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν ποίμνιον says Peter. It is therefore false what Bellarmine in book 1 on the Roman Pontiff c. 12. argues, that the Roman Pontiff has succeeded Peter in the Apostleship, insofar as that includes the faculty of establishing new laws, and supreme power over all Churches. For the Apostleship was an extraordinary office; the Presbyterate is an ordinary Ecclesiastical office. Between Apostles and Presbyters this is the difference, that the Apostles received the mandate of preaching the Gospel to every creature Mark 16. v. 15. and teaching all nations Matt. 28. v. 19.; but to the Presbyters it was said, feed the flock which is among you, therefore they have distinct Dioceses, distinct sheepfolds, distinct flocks. But what was said concerning Presbyters, the same must be understood concerning Bishops, since in the Scriptures the same are Presbyters who are Bishops and vice versa. If the Pontiff has received those things which are proper to an Apostle, he will certainly also be an Apostle, not a Roman Bishop. If the Pontiff succeeded Peter as an Apostle, it would follow that the Apostles would have appointed other Apostles in the Church after themselves, not Pastors and Bishops.

16. Feed, τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον τοῦ θεοῦ. It is therefore false, what Hadrian Saravia the Calvinist in his book on the different degrees of Ministers, chapter 16 and following, establishes, that the Apostleship still flourishes in the Church and that all Bishops are still endowed with Apostolic authority. In the Apostles three things can be considered. 1. The ministry of teaching the Gospel and administering the Sacraments with the power of the keys. 2. ἐπισκοπὴ inspection not only of the Lord's flock, but also of other Presbyters. 3. The power of preaching in the whole world, joined with immediate calling, the gift of miracles, ὑπεροχῇ and authority αὐτοπίστῳ and the privilege of infallibility. With respect to the first, all are true and sincere Ministers of the Church; with respect to the second, all Bishops are called successors of the Apostles by Ecclesiastical custom of speaking. Iren. lib. 3. adv. haeres. cap. 3. Cyprian. lib. 4. Epist. 9. Jerome in Epist. ad Evagrium. With respect to the third, in which the Apostleship also properly consists, there was no successor of the Apostles, but the Apostleship was a temporary and extraordinary order, which ceased together with them in the Church, and therefore was not propagated to the Ministers of the Church of subsequent times, which can be proven from the lack of 1. power proper to the Apostles. 2. immediate vocation. 3. absolute infallibility. 4. θαυματουργίας miraculous. 5. preaching restricted to no certain place. 6. vision of Christ in the flesh, Compare the tract on the Ministry of the Church §. 220.

17. Feed τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν πόιμνιον. Blessed Luther urges this against the dominion of the Pope and the Bishops, which they arrogate to themselves in the Church. It is said, he says, τὸ ποίμνιον ἐν ὑμῖν but not ὑφ᾽ ὑμῶν, the flock of Christ is among you, but not under your feet. A parallel passage exists Acts 20. verse 28. Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock ἐν ᾧ in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as Bishops. That of Sirach can also be accommodated here chap. 32. verse 1. ἡγούμενον they have appointed you, do not be exalted, be to them as one of them. Bernard Epist. 42. to Henry Archbishop of Sens. By the example of the Apostle you will honor your ministry, I say ministry, not dominion.

18. Feed μὴ αἰσχροκερδῶς. And yet among the Pope and the Papal Bishops reigns αἰοχροκερδεία, as the trading of Masses, Indulgences, the Jubilee, the Penitentiary Tax of the Roman Curia testify, in which for any sin a certain price is exacted, palls, annates, profits from harlots and concubines, bulls of dispensations, and who could enumerate all the nets of money, so that deservedly that Petrine 2. Epist. 2. verse 3. can be applied to the Papal Clerics ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλαστοις λόγοις ὑμᾶς ἐμπορέυσονται. Salmero on this passage. Avarice (the Apostle in this place) wishes to be far from a Bishop, which is always called by the Apostles filthy lucre, which pertains to Bishops, who first seek nothing else than the fruits of the sheep and how much pension they can pay, which also they might be able to bring temporal advantages to their servants or kinsmen. Wherefore the Lord deservedly cast out those selling and buying from the temple, and Elisha struck his servant Gehazi with leprosy, and Peter cursed Simon wishing to buy the Holy Spirit, so that he might later sell it.

19. Presbyters are forbidden to lord it over the flock. But the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself dominion, not only over the remaining Bishops, but even over Emperors, Kings, and Princes, and furthermore he claims for himself power over the universal Church to promulgate laws which bind the whole Church, he wishes to be judged or reproved by no one, even if he leads innumerable souls in droves with him into hell. c. Si Papa Dist. 40. The Pontiff is commanded ἐπισκοπεῖν, he is forbidden κατακυριέυειν. Therefore let him feed with the word of doctrine, but let him not arrogate to himself the power of commanding. Luth. in h. l. Bernh. Epist. 230. to the Roman see. And formerly you were lording it over the Clergy against the Apostle Peter, indeed you were even lording it over the faith of the whole world against his Co-Apostle Paul: but you have added something new, usurping even more over religion itself, what remains, except that you add that you also lord it over the Holy Angels themselves.

20. Presbyters are forbidden to lord it over the flock. But the Roman Bishops lord it over the flock, so that the Prophetic saying may deservedly be used of them Ezech. 34. v. 4. With austerity you ruled them and with cruelty. Erasmus in h. l. This precept of the Prince of the Apostles (not lording it over the Clergy) ought to be inscribed in golden letters in all the courts of all Bishops. Feed, he says, the flock, do not oppress, do not plunder, and that not by compulsion, as if by duty, but from sincere affection, as fathers: nor for the sake of base gain, as if foreseeing the plague of the Church that would arise from this. Finally, do not lord it in the manner of Kings, but feed by example, conquer by good deeds. Now the common herd of Bishops hears nothing from learned flatterers, except dominions, jurisdictions, swords, keys, powers. And hence the pride of some is more than Royal, the cruelty more than Tyrannical. Now we flatter the Roman Pontiff with great volumes, attributing to him power equal to Christ's, whence it happens that the Christian world sometimes can scarcely bear the dominion and clamor of this man and his Cardinals, and can scarcely suffice for their avarice. Estius in h. l. The Apostle forbids that which he had heard his Lord forbidding in those words, The Princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them. It shall not be so among you. Matth. 20. For not only are those said to lord it over others who convert and refer the power which they have over them to their own utility, of which kind is the power of masters over servants: but also those who, in the manner of the Princes of this age, command with ostentation of power, and do not go out into public except with a retinue and a pomp of followers, clearly so that they may strike terror into their subjects. And yet Christ wished that humility and gentleness should appear more in the pastors and rulers of the Church than the ostentation and severity of power: and love more than terror, so that there may be absent not only the spirit, but even the appearance of lording it over the subject people, and that they should rather conduct themselves through humility as ministers of those over whom they preside, procuring their spiritual utility with all zeal.

21. By Cleros the Apostle understands the Lord's flock, as we have proved above, and as even those from the Papists themselves admit: Cajetan, Gagnaeus, Titelmann, Jansenius, Emanuel Sa, Estius, etc. Therefore, it is to be disapproved that ecclesiastical persons in the Papacy claim the name of Clerics for themselves alone. c. Clericus caus. 12. q. 1. Bellarm. lib. 1. de membr. Eccles. milit. cap. 1. Gregorius de Valent. tom. 4. Disp. 9. q. 5. punct. 2. Ministers of the Church are called Clerics, either because they are peculiarly of the lot, or inheritance, of the Lord, insofar as they are singularly enslaved to divine worship, or because the Lord is peculiarly their lot or portion. They object, if even the whole Church is understood by the Clergy, nevertheless that name can be peculiarly attributed to the Ministers, since by reason of their office they pertain more to God than the rest of the Christians. I respond: the question is not about whether there is a distinction between Pastors and the flock, nor about whether in a sound sense the name of Clerics can be peculiarly attributed to the Ministers of the Church, since not only by reason of common Christianity, but also by reason of their peculiar office they look to the lot of the Lord, in which sense the name of Clerics was attributed to the Ministers of the Church by certain Fathers, Tertull. de monogam. Orig. homil. 7. in Ierem. Epiphan. in Epist. ad Ioh. Hierosolym. Euseb. lib. 5. c. 28. Socrat. lib. 5. cap. 2. & 16. Hieronym. in Epist. ad Nepotian. But that is what is at issue in the question, whether sacred Scripture peculiarly calls the Ministers of the Church by this name, which the Papists affirm, but we deny. Then also that is especially questioned, whether in the Papist sense the Ministers of the Church are rightly called, or can be called, Clerics, which we likewise deny. We understand, however, the Papist sense, that they distinguish Clerics from Laity in such a way that they attribute to them such a prerogative and excellence, which includes αὐτοκρατορικὴν the authority of commanding and the free power of governing the Church, but this from the of Scripture they exclude them from the reading, from the examination of doctrine, and from the participation of the Eucharistic chalice, so that they may entirely exempt them from the power of the political Magistrate, but in truth arrogate to themselves an authentic authority over them.

22. Presbyters ought to be examples of the flock. But the Roman Pontiff is the man of sin2. Thess. 2. v. 3. given over to sin, and making others sin through forced celibacy, through the impulse to inflict persecutions upon the confessors of the Gospel. Pontifical Bishops likewise are not examples of the flock, but they bind heavy and unbearable burdens, and lay them on the shoulders of men, but they themselves will not move them with their finger. Matth. 23. v. 4. Ioh. Aventinus lib. 1. Annal. The decurions of the mystics and the Parish priests with impunity and everywhere in heat, adulteries, and debaucheries contaminate everything, they love, they drink, they violate many virgins in one year, and they fill under the surface of piety, they revel, they defraud, they plunder, they litigate, they tear apart temples and Priesthoods, they exchange them as if they were horses for sale, they trade in Ceremonies, they huckster religions, they fornicate, they act lasciviously, they hunt, they wage war, they thirst for and shed human blood with impunity, they practice robbery etc. Compare the tract on the Church §. 265.

23. The coming of Christ to judgment is called φανέρωσις in this place and Coloss. 3. v. 4.1. Ioh. 2. v. 28.cap. 3. v. 2. ἐπιφάνεια τῆς παρουσίας 2. Thessal. 2. v. 8. ἐπιφάνεια τῆς δόξης Tit. 2. v. 13. ἐπιφάνεια τοῦ Χριστοῦ 1. Tim. 6. v. 14.2. Timoth. 4. v. 1. ἀποκάλυψις 1. Corinth. 1. v. 7.2. Thess. 1. v. 7. etc. Therefore the Calvinists err, who oppose the return of Christ to judgment to his presence with us in these lands; Although Christ according to both Natures is present with us according to his infallible promise Matth. 18. vers. 20.cap. 28. vers. 19. nevertheless that presence is invisible, but on the day of judgment Christ will be so revealed, or manifested, that he may be seen by all.

24. Christ alone is ἀρχιποιμὴν. Therefore the Roman Pontiff sins by selling himself as the primary Pastor, the head and bridegroom of the Church. The Council of Carthage III. can. 26. established, that the Bishop of the first see should not be called Prince of Priests or supreme Priest, which was repeated in the African Council in the time of Boniface I. and inserted into the Canon law c. Sedis. c. Nullus c. Ecce dist. 99. Bernard in Epistle 237 warns Pope Eugenius, that as the heir of Peter he should listen to Peter, and not call the Church Sarai, i. e. My Lady, but Sara, that is, Lady Absolutely, because she is the Lady and wife of Christ, who is the true Patriarch and Abraham of the Church. Cyprian in the Council of Carthage: For none of us sets himself up as a Bishop of bishops, or by tyrannical terror forces his colleagues to the necessity of obedience. Estius objects in this place: Christ is the primary Prince of Pastors, whose sheep are even the Pastors themselves, redeemed like the other sheep by His blood. For Peter, who writes here, was indeed himself also a prince of Pastors, but a secondary and vicarious one. I respond: 1. These things contain a begging of the question. Peter calls himself a fellow-elder, but Christ alone the Prince of Pastors. 2. Christ communicates being a pastor to the Ministers of the Church, but He does not communicate being the head and Prince of Pastors. 3. To say a secondary Prince of Pastors is to say an opposite in an appositive. He who is also secondary is not the prince of Pastors. 4. Will they also appoint some secondary and vicarious Bridegroom? Christ alone, as He is the head and Bridegroom of the Church: so also He alone is the Prince of Pastors; He admits no one into the partnership of this dignity and power.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Salmero comments on verse 1 thus: The Apostle descends to this exhortation, because it pertained to the Roman Bishop himself, the supreme Pastor of the Lord's fold, to prescribe laws and precepts to the inferior Pastors and those called into a share of the solicitude, etc. For this reason he sent this doctrine, written from the city of Rome, so that all posterity might understand that laws and judgments were to be received from that Pastor or Bishop who is set over that city, since it was said to him, feed my sheep, confirm your brothers. And afterwards on verse 2: Peter received a universal Episcopate and Pastorate over all the Churches of Christ and over all the sheep which are called Christ's, and even over all the Apostles themselves. Ibid: As far as internal matters are concerned, Christ still lives and reigns, and with every private Pastor He feeds the flock: but as far as external matters and sensible presence are concerned, i. e., the preaching of the Sacraments and obedience, He left one and external Universal Pastor, that is, Peter, and the successor of Peter, with whom, having the care of all the sheep, He might rule the Universal Church. Lorinus in this place: A particular pastor has dioceses and parishes and his own sheep; only the successor of Peter feeds all with primary power. To the Apostles, by the privilege of Christ, while saving that prerogative of Peter, no limits were prescribed in the world, in which matter the others after them Bishops do not succeed them, just as they do not constitute other Bishops, as the Apostles themselves used to do, but the successor of Peter himself, assigning to each one, as he wishes, sheep, and indicating what kind and how great an amplitude of jurisdiction, he himself being the pastor of all pastors. Turrianus thinks in book 2 for the Epistles of the Pontiffs, chapter 9, this is indicated here by Peter with those words, feed the flock of God which is among you. Estius on verse 1, He turns his exhortation to the pastors of the churches, i.e., to the Bishops or Presbyters, mindful of his own office and power received from Christ Matth. 16. Luc. 22. Ioh. 21. For with the same authority with which he admonishes the Bishops of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, which regions he named at the front of the Epistle, he could also admonish the remaining Bishops everywhere constituted. Wherefore this passage also is of primary value for confirming the primacy of Peter over the universal Church. Resp. 1. The cause of this exhortation to the Presbyters is not the Monarchical power of Peter, but his Apostolic authority. 2. In this very exhortation he calls himself a fellow-presbyter and a witness of the sufferings of Christ. He therefore implies that he is writing as one of the pre-elected witnesses of Christ Actor. 10. v. 41., that is, as an Apostle of Christ, to whom the care of the entire Lord's flock was commended Ioh. 21. v. 15. 3. If Monarchical power could be inferred from an exhortation to Presbyters, it could also be concluded in a similar way concerning Paul. Act. 20. v. 28. 1. Tim. 3. v. 2. Tit. 1. v. 6. 4. For Lorinus writes expressly on this passage, Paul uses the phrase of ruling the flock in a similar exhortation to the Bishops. Act. 20. v. 28. 5. Salmero speaks alternatively. The Apostle descends, he says, to this exhortation, since he had said above, As each one has received grace, administering it to one another, etc., or because it pertained to the supreme Pastor of the Lord's sheepfold, the Roman Bishop, to prescribe laws and precepts to the inferior Pastors. Therefore he himself doubts whether Monarchical power is the true cause of this exhortation. 6. What is said to the Presbyters, feed τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον τοῦ θεοῦ,, from that it is rightly inferred that, by reason of the Apostolic office, not a particular but a universal care of the Church and the feeding of the entire Lord's flock was committed to Peter, but Monarchical power is not yet proven from that, since the same command was given to all the Apostles Matth. 28. vers. 19. Marc. 16. vers. 15. and Paul attributes to himself the solicitude of all the churches 2. Cor. 11. v. 28. 7. Furthermore, from this it can be proven against the Papists that Peter did not preside over the Roman see for 25 years, for that with the administration It is by no means fitting for an apostolic office. 8. τὸ παρακαλεῖν, the Vulgate rendered to beseech. But if he had wished to exercise monarchical power, he would have admonished the presbyters of their duty not by beseeching, but by commanding.

2. Lorinus comments thus on verse 1: He who has the passion of Christ before his eyes, and suffers with the same in mind or even in body, by either voluntarily tormenting himself or willingly enduring pains coming from anywhere, more easily draws others to the love of that same Christ. I reply: by voluntary torment of the body, Lorinus points his finger at voluntary flagellations undertaken with the opinion of satisfaction. But concerning those, there exists no command in the Scriptures, no approved example, no promise. Beautifully, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples in his annotations on Col. 3. The members of Christ are spiritual, the members of the flesh are carnal, as are carnal affections. And these are to be mortified with their acts. But by what things are these mortified? Is it by the precepts or doctrines of men, by private or public macerations of the flesh, in which men trust, and think themselves in some way righteous from their works, and lament others who are not their own donkey-drivers, as if for that reason fearing for their salvation? This is a humility of sense and earthly humility, not the humility of the Spirit, and divine humility, by which even the highest powers, which stand around the highest throne of God, fall down in the sight of the throne upon their faces. What therefore mortifies? Certainly those things most of all which are of the Spirit, in which we have help, nay, our entire strength from above, not those which are exterior and come from below. Among which spiritual things indeed, that which obtains the highest and chief place for this mortification of carnal affections as the victory of the members of the flesh, is the love of God, and the love of neighbor.

3. The same author comments thus on this place: The ancient rite of signing oneself with the cross by a preaching Bishop, or another, and by a Deacon reciting the Gospel, and by others who were listening, could look to this. Cornelius à Lapide on verse 1: The Pontiff wears an adamantine cross on his breast, so that he may remember the cross and the passions of Christ continually. I reply: 1. We do not simply disapprove of the sign of the cross, but we use it, both for the testimony of our faith, that we believe in CHRIST crucified, whence we imprint that sign on our forehead and breast, so that we may testify that we are not at all ashamed of CHRIST, but have him in our heart; and then to the admonition of enduring the cross on account of the confession of CHRIST. 2. But the Papists attribute ἄτερ γραφῆς spiritual effects to the sign of the cross, which we can in no way prove. Bellarm. lib. 2. de Imag. cap. 30. That there are wonderful effects of the cross, it terrifies and puts to flight demons, drives away diseases and all evils, it sanctifies those things upon which it is imprinted. 3. Peter was a witness of the sufferings of Christ, not through the figuration of the cross, but through the preaching of the Gospel concerning Christ crucified, and through the patient endurance of persecutions brought upon him on account of the name of Christ.

4. Estius on verse 2 comments thus, ποιμάνατε not only signifies the care and provision of fodder; but the entire rule or government, which a Shepherd by office bestows upon the sheep, whence the old Interpreter is accustomed to render that Greek word with the verb to rulePsalm. 2. vers. 9.Psalm. 23. vers. 2. &c. Jerome Epistle 85. cites the passage thus, Rule the flock of Christ. And the Kings of this age are called shepherds of men and peoples.Jeremiah 25. v. 34. Resp. 1. Estius immediately adds, that Hilary inPsalm. 2. the word ποιμαίνειν explains as to rule pastorally, and adds the exposition of John Hessels (which Salmero very ignorantly attributes to Hilary.) The sheep of Christ are ruled pastorally, while the fodder of Christian doctrine is provided to them not only by public preachings and exhortations, but also by secret and private instructions, consolations, and corrections. Likewise while the Sacraments are sedulously administered to them, while the best examples of life are proposed to them, while their temporal necessities are cheerfully relieved, while useful laws and precepts are prescribed, while one prays, groans, weeps, and sacrifices for them before God most solicitously and frequently. Such pastoral rule (if that which is added concerning laws and sacrifice be explained according to the phrase of Scripture,) we by no means deny to belong to Bishops. They ought not only to lead their hearers to salutary pastures, but also to rule them with the staff of the word Zechariah 11. v. 7. both pertain to the Pastoral office. 2. But the Roman Bishops, by no means content with these limits, attribute to themselves in Ecclesiastical matters a αὐτοκρατορικὸν and absolute rule. 3. Nay, they even join political dominion to it, and wish to rule after the manner of the Princes of this age, which is not only by no means from the word of feeding it can be deduced, but it also most strongly opposes the same, Compare the tract on the Ministry of the Church §. 197. & following.

5. Lorinus on v. 2. comments thus. Bishops are accustomed to sit in a more elevated place in the Church, and thus to look upon all, and to be looked upon by all. Martinus Polonus in his Chronicle relates, that Clement decreed that the Episcopal chair should be placed in a more eminent place, in which the Bishop sitting might be able both to look around at all, and to be seen by all. Cornel. à Lapide on v. 2. The Bishop sits in the Church on a higher throne, so that he may be able to survey, rule, and correct all, and in turn to be seen and heard by all. Resp. By τὸ ἐπισκοπεῖν not only the gaze of bodily eyes, but also and even most especially the vigilance of the mind in administering the Episcopal office is required. Nor should the Bishop be so solicitous about a wooden or stone more eminent chair, as about the chair of doctrine, so that he may feed the people committed to his faith with the food of doctrine, and shine before them with the good example of his life. Bishops in the Papacy have retained wooden chairs, but they have cast the duty of teaching and of overseeing onto the shoulders of others.

6. Bellarmine, book 5 of the Roman Pontiff, chapter 10, gathers from the word κατακυριέυειν, that only violent and Tyrannical dominion is prohibited, but not such dominion as can be that of pious Kings and Princes. The Lord, he says, in those words, The Kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship, but you not so, does not prohibit to Bishops such dominion as can be that of pious Kings and Princes, but such as is that of Kings ignorant of GOD, who are rather Tyrants than Kings, since in the Greek it is κατακυριέυειν, which is to dominate violently. Lorinus in this place, page 552. κατακυριέυειν indicates Tyrannical dominion. page 555. The participle κατακυριέυοντες signifies violent dominion with austerity and power, such as CHRIST says the Kings of the Gentiles were accustomed to use, Matth. 20. vers. 25. Marc. 10. vers. 42. &c. To which could be referred that of Calvin in his commentary on this place, Because the preposition κατὰ is almost always taken in a bad sense, Peter here censures preposterous domination, such as is that of those who, not considering themselves to be ministers of Christ and the Church, desire something more. Resp. 1. That which Matthew and Mark call κατακυριέυειν & κατεξουσιάζειν,, that Luke chapter 22. vers. 25. simply calls κυριέυειν & ἐξουσιάζειν,, which Lorinus could not deny. And yet if in the preposition κατὰ there were a certain necessary restriction of dominion to Tyranny, Luke, who wrote after Matthew and Mark, would not have permitted the same. 2. The Vulgate version rendered the word κατακυριέυοντες in this place simply as dominating. But because of the thunderbolt of the Council of Trent, it is not permitted for Papists to depart from that Vulgate version. 3. Paul not only κατακυριέυειν, but also κυριέυειν derogates from himself and the remaining Apostles 2. Corinth 2. v. 24. οὐ κυριέυομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως. 4. The word κατακυριέυειν Act. 19. vers. 16. is used simply for dominion or prevailing. Ier. 3. vers. 14. it is attributed to God himself, Psal. 72. v. 8.Psal. 110. v. 3. to Christ himself, from whom tyrannical dominion and abuse of power is very far removed. 5. Those κατακυριέυοντας καὶ κατεξουσιάζοντας, of whom Christ Matth. 20. v. 25. speaks, he says are called εὐεργέτας, but those who exercise tyrannical dominion do not deserve to be called εὐεργέται. Christ was derogating from the Apostles such a command as they themselves were aspiring to, otherwise the answer would not have been accommodated to the question. Now indeed the Apostles were not aspiring to tyrannical command, but to political principate and dominion, because they were fostering carnal opinions about the earthly kingdom of the Messiah. Christ disapproves of and detests tyrannical dominion, such as that of certain Gentile Kings, among Christian Kings themselves. And yet he grants that dominion of which he speaks to political Kings, but removes it from the Apostles and their successors in the office of teaching. Therefore 6. Ecclesiastical persons are called by the Holy Spirit Ministers of the Church, but not Princes and Lords of the Church. They are indeed called absolutely Kings Psal. 68. v. 13. and Princes Psalm. 45. vers. 17. but not on account of some political and Monarchical dominion over the Church, but in that signification by which, on account of the Spiritual kingdom, the remaining pious are also called Kings 1. 1. Petr. 2. v. 9.Apoc. 1. v. 6. and on account of the eminence of the gifts with which they are instructed. 7. We urge the opposition in the saying of Peter, οὐ κατακυριέυοντες τῶν κλήρων, ἀλλὰ τύποι γινόμενοι τοῦ ποιμνίου. Therefore Bishops ought to preside by example rather than by command. Compare Harm. Evang. chap. 73. page 141. where the exceptions of the adversaries were answered.

7. Salmero comments thus on v. 3. By Clergy the Apostle understands the sacred assembly ascribed to the ministry of the altar etc. This name is hadNum. 12. and Deut. 18.where the Lord is called the lot and portion of the Levites and

Of the Priests. Cornel. à Lapide on this passage: That sense, by which Clerics are understood through the Clergy, is very congruent. 1. because it is prone that some Bishops of a clearer mind might wish to dominate over the Clergy, for this is more subject to them than the Laity are, 2. because in the Clergy there are properly Clerics, i. e. various lots and degrees of Clerics, 3. because Bishops and Pontiffs have prescribed many laws, canons, rites and Ceremonies to Deacons and other Clerics. 4. many read in the Clergy as in the Clera and explain it concerning Clerics. as the VII general Synod. can. 4. 5. because Peter alludes to the Levites, who in the O. T. were the Lord's Clergy, i. e. lot and inheritance Num. 16. v. 20. Deut. 18. v. 2. Lorinus on this passage: It is not entirely certain whether by the Clergy is designated that certain degree in the Church which is called Clerical, and according to the etymology looks to the peculiar lot of God, to which he is dedicated by a certain proper rite, which others, whom we name Laity as if popular, are not, or whether the whole flock of Christ, and as many as are comprehended in the bosom of the Church, ought to be understood by the voice of the Clergy &c. the common opinion of the many ought to prevail over a few more recent ones, or the Syriac edition, or even Cyril in the declaration of the present passage, and lest we even in this matter favor heretics, and also the heretical Author of the Thesaurus of the Greek language, who thus interpret Peter in this place, it behooves us to abstain from the former interpretation. Resp. 1. Above in q. 11 we demonstrated with evident arguments that by Clergy the Lord's flock is understood in general, not inferior Presbyters in species. 2. Estius saw that dissertation of Lorinus concerning this little word to be sufficiently prolix, nor yet could he be moved to confirm it with his suffrage, but rather disputes against it. 3. Nor could Lorinus deny that many Papist writers embrace our exhortation, whom we enumerated above in the said place. Lorinus prefers the ancients to the more recent in this question, whereas elsewhere in the question concerning the immaculate conception of the virgin they prefer the more recent to the ancients. 4. In the adduced O. T. passages the reason is given why God did not wish a certain portion of the land of Canaan to be assigned to the Levitical tribe to be possessed by inheritance with the remaining Israelites, because namely the Lord is their lot or inheritance, i. e. as is explained elsewhere throughout, because they ought to be sustained from the sacrifices, victims, the ransom of the firstborn, firstfruits &c. offered to the Lord Deuter. 18. vers. 1. There shall not be to the Priests, the Levites a part and inheritance with Israel, they shall eat the fire-offerings or oblations and his inheritance. But what is this to the ministers of the Church of the N. T. to whom αἰτιολογίας, the explanation of that can in no way be adapted. 5. In the primitive Church, in an orthodox sense, Ministers of the Church were called Clerics, because τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας they receivedActs 1. verse 17. Isidore, book of Etymologies, chapter 12, and it is cited in c. Cleros dist. 21. We believe that Cleros and Clerics are so called from this, because Matthias was elected by lot, whom we read was the first to be ordained by the Apostles. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: Some think that the term Clergy was attributed to Clerics from the election of St. Matthias, who was elected to the Apostleship by Cleros, that is, by lot, from which you may see how ancient the name of Clergy and Cleric is, and its distinction from the Laity, which heretics wrongly deny. But Cornelius confuses the occasion of this appellation, which could have been the election of Matthias by lot, and its origin, which is not of the same antiquity as the election of Matthias.

8. Estius on verse 4 annotates thus: Since a crown is a reward and the wages of victory, it follows by an argument from relatives that a man fighting and conquering merits the glory of the heavenly kingdom, and therefore those who deny the merits of good works are vehemently mistaken. I say merits, which nevertheless are themselves also gifts of God. Resp. 1. A reward in general is said to be whatever is given to someone after labor has been performed, whether it is done freely or out of debt; whether it is much or little; whether it corresponds to the labor or less, and therefore there is not a perpetual relation between reward and merit, since a reward has a place somewhere where merit is not given. Gen. 15. v. 1.Psalm 127. v. 3.Rom. 4. v. 4. etc. 2. When a reward is promised to those who work well out of faith, the reward is to be understood according to grace, not according to the debt of justice, because eternal life is not the merit of our works, but χάρισμα a gratuitous gift of God in Christ Rom. 6. v. 23. Ambrose, book 1, Epistle 1: One thing is the reward of liberality and grace, another is the stipend of virtue, another is the remuneration of labor. Lyranus on chapter 10 of John: Heavenly glory is not properly called a reward, but only broadly, insofar as everything that is rendered as a prize for labor is called a reward. The reason for this, however, is because an inheritance is distinguished from a reward properly so called, just as a son, to whom an inheritance is owed, is distinguished from a hired laborer, to whom a reward is owed: but heavenly glory is rendered to the faithful as an inheritance to children, for which reason it does not have the nature of a reward. Without a doubt, Lyranus refers to the Apostolic passage Col. 3. v. 24. in which the rewards of good works are called ἀνταπὸδοσις τῆς κληρονομίας. 3. Therefore, when Estius argues, that reward and merit are relative, that reward is rendered to merits, just as grace is given freely, then he proceeds from the property of one species to the property of the genus, which is ἀσυλλόγιστον. 4. In this statement, it is not the meritorious cause of eternal life that is described, but the condition and quality of the Pastors who are to be saved. The crown of glory and of life is promised to faithful Pastors, not because their faithfulness, being already in many ways owed to GOD beforehand and imperfect, is merit properly so called, but because GOD, out of grace, gave to faithful Pastors the promise of a most bountiful retribution.

9. Salmero gathers from this passage the aureole or little crown of faithful Pastors. The crown of unfading glory, he says, is more than eternal life, because it signifies a certain higher degree of eternal life above others. Wherefore, after Daniel had said that many would rise again, some to eternal life, others to everlasting reproach, he adds something peculiar about the Teachers. But they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament &c. Lorinus on this passage says, Hugo and Thomas the Englishman interpret it as the aureole crown, which is attributed to Teachers. Indeed, among Paul, the same are Pastors and Teachers Ephes. 4. v. 11. &c. but I do not think that an aureole is decreed for every one who teaches and also preaches, but for him who in that kind, either by writing or by word, has notably illustrated the Church, and has carried off an egregious victory over the Devil, by driving him from the hearts and minds of others, as far as in him lay, by showing the truth and detecting frauds and customs. Resp. 1. We do not deny that there will be degrees of glory in eternal life, and that GOD, out of grace, will reward not only with temporal but also with eternal rewards the labors and sufferings of the pious which they have sustained for Christ's sake; meanwhile, we can by no means approve the Papal doctrine concerning aureoles, both because of the condition of the foundation, which is the doctrine of works of supererogation, and because of the rash decision. Compare the treatise on eternal life §. 160. 161. 2. That by the crown of glory here is not understood an aureole, but eternal life itself, Estius teaches in his commentary on this passage. Hesselius, he says, interprets the crown of glory as a very glorious crown, since it does not simply signify eternal life, but a higher degree above others &c. There are those who interpret this crown as an aureole, which is attributed to teachers, such as Hugo the Cardinal and Thomas the Englishman. But it is more probable that the principal (essential) reward is understood, which is also elsewhere called a crown it is usually signified by the name, as Jacob. 1. he shall receive the crown of life, which GOD has promised to those who love him.

Observations. 1. Christians ought to edify one another and exhort to good. 1. Thess. 5. v. 11. but especially this is incumbent upon the Ministers of the Church, to whom the Apostolic precept primarily pertains Rom. 12. v. 7. εἔτε ὁ διδάσκων, ἐν τῆ διδασκαλὶα, v. 8. εἴτε ὁ παρακαλῶν, ἐν τῇ παρακλήσει, (where by διδάσκοντας are understood those who explained Christian doctrine and defended it against corruptions without application to the hearers or admonition, just as is accustomed to be done today in the schools 1. Cor. 12. v. 28.Eph. 4. v. 11. by παρακαλοῦντας Pastors, who not only explained the truth of the doctrine, but also applied it to use, by exhorting, consoling, reproving, and admonishing, as the necessity of the hearers, committed to their faith, required.)

2. That the Apostle might leave an example of humility to his successors in the office of teaching, he beseeches and exhorts, he who could have commanded. 1. Tim. 5. v. 1. Do not rebuke an elder, but beseech him as a father, the younger ones as brothers.

3. For the same purpose he calls himself συμπρεσβύτερον, although he was an Apostle, which is the highest rank of Ecclesiastical Ministry 1. Cor. 12. vers. 28.Eph. 4. v. 11.

4. Peter shows, where Christians are, there also are sufferings, writes Blessed Luther in his commentary on this place. A true Christian is also a cross-bearer.

5. Pastors of the Church, by the example of Peter, ought to be witnesses of the sufferings of Christ, not only by preaching Christ crucified 1. Cor. 1. v. 2. 3. but also by patiently tolerating persecutions brought upon them for the confession of Christ. If I feared the cross, I would not preach the cross of Christ, said the Apostle Andrew, when led to the punishment of the cross. Cyprian, Epist. 55 to Cornelius, calls himself honored by the testimony of the Lord's condescension, because it had been granted to him to suffer for Christ.Phil. 1. vers. 29.

6. Those who suffer adversity for the sake of the truth of the Gospel, by that very fact confirm and seal the Evangelical truth. 1. Tim. 6. v. 13. it is said Christ gave testimony under Pilate of a good confession, because he suffered death itself for the confession of the truth, which example of constancy all the truly pious, especially the Ministers of the Church, ought to imitate, But also the of the Martyrs Passions offer public testimony to the truth of heavenly doctrine, whence they are called κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν Martyrs.

7. With an unbroken bond, Peter joins the future glory of the heavenly kingdom to passions endured for the sake of the confession of Christ 2. Tim. 2. v. 12. If we endure, we shall also reign with him. Calamity is the flower of eternal life; let us not fear to pluck the flower on account of the fruit. August. in Ps. 36. Do not wonder that you are prepared in labors; you are being prepared for something great.

8. The pious in this life have a certain foretaste of eternal happiness and in a way begin to be glorified, while they are certain from faith that, just as they are conformed in this to the image of the crucified Christ, so also they are to be conformed at some time to his glorious image. Rom. 8. v. 29.

9. That foretaste of happiness, just as it did not at all exalt Peter into pride, so also it does not at all exalt the pious, but rather renders them grateful toward God and dutiful toward their neighbor, so that by the example of Peter they may glory in passions and exhort others to the parts of their owed duty, so that they themselves may also become participants of the same glory.

10. Presbyters ought to feed the flock committed to them. Bede in this place: Just as the Lord ordered Peter (as an Apostle) to have care of his whole flock, that is, the Church: so Peter rightly commands the following pastors of the Church that each one should protect the flock of GOD that is with him with solicitous governance. In the Syriac edition, the title noted before this chapter advises that this first part of it is recited on the 14th Sunday after Pentecost and at the election or ordination of Bishops. Doubtless because it exhibits a most beautiful mirror of the Pastoral office.

11. That feeding is done by teaching, exhorting, arguing, consoling, correcting, etc.; it is done by teaching and leading; by correcting and amending; by counseling and consoling. Bernh. serm. 2. de resurr. Feed with the mind, feed with the mouth, feed with work; feed with the prayer of the soul, the exhortation of the word, the exhibition of example. A good pastor ought to provide his sheep with the fodder of salutary doctrine learnedly; the examples of good conduct holily; the subsidies of charity piously. Let him feed with the word, let him feed with example, let him feed with the suffrage of prayers. Bernh. Epist. 201.

12. From the example of Christ, who calls himself the good Shepherd John 10. v. 11., it must be learned how the sheep are to be fed. Ezech. 34. v. 15. I will feed my sheep, etc., says the Lord: v. 16. That which had perished, I will seek; that which was wandering, I will bring back; that which had been broken, I will bind up; that which was weak, I will strengthen; and that which is fat and strong, I will guard, and I will feed them in judgment.

13. It is not enough to lead the flock to salutary pastures, but it is also necessary to drive the wolves away from the sheepfold. He who does not watch against the wolf for the sheep differs nothing from a wolf. Luth. tom. 2. Ien. f. 3816. A good shepherd nourishes the flock with pious songs; he is not accustomed to neglect the weapons which make for the overthrow of impiety, but rather, singing the things that are of the Spirit, he also takes up arms against the wolves.

14. The doctrine of Christ alone is the salutary food of the soul. Therefore, they are not true Pastors who either abstain entirely from the office of teaching, or propose human dreams to the sheep as if they were deadly poisons.

15. As Pastors are said to be in the flock, so the flock in turn is said to be in the Pastor. This is because the Pastor is joined to the flock and the flock to the Pastor by the bond of both charity and duty.

16. All things, indeed, which are in heaven and on earth are God's, yet the Church is His own property and inheritance, His own sheepfold and dear possession. This very thing can and ought to stir up Pastors to vigilance most of all, because they know that the flock committed to them is the flock of GOD, that is, chosen by GOD, and the flock of Christ, that is, redeemed by Christ.

17. The episcopate is one and undivided, of which a part is held by each in its entirety, says Cyprian in his book on the unity of the prelates. To individual pastors a portion of the flock has been assigned, which each one may rule and govern, being about to render an account of his act to the Lord, says the same in book 1, Epistle 3.

18. The Pastors of the Church are reminded not only of ποιμαίνειν but also of ἐπισκοπεῖν,, the precept of labor in feeding; and of the prudence and vigilance in inspecting them. August. book 19 de Civ. DEI chap. 9. The name of episcopate is of work, not of honor, for ἐπισκοπεῖν is to superintend, so that he may understand that he is not a bishop who has loved to preside, not to be useful. Isid. Pelusiota book 1, Epistle 149. From the name itself it is perceived that a bishop ought to watch, and to be an eye in every part, looking out upon all things, and neglecting nothing. Bernh. in his sentences. It is for pastors to watch over the flock for three necessary reasons, namely for discipline, for custody, and for prayers. For discipline, on account of the correction of morals, lest the committed flock fail through its own trouble. For custody, on account of diabolical suggestion, lest it be seduced by hostile craftiness. For prayers, on account of the urgency of temptations, lest it be overcome by pusillanimity.

19. That ἐπισκοπεῖν also requires this, that the Pastor not only may he look out for all, but also for each individual. Acts 20. v. 28. Take heed to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, etc. v. 31. Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears. Ezek. 3. v. 17. chap. 33. v. 7. Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel (in general) v. 18. When I say unto the wicked, (in particular) thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, his blood will I require at thine hand. Heb. 13. v. 17. Obey them that have the rule over you, for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account. Concerning Gregory Thaumaturgus, Bishop of Neocaesarea, Gregory of Nyssa records in his life, that he instructed individuals in virtue appropriate to their own station. He exhorted the young to modesty, the old to patience, servants to obedience, that they might be faithful and compliant toward their masters, masters to clemency, that they might show themselves humane toward their subjects, the poor to the contempt of wealth, that they might consider virtues to be true riches, the rich to beneficence, that they might give alms to the needy, thinking that they were not masters of their wealth, but stewards; he inculcated chastity in women, obedience in children, discipline in parents; he brought consolation to the mourning, counsel to the doubtful, aid to the afflicted, becoming all things to all men. 1 Cor. 9. verse 23.

20. Gregory of Nazianzus in his Apology, when he had said, that which is expressed by force and necessity is by no means to be praised, he adds the passage presently cited. Therefore, our law and our lawgiver have ordained this most of all, that the flock be fed not by compulsion, but spontaneously and with a willing mind. Ambrose in Ps. 118. octonary 14, expounding the words of the Psalmist, Accept, I beseech thee, the freewill offerings of my mouth, O Lord, etc. shows in many ways that it matters a great deal whether you do something out of will or out of necessity, as to what pleases GOD, and he urges above all the Apostolic passage 1 Cor. 9. v. 17. If I do this thing willingly, I have a reward, ibid. The Lord approves the spontaneous actions of his servants rather than those that are forced; therefore he makes them free from servants, so that we may offer the gifts of our wills rather than the obsequies of necessities. To which also may be referred that which Peter in this place requires, a liberal mind and affection in the Pastoral office.

21. Bede on this passage comments thus. He provides by compulsion who, on account of a lack of temporal things, not having wherewith to live, therefore preaches the Gospel, that he may live of the Gospel. On the contrary, he provides spontaneously, who preaches the word of GOD with a view not to any earthly thing, but only to the heavenly reward. Afterwards he adds, that all works of religion ought to be done spontaneously, which he declares by the example of the Israelites in the O. T. According to that, he says, example of the construction of the tabernacle, which prefigures the present construction of the Church, where both the whole multitude of the children of Israel offered with a most prompt and devoted mind the first-fruits to the Lord, giving everything of their own free will for the doing of the work of the tabernacle, and the craftsmen themselves offered themselves of their own free will to do the work.

22. Ἀισχροκερδεία in every state of life, but especially in the Ecclesiastical Ministry, is to be detested. Those are said αἰσχροκεοδῶς to provide for the flock, who exercise so holy a ministry for the sake of gain, and seek to be enriched from the office of pastoral care. Bede in this place: He provides for the flock of GOD for the sake of filthy lucre, who preaches on account of gain and earthly advantages, since all works of religion ought to be done spontaneously. Concerning such various Pastors, most grave complaints exist in the Prophets. Esai. 56. v. 11. Most impudent dogs, they have not known satiety; the Pastors themselves have not known understanding; all have turned aside to their own way, every one to his own avarice. Ierem. 6. v. 13. cap. 8. v. 10. From the least even to the greatest, all are eager for avarice, and from the Prophet even to the Priest, all practice deceit. Ezech. 13. v. 19. for a handful of barley and a piece of bread you profane me before my people &c., lying to my people who believe in lies. Ezech. 34. v. 2. Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who were feeding themselves! Mich. 3. v. 5. Thus says the Lord concerning the Prophets who seduce my people, who bite with their teeth and preach peace: and if anyone does not give something into their mouths, they sanctify war against him. 1. Tim. 6. v. 5. they suppose that godliness is a way of gain. On the contrary, however, faithful Pastors are described as being as far as possible from this vice Num. 16. v. 15. 1. Sam. 12. v. 3. Act. 20. v. 33. 1. Tim. 3. v. 3. Tit. 1. v. 7. Jerome to Nepotianus: I beseech you, and I will warn you again and again, do not think the office of the Clergy is a kind of ancient military service, that is, do not seek the gains of the world in the service of Christ, do not have more than when you began to be a Cleric &c. There are some Clerics who possess wealth under the poor Christ, which they had not possessed under the rich and deceitful Devil, so that the Church sighs for them as rich, whom the world previously held as beggars &c. Flee from the merchant Cleric, and from the one who is rich from being needy, and glorious from being ignoble, as a kind of plague. Bernard, Epistle 24 to Gilbert the Bishop that true and undoubted wisdom is, which despises base gains, and judges it unworthy of itself to enjoy the same fellowship with the servitude of idols.

23. The Church is bound to pay stipends to Pastors and indeed liberally, lest there be for them an occasion of neglected duty or even of seeking αἰσχροκερδείας. 1. Cor. 9. v. 7. and following. Galat. 6. v. 6.1. Timoth. 5. v. 17. & 18.

24. There are three plagues of the Ecclesiastical Ministry, ἀεργία, αἰσχροκερδεία & φιλοπρωτεία, ambition, tyranny, and the lust for dominating. Epist. Ioh. 3. v. 9.

25. Therefore, just as the desire for base gain is forbidden to Presbyters, so too is the desire for dominion. Let them consider that they are not lords of the Churches, but ministers, 1. Cor. 4. v. 21. All things are yours v. 22. Whether Paul, or Apollo, or Cephas, etc., all things are yours. Let them consider that it is entrusted to them to minister to others the grace divinely given to them. As good stewards of the manifold grace of GOD. 1. Petr. 4. v. 10. Let them consider that a curse is denounced against those Pastors who rule with austerity and cruelty Ezech. 34. v. 4. who bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on the shoulders of men, but they themselves will not move them with their finger. Matth. 23. v. 4. Let them consider that they preside for this purpose, that they may excel in holiness, and shine before others in humility, and not that they may show off their power and severity. Let them consider that not absolute dominion over the flock, but the care of feeding it is enjoined upon them. Lyranus in h. l. Let not Presbyters be elevated through the pride of the nature of prelacy.

26. The Church is the inheritance and property of the Lord. Christ acquired the Church for Himself with His own blood. Act. 20. v. 28. He therefore alone is the Lord of the Church. He let out the cultivation of this vineyard of His to others, but He Himself alone is and remains the Lord. Matth. 21. v. 33.

27. Pastors ought not only to teach by word, but also by example; let them show themselves as a living image of piety and virtue, let them go before their hearers in the study and race of virtue. Ioh. 10. v. 4. The shepherd goes before the sheep, and the sheep follow him. Phil. 3. vers. 17. Be imitators of me. 2. Thessal. 3. vers. 9. Not as though we did not have the power, but that we might give ourselves τύπον to you to imitate us. 1. Timoth. 4. v. 12. Be a pattern of the faithful in word, in conversation, in charity, in faith, in chastity. Tit. 2. vers. 7. In all things show yourself τύπον a pattern of good works in doctrine, integrity, gravity, incorruptibility: on which passage Jerome comments thus. Paul desires that Timothy;

or whoever is a prelate is like an archetype or primary form, from which living images of virtues are expressed by the features of an honest life transferred into themselves. Therefore, the life of a Pastor ought to be such that not only whatever he says, but also whatever he does, is a teaching for his hearers. How can they inform others, who are unformed and monstrous in themselves, says Lyranus in this place. But it is a monstrous thing to have the highest rank and the lowest mind; the first seat and the lowest life; a grandiloquent tongue and an idle life; much speech and no fruit; a grave countenance and a light act; huge authority and wavering stability, as Bernard writes in book 2 of his work On Consideration to Eugene, chapter 8. What we are by profession, let us demonstrate by action rather than by name, so that the name may agree with the action, and the action may respond to the name, lest the name be empty and the crime immense: lest there be sublime honor and deformed life; lest there be a deific profession and an illicit action; lest there be religious attire and irreligious progress; lest there be an exalted rank and a deformed excess; lest a more sublime chair be held in the Church, and the conscience of the Priest be found lower; lest we simulate the speech of a dove, and have the mind of a dog, says Ambrose in his book On the Dignity of the Priesthood, chapter 3, volume 4 of his works, folio 179.

28. Hearers, having followed their Pastors in the way of piety and virtue, should likewise become τύποι to other believers. 1. Thess. 1. v. 6. You became imitators of us and of the Lord. vers. 7. so that you became τύπος to all believers in Macedonia.

29. Faithful Pastors in this age are accustomed to receive the hatreds and ingratitude of the world in place of a reward; therefore, let them look toward the future age outside of this world, and oppose the promised heavenly rewards, stored up with Christ, to the hatreds of Satan and the world, by the hope of which they ought to overcome all dangers and adversities, and rouse themselves to execute their office with the greatest diligence. Luth. in this place. The office of Pastors is too sublime to be compensated in this life; a copious reward is prepared for them in heaven. Dan. 12. v. 3. Matth. 25. v. 21. 2. Tim. 4. v. 8.

30. Christ is the Prince of Pastors, the primary Pastor, the great Pastor of the sheep Hebr. 13. v. 20., indeed one Ezech. 34. v. 23.; his sheep are his own, the remaining Pastors are also his own, likewise redeemed with the sheep by his blood. Act. 20. v. 28. Bened. Arias in this place. Christ is the prince of Pastors by right, by office, by example.

31. The heavenly reward promised by the prince of Pastors to faithful Pastors, and to be rendered in its own time, is called a crown of righteousness 1. Timoth. 4. vers. 8. partly because Christ by His perfect obedience and righteousness has merited it, partly because God has promised it to those who serve Him faithfully, and who are zealous for holiness and righteousness 1. Corinth. 9. vers. 25.crown of lifeIac. 1. v. 12.Apoc. 2. v. 20. because those to whom this crown will be given will be made partakers of true and eternal life; and the crown of glory in this place, because it will render those glorious and illustrious upon whom it is placed by Christ.

32. The name crowns can warn faithful pastors especially of three things. First, that no small struggle is set before them in the Ministry. 2. Timoth. 2. v. 5.He who struggles will not be crowned, unless he has struggled lawfully. For unless one struggles, no crown is given. 2. That after the struggle has been endured, heavenly rewards are to be expected by them. The end of a strong fight is victory; the consequence of victory is a crown. 3. That those future rewards will be eternal. Lyranus in this place: Eternal life is a crown, because it has neither beginning nor end.

33. The consideration of all these things ought to excite pastors to alacrity in performing their duty. A far greater reward is promised by Christ to faithful pastors than to Jacob, who was so heavily occupied in feeding the flocks of his father-in-law. Gen. 31. v. 31. Gregory, book 7, Epistle 48: If he who fed the sheep of Laban labors and keeps watch in such a way, to how much labor and to how many vigils ought he to attend who feeds the sheep of God? To whom also divine and heavenly rewards are promised.

34. The more numerous the requirements of a faithful pastor are, the rarer the examples of faithful pastors are, and the greater the rewards promised to faithful pastors, the greater ought to be the reverence of the Lord's flock toward faithful pastors.

35. The younger ought to be subject to the elders, let them allow themselves to be warned by them, as being taught by long experience of things and less prone to the dominion of the passions, let them show reverence and obedience to them, and obey their holy warnings.

36. This is conformable to the divine command Lev. 19. vers. 32.Before the hoary head you shall rise, and honor the person of the old man; this is conformable to the law of Nature, to right reason, to the sayings and examples of the sounder Gentiles, who believed this to be a great crime and one to be atoned for by death, if a youth had not risen before an old man.

BUT ALL OF YOU INSINUATE HUMILITY TO ONE ANOTHER, BECAUSE GOD RESISTS THE PROUD, BUT GIVES GRACE TO THE HUMBLE.

Connection. 1. To the special exhortation directed to the Presbyters by the dignity of their office, and to the younger by age, the Apostle adds a general exhortation directed to all men of whatever status, condition, and age, in which first of all he commends humility to all.

2. The Apostle had commanded that the younger ought to be subject to the elders. He amplifies this precept with a kind of correction, by which he extends it to all, and by transferring the hypothesis to the thesis, he asserts that all ought to be subject to one another through humility. Bede in this place Lest the Prelates, hearing (that the precept of subjection is given to the younger) should think that the rights of humility due were to be observed only by their subjects, and not also by themselves, he immediately added by admonishing generally; but all of you insinuate humility.

3. The plague of obedience is pride, for unless those high and lofty spirits with which man is swollen are subdued, no one will want to yield to another; therefore, after the Apostle had exhorted the younger to subjection and reverence toward the elders, he exhorts both them and in general all to humility.

Disposition. It is proposed in this verse. 1. The Apostolic exhortation. 2. The reason for the exhortation. The exhortation is twofold. 1. To mutual subjection. 2. To the flight of pride. The reason for the exhortation is sought from the consequences both of pride and of humility ἀντιθετικῶς opposed to one another.

Exposition. πάντες δὲ ἀλλήλοις ὑποτασσόμενοι τὴν ταπεινοφροσύνην ἐγκομβώσασθε. The Vulgate rendered it. But all of you insinuate humility to one another. But in the Greek text is added ὑποτασσόμενοι; all of you being subject or subjecting yourselves to one another, for it is a participle of the present tense, or as some Codices read ὑποτάσσεσθε subject yourselves. Some Codices omit the adversative δὲ, whence some Interpreters establish this as if it were a correction ἀσυνδέτως added. But it is held in the more approved and more numerous Codices, and the universality of the precept requires it entirely, through a kind of correction as it were of the special by the precept of the subject, so that the little word μᾶλλον. is understood. Altogether the younger ought to be subject to the elders, but all rather ought to be subject to one another. The Syrian Interpreter not only omitted the little word δὲ, but also the universal πάντες as well as the participle ὑποτασσόμενοι entirely; therefore he does not establish a new precept here, but joins it with the preceding precept given to the younger in particular, in this way. And you younger, subject yourselves to your elders, and clothe yourselves inwardly with humility of mind one toward another. But the Syriac version, since it is a stream, ought not to prejudice the Greek fountain. Concerning the meaning of the word ἐγκομβώσασθε, the opinions of the Interpreters vary greatly. 1. The Vulgate rendered it Insinuate. Bede follows it in his commentary. All, he says, are commanded to insinuate the virtue of humility. The old Interpreter seems to have read ἐγκολπώσασθε, insinuate, hide, comprehend with a distended bosom. Carry it always in your bosom and breast as a most dear thing, or as the interlinear gloss explains, always have it in your bosom. Insinuate in this meaning does not occur among approved Latin writers, but it signifies something else to them, which Lyranus and John Huss expressed thus. Insinuate, i.e., show outwardly by work, do not only have it in the mind. Lyranus. Demonstrate by words and works, so that you may excite one another to works of humility. Others, insinuate, i.e., send into the bosom of others by your example. Salmero, seeking a support for the Latin version, explains it thus. To insinuate is properly to join and as it were to insert oneself secretly and cautiously into the bosom. But anyone sees that this meaning is foreign. For who would say that we ought to insert ourselves secretly and cautiously into the bosom of humility? Or how can this meaning be deduced from the Greek word ἐγκομβώσασθε?? 2. The Syrian rendered it by the word [consult facsimile image] in Ethpael, which is used twice in the N. T. Acts 12. v. 8. where in Greek it is περιβάλου τὸ ἱμάτιόν σου wrap yourself in your covering, and in this place, clothe yourselves inwardly, [consult facsimile image] which the Syrian added for the sake of ἐξηγήσεως, so that he might express the emphasis of the preposition ἐν in the word ἐγκομβώσασθε. This meaning of wrapping and clothing agrees with the use of the word ἐγκομβώσασθε among Greek writers. Pollux, book 4, chapter 18, writes τῇ τῶν δούλων ἐξωμίδι προσκεῖσθαι καὶ ἱματίδιον τὶ λευκὸν, that ἐγκόμβωμα or ἐπίβλημα is named.

Hesychius ἒγκομβωθείς explains δεθεὶς & ἐγκεκόμβωται, he brings forward for the pious ἐνειληταί. Item κομβώσασθαι he explains στολίσαθαι and κόσσυμβοι or κοσσύμβην, he says it was ἐγκόμβωμα καὶ περιζωμα Ἀιγύπτων.. Oecumenius seems to have followed this meaning, who rendered it, gird yourselves. Thus, therefore, the metaphor would be drawn from a type of garment tied into a knot, which servants once used, which was called ἐγκόμβωμα, so that the sense may be: Put on humility and embrace it on every side, just as a garment covers the whole body. Like a garment tied in a knot, retain humility joined to you, lest it be shaken off anywhere. The Apostle uses a similar phrase Col. 3. v. 12. ἐνδύσασθαι ταπεινοφροσύνην. 3. Related to this explanation is that by which ἐγκομβώσασθε is explained as knot, bind, that is, tightly bind humility to yourselves. For as we warned before, that type of garment which was called ἐγκόμβωμα was accustomed to be tied into a knot. Henricus Stephanus cites from a certain old Lexicon that ἐγκόμφωμα is τὸν δεσμόν τῶν χειριδων.. Suidas, ὁκόμβος, (from which κόμβωμα & ἐγκόμβωμα) ἐστι τῶν δύο χειριδίων, ὃθαν τις δήσῃ ἐπὶ τὸν ἲδιον τράχηλον. Erasmus rendered, have humility fixed. Humility ought to be so tightly bound that not even the Devil himself can untie this bond. In the same way Vatablus: Have humility fixed to you, or hold it tightly or bound with knots. Pagninus: Have humility bound to you, for κόμβος signifies a knot. Camerarius in his notes ἐγκομβὼσασθε bind, fasten. The sense therefore will be: Bind and knot humility with the tightest knots, lest it slip away. To this can be referred that κόμβος for Hesychius is the same as κόσυμβος, i.e., ἀνάδεσμα, ὅπερ αἱ κρισσαὶ φοροῦσιν ὃμοιον ἀσπιδίσκῳ.. For Suidas it is likewise ἀνάδεσμος & χιτὼν κρισσωτὶς.. For a knot and ἀναδέσματι it is taken Exod. 28. v. 39. where οἱ κόσυμβοι τῶν χιτώνων ἐκ βύσσου are the knots of the tunics of fine linen, for which the version of the Hebrew text has, you shall weave the tunic of fine linen, Pollux book 2, in the title concerning tonsure and hair, takes it for a knot of hair. In the same chapter Exod. verse 4. χιτὼν κοσυμβωτὶς is a tunic tied with knots. 4. Not far from this explanation departs that by which ἐγκομβώσασθε is explained as adorn yourselves. For a garment not only covers the body, but also adorns it. And στολίσασθαι,, by which Hesychius explains the word ἐγκομβώσασθαι, signifies not only to be clothed, but also to be adorned. For Suidas κομβώματα are τὰ καλλωπίσμαθα ornaments.

The Royal Bible in this passage reads ἐγκομβώσασθε for ἐγκομπώσασθε;, but in Suidas ἐγκομπώσασθαι is explained by στολίσασθαι.. Thus, therefore, the doors of the senses. Be adorned within with humility. Although Beza in his annotations rejects the third meaning as metaphorical and by no means suitable to this passage, nevertheless, since examples of these three latter meanings have been brought forward, and they do not conflict with one another in the least, but are subordinate, therefore none of them can be simply rejected.

Ταπεινοφροσύνη is indeed used in a bad sense Coloss. 2. v. 18., where it is joined with θρησκεία τῶν Αγγέλων., and cap. eiusd. vers. 23., where it is joined with ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ καὶ ἀφειδία σώματος,; it signifies, therefore, a foolish dejection of mind, but in other sayings of Scripture it denotes that Christian virtue, nay, the foundation of all virtues, when someone thinks modestly of himself and is of a humble mind, ὁ γὰρ ταπεινόφρων ἒστιν ὁ ταπεινὰ φρονῶν Act. 20. v. 19.Eph. 4. v. 2.Phil. 2. v. 3.Col. 3. v. 12. The Syrian in this passage rendered it by [consult facsimile image] humility, meekness, gentleness, etc. of mind, for these virtues are related to ὃτι ὁ θεὸς ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν,. The passage is taken from Prov. 3. v. 34. according to the Septuagint Interpreters, except that for ὁ θεὸς there is read κύριος.. James cites this sentence with the same words cap. 4. v. 6.; in the Hebrew text in Solomon it is held: He himself will mock the mockers, and to the meek he will give grace; but without any variation of sense.

Ὑπερήφανοι are called proud and haughty men. Luc. 1. v. 51.Rom. 1. v. 30.2. Tim. 3. v. 2. Eustathius reports that ὑπερήϕανος has a pleonasm of the letter η,, so that it is as if ὑπέρϕανος from ὑπερϕαίνομαι I stand out above others. For he who is proud and arrogant presents himself to be seen above others, namely, lifting himself up above them. In Demosthenes in Midiam, ὑπερηϕανία καὶ ὑπεροψία are joined as ἰσοδυναμοῦντα.. Eustathius explains the participle ὑπερηφανέοντες in Homer Iliad λ. as ὑπερφρονοῦντες,; for from pride the contempt of others is born. The LXX use for גאה or גאיון swollen, haughty Iob. 40. vers. 7.Psal. 93. v. 2. etc., for גבה sublime Ps. 100. v. 7. ὀφθαλμὸι ὑπερήφανοι, whom Esai. 5. vers. 15. they call ὀφθαλμοὺς μετεώρους, for זר or זרון proud, elated from the root זור he swelled, he boiled over with pridePsal. 118. v. 21.51.69. &c. Ier. 43. v. 2. for רם or מרום elated, elevated,2. Reg. 22. v. 28.Iob. 38. v. 15. &c. for pride shines forth from the eyes, words, gestures, and clothes; and it leaves traces of itself everywhere through all the members of the body. The Syrian rendered [consult facsimile image] those who elevate and exalt themselves, ὑψοῦσιν ἑαντοὺς, as they are called Luc. 18. Vers. 13.

The word ἀντιτάσσεσθαι is to be military, from the opposite side as if to draw up a battle line, to stand against in battle. Plutarch in Caesar speaking about Brutus. άντιταχθεὶς δὲ Αντωνίῳ καὶ φιλίππῳ, ἀντιτά-ττεσθαι, says Budaeus, just as άντιπαρατάττεσθαι is to be drawn up from the opposite side in battle line so that the left wing of the adversaries is against our right; thence οἱ ἀντιτεταγμένοι are called enemies, and ἡ ἀντίταξις is the drawing up of a battle line against an enemy. This meaning fits this passage beautifully. For the proud are as it were invaders of divine glory, while they snatch to themselves what is God's; but against invaders and robbers an armed force is accustomed to be opposed. Ambrose in Psal. 118. octon. 7. tom. 4. fol. 464. God, as the repeller of his own insult, undertakes a certain special struggle against pride. The emphasis of this word is explained Iud. 2. v. 15. Wherever the Israelites went out, the hand of the Lord was against them for evil, so that they could not stand before their enemies, as is gathered from the preceding verse. God himself was drawing up a battle line against the Israelites, and was granting victories to their enemies, but on the contrary was resisting the attempts of the Israelites. Then ἀντιτάσσεσθαι in general signifies to resist, to fight back, to be an adversary, whether that happens by words or by deeds, Act. 18. v. 6. ἀντίτασσομένων αὐτῶν καὶ βλασφημούντων. Rom. 13. Vers. 2. ὁ ἀντιτασσόμενος τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ διαταγῇ ἀνθέστηκεν. Iac. 5. Vers. 6. ὁ δίκαιος ἀντιτάσσεται ὑμῖν. which meaning can likewise be accommodated to this place. For God opposes the attempts of the proud both by words and by deeds, and hinders them. The Syrian has the word [consult facsimile image] he met, he opposed, Act. 17. vers. 17. thence [consult facsimile image] ἐνάντιος. adversary, enemy Ioh. 19. v. 12. because God has pride and the proud in hatred.

By ταπεινοὺς are understood in this place ταπεινόφρονες, τοῖς ὑπερηθανοις who are opposed, as the antithesis teaches. It signifies, therefore, not so much a humble state as a cast-down mind and a humble affection, in which meaning it is used Matth. 11. v. 29.Luc. 1. v. 52. etc. In the Hebrew text Prov. 3. v. 34. there is held the little word עניים which properly signifies the meek, because humility is the mother of meekness, thence צני Zach. 9. v. 9.Matthaeus cap. 21. v. 5. rendered πραΰς. The LXX use ταπεινὸς for דכאי־רוח who are compressed or humble in Spirit.Psalm. 33. v. 18. for צנוע which signifies him who is of a cast-down and humiliated mind. Prov. 11. v. 2. for שפל humiliatedPsal. 137. v. 7.Ezech. 21. v. 25. etc. The Syrian has the noun [consult facsimile image] which likewise signifies ταπεινὸν & πρᾷον humble and meek.Matth. 5. v. 5.cap. 11. v. 28.cap. 21. Vers. 5.12. v. 16.1. Thess. 2. v. 7.

Χάρις in the Scriptures signifies: 1. favor. 2. gifts given out of grace. Both significations have a place here. For God gives grace to the humble, among others he makes them gracious and dear, so that they may emerge, as is said concerning Joseph Gen. 39. v. 4. he found grace in the eyes of Potiphar his master. He also heaps upon them gifts of grace or χαρίσμασι, so that it may appear that they themselves are dear to God and to men.

Latin:

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quinam per Presbyteros intelligantur? Quamvis nomen πρεσβυτέρων quandoque simpliciter de aetate in Scripturis sacris intelligatur Luc. 15. v. 25.Ioh. 8. v. 9.Act. 2. v. 17.1. Tim. 5. v. 1. &c. quibus opponuntur νεώτεροι sive νεανίσκοι, in qua significatione in hoc ipso capite v. 5. Apostolus noster hoc nomine utitur: ex verbo tamen pascendi in v. 2. manifestum est, nomen Presbyteri hoc loco esse officii & dignitatis nomen, quo appellati olim fuêre Ecclesiarum praepositi. Rectiùs ergò fecisset Latinus Interpres, si nomen Presbyteri ex Graeco retinuisset, ut fecit Hieronymus Epist. 85. ad Evagrium. Cùmque ex 1. Tim. 5. v. 17. colligi possit, duplices fuisse in Ecclesia Presbyteros, sive duos Presbyterorum ordines. Quidam enim laborabant in verbo & doctrina, h. e. erant pastores & doctores Ecclesiae, quidam vero erant duntaxat ἡγούμενοι, qui unà cum doctoribus Ecclesiam gubernabant, & curam doctrinae ac disciplinae habebant, manifestum est, Petro de priore Presbyterorum ordine hoc loco agere.

Q. 2. Quare Ecclesiae Doctores vocentur Presbyteri? Resp. 1. quia vel aetate vel senili prudentiâ alios antecellere debent. 2. quia plerunque ex Senioribus eligebantur, sicut etiam illi, qui Reipubl. praesunt, Senatores vocantur, propterea quòd plerumque ex Senioribus Senatus colligitur, unde à Senibus nomen mite Senatus habet, atque apud Homerum Iliad. β γέροντεςdicuntur iidem, quiἀριστῆες.Iob. 12. v. 12.In senibus est sapientia, & in multo tempore est prudentia. Neque tamen ex solis senibus constituebatur πρεσβυτερεῖον, sed etiam iuniores quandoque in illud cooptabantur, ut exemplum Timothei ostendit, de quo Apostolus dicit, 1. Tim. 4. vers. 12.Nemo iuventutem, tuam contemnat: interim totum Collegium respectu potioris partis Presbyterium fuit appellatum.

Q. 3. An hoc nomine etiam simplices Presbyteri, qui non sunt simul Episcopi, comprehendantur? Estius negat, sic enim in hunc locum commentatur. Quatenus nomen Presbyteri generale sit etiam usu Apostolorum, ut omnes, qui sunt ordinis Sacerdotalis, complectatur, utPhilipp. 1.1. Tim. 3. & 5.Tit. 1.principaliter tamen hoc sermone solos Episcopos convenit Petrus, ut qui soli propriè & plenà ratione sunt Dominici gregis pastores, non in partem operis vocati, velut parochi, sed absolutam & illimitatam, quod ad ius divinum attinet, exercendi in suo grege pastoralis officii, potestatem habentes, ad quos proinde spectat non tantùm praedicare Dei verbum, & Sacramenta ministrare, quod utrumque Parachi faciunt, verùm etiam leges ponere, & transgressores punire, & contumaces ab Ecclesia per excommunicationem eiicere, unde & in canonibus & apud veteres ipsi soli vocaentur Pastores. Sed & PaulusEph. 4. pastores & doctores nominans solos Episcopos intellexit. Sed rectiùs dicitur, Presbyterorum nomen esse commune nomen omnium ministrorum verbi. 1. Fatetur ipse Estius, ex usu Apostolorum nomen hoc omnes, qui sunt Sacerdotalis ordinis complecti, ut patet Act. 14. v. 23.cap. 15. v. 2. & seqq. cap. 20. v. 17.1. Tim. 5. v. 17.Tit. 1. v. 5.Iac. 5. v. 14. &c. 2. Nulla cogimur necessitate, ab hac usitata significatione discedere, cum ea, quae Apostolus hoc loco Presbyteris praescribit, ad omnes Ecclesiae ministros pertineant. 3. Iubentur quidem ἐπισκοπεῖν, at ex eo probari nequit, solos Episcopos inspectioni aliorum Ecclesiae Doctorum praepositos hic intelligi, cum iubeantur ἐπισκοπεῖνgregi Dominico, quod omnibus Pastoribus est commune. 4. Leges ponere, transgressores punire, excommunicare contumaces &c. non pertinet ad solos Episcopos, sed ad totum Presbyterium, imò ad totam Ecclesiam, cuius consensus accedere debet Act. 15. v. 22.1. Cor. 5. v. 4. proinde etiam absolutam & illimitatam potestatem Episcopis Ecclesiae minimè concedimus. 5. Et pastorum & doctorum nomen generale est, ad omnes Ecclesiae ministros pertinens, unde Hieron.

in comm. h. l. & Augustinus Epist. 59. ad Paulin. notant, quod cum in caeteris Apostolus discreverit officiorum genera, hic duo coniunxerit. Neque enim dixit, quosdam pastores, quosdam doctores, sed alios pastores & doctores, quòd quicunque sunt pastores, iidem etiam debeant esse doctores. Cornelius à Lapide discedens ab Estio dicit, Seniores hîc intelligi tùm aetate, tùm dignitate & Sacerdotio, sive id mimus sit & vulgare, sive maius, puta Episcopatus.

Q. 4. Quare ultimo demum loco Apostolus Presbyteros sui Admoneat officii? Resp. 1. Quia ipsorum ordo reliquis ordinibus aestatibus est praestantior, ideò per gradus quasi ascendendo post diversa monita, sub ditis, servis, uxoribus & maritis in ordine oeconomico & politico constitutis tradita, Presbyteros, qui animarum curam gerunt, & in Ecclesiastico ordine constituti sunt, compellat. 2. Ut regni salus in Rege, ovium incolumitas in Pastore, membrorum sanitas in capite consistit: sic Ecclesiarum salus in Praepositis sive Presbyteris. Quemadmodum videns arborem, foliis pallentibus marcidam, intelligis, quòd aliquam culpam habeat circa radicem: ita cum videris populum indisciplinatum, sine dubio cognosce, quòd Sacerdotium eius non est sanctum, inquit Chrysostomus de symb. Meritò igitur exhortationem ad Presbyteros Apostolus ad locum ultimum reiecit, cum ab illis reliquorum Ordinum salus pendeat. 3. Cum Presbyteri alios in vita & moribus instruant, paucioribus, admonitionibus prae reliquis Ordinibus indigere videbantur.

Q. 5. Quo fine Apostolus se appellet testem passionum Christi? Resp. 1. Ut eò maiorem autoritatem ac fidem exhortationi suae conciliet. Quia enim fidelem Christi ministrum isthac passionum tolerantia sese comprobavit, ideò aequum est, admonitioni eius ex fideli corde profectae locum relinqui. 2.
