Nomine vero subiectionis complectitur Apostolus omne subiectionis & officii genus, quod iuniores debent Senioribus, videl. quòd debeant Senioribus assurgere, eos verbis, gestibus & opere ipso honorare, eorum monitis parere ac morem gerere, ipsis cedere, adeoque venerandam ipsorum caniciem in precio habere.

## 5:6
HUMBLE YOURSELVES THEREFORE UNDER THE MIGHTY HAND OF GOD, THAT HE MAY EXALT YOU IN THE TIME OF VISITATION.

Connection. 1. The Apostle repeats the exhortation to humility, and confirms the argument of the exhortation that has been adduced from the power of Him who requires humility, and has promised that He will exalt the humble. God has enough strength, he says, to resist the proud, and to exalt the humble, therefore study humility seriously. The illative particle οὖν, proves this connection, which shows that this sentence is deduced from the former.

2. A new argument of exhortation can also be established here, drawn from the will of God. By humbling ourselves we submit to the hand of the Lord, and we demonstrate that the hope of future exaltation flourishes in our heart.

3. The Apostle persists in the military metaphor. Men through the sin of the corrupt and depraved, draw up their battle line as it were against GOD, whom GOD opposes from the opposite side, and while the humble indeed submit themselves under his powerful hand, whom he also receives into his own faith and protection, the proud, however, continuing to move weapons against him, are prostrated by the powerful hand of GOD.

4. He explains what that grace is, which he had said in the preceding verse is given by GOD to the humble, and he transfers the thesis to the hypothesis. GOD gives grace to the humble. Be humbled therefore under the powerful hand of GOD, that he may also exalt you. Bede in h. l. What that same grace is, which GOD confers upon the humble, he explains consequently, when by admonishing he adds. Be humbled therefore under the powerful hand of GOD, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation. This grace therefore he bestows upon the humble, that by how much the more they shall have been humbled on account of him in the time of the struggle, by so much the more gloriously they may be exalted by him in the time of retribution.

5. He meets a tacit objection, and indeed a double one. 1. When we are warned about the pursuit of humility, our refractory flesh retorts. Why should I submit myself to him, when I am not inferior to him. The Apostle answers. He who on account of the command of GOD and in the fear of the Lord submits himself to another, does not submit himself to man, but to GOD, inasmuch as he who commanded it, and holds it pleasing, and wishes to reward it with prizes. 2. The refractory flesh retorts this also. If I shall have submitted myself to all, they will make a footstool of my feet out of me. The Apostle answers, your humility will by no means be a loss to you, because GOD will exalt you at the just time.

6. He explains also the manner and reason for us to be humbled, namely that we may acknowledge the powerful and invincible hand of GOD, and on that account humbly submit ourselves to GOD, and on account of GOD to men.

Disposition. 1. Repetition of the exhortation. 2. Double argument of the exhortation. The former taken from the power of GOD. The latter from the benevolence of GOD. Submit yourselves to GOD, and to men on account of GOD, who by his powerful hand can cast down the proud and lift up the humble. So it will come to pass, that he will exalt you and make you glorious in the glorious coming of Christ to judgment.

Exposition of the text. Ταπεινώθτε οὖν ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ θεοῦ. The Vulgate rendered it, be humbled. But it ought to have been rendered, be ye humbled, for the Apostle continues the exhortation. The Syriac has The word [consult facsimile image] in the Ethpael, dismiss yourselves, signifies indeed a reciprocal action.

By the κραταιὰν powerful, robust, and valid hand of God, his very omnipotence is designated, which Ex. 14. v. 31. is called great hand, cap. 3. v. 19. valid hand, cap. 32. v. 11. robust hand, Deut. 3. v. 24. most strong hand, Matth. 26. v. 64. right hand of power, by which he is powerful both to depress and prostrate the proud, and to defend and exalt the humble. A parallel passage exists Iac. 4. v. 6. God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. v. 7. ὑποτάγη τε οὖν τῷ θεῷ. v. 10. ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον τοῦ κυρίου καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς. ἵνα ὑμᾶς ὑψώση ἐν καιρῷ. The Vulgate adds, in the time of visitation, just as also the Royal and another Codex read ἐν καιρῷ ἐπισκοπῆς. But most Greek Codices read simply ἐν καιρῷ. προσδιορισμὸς that one seems to have been transferred here from cap. 2. vers. 12. they may glorify God ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπισκοπῆς. The Syriac rendered [consult facsimile image] [consult facsimile image] in a convenient or just time. For καιρὸς does not denote simply time, but determinately a convenient and opportune time, whence Erasmus in this place rendered, that he may exalt you, when it will be opportune, when it will seem opportune to him; when he will judge it to be expedient for you either in this age, or in the day of judgment.

Latin:

HUMILIAMINI IGITUR SUB POTENTI MANU DEI, UT VOS EXALTET IN TEMPORE VISITATIONIS.

Connexio. 1. Repetit Apostolus exhortationem ad humilitatem, & adductum exhortationis argumentum confirmat à potentia illius, qui humilitatem requirit, & humiles sese exaltaturum promisit. Sat virium, inquit, Deus habet ad resistendum superbis, & exaltandum humiles, ideò humilitati seriò studete. Hanc connexionem probat particula illativa οὖν, quae ostendit hanc sententiam deduci ex priore.

2. Potest etiam novum hîc statui exhortationis argumentum, ductum à Dei voluntate. Humiliando submittimus nos manui Domini, & futurae exaltationis spem in corde nostro vigere demonstramus.

3. Persistit Apostolus in metaphora militari. Homines per peccatum corrupti ac depravati, aciem quasi contra DEUM instruunt, quos DEUS ex adverso oppugnat, ac humiles quidem se sub potenti ipsius manu submittunt, quos etiam in suam fidem ac tutelam recipit, superbi verò, arma adversus ipsum movere pergentes, potenti manu DEI prosternuntur.

4. Exponit, quae sit illa gratia, quam humilibus à DEO dari in versu praecedente dixerat, ac thesin ad hypothesin traducit. DEUS humilibus dat gratiam. Humiliamini ergò sub potenti DEI manu, ut etiam vos exaltet. Beda in h. l. Quae sit eadem gratia, quam confert humilibus DEUS, consequenter exponit, cum admonendo subiungit. Humiliamini igitur sub potenti manu DEI, ut vos exaltet in tempore visitationis. Hanc ergò gratiam humilibus tribuit, ut quò magis humilitati fuerint propter ipsum tempore certaminis, eò glorio siùs exaltentur ab ipso tempore retributionis.

5. Occurrit tacitae obiectioni, & quidem duplici. 1. Quando de studio humilitatis monemur, caro nostra refractaria regerit. Cur illi me subiicerem, cum ipso non sim inferior. Respondet Apostolus. Qui propter mandatum DEI & in timore Domini sese alteri subiicit non homini, sed DEO sese subiicit, quippe qui id praecepit, & gratum habet, & praemiis vult remunerari. 2. Regerit & hoc caro refractaria. Si me omnibus subiecero, scabellum pedum ex me facient. Respondet Apostolus, humilitas vestra nequaquam vobis erit damno, quia DEUS iusto tempore vos exaltabit.

6. Exponit etiam modum ac rationem nos humiliandi, videlicet ut agnoscamus potentem & invictam DEI manum, ac propterea humiliter nos subiiciamus DEO, & propter DEUM hominibus.

Dispositio. 1. Exhortationis repetitio. 2. Duplex exhortationis argumentum. Prius desumtum à DEI potentia. Posterius à DEI benevolentia. Subiicite vos DEO, & hominibus propter DEUM, qui potente suâ manu superbos deiicere & humiles extollere potest. Ita futurum, ut vos exaltet & gloriosos faciat in glorioso Christi ad iudicium adventu.

Textus expositio. Ταπεινώθτε οὖν ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ θεοῦ. Vulg. reddidit, humiliamini. Sed reddendum erat, humiliemini, continuat enim Apostolus exhortationem. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] in Ethpael, dimittite vosipsos, significat enim actionem reciprocam.

Per κραταιὰν potentem, robustam ac validam Dei manum ipsius omnipotentia designatur, quae Ex. 14. v. 31. vocatur manus magna,cap. 3. v. 19.manus valida,cap. 32. v. 11.manus robusta,Deut. 3. v. 24.manus fortissima,Matth. 26. v. 64.dextra virtutis, quâ potens est tùm superbos deprimere ac prosternere, tùm humiles defendere & exaltare Locus parallelus extat Iac. 4. v. 6.Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam.v. 7.ὑποτάγη τε οὖν τῷ θεῷ.v. 10.ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον τοῦ κυρίου καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς. ἵνα ὑμᾶς ὑψώση ἐν καιρῷ. Vulgata addit, in tempore visitationis, sicut etiam Regius & alter Codex legunt ἐν καιρῷ ἐπισκοπῆς. Sed plerique Codices Graeci simpliciter legunt, ἐν καιρῷ. προσδιορισμὸς ille videtur huc translatus ex cap. 2. vers. 12.glorificent Deumἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπισκοπῆς. Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image][consult facsimile image]in tempore conveniente sive iusto.καιρὸς enim non simpliciter tempus, sed determinatè conveniens & oportunum tempus denotat, unde Erasmus h. l. reddidit, ut vos extollat, cum erit oportunum, cum ipsi videbitur oportunum; cum iudicabit id vobis expedire vel in hoc seculo, vel in die iudicii.

## 5:6-11 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. Who are understood by the little word πάντες; Resp. Some think that this precept of humility pertains only to the younger ones, whom the Apostle therefore wishes to be humble, because Where humility is lacking, there obedience cannot have a place. But it is more correctly said that this is a general precept, pertaining to all men of whatever status, condition, and age, because it is subjoined to the special precept given to the younger ones by an adversative particle, and is therefore amplified as if by a certain correction. I said that the younger ought to be subject to the elders, but it is truer that all ought to be subject to one another through humility.

Q. 2. Why does the Apostle commend humility to all, and therefore also to Presbyters? Resp. Bede in his commentary on this passage: Lest the prelates, hearing this, should think that the rights of humility due were to be observed only by their subjects and not also by themselves, he immediately added by way of general admonition: 'All of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another.' For he says 'all,' both elders and adolescents, who are commanded to clothe themselves with the virtue of humility, and these, namely, by ruling, and those by obeying humbly. Which we read was done in the case of Peter himself and by him, when, as he was entering Caesarea, Cornelius met him and humbly prostrated himself at his feet, and he more humbly raised him up, saying, 'Arise, I myself am a man,' etc. Therefore, he teaches by example or also insinuates by word that all should have humility toward one another, because he knew that the vice of pride, which cast the Angels from heaven, was to be avoided by all, and he terrifies and restores all wholesomely by adding the sentence of Solomon.

Q. 3. How does the version of the LXX Interpreters Prov. 3. v. 34. which Peter follows, agree with the Hebrew text, which alone is authentic? Resp. The Hebrew text word for word is thus: He (the Lord) will mock the mockers, and to the meek he will give grace. The version of the LXX Interpreters is thus: The Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, which κατὰ πόδα Peter follows, except that for κύριος he substitutes ὁ θεὸς. There is no diversity here in sense. For 1. proud men are truly mockers, who with a high brow despise everyone and laugh at those who advise rightly. 2. God resists the proud, and by resisting them He mocks them, by eluding and frustrating their efforts and pursuits, by which they seek their own excellence. But also by deposing them from their seat He renders them contemptible, which is the property of one who mocks. 3. The humble are also the meek, just as the proud are irascible and boastful. The Hebrew ענוים descends from the root ענה which signifies to have been afflicted, humbled, and depressed, Es. 25. v. 5. cap. 31. v. 4. therefore ענוים signifies not only the meek, but also the humble and the humbled or afflicted.

Q. 4. What is to be understood by humiliation under the hand of God? Bede in his commentary explains it in three ways. Humiliation, he says, can in this place be accepted in many ways, that is, both that by which anyone beginning the way of virtues is healthily worn down for the washing away of the sins which he had committed; and that which is exhibited by the more perfect to God or to their neighbor in peace with spontaneous devotion of mind regarding surrounding things; and also that by which, when the whirlwinds of persecutions rush in, the unconquered mind is armed through the virtue of patience. To every kind of humility devoted to God, however, there succeeds that reward, that those who humble themselves in the time of their pilgrimage may be exalted in the time of His visitation. Properly and directly the Apostle treats of that virtue by which one acknowledges his own infirmity, humbles himself before GOD in true fear, and reverently submits himself to others, honoring the gifts of GOD in them.

Q. 5. Why does he make mention of the powerful hand of God, under which all ought to humble themselves? Resp. He adds this epithet, most suited to the proposed exhortation, for this reason: 1. that it may strike more terror into the haughty and swollen, lest they attempt to rise up against God. As if to say: You cannot escape the most powerful hand of God; whether you wish it or not, you are compelled to be subjected to it. 2. that it may raise up the oppressed and humble with consolation. As if to say: The hand of God is powerful to depress the proud, who insult others and trample them with their feet; and conversely, to defend the humble, who flee to Him, under His protection against all the insults of the proud, and to lift them on high.

Q. 6. What is understood by τὸν καιρὸν in this place? Resp. Some understand determinately the day of the coming of the Lord and the Universal judgment, which is called by antonomasia the time Matt. 8. v. 29. Have you come before the time to torment us? Mark 13. v. 33. You do not know when the time is. Luke 21 v. 8. the time, that is, of judgment, draws near. To which could also be referred Acts 1. v. 7. chap. 3. v. 24. 1. Cor. 4. v. 5. Gal. 6. v. 9. 1. Thess. 5. v. 1. 1. Tim. 6. v. 15. 1. Pet. 1. v. 5. And likewise those sayings in which the day of judgment and the coming of Christ is called absolutely ἡμέρα. 2. Tim. 4. v. 8. Heb. 10. v. 25. They think, therefore, that exaltation is assigned to the extreme time of retribution because the most powerful rewards of the pious are deferred to the day of judgment and the future life. Matt. 19. v. 29. Mark 10. v. 30. But it is more correctly said that by καιρὸν in this place is understood any opportune time of exaltation, whether it pleases God to lift us up in this or in the future age.

Q. 7. Why does the Apostle join this προσδιορισμὸν to the promise of future exaltation? Resp. 1. So that he may meet the scandal which is accustomed to arise from the pride of the impious. For he wishes to say this: The impious will not always be proud, and oppress others, nor will the humble always lie in the dust, but there will be a time when those will be humbled, but these will be exalted. 2. So that he may remedy haste, lest we seek to be exalted through illicit means before the time established by God, and thus by our own counsels, strive to anticipate the divine will.

Q. 8. Why does the Apostle use the word for casting? Resp. So that he may teach that those anxieties which press upon us are a huge weight, for the bearing of which we are not equal; it is required, therefore, that we relieve ourselves of this weight and burden as quickly as possible, and deposit it into the powerful hand of God, of which he had made mention in the preceding verse.

Q. 9. Does the Apostle speak of the sobriety of the mind, or indeed of the body? Calvin explains it concerning the sobriety of the mind. He uses a double metaphor, he says, that they should be sober, and keep watch. Lorinus notes, it is not improbable that sobriety in this place denotes moderation in prudence, or in the care of passing life, of which mention preceded most closely, and at the same time in believing, lest we wish to investigate too curiously those things which are proposed simply to be believed. It is favored by the fact that a little later we are admonished to resist the adversary the Devil in faith &c. Furthermore, since Paul commands, Rom. 12. v. 6. that no one should think more than is fitting, but εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν, which Irenaeus lib. 5. c. 20. renders as prudence; Jerome lib. 1. contra Iovin. as modesty. Augustine Epist. 47. as temperance. This temperance is a measure of containing oneself within boundaries, lest we seek a superfluous knowledge of the mysteries of faith. An argument could be added, that the Apostle uses not only cap. 1. v. 13. but also cap. 4. v. 7. νήφειν for the vigilance and sobriety of the mind, for he says νήφειν εἰς τὰς προσευχὰς. But the Apostle speaks directly and principally of the sobriety of the body, because he took this exhortation from the words of Christ Luc. 21. vers. 34. and because through drunkenness not a window, but a double-doored gate is opened to Diabolical temptations. Secondarily and less principally, we do not deny that the same exhortation is referred to the sobriety of the mind. For σωφροσύνη is said as if σώζουσα τὴν φρόνησιν, or σωτηρία φρονήσεως according to Plato in the Cratylus, and the sobriety of the body can also have the sobriety of the mind joined to it, which by no means consists with drunkenness and gluttony.

Q. 10. Whether the Apostle speaks of the wakefulness of the mind, or indeed of the body? Some receive this exhortation concerning the wakefulness of the body. 1. because γρηγορεῖν is properly used concerning the wakefulness of the body. Nehem. 7. vers. 3. Matth. 26. v. 40. Marc. 14. v. 37. 1. Thessal. 5. v. 10. &c. 2. because the preceding word concerning the sobriety of the body νήφειν is used. 3. because in the parallel passage. Luc. 21. v. 36. not only the wakefulness of the mind, but also of the body is required. For although Christ does not prohibit natural sleep, which no man in this life can lack for the preservation of health, yet He teaches that moderation must be applied to it, just as in food and drink. 4. Those who indulge too much in sleep are slothful and remiss in the works of their vocation, and have dulled senses. A full and idle belly cannot resist the Devil, says Luther in this place. 5. from the word γρηγορεῖτε the pious ancients took the occasion of introducing the rite of nocturnal vigils and prayers into the Church, as appears from Lactant. lib. 7. Instit. cap. 19. Gregor. Nyssen. on the feast of Easter. But although all these things are correct, it is said more rightly that the Apostle treats either solely or primarily of the wakefulness of the mind. 1. because we must fight against Satan not so much by the wakefulness of the body as by the wakefulness or vigilance of the mind. 2. without the vigilance of the mind, the wakefulness of the body profits little, since the Devil, our adversary, never takes sleep, but is perpetually awake. 3. Christ in the parallel passage Luc. 21. v. 36. speaks primarily of the vigilance of the mind, for He adds, watching at all times. 4. because that metaphorical meaning of the word γρηγορεῖν, by which it is taken for all vigilance, is far more customary to Christ and the Apostles. Matth. 25. v. 13. Luc. 12. v. 37. Act. 20. v. 31. 1. Cor. 16. v. 13. Coloss. 4. vers 2. 1. Thess. 5. v. 6. Apoc. 3. v. 2. cap. 3. v. 3. cap. 16. v. 15. 5. The Apostle shows that with the sobriety of the body, which brings with it the moderation of sleep, the vigilance of the mind must be joined. 6. Most interpreters explain it in the same way. The Syrian rendered it, be mindful or be remembering. Interlinear Gloss: Watch, not intent upon the delights of the world. Just as bodily drunkenness generates sloth and sleep: so also those who gorge themselves with earthly cares or pleasures, oppressed by spiritual lethargy, think of nothing. Lyranus: Watch, i. e. diligently beware of sins.

Q. 11. What is denoted by this spiritual vigilance? We said in Harm. Evang. chap. 162, that Christ in the parallel passage Luke 11. v. 36. requires from us through the precept of vigilance: 1. a daily remembrance of the last day, and a perpetual expectation of His advent, as is evident from the parable of the servants, who are vigilantly awaiting the return of their Lord from the wedding, to whom Christ wishes the faithful to be similar. Luke 12. v. 36. etc. 2. a solicitous care and daily preparation for the day of judgment, as is evident from the fact that Christ subjects to this precept ἐξηγήσεως in the passage at Matthew chap. 24. v. 44.: Be ye ready. 3. perpetual sobriety, as is evident from the fact that the precept of vigilance in Luke is subjected to a dehortation from surfeiting and drunkenness; as also from the parallel passage 1. Thess. 5. v. 4. and following. 4. diligence in the works of one's calling, as is evident from 2. Tim. 4. v. 5. and from the parable of the talents distributed among the servants, subjected to this precept in chap. 25. Matth.. 5. the flight from security and sins, as the comparison of the last times and the antediluvian times shows, which is prefixed to this precept of vigilance in the Evangelists; as also the parallel passages 1. Thess. 5. v. 3. and following, Apocal. 16. v. 15. etc. 6. prudence in avoiding the snares of Satan and the world. For just as he who sleeps corporally does not guard himself against the snares of thieves or enemies: so he is to be considered to sleep spiritually who does not observe the μεθοδείας. of the Devil Eph. 6. v. 11. and the various snares of this perverse age. 7. a circumspect custody of body and soul, because vigilance provides no mediocre support to the pursuit of virtue, viz. chastity, sobriety, and prayer. Therefore, because Peter repeats this exhortation from the mouth of his Master, all these things can also be accommodated to the present precept of vigilance. But especially by vigilance the Apostle in this place understands an attentive and solicitous care for salvation against the snares of Satan, with a metaphor taken from military sentinels. Just as a soldier placed on watch by a leader of war ought not to hang his arms on the wall and sleep soundly, but stand clothed in his arms and keep watch: so the pious ought to be fortified with the spiritual armor of faith, hope, and charity. Since they are children of light, let them cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light Rom. 13. v. 12.

Q. 12. Whether by the name of the Devil the Prince of evil Spirits is understood? The name Devil in the Scriptures is not used in one way only. For it is accepted either as a proper name, or as an appellative. In the former signification it is attributed. 1. To the Prince and head of the evil Spirits Matth. 25. v. 41.Apoc. 12. v. 9. in which sense it can also be understood that Christ is said to be tempted by the Devil Matth. 4. v. 1.Luc. 4. v. 2. for without doubt no common Devil attacked him, but the Prince of the malignant Spirits exerted all the powers of his might and knowledge against him, whence Luc. 4. v. 13. it is said, that when all temptation was finished, i. e. when all forces and deceits had been tempted in vain, the Devil departed from him. 2. To the entire assembly of malignant Spirits, Luc. 8. v. 12.Act. 10. v. 38.Eph. 6. v. 11. &c. Scripture is accustomed to speak of evil Spirits in the singular number, because under their head they constitute a certain society and kingdom, which is opposed to Christ and his kingdom. 3. To impious men, who are the instruments and children of the Devil, as Christ calls them Ioh. 8. v. 44. and Paul Act. 13. v. 10. Thus Christ Ioh. 6. v. 70. calls Judas his betrayer a Devil, because in the crime of betrayal he offered himself as an instrument of the Devil, belonged to the kingdom of the Devil, Satan had entered into him Luc. 22. v. 3. and he was ἐνδιαβολισμένος, spiritually possessed by the Devil, a slave and sewer of Satan. In the first signification the name of Devil is taken ἀτόμως, in the second συναγωγικῶς, in the third μετωνυμικῶς. The name of Devil is taken appellatively for any slanderer, which signification, however, could conveniently be referred to the one immediately preceding, because slanderers are instruments of the Devil. Eph. 4. v. 27.1. Tim. 3. v. 6. In this place the name of Devil is taken συναγωγικῶς, since the pious must struggle with the whole phalanx of Diabolical powers. Eph. 6. v. 12. Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against Princes and powers, against κοσμοκράτορας the darkness of this world, against spiritual i. e. Spirits of wickedness.

Q. 12. Why is the Devil compared to a lion? Resp. 1. on account of strength and validity. Prov. 30. v. 30. A lion, the strongest of beasts. Heb. strong among animals or among animals, he will not fear the encounter of any. Heb. he will not turn back from the face of any. Epiph. heres. 78. A lion is an animal most solid in strength, and, so to speak, most royal over other animals. Thus it is said of the Devil under the figure of Leviathan Iob. 41. vers. 25. He has no likeness on earth, who was made so that he would fear no one. 2. on account of cruelty. He is compared to a roaring lion i. e. a famished one. A famished lion or one deprived of its cubs invades, tears apart, and devours whoever it meets, whether men or beasts. Thus the Devil exercises the greatest cruelty against men. The lion delights in blood: thus the Devil is bloodthirsty and cruel, he is not content with the fortunes of men, but seeks their blood, nay, their very soul. 3. on account of courage. The lion is courageous and bold because of his redness: thus the Devil is not only most robust in strength, but also most prompt in boldness. 4. on account of cunning. Augustine, conc. 2. on Psalm 90 and tract. 10. on John, thinks that the Devil is compared to a lion, on account of manifest persecution against the Martyrs: to a Dragon on account of hidden persecution, which he stirs up through heretics, so that the lion, raging openly, seeks whom he may devour; the Dragon when he lies in wait; but cunning is not lacking to the lion either, therefore the Devil is compared to a lion not only on account of cruelty, but also on account of cunning. Psalm 10 v. 8 He lies in wait in secret as a lion in his den. The lion hides the tracks of his feet by drawing his tail over the sand. Epiphanius, to the Physiologus, chap. 1. He walks with twisted feet, and with his claws hidden inside as if in a sheath. Isidore, book 1. Etymologies, chap. 2, from Plutarch in his work on the comparison of animals, compares that which they assert he does especially in the winter time, so that he may not be discovered and caught by hunters from the tracks left in the snow: thus the Devil covers the tracks of his temptations, and proposes vices to men under the appearance of virtue, concerning which matter Nazianzen discourses most beautifully in his poem on virtue:

—————— Παλλάκι δὲ ἆυτε Ἐσθλοῦ τ᾽ ἡδὲ κακοῖο διάκρισιν ἐχθρὸς ἂμερσεν Ὣς θὴρ κερδάλεος τις ὑπ᾽ ἲχνεσιν ἲχνια βάλλων Ὣς κεν θηρητῆρα καλοῦ πλάξειε δολοῖσι. Often the deceitful enemy again takes away my discernment of good and evil, blinding my eyes, as a cunning beast that casts tracks upon tracks, so that by this art he might deceive the hunter of virtue.

The lion sleeps with open eyes, or rather he is awake while sleeping, and moves his tail, whence some think, that the lion never sleeps, for he has huge eyes, but thin eyelids, so that he cannot cover his whole eyes, and therefore the lion is called ὰ λὰω i. e. I see, who is ὀξυδερκὴς: thus the devil is ever-watchful, so that he may harm man. 5. on account of the desire to harm. The Apostle does not simply compare the Devil to a lion, but to a roaring and prowling lion seeking whom he may devour. Aristotle, book 9 of the History of Animals, chapter 44, and Pliny, book 8 of the Natural History, chapter 16, record that lions in the time of their old age, when they cannot hunt because of the weakness of their body and the loss of their teeth, approach cities so that they may seek men to be devoured. Thus the Devil is a veteran lion, most greedy for human blood, yet with this difference in him, that the number of his years has neither diminished his power, nor his knowledge, nor his desire to do harm, but rather has increased them. 6. because of the quality of those things which are contrary to the lion. Solinus in his Polyhistor records that the lion is terrified by the crowing of a cock, the cause of which he writes is unknown to him. Aelian, book 8 of the History of Animals, chapter 28, and those who seek it out do not attain it. The Devil is not only terrified by the prayers of the pious, but is even put to flight. Luke 22, v. 40. Pray, that you may not enter into temptation. Aristotle, book 9 of the History of Animals, chapter 44, records that the lion especially fears fire, citing that Homeric line, καιόμεναι τε δεταί, τὰς τετρεῖ ἰσθνμένός περ And burning torches, which, however much he may rage, he dreads: Thus the spiritual fire of faith, kindled in the heart by the Holy Spirit, is a great terror to the Devil.

Q. 14. Why is the Devil compared to a roaring lion? Resp. 1. because of his zeal for harming. As a hungry lion seeks food: so the Devil solicitously seeks the souls of men. 2. because of terror. The roar of a lion strikes such terror into animals that they stand motionless: Thus the Devil sometimes terrifies with threats, sometimes flatters and seduces with allurements. 3. because of the harm which he inflicts upon men. The Ordinary Gloss on this passage: As the roar of a lion hinders the ears so that they may not receive another sound: Thus the Devil, by terrifying the minds of the faithful and suggesting illicit things, turns them away from the path of truth, so that they may not hear the voice of Christ.

Q. 15. Why is the Devil said to περιπατεῖν go about? Resp. Cyprian, in his sermon on zeal and envy, thinks that the metaphor is drawn from an enemy of a besieged city, surveying the walls all around. He goes about, he says, us one by one, and as an enemy besieging those shut in, he explores and tests the walls, whether there is any part of the members less stable and less faithful, by whose approach he might penetrate to the interior. Bernard, sermon 12 on the Psalm He who dwells, etc. Let us say that the ways of the Devil are circumvention and going about. For he uses the latter toward us, the former in himself. He is always exalted, but he is always cast down. His pride always ascends, it is always humbled, etc. He ascends by the zeal of vanity, he descends by the envy of malice. Whose ascent is lying, his descent is cruel. The Apostle looks especially to an insatiable desire for harming, overthrowing, and devouring in the Devil, such as appears in the famished lion, going about that he may investigate prey.

Q. 16. Why should the Apostle warn the pious beforehand concerning these snares and desire for harming of the Devil? Resp. 1. That he may shake off from them security, which is the first snare of the Devil. For first the Devil attempts to make us secure. Then from security he precipitates us into sin. Thirdly, he labors to drag us from sin into eternal destruction. 2. That he may impel them to more ardent prayers. For prayer is a sacrifice pleasing to God, a most safe protection for man, but a whip to the Devil. 3. That he may commend to them confidence in God. Chrysostom, book 1 to Stagyrus! He who perceives danger to be imminent upon him, runs with greater desire to him whom he can protect, just as infant children when they have seen something horrible, flee immediately to the bosoms of their mothers, and hanging from their garments, they guard and protect themselves, outside of which time they sometimes do not even allow themselves to be drawn by blandishments.

Q. 17. What is to be understood by τί resisting the Devil? Resp. To resist the Devil is: 1. Not to consent to his temptations, to which the Apostolic saying is accommodated by some. Eph. 4. v. 27. Do not give place to the Devil, inasmuch as he possesses the minds of the angry. Bernard, Epist. 1. Col. 757. The adversary follows you more willingly when you are fleeing than he sustains you when you are fighting back, and he insists more boldly on the back than he resists in the face. Doubtless the first impetus of diabolical temptation is most sharp, which if anyone has bravely sustained, in the second assault he will find this enemy weaker, for by as much as he has been repelled, by so much the more he cools and fails. When the Devil is resisted and his temptation is repelled, he is weak as an ant; but when his suggestion is received, he is a strong lion. 2. To fight against him, fortified with spiritual armor Eph. 6. v. 12. and following. But to this armor belongs: First, the sword of the word. Eph. 6. v. 17. Hebr. 4. v. 12. Apoc. 1. v. 16. Just as enemies are put to flight by a sword, so by the word of God we can drive away and put to flight all the snares, all the machinations of the Devil. Christ commended this sword to us by his own example, when to the individual temptations of the Devil he set back some oracle of Scripture Matth. 4. vers. 4. 7. and 10. Secondly, the shield of faith Ephes. 6. v. 16. to which Peter also refers in this place, when he adds: Whom resist, strong in the faith. For as with a shield the weapons of the adversaries are received and repelled, thus in the shield of faith we can extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one. Thirdly, the sling of prayers projected from faith. Matth. 17. v. 21. C. 26. v. 41. Eph. 6. v. 13. v. 18. Just as David prostrated Goliath with stones projected from a sling: So we can conquer the Devil with prayers. Our strength against the Devil consists in prayers, because through them we are rendered participants of divine virtue. To prayers are also to be referred the Psalms, concerning which Ephrem lib. 2. de compunct. cordis cap. 2. Just as dust is scattered and attacked by the vehemence of the wind: so also our adversary is reduced to nothing, when our voice resounds in the praises of God, and our prayers full of tears are exhibited to God. Fourthly, the helmet of vigilance, to which the Apostle referred us in the preceding verse, by which we are intent upon all the snares of this enemy of ours and μεθοδείας solicitously beware, lest through security and consent into sins we open an approach to him; by which in the time of truces we may think about this spiritual war, and prepare ourselves for it; by which according to the rule of Gerson lib. de remed. contra Pusillan. in whatever temptation, by which we are attacked, we should always object the contrary, and therefore before sin we should think of divine justice, lest we consent to it; after sin divine mercy, lest we despair.

Q. 18. Whether by τά παθήματα are the temptations of Satan, or the persecutions of the world understood? Resp. The former exposition is favored by the fact that the Apostle here instructs us how we can resist our enemy the Devil. The latter, however, by the fact that the passions which are inflicted upon the brotherhood dispersed through the world seem to be persecutions. But both expositions can be joined, since the Devil endeavors to lead us away from the true faith, and to impel us to apostasy, not only through interior temptations, but also through exterior and open persecutions. Both παθημάτων kinds can and ought to be resisted by faith, to both are the pious dispersed through the whole world subject.

Q. 10. In what sense is the word grace taken in this place? Resp. The word grace used of God. 1. signifies his goodness, favor, mercy. 2. μετωνυμικῶς a gift given out of grace, which is called χάρισμα. According to the former signification God is called the God of all; grace, in that sense in which he is called the father of mercies, and the God of all, consolation 2. Cornith. 1. v. 3. because viz. he is merciful and rich in grace.

Eph. 2. vers. 7. by which reasoning the added little word πάσης denotes not so much distribution, as perfection. Luth. in comm. h. l. Gott gibt allen Gnade / und nicht ein Stu ct der Gnade / sondern reichlich alle Gnade. According to the latter meaning, He is called the God of all grace, because from Him benefits and goods of every kind descend to us Iac. 1. v. 17. He is the fountain and author of all spiritual gifts. Both meanings can be joined without any absurdity. For the Apostle recalls to the faithful, whom he encourages against the temptations of Satan and the persecutions of the world, the grace of election, calling, justification, regeneration, renovation, etc., and thus all spiritual benefits already received before, from which they ought to conceive confidence concerning the grace that preserves, confirms, strengthens, and perfects, or consummates, in temptations and persecutions.

Q. 20. Why does he make mention of the calling? Resp. 1. because among the spiritual benefits which God has conferred upon the faithful in time, it is the first of all. 2. because in it the gratuitous grace of God shines forth most especially, in that He has called us into His glory, neither seeking it, nor thinking about it. 3. because the same confirms us concerning preservation in faith unto eternal life. Phil. 1. v. 6. He who began a good work in you, will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ. 4. Just as Peter at the beginning of this Epistle had celebrated the benefit of the gratuitous calling, and had commended it to the faithful to be worthily weighed: cap. 1. v. 15. so he returns to the celebration of the same toward the end of the Epistle, so that, worthily esteeming this fountain of the remaining spiritual benefits, they may both give thanks to God, by whom they were called, and conduct themselves worthily of that calling.

Q. 21. Of what calling does the Apostle speak? They distinguish between internal and external calling, efficacious and inefficacious. They call that external which occurs through the external Ministry of the word, and is common to all constituted in the external society of the Church, whether they obey that calling or deny assent. They call that internal which occurs through the internal illumination of the Holy Spirit, and is proper to the faithful alone, those true and living members of the Church, inasmuch as they provide assent to that calling and obey the same. But this distinction must be rightly explained, lest the internal efficacy of the Holy Spirit be separated from the external Ministry of the word, nor should the interior assent be attributed to the natural powers of free will, or even the cause of denied assent be attributed to some absolute decree of reprobation. Some distinguish thus. Calling is considered either by reason of the term from which, i. e. of God calling through the word, or by reason of the term to which, i. e. of man providing assent to the calling. It is manifest that the Apostle speaks of a calling not only exterior, but also interior and efficacious, since he addresses those who truly believe, to whom he also promises preservation in the faith against all the insults of Satan and the world.

Q. 22. What is that eternal glory of God, to which the faithful are called? The name of glory could be expounded actively with respect to the called, in this sense. God out of grace has called you, that you may eternally glorify Him, because the ultimate end not only of calling, but also of all other spiritual benefits, and thus even of glorification itself or introduction into the possession of eternal life, is the glory of God to be celebrated by Angels and elect men for all eternity, in which sense the Apostle says Ephes. 1. v. 6. that God has predestined us unto the adoption of children by Christ Jesus to the praise of the glory of his grace, i. e. of his glorious grace, or even of his glory, glorious or to be conferred freely through a Hebraism. For when two nouns are joined in the state of regimen among the Hebrews, sometimes the former, sometimes the latter serves in the place of an adjective. Because however it follows, ἐν ἧ ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς, therefore the former, namely the little word δόξης is more correctly expounded by an adjective. Thus Paul says, that God makes known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he has prepared unto glory, i. e. that it may be celebrated by the elect for all eternity. Rom. 9. v. 23. But the name of glory in this place is more correctly expounded passively, in this sense. God out of grace in Christ has called you, that he may make you partakers of his eternal glory in the heavenly kingdom. For the Apostle expounds the beginning of that glorification, which is gratuitous calling; the means, which is preservation and confirmation in sufferings; and the end, which is the collation of heavenly and eternal glory; and he teaches that all these benefits happen to us in CHRIST, and on account of CHRIST. Therefore, parallel to this place of ours is the Pauline passage Rom. 8. v. 28. We know that to those who love God, all things (and consequently even the very sufferings of this time vers. 18.) work together for good, to those who are called according to his purpose. vers. 29. For whom he foreknew ( προγνώσει of faith) he also predestined to be made conformable to the image His own Son (first indeed in this life through the cross and ignominy, then in the future through light and glory) that he might be the firstborn among many brethren (that he might have many brothers as partners of his heavenly inheritance and glory, among whom, however, he himself as firstborn and head might hold the primacy) v. 30. And whom he predestinated (from eternity in Christ) these also (in time) he called (where is understood the calling with the term to which, namely joined with acceptance on the part of those called.) Whom he called, these also he justified (through faith in Christ.) Whom he justified, these also he glorified (by the progress of virtues and eternal beatitude, as Anselm explains in this place.) This is the golden chain of salvation extending from eternity into eternity, the beginning of which is our election, the middle, calling, justification, preservation in the cross etc., the end our glorification. August. soliloq. cap. 28. Whom God predestinated before the world, he called from the world, justified in the world, him he will certainly magnify after the world. serm. 16. de verb. Apost. he predestinated us, before we were; he called, when we were turned away; he justified, when we were sinners; he glorified, when we were mortal. Bernh. de verbis Sap. 5. The kingdom of God is granted, promised, shown, and received. It is granted in predestination, promised in calling, shown in justification, received in glorification.

Q. 23. Why does the Apostle add this προσδιορισμὸν in Christ Jesus? Resp. 1. because the calling was made in Christ Jesus, or on account of Christ. 2. to the merit of Christ not only the grace of calling, but also every subsequent grace, and thus also preservation and confirmation in the cross, is uniquely to be ascribed. 3. Christ is the foundation of that eternal glory, because it is acquired by his merit, and is given to us through him.

Q. 24. In what sense is glory attributed to God in δοξολογία ? Resp. The glory of God is taken in two ways 1. οὐσιωδῶς, as it denotes the essential properties of God. 2. σχετικῶς, as it denotes the acknowledgment and celebration of that majesty, which is subjectively in rational creatures acknowledging and proclaiming God. In the former signification God is called the God of glory, i. e. glorious, great, most high Act. 7. v. 2. In the latter signification we are commanded to give glory to God, to extol the glory of God, to magnify God etc. Both significations have a place here. The former is favored by the fact that with glory here is joined κράτος; the latter, that the Apostle in this δοξολογία glorifies God, and intimates by his own example that He is to be glorified by all. To glorify God is nothing other than to acknowledge and proclaim the majesty, power, and sublimity of God, and thus the former meaning is the foundation of the latter.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Be all subject one to anotherv. 5.But younger ones be subject to the elders same verse. If passive subjection belongs to the elders i. e. that others ought to subject themselves to them, how will active subjection belong to them themselves i. e. that they themselves ought to subject themselves to others? Add that the distinction of states is divinely ordained, so that the people or citizens may be subject to the Magistrate, who for that reason are also called subjects; so that hearers may be subject to Teachers, children to parents, servants to masters, wives to husbands. 1 Pet. 2 v. 13. & 18.ch. 3 v. 1. &c. Resp. 1. Some expound this Apostolic precept distributively, in that sense in which ch. 4 v. 9. all are commanded to exercise hospitality one to another, i. e. that some toward others, the rich toward the poor, those having their own homes toward exiles, should exercise hospitality. Thus, therefore, the sense would be, that not all ought to be subject to all, but some to others, inferiors to superiors, wives to husbands, children to parents, servants to Masters. But by this reasoning that precept would clearly agree with the preceding one, for the Apostle had already said before that the younger ought to be subject to the elders. 2. Because, therefore, the Apostle adds this to the preceding one as if by a certain correction, it is more rightly expounded generally, that all without exception ought to be subject one to another, in that sense in which Paul commands the same thing in places parallel to this one of ours. Rom. 12 v. 10.In honor preventing one another.Eph. 5 v. 21.Being subject one to another in the fear of ChristPhil. 2 v. 3. through humility, or in humility esteeming others better than themselves. 3. From which last passage it shines forth that the precept of humility is given to all in this place, for this virtue ought to be common to all; nay, rather, those whom God has raised to a high degree of honor and dignity in this world ought to pursue it most of all. Sir. 3 v. 20.The greater you are, the more humble yourself.Luke 14 v. 8.do not sit down in the first place &c. Through this virtue it happens that no one, however much he may shine with sublimity, despises another, but that he cherishes him as a partner of the same humanity, nay, of brotherhood and inheritance, prevents the other with honor, treats him humanely, lives with him in a friendly and concordant manner, and acknowledges his own infirmity and the gifts of God in others.

4. After, therefore, the Apostle had said, that the younger ought to be subject to the elder, he admonishes all in general, and consequently the elders themselves also, that through humility they should be subject to one another; he requires, therefore, that the elders should not despise the gifts of the younger, who are endowed with piety, doctrine, and judgment, but should even reverently acknowledge them. 1. Tim. 4. v. 12. They should listen to those who advise them rightly, and in general all others should submit themselves to one another out of true humility. 5. Through this correction, the Apostle wishes to bring everyone to equality and concord. For neither, when the younger are commanded to be subject to the elders, is power αὐτοκρατορικὴ, or license to do whatever they please given to the elders by that very fact, but they themselves also are brought into order by the precept of humility, so that there may be mutual subjection, mutual honor, mutual reverence, etc. Gregory, lib. 34. moral. cap. 16. (al. 17.), citing the Apostolic passage Phil. 2. v. 3. Esteem all others superior to yourselves, adds: Lest while one humbles himself to another, the humiliation should turn into pride for the other, he well admonished both parties, that in the thoughts of the heart I should prefer him to myself, and in turn he should prefer me to himself, so that when the heart is pressed lower on both sides, no one may be lifted up by the honor bestowed. Bede in h. l. Lest the Prelates, hearing these things, should think that the rights of humility are to be observed only by their subjects and not also by themselves, he immediately adds by admonishing generally, but all of you insinuate humility to one another. For he says all, both elders and adolescents, who are commanded to insinuate the virtue of humility, and these, namely, by ruling, and those by obeying humbly.

2. God resists the proud, namely as a just judge depressing and confounding them v. 5. But sometimes He wholesomely depresses certain ones, so that He may exalt them by His goodness. Resp. Pride is innate to all men after the fall, because that serpentine , You shall be as Gods, was once implanted in the hearts of all through corrupt Nature. Therefore, God depresses all through the preaching of the law, through the sending of the cross, and by other means. As many as are depressed by God and humble themselves before Him, by acknowledging their own unworthiness and infirmity, and by imploring the grace of God, to them this depression is wholesome, and leads to exaltation: but as many as continue to struggle against God through impenitence and pride, He so depresses them that He confounds them, destroys them, and casts them into the dust, nay, into hell.

3. God gives grace to the humblev. 5.But the humble are already before God in grace. Resp. James chapter 4. v. 6. shows the manner of reconciliation, for he gives greater grace. For those who humble themselves before God and, emptied of all confidence in their own virtue, wisdom, justice, etc., seek whatever is good, and thus their justice, life, and salvation in God alone, in them he increases the grace previously given, and subsequently adds greater gifts of grace to the former. Namely, God gives one grace after another; after the grace of conversion he gives the grace of justification; after the grace of justification, he gives the grace of sanctification; after the grace of sanctification, he gives the grace of glorification.

4. Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in time.v. 6.But we ought not to do good works with a view to a reward, but to offer filial obedience to God. Resp. 1. The little word ἵνα is not placed as τελικῶς, but as ἐκβατικῶς, so that the sense may be, it will come to pass that God will exalt you at the just time. 2. The promises concerning the rewards of good works ought to excite in us a zeal for doing good, therefore we ought to shake off the torpor of the flesh clinging to us Matt. 26. v. 41.Gal. 5. v. 17. by the consideration of rewards and punishments, of which the former are proposed for good works, the latter indeed for evil works. Thus when the flesh solicits us to pride, we ought to think that God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, and exalts them. Lorinus acknowledges this at this Apostolic passage, noting thus: We ought not in humility to propose to ourselves exaltation as the primary end. Yet since this has a connection with that, one can be excited by the hope of reward by first proposing to himself God alone as the end.

5. Cast all your anxiety upon him.vers. 7. But Rom. 12. v. 9.he who rules, let him rule in anxiety, i.e.v. 11.not slothful in anxiety.Eph. 4. v. 3.anxious to keep the unity of the Spirit. Resp. 1. Because in this place is held the little word μεριμνᾶς, Rom. 12. v. 8. & 11.Ephes. 4. v. 3. the little word σπουδῆς, thence Jerome in chapter 6 of Matthew seems to distinguish between σπουδῆν & μεριμνὰν, the former being commanded, the latter indeed being prohibited saying. Care, he says, for that which Nature bestows upon all, and is common to beasts and cattle and men, we are not entirely freed from (which is accustomed to be called σπουδὴ i.e. honest zeal) but it is commanded to us, that we be not anxious about what we may eat, (this is μέριμνα ) because in the sweat of your face you shall prepare let us seek bread for ourselves. Labor must be exercised, anxiety must be removed. 2. In the same place he distinguishes between anxiety about bodily food and clothing, and anxiety about spiritual food and clothing, saying that the former is prohibited, but the latter is commanded. This, he says, which is said: Do not be anxious for your soul, what you may eat, nor for your body, what you may put on, let us take as concerning carnal food and clothing. But concerning spiritual foods and garments we ought always to be anxious. 3. But not only the little word σπουδή & σπουδάζειν, but also μέριμνα & μεριμνᾶν is sometimes taken in a good sense, and is used for a care that is not only lawful, but also commanded. 1. Cor. 7. vers. 34. ἡ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾶ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου cap. 12. v. 25. ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων μεριμνῶσι τά μέλη 2. Cor. 11. v. 28. ᾑ ἐπισύστασίς μου ἡ καθ᾿ ἡμέραν ἡ μέριμνα πασῶν τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν Phil. 2. v. 20. οὐδένα ἔσχω ἰσόψυχων, ὃστις γνησίως τά περὶ ύμῶν μεριμνήσει. So also the LXX Interpreters Ps. 37. v. 19. μεριμνήσω ὑπὲρ τῆς ἁμαρτίας μου. Prov. 17. v. 12. ἐμπεσεῖται μέριμνα ἄνδρινοήμονι. Sap. 12. v. 22. ἳνα σου τὴν ἀγαθόπητα μεριμνῶμεν. 4. Even moderate care for bodily sustenance and clothing is not simply prohibited, and conversely, there can be such a solicitude about spiritual food and clothing that is inordinate and reprehensible. 5. More rightly, therefore, a distinction is made between the solicitude of duty, which is ordered; and inordinate solicitude joined with doubt and diffidence. The Apostle himself had commanded the solicitude of duty a little before, when he ordered the Presbyters to feed the flock committed to them ἐπισκοποῦντες vers. 2. but in this place, from the mouth of the Master, he prohibits solicitude joined with diffidence Matth. 6. v. 25. and following, an anxious care about the outcome of our affairs, such as was Martha's, of whom it is said Luc. 10. v. 40. περιεσπᾶτο περὶ πολλὴν διακονίαν v. 41. Μάρθα μεριμνᾶς καὶ τυρβάζῃ περὶ πολλὰ, 6. Therefore the Apostle commends God's providence and fatherly care for us, he does not remove holy solicitude, whether of duty or of salvation. He does not persuade to ignorant idleness Eph. 4. v. 28. nor does he prohibit the care of one's vocation, diligence, and prudence in the administration of a duty entrusted, but he warns that we should not wear ourselves out with anxious and unnecessary solicitude. Philip. 4. vers. 5. The Lord is near vers. 6. μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε. Lyranus in h. l. Not that they should omit doing what is in them, for this would be to tempt God, but that they themselves should believe they will attain every good through the power of God. 7. He requires that in all our care about necessary things from fatherly Let us depend entirely upon the care and providence of God, and let us humbly expect from Him, as from a most kind father, all our things of which we are in need. Matth. 6. v. 32. Your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things; whence Peter immediately adds, for He has care of you. However, it is agreed that among those means through which God has determined to supply necessary things to us, there is also our labor, our prayers, and indeed even our care; therefore, Peter does not simply exclude it, but only that solicitude which is inordinate, anxious, and joined with diffidence.

6. Your adversary the Devil goes about like a roaring lion v. 8. But Apoc. 20. v. 1. He saw an Angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss, and a great chain in his hand. v. 2. And he apprehended the Dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years. v. 3. And he cast him into the abyss, and closed and sealed over him, etc. Response: This binding of Satan is not to be taken absolutely, as if Satan, in those thousand years in which he is bound, could no longer seduce anyone and draw them into his nets, but comparatively, that in those thousand years with respect to the nations, Satan was then in a certain way bound, so that he could not further propagate gentile idolatry by his persecutions. Compare disp. 3. de nov. fanat. th. 15. & seqq.

7. The Devil goes about seeking whom he may devour v. 8. But Ioh. 12. v. 31. Now is the judgment of the world, now the prince of this world shall be cast out. cap. 16. vers. 11. The prince of this world has been judged. Roman. 16. vers. 20. The GOD of peace will crush Satan under your feet speedily. Response: Although CHRIST by His passion, death, resurrection, and ascension has conquered and captivated the Devil, and although He also takes care that this victory of His be offered to all through the preaching of the Gospel, and grants the same to believers, nevertheless a full and perfect victory over Satan will finally be obtained by believers on the day of judgment; in this life that enemy does not cease to tempt the pious. For since that impudent one dared to attack the head of the pious, Christ, with his temptations, it is easily gathered that he will much less abstain from the pious, as being members of CHRIST. Meanwhile, his power is subject to the power of CHRIST, so that he cannot either tempt or harm when he wishes and as much as he wishes, but only insofar as this is permitted to him for us, now to be humbled, now to be tested. Bede on chapter 12 of John, upon the words: Now the prince of this world shall be cast out. What then, someone might say, because the Devil is cast out from the hearts of believers, does he now tempt no one among the faithful? Indeed, he does not cease to tempt. But it is one thing to reign within, another to attack from without. It is one thing to wound, another to kill. But if he wounds, there is one present who heals, because just as it was said to those fighting: These things I write to you, that you may not sin: so let those who are wounded hear what follows. And if you have sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just. And he is the propitiation for our sins. For what were we, when we say: Forgive us our debts, unless that our wounds might be healed? And what else do we ask, when we say: And lead us not into temptation? unless that he, who lies in wait, may either certainly not break in from the outside, or deceive us by no fraud, or subvert us by no machines. When he does not hold the place of the heart, where faith dwells, he has been cast out. But unless the Lord shall have guarded the city, he who guards it watches in vain. Do not therefore presume about yourselves, if you do not wish to recall the Devil, who has been cast out, back inside.

8. Whom resist, strong in faith.v. 9. But it is not enough to resist the Devil, but it is necessary to fight against him, and to conquer him with spiritual weapons. Resp. He who resists the enemy also fights against the enemy; therefore τὸ ἀντιστῆναι also embraces the spiritual fight against Satan, as we have warned above. But Peter commands this in this place, just as Paul Ephes. 6. v. 13. and James cap. 4. v. 7. command to resist, because, when we resist the temptations of the Devil with the shield of faith held up, his fiery darts are extinguished Ephes. 6. v. 16. and he himself is rendered weak for tempting. Through resistance, therefore, we carry off the victory over Satan. For we cannot finish off this evil Spirit with bodily weapons, but it is sufficient if we repel him with his temptations, and refuse to give place to his inspirations in our heart. August. serm. 41. de verb. Domini. Christ could have made bread from stones, but he did not, so that he might despise the will of the tempter. For the tempter is not otherwise conquered, unless he is despised.

9. Whom resist, strong in faith.v. 9. But Matth. 5. v. 36. Do not resist τῷ πονηρῷ, i. e. the Devil, as some of the ancients explain. Resp. Indeed, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Euthymius in their commentary on that place understand the Devil through τὸν πονηρὸν because of the added article, who is called ὁ πονηρὸς Matth. 13. v. 19. & 38.Ephes. 6. v. 16.1. Ioh. 2. v. 13. & 14.cap. 3. v. 12.cap. 5. v. 18. according to their hypothesis it must be answered, that one must not resist the Devil, namely by his instruments inflicting injuries upon us, yet one must resist the Devil in his temptations which he strives not to seduce. But it is more correctly said, that by πονηρὸν is not understood the Devil, but evil, which the impious inflict upon us, which Christ teaches is not to be resisted, namely by private individuals, and out of a private desire for vengeance. Nor is it perpetual, that by πονηρὸν with the prepositive article the Devil is understood. Matth. 5. v. 37.cap. 6. v. 13.Luc. 11. v. 4.2. Thessal. 3. v. 3.1. Ioh. 5. v. 19.

10. The God of all grace, who has called you into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, he himself will perfect youv. 10.But experience testifies, not all, who have been called by God, are so perfected, strengthened, supported, founded by God, that they become partakers of eternal salvation. Resp. The Apostle understands τοὺς κλητοὺστκατὰ πρόθεσεν Rom. 8. vers. 28. whom he predestined, he justified, he glorified. v. 30. who by the power of God are guarded through faith unto salvation.1. Petr. 1. v. 5. Holy Scripture describes those in such a way, that the beginning ὑποστάσεως until the end they hold firmHebr. 3. v. 14. that they make their calling and election firm2. Petr. 1. v. 10. that laying aside every weight and τὴν εὐπερίστατον ἁμαρτίαν through patience they run the proposed to them ἀγῶνα. Hebr. 12. v. 1. that which cannot be said of all those called altogether.

11. You having suffered a little.v. 10.But experience testifies, that some are subject to the cross and afflictions through the whole course of life. Resp. Our passions are light and brief, if they are compared with the eternal glory, which will sometimes follow them. Rom. 8. v. 18.2. Cor. 4. v. 17. Aug. in Manuali cap. 15. O my soul, if it were necessary for us to endure torments daily, if to tolerate hell itself for a long time, so that we might be able to see CHRIST in glory, and be associated with his saints, would it not be worthy to suffer everything, which is sad, so that we might be held as partakers of so great a good, and so great a glory?

12. He himself has founded you v. 10. But Matth. 7. v. 24.Everyone, who hears these words of mine and does them, will be likened to a wise man, who built his house upon the rock.1. Thess. 5. v. 11. οἰκοδομεῖτε εἰς τὸν ἕνα. Resp. the reborn man builds himself and others not principally, but ministerially;

not by natural powers, but by new powers given by the Holy Spirit.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Be all subject one to another, be clothed with humility, says Peter verse 5. Therefore, the intolerable pride of the Roman Pontiff is to be condemned, who lies that he is the successor of Peter, by which he exalts himself not only above Emperors, Kings, and princes on earth, but even above the Angels, nay, God himself in heaven. Ceremon. lib. 3. sect. 1. The Pope does not show reverence to any man. Anton. Forent. in summ. The Pope is greater than an Angel. Clement VII in the Bull of the Jubilee commands the Angels to take the souls of those who die on the journey toward Rome from purgatory and introduce them into the absolute glory of Paradise. In the Lateran Council, Julius II allowed it to be acclaimed to him by the Fathers: You are all things, and above all things, all power is given to you in heaven and on earth. He says that he can make justice out of injustice. C. Quanto de translat. in Glossa; that he can dispense from law above law cProposuit de concess. Pretending It is disputed almost more busily concerning the power of the Roman Pontiff than concerning the power of God himself, while it is asked etc. whether he can abrogate what has been decreed by Apostolic writings, whether he can establish something that conflicts with Evangelical doctrine, whether he can establish a new article of faith etc. Erasmus in annot. ad 1. Tim. 1. p. 465.

2. Peter says to all: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Therefore, it cannot be proven what some dispute subtly, that what is said about Christ must be understood exclusively Phil. 2. verse 8. he humbled himself. Only, they say, Christ humbled himself, because no one could humble him, he had in himself no cause for humiliation, that is, no defect after such glory, and the fame of his doctrine and miracles, he suffered such things, which he foresaw and willed; and the greater the humiliation; the higher the state from which it came. Only Christ was humble of heart, that is, not by judgment, because he did not judge that necessary, or a cause in himself, as Lorinus writes ad v. 5 from Bernard serm. 42. in Cant. But the same Lorinus ad verse 6 more correctly annotates thus. Humble yourselves, namely, spontaneously, or humble yourselves, humble your souls. Which modes of speaking, since we read them used not rarely concerning others, I do not think force should be applied, when Paul asserts concerning Christ Phil. 2. verse 8. that he humbled himself, as if it could not befit others. Christ indeed is one, because as God he did not have one from whom he could be subjected and humbled, and for this reason he alone humbled himself; every pure creature, subjected to nothingness, from which God raised it up, is subjected to God, who could reduce it to nothingness. Man, moreover, because of sin, which is below nothingness, and on account of so many calamities to which he is subjected, has very many and most grave causes for humility.

3. Exaltation, both in this life and especially in the future life, which is promised to the pious who humble themselves before God out of faith, arises from grace; for the Apostle had premised v. praeced. God gives grace to the humble, and in this verse he adds: humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in time. Estius in his annotations to this place: He clearly signifies that that exaltation of the future age is included under the name of grace, of which he had spoken. He gives grace to the humble. It is false, therefore, that it is taught by the Papists that eternal life is given from merit, or on account of the merits of works.

4. He has care for you, says the Apostle v. 7. This must be opposed to those philosophers of whom Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho p. 168 thus discourses: Certain philosophers desire to persuade us that God indeed takes care of this universe and of the genera and species themselves, but not likewise of me and of you and of each one individually, otherwise, they say, we would not implore him with prayers all day and night. Clement of Alexandria, book 5 of the Stromata, p. 275, attributes to Aristotle that he restricted divine providence only to the celestial bodies, from which error, however, some attempt to free him.

5. Peter commands that one must be zealous for sobriety and be vigilant, so that we may be able to resist our adversary the Devil by faith. v. 8. It is therefore erroneous what is taught by the Calvinists, the architects of the absolute decree, that those who have been rejected by the absolute decree of reprobation either cannot struggle out of the snares of Satan, or must necessarily succumb to his temptations. Hence Faustus, book 1 on free will, chapter 10, in volume 4 of the Library of the Fathers, proves from this apostolic passage that no one is assigned to the Devil without regard to free evil works. For unless the reborn could freely resist or yield to the Devil and his temptations, they would be exhorted to resist in vain, and the Devil would also seek in vain those whom he might devour.

6. The Devil our adversary goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. v. 8. This must be opposed both to the Sadducees and the Libertines, who established that evil spirits are not truly ὑφιστάμενα, but evil affections and vicious thoughts of the flesh, by which we are solicited to sin: or even the just judgments of God, when on account of sins committed we are subjected to punishments according to our deserts, then to the Epicureans who utterly deny God and hell. Salmero Disp. 8. on this Epistle of Peter. There are those who think that there are no Devils, from whose snares they are therefore less on their guard, and they themselves, being most crafty, attempt to persuade this, so that they may be able to harm more, and they suggest Sophistical reasons, so that the simple and unwary may believe less. When they see those possessed, and perceive that certain admirable things are done by them, they attribute them to melancholy or to menstrual cycles, or to the influences of the stars, and thus they themselves are Devils to themselves, by whom they are deluded, although every sect professes that Demons are enemies of men. From which latter words it appears that Salmeron is disputing against certain Papists embracing the error of the Sadducees, just as Ambrosius Catharinus also disputes against them in his commentary on this place.

7. We can and ought to resist the Devil by faith v. 9. It is therefore erroneous what the Papists establish, that faith is merely Historical knowledge and assent, and not trust. That this argument may be more evident, it is to be noted by what reason one resists the Devil through faith. It is done 1. by seeking remedies against the temptations of Satan from the word of God. When the Devil attacked Christ with his temptations, Christ responded to each temptation from the word of God. The sayings of Scripture are those sharp stones, with which we can prostrate this infernal Goliath by the example of David. 2. by apprehending consolation from the Evangelical promise, that Christ by his passion, death, resurrection, etc., conquered Satan, and wishes to make us participants of his victory. If you have the word of God in your heart, says Luther on this place, and keep it by faith, the Devil cannot triumph over you, but is forced to yield. The word, therefore, is to be held with firm and strong faith. He was snatching the word from Eve, and was supplanting her with his temptations, namely because she was not firmly keeping it. 3. by observing the snares of Satan. Faith is the eye of the soul, by which we can see and beware of the snares of this our enemy, hence Cant. 1. v. 15. the eyes of the Bride are called spiritual eyes of doves, of which the pious ancients write thus. Origen. homil. 3. in Levit. They say that this kind of bird, when they have come to the waters, because they are accustomed to suffer the injuries of the hawk there, detect the enemy coming from above by the shadow of the flying one cast upon the waters and by the sharpness of their eyes and

to escape the fraud of imminent danger by the benefit of the waters. Gregory on chapter 5 of Canticles: The Scriptures are most full streams, near which the holy doves reside, where they both behold the flying proudly, and with head submerged elude the cunning of the pursuer. Bernard, sermon 55 on the manner of living well: Just as doves are accustomed to reside by the streams, so that they may see the shadow of flying birds in the water, upon which casting themselves they escape the rapacious claws. For holy men perceive the frauds of the Demon in Scripture, and from the description, as if from a shadow which they see, they recognize the enemy and escape his deception. 4. By uniting us with Christ. True faith embraces Christ with all his benefits, and unites us with Christ, that he may dwell in our hearts Eph. 3. v. 17. that he may remain in us and we in him John 15. v. 4. Therefore, just as faith possesses Christ the victor over Satan, so also it relies upon the power of the same in the battle against Satan. Faith looks upon and apprehends that lion of the tribe of Judah Rev. 5. v. 5 who conquered this infernal lion and makes believers participants of this victory of his. The victory of the Lord is the triumph of the servants, says Jerome on chapter 4 of Matthew. 5. By seeking help against Satan from God. True faith pours forth prayer, by which we implore and obtain defense against Satan from Christ our Leader. Our victory against Satan consists in prayers proceeding from faith and leaning upon the word of God. Prayer is the harp of David, which drives away this malignant Spirit 1 Sam. 16. verse 23. it is the jawbone of Samson, which prostrates this enemy Judg. 15. verse 15. Macarius, homily 43, page 475, ἐὰν ὦσιν οἱ δαίμονες ἰσχυροὶ ὡς ὂρη ἰσχυρὰ, ὑπὸ τῆς εὐχῆς καίονται, καθάπερ ὁ κηρὸς ὑπὸ πυρὸς, If the Demons are strong in power not unlike mountains, they will be burned up by prayer: just as wax by fire. All these things show that the faith by which we resist the Devil is not a bare knowledge and assent common even to hypocrites, but a fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ and the Evangelical promise. The Adversaries themselves are forced to acknowledge this, whose eyes the brightness of truth has struck, so that they might rise to our opinion in the commentary on this place. Salmero on this place writes thus on page 107: The Apostle wishes them to be strong in faith or trust of divine mercy, and which embraces Christ himself fighting for us and who says concerning the afflicted: I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him and glorify him. He also has with him the Holy Spirit, who is of Christ, who is creator and infinite of virtue against the wicked and powerless Spirit if it has not stood through us. Lorinus on v. 8. p. 575. We are commanded to resist the adversary the Devil in faith, which can denote either simple assent or confidence. The same on v. 9. To faith itself according to itself is deservedly attributed resistance just as the account of a shield, which we can call the shield of truth, by which those surrounded do not fear from the terror of the night, from the arrow flying in the day, from the business walking in darkness, from the assault and the noonday Devil. Psal. 91. v. 6. You would rightly call faith the right eye, because it sees natural and supernatural things, whereas reason as the left eye judges only of natural things etc. Estius on this place. Blessed Peter teaches that the temptations of the Devil, whether open or hidden, must be resisted by the firmness of faith, by which, namely, we not only believe the promises of God without doubt, but also excite in ourselves confidence of obtaining them, with the power and truth and mercy of God through Christ proposed before our eyes. For grace and truth came through Jesus Christ Ioh. 1. v. 17. and this is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith 1. Ioh. 5. v. 4. The world, therefore, and the Prince of the world Cornel. à Lapide on this place. Faith implores the help of God to fight bravely, whence through faith Christ dwells in our hearts Ephes. 3. v. 17.

8. By faith we resist the Devil. v. 9. Therefore true faith is not a dead thing separated from the remaining virtues and good works, as the Papists teach, but a living and efficacious thing through charity, humility, prayer, patience etc. Gal. 5. v. 6. Lorinus on this place. Faith strikes terror into the Demons, either by the humility and simplicity of assent, or by the detection of his frauds, or by the proposition of every kind of remedy against him, or, so to speak, by the fortification which is made by virtues or other gifts, by which faith takes root in us. These are in the intellect, the gifts of knowledge, understanding, wisdom; in the affection, charity, in which when we are rooted and founded, Christ dwells more firmly in our hearts through faith. Ephes. 3. v. 17. furthermore patience and long-suffering, which wonderfully strengthen. Coloss. 1. vers. 11. Estius on this place. This faith so far from excluding hope and charity, that it brings them with it. For faith is hoping, loving, invoking, obeying, justifying, working, and therefore living, not idle, not dead. Cornel. à Lapide on this place. Under faith as a root understand hope, prayer, charity. For faith strengthened by hope, armed by prayer, ignited by charity overcomes the Devil.

9. Lorinus on this v. 9. annotates thus It is worthy of note in this and that in the former verse and the one following, three precepts are contained, by which the sum of Evangelical perfection is comprised, namely abstinence from evil, which sobriety denotes; works of justice, which are signified through vigilance and resistance against the Devil; hope of eternal life, concerning which in the latter member of the present verse and the following verse. In the first chapter vers. 13. mention of these same three was made, when concerning loins girded and sobriety, when concerning children of obedience not conformed to the former ignorances, and that they should be holy in all conversation, and that we should hope perfectly in that grace which is offered in the revelation of Jesus Christ. Concerning these three Paul discoursed before Felix Actor. 24. vers. 25. that is, concerning justice and chastity and future judgment, as Augustine noted in sermon 39. on the words of the Lord. From these we conclude thus. Those to whom are proposed precepts, in which the sum of Evangelical perfection is comprised, they also live in that state in which they can aspire to Evangelical perfection. But not only to Monks or Clerics, but to all Christians entirely are proposed precepts, in which the sum of Evangelical perfection is comprised. Therefore not only Monks or Clerics, but all Christians entirely live in that state in which they can aspire to Evangelical perfection. This conclusion fights with the Papist hypothesis, that only Monks live in a state of perfection to be acquired, Clerics especially Bishops in a state of acquired perfection. It is, however, conformable to the Apostolic saying Coloss. 1. v. 28. We announce Christ, admonishing every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect, in Christ Jesus.

10. The God of all grace called us in CHRIST certainly out of grace. v. 10. for thus it is expounded Gal. 1. vers. 6. he called you ἐν χάριτι Χριστοῦ. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. God called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before secular times. Therefore calling is not made from the merits of works. This is to be opposed to the doctrine of the Papists concerning the merit of congruity, and dispositions toward justification.

11. The God of all grace called us in Christ Jesus to his eternal glory. vers. 10. Therefore eternal life does not befall us on account of the merits of our works, as the Papists teach, but is χάρισμα the gratuitous gift of God in Christ. As calling is gratuitous, so also predestination is gratuitous. As predestination is gratuitous, so also justification is gratuitous. As justification is gratuitous, so also glorification is gratuitous. Conversely, as calling was made in Christ, so also predestination was made in Christ. As predestination was made in Christ, so also justification was made in Christ.
