As justification was made in Christ, so also glorification is made in Christ, so that thus the beginning, middle, and end of our salvation may depend upon the sole grace of God exhibited to us in Christ Jesus. Eph. 1. vers. 4. & following. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9.

12. The God of all grace, who has called us to his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, he himself will perfect, confirm, strengthen, and establish us.vers. 10. Therefore we ought not to doubt concerning the salvation to which we have been called in Christ, but, relying on this promise, let us certainly conclude that he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion even unto the day of Jesus Christ. Philip. 1. vers. 6. If our calling is founded in CHRIST, and reaches even unto eternal glory, it will certainly not be empty and in vain. Roman. 11. vers. 29. ἀμεταλέλητα τὰ χαρίσματα, καὶ κλῆσις τοῦ θεοῦ. This is to be opposed to the Papists, the patrons of doubt.

13. It is God who perfects, stabilizes, corroborates, and establishes us. Therefore there are no powers in spiritual matters; from ourselves as from ourselves we cannot cooperate either in the first conversion, or in the preservation of faith, or in holy conduct, but whatever good we do, that whole and entire thing is from powers newly gifted by grace. 2. Cor. 3. v. 5. This is to be opposed to the Papists who defend free will in spiritual matters.

14. The God of all grace, who has called us to his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, he himself will perfect, stabilize, corroborate, and establish us, v. 10. certainly from the same grace from which he called us. Therefore perseverance is not a merit of our works, but a gratuitous gift of God. Prosper, book I, on the calling of the Gentiles, chapter 10: That to perfect and persevere in faith and in good works even unto the end is of divine gift and aid, the authority of the holy scriptures confirms. To prove that, he brings forward the sayings Phil. 1. v. 6.cap. 2. v. 13.1. Thess. 3. v. 13.1. Cor. 1. v. 4. & following Rom. 8. v. 35.1. Thessal. 5. v. 23.2. Thess. 2. v. 15. & finally he adds:

Let us also hear the Apostle Peter, from where he teaches the virtue of perseverance to be. But the God, he says, of all grace, who has called you into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will himself perfect, confirm, and strengthen you, etc. Bellarmine, book 5 on Justification, chapter 22, section 1. Concerning restoration after a fall, and perseverance until the end, the opinion of the Theologians is in agreement, that it does not fall under merit of condignity. Pererius, Disputation 26 on chapter 14 of John, page 401. A man cannot properly and worthily merit perseverance in good until the end, but just as the donation of first grace is gratuitous, and not on account of any merit of man properly so called, so also the preservation of that very grace until the end is a gift of God, in no way comparable to the merits of man. This must be opposed to the Pelagians, who assert that perseverance depends on one's own merits, from whom the Papists can with difficulty be torn away, who teach that good works truly merit the increase of grace, eternal life, and the attainment of eternal life itself, and even the increase of glory. Council of Trent, session 6, canon 32. Bellarmine, book 5 on Justification, 1. For if the gift of perseverance does not fall under merit, then certainly also the increase of grace and the attainment of eternal life do not fall under merit. The connection is proven, because without the gift of perseverance eternal life happens to no one, and the preservation and strengthening in good also pertains to the increase of grace.

15. Peter testifies that καταρτισμὸν, absolution, perfection, or consummation is necessary for the faithful, so that, namely, the knowledge of God and piety may be absolved and perfected in them. Therefore, the faithful in this life are not perfect, but it is required of them to make progress. This must be opposed to the Papists who champion the perfection of works and the perfect fulfillment of the law, as also to other Perfectionists.

Έκδίκησις. 1. Estius on James 4:6 annotates thus. This sentence confirms (God gives grace to the humble) the Catholic doctrine, which teaches that a justified man merits the increase of grace by good works, and especially by humility. God resists the proud, and humbles them, because their pride merits this; he gives grace to the humble, and exalts them, because their humility merits that. Response 1. We invert the argument. That which God gives to the humble is grace or a gratuitous gift. Therefore, it does not befall them on account of the merits of works. For grace is not grace in any way, if it is not gratuitous in every way Rom. 11:6 If by grace, then it is no longer of works; if of works, then it is no longer of grace.

2. Those are understood who, having been anticipated by the grace of God, as Estius concedes, and it is gathered from the fact that God is said to give greater grace in James. But as the first calling is gratuitous, so also is preservation in good gratuitous, since God gives grace for grace. John 1. verse 16. 3. Thence Estius on verse 5 of our chapter comments thus. To the humble, by this very fact that they are already humble, having been anticipated by the grace of God, He gives more ample grace, increasing what He gave and heaping up prior things with new gifts of His grace one after another, finally exalting them through glory in the future age, which is itself also grace, as Paul testifies. The grace of God is eternal life, which Peter also signifies in the following verse. Therefore all things which are given to the humble in place of a reward are gratuitous gifts. 4. The reason for the punishments which are inflicted upon the proud and the rewards which are given to the humble is therefore different. For evil works deserve punishments, but good works do not deserve rewards, since they are already owed beforehand, they are imperfect, they are contaminated by the stain of sin, etc. Romans 6. verse 23. The wages of sin is death, but eternal life is χάρισμα the gratuitous gift of GOD in CHRIST JESUS.

2. James of Vitry, sermon 2 on the 3rd Sunday after Pentecost, says hand in v. 6 is taken for the Son of God, whose affixed hands conquered the world, and invite us by such a great example to humility. I reply, certainly Christ is the power of God 1. Cor. 1. v. 24. but personal. Peter, however, speaks here of the essential power of God common to all three persons of the Godhead. For exaltation is a work ad extra, and therefore that which operates in it is the one Godhead common to the three, as Nazianzen speaks, oration 2 on Theology.

3. Estius on this verse annotates thus. The Apostle rightly assigns the exaltation to the final time of retribution, because the exaltation of the present time, besides the fact that it does not correspond to the proportion of merits, is fleeting and very small with respect to future glory. I reply 1. we showed above that by καιρὸν it is not determinately understood here as the day of judgment, but in general and indeterminately as an opportune time either in this or in the future age. Corn. à Lap. on this place. In the time of visitation, by which, namely, God will visit you, that He may reward your humility, and exalt you either in this life, or in the future. Τὸ of visitation is not in the Greek, but it is understood, for καιρὸς signifies an occasion, an opportunity, a convenient time, which is the time of visitation. Whence the Syrian translates, in a congruent time. Tigur. when it will be opportune, Pagn. in an opportune time 2. lest indeed we can merit the exaltation of the present time by our humility, when we cannot even merit a small crumb of bread, but are compelled by humble prayer to beg it daily from God. Matth. 6. v. 11.3. Estius confesses, that that exaltation is included under the preceding name of grace. How, therefore, will it correspond to the proportion of our merits?

4. Franciscus Turrianus, book 2 de dogm. charact., accepts that commandment of casting anxiety upon God concerning the Priests who are Ministers of the Eucharist, to whom it is commanded that not only anxiety simply, but all anxiety must be cast upon God, for the reason that they ought either to lack wives or not have the use of them. Resp. 1. The Davidic and Petrine commandment is general, pertaining not only to the Ministers of the Church, but to all Christians; nor does it pertain only to the celibate, but also to the married, as the circumstances of the text in both places evidently show. 2. The Apostle warns beforehand that those who live in marriage will have tribulation of the flesh 1. Cor. 7. v. 28. and asserts that the same are anxious about the things that are of the world v. 33. to provide necessary things for themselves, their family, and their wife, as Lyranus notes in the same place. Therefore, the commandment concerning casting all anxiety upon God pertains more to the married than to the celibate. Papal Bishops indeed lack wives, meanwhile they are immersed in the anxieties of this age on both ears, since they exercise political dominion. Therefore, lacking wives and casting all anxiety upon God are not necessarily and perpetually connected.

5. Lorinus on v. 7 notes thus: If any others, much more those who are addicted to another's care for God by the institution of their life (he understands Monks) ought to strip off, cast away, and throw off all anxiety, etc., also avoiding the care of a sick body and the procurement of medicines, since, says Ephrem serm. de fide tom. 1. he who cures the diseases of the soul is God, he will also cure those of the body. To which can be referred that of Bernard serm. 30. super Cant. col. 570. Hippocrates and his followers teach how to save souls in this world. He who loves his soul, says Christ, loses it. He who loses it, either by placing it as a Martyr, or by afflicting it, as a penitent, will save it. Likewise what is held in c. Contraria dist. 5. de conservatione. The precepts of medicine are contrary to the divine condition, which call one back from fasting, do not allow one to work by lamplight, and lead one away from every intention of meditation, thus he who has given himself to medicines, denies himself to himself. Resp. 1. all anxiety upon God is for that reason to be cast away, so that nevertheless we do not neglect the means of health either to be preserved or to be recovered, ordained by God. Sir. 38. v. 1. & following. 2. The Apostle disapproves of hypocritical τοῦ σώματος ἀφειδίαν Col. 2. v. 23. but on the contrary commands τιμὴν to be shown to it & grants πρόνοιαν σαρκὸς ποιεὶσθαι, provided it is not done εἰς ἐπιθυμίας. Rom. 13. v. 14. 3. God is the author of medicine and medicaments, therefore he who despises them, despises God himself, their author; he who rashly rejects them when they are at hand, tempts God. The health not only of the soul, but also of the body is a gift of God, therefore neither is to be neglected, or the care of it entirely cast away. 4. The precepts of medicine are not contrary to the divine condition or the word of God, for the canons of physicians recommend moderate fasts, nor do they lead away entirely from the intention of meditation, but they inculcate that Hippocratic πᾶν τὸ πολὺ πολέμιον τῇ φύσει μετρὸν δ᾿ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστον.

6. Franciscus Turianus in book 2 of de dogm. charact., and following him Gregorius de Valentia in volume 4, Disp. 9, point 5, §. 1, restrict the precept of sobriety and vigilance to Bishops alone, and infer the celibacy of the Clergy from it. But Lorinus refutes them in his annotations to this place. We must be vigilant, he says, (all of us) lest we be intercepted by the snares of Satan, who sagaciously seeks all ways of harming and gapes most greedily for our prey. Wherefore this passage does not pertain here to Bishops alone and Priests who are ministers of the Eucharist, although Valentia also thinks so with Turrianus. Nor does it matter that Peter now demands sobriety absolutely; in the preceding chapter v. 7. for prayers, as if continence ought always to be observed by some, and by others for a time and for the sake of prayer, for the speech is equally general here and there. He says this most correctly. And all the circumstances of the text and the comparison of parallel places of Scripture show that this precept of sobriety and vigilance is general, which is confirmed most of all by the reason added to this precept.

7. But the same Lorinus annotates thus on this verse 8. Temperance must be studied, the first wound of which was inflicted upon the human race by the most crafty serpent Gen. 3. v. 1. & following. The tempter also solicited Christ concerning gluttony Matth. 4. v. 3. Resp. 1. The Devil first of all solicited Eve to doubt, diffidence, and incredulity, because he attempted to snatch the word from her heart. Why has God said etc. Only afterwards does it follow. The woman saw that the tree was good for food. 2. The first temptation also, by which the Devil attacked Christ, was likewise a temptation of diffidence. Mr. Chemnitius, chapter 19, Harm. Evang., p. 41. The Devil seizes and in all these temptations agitates the paternal voice. You are my son, and that for these reasons especially. 1. Because he feared for his head, which he knew was to be crushed by the Messiah, the Son of God: therefore by tempting he wished to explore whether that Jesus, declared by the voice of the Father at the Jordan, was the true Messiah, the Son of God, so that he might beware of him. 2. Since, however, he did not see in Christ, even after he had been announced by the voice of the Father, such external magnificence as would seem either to befit the Son of God or to correspond to the oracles of the Prophets, he began to mock him by the agitation of the paternal voice. 3. So that, just as he had done Genes. 3. vers. 4. he might argue that that voice of God was either of falsehood or of vanity. 4. So that he might snatch from Christ the faith in the paternal voice and the confidence conceived from it. 5. So that on that occasion he might induce Christ into the sin of diffidence, or presumption, or ostentation, or defection.

8. The same Lorinus on this verse, p. 580, writes thus. The tyranny of the Devil has been repressed, which Christ hints at through the casting out of the Prince of this world outside, and through the stronger one who conquered the strong armed man, so that he does not hold captives to his own will, does not so work his works in men, does not sift like wheat, does not so easily sow tares over, but his thoughts and snares are better known and conquered; God does not so much admit accusations against us, he does not dare to come so freely among the sons of God, inasmuch as he is trodden and crushed by the feet of the faithful; and in exorcisms he is more frequently blown away. Resp. 1. That peculiar power of casting out demons with authority was proper to the primitive Church near the times of the Apostles. Marc. 16. v. 15. Justin in Dial. with Trypho, Tertullian de coron. milit. and in Apolog. c. 32, Cyprian to Demetrianus, Lactantius lib. 2. Instit. c. 16, etc. Therefore, the Papist Exorcists, boasting that they can expel the Devil with conceived words and certain ceremonies, rashly arrogate this to themselves; today we can fight against them only with the word and prayers. Origen, in chapter 17 of Matthew, If at any time it behooves us to help the obsessed, let us not speak with the Spirit either by adjuring or by commanding, as if he hears us, but let us persevere by applying ourselves only to prayers and fastings. 2. But if by exsufflation Lorinus understands the exorcism which is applied in Baptism, we say that that exorcism, with the cessation of this gift of casting out demons, belongs to the ceremonies Celestine, in chapter or distinction 4 of the consecration, decrees that the translation of Baptism (since through Baptism we are liberated from the kingdom and power of Satan and received into the kingdom of Christ) is a σημαντικὸν signifying the power of original sin and the liberation from it through Christ, that all are to be kept from Baptism, from whom the Devil has not been expelled through adjurations and exsufflations. The gloss adds there, This is not to be understood simply, because the Demon is cast out before Baptism, since until the dipping we are of the Devil's household and his members. He therefore establishes that the Devil is not cast out by exorcism, but that his being cast out is signified.

9. Corn. à Lap. on this passage: The Church begins the Compline from these words of the Holy Father (Be sober and watch) and by them warns the faithful that they should be sober and watchful for praying and resisting the Devil, and therefore, about to go to bed, they should seriously commend themselves to the guardian Angel and the tutelary Saints. Resp. 1. If it is said that they should commend themselves to the guardian Angel in the sense that it is the same as commending themselves to God through pious prayers to be guarded by the Angel, we acknowledge that this rule is conformable to the divine word. But if it is said in the sense that it is the same as invoking the guardian Angel and commending oneself to him through prayers, then we deny that this is conformable to the word of God. Apoc. 19. v. 10.c. 22. v. 9. 2. There is deep silence in the Scriptures concerning tutelary saints. The Gentiles had their tutelary Gods, but Christians flee uniquely to the protection of God in all adversities.

10. The same author on these words annotates thus: The Devil is antonomastically called Lucifer, the Prince of Demons Matth. 4. v. 1. Lucifer therefore goes about not so much by himself (for he is bound in hell Apoc. 20. v. 2.) as through his henchmen, for each of these is called and is a Devil. Resp. 1. We have explained above how that binding of Satan is to be accepted ἐναντιοφ. 6. 2. If the Devil could not go about and harm by himself, he could not go about and harm even through his henchmen. 3. Just as no one of the good Angels is not prepared for the guardianship of man: so no one of the evil Angels is not desirous and prompt to inflict harm upon man.

11. Estius on verse 9 annotates thus: Therefore the victory by which we overcome the Devil and all his temptations is ascribed to faith, because faith shows the goods to be hoped for and excites us to seize them, and animates us, and teaches from where the aids are to be sought by which we may resist the adversary. Resp. These things are indeed said truly, but imperfectly. For faith not only teaches from where the aids are to be sought by which we may resist the adversary, nor only it shows the goods to be hoped for and excites us to lay hold of them, but it also apprehends the Evangelical promise, and in it Christ the victor over Satan, in whom we are strong to resist all the insults of Satan; it also takes refuge through prayers to God, and obtains from Him the strength and vigor for fighting, and the grace for overcoming. Compare the things said above ἐλέγχῳ in the seventh.

12. Lorinus comments on this verse thus. Who is ignorant of the regions which the pestilence of heresy has pervaded, or where, in a more languid faith, the corruption of morals, and how much Magical superstition has prevailed? Resp. 1. If judgment is to be made concerning the pestilence of heresy from Magical superstition, the Papacy will be the sink of heresies, because nowhere does superstition and Magic reign more, as manifest experience testifies. 2. In the time of the dominant Papacy, the apparitions and illusions of specters were frequent, but those have disappeared at the light of the Gospel.

13. The same Lorinus writes thus on verse 10. In a similar form, by which God is called the God of all grace, and the father of mercies by the Church, Mary is called the mother of mercy and grace, either because she bore Christ the author of these, or because she obtains them for us: or because she is the special mother of those who have obtained grace and mercy, or because by a Hebrew phrase it means the same to be Queen or mother of grace and mercy, as to be gracious, or grateful and merciful. For almost the same reason we read that certain men were called men of mercy, Sir. 44. v. 10. but also the bowels of the mercy of our God are spoken of, because they are mercy. Luc. 1. v. 78. Resp. 1. Scripture asserts that God is the God of all grace, and the father of mercies 2. Cor. 1. v. 3. and in this place. But it nowhere asserts that Mary is to be invoked as the mother of grace and mercy. 2. The first reason, that the Mother is called the mother of grace because she bore Christ the author of grace, is foreign. For by this reasoning Mary could be said to have created heaven and earth, because she gave birth to Him who created heaven and earth, to have performed the work of redemption, and to have satisfied for the sins of the whole world, because she gave birth to Him who performed the work of redemption, and satisfied for the sins of the whole world. By this reasoning it could also be said of the mother of Lorinus that she wrote commentaries on the Epistle of St. Peter, because she gave birth to him who wrote those commentaries. 2. The other reason, that Mary is called the mother of grace because she obtains it for us, indeed agrees with the intention of those who [use] that hymn Salve Regina, and likewise composed prayers, 'Mary, Mother of Grace,' etc. it also agrees with that which Bernhardus de Busta writes in his Mariale, dedicated to the Roman Pontiff Alexander VI, book 1, chapter 2. Often those whom the justice of the Son condemns, the mercy of the Mother frees; hence one must appeal from the court of the justice of God to the court of the mercy of the Mother. In the Legend of the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin, example 42, it is read thus: A certain nobleman, Theophilus, had abjured God, the Baptist, Christ, and Mary. When he repented of the deed, he could obtain no pardon from Christ, which, however, he easily obtained from Mary. Vincentius Bunus, Jesuit, in Meditations on the Principal Mysteries of the Life and Passion of Christ, part 1, meditation 1, page 13: If Mary is full of grace, and is the inventress of grace before God, let us all, as many as are needy and desirous of grace, approach her. For God, in order to honor his Mother, poured into her the fullness of grace, so that we might understand that if there is any hope, if there is any good, if there is any salvation in us, it all redounds from Mary as Mediatrix. But this reasoning does not at all agree with the Holy Scriptures, since they propose only Christ to us as the author of grace and our Mediator with God, but nowhere assign to Mary that she either obtained grace for us by her own merits, or that she was religiously invoked so that she might obtain grace for us from God. 4. The third reason, that she is the special mother of those who have obtained grace and mercy, is understood by Lorinus in this sense, that she hears their prayers, grants them forgiveness of sins, defends them in dangers, and receives them at the hour of death, for the Roman Church asks for all these things from Mary in its hymns and public prayers. But taken in that sense, this reason is likewise ἄτερ γραφῆς. 5. The fourth reason is indeed conformable to Scripture, because Mary is gracious and pleasing to God, in that she found grace before God Luke 1, v. 31, nor did heavenly glory extinguish in her the affection of mercy, since charity is more perfect in eternal life than in this life, but the same is not conformable to the intention of those who, in the hymns and prayers accustomed to be sung in the Roman Church, call her the Mother of Grace.

14. The same Lorinus annotates on the same verse thus: To say that you could now be called God by the name of John, which signifies the grace of God or the God of grace. Resp. 1. One must speak chastely and cautiously about God and divine things; that God is called John will not be found in Scripture nor in the Fathers. 2. The name John is derived from חנן which signifies he has had mercy, he has been gracious, he has followed with grace, he receives into grace, he has given out of grace.

The prefix Iod is a formative of a proper noun, but John is not derived from the noun יה which is contracted from the proper name of God, Jehovah. 3. But even if it were formed from חנן & יה, it would still not signify God giving out of grace, but a man enjoying the grace of God, and receiving good things from God out of grace, as is evident from the names Azariah, Zechariah, Hezekiah, etc.

15. Salmero on the same verse comments thus: He himself will perfect by charity, rendering all things perfect; he will confirm by living hope; he will solidify by strong and efficacious faith. I respond: indeed, faith, hope, and charity pertain to this καταρτισμὸν, στήριξιν, σθένωσιν καὶ θεμελίωσιν; meanwhile, our perfection, strength, and hope before God do not consist in our charity, which is imperfect and languid in this life, but solely in Christ apprehended through true faith, and dwelling in our hearts through faith. Eph. 3. v. 17. For by faith we apprehend the benefits of Christ, among which is the victory over Satan; by faith we obtain from God through prayers the strength of the soul and the powers to fight against Satan; by faith we are guarded by the power of God unto salvation, says our Apostle cap. 1. v. 5. More correctly, therefore, Lorinus writes thus on this passage, p. 587: It is probable, as Gagneius hints, that the same thing is exaggerated with many words signifying almost the same thing, namely, how great is the power of faith and of patience or perseverance against the Devil, etc. The Syrian Interpreter seems to have intended this also in the present place. So that when we have endured these slight oppressions, we may be strengthened, and confirmed, and persist in him (Christ Jesus) forever. Nevertheless, the Greek words have great force besides the word καταρτίσαι, (which signifies to restore, to compose, to fit, to complete, to instruct, to perfect) namely στηρίξαι to establish firmly and to prop up, and by translation to confirm, which is doubtful, σθενῶσαι ἀσθένος to strengthen, θεμελιῶσαι from θεμέλιον to found, all of which aptly agree with faith, which is first in the eternal spiritual foundation and ὑπόστασις Hebr. 1. v. 11. and therefore to it Christ said, brothers, στηρίζειν for whose faith he had prayed, that it might not fail, Luc. 22. v. 32. and upon whom he had founded his Church. Matth. 16. v. 18.

Διδασκαλίαι. 1. The precept of humility is common to all, not only to the younger, but also to the Elders; not only to inferiors, but also to superiors. Rom. 12. v. 10. outdoing one another in honor.

v. 16.Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate.Eph. 5. v. 21.Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.Phil. 2. v. 3.In lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.v. 5. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ v. 8.he humbled himself. Bernh. serm. 4. super Missus est. It is no great thing to be humble in abjection, it is a truly great and rare virtue to be humble when honored.

2. Humility, as it is commanded to all, so also is it most necessary for all, and to be strictly guarded by all. The Apostle commands that humility be bound and knotted with the tightest knots, lest it slip away. For humility is indeed necessary, yet so difficult, that unless it be retained with great care and vigilance, and as it were bound, it might very easily slip away upon any occasion arising. August. Epist. 56. Unless humility shall have preceded, accompanied, followed, and been set before all things whatsoever we do well; and been placed before us, that we may look upon it; and been placed beside us, that we may cling to it; and been placed upon us, that we may be restrained by it; pride snatches away from our hand everything while we are already rejoicing over some good deed.

3. Humility is not only a virtue, but also the foundation of the remaining virtues. You think to build a great structure of virtues, think first of the foundation of humility. It is not only a virtue, but also the ornament and treasure of the remaining virtues. Basilius serm. de abdic. rerum. Humility is the dragnet which embraces all virtues. Cassianus collat. 15. cap. 7. Humility is the mistress of all virtues, it is the most firm foundation of the heavenly building. Ioh. Huss. in 1. Petr. 3.He who gathers other virtues without humility, carries dust into the wind.

4. Humility is the most beautiful garment of the pious, with which they cover their virtues; lest on account of them they exalt themselves before God or men, with which also they cover the infirmities of their neighbor, lest on account of them they despise their neighbor with a high eyebrow. Just as in a pleated garment the exterior fold, or the one standing out, accommodates and insinuates itself to the interior or more depressed fold, and vice versa the interior to the exterior: so through humility the superior accommodates himself to the inferior, and in turn the inferior to the superior, so that one garment of concord and peace may be fashioned from humility. Coloss. 3. v. 12. ἐνδύσασθε τὴν ταπεινοφροσύνην.

5. Moreover, humility is such a virtue, by which one in the true fear of God acknowledges his own infirmity and unworthiness, keeps himself within the bounds of his calling, nor does he desire things greater than his strength, thinks modestly of himself and his gifts, conducts himself moderately in speech and gesture, but in his neighbor he reverently acknowledges the gifts of God, esteeming him as superior and promptly serving him with every kind of duty. Nazianzen, oration 13. Humility is situated not in clothing or the bowing of the neck or the submission of the voice, but in the constancy of the mind. Bernard on the degrees of humility. Humility is a virtue by which one becomes vile to himself from the truest knowledge of himself.

6. The proud oppose themselves to God, and as it were declare war upon Him, therefore God resists them, blocking for them the way of escaping, hindering their attempts and disturbing their counsels. Chrysostom, homily 3 on the words of Isaiah. The Apostle did not simply say: God dismisses the proud and abandons them in their sins, and strips them of His help, but He resists and opposes, as if in a battle line well-disposed against an opponent, not that God has need of an arrayed battle line or a fight, since nothing is weaker than a proud man, inasmuch as he is blinded in his eyes, with which he might see God, and is exposed to the injury of all. But for God, however strong and powerful a proud man might be, His will suffices to overturn everything. He resists, therefore, to declare vehement hatred toward the proud. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epistle 164. God resists the proud, since indeed He also opposed their Prince from the beginning. Consider therefore how great a thing it is, both to have God ἀντίμαχον, and the ancient enemy συμμέτοχον

7. The remaining sins flee from God, pride alone opposes itself to God; the remaining sins depress man, pride alone raises him up against God. Hence also God in turn opposes Himself to the proud, inasmuch as He could not endure arrogance either in heaven or on earth. Judith 9. v. 16. The proud from the beginning have not pleased thee. Sir. 10. v. 16. The Lord hath made the proud contemptible and hath destroyed them even to the end. v. 17. God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes and hath set up the meek in their stead. v. 18. God hath made the roots of proud nations to wither and hath planted the humble in their stead. v. 21. God hath destroyed the memory of the proud and hath left the memory of the humble in mind. Luke 1. v. 51. He hath scattered the proud in the conceit of their heart. c. 14. v. 10. c. 18. v. 13. Everyone that exalteth himself shall be humbled. John Huss in this place. The great vice of pride, through which the Angel lost heaven, man lost Paradise, Saul lost the kingdom. Examples of pride punished in the evil Angels, in Pharaoh Ex. 5. v. 2. in Nebuchadnezzar Dan. 4. v. 30. etc.

8. God sometimes healthfully humbles the proud, converting them to Himself and inspiring in them the grace of humility, which is a work of mercy: sometimes, however, He so depresses the proud that He oppresses and overthrows them, which is a work of justice.

9. Humility is not only a grace, but also a vessel of graces. For God continually gives greater grace to the humble; therefore, He pours other virtues and other charisms into humility as if into a vessel, so that they may be properly preserved in it. Valleys are fruitful and abound with grainPsal. 65. v. 14. that is, the humble abound in virtues. Valleys are exaltedEs. 40. vers. 4. that is, the humble are filled with the gifts of graces. God sends forth springs in the valleysPsal. 104. v. 10. that is, the springs of divine grace gush forth in the hearts of the humble. Streams of grace flow downward, not upward. Waters seek sloping places: thus grace does not flow except into humble hearts, Bernh. serm. 4. on Missus est. Just as the seat of waters is the humility of the valleys, so the seat of grace is the humility of men. Valleys are irrigated by heavenly rains and become more fruitful than the highest peaks of the mountains. August. serm. 27. on the words of the Lord on the words Luc. 10. v. 39.Mary was sitting at the feet of our head. The more humbly she sat, the more she received. For water flows together to the humility of the valley, it flows away from the swellings of the hill. Examples of humility rewarded with greater grace by God in Joseph, David, Daniel, Esther, Mary, etc.

10. It truly befits the pious that first of all they humble themselves before God, lest they be forced to hear that Ex. 10. vers. 3.How long do you refuse to submit to me! then also that for the sake of GOD they humble themselves before others.

11. We humble ourselves before God by humbly acknowledging the foulness of our sins on one side, and the divine majesty and purity on the other side, by submitting ourselves to the powerful hand of God, and by committing ourselves entirely to His will. We humble ourselves before men by acknowledging that they are superior to us by reason of their gifts and by reverently submitting ourselves to them. The Apostle immediately joins the commandment of humility toward one's neighbor with the commandment of humiliation under the powerful hand of God; for he commands us to be humbled before God for this reason, that we may be humane and gentle toward our brothers, and not refuse out of true humility to submit ourselves to them, as the reason of charity demands. Therefore, those who are arrogant against men, they exalt themselves against God Himself.

12. The repetition of the commandment concerning humility insinuates the necessity of this virtue, but censures the hypocrisy of men who feign it outwardly. Jerome to Celantia: Many have the appearance of humility, few follow the truth.

13. The end of humility is glory, the end of pride is ignominy. Prov. 11. v. 2. נא זדון ויבא קלון When pride comes, then comes ignominy, and with the humble is wisdom. ἀρίστη ὁδὸς ὑψώσεως ἡ ταπείνωσις Iob. 5. v. 11. God sets the humble on high, cap. 22. v. 29. He who has been humbled shall be in glory, and he who has cast down his eyes, he shall be saved, Psal. 18. 28. You will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud. Prov. 29. v. 33. Humiliation follows the proud, and glory shall uphold the humble in spirit. Luc. 1. v. 52. He has exalted the humble cap. 14. v. 10. cap. 18. v. 13. He who humbles himself shall be exalted. Humility is like Jacob's ladder, which carries us up from earth to heaven Gen. 28. v. 12. Nazianzen, oration 48: Christ taught by His own example that the outermost path to sublimity is humility. Phil. 2. v. 8. He humbled Himself v. 9. therefore God has exalted Him to the highest sublimity. Aug. sermon 53 on the words of the Lord: If you cast yourself down, God lifts you up. If you exalt yourself, God casts you down.

14. There are, as it were, two hands of GOD, under which we ought to humble ourselves; one depresses the proud, the other exalts the humble.

15. The time of the promised exaltation must be patiently awaited and committed to God, whether and when He wills to exalt us, whether that happens in this or in the future age. Lord, I may be to You as my hand is to me. Son of God, as You will and as You know, have mercy on me. Rabanus on chapter 8 of Judith.

16. The time of this life is for the most part a time of humiliation; exaltation will sometimes follow on the day of judgment. An example is proposed in Christ our head, who, crowned with honor and glory in His resurrection, Psal. 8. v. 6. was exalted in His ascension to the right hand of His Father. Act. 2. v. 33.

17. Clement, at the beginning of the Recognitions, writes that this was the teaching of Peter: We Christians are anxious about no thing or event, but in the providence of God We rest completely, knowing that we are a care to Him, and are directed by Him in all things, so that all things may turn out for our good. That seems to be requested from this Apostolic passage. Clemens Alexandr. lib. paedag. cap. 5. Let us imitate children, by acknowledging God alone as Father, having laid aside cares about food, by clinging to the Father alone. Chrysostomus homil. 56. ad popul. Antioch. & homil. 69. in Matth. Do not care for your own things, but entrust them to God, for if you are anxious, you are anxious as a man, but if you let them go, God will provide. Therefore, so that He may take great providence of them, commit all things to Him alone. But if you yourself, having omitted spiritual things, handle them, He will not take much care of them. Therefore, so that these things may be well arranged for you, and you may be freed from all care, despise worldly things: For thus you will have both earth with the heavens and will attain future goods.

18. Indeed, just as infants cast all their anxiety into the bosom of their mother, in which they sweetly recline and sleep: so let the faithful person deposit all his anxiety into the bosom of God, as being his heavenly Father. Psal. 37. v. 5.Commit your way to the Lord.Psal. 55. v. 23.Cast your burden upon the Lord. He promised, I will not leave you, nor forsake you.Ios. 1. v. 5.Hebr. 13. v. 5.If a mother forgets her infant, He will also forget us.Esai. 49. v. 15.

19. Μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε, Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.Phil. 4. v. 6. Therefore it is for the pious to be anxious for nothing, but to pray much. We, on the contrary, are for the most part very anxious, but pray little.

20. The cares that press upon us are like a great burden; but especially our sins are a heavy burden pressing us down even to hell. Psal. 38. v. 5.My iniquities are like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me. Because of them we are sometimes a burden to ourselves Iob. 7. v. 20.I have become a burden to myself. Therefore, we ought to cast the burden of cares through true trust in God, and the burden of sins upon Christ through true repentance. For He ἄιρει takes upon Himself and takes away from the midst the sins of the world. Ioh. 1. v. 29.

21. He who is pressed by a great burden, which he is not able to bear, labors to cast it far from himself quickly and with a certain vehemence; thus let us cast the burden of our cares quickly and far from us, directing that projection of ours solely toward God as the target.

22. Those who cast their cares upon God feel the peace of conscience, and are peaceable toward men, just as he who is relieved of a burden completes his journey more easily. When we are firmly persuaded that God wishes to take upon Himself the cares we have cast upon Him, the mind will be easily composed to patience and gentleness.

23. Let the faithful ascend Mount Moriah daily with Abraham, using as a proverb that saying, The Lord will provide, Genes. 22. v. 8. On the mount the Lord will provide, v. 14. namely, on that mount of divine providence, from which help descends to us. Psal. 121. Bernh. serm. 9. in Psalmum. He who dwells. Why, if we know these things, why do we hesitate to cast away entirely miserable, vain, useless, and seductive hopes, and to cling with the whole devotion of the soul, with the whole fervor of the Spirit, to this one hope, so solid, so perfect, so blessed? Theodoret. in Psal. 54. upon the words. Cast your thought upon the Lord: Against the ship of the mind fluctuating with the waves of anxieties, the anchor of hope in God must be cast, for He Himself is the pilot.

24. Although in general all things are subject to divine providence, so that nothing at all is understood to be excluded from it Sap. 8. v. 1. cap. 12. v. 13. & 15. Hebr. 1. v. 3., nevertheless, those who believe in Christ are specially the care of God. They are the kernel of the human race, for whose sake the world is still sustained and preserved by God; if it were without them, the world would be destroyed in a moment and reduced to nothing. They are the beloved children of the heavenly householder, for whose sake He moderates and governs all things in His house. Deut. 32. v. 9. The Lord's portion is His people Jacob, etc. Psal. 77. v. 21. You led Your people like sheep. 1. Tim. 4. v. 10. God is the Savior of all men, especially of the faithful.

25. Bernh. serm 68. in Cant. warns. That Peter did not say, cast all your anxiety upon Him, so that He might have care for you, but because He has care for you, openly showing to the Church of the saints not only that it is beloved, but that it was beloved first. Attend to Him, because He attends to you.

26. An inexplicable consolation lies hidden in this care of God for us and concerning us. For if we are a care to God, then He is our Father, He is our provider, He is our patron, etc. Psal. 40. v. 18. I am afflicted and poor, the Lord is solicitous for me, or thinks for me, upon which words Aug. comments thus. He who had care of you before you were, How will He not have care, since you are already this, which He willed that you should be? For you are already faithful, you already walk in the way of justice, etc. He is nowhere lacking to you; do not you be lacking to Him, do not you be lacking to yourself.

27. Upon God we have been cast from the womb Psalm. 22. v. 10., that is, into His own faith and protection; therefore we ought also to cast all our anxiety upon Him. He has care for us. Therefore we ought to cast all our care upon Him. He can bring aid to us, as an omnipotent God; He bears care for us, as a faithful father. Matth. 6. v. 36. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Aug. lib. 3. Confess. cap. 1. O You good omnipotent One, who so cares for each one of us, as if You care for him alone, and so for all as if for individuals.

28. From the mouth of Christ their Master, the Apostle repeats the precept of sobriety and vigilance Luc. 21. v. 34. Take heed, lest your hearts be burdened with surfeiting. Paul inculcates the same 1. Thess. 5. v. 5. All you are children of light, and children of the day; we are not of the night nor of darkness. v. 6. Therefore let us not sleep as others do, but let us watch and be sober.

29. It is first to be sober, then to watch, because sobriety is the parent of vigilance, just as, on the contrary, satiety provokes sleep, and surfeiting is the mother of slumber.

30. Sobriety consists in the moderation of food and drink and diligent care, lest hearts be burdened with surfeiting, through which men are rendered inept for prayers and works of piety, as also for their vocation. Hieron. lib. 2. adv. Iovin. cap. 6. Reason ought to be present, that we may take such and so great foods, by which the body is not burdened and the liberty of the soul is not weighed down.

31. Vigilance consists in provident care, lest through security and negligence we be led into errors or crimes by the snares of Satan, and thus fall away from the grace of God and eternal salvation. Phil. 2. v. 12. With fear and trembling work out your salvation. Cyrillus Hierosolymit. catech. 4. Work with divine grace with a sober mind, and with watching eyes, that we may avoid tares for wheat, the wolf for the sheep, the Devil for a good Angel. August. serm. 23. de verb. Dom. cap. 10. Watch with your heart, watch with faith, watch with hope, watch with charity, watch with works.

32. The precept of watching also warns of this, that we should not grow sluggish in the course of piety, that we should not love the world, and those things which are in world 1. John 2. v. 15. for what else are the honors, pleasures, and riches of this world, than sweet dreams, with which the lovers of the world delight themselves? so that we may be occupied in perpetual watchfulness, so that we may be attentive on every side to μεθοδείας & the stratagems of Satan.

33. The most grave danger to which we are subject at every moment ought to move us to sobriety & vigilance, namely the snares of the Devil, who is perpetually intent upon our seduction & destruction. Matt. 26. v. 41. Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. B. Luther on this passage: Such is our life, as if a traveler were to come into an inn, in which all the inhabitants were thieves; there he would certainly watch, arm himself, and fortify himself.

34. The Devil perpetually watches to attack us; it is therefore necessary that we watch to resist him. Cyprian, tract on Zeal & Envy: Against all the deceitful snares or open threats of the Devil, one ought to stand instructed in spirit and armed, as prepared always to fight back as the enemy is always prepared to attack. Jerome, Epistle 1 to Heliodorus: This lion lies in wait in his den, he lies in wait to seize the poor, and do you, covered by the shade of a leafy tree, take soft sleep, about to be prey?

35. The Devil is our adversary, who wages implacable hatred & war with us ἀσπονδον. Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against Princes and powers; against κοσμοκράτορας etc. Eph. 6. v. 12. Various are his μεθοδείαι v. 11. his darts are fiery v. 16. Enmities between him and us were established in Paradise Gen. 3. v. 15. in Baptism we renounced him and all his works; hence he is our perpetual adversary, & the life of man upon earth is a perpetual warfare. Job 7. v. 1.

36. The Devil does not idle, does not grow weary, is not affected by boredom, but driven by a desire to harm, he is perpetually on the move, & walks about. Hence he is also compared to a hunter diligently tracking wild beasts and setting snares for them Psalm 91. v. 3. In the hunter we discern first vigilance, because he rises at the crack of dawn to track wild beasts while they are still resting in their lairs. Secondly, indefatigable industry, because he shakes every bush, spares no labor, endures rain, heat, cold, hunger, thirst, in order to catch the beasts. Thirdly, fraudulence, because he devises many arts & snares by which he may oppress the unwary beasts. Fourthly, vigilance, because with great force upon the prey offered and captured it rushes, all of which can be applied to the Devil.

37. The Devil goes about, like an enemy surrounding a city with a military army, seeking in what part he might break in. Cyprian, sermon on Zeal and Envy. He goes about us one by one, and like an enemy besieging those shut in, he explores the walls, and tests whether there is any part of the walls less stable and less trustworthy, by whose entrance he might penetrate to the interior. He offers to the eyes alluring forms and easy pleasures, so that by sight he may destroy chastity; he tests the ears through melodious music, so that by the hearing of sweeter sound he may loosen and soften Christian vigor. He provokes the tongue to reviling, he incites the hand to the petulance of slaughter by provoking injuries; so that he may make one a defrauder, he sets forth unjust gains: so that he may capture the soul with money, he introduces dangerous profits; he promises earthly honors, so that he may take away heavenly ones: he displays false things, so that he may steal away true ones, and when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens boldly and openly, intending the terror of turbulent persecution, always restless and hostile for the sake of overcoming the servants of God, deceitful in peace, violent in persecution, which passage of Cyprian, Bede brings forward in full in his commentary on this place. Jerome, Epistle 1 to Heliodorus. Thence luxury pursues me, thence avarice tries to break in, thence my belly wishes to be God to me instead of Christ: lust compels me to put to flight the Holy Spirit dwelling within, so that I may violate His temple; the enemy pursues me, I say, to whom there are a thousand names, a thousand arts of harming, etc. In that heat, the Charybdis of luxury devours salvation. There, with a maidenly mouth, lust, smiling like Scylla, flatters to commit the shipwrecks of modesty. Here is a barbarian shore, here the Devil, a pirate with his companions, carries chains for those to be captured, etc. Leo, sermon 7 on the Nativity. He knows to whom he should apply the goad of cupidity, to whom he should introduce the allurements of gluttony, to whom he should apply the incitements of luxury, to whom he should pour the poison of envy: he knows whom he may disturb with error, whom he may deceive with joy, whom he may oppress with fear, whom he may seduce with admiration. Bernard, sermon 67 on the manner of living well, col. 1741. The Devil tempts man more from that part by which he sees him to be easily inclined to vices through an excrescent humor, so that according to the mixture of the humor he may apply the temptation. Compare Lactantius, book 6 of the Institutes.

38. The Devil goes about seeking prey. Therefore he neglects to tempt those, chapter 4, whom he already possesses beforehand by quiet right. His food is choice meat Hab. 1. v. 16. which Jerome, Epistle 22, and Gregory in 1 Kings 9 apply here. Rightly Cyprian, book 1, Epistle 1. The Devil does not seek those whom he has already subdued, nor does he desire to overthrow those whom he has already made his own. The enemy and foe of the Church, whom he has alienated from the Church and led outside, as he despises and passes over captives and the bound, he proceeds to harass those in whom he perceives Christ to dwell.

39. The Devil circles like a wolf around the sheepfolds; yet he does not enter, unless someone voluntarily opens the door of his heart to him; he does not slip in, he does not break in, unless admitted. Chrysost. on ch. 4 of Matt. He can suggest, he cannot compel. He can persuade, he cannot precipitate, says Jerome on ch. 4 of Metaph.

40. The Devil is compared to a roaring lion, a lurking serpent, a watchful dragon Isa. 27. v. 1.Apoc. 12. v. 3. & 9. a stinging scorpion Luke 10. v. 19. a snatching bird Matt. 13. v. 4. & 19. The Syrians call the Devil דיוא from the Hebrew דאה which signifies vulture or kite. Matt. 9. v. 32.ch. 10. v. 8. &c.

41. Let us oppose to this roaring lion the lion of the tribe of JudahApoc. 5. v. 5. by whom he was conquered and bound. Bernard, sermon 13 on Ps. 9. he dwells &c. Your adversary as a roaring lion, says Peter. Thanks to that great lion of the tribe of Judah: that one can roar, he cannot strike. Let him roar as much as he wants, provided the sheep of Christ does not flee. How much he threatens, how much he exaggerates, how much he attempts, let us not be beasts, so that the empty roar of that one might prostrate us. For thus they claim, who have investigated such things more curiously, that at the roar of a lion no beast can stand, not even that which resists against his blow with all its spirit, and for the most part overcomes the striker, which does not sustain the roarer. Truly a beast, truly devoid of reason, is he who is so pusillanimous that he yields to fear alone, who, conquered by the mere exaggeration of future labor, is prostrated before the conflict not by a weapon, but by a trumpet. You have not yet resisted unto blood, says that strenuous leader, who knew the roar of this lion to be vain. And another one: Resist, he says, the Devil and he will flee from you. Gerson, on the consolation of Theology, book 3, prose 4. God terrifies the bound infernal lion, lest he rage as much as he would like; it is not he, but the one holding him who must be entreated.

42. Three kinds of weapons are shown to us against the assault of the Devil. 1. resistance. The first step to victory is to resist, because the Devil, when he is resisted, is weak as an ant; but when his suggestion is received, he is strong as a lion. 2. strength of mind, because it is not his power that makes the Devil strong, but our negligence. Bernard, Epistle 1, col. 757. The adversary pursues you more willingly when you are fleeing than he sustains you when you are fighting back, and more boldly he presses from behind, rather than resists in the face. 3. Faith, which is that most strong shield, by which we can receive and extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one. Eph. 6. v. 16. Thomas Anglicus on this passage: Just as in the Devil perversity is denoted by the name of adversary; strength by the name of lion; cruelty, when he is said to be roaring; solicitude, when he is said to seek by going about: so it is required of us against the first, that we resist; against the second, that we be strong; against the third, that we have the meekness of faith; against the last, that we watch.

42. In the word apprehended by true and firm faith consists all our victory against the Devil. Equipped with this sword of the Spirit, protected by this shield of the word, we can resist all the temptations of Satan. If the Devil desires to persuade us of a false dogma, let us oppose the antidote of the heavenly word. If he wishes to impel us to the desire for vengeance, to lust, and to other sins, let us oppose the divine threats. If he inspires doubt and strives to render us faint-hearted, let us oppose the divine promises. No temptation of the Devil can be named, against which there is not held a special antidote in the word of God.

44. The Devil is put to flight by faith, just as a lion by fire. In faith is victory against Satan, because faith unites us with Christ the victor. Isidorus lib. 3. de summ. bono cap. 5. By the incredulous the Devil is feared as a lion, by those strong in faith he is despised as a worm and, once shown for a moment, is repelled.

45. When the Apostle had said that we are attacked by Satan, he immediately embraces every kind of affliction under the name τῶν παθημάτων, from which it appears that even in other adversities one must wrestle with him, inasmuch as through them he solicits us to impatience.

46. A great argument of consolation in persecutions on account of the Evangelical truth is the fellowship of other believers. For since they are our brothers, therefore we ought not to refuse a common lot with them, nor demand our own. I am not better than my fathers, said the prophet Elijah. 1. Reg. 19. v. 4. Let us also say: We are not better than our brothers. Beda on this passage: That which the righteous have always suffered from the foundation of the world, let us be ashamed that we alone before all others are unable to endure.

47. Not only of afflictions, but also of prayers and of the struggle against Satan, fellowship with the remaining faithful intercedes for us. They are not only our παθημάτων συμμέτοχοι, but also in prayers and the fight against Satan our συμπαλαιστρίται and σύμμαχοι. Therefore this consolation does not consist only in example, but also in the unity of faith, in which all the faithful in Christ the victor and their head fight strongly against the common enemy, and in the conjunction of prayers, by which in this fight συναγωινζουσι, and they help one another. Hence in the spiritual πανοπλίᾳ the Apostle also makes mention of προσκαρτερήσεως and δεήσεως περὶ πάντων τῶν ἁγίων. Ephes. 6. vers. 18. Oecumenius in this place Fellowship of companions lightens the burden, so that you may show greatness of soul against the adversary the Devil, because we are not alone, who fight with him, but all the good and the elect of Christ.

48. Believers are brothers, who have one father in the heavens, from whom they expect the same inheritance. Eph. 4. v. 4. & 6. They also have a common brother Christ, on account of whom and through whom they have been adopted by God into sons, and joined by his Spirit; furthermore they have a common mother the Church, which cherishes them in her bosom. Minutius Felix in Octavius. We are called brothers, as men of one God the parent, as partners of faith, as co-heirs of hope. Because therefore the faithful are brothers, therefore their affection ought to be brotherly. If concord of brothers according to the flesh is natural, much more ought concord to be commended to spiritual brothers.

49. The sufferings, which weigh upon us, are accomplished in the brotherhood, which is in the world. Namely because Christ the head of the mystical body suffered in the world, therefore it behooves all true and living members of the mystical body, which is the Church, to suffer in this world, so that the measure of sufferings defined by God in this mystical body may be completed. Col. 1. v. 24.

50. God is the God of all grace and of all charisms. Therefore to Him every good and every gift is to be attributed Iac. 1. vers. 17. and according to the will of God is to be communicated with others 1. Petr. 4. vers. 10.

51. God is the God of grace, He is also the God of glory. Act. 7. vers. 2. the Lord will give grace and glory. Psal. 84. v. 12. As He is the God of all grace, so also the father of mercies 2. Cor. 1. v. 3. namely because from His grace and mercy various benefits come to us, among which is the gift of the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of graceZach. 12. v. 10.Hebr. 10. v. 29. and the gift of eternal life, which is χάρισμα in Christ Jesus.Rom. 6. v. 23.

52. Our calling is purely gratuitous, as having proceeded from GOD, the source of all grace. Therefore, let us give due thanks to GOD, by whom we have been called, and let us conduct ourselves in a manner worthy of that calling. Ephes. 4. vers. 1.

53. Three things are most aptly joined by the Apostle: calling, which is the beginning of our salvation, through which we have been called to eternal glory; Christ, who is the merit of our salvation and the way to that glory Ioh. 14. vers. 6.; and eternal glory, which is the end and full possession of our salvation, and which is established for us solely through Christ Rom. 6. vers. 23.Eph. 2. v. 8.Tit. 3. vers. 5. The Law says that obedience perfectly rendered to it is the way to that glory, but the Gospel teaches that Christ is the way, whence here we are said to be called in Christ to the eternal glory of God.

54. When the Apostle attributes καταρτισμὸν, στήριξιν, σθένωσιν and θεμελίωσιν, to divine grace, he shows the beginning, the middle, and the end of our salvation, and thus also that our perseverance is the work of God; he also warns us of our infirmity in bearing the cross patiently, and impels us, as we flee to God through earnest prayers, to ask from Him for preservation in good and the completion of the good work.Phil. 1. v. 6.

55. Because the Apostle expresses our preservation in good in many words, by that very fact he shows that it is of altogether great difficulty to persevere in good until the end and to endure in the cross, and therefore that there is also need for the special grace and power of God. 1. Petr. 1. vers. 5.

56. The eternal glory of God, to which those believing in Christ have been called, is opposed to the eternal ignominy and reproach to which the Devil and all the damned will be subject on the day of judgment and in the fire of hell. Esai. 66. v. 24. they shall be an abomination to all flesh.Dan. 12. v. 2. they shall awake to everlasting shame.

57. In persecutions for the sake of the Gospel, let us be comforted both by the brevity of afflictions which are to be ended with this life Esai. 54. v. 7. & 8.2. Cor. 4. v. 17.1. Petr. 1. v. 6. and by the sweetness of the divine presence Psal. 91. v. 15.Esai. 43. v. 2. etc.

58. As often as we happen to make mention of the benefits of God, we ought to break forth into the glorification of the divine name. For to that end God confers His benefits upon us, that He may be glorified by us in this and the future life. Bernard, sermon against ingratitude, Happy is he who, at every gift of grace, returns to Him in whom is the fullness of all graces.

59. Two greatest things are sought by men; glory, or the celebrity of fame, and empire or power, but both are to be uniquely attributed to God through glorification. Just as all rivers arise from the sea: so all good things flow forth from the fountain of divine grace. Therefore, just as all rivers return to the sea, so all good things are to be referred to God through thanksgiving and glorification Eccl. 1. v. 1.

60. The use of goods divinely bestowed upon us is owed to our neighbor, the glory of them is owed to GOD. Augustine, soliloquies, chapter 15, He who seeks glory for himself from Your good, O Lord, and not for You, this man is a thief and a robber, and is like the Devil, who wanted to steal Your glory.

61. To God alone belongs strength and empire. He is the only powerful King of Kings, and Lord of lords 1. Tim. 6. v. 15. Yours, O Lord, is magnificence and glory, and victory, and to You is praise, for all things which are in heaven and on earth are Yours: Yours, O Lord, is the kingdom, and You are exalted above all Princes; Yours are riches and Yours is glory, You rule over all, in Your hand is virtue and power, in Your hand it is to magnify and strengthen everyone, says David 1. Paral. 29. v. 11. & 12. Thence also among the Hebrews God is called האל that strong one, and by more recent Jews הגבורה κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν that supreme power, God in His fortitude and power. To which can be referred what Luke cap. 22. v. 69. says, the son of man sitting ἐκ δεξιῶν τῆς δυνάμεως τοῦ θεοῦ that Matthew c. 26. v. 64. simply expresses thus, The Son of man sits ἐκ δεξῶν τῆς δυνάμεως.

62. Because all and every good of ours, which we have, descends from God: because it is the benefit of God alone that we are called to eternal glory, that we are preserved in persecutions, that we work well, that we overcome the temptations of Satan, that we are perfected, established, strengthened, founded, etc., therefore let us celebrate Him with perpetual proclamations of praise. A spiritual and pleasing sacrifice to God is the proclamation of divine praises. In turn, because God alone holds supreme dominion in heaven and on earth, therefore let us fear Him alone, let us seek help and defense from Him, let us humbly submit ourselves to Him, etc.

Latin:

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quinam intelligantur per voculamπάντες; Resp. Quidam existimant, praeoeptum hoc humilit atis tantùm ad iuniores pertinere, quos propterea Apostolus velit esse humiles, quia ubi humilitas deest, ibi obedientia locum habere nequit. Sed rectiùs dicitur, esse hoc praeceptum generale, ad omnes cuiuscunque status, conditionis & aetatis homines pertinens, quia praecepto speciali iunioribus dato, per particulam adversativam subiicitur, ac proinde quasi correctione quadam amplificatur. Dixi, iuniores debere subiici senioribus, sed verius est, omnes per humilitatem debere sibi invicem subiici.

Q. 2. Quare Apostolus omnibus, ac proinde etiam Presbyteris humilitatem commendet? Resp. Beda in comm. h. l. Ne praelati audientes putarent solummodò subditis suis, & non etiam sibi debitae humilitatis iura esse servandae, continuò generaliter admonendo subiecit. Omnes autem invicem humilitatem in sinuate. Omnes etenim dicit & seniores & adolescentes, qui iubentur humilitatis insinuare virtutem, & hi videl, regendo & illi obsequendo humiliter. Quod apud ipsum Petrum & in ipso factum legimus, cum intrante eo Caesaream Cornelius occurrens pedibus se eius humiliter stravit, & ille humiliùs levavit eum dicens, surge & ego homo sum &c. Omnes ergò humilitatem habere ad alterutrum vel exemplo docet, vel etiam verbo insinuat, quia nimirum omnibus superbiae vitium, quod Angelos de coelo deiecit, noverat esse cavendum, omnes adiuncta Salomonis sententia terret salubriter ac refovet.

Q. 3. Quomodo versio LXX. Interpp.Prov. 3. v. 34.quam Petrus sequitur, conveniat cum textu Hebraeo, qui solus est authenticus? Resp. textus Hebraeus ad verbum sic habet: Ipse (Dominus) deludet illusores, & mansuetis dabit gratiam. LXX. Interpp. versio sic habet. Dominus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam, quam κατὰ πόδα sequitur Petrus, nisi quod pro κύριος reponit ὁ θεὸς. Nulla hîe in sensu diversitas. Nam 1. homines superbi verè sunt illusores, qui alto supercilio omnes contemnunt, & recta monentes rident. 2. Deus resistit superbis, & resistendo eos deludit, eludendo atque frustrando eorum conatus & studia, quibus suam quaerunt excellentiam. Sed & de sede eos deponens contemtibiles eos reddit, quod proprium est deludentis. 3. humiles sunt etiam mansueti, sicut superbi sunt iracundi & iactabundi. Hebraeum ענוים descendit à rad. ענה quod significat afflictus, humiliatus & depressus fuit,Es. 25. v. 5.cap. 31. v. 4. significat ergò ענוים non solùm mansuetos, sed etiam humiles & humiliatos sive afflictos.

Q. 4. Quid per humiliationem sub manu Dei intelligatur? Bedain comm. tribus modis exponit. Potest, inquit, humiliatio hoc in loco multifariè accipi, hoc est, & ea, quâ incipiens quisque viam virtutum pro abluendis, quae commiserat, peccatis salubriter atteritur; & illa, quae spontaneâ mentis devotione à perfectioribus Deo vel proximio in pace exhibetur rerum circumstantium; nec non ea, quâ incur santibus persecutionum turbinibus invictus per patientiae virtutem animus armatur. Omni autem generi Deo devotae humilitatis merces succedit illa, at qui se tempore peregrinationis suae humiliant, tempore visitationis eius exaltentur. Propriè & directè Apostolus agit de virtute illa, quâ quis infirmitatem suam agnoscit, in vero timore se coram DEO humiliat, & aliis reverenter sese subiicit, dona DEI in illis honorando.

Q. 5. Quare mentionem faciat potentis Dei manus, sub qua omnes se humiliare debeant? Resp. Epitheton hoc, ad propositam exhortationem perquàm accommodatum, ideò addit. 1. ut fastuosis ac turgidis plus terroris incutiat, ne contra Deum insurgere tentent. q. d. Non potes effugere potentissimam Dei manum, velis nolis, ei subdi cogeris. 2. ut oppressos atque humiles consolatione erigat. q. d. Potens est Dei manus, ad superbos, qui aliis insultant, & pedibus suis eos conculcant, deprimendos; & vicissim ad humiles, qui ad ipsum confugiunt, sub tutela sua contra omnes superborum insultus defendendos, & in altum evehendos.

Q. 6. Quid perτὸν καιρὸνhoc loco intelligatur? Resp. quidam determinatè intelligunt diem adventûs Domini & Universalis iudicii, qui antonomasticè vocetur tempus Matth. 8. v. 29.Venisti ante tempus nos torquereMarc. 13. v. 33.Nescitis quando tempus sit.Luc. 21 v. 8.tempus, se. iudicii appropinquat. Quò etiam referri posset Act. 1. v. 7.cap. 3. v. 24.1. Cor. 4. v. 5.Gal. 6. v. 9.1. Thess. 5. v. 1.1. Tim. 6. v. 15.1. Petr. 1. v. 5. Itemque dicta illa, in quibus dies iudicii & adventus Christi absolutè vocatur ἡμέρα.2. Tim. 4. v. 8.Hebr. 10. v. 25. Existimant igitur, exaltationem propterea extremo retributionis tempori assignari, quia potissima piorum praemia differuntur in diem iudicii & futunam vitam. Matth. 19. v. 29.Marc. 10. v. 30. Sed rectiùs dicitur, per καιρὸν hoc loco intelligi quodvis oportunum exaltationis tempus, sive Deo placeat in hoc, sive in futuro seculo nos evehere.

Q. 7. Quare Apostolus huncπροσδιορισμὸνpromissioni seuturae exaltationis coniungat? Resp. 1. ut occurrat scandalo, quod ex impiorum fastu oriri solet. Hoc enim vult dicere: Non semper impii superbient, & alios depriment, nec semper humiles in pulvere iacebunt, sed erit tempus, quo illi humiliabuntur, hi vero exaltabuntur. 2. ut medeatur festinationi, ne per media illicita ante tempus à Deo constitutum exaltari quaeramus, sicque nostris consiliis, voluntatem divinam antevertere nitamur.

Q. 8. Quare proiiciendi verbo Apostolus utatur? Resp. ut doceat, solicitudines illas, quae nos premunt, esse ingens pondus, cui ferendo nos non simus pares, requiri igitur, ut hoc pondere atque onere nos quàm fieri potest citissimè levemus, & in potentem Dei manum, cuius in praeced. versiculo mentionem fecerat, illud deponamus.

Q. 9. An de mentis, an vero corporis sobrietate Apostolus loquatur? Calvinus de sobrietate mentis exponit. Duplici, inquit, metaphorâ utitur, ut sobrii sint, & excubias agant. Lorinus annotat, non esse improbabile, sobrietatem hoc loco denotare modum in prudentia, curave transigendae vitae, de qua praecessit proximè mentio, simulque in credendo, ne curio siùs velimus, quae simpliciter proponuntur credenda, scrutari. Favet, quod paulo pòst admonemur, adversario Diabolo resistere in fide &c. Praeterea, quoniam Paulus praecipit,Rom. 12. v. 6.ne sapiat quis plusquàm oportet, sedεἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν,quod Irenaeus lib. 5. c. 20. reddit ad prudentiam; Hieronymus lib. 1. contra Iovin. ad pudicitiam. Augustinus Epist. 47. ad temperantiam. Haec temperantia modus est, sese intra terminos continendi, ne superflum quaeramus fidei mysteriorum cognitionem. Posset addi argumentum, quod Apostolus non solùmcap. 1. v. 13.sed etiamcap. 4. v. 7.νήφεινpro mentis vigilantia & sobrietate usurpet, dicit enimνήφειν εἰς τὰς προσευχὰς. Sed directè & principaliter loquitur Apostolus de sobrietate corporis, quia desumsit hanc exhortationem ex verbis Christi Luc. 21. vers. 34. & quia per ebrietatem Diabolicis tentationibus non fenestra, sed bipatens ianua aperitur. Secundariò & minùs principaliter ad mentis sobrietatem eandem exhortationem referri, non abnuimus. σωφροσύνη enim dicitur quasi σώζουσα τὴν φρόνησιν, vel σωτηρία φρονήσεως apud Platonem in Cratylo, ac sobrietas corporis etiam mentis sobrietatem coniunctam habere potest, quae cum ebrietate & crapulâ minimè consistit.

Q. 10. An de mentis, an vero corporis vigiliâ Apostolus loquatur? Quidam de corporis vigiliâ exhortationem hanc accipiunt. 1. quiaγρηγορεῖνpropriè de corporis vigiliâ usurpatur.Nehem. 7. vers. 3.Matth. 26. v. 40.Marc. 14. v. 37.1. Thessal. 5. v. 10. &c. 2. quia de corporis sobrietate praecedens verbumνήφεινusurpatur. 3. quia in loco parallelo.Luc. 21. v. 36.non solùm mentis, sed etiam corporis vigilia requiritur. Quamvis enim Christus non prohibeat somnum naturalem, quo advaletudinis conservationem nemo hominum in hac vitâ carere potest, tamen in eo aequè, ac in cibo & potu, moderationem adhibendam esse docet. 4. Qui somno nimiùm indulgent, in operibus vocationis sunt desides & remissi, ac obtusos habent sensus. Plenus & ignavus venter non potest Diabolo resistere, inquit Lutherus in h. l. 5. ex verboγρηγορεῖτεpii veteres occasionem acceperunt introducendi ritum nocturnarum vigiliarum & precum in Ecclesiam, ut apparet ex Lactant. lib. 7. Instit. cap. 19. Gregor. Nyssen. de festo Paschatis. Sed quamvis haec omnia rectè se habeant, de mentis tamen vigiliâ Apostolum vel unicè, vel potissimùm agere rectiùs dicitur. 1. quia non tàm corporis, quàm mentis vigiliâ sive vigilantiâ contra Satanam pugnandum. 2. absque mentis vigilantiâ corporis vigilia parùm prodest, cùm Diabolus adversarius noster nunquam somnum capiat, sed perpetuò vigilet. 3. Christus in loco parallelo Luc. 21. v. 36. de mentis vigilantia potissimùm loquitur, addit enim, vigilantes omni tempore. 4. quia significatio illa verbi γρηγορεῖν metaphorica, quâ pro omni vigilantiâ accipitur, Christo & Apostolis longè usitatior. Matth. 25. v. 13.Luc. 12. v. 37.Act. 20. v. 31.1. Cor. 16. v. 13.Coloss. 4. vers 2.1. Thess. 5. v. 6.Apoc. 3. v. 2.cap. 3. v. 3.cap. 16. v. 15. 5. Ostendit Apostolus, cum sobrietate corporis, quae moderationem somni secum affert, coniungendam esse vigilantiam mentis. 6. Eodem modo exponunt plerique Interpretes. Syrus reddidit, mementote sive memores estote. Glossa interlinearis: Vigilate, non intenti delectationibus seculi. Quemadmodum ebrietas corporalis ignaviam & somnum generat: ita quoque illi, qui se terrenis curis aut voluptatibus ingurgitant, spirituali veterno oppressi nihil cogitant. Lyranus: Vigilate, i. e. diligenter à peccatis praecavete.

Q. 11. Quid per hanc spiritualem vigilantiam denotetur? Diximus in Harm. Evang. cap. 162. Christum in loco parallelo Luc. 11. v. 36. per vigilantiae praeceptum à nobis requirere. 1. quotidianam, novissimi diei memoriam, & perpetuam adventûs sui expectationem, uti patet ex parabola de servis, reditum Domini sui è nuptiis vigilanter expectantibus, quibus Christus vult fideles esse similes. Luc. 12. v. 36. &c. 2. solicitam curam & quotidianam ad diem iudieii praeparationem, uti patet ex eo, quod Christus huic praecepto ἐξηγήσεως loco apud Matthaeum cap. 24. v. 44. subiicit: Estote parati. 3. perpetuam sobrietatem, uti patet ex eo, quòd praeceptum vigilantiae apud Lucam subiicitur dehortationi à crapula & ebrietate; uti etiam ex loco parallelo 1. Thess. 5. v. 4. & seqq. 4. in operibus vocationis sedulitatem, uti patet ex 2. Tim. 4. v. 5. & ex parabolade, talentis inter servos distributis, huic praecepto in cap. 25. Matth. subiecta. 5. securitatis & peccatorum fugam, ut ostendit collatio temporum novissimorum & antediluvianorum, quae huic vigilantiae praecepto apud Evangelistas praemittitur; uti etiam locorum parallelorum 1. Thess. 5. v. 3. & seqq. Apocal. 16. v. 15. &c. 6. in cavendis Satanae & mundi insidiis prudentiam. Ut enim, qui corporaliter dormit, non cavet sibi ab insidiis furum vel hostium: sic spiritualiter dormire censendus est, qui non observat Diaboli μεθοδείας.Eph. 6. v. 11. & varias perversi huius seculi insidias. 7. circumspectam corporis & animae custodiam, quia vigilantia studio virtutis, sc. castitati, sobrietati, orationi adminiculum non mediocre praestar. Quia ergò Petrus ex ore Magistri sui hanc exhortationem repetit, ideò haec omnia etiam ad praesens vigilantiae praeceptum accommodari possunt. Cumprimis vero per vigilantiam Apostolus hoc loco intelligit attentam & sollicitam salutis curam adversùs Satanae insidias, metaphorâ à castrensibus excubitoribus sumtâ. Quemadmodum miles in excubiis à Duce belli constitutus, non debet arma sua è pariete suspendere, atque altùm dormire, sed stare armis suis indutum & vigilare: sic pii debent esse muniti spirituali armaturâ fidei, spei & caritatis. Cùm sint filii lucis, abiiciant opera tenebrarum, & induant arma lucisRom. 13. v. 12.

Q. 12. An Diaboli nomine Princeps malorum Spirituum intelligatur? Nomen Diaboli in Scripturis non uno modo usurpatur. Accipitur enim vel ut proprium, vel ut appellativum. In priore significatione tribuitur. 1. Principi & capiti malorum Spirituum Matth. 25. v. 41.Apoc. 12. v. 9. quo sensu etiam accipi potest, quod Christus dicitur à Diabolo tentatusMatth. 4. v. 1.Luc. 4. v. 2. procul dubio enim non gregarius aliquis Diabolus ipsum oppugnavit, sed Princeps malignorum Spirituum omnes potentiae & scientiae suae vires adversus cum exeruit, undè Luc. 4. v. 13. dicitur, quod consummatâ omni tentatione, i. e. omnibus viribus & fraudibus frustrà tentatis Diabolus ab eo recesserit. 2. universo caetui malignorum Spirituum, Luc. 8. v. 12.Act. 10. v. 38.Eph. 6. v. 11. &c. Solet autem Scriptura de malis Spiritibus loqui numero singulari, quia sub capite suo constituunt certam quandam societatem ac regnum, quod Christo & ipsius regno opponitur. 3. hominibus impiis, qui sunt organa ac filii Diaboli, ut ipsos vocat Christus Ioh. 8. v. 44. & Paulus Act. 13. v. 10. Sic Christus Ioh. 6. v. 70. Iudam proditorem suum vocat Diabolum, quia in proditionis scelere sese organum Diaboli praebuit, ad regnum Diaboli pertinuit, Satanas, in ipsum intraverat Luc. 22. v. 3. ac fuit ἐνδιαβολισμένος, spiritualiter à Diabolo obsessus, Satanae mancipium & cloaca. In primâ significatione nomen Diaboli accipitur ἀτόμως, in secundâ συναγωγικῶς, in tertia μετωνυμικῶς. Appellativè sumitur nomen Diaboli pro quovis calumniatore, quae tamen significatio commodè referri posset ad proximè praecedentem, quia calumniatores sunt organa Diaboli. Eph. 4. v. 27.1. Tim. 3. v. 6. Hoc loco nomen Diaboli accipitur συναγωγικῶς, siquidem piis cum totâ Diabolicarum potestatum phalange est conflictandum. Eph. 6. v. 12.Non est nobis colluctatio adversus carnem & sanguinem, sed adversus Principes & potestates, adversùsκοσμοκράτοραςtenebrarum huius seculi, adversus spiritualia i. e. Spiritus nequitiae.

Q. 12. Quare Diabolus comparetur leoni? Resp. 1. propter robur ac validitatem. Prov. 30. v. 30.Leo bestiarum fortissimus. Hebr. fortis in animali sive inter animalia, ad nullius pavebit occursum. Hebr. non revertetur à facie cuius quam. Epiph. heres. 78. Leo est animal robore solidissimum, &, ut ita dicam, regalissimum super alia animalia. Sic de Diabolo sub figura Leviathan. dicitur Iob. 41. vers. 25.Non habet in terris similem, qui factus est, ut neminem timeret. 2. propter crudelitatem. Comparatur leoni rugienti i. e. famelico. Leo famelicus vel catulis orbatus obvios quosque, vel homines, vel bestias invadit, discerpit, devorat. Sic Diabolus maximam adversùs homines crudelitatem exercet. Leo sanguine delectatur: sic Diabolus est sanguinarius & crudelis, non contentus est hominum fortunis, sed sanguinem, imò animam ipsorum expetit. 3. propter animositatem. Leo ob rubor animosus est & audax: sic Diabolus non solùm viribus est robustissimus, sed etiam audaciâ promtissimus. 4. propter calliditatem. August. conc. 2. in Psalm. 90. & tract. 10. in Ioh. existimat, Diabolum comparari leoni, propter manifestam persecutionem contra Martyres: Draconi propter occultam, quam per haereticos excitat, ita ut apertè saeviens leo quaerat quem devoret; Draco quando insidietur; sed non deest etiam leoni astutia, proindè non tantùm propter crudelitatem, sed etiam propter calliditatem Diabolus leoni comparatur. Psal. 10. v. 8.Insidiatur in abscondito quasi leo in speluntâ. Leo vestigia pedum suorum arenâ per caudam attractâ abscondit. Epiphan. ad Physiolog. cap. 1. Contortis ingreditur pedibus, ac tanquam vagina conditis intus unguibus. Isidor. lib. 1. Etymol. cap. 2. ex Plutarcho in opusc. de animant. comparat. id quod hyberno tempore potissimùm ipsum facere asserunt, ne ex relictis in nive vestigiis à venatoribus deprehendatur & capiatur: sic Diabolus tentationum suarum vestigia tegit, ac vitia sub specie virtutis hominibus proponit, quâ de re Nazianz, in carm. de virtut. pulcherrimè disserit:

—————— Παλλάκι δὲ ἆυτεἘσθλοῦ τ᾽ ἡδὲ κακοῖο διάκρισιν ἐχθρὸς ἂμερσενὫς θὴρ κερδάλεος τις ὑπ᾽ ἲχνεσιν ἲχνια βάλλωνὫς κεν θηρητῆρα καλοῦ πλάξειε δολοῖσι.Saepe mihi rursus delectum subdolus hostisVirtutis vitiique adimens mea lumina fallit,Ut fera signa pedum, quae signis callida turbat,Hac venatorem virtutis laedat ut arte.

Leo apertis dormit oculis, imò dormiendo vigilat, caudamque movet, unde quidam putant, leonem nunquam dormire, habet enim oculos ingentes, palpebras v. exiles, ut totos oculos tegere nequeat, ideoque dictus leoὰ λὰω i. e. video, quis estὀξυδερκὴς:sic diabolus pervigilest, ut homini noceat. 5. propter nocendi cupiditatem. Apostolus non simpliciter comparat Diabolum leoni, sed leoni rugienti ac circumeundo quaerenti, quem devoret. Aristot. 9. de Hist. animal. cap. 44. & Plinius lib. 8. N.
