Deut. 32. v. 9.pars Domini populus eius Iacob &c.Psal. 77. v. 21.deduxisti sicut oves populum tuum.1. Tim. 4. v. 10.Deus est Salvator omnium hominum, maximè fidelium.

25. Bernh. serm 68. in Cant. monet. Petrum non dixisse, omnem solicitudinem proiicite in eum, ut sit ipsi cura de vobis, sed quia ipsi cura est de vobis, apertè monstrans Ecclesia sanctorum non modò quoniam dilecta, sed quod prius dilecta fuerit, quidem. Intendite illi, quia ipse intendit vobis.

26. Inexplicabilis in hac Dei pro nobis ac de nobis cura latet consolatio. Si enim Deo curae sumus, ergò ipse pater noster, ipse provisor noster, ipse patronus noster &c. Psal. 40. v. 18.Ego afflictus sum & pauper, Dominus solicitus est mei, vel cogitat pro me, in quae verba Aug. sic commentatur. Qui habuit tui curam antequam esses, quomodo non habebit curam cum iam hoc es, quod voluit, ut esses? Iam enim fidelis es, iam ambulas in via iustitiae &c. nusquam tibi deest, tu illi noli deesse, tu tibi noli deesse.

27. In Deum proiecti sumus ab uteroPsalm. 22. v. 10. hoc est, in ipsius fidem & clientelam, ergò etiam in ipsum omnem nostram solicitudinem proiicere debemus. Ipsi cura est de nobis. Ergò in ipsum omnem curam nostram coniicere debemus. Opem nobis ferre potest, ut Deus omnipotens, curam nostri gerit, ut fidelis pater. Matth. 6. v. 36.Novit pater vester, quia his omnibus indigetis. Aug. lib. 3. Confess. cap. 1. O tu bone omnipotens, qui sic curas unumquemque nostrûm, tanquam solum curas, & sic omnes tanquam singulos.

28. Ex ore Christi Magistri sui repetit Apostolus sobrietatis & vigilantiae praeceptum Luc. 21. v. 34.Attendite, ne corda vestra graventur crapula. Idem inculcat Paulus 1. Thess. 5. v. 5.Omnes vos filii lucis estis, & filii diei, non sumus noctis neque tenebrarum.v. 6.Igitur non dormiamus sicut caeteri, sed vigilemus & sobrii simus.

29. Prius est sobrium esse, deindè vigilare, quia sobrietas est vigilantiae parens, sicut contra saturitas somnum provocat, & crapula est mater dormitionis.

30. Sobrietas consistit in moderatione cibi & potus ac diligenti curâ, ne corda graventur crapula, per quam ad preces & opera pietatis, uti etiam vocationis homines inepti redduntur. Hieron. lib. 2. adv. Iovin. cap. 6. Adesse debet ratio, ut tales ac tantas sumamus escas, quibus non oneretur corpus & libertas animae praegravetur.

31. Vigilantia consistit in provida cura, ne per securitatem ac negligentiam in errores aut scelera insidiis Satanae inducamur, ficque gratiâ Dei & aeternâ salute excidamus. Phil. 2. v. 12.Cum timore & tremore salutem vestram operemini. Cyrillus Hierosolymit. catech. 4. Opus cum divina gratia sobriâ mente, & vigilantibus oculis, ut Zizania vitemus pro tritico, pro ove lupum, Diabolum pro Angelo bono. August. serm. 23. de verb. Dom. cap. 10. Corde vigila, fide vigila, spe vigila, caritate vigila, operibus vigila.

32. Vigilandi praeceptum etiam hoc monet, ut non segnescamus in pietatis cursu, ut non diligamus mundum, & ea, quae sunt in mundo 1. Ioh. 2. v. 15. quid enim aliud sunt honores, voluptates, divitiae huius mundi, quàm suavia somnia, quibus mundi amatores sese oblectant? ut versemur in perpetuis excubiis, ut attenti simus omni ex parte ad μεθοδείας & stratagemata Satanae.

33. Ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam permovere nos debet gravissimum periculum, cui singulis momentis sumus subiecti, videlicet insidiae Diaboli, qui in seductionem & exitium nostrum perpetuò est intentus. Matth. 26. v. 41.Vigilate & orate, ne intretis in tentationem. B. Lutherus in h. l. Talis vita nostra, ac si peregrinus veniret in hospitium, in quo omnes incolae essent latrones, ibi certè vigilaret, sese armaret ac muniret.

34. Diabolus perpetuò vigilat ad nos oppugnandos, necessarium igitur est, ut vigilemus ad ei resistendum. Cyprian. tract. de Zelo & livore. Contra omnes Diaboli vel fallaces insidias, vel apertas minas stare debet instructus animis & armatus, tàm paratus semper ad repugnandum, quàm est ad impugnandum semper paratus inimicus. Hieronymus Epist. 1. ad Heliodor. Insidiatur hic leo in spelunca sua, insidiatur ut rapiat pauperem, & tu frondosae arboris tectus umbraculo molles somnos futurus praeda capis?

35. Diabolus est noster adversarius, qui odium implacabile & bellum nobiscum gerit ἀσπονδον. Non est nobis colluctatio adversus carnem & sanguinem, sed adversus Principes & potestates; adversus κοσμοκράτορας &c. Eph. 6. v. 12. variae eius sunt μεθοδείαιv. 11.tela eius sunt ignitavers. 16. Inimicitiae inter ipsum & nos in Paradiso sunt constitutae Gen. 3. v. 15. in Baptismo ipsi & omnibus eius operibus renunciavimus, inde est perpetuus noster adversarius, & vita nostrae super terram est militia perpetua.Iob. 7. v. 1.

36. Diabolus non otiatur, non delassatur, non afficitur taedio, sed cupiditate nocendi impulsus perpetuò caruit, & obambulat. Inde etiam comparatur venatori solicitè feras investiganti, & laqueos eis ponenti Psalm. 91. vers. 3. In venatore deprehendimus primò vigilantiam, quia summo mane surgit, ut feras in cubilibus suis adhuc quiescentes investiget. Secundò indefessam industriam, quia omnia arbusta excutit, nulli labori parcit, tolerat imbres, aestum, frigus, famem, sitim, ut feras capiat. Tertiò fraudulentiam, quia multas vovit artes & insidias, quibus in cautas feras opprimat. Quartò vigilantiam, quia magno impetu in praedam oblatam atque captam irruit, quae omnia ad Diabolum accommodari possunt.

37. Circuit Diabolus, velut hostis urbem exercitu militari circumdatam quaerens, quâ parte irrumpere possit. Cyprianus serm. de Zelo & livore. Circuit ille nos singulos, & tanquam hostis clausos obfidens, muros explorat, & tentat, an sit pars aliqua murorum minùs stabilis & minùs fida, cuius aditu ad interiora penetretur. Offert oculis formas illices & faciles voluptates, ut visu destruat castitatem, Aures per canoram Musicam tentat, ut soni dulcioris auditu solvat & molliat Christianum vigorem. Linguam convitio provoeat, manum iniuriis lacessentibus ad petulantiam caedis instigat; ut fraudatorem faciat, lucra opponit iniusta: ut animam pecunia capiat, ingerit periculosa compendia honores terrenos promittit, ut coelestia adimat: ostèntat falsa, ut vera surripiat, & cum latenter non potest fallere, exertè atque apertè minatur, terrorem turbidae persecutionis intentans, ad debellandos Dei serves inquietus semper & infestus, in pace subdolus, in persecutione violentus, quem Cypriani locum integrum Beda in comm h. l. adducit. Hieronymus Epist. 1. ad Heliodor. Inde me persequitur luxuria, inde avaritia conatur irrumpere, inde venter meus vult mihi esse Deus pro Christo: compellit libido, ut habitantem Spiritum S. fugem, ut templum eius violem, persequitur inquam me hostis, cui nomina mille, mille nocendi artes &c. In illo aestu Charybdis luxuriae salutem vorat. Ibi ore virgineo ad pudicitiae perpetranda naufragia Scylla ceu renidens libido blanditur. Hîc barbarum littus, hîc Diabolus pirata cum Sociis portat vincula capiendis &c. Leo serm. 7. de nativit. Novit, cui adhibeat aesius cupiditatis, cui illecebras gulae ingerat, cui apponat incitamenta luxuriae, cui infundat virus invidiae: novit, quem errore conturbet, quem gaudio fallat, quem metu opprimat, quem admiratione seducat. Bernh. serm. 67. de modo bene viv. col. 1741. Amplius tentat Diabolus hominem ex parte illa, quâ eum videt per excrescentem humorem facilè inclinari ad vitia, ut secundùm humoris conspersionem adhibeat & tentationem. Confer Lactant. lib. 6. Instit.

38. Diabolus circuit quaerens praedam. Ergò negligit hos centare, cap. 4. quos iam antè quieto iure possidet. Esca eius cibur electusHab. 1. v. 16. quod huc accommodant Hieronymus Epist. 22. & Gregorius in 1. Reg. 9. Rectè Cyprianus l. 1. Epist. 1. Non quaerit Diabolus eos, quos iam subegit, aut gestit evertere, quos iam suos fecit. Inimicus & hostis Ecclesiae, quos alienavit ab Ecclesia & foras duxit, ut captivos & vinctos contemnit & praeterit, eos pergit lacessere, in quibus Christum cernit habitare.

39. Circuit Diabolus ut lupus ovium caulas; non tamen intrat, nisi spontè quis ianuam cordis sui ei aperiat; non illabitur, non irrumpit, nisi admissus. Chrysost. in cap. 4. Matth. Suggerere potest, cogere non potest. Persuadere potest, praecipitare non potest, inquit Hieronymus in cap. 4. Metaph.

40. Confertur Diabolus leoni rugienti, serpenti insidianti, Draeoni vigilanti Esai. 27. v. 1.Apoc. 12. v. 3. & 9. scorpioni pungenti Luc. 10. v. 19. volucri rapienti Matth. 13. v. 4. & 19. Syri Diabolum vocant דיוא ex Hebraeo דאה quod vulturem sive milvum significat. Matth. 9. v. 32.cap. 10. v. 8. &c.

41. Leoni huic rugienti opponamus leonem de tribu IudaApoc. 5. v. 5.à quo victus est & vinctus. Bernhardus serm. 13. in Psal. 9. habitat &c. Adversarius vester tanquam leo rugiens ait Petrus. Gratias magno illi leoni de tribu Iuda: rugire iste potest, ferire non potest. Rugiat, quantum vult, tantùm non fugiat ovis Christi. Quanta minatur, quanta exaggerat, quanta intentat, non simus bestiae, ut nos prosternat vacuus illo rugitus. Sic enim perhibent, qui talia curio siùs vestigaverunt, ad rugitum leonis nullam bestiam stare posse, ne eam quidem, quae adversus ictum eius tota animositate repugnat, & plerunque, superat ferientem, quae non sustinet rugientem. Verè bestia, verè rationis expers, qui tam pusillanimis est, ut solo timore cedat, qui sola futuri exaggeratione laboris victus, ante conflictum non telo, sed tubâ prosternitur. Nondum restitistis usque ad sangvinem, ait strenuus ille dux, quileonis huius noverat vanum esse rugitum. Et alius quidam: Resistite, inquit, Diabolo & fugiet à vobis. Gerson. de consolat. Theol. lib. 3. prosa. 4. Terret Deus ligatum leonem infernalem, ne furiat, quantum vellet, non ille, sed detinens eum rogandus est.

42. Tria adversus Diaboli oppugnationem monstrantur nobis armorum genera. 1. resistentia. Primus ad victoriam gradus est resistere, quia Diabolus, cum ei resistitur, debilis est ut formica; cum vero eius suggestio recipitur, fortis est ut leo. 2. robur animi, quia fortem Diabolum facit non illius potentia, sed nostra negligentia. Bernhardus Epist. 1. col. 757. Libentiùs te insequitur adversarius fugientem, quàm sustineat repugnantem, & audacius insistit à tergo, quàm resistat in faciem. 3. Fides, quae est scutum illud fortissimum, quo omnia tela nequissimi ignea excipere & extinguere possumus. Eph. 6. v. 16. Thomas Anglicus in h. l. Quemadmodum in Diabolo perversitas denotatur per nomen adversarii; robur per nomen leonis; crudelitas, cum rugiens dicitur; solicitudo, cum circumeundo quaerere: sic à nobis exigitur contra primum, ut resistamus; contra secundum, ut simus fortes; contra tertium, ut fidei mansuetudinem habeamus; contra ultimum, ut vigilemus.

42. In verbo verâ & firmâ fide apprehenso consistit omnis nostra contra Diabolum victoria. Hoc Spiritus gladio instructi, hoc verbi scuto muniti omnibus Satanae tentationibus resistere possumus. Si falsum dogma Diabolus nobis persuadere cupit, opponamus antidotum coelestis verbi. Si ad vindictae cupiditatem, ad libidinem & alia peccata nos impellere voluerit, opponamus divinas comminationes. Si dubitationem inspirat & pusillanimes nos reddere teneat, opponamus divinas promissiones. Nulla potest nominari tentatio Diaboli, contra quam non habeatur speciale alexipharmacum in verbo Dei.

44. Diabolus fugatur fide, sicut leo igne. In fide contra Satanam victoria, quia fides cum Christo victore nos unit. Isidorus lib. 3. de summ. bono cap. 5. Ab incredulis Diabolus ut leo timetur, à fortibus in fide ut vermis contemnitur atque ad momentum ostensus repellitur.

45. Cum Apostolus à Satana nos oppugnari dixisset, statim omne genus afflictionum nomine τῶν παθημάτων complectitur, ex quo apparet, etiam in reliquis adversis cum ipso luctandum esse, quippe per quae ad impatientiam nos solicitat.

46. Magnum consolationis in persecutionibus propter veritatem Evangelicam est argumentum societas aliorum fidelium. Cùm enim illi sint fratres nostri, ideò non debemus communem cum ipsis sortem recusare, nec propriam postulare. Non sum melior Patribus meis, dicebat Elias propheta. 1. Reg. 19. v. 4. dicamus & nos: Non sumus meliores fratribus nostris. Beda in h. l. Quod à constitutione mundi semper passi sunt iusti, pudeat nos solos prae omnibus sustinere non posse.

47. Non afflictionum tantùm, sed etiam precum ac pugnae contra Satanam, societas cum reliquis fidelibus nobis intercedit. Non solùm sunt nostrorum παθημάτων συμμέτοχοι, sed etiam in precibus & pugna contra Satanam nostri συμπαλαιστρίται atque σύμμαχοι. Ergò haec consolatio non tantùm consistit in exemplo, sed etiam in fidei unitate, in qua omnes fideles in Christo victore & capite suo fortes contra communem hostem pugnant, & in precum coniunctione, quibus in hac pugna συναγωινζουσι, seseque mutuò adiuvant. Inde in spirituali πανοπλίᾳ Apostolus etiam mentionem facit προσκαρτερήσεως ac δεήσεως περὶ πάντων τῶν ἁγίων.Ephes. 6. vers. 18. Oecumenius in h. l. Gravitatem alleviat societas consortum, ut animi magnitudinem contra adversarium Diabolum praester, quia non soli sumus, qui cum eo pugnamus, sed omnes boni & Christi electi.

48. Credentes sunt fratres, qui habent unum patrem in coelis, à quo eandem expectant hereditatem. Eph. 4. v. 4. & 6. Communem etiam habent fratrem Christum, propter quem ac per quem à Deo in filios adoptati sunt, & Spiritu eius coniuncti; communem insuper habent matrem Ecclesiam, quae ipsos sinu suo fovet. Minutius Felix in Octavio. Fratres vocamur, ut unius Dei parentis homines, ut consortes fidei, ut spei coheredes. Quia ergò fideles sunt fratres, ideò affectio ipsorum debet esse fraterna. Si fratrum iuxta carnem concordia est naturalis, multò magis fratribus Spiritualibus concordia debet esse commendata.

49. Passiones, quae nobis incumbunt, eaedem in fraternitate, quae est in mundo, perficiuntur. Nimirum quia Christus corporis mystici caput in mundo passus est, ideò omnia vera & viva corporis mystici, quod Ecclesia, membra in hoc mundo oportet pati, ut mensura passionum à Deo definita in hoc mystico corpore compleaetur. Col. 1. v. 24.

50. Deus est Deus omnis gratiae & omnium charismatum. Ipsi ergò omne bonum & omne donum acceptum ferendum Iac. 1. vers. 17. & iuxta Dei voluntatem cum aliis communicandum 1. Petr. 4. vers. 10.

51. Deus est Deus gratiae, est etiam Deus gloriae. Act. 7. vers. 2.gratiam igitur & gloriam dabit Dominus.Psal. 84. v. 12. Ut est Deus omnis gratiae, ita quoque pater misericordiarum2. Cor. 1. v. 3. nimirum quia ex ipsius gratia & misericordia varia beneficia ad nos proveniunt, inter quae est donatio Spititus sancti, qui est Spiritus gratioZach. 12. v. 10.Hebr. 10. v. 29. ac donatio vitae aeternae, quae estχάρισμαin Christo Iesu.Rom. 6. v. 23.

52. Vocatio nostra est merè gratuita, utpote à DEO omnis gratiae profecta. Gratias ergò DEO, à quo vocati sumus, debitas agamus, & vocatione illâ dignos nos geramus. Ephes. 4. vers. 1.

53. Tria aptissimè coniunguntur ab Apostolo, vocatio, quae est salutis nostrae principium, per quam ad gloriam aeternam sumus vocati; Christus, qui est salutis nostrae meritum & via ad illam gloriam Ioh. 14. vers. 6. & gloria aeterna, quae est salutis nostrae finis & plena possessio, quaeque persolùm Christum nobis constat Rom. 6. vers. 23.Eph. 2. v. 8.Tit. 3. vers. 5. Lex dicit, obedientiam sibi perfectè praestitam esse viam ad illam gloriam, sed Evangelium docet, Christum esse viam, unde hîc in Christo dicimur vocati ad aeternam Dei gloriam.

54. Quando Apostolus divinae gratiae tribuit καταρτισμὸν, στήριξιν, σθένωσιν ac θεμελίωσιν, ostendit principium, medium & finem nostrae salutis, adeòque etiam nostram perseverantiam esse opus Dei; admonet etiam nos nostrae infirmitatis in cruce patienter ferenda, & impellit nos, ut ad Deum per serias preces confugientes ab ipso conservationem in bono & consummationem operis boni petamus.Phil. 1. v. 6.

55. Quod pluribus verbis nostram in bono conservationem Apostolus exprimit, eo ipso ostendit, magnae omninò difficultatis esse ad finem usque in bono perseverare & in cruce perdurare, proinde etiam speciali Dei gratiâ & virtute opus esse. 1. Petr. 1. vers. 5.

56. Gloria Dei aeterna, ad quam credentes in Christo vocati sunt, opponitur aeternae ignominiae & opprobrio, cui Diaboli & omnes damnati in die iudicii & in igne inferni erunt obnoxii. Esai. 66. v. 24.erunt abominatio omni carni.Dan. 12. v. 2.evigilabunt in ignominiam sempiternam.

57. In persecutionibus propter Evangelium soletur nos, tùm afflictonum cum hac vita terminandarum brevitas Esai. 54. v. 7. & 8.2. Cor. 4. v. 17.1. Petr. 1. v. 6. tùm divinae praesentiae suavitas Psal. 91. v. 15.Esai. 43. v. 2. &c.

58. Quoties in beneficiorum Dei mentionem incidimus, in glorificationem divini nominis erumpere debemus. Eo namque fine Deus sua in nos confert beneficia, ut in hae & futura vita à nobis glorificetur. Bernhardus serm. contra ingrat. Felix est, qui ad singula dona gratiae redit ad eum, in quo est plenitudo omnium gratiarum.

59. Duo maximi ab hominibus fiunt; gloria, sive famae celebritas, & imperium sive potestas, utraque vero unicè Deo per glorificationem tribuenda. Sicut omnia flumina ex mari oriuntur: ita omnia bona ex fonte divinae gratiae profluunt. Ut ergò omnia flumina in mare revertuntur, sic omnia bona per gratiarum actionem & glorificationem ad Deum sunt referenda Eccl. 1. v. 1.

60. Usus bonorum divinitùs in nos collatorum debetur proximo, gloria illorum debetur DEO. August. soliloq. cap. 15. Qui de bono tuo ô Domine gloriam sibi quaerit & non tibi, hic fur est & latro, & similis est Diabolo, qui voluit furari gloriam tuam.

61. Deo soli competit robur & imperium. Ipse est solus potens Rex Regum, & Dominus dominantium1. Tim. 6. v. 15.Tua est Domine magnificentia & gloria, atque victoria, & tibi laus, cuncta enim, quae in coelo sunt & in term, tua sunt: tuum, Domine, regnum, & tu es elevatus super omnes Principes; tuae divitiae & tua est gloria, tu dominaris omnium, in manu tua virtus & potentia, in manu tua magnificare & confortare unumquemque, inquit David 1. Paral. 29. v. 11. & 12. Inde etiam apud Hebraeos Deus vocatur האלille fortis, & à recentioribus Iudaeis הגבורהκατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν summa illa potestas, Deus in sua fortitudine & potentia. Quò referri potest, quae Lucas cap. 22. v. 69. dicit, filium hominis sedereἐκ δεξιῶν τῆς δυνάμεως τοῦ θεοῦ illud Matthaeum c. 26. v. 64. simpliciter sic efferre, Filius hominis sedetἐκ δεξῶν τῆς δυνάμεως.

62. Quia totum & omne bonum nostrum, quod habemus, à Deo descendit: quia solius Dei beneficium est, quod sumus ad aeternam gloriam vocati, quod in persecutionibus conservamur, quod benè operamur, quod Satanae tentationes superamus, quod perficimur, stabilimur, roboramur, fundamur &c. ideò perpetuis laudum praeconiis ipsum celebremus. Spirituale & Deo gratum sacrificium est laudum divinarum praeconium. Vicissim quia solus Deus supremum in coelo ac terra obtinet dominium, ideò ipsum solum timeamus, ab ipso auxilium & defensionem petamus, ipsi humiliter nos subiiciamus &c.

## 5:7
CASTING ALL YOUR ANXIETY UPON HIM, BECAUSE HE HAS CARE FOR YOU.

Connection. 1. The Apostle continues in the response to the objection that contempt and oppression follow humiliation, and he commends the providence of God even more expressly. We think that by our submission and modesty the reins are loosened for the lust of the impious, so that they may insult us with greater audacity and petulance. But the Apostle responds that this thought and care is to be cast into the bosom of God, lest anyone fear that he will be despised by too much self-dejection.

2. Because the humble are for the most part trampled and harassed by the more powerful who behave themselves more insolently, by a certain prolepsis he warns that they should cast all care upon God, and in his providence humbly acquiesce, lest they grow weary under this burden, and begin to murmur out of impatience. Many cares and many anxieties weigh upon the humble: he shows, therefore, upon whose shoulders they ought to cast them, and to unburden themselves of them, so that humility may be joyful and peaceful.

3. The participle ἐπιῤῥίψαντες placed in the aorist shows that this sentence refers to the preceding verb ταπεινώθητε, and has been added so that it may be signified what, among other things, that humiliation of ours under the mighty hand of God demands, namely, the casting of all our cares upon God. Some, however, prefer that the participle ἐπιῤῥίψαντες is placed in the stead of the indicative through a common Hebraism.

4. Luther in this place teaches such a connection. No one humbles himself with a calm mind, since that serpentine seed is implanted in the hearts of all men by Nature, You shall be as Gods. Gen. 3. v. 5. Therefore Peter invites us to the study of humility with the most gentle words.

5. To the exhortation to humility, the Apostle adds an exhortation to filial trust, admonishing that we cast all our care and anxiety upon God, having considered both His power, of which he had made mention in the preceding, and His fatherly benevolence, of which he adds, for He cares for you.

Disposition. There are two parts of the verse. 1. The Apostolic admonition to filial trust, which is amplified by a note of Universality, casting all your anxiety upon Him. 2. The argument of this admonition taken from the special providence and fatherly care of God.

Exposition of the text. Πᾶσαν τὴν μέριμναν ὑμῶν ἐπιῤῥίψαντες ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν. The Vulgate rendered it, casting all your anxiety upon Him. But in the Greek it is an aorist. Having cast all your anxiety upon Him, or as Erasmus rendered it, having thrown all care upon Him. The passage is taken from Ps. 55. v. 23. ἐπιῤῥίψον ἐπὶ κύριον τὴν μέριμνάν σου, where in the Hebrew it is השלך cause to be sent, or cast upon the Lord יהבך your burden, for so the Hebrews explain it by פעונך your load. LXX. μέριμνάν σου, whereas otherwise יהב signifies a gift, by which reasoning the sense would be, whatever you seek to be given or gifted to you, cast upon the Lord.

The word ἐπιῤῥίπτειν is used only twice in the New Testament, in this place and Luke 39. v. 35. where the discourse is about the hurried casting of garments upon the colt, which meaning can be beautifully accommodated here, so that the sense may be that we ought not to struggle for a long time with the weight of our cares, but immediately relieve ourselves of it and cast it upon the Lord. The interlinear Gloss adds, casting all your care upon him as an anchor in the sea. The Syriac has the word [consult facsimile image] he cast away, he cast forth.

Μέριμνα signifies a solicitous and doubtful care, which divides the mind into different parts as it were, from μερίζειν τὸν νοῦν,, which effect of care Virgil most elegantly expressed in the 4th Aeneid, where, when he had said,

——— he fluctuates with a great tide of cares, he adds, And he divides his swift mind now hither, now thither, And snatches it into various parts, and turns it through everything.

Μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτον Matt. 13. v. 22.Mark 4. v. 19. are called cares concerning food and clothing, concerning acquiring and preserving riches, which are otherwise called μέριμναι βιωτικαὶ Luke 21. v. 34. μέριμναι τῶν τοῦ κόσμου 1. Cor. 7. vers. 33. & 34. The Syriac has the noun [consult facsimile image] from the root [consult facsimile image] he was solicitous. Places parallel to this one of ours are Matt. 6. v. 25.Luke 12. v. 22. μὴ μεριμνᾶτε τῆ ψυχῆ ὑμῶν Matt. 6. v. 34. μὴ οὖν μεριμνήσατε εἰς τὸ ἄυριον. Phil. 4. v. 6. μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε. The little word πᾶσαν is ἐμφατικὴ, all your care, whatever cares weigh upon you, cast that whole and entire thing upon him. The interlinear Gloss, Cast all care of body and soul upon him. ὅτι αὐτῷ μέλει περι ὑμῶν. In Psalm 55. v. 23. from which this sentence is brought, it is added והוא יכלכלך and he himself will nourish you, he will not give the righteous to shaking forever. כלכל & יכל is, he sustained, he bore, he carried Job 31. v. 23.v. 2.Mal. 3. v. 2. The sense therefore is, God will not only bear the weight of your cares, but he will also carry and support you yourself. It also signifies he nourished, he fed, Gen. 45. v. 11.2. Sam. 19. v. 32.Zech. 11. v. 16. as the Targum rendered יזון, and the LXX διατρέψει, as also the Latin version, He himself will nourish you. Peter gathers the genus from the species. For God, for him who in true confidence casts all his anxiety upon Him, not only provides for food, but also defends him, delivers him, and provides for him all things which are necessary for this and the future life. Peter embraces all these things when he says, He has care for you, He himself knows and loves you, He pursues you with special favor, He knows what you need Matt. 6. v. 32. what evils press upon you, what dangers hang over you. The Syrian has the word [consult facsimile image] which means by ceasing he made void, and through ἀντὶφρασιν it was a care to him, anxiety lay upon him 1. Cor. 9. v. 10. The sense therefore is, He himself anxiously cares for you, therefore there is no reason why you should macerate yourselves with useless cares and anxieties. And because words of affection among the Hebrews connote effects, therefore through this care and anxiety of God it is insinuated that He is going to be present to us with His help and protection, about to defend and deliver us, just as it is said in the parallel passage Phil. 4. v. 5. The Lord is near. v. 6. be anxious for nothing.

Latin:

OMNEM SOLICITUDINEM VESTRAM PROIICIENTES IN EUM, QUONIAM IPSI CURA EST DE VOBIS.

Connexio. 1. Pergit Apostolus in responsione ad obiectionem, quòd contemtus & oppressio humiliationem sequatur, & expressiùs adhuc Dei providentiam commendat. Putamus nostrâ submissione & modestiâ frena laxari impiorum libidini, ut maiore audacia ac petulantiâ nobis insultent. Sed respondet Apostolus, in sinum Dei hanc cogitationem atque curam esse coniiciendam, ne quisquam nimia sui deiectione se contemtum iri metuat.

2. Quia humiles plerunque à potentioribus insolentiùs sese gerentibus calcantur ac divexantur, per prolepsin quandam monet, ut omnem curam in Deum coniiciant, & in ipsius providentia humiliter acquiescant, ne sub hoc onere fatiscant, & ex impatientia obmurmurare incipiant. Multae humilibus incumbunt curae multae solicitudines: ostendit igitur, in cuius humeros eas reiicere, seseque illis exonerare debeant, ut sit laeta & pacata humilitas.

3. Participium ἐπιῤῥίψαντες in aoristo positum ostendit, hanc sententiam referri ad verbum praecedens ταπεινώθητε, & additam esse, ut significetur, quid inter alia postulet illa nostri humiliatio sub potenti manu Dei, videlicet omnium curarum nostrarum in Deum coniectionem. Quidam tamen malunt participium ἐπιῤῥίψαντες per usitatum Hebraismum positum esse loco indicativi.

4. Lutherus in h. l. tradit eiusmodi connexionem. Nemo se aquo animo humiliat, cum semen illud serpentinum sit omnium hominum cordibus per Naturam insitum, Eritis sicut Dii.Gen. 3. v. 5. ideò Petrus blandissimis verbis ad studium humilitatis invitat.

5. Exhortationi ad humilitatem subiungit Apostolus exhortationem ad filialem fiduciam, admonens, ut omnem nostram curam & solicitudinem in Deum coniiciamus, consideratâ tùm eius potentiâ, de qua in praecedentibus mentionem fecerat, tùm paterna benevolentia, de qua subiungit, ipsi enim curae est de vobis.

Dispositio. Partes versiculi duae sunt. 1. Apostolicum ad filialem fiduciam monitum, quod amplificatur per notam Universalitatis, omnem vestram solicitudinem proiicientes in eum. 2. Moniti huius argumentum à speciali Dei providentia & cura paterna desumtum.

Textus expositio. Πᾶσαν τὴν μέριμναν ὑμῶν ἐπιῤῥίψαντες ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν. Vulg. reddidit, omnem solicitudinem vestram proiicientes in eum. Sed in Graeco est aoristus. Omni solicitudine vestrâ proiectâ in eum, vel ut Erasmus reddidit, omni curâ coniectâ in eum. Locus desumtus est ex Ps. 55. v. 23.ἐπιῤῥίψον ἐπὶ κύριον τὴν μέριμνάν σου, ubi in Hebraeo est השלךfac mitti, vel proiice super Dominumיהבךpondus tuum, ita enim exponunt Hebraei per פעונךonus tuum. LXX.μέριμνάν σου, cum aliàs יהב significet donum, quâ ratione esset sensus, quicquid tibi dari, donarive expetis, super Dominum proiice.

Verbum ἐπιῤῥίπτειν bis duntaxat in N. Test. usurpatur, hoc loco & Luc 39. v. 35. ubi de festinata vestimentorum in pullum iniectione sermo est, quae significatio pulchrè huc accommodari potest, ut sit sensus, quòd cum pondere curarum nostrarum non debeamus diu luctari, sed statim eo nos levare, & in Dominum illud coniicere Gloss. interl. addit. omnem solicitudinem vestram proiicientes in eum tanquam anchoram in mari. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image]abiecit, proiecit.

Μέριμνα significat curam solicitam ac dubiam, quae mentem in partes diversas velut dividit, à μερίζειν τὸν νοῦν, quem curae effectum elegantissimè expressit Virgilius 4. Aeneid. ubi cum dixisset.

——— magno cur arum fluctuat aestu, subiungit,Atque animum celerem nunc huc, nunc dividit illuc,In partesque rapit varias, perque omnia versat.

Μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτονMatth. 13. v. 22.Marc. 4. v. 19. dicuntur solicitudines de victu & amictu, de divitiis acquirendis & conservandis, quae aliàs vocantur μέριμναι βιωτικαὶLuc. 21. v. 34.μέριμναι τῶν τοῦ κόσμου1. Cor. 7. vers. 33. & 34. Syrus habet nomen [consult facsimile image] à rad. [consult facsimile image]solicitus fuit. Loca huic nostro parallela sunt. Matth. 6. v. 25.Luc. 12. v. 22.μὴ μεριμνᾶτε τῆ ψυχῆ ὑμῶνMatth. 6. v. 34.μὴ οὖν μεριμνήσατε εἰς τὸ ἄυριον.Phil. 4. v. 6.μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε. Vocula πᾶσαν est ἐμφατικὴ, omnem solicitudinem vestram, quicquid curarum vobis incumbit, illud totum & omne in ipsum proiicite. Gloss. interlin. Omnem solicitudinem corporis & animae in ipsum proiicite.ὅτι αὐτῷ μέλει περι ὑμῶν. In Psalmo. 55. v. 23. ex quo haec sententia est adducta, additur והוא יכלכלך& ipse te enutriet, non dabit in seculum nutationem iusto.כלכל & יכלest, sustinuit, tulit, portavitIob. 31. v. 23.v. 2.Mal. 3. v. 2. Sensus igitur est, Deus non solùm pondus tuarum curarum, sed etiam teipsum feret & portabit. Significat etiam nutrivit, aluit, Gen. 45. v. 11.2. Sam. 19. v. 32.Zach. 11. v. 16. quomodo reddidit Targum יזון, & LXX. διατρέψει, uti etiam Latina versio, ipse enutriet te. Potrus ex specie colligit genus. Deus enim illi, qui in vera fiducia omnem solicitudinem suam in ipsum proiicit, non sosolùm de alimentis prospicit, sed etiam ipsum defendit, liberat eique omnia praestat, quae ad hanc & futuram vitam ipsi necessaria. Haec omnia complectitur Petrus, quando dicit, ipsi cura est de vobis, ipse novit & diligit vos, speciali favore vos prosequitur, novit quibus indigeatis Matth. 6. vers. 32. quae mala vos premant, quae pericula vobis impendeant. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] quod significat cessando irritum fecit, & per ἀντὶφρασινcurae ipsi fuit, solicitudo ipsi incubuit1. Cor. 9. v. 10. Sensus igitur est, ipse solicitè vos curat, ergò non est, quod inutilibus curis ac solicitudinibus vos maceretis. Et quia verba affectûs apud Hebraeos connotant effectus, ideò per hanc Dei curam & solicitudinem insinuatur, quod auxilio & praesidio suo nobis praesto sit futurus, nos defensurus & liberaturus, sicut in loco parallelo dicitur Phil. 4. v. 5.Dominus prope est.v. 6.nihil soliciti sitis.

## 5:8
BE SOBER, AND WATCH, BECAUSE YOUR ADVERSARY THE DEVIL AS A ROARING LION GOES ABOUT, SEEKING WHOM HE MAY DEVOUR.

Connection. 1. After the Apostle had exhorted everyone to humility and confidence, now furthermore he exhorts them to sobriety and vigilance.

2. Already before in the preceding chapter, verse 7, he had given the precept of sobriety and vigilance to those to whom he writes, but in this place he repeats it anew on account of the supreme necessity of this virtue, so that they might have it commended to themselves with greater zeal.

3. Christ Luke 21. v. 34. and 36. had joined the dehortation from gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and the exhortation to vigilance opposed to it; Peter, insisting upon the footsteps of this his Master, after he had taught that all anxiety must be cast upon God, subjoins the exhortation to sobriety and vigilance.

4. The interlinear Gloss hands down such a connection. Thus cast your care upon God, so that you also may work together with the assisting grace. Lest we abuse that consolation, that God has care for us, unto security, the Apostle warns us concerning the snares of Satan. Bernh. serm. 11. in Psal. 90. Just as God is solicitous for us, and has care for us: So the Devil is solicitous, that he may slaughter and destroy us, and his one care is, lest by chance he who has turned away, should return.

Disposition. There are two parts of the verse. 1. The Apostolic exhortation. 2. The reason for the exhortation. The exhortation requires. 1. sobriety. 2. vigilance. The reason for the exhortation is sought from the danger in which the pious live as long as they live on this earth, namely from the snares of the Devil. He amplifies that danger by two adjuncts of our enemy. 1. From the strength and validity of the Devil, when he compares him to a lion. 2. From the desire of harming, when 1. he calls him our ἀντίδικον. 2. compares him to a roaring lion. 3. he attributes to him the zeal of swallowing us up.

Exposition of the text. Νήψατε, γρηγορήσατε. The Vulgate rendered it. Be sober and watch. But in the Greek ἀσυνδέτως these are joined not without emphasis. Be sober, watch. The Syrian likewise added the copulative O. Concerning the word νήψατε we have treated above cap. 1. vers. 13. cap. 4. vers. 7. The Vulgate Interpreter had translated that in that place, watch, but because he saw that, on account of the following word γρηγορῄσατε it could not be rendered thus in this place, therefore he translated, be sober, which meaning he could have followed above as well. The Syrian in this place likewise, as in cap. 4. vers. 7. rendered [consult facsimile image] watch, which Matth. 24. vers. 42. uses for γρηγορεῖτε, lest therefore he should be forced to repeat the word of watching twice in this place, for γρηγορεῖτε, which follows in the Apostle, he placed another, concerning which we shall see later. It is most simply established that τὸ νήφειν here signifies sobriety, that is, temperance in food and drink, so that in this way the Apostolic precept may agree with the Lord's precept Luc. 21. v. 34. Take heed, lest your hearts be burdened with surfeiting and drunkenness. 1. Thessal. 5. vers. 8. But we who are of the day, νήφομεν 2. Timoth. 4. vers. 5. νῆφε ἐν πᾶσιν. 1. Petr. 1. vers. 13. νήϕοντες.

Γρηγορεῖν, and what is more customary ἐγρηγορεῖν, is properly used concerning the wakefulness of the body Nehem. 7. v. 3. Matth. 26. v. 40. Marc. 14. vers. 37. 1. Thess. 5. v. 10. and is opposed to the word καθέυδειν. But in this place metaphorically is understood as the wakefulness of the soul and the vigilance of the mind, whence Ioh. Huss. at this place rightly annotates thus: Be sober in body, be vigilant in mind. Examples of this meaning, which is more frequent in Christ and the Apostles than the former, occur everywhere Matth. 25. v. 13. Luc. 12. v. 37. Act. 20. v. 31. 1. Cor. 16. v. 13. Col. 4. v. 2. 1. Thess. 5. v. 6. Apoc. 3. v. 2. cap. 3. v. 3. cap. 16. v. 15. The LXX use this verb for שקד he watched over some thing, he was intent upon some business, he was solicitous about some matter Ier. 1. v. 12. cap. 31. v. 28. Thren. 1. v. 1. etc. and it always includes a certain alacrity of mind, which meaning approaches most closely to the metaphorical. The Syrian in this place rendered it by [consult facsimile image] be mindful, as if in Greek it were μνήσθητε or μνημονέυετε, for which the Syrian uses this word Iohann. 15. vers. 20. because that spiritual vigilance includes among other things also this, that we be mindful of those things which Christ and the Apostles foretold to us, as also of the consolation which they proposed to us in the word. The places parallel to this of ours are. Matth. 24. vers. 42. γρηγορεῖτε watch, because you do not know at what hour the Lord is to come. c. 15. v. 13. γρηγορεῖτε watch, because you know neither the day nor the hour in which the son of man will come. cap. 26. v. 41. γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσέυχεθε. Marc. 13. v. 33. ἀγρυπνεῖτε καὶ προσέυχεθε. v. 35. γρηγορεῖτε watch, because you do not know when the master of the house will come. v. 37. What I say to you, I say to all γρηγορεῖτε. cap. 14. v. 38. γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσέυχεσθε. Luc. 21. vers. 36. ἀγρυπνεῖτε ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ δεόμενοι. 1. Cor. 16. v. 13. γρηγορεῖτε, στήκετε ἐν τῆ πίστει. Eph. 6. v. 18. ἀγρυπνοῦντες ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει καὶ δεήσει. Col. 4. v. 2. τῇ προσευχῇ προσκαρτερεῖτε, γρηγοροῦντες ἐν αὐτῇ. 1. Thess. 5. v. 6. γρηγορῶμεν καὶ νήφωμεν, 1. Petr. 4. v. 7. σωφρονήσατε καὶ νήψατε εἰς τὰς προσευχὰς. Apoc. 3. v. 2. γίνου γρηγορῶν. from which parallel places the best exposition of all of this precept concerning vigilance is gathered.

Ὅτι ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν διάβολος ὡς λέων ὠρυόμενος περιπατεῖ, ζητῷν τινα καταπίῃ. This is the reason for the precept toward sobriety and vigilance, in which there are as many weights of sentences as there are words.

First, he calls that enemy of ours, with whom ἄσπονδον and a perpetual war intervenes for us, our ἀντίδικον. Ἀντίδικος properly it is an adversary litigating in judgment against another, in which meaning it is used Matth. 5. vers. 25. παραδῶ ὁ ἀντίδικος τῷ κριτῇ ibid. Be well-disposed τῷ ἀντιδίκω σου. Luke 12. v. 58. μετὰ τοῦ ἀντιδίκου σου εἰς ἀρχοντα. chap. 18. v. 9. ἐκδίκησόν μου ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀντιδίκου. Aeschines against Ctesiphon. καὶ τοὺς λόγους ἐκφέρων τοῖς ἀντιδίκοις. In Plato, book 12 of the Laws, ἀντιδικοῦντες ἑκατέροι they are called actor & defendant. When therefore Peter calls the Devil our ἀντίδικον. he warns us that he is our κατήγορος κατηγορῶν ἡμῶν ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς Apoc. 12. verse 10. because τοῦ ἀντιδίκου ἔστιν ἡ κατηγορία ἐνώπιον τοῦ κριτοῦ. the LXX Isaiah 41. v. 11. use for איש ויב a man of a lawsuit or of contention, who is described in the same place ἐξηγητικῶς as being incensed against someone 1. Sam. 2. v. 9. for מריב contending or quarreling. The Syrian rendered it [consult facsimile image] i.e. Lord or possessor of hatred, that is, your enemy, who perpetually burns with hatred against you. Moreover, the name ἀντίδικος corresponds to the Hebrew שטן adversary, enemy Num. 22. v. 22. 1. Sam. 29. v. 4. which is attributed through ἀντονομασίαν to the Devil, who is the sworn and perpetual enemy of the human race Job 1. verse 6. Zech. 3. verse 1. etc. 2. Cor. 12. v. 7. Apoc. 12. verse 9. Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho, p. 259, thinks that the name שטן is composed of שטה he turns himself away, he withdrew, he declined, and נס serpent נחש serpent, but the Arameans elide the ח guttural, therefore it becomes נש, for ש they place ס ) for thus he writes. Moses calls the Devil a serpent, by Jesus he is called Satan, the name being congruent with the very things which he did, and indicating that it is composed from there. For Sata in the voice of the Jews and Syrians is an apostate and deserter, but the name Nas, from which by interpretation he is also called a serpent, is the same as Sata explained in the Hebrew language, from both of which one compound name is made, Satanas. Irenaeus insists on the footsteps of Justin, book 5, chapter 18, p. 343. The word Satana in Hebrew signifies an apostate, for he who was previously a good Angel turned himself away from God and defected. But it is more correctly deduced from שטן, which signifies he has acted as an adversary, he hindered, he disparaged. 1. Because the Holy Spirit himself shows this etymology Zech. 3. verse 1. And he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the Angel of the Lord והשטן and Satan was standing at his right hand לשטנו so that it might truly be what was said, that he might act as an adversary to him. 2. Because in the N.T. he is called Σατᾶν & Σατανᾶ 2. Cor. 12. v. 7. Which Apoc. 12. v. 9. chapter

20. v. 2. it is called Σατανᾶς,, that happens by Greek inflection. 3. because our Apostle interprets this name by ἀντίδικον. Aug. in qq. ex N. T. q. 90. The name Satan is a name of work, not of Nature. Caesarius Dial. 1. Thence that malignant Spirit is called Satan, because he is opposed to GOD & to men.

Secondly, he calls that enemy of ours διάβολον,, by which name he is everywhere distinguished in the N. T. Matth. 4. vers. 1. & following cap. 13. v. 39.cap. 25. v. 41.Luc. 4. v. 2. Moreover ὁ διάβολος ἀπὸ τοῦ διαβάλλειν is said to calumniate, whence the appellative name διαβόλου is sometimes used for a man a calumniator 1. Timoth. 3. vers. 11.2. Timoth. 3. vers. 3.Tit. 2. vers. 3. in which sense some also take the passage Eph. 4. v. 27. & 1. Timoth. 3. v. 6. Why this name is attributed to Satan, the pious ancients explain the cause of that matter most beautifully. Iustinus in paraen. 1. ad Graecos p. 21. ἐχθρὸν τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος Διάβολον αἱ θειαὶ γραφαί καλοῦσιν ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης αὐτοῦ πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον διαβολής τάυτης τῆς προσηγορίας τυχόντα. The divine Scriptures call the Devil the enemy of the human race from his first calumny against man, and an appellation of this kind was imposed by accusation. Lactantius lib. 2. Instit. cap. 8. p. 93. We call the Devil a criminator, for the reason that he brings to GOD the crimes into which he himself entices. Chrysostomus homil. 2. in 2. Corinth. He is called Devil, firstly, because he accuses GOD before men, since, namely, he constructs a calumny of divine mercy, and solicits men to desperation. Secondly, because he accuses men before GOD Apocal. 12. v. 10. since he exaggerates before the divine judgment the sins into which he has precipitated them, or calumniates that they serve GOD only for the sake of reward. Iob. 1. v. 9. Thirdly, men among themselves in turn, when he occupies the tongue of one, namely, of him who brings forth calumnies; but the ears of another, namely, of him who delights in calumnies, and by this reason he furthermore harms the reputation of a third, alien person. There are allusive etymologies, when a Latin derivation is sought for the origin of this Greek word. Gersoni tract. 8. super Magnificat, The Devil is said as if flowing downwards, the reason for which etymology Bonaventura explains lib. 2. sent. dist. 5. q. 1. He is called Devil, because he flowed downwards, and from this he was confirmed in his malice, and therefore the Master, describing a perfect aversion, such as is in the Devil, not such as is in sinful men, says that to be averted is to have hatred or to envy. For the Devil, not being able to ascend, but being compelled to descend, he hates the just God, and envies His excellence. Some of the Scholastics think that Devil is said from dia, which is two, and bolus, because when he drags a man into his snare, he makes two morsels out of him, while he destroys his body and soul. The Syrian rendered the name διαβόλου in this place by [consult facsimile image], having followed the LXX interpreters in this part, who likewise place the name διαβόλου, when in the Hebrew there is שפן 1. Paral. 21. vers. 1.Iob. 1. v. 6. & seqq. cap. 2. v. 1. & seqq. Zach. 3. v. 1. & 2. The reason seems to be this, because he who contends with someone in judgment, and is his שפן or ἀντίδικος,, is usually accustomed to pervert his cause with calumnies, a thing which fits that adversary of ours beautifully. Some wish that Devil is so called from this, because he is an impostor and a deceiver, so much so that he makes enemies even out of friends, and thus often separates those most closely joined. But the etymology of this name does not fit for any other reason, except because calumny usually has craftiness joined to it, and draws with it the dissolution of friendship.

Thirdly, the Apostle compares our enemy to a lion. The name lionApocal. 5. v. 5. is attributed to Christ, who is called the lion of the tribe of Judah, on account of His strength and divine power Prov. 30. v. 30. in which respect it is also attributed to God Amo. 3. v. 8.Thren. 3. v. 10. where at the same time there is a regard for the effect of divine judgments. In Christ, a peculiar reason is added for which He is compared to a lion, namely, on account of the resurrection. Bernh. serm. 1. in die pasch. col. 130. The lamb was slain, but the lion conquered. The lion is said to awaken its cubs with its voice. Christ raised Himself from the dead, and by the efficacy of His voice will one day recall all the dead to life,Iohan. 5. vers. 28. Origen homil. 17. in cap. 49. Genes. applies to the rising Christ, that the lion's cubs sleep for three days and three nights when they are first born, but afterwards are awakened by the roar of their parent. August. serm. 174. de temp. Christ is a lion, on account of fortitude; a lamb, on account of innocence; a lion, because He conquered; a lamb, because He was meek. Some add, that Christ is compared to a lion, not only on account of fortitude and on account of the resurrection, but also on account of sovereignty, on account of a nature devoid of fear, and on account of vigilance. Here, however, the similitude taken from the lion is taken in a bad sense, when the Devil is compared to a lion primarily on account of cruelty. August. serm. 46. de diversis cap. 2. Christ is a lion on account of fortitude, the Devil because of ferocity; the former a lion for conquering, the latter a lion for harming. Therefore, a rule is to be noted in this place. Names placed metaphorically are sometimes taken in a good sense, sometimes in a bad sense. Aug. lib. 3. de doctr. Christ. cap. 25. Sacred Scripture contains many things, of which some are taken in a contrary, some in a different, some in an ambiguous meaning. Thus the serpent is in a good sense Matth. 10. v. 16. & in a bad sense 2. Corinth. 11. vers. 3. leaven is placed in praise Matth. 13. v. 33. & in reproach Matth. 16. vers. 6.1. Cor. 5. v. 7. Related to this Apostolic place is the meaning by which cruel men & enemies of the Church are called lionsPsalm. 22. v. 22.Psal. 35. v. 17.Psalm. 91. v. 13. &c. 2. Timoth. 4. v. 17. The Syrian in this place has the name [consult facsimile image] which properly signifies a larger lion, which now seizes and tears apart prey. The Hebrew אריה Heem. is by some compared with ואה he saw & ירא he feared, & is explained כל הראה אותו ירא ממנו Everyone seeing him, fears from him. Both illustrate this similitude, by which the Devil is compared to a lion.

Fourthly, the Devil is not simply compared to a lion, but to a roaring lion. ώς λέων ὠρυόμενος. Hesychius notes, ὠρύεσθαι that it is peculiarly said ἐπὶ λιμῷ κλαιόντων λύκων ἣ λεόντων ἢ κυνῶν. Apollonius Rhodius lib. 4. Argon. uses the word ὠρύεται. regarding a lion. The name ἀρύωμα derived from this word Ezech. 19. v. 7. is used regarding a lion.

ἠφάνισε γῆν καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς ἀπὸ φωνῆς ὠρυώματος αὐτοῦ, from the voice of his roaring, for this wailing or cry of famished lions is properly called roaring among the Latins. Amo. 3. v. 8. regarding this roaring of a lion the word ἐρεύξεται, is used, where in the Hebrew the word שאג he roared is held, for which Iud. 14. v. 5.Psalm. 21. vers. 13.Psalm. 37. v. 8.Ps. 103. v. 22. &c. elsewhere the LXX. use the word ὠρύεσθαι. Ambros. lib. 6. hexamem. c. 3. records, that a famished lion strikes terror into living creatures with his voice, so that they fail as if stunned and struck by force. Prov. 28. v. 15. a roaring lion is called נהם by which word the Syrian also uses here, where the LXX. translated λέων πεινῶν hungry. Basilius homil. 9. in Hexaëm. Nature has provided the lion with such instruments for eliciting a voice, that many living creatures far swifter than he are often captured by his roaring alone, to which they accommodate that Amos 3:8 The lion roars, who will not fear? Pliny, book 8, chapter 16. Aristotle, on the History of animals, chapter 44. When he is hungry, the lion roars more fiercely. Plutarch, in his book on the Nature of animals, discusses this roaring of the lion a little differently. The lion, he says, is a social animal. When they are heavy with years and already worn out, they are led by the younger ones to a common hunt, and when they have lost heart in the chase, they sit and wait for the outcome. Meanwhile, the young ones do the work. As soon as they have succeeded, they give a signal with a cry tempered into the form of a calf's lowing, and they call the old ones. They, as soon as they have sensed it, run up and enjoy the prey in common. But because the Apostle immediately adds, seeking whom he may devour, it is manifest from that, that he is not speaking of the roar which lions emit when prey has already been found, of which Psalm 22:14 as a lion ravening and roaring. Isaiah 31:4 If a lion and a lion's whelp roar upon their prey. Amos 3:4 Will a lion roar in the forest, when he hath no prey? But [he speaks] of that which is an indication of hunger, of which Psalm 104:21 The young lions roaring after their prey, and seeking their meat from God. Therefore the Devil is compared to a famished lion, and one roaring out of impatience of hunger, because he insatiably desires our destruction, nor does any prey suffice for him.

Fifthly, this adversary of ours is said περιπατεῖν to walk about. The Apostle persists in the metaphor, because a famished lion runs about, solicitously inquiring for prey. Some, however, prefer that the metaphor is drawn from a hunter, to whom the Devil is compared Psalm 91:3 because as a hunter he rises at the crack of dawn, so that he may investigate the wild beasts still resting in their lairs, and he shakes all the bushes, sparing no labor, enduring rains, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, so that he may catch the wild beasts: so the Devil with indefatigable zeal is intent upon all opportunities, so that he may drive man into the nets of either errors or sins. Lyranus notes here, the Devil roars through cruelty, he goes about through malice. B. Luther notes, that the Devil is therefore called περιπατεῖν, because he does not meet one in the open, but lies in wait in secret; attacking us from every side, now from this way, now from that, and such is his impudence, he does not cease to attack once and again after being repulsed. The Apostle also seems to look back to Job 1:7 where Satan, being asked by the Lord, whence he comes, answers, from going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it, where in the Greek version of the LXX Interpreters it is held. περιελθὼν τὴν γῆν καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσας τὴν ὑπ᾽ οὐρανὸν πάρειμι. chapter 2:2 διαπορευθεὶς τὴν ὑπ᾽ οὐρανὸν καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσαςντὴν σύμπασαν πάρειμι. It also looks to the saying of Christ Luke 11. verse 24. When the unclean Spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through dry places, seeking rest &c.

Sixthly, it is said ζητεῖν τινα καταπίῃ to seek with the greatest zeal (for we showed this to be the emphasis of the word ζητεῖν, in Harm. chap. 148. page 664. chap. 152. p. 964.) who does not injure in any way or wound lightly, but swallows up and devours completely. For that is what καταπίνειν signifies Matt. 23. verse 24. 1. Cor. 15. verse 54. Heb. 11. verse 29. which the Syrian rendered by [consult facsimile image] he swallowed, he absorbed. Chrysost. homil. 22. to the people of Antioch. He goes about seeking, not whom he may bite or break, but whom he may devour. Two Royal Codices, and as many others, read ζητᾶν τινα καταπιεῖν, seeking someone to devour. The Interpreter, whom Augustine follows, seems to have read ζητῶν τι καταπιεῖν. For thus he cites this passage in the book of fifty homilies, hom. 35. Your adversary the Devil, as a roaring lion, seeking something to devour. But this seems to have been done by the fault of the scribes. For in homil. 46. of the same work it is read, seeking someone to devour. The more approved and more numerous Greek Codices have ζητῶν τινα παταπίῃ seeking whom he may devour, by incorporating him to himself through mortal sin, as Lyranus notes on this passage. Everywhere that enemy of ours spreads his snares, and stretches nets for us, so that he may drag us into sins Psalm 91. verse 3. he will deliver you from the snare of the hunter. 1. Tim. 3. verse 17. lest he fall into the snare of the Devil. 2. Tim. 2. verse 26. that they may recover themselves from the snares of the Devil, by whom they are held captive to his will. But those whom the Devil has dragged into the nets of sins are said to have been devoured by him, because he has reduced them into his power, and united them to himself by a spiritual bond. Just as between God and pious men there is such a close union, that on account of it the pious are called partakers of the divine Nature 2. Pet. 1. verse 4. children of God John 1. v. 12. one Spirit with God 1. Cor. 6. v. 17. and God is said to make his abode with them John 14. v. 23. so conversely between the Devil and the impious there is such a close bond of kinship and συνδεσμὸς, as Peter speaks Acts 8. v. 23. that the impious are called children of the Devil John 8. v. 44. Acts 13. verse 10. even the Devil himself John 6. v. 70. and the Devil is said to enter into them Luke 22. v. 3. they are ἐνδιαβολισμέι οι, spiritually possessed by the Devil, and as it were incorporated into him.

Latin:

SOBRII ESTOTE, & VIGILATE, QUIA ADVERSARIUS VESTER DIABOLUS TANQUAM LEO RUGIENS CIRCUIT, QUAERENS, QUEM DEVORET.

Connexio. 1. Postquam ad humilitatem & fiduciam omnes fuisset Apostolus exhortatus, iam porrò eos ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam hortatur.

2. Iam antè cap. praeced. 4. vers. 7. praeceptum sobrietatis & vigilantiae illis, ad quos scribit dederat, sed hoc loco illud denuò repetit ob summam huius virtutis necessitatem, ut maiori studio eam sibi habeant commendatam.

3. Christus Luc. 21. v. 34. & 36. dehortationem à crapula & ebrietate ac curis huius vitae, eique oppositam exhortationem advigilantiam coniunxerat, huius utpote Magistri sui vestigiis insistens Petrus, postquam omnem solicitudinem in Deum proiiciendam esse docuerat, subnectit exhortationem ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam.

4. Glossa interlinearis eiusmodi connexionem tradit. Ita proiicite curam vestram in Deum, ut & vos collaboretis coadiutrici gratiae. Ne consolatione illa, quod Deo sit cura de nobis, ad securitatem abutamur, praemonet nos Apostolus de Satanae insidiis. Bernh. serm. 11. in Psal. 90.Sicut Deus solicitus est nostri, & ipsi cura est de nobis: Sic Diabolus solicitus est, ut nos mactet & perdat, & una ei cura, ne fortè qui aversus est, revertatur.

Dispositio. Partes versiculi duae sunt. 1. Apostolica exhortatio 2. Exhortationis ratio. Exhortatio requirit. 1. sobrietatem. 2. vigilantiam. Ratio exhortationis petita est à periculo, in quo pii versantur, quamdiu in his terris vivunt, videlicet ab insidiis DiaboliPericulùm illud amplificat duobus hostis nostri adiunctis. 1. à Diaboli robore & validitate, quando eum comparat leoni. 2. à nocendi cupiditate, quando 1. eum vocat nostrum ἀντίδικον. 2. comparateum leoni rugienti. 3. tribuit ei studium nos deglutiendi.

Textus expositio. Νήψατε, γρηγορήσατε. Vulgata reddidit. Sobrii estote & vigilate. Sed in Graeco ἀσυνδέτως non sine emphasi haec coniunguntur. Sobrii estote, vigilate. Syrus itidem addidit copulativum O. De verbo νήψατε egimus superiùs cap. 1. vers. 13. cap. 4. vers. 7. Vulgatus Interpres eo loco istud verterat, vigilate, sed quia vidit, propter verbum sequens γρηγορῄσατε illud non posse hoc loco sic reddi, ideò vertit, sobrii estote, quam significationem etiam sequi potuisset superiùs. Syrus hoc loco itidem, ut in cap. 4. vers. 7. reddidit [consult facsimile image]vigilate, quod Matth. 24. vers. 42. utitur pro γρηγορεῖτε, ne ergò vigilandi verbum bis repetere hoc loco cogeretur, pro γρηγορεῖτε, quod apud Apostolum sequitur, aliud posuit, de quo postea videbimus. Simplicissimè statuitur, τὸ νήφειν hîc significare sobrietatem, hoc est, temperantiam in cibo & potu, ut hac ratione praeceptum Apostolicum congruat cum praecepto Dominico Luc. 21. v. 34.Cavete, ne corda vestra graventur crapulâ & ebrietate.1. Thessal. 5. vers. 8.Nos autem qui diei sumus,νήφομεν2. Timoth. 4. vers. 5.νῆφε ἐν πᾶσιν.1. Petr. 1. vers. 13.νήϕοντες.

Γρηγορεῖν, & quod usitatius ἐγρηγορεῖν, propriè de corporis vigilia usurpatur Nehem. 7. v. 3.Matth. 26. v. 40.Marc. 14. vers. 37.1. Thess. 5. v. 10. ac opponitur verbo καθέυδειν. Sed hoc loco metaphoricè de animi vigilia ac mentis vigilantia accipitur, unde Ioh. Huss. ad h. l. rectè sic annotat. Sobrii estote corpore, vigilate animo. Huius significationis, quae Christo & Apostolis magis frequens, quàm prior, exempla passim occurruntMatth. 25. v. 13.Luc. 12. v. 37.Act. 20. v. 31.1. Cor. 16. v. 13.Col. 4. v. 2.1. Thess. 5. v. 6.Apoc. 3. v. 2.cap. 3. v. 3.cap. 16. v. 15. LXX. utuntur hoc verbo pro שקדinvigilavit alicui rei, intentus fuit ad aliquod negotium, solicitus fuit de aliquareIer. 1. v. 12.cap. 31. v. 28.Thren. 1. v. 1. &c. ac semper alacritatem quandam animi includit, quae significatio ad metaphoricam proximè accedit. Syrus hoc loco reddidit per [consult facsimile image]memores estote, ac si in Graeco esset μνήσθητε vel μνημονέυετε, pro quo hac voce utitur Syrus Iohann. 15. vers. 20. quia spiritualis illa vigilia inter alia etiam hoc complectitur, ut memores simus eorum, quae Christus & Apostoli nobis praedixerunt, ut & consolationis, quam in verbo nobis proposuerunt. Loca huic nostro parallela sunt. Matth. 24. vers. 42.γρηγορεῖτεvigilate, quia nescitis, quâ horâ Dominus venturus sit.c. 15. v. 13.γρηγορεῖτεvigilate, quia nec diem nec horam scitis, in quae filius hominis veniet.cap. 26. v. 41.γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσέυχεθε.Marc. 13. v. 33.ἀγρυπνεῖτε καὶ προσέυχεθε.v. 35.γρηγορεῖτεvigilate, quia nescitis, quando Dominus domus veniet.v. 37.Quod vobis dico, omnibus dicoγρηγορεῖτε.cap. 14. v. 38.γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσέυχεσθε.Luc. 21. vers. 36.ἀγρυπνεῖτε ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ δεόμενοι.1. Cor. 16. v. 13.γρηγορεῖτε, στήκετε ἐν τῆ πίστει.Eph. 6. v. 18.ἀγρυπνοῦντες ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει καὶ δεήσει.Col. 4. v. 2.τῇ προσευχῇ προσκαρτερεῖτε, γρηγοροῦντες ἐν αὐτῇ.1. Thess. 5. v. 6.γρηγορῶμεν καὶ νήφωμεν,1. Petr. 4. v. 7.σωφρονήσατε καὶ νήψατε εἰς τὰς προσευχὰς.Apoc. 3. v. 2.γίνου γρηγορῶν. ex quibus locis parallelis omnium optima huius praecepti de vigilantia expositio colligitur.

Ὅτι ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν διάβολος ὡς λέων ὠρυόμενος περιπατεῖ, ζητῷν τινα καταπίῃ. Haec est praecepti ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam ratio, in qua tot sententiarum pondera, quot verba.

Primò hostem illum nostrum, cum quo ἄσπονδον ac perpetuum nobis intercedit bellum, vocat nostrum ἀντίδικον. Ἀντίδικος propriè est adversarius in iudicio litigans contra alium, in qua significatione usurpatur Matth. 5. vers. 25.παραδῶ ὁ ἀντίδικος τῷ κριτῇ ibid. Esto benevolusτῷ ἀντιδίκω σου.Luc. 12. v. 58.μετὰ τοῦ ἀντιδίκου σου εἰς ἀρχοντα.cap. 18. v. 9.ἐκδίκησόν μου ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀντιδίκου. Aeschines in Cresiphontem. καὶ τοὺς λόγους ἐκφέρων τοῖς ἀντιδίκοις. Apud Platonem lib. 12. de legibus, ἀντιδικοῦντες ἑκατέροι dicuntur actor & rtus. Quando igitur Petrus Diabolum vocat nostrum ἀντίδικον. admonet nos, quòd sit noster κατήγορος κατηγορῶν ἡμῶν ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸςApocal. 12. vers. 10. quia τοῦ ἀντιδίκου ἔστιν ἡ κατηγορία ἐνώπιον τοῦ κριτοῦ. LXX. Esai. 41. v. 11. utuntur pro איש ויבvir litis sive contentionis, qui ibidem ἐξηγητικῶς sic describitur, quòd sit contra aliquem succensus 1. Sam. 2. v. 9. pro מריבcontendens sive rixans. Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image]q. d. Dominus vel possessor odii, h. e. inimicus vester, qui perpetuo adversus vos odio flagrat. Caeterùm nomen ἀντίδικος respondet Hebraeo שטןadversarius, hostisNum. 22. v. 22.1. Sam. 29. v. 4. quod per ἀντονομασίαν tribuitur Diabolo, qui est iuratus ac perpetuus humani generis hostis Iob. 1. vers. 6.Zachar. 3. vers. 1. &c. 2. Corinth. 12. v. 7.Apocal. 12. vers. 9. Iustinus in Dial. cum Tryphone p. 259. existimat, nomen שטן esse compositum ex שטהavertit se, recessit, declinavit, &נסserpensנחשserpens, sed Aramaei elidunt ח guttutalem, inde ergò fit נש, pro ש ponunt ס) sic enim scribit. Diabolum Moses vocat serpentem, à Iesu appellatur Satanas, nomen cum rebus ipsis, quas egit congruens, indeque compositum obtinere indicante. Nam Sata Iudaeorum & Syrorum voce apostata & desertor est, nomen autem Nas, unde interpretatione etiam serpens vocatur, idem est, quod Sata Ebraeorum expositum sermone, ex quibus utrisque unum nomen compositum fit Satanas. Iustini vestigiis insistit Irenaeus lib 5. cap. 18. p. 343. Satana verbum Hebraicè apostatam significat, qui enim priùs bonus Angelus erat, à Deo sese avertit & defecit. Sed rectiùs dedu citur à שטן, quod significat adversatus est, impediit, detraxit. 1. quia hanc etymologiam monstrat ipse Spiritus S. Zachar. 3. vers. 1.Et ostendit mihi Iosua Sacerdotem magnum stantem coram Angelo Dominiוהשטן& Satan stabat ad dextram eiusלשטנו ut verè esset, quod dicebatur, ut adversaretur ei. 2. quia in N. T. dicitur Σατᾶν & Σατανᾶ2. Cor. 12. v. 7. Quod Apoc. 12. v. 9. cap.

20. v. 2. vocatur Σατανᾶς, id fit Graecâ inflexione. 3. quia Apostolus noster hoc nomen interpretatur per ἀντίδικον. Aug. in qq. ex N. T. q. 90. Nomen Satan est nomen operis, non Naturae. Caesarius Dial. 1. Inde malignus ille Spiritus dicitur Satan, quia DEO & hominibus adversatur.

Secundò hostem illum nostrum vocat διάβολον, quo nomine passim in N. T. insignitur. Matth. 4. vers. 1. & seqq. cap. 13. v. 39.cap. 25. v. 41.Luc. 4. v. 2. Dicitur autem ὁ διάβολος ἀπὸ τοῦ διαβάλλεινcalumniari, unde διαβόλου nomen appellativum quandoque pro homine calumniatore usurpatur 1. Timoth. 3. vers. 11.2. Timoth. 3. vers. 3.Tit. 2. vers. 3. quo sensu etiam quidam accipiunt locum Eph. 4. v. 27. & 1. Timoth. 3. v. 6.Quare Satanae hoc nomen tribuatur, eius rei causam pulcerrimè explicant pii veteres. Iustinus in paraen. 1. ad Graecos p. 21. ἐχθρὸν τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος Διάβολον αἱ θειαὶ γραφαί καλοῦσιν ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης αὐτοῦ πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον διαβολής τάυτης τῆς προσηγορίας τυχόντα.Hostem humani generis Diabolum divinae vocant Scripturae à prima sua adversus hominem calumnia, & criminatione appellatio huiusmodi imposita. Lactantius lib. 2. Instit. cap. 8. p. 93. Diabolum criminatorem vocamus, propterea quod crimina, in quae ipse illicit, ad DEUM defert. Chrysostomus homil. 2. in 2. Corinth. Diabolus vocatur, primò, quia DEUM incusat apud homines, quoniam scil. divinae misericordiae calumniam struit, & ad desperationem homines solicitat. Secundò, quia homines accusat apud DEUMApocal. 12. v. 10.quoniam peccata, in quae eos praecipitavit, coram divino iudicio exaggerat, vel mercedis tantùm causa illos DEO servire calumniatur.Iob. 1. v. 9.Tertiò, homines inter se invicem, quando unius, videlicet eius, qui calumnias profert, linguam; alterius verò, videlicet eius, qui calumniis delectatur, aures occupat, & hac ratione tertiae alienius personae famam insuper laedit. Allusivae etymologiae sunt, quando huius vocabuli origine Graeci derivatio Latina quaeritur. Gersoni tract. 8. super Magnificat, Diabolus dicitur quasi deorsum fluens, cuius etymologiae rationem exponit Bonaventura lib. 2. sent. dist. 5. q. 1. Dictus est Diabolus, quia deorsum fluxit, & ex hoc in sua malitia firmatus fuit, & ideò Magister describens perfectam aversionem, qualis in Diabolo, non qualis in hominibus peccat oribus dicit, quòd averti est odio habere vel invidere. Diabolus enim non valens conscendere, sed compulsus descendere odit Deum iustum, & invidet excellentiae eius. Quidam ex Scholasticis Diabolum dictum putant ex dia, quod est duo, & bolus, quia quando hominem in nassam suam pertrabit, duos ex ipso facit bolos, dum ipsius corpus & animam perdit. Syrus nomen διαβόλου hoc loco reddidit per [consult facsimile image] secutus hac in parte LXX. Interpp. qui itidem ponunt nomen διαβόλου, quando in Hebraeo est שפן1. Paral. 21. vers. 1.Iob. 1. v. 6. & seqq. cap. 2. v. 1. & seqq. Zach. 3. v. 1. & 2. Ratio videtur esse ea, quia qui in iudicio cum aliquo contendit, & est eius שפן vel ἀντίδικος, solet plerunque calumniis causam eius pervertere, id quod pulchrè adversario illi nostro congruit. Quidam volunt, Diabolum ex eo sic dictum, quòd sit impostor & fallax, adeò ut ex amicis etiam inimicos faciat, adeoque coniunctissimos saepe dirimat. Sed non aliâ ratione congruit nominis huius etymologiae, nisi quia calumnia calliditatem plerunque coniunctam habet, & dissolutionem amicitiae secum trahit.

Tertiò comparat Apostolus hostem nostrum leoni. Nomen leonisApocal. 5. v. 5. tribuitur Christo, qui vocatur leo de tribu Iudae, ob robur & potentiam divinam Prov. 30. v. 30. quo respectu etiam. Deo tribuitur Amo. 3. v. 8.Thren. 3. v. 10. ubi simul habetur respectus ad effectum iudiciorum divinorum. In Christo accedit peculiaris, ratio, ob quam leoni comparatur, videl. ob resurrectionem. Bernh. serm. 1. in die pasch. col. 130. Occisus est agnus, sed leo vicit. Leo catulos voce suâ excitare dicitur. Christus seipsum ex mortuis suscitavit, & vocis suae efficacia aliquando omnes mortuos in vitam revocabit,Iohan. 5. vers. 28. Origenes homil. 17. in cap. 49. Genes. ad Christum resurgentem applicat, quòd catuli leonis tribus diebus ac tribus noctibus dormiunt, cum primùm nascuntur, postmodùm vero genitoris rugitu excitantur. August. serm. 174. de temp. Christus leo, propter fortitudinem, agnus, propter innocentiam; leo, quia victus, agnus, quia mansuetus. Quidam addunt, Christum conferri leoni, non solùm propter fortitudinem & propter resurrectionem, sed etiam propter principatum, propter Naturam timoris expertem & propter vigilantiam. Hîc vero similitudo à leone petita in malam partem accipitur, quando Diabolus potissimùm propter crudelitatem leoni comparatur. August. serm. 46. de diversis cap. 2. Christus leo propter fortitudinem, Diabolus propter feritatem; ille leo ad vincendum, iste leo ad nocendum. Notanda ergò hoc loco regula. Nomina metaphoritè posita, quandoque in bonam, quandoque in malam partem accipiuntur. Aug. lib. 3. de doctr. Christ. cap. 25. Sacra Scriptura plurima continet, quorum quaedam in contrariam, quaedam in diversam, quaedam in ambiguam significationem accipiuntur. Sic serpens in bono est Matth. 10. v. 16. & in malo 2. Corinth. 11. vers. 3. fermentum ponitur in laude Matth. 13. v. 33. & in vituperio Matth. 16. vers. 6.1. Cor. 5. v. 7. Cognata huic loco Apostolico est significatio ea, quâ homines crudeles & Ecclesiae hostes dicuntur leonesPsalm. 22. v. 22.Psal. 35. v. 17.Psalm. 91. v. 13. &c. 2. Timoth. 4. v. 17. Syrus hoc loco habet nomen [consult facsimile image] quod propriè significat leonem grandiorem, qui iam praedam rapit & discerpit. Hebraeum אריה Heem. à quibusdam confertur cum ואהvidit & יראtimuit, & exponitur כל הראה אותו ירא ממנוOmnis videns eum, timet ab eo. Utrumque illustrat hanc similitudinem, quâ Diabolus leoni comparatur.

Quartò non simpliciter confertur Diabolus leoni, sed leoni rugienti. ώς λέων ὠρυόμενος. Hesychius annotat, ὠρύεσθαιpeculiariter diciἐπὶ λιμῷ κλαιόντων λύκων ἣ λεόντων ἢ κυνῶν. Apollonius Rhodius lib. 4. Argon. de leone usurpat verbum ὠρύεται. Nomen ἀρύωμα ex hoc verbo deductum Ezech. 19. v. 7. de leone usurpatur.

ἠφάνισε γῆν καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς ἀπὸ φωνῆς ὠρυώματος αὐτοῦ, à voce rugitus sui, nam hic leonum famelicorum eiulatus sive clamor, apud Latinos propriè vocatur rugitus.Amo. 3. v. 8. de hoc leonis rugitu usurpatur verbum ἐρεύξεται, ubi in Hebraeo habetur verbum שאג rugivit, pro quo Iud. 14. v. 5.Psalm. 21. vers. 13.Psalm. 37. v. 8.Ps. 103. v. 22. &c. alibi LXX. utuntur verbo ὠρύεσθαι. Ambros. lib. 6. hexamem. c. 3. memorat, leonem famelicum voce suâ terrorem animantibus incutere, ut quasi vi attonita atque icta deficiant.Prov. 28. v. 15.leo rugiens vocatur נהם quâ voce etiam Syrus hîc utitur, ubi LXX. verterunt λέων πεινῶνesuriens. Basilius homil. 9. in Hexaëm. Leoni tanta vocis elicendae Natura praestitit instrumenta, ut animantium complura longè ipso celeriora solo saepè rugitu capiantur, quò accommodant illud Amos. 3. v. 8.Leo rugit, quis non timebit? Plin. lib. 8. cap. 16. Aristot. de Histor. anim. cap. 44. Cùm esurit, saeviùs rugit leo. Plutarchus lib. de Natura animal. paulo aliter de hoc leonis rugitu disserit. Est, inquit, leo socium animal. Graves annis & confecti iam, in communem à iunioribus venatum ducuntur, ac ubi cursu despondêre animum, sedent eventumque praestolantur. Iuvenes interea rem agunt. Mox ut successit, clamore in vitulini mugitus formam temperato signum dant, vocantque senes. Illi statim, ut sensêre, accurrunt ac in commune praedà fruuntur. Sed quia statim addit Apostolus, quaerens quem devoret, ex eo manifestum est, ipsum non loqui de rugitu, quem leones edunt, inventâ iam praedâ, de quo Psal. 22. v. 14.sicut leo rapiens & rugiens.Esai. 31. v. 4.Si rugiat leo & catulus leonis super praedam suam.Amos. 3. v. 4.Nunquid rugiet leo in saltu, nisi habuerit praedam. Sed qui famis est indicium, de quo Psalm. 104. v. 21.Catuli leonum rugientes, ut rapiant & quaerant à Deo escam sibi. Comparaturigitur Diabolus leoni famelico, & prae impatientia famis rugienti, quia perniciem nostram inexplebiliter appetit, nec ulla praeda ei sufficit.

Quintò dicitur hic noster adversarius περιπατεῖνobambulare. Persistit Apostolus in metaphora, quia leo famelicus discurrit, solicitè inquirens praedam. Quidam tamen malunt, metaphoram esse ductam à venatore, cui Diabolus comparaturPsalm. 91. v. 3.quia ut venator summo mane surgit, ut feras in cubilibus suis adhuc quiescentes investiget, ac omnia arbusta excutit, nulli labori parcens, tolerans imbres, frigus, aestum, famem, sitim, ut feras capiat: sic Diabolus indefesso studio in omnes occasiones intentus est, ut hominem vel in errorum, vel in peccatorum retia impellat. Lyranus hîc annotat, Diabolum rugire per saevitiam, circuire per malitiam. B. Lutherus annotat. propterea Diabolum diciπεριπατεῖν,quia non occurrit in manifesto, sed insidiatur in occulto; omni ex parte, modò ex hac, modò ex illa nos invadens, ac quae est eius impudentia, non cessat invadere semel atque iterum repulsus. Videtur etiam Apostolus respicere ad Iob. 1. v. 7. ubi Satan à Domino interrogatus, unde veniat, respondet, à circumeundo terram & à per ambulando eam, ubi in Graeca LXX. Interp. versione habetur. περιελθὼν τὴν γῆν καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσας τὴν ὑπ᾽ οὐρανὸν πάρειμι.cap. 2. v. 2.διαπορευθεὶς τὴν ὑπ᾽ οὐρανὸν καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσαςντὴν σύμπασαν πάρειμι. Respicit etiam ad dictum Christi Luc. 11. vers. 24.Cùm immundus Spiritus ab homine exierit, ambulat per loca arentia, quaerit requiem &c.

Sextò dicitur ζητεῖν τινα καταπίῃsummo studio quaerere (hanc enim esse emphasin verbi ζητεῖν, ostendimus in Harm. cap. 148. pag. 664. cap. 152. p. 964.) qui non qualitercunque laedat vel leviter vulneret, sed penitus deglutiat atque devoret. Id enim significat καταπίνεινMatth. 23. vers. 24.1. Cor. 15. vers. 54.Hebr. 11. vers. 29. quod Syrus reddidit per [consult facsimile image]deglutiit, absorpsit. Chrysost. homil. 22. ad popul. Antioch. Circuit quaerens, non quem mordeat vel frangat, sed quem devoret. Regii duo Codices, aliique totidem legunt ζητᾶν τινα καταπιεῖν,quaerens aliquem devorare. Interpres, quem-sequitur Augustinus, legisse videtur ζητῶν τι καταπιεῖν. Sic enim adducit hunc locum in libr. quinquag. homiliarum hom. 35. Adversarius vester Diabolus, tanquam leo rugiens, aliquid devorare quarens. Sed hoc videtur vitio librariorum factum. Nam eiusdem operis homil. 46. legitur, aliquem devorare quaerens. Probatiores & plures Codices Graeci habent, ζητῶν τινα παταπίῃquaerens quem devoret, incorporando sibi per mortalem culpam, ut Lyranus ad h. l. annotat. Quaquaversum hostis ille noster expandit suos laqueos, & retia nobis tendit, ut in peccata nos pertrahat Psalm. 91. vers. 3.liberabit te de laqueo venatoris.1. Tim. 3. vers. 17.ne incidat in laqueum Diaboli.2. Tim. 2. vers. 26.ut resipiscant à Diaboli laqueis, à quo capti tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem. Quos vero Diabolus in peccatorum retia pertraxit, eos devorasse dicitur, quia in suam eos potestatem redegit, eosque sibi spirituali vinculo univit. Quemadmodum inter Deum & pios homines tam arcta est unio, ut propter eam pii dicantur divinae consortes Naturae2. Petr. 1. vers. 4.filii DeiIoh. 1. v. 12.unus cum Deo Spiritus1. Cor. 6. v. 17. ac Deus dicitur apud illos mansionem facere h. 14. v. 23. sic è converso inter Diabolum & impios tàm arctum est cognationis vinculum ac συνδεσμὸς, ut loquitur Petrus Act. 8. v. 23. ut impii dicantur filii DiaboliIoh. 8. v. 44.Actor. 13. vers. 10.imà ipst DiaboliIob. 6. v. 70. ac Diabolus dicitur in eos intrareLuc. 22. v. 3. sunt ἐνδιαβολισμέι οι, spiritualiter à Diabolo obsessi, & ipsi quasi incorporati.

## 5:9
WHOM RESIST, STRONG IN THE FAITH, KNOWING THAT THE SAME AFFLICTION IS ACCOMPLISHED IN YOUR BRETHREN THAT ARE IN THE WORLD.

Disposition. The parts of the verse are two. The former προτρεπτικὴ. the latter παρακλητικὴ.

Connection by reason of the former part. 1. Because the Apostle had depicted the cruelty and desire to harm, with which the Devil burns against us, under the figure of a lion, he now furthermore shows how his snares are to be resisted, namely through faith.

2. He therefore exhorts those to whom he writes to constancy in faith, and to a confident apprehension of the merit of Christ, offered in the word of the Evangelical promise, inasmuch as through it they can bravely overcome all the snares and temptations of Satan.

3. Just as James chap. 4. v. 7. joined the exhortation to resist the Devil with the exhortation to humble oneself before God. Submit yourselves, he says, therefore to God, resist the Devil, and he will flee from you: So also Peter in this place connects both exhortations. ver. 6. & 9.

4. In the verse immediately preceding, the Apostle had exhorted the faithful to sobriety and vigilance, but because sobriety and vigilance are not yet sufficient for avoiding the snares of Satan and overcoming his temptations, since they only render the body suitable and remove the occasions of sin, but the sword, with which one must fight against Satan, is the word and faith Eph. 6. v. 16. &. 17. therefore he now furthermore refers them to this true and strong armor against Satan. B. Luther on this place.

5. Just as the power and fraudulence of the enemy ought to sharpen our vigilance, and render us more solicitous: So there would be a danger, lest the mind, oppressed by immoderate terror, should collapse, unless at the same time the hope of victory against the enemy were shown. That indeed is contained in the exhortation to resist through faith. For the exhortation to fight would be in vain, unless at the same time the hope of overcoming the enemy were shown.

Connection by reason of the latter part. 1. He joins not only implicit, but also explicit consolation to the exhortation of the Apostle, when he says that those temptations of Satan are common to the rest of the faithful, leaving it to be understood from this that we do not fight alone against this enemy, but have many fellow-wrestlers in the world. Bede in h. l. Be so much the stronger in faith, have so much the greater confidence for overcoming the wiles of the Devil, by how much it is certain that you are not tempted alone, but the very suffering which wearies you is also common to the Church of Christ which is throughout the whole world, and therefore to your brotherhood: and that which the righteous have always suffered from the foundation of the world, let it shame you not to be able to endure alone before all others.

2. Because he shows that the struggle with Satan is common to those tempted with the rest of the brothers in the world, by that very fact he raises them into a certain hope that they will also obtain a common victory with them; therefore, he not only exhorts them by the example of the brothers to constancy in faith and strength of mind in the fight against Satan, but also consoles them with the aid of the whole brotherhood and the hope of victory. Lyranus in h. l. Resist the Devil, just as they also (through faith, so also you will carry off the victory from Satan just as they also.) Oecumenius in h. l. This application of allied hands, as it were, contributes much in lifting the weight.

3. Those who determine that by τὰ παθήματα not the temptations of Satan, but the persecutions of the world are to be understood, think that the faithful are fortified by these words against the persecutions of the world by the consolation of the equal condition of the brothers, i.e., of the associates of the Christian faith in the whole world. For no one ought to seek for himself a better lot than that which is of the rest of the brothers in the world. A common fatherhood and a common inheritance require a common lot of brotherhood.

Exposition of the text. ᾧ ἀντίστητε στερεοὶ τῇ πίστει. The Vulgate rendered: Whom resist, strong in faith. The Greek properly has: Whom resist, solid, or firm in faith. The Syriac rendered: Stand, rise up against him [consult facsimile image] strengthened, established, confirmed in faith. For [consult facsimile image] formed from the Hebrew ישר to be straight, with י cut off and ו repeated, signifies to be strengthened in the straight way. The interlinear gloss adds: Let faith be as a wall. Parallel passages are Eph. 6. vers. 13. Take the armor of God, that you may be able ἀντεστῆται. vers. 14. Stand, having your loins girt about with truth v. 16. In all things taking the shield of faith, wherewith you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one. Iac. 4. v. 7. Resist the Devil, and he will flee from to you John 5. verse 4. This is the victory, which overcomes the world (and the Prince of the world, SatanJohn 16. v. 11.) our faith. εἰδότες, τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελφότητι ἐπιτελεῖσθαι. The participle εἰδότες shows that this latter part depends on the former. It must therefore be referred either to the verb ἀντιστῆτε, or to the noun στερεοὶ, but the matter in both cases comes to the same thing. For the sense is that this ought to confirm us in faith, and animate us to resist the Devil, because we know that the same sufferings are common to us with the rest of the faithful in the world. The Syrian resolves it into a verb, Stand against him confirmed in faith, and know.

Τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων are τὰ αὐτὰ παθήματα, with the customary change of ἐνάρθρως having been made. The Vulgate rendered it, the same suffering. But in the Greek it is plural, the same sufferings, in which way also the Syrian rendered it, [consult facsimile image] from the root [consult facsimile image] or [consult facsimile image] to suffer.

By τὴν ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελφότητα the Apostle understands the spiritual brotherhood, i.e., the multitude of spiritual brothers, or the assembly of the faithful, joined to us by the spiritual bond of the same faith, because all truly faithful are brothers among themselves under one heavenly father. Matt. 23. verse 8. & 9. In the same signification our Apostle uses the word ἀδελφότητος. chap. 2. of this Epistle verse 17. τὴν ἀδελφότητα ἀγαπᾶτε. The Syrian resolves the abstract into the concrete. [consult facsimile image] [consult facsimile image] against your brothers. Concerning προσδιορισμὸν τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ἀδελφότητι, the participle οὔσῃ or διαγούσῃ. must be understood. Moreover, there can be a double sense of this προσδιορισμοῦ, either by reason of place, because the faithful are dispersed through the whole world, and therefore these sufferings happen to the faithful promiscuously everywhere among the nations; or by reason of time, because the necessity of fighting, as long as we live in this age, awaits us. Both significations agree with the little word κόσμου and the analogy of faith, yet the former seems to approach the text more. John Huss, after he had reviewed the former explanation, adds another and clearly new one, in which the little word κόσμου is taken by reason of the object placed.
