Knowing, he says, the same suffering, that is, tribulation and temptation, similar to that which you sustain, to be happening to your brotherhood; which is in the world, that is, to your brothers, who are dispersed throughout the world, as if he were saying. Do not think that you alone sustain these things, nay, this is common to all the saints, etc. Or thus. Knowing that the same suffering is happening to your brotherhood, which is in the world, that is, which the Devil inflicts upon worldly people, that is, to us brothers, by emphasis, with the abstract placed for the concrete, indeed Do not think that you are tempted less because you are faithful, nay, rather more. But anyone sees that this exposition is forced. For the Apostle does not say τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημὰτων τῶ κόσμῳ καὶ τῇ ἀδελφότὴτι ἐπιτελεῖσθαι but τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελφότητι.

The Vulgate rendered the word ἐπιτελεῖσθαι as to happen. The Greek properly has, to be perfected, to be consummated, to be fulfilled. Luke 13. verse 32. Romans 15. verse 28. 2. Corinthians 7. v. 1. etc. The LXX use it for כלה he absolved, he finished. 1. Kings 3. v. 12. The Syrian has the word [consult facsimile image] it happened, it befell, it came to pass, which is used only once in the N. T. The Arab uses it Mark 10. verse 32. 1. Corinthians 10. v. 11. But the word ἐπιτελεῖσθαι to be perfected, to be consummated, is emphatic. For Peter looks to this. 1. to the decree of God, by which from eternity He ordained that the elect should not arrive at heavenly glory without sufferings. Romans 8. verse 29. Acts 24. v. 22. this decree of God must altogether be perfected and consummated in this age. 2. to the sufferings of Christ, about which the simple word τελεῖσθαι, with which it is compounded is of the same meaning, or intends the same, is used Luke 18. v. 31. John 19. v. 28. & 30. Acts 13. v. 29. For the sufferings which began in the personal body of Christ, the same are consummated in His spiritual and mystical body, whence Paul in a place parallel to this of ours says, that he παθήμασι ἀνταναπληροῦν τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν θλίψεων τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν τῇ σαρκί σου. his Colossians 1. v. 24. 3. to the utility of the cross. The faithful cannot be perfected in the pursuit of piety without the cross, inasmuch as through it the mortification of the old man & the necessary renewal is perfected more and more day by day. 2. Corinthians 4. v. 16. Our inner man is renewed from day to day v. 17. for that which is momentary and light of our tribulation in the present, works for us above measure in sublimity an eternal weight of glory. Cajetan in this place Sufferings do not harm, but rather lead to perfection. 4. to the brevity of the cross. Sufferings are sent in this age, when they are finished and perfected with this age.

Latin:

CUI RESISTITE, FORTES IN FIDE, SCIENTES EANDEM PASSIONEM EI, QUAE IN MUNDO EST, VESTRAE FRATERNITATI FIERI.

Dispositio. Partes versiculi duae sunt. Prior προτρεπτικὴ. posterior παρακλητικὴ.

Connexio ratione prioris partis. 1. Quia sub figura leonis crudelitatem & nocendi cupiditatem, quâ Diabolus adversus nos flagrat, Apostolus depinxerat, iam porrò ostendit, quomodo illius insidiis sit resistendum, videlicet per fidem.

2. Hortatur igitur eos, ad quos scribit, ad constantiam in fide, & ad fiducialem apprehensionem meriti Christi, in verbo promissionis Evangelicae oblati, utpote per quam omnes Satanae insidias & tentationes fortiter superare possint.

3. Sicut Iacobus cap. 4. v. 7. coniunxit exhortationem ad resistendum Diabolo cum exhortatione ad se humiliandum coram Deo. Subditi, inquit, estote Deo, resistite a. Diabolo, & fugiet à vobis: Ita quoque Petrus hoc loco utramque exhortationem connectit. vers. 6. & 9.

4. In versu proximè praecedente exhortatus fuerat Apostolus fideles ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam, quia vero sobrietas & vigilantia nondum sufficiunt ad cavendas Satanae insidias & tentationes eius superandas, siquidem corpus duntaxat idoneum reddunt, & peccandi occasiones demunt, gladius verò, quo contra Satanam pugnandum, est verbum & fides Eph. 6. v. 16. &. 17. ideò ad hanc veram & fortem contra Satanam armaturam iam porrò eos remittit. B. Lutherus in h. l.

5. Sicut hostis potentia & fraudulentia vigilantiam nostram acuere, ac nos magis solicitos reddere debet: Ita periculum esset, ne immodico terrore animus oppressus concideret, nisi simul spes victoriae adversus hostem ostenderetur. Ea vero in exhortatione ad resistendum per fidem continetur. Frustranea namque esset ad pugnandum exhortatio, nisi de superando hoste simul spes ostenderetur.

Connexio ratione posterioris partis. 1. Non solùm implicitam, sed etiam explicitam consolationem exhortationi coniungit Apostolus, quando tentationes illas Satanae cum reliquis fidelibus communes esse dicit, ex quo intelligendum relinquit, nos non solos contra hunc bostem pugnare, sed multos in mundo habere sympalaestritas. Beda in h. l. Tantò fortiores estote in fide, tantò maiorem habetote fiduciam ad superandas Diaboli versutias, quantò constat, quia vos non soli tentamini, sed ipsa passio, quae vos fatigat, eiquoque quae per totum mundum est Ecclesiae Christi, vestrae inde licet fraternitati communisest: & quod à constitutione mundi semper passi sunt iusti, pudeat vos solos prae omnibus sustinere non posse.

2. Quia certamen cum Satanâ tentatis cum reliquis in mundo fratribus commune esse ostendit, eo ipso in spem certam eos erigit, fore ut cum illis etiam communem obtineant victoriam, proinde non solùm exemplo fratrum ad constantiam in fide, & robur animi in pugna contra Satanam eos hortatur, sed etiam subsidio totius fraternitatis & spe victoriae eosdem consolatur. Lyranus in h. l. Resistite Diabolo, sicut & ipsi (per fidem, ita quoque victoriam à Satana reportabitis sicut & ipsi.) Oecumenius in h. l. Sociarum ista veluti manuum admotio in sublevando pondere multum confert.

3. Qui per τὰ παθήματα non Satanae tentationes, sed mundi persecutiones intelligendas esse statuunt, existimant, muniri his verbis fideles contra persecutiones mundi solatio à pari conditione fratrum h. e. fidei Christianae sociorum in toto mundo. Nemo enim debet meliorem sibi sortem expeterê, quàm quae est reliquorum in mundo fratrum. Communis paternitas & communis haereditas communem fraternitatis sortem requirit.

Textus expositio. ᾧ ἀντίστητε στερεοὶ τῇ πίστει. Vulgata reddidit. Cui resistite fortes in fide. Graeca propriè habent. Cui resistite solidi, vel firmi fide. Syrus reddidit: State, insurgite contraeum[consult facsimile image]corroborati, stabiliti, confirmati in fide.[consult facsimile image] enim formatum ab Hebraeo ישר rectum esse, abscisso י & repetito ו significat corroborari in recto. Glossa interlinearis addit. Fides sit quasi murus. Loca parallela sunt Eph. 6. vers. 13.Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitisἀντεστῆται.vers. 14.State succincti lumbos vestros in veritatev. 16.In omnibus sumentes scutum fidei, in quo possitis omnia nequissimi tela ignea extinguere.Iac. 4. v. 7.Resistite Diabolo, & fugiet à vobis Iohan. 5. vers. 4.Haec est victoria, quae vincit mundum (ac mundi Principem, SataenamIohan. 16. v. 11.) fides nostra.εἰδότες, τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελφότητι ἐπιτελεῖσθαι. Participium εἰδότες ostendit, posteriorem hancce partem pendere à priori. Referri igitur debet vel ad verbum ἀντιστῆτε, vel ad nomen στερεοὶ, sedres utrobique eodem redit. Sensus enim est, hoc debere in fide nos confirmare, & ad Diabolum resistendum animare, quòd sciamus, easdem passiones cum reliquis in mundo fidelibus nobis esse communes. Syrus resolvit in verbum, State contra eum confirmati in fide, & scitote.

Τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων sunt τὰ αὐτὰ παθήματα, usitatâ mutatione ἐνάρθρως facta. Vulg. reddidit, eandem passionem. Sed in Graeco est plurale, easdem passiones, quo modo etiam Syrus reddidit, [consult facsimile image] à rad. [consult facsimile image] vel [consult facsimile image]pati.

Per τὴν ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελφότητα intelligit Apostolus fraternitatem spiritualem, i. e. multitudinem spiritualium fratrum, sive coetum fidelium, spirituali eiusdem fidei vinculo nobis coniunctorum, quia omnes verè fideles inter se fratres sunt sub uno patre coelesti. Matth. 23. vers. 8. & 9. In eadem significatione noster Apostolus voce ἀδελφότητος utitur. cap. 2. huius Epist. vers. 17.τὴν ἀδελφότητα ἀγαπᾶτε. Syrus abstractum resolvit in concretum. [consult facsimile image][consult facsimile image]contra fratres vestros. Circa προσδιορισμὸν τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ἀδελφότητι, subintelligendum participium οὔσῃ vel διαγούσῃ. Duplex autem potest esse huius προσδιορισμοῦ sensus, vel ratione loci, quod fideles per totum mundum sint dispersi, ac proinde promiscui ubique gentium hae passiones fidelibus obveniant; vel ratione temporis, quod pugnandi necessitas, quamdiu in hoc seculo vivimus, nos maneat. Utraque significatio congruit voculae κόσμου & fidei analogiae, prior tamen magis videtur ad textum accedere. Iohannes Huss postquam priorem explicationem recensuerat, aliam ac planè novam subiungit, in qua vocula κόσμου ratitione obiecti posita accipitur. Scientes, inquit, eandem passionem, idest, tribulationem & tentationem, similem ei, quam vos sustinetis, fieri vestrae fraternitati; quae in mundo est, h. e. fratribus vestris, qui sunt per mundum dispersi, quasi dicat. Non aestimetis haec vos solos sustinere, imò hoc est commune omnibus sanctis &c. Vel sic. Scientes eandem, passionem ei, quae in mundo est, id est, quam facit Diabolus mundanis, vestrae fraternitati fieri, id est, nobis fratribus, per emphasin, posito abstracto pro concreto, quidem Non putetis minùs tentari, quia fideles estis, imò magis. Sed quilibet videt, hanc expositionem esse coactam. Neque enim dicit Apostolus, τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημὰτων τῶ κόσμῳ καὶ τῇ ἀδελφότὴτι ἐπιτελεῖσθαι sed τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελφότητι.

Verbum ἐπιτελεῖσθαι Vulgata reddidit fieri. Graeca propriè habent, persici, consummari, impleri.Luc. 13. vers. 32.Roman. 15. vers. 28.2. Corinth. 7. v. 1. &c. LXX. utuntur pro כלהabsolvit, finivit.1. Reg. 3. v. 12. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image]accidit, contigit, evenit, quod semel tantum, in N. T. usurpatur. Arabs eo utitur Marc. 10. vers. 32.1. Corinth. 10. v. 11. Sed verbum ἐπιτελεῖσθαιperfici, consummari, est emphaticum. Respicit enim eo Petrus. 1. ad decretum Dei, quo ab aeterno constituit electos, non sine passionibus ad gloriam coelestem pervenire. Roman. 8. vers. 29.Actor. 24. v. 22. hoc decretum Dei omninò oportet in hoc seculo perfici ac consummari. 2. ad passiones Christi, de quibus simplex verbum τελεῖσθαι, cum quo compositum est eiusdem significationis, vel eandem intendit, usurpatur Luc. 18. v. 31.Iohan. 19. v. 28. & 30.Actor. 13. v. 29. Quae enim passiones in personali corpore Christi coeperunt, eaedem in spirituali ac mystico eius corpore consummantur, unde Paulus in loco huic nostro parallelo dicit, se suisπαθήμασι ἀνταναπληροῦν τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν θλίψεων τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν τῇ σαρκί σου.Col. 1. v. 24. 3. ad crucis utilitatem. Fideles non possunt in studio pietatis perfici absque cruce, utpote per quam mortificatio veteris hominis & renovatio necessaria indies magis magisque perficitur. 2. Corinth. 4. v. 16.Interior noster homo de die in diem renovaturv. 17.id enim quod in praesentiest momentaneum, & leve tribulationis nostrae supra modum in sublimitate aeternum gloriae pondus operatur. Caietanus in h. l. Passiones non nocent, verùm ad perfectionem ducunt. 4. ad crucis brevitatem. Passiones in hoc seculo immittuntur, cum hoc seculo finiuntur & perficiuntur.

## 5:10
BUT THE GOD OF ALL GRACE, WHO CALLED US INTO HIS ETERNAL GLORY IN CHRIST JESUS, AFTER YOU HAVE SUFFERED A LITTLE WHILE, HE HIMSELF WILL PERFECT, CONFIRM, AND STRENGTHEN YOU.

Connection. 1. Most interpreters begin the conclusion of the Epistle from this verse, which they think is concluded with a pious wish after the example of the Pauline Epistles. But because in this verse another argument of consolation is proposed, against persecutions to be endured on account of the confession of the Gospel, and because the concluding wish follows only in v. 14, therefore this verse is more correctly referred here to the ἐργασίαν of the Epistle itself.

2. Some take these words as a pious wish and a serious prayer. For they think that the Apostle wishes for the faithful to whom he writes, both consummation or perfection, that is, full knowledge of the divine will, and full ability to do those things which please God: and also constancy in the faith. And likewise that he prays for the same, that God through the Holy Spirit may work in their hearts those things to which he had exhorted them thus far, from which they gather that the Apostle wished to perform the office of a faithful Minister and Doctor of the Church; since it is his duty not only to propose the sound doctrine of faith and to exhort to constancy in faith and the remaining Christian virtues, but also to seek the increase from God. But it is more correctly said that an argument of consolation is contained in these words, to be embraced by firm faith in the persecutions of the world and the temptations of Satan, taken from the promise of God, that in temptations and the cross, he wills to strengthen and confirm us by his divine will. And likewise from the brevity of those afflictions, that they are small and transitory.

3. Lyranus provides such a connection: Because such resistance against the Devil needs divine assistance, therefore he adds: But the God of all grace, etc. Certainly, the help and protection of God against all the temptations of Satan, against the hatreds and persecutions of the world, against the allurements and seductions of the flesh, renders us invincible.

4. John Huss says, that the Apostle in this general exhortation requires three things from all the faithful. 1. that there ought to be humiliation of the mind from sight. 2. that there ought to be attentive watching against the Devil. 3. that there ought to be an act of thanksgiving concerning benefits, which third member he asserts is contained in this verse. But it is more correctly said, not for the sake of both exhortation and consolation, this sentence is annexed to the preceding ones.

Disposition: Various arguments of consolation against the temptations of Satan and the persecutions of the world are contained in this verse. 1. From the abundance of divine grace. God, who chose, called, and justified you, and whom you acknowledge, invoke, and worship according to the revealed word, etc., is the God of all grace. Therefore, He will be present with you in the cross with His grace and help. 2. From the kindness of the divine calling. God called you into His eternal glory in Christ Jesus. Therefore, the good work which He began in you, He will most kindly perfect. 3. From the brevity of sufferings. That which you endure in this life is a little thing, both with respect to magnitude and with respect to duration. Therefore, all of it must be borne patiently. 4. From the variety of divine benefits. He Himself will perfect, confirm, strengthen, and settle you. Therefore, nothing of those things which are required for constancy in faith and perseverance will be lacking to you.

Exposition. ό δε θεὸς πάσης χάριτος. Just as Paul 2. Cor. 1. v. 3. calls God θεὸν πάσης παρακλήσεως, because all solid and life-giving consolation descends solely from Him, so Peter in this place calls Him the God of all grace, because, namely, He is the fountain of all grace and of all good things, not only temporal and bodily, but also and even most especially spiritual and eternal. The Syrian omitted the name πάσης, and separated these words from the following ones, rendering the text thus: But the God of grace is He who called us etc. But the little word πάσης is emphatic in this place. Because God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is the God of all grace, of every saving good to be expected from Him, therefore in temptations and persecutions He will not withdraw from you His grace, His protection, and His help. Also emphatic is that which in the Greek text these words, ὁ δὲ θεὸς πάσης χάριτος are joined with the following αὐτὸς καταρτίσει. For the Apostle shows that from the same fountain of grace both the first calling to heavenly glory and the final consummation of this benefit, namely, preservation in good and introduction into heavenly glory, proceed.

Ὁ καλέσας ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον αὐτοῦ δὸξαν ἐν Χριστῷ Ιησοῦ. Certain codices read ἡμᾶς, just as the Vulgate Interpreter and the Syrian paraphrast also read. The blessed Luther followed the same reading in the vernacular version, by what reasoning the Apostle associates himself through ἀνακοινωσιν with those who suffer and experience divine help on the cross. Apoc. 1. v. 9. I John your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience in Christ Jesus. The other reading, which has ὑμᾶς, in the second person, is supported by the fact that in the following words of this verse everyone reads ὑμᾶς. in the same way. The Apostle expresses in these words, first, the principle or efficient cause of the calling, which is God, of whom 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. who hath called us with a holy calling. Second, the impulsive cause, which is the gratuitous mercy of God, which the Apostle hints at when he calls God, who called us, the God of all grace. Certainly, therefore, even the grace of the calling descends solely from Him. Third, the object of the calling, which are those believing in Christ, whom he had ordered a little before to be στερεοὺς τῇ πίστει. Fourth, the end of the calling, which is heavenly and eternal glory. The Syrian περιφραστικῶς rendered it, called you into his eternal glory, He emphatically calls that glory the eternal glory of God, not only because the glory of God will shine forth most greatly in the blessedness of the elect, but also because God will make the elect participants in a certain way of His eternal glory. The Apostle looks back to v. 1. of this chapter, in which he had called himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ and also a partaker of that glory that shall be revealed in time to come. Fifth, the meritorious cause of the calling, which is Christ. That προσδιορισμὸς can indeed, with the analogy of faith safe, be referred both to the little word ὑμᾶς: He called you existing in Christ Jesus, i.e., through faith, because only those perseveringly believing in Christ will be rendered participants of that eternal glory, and to αἰώνιον θεοῦ δόξαν, because eternal glory is not obtained finally except in Christ, i.e., on account of Christ, just as Rom. 6. v. 23. it is said, that eternal life is χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν χριστῷ, But it is most simply referred to the participle καλέσας, because the calling to eternal glory comes to us on account of the merit of Christ, since all spiritual benefits are to be credited to Him, the first of which is eternal election, and in time the calling, the last eternal glorification. 1. Cor. 1. v. 2. sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints. Gal. 1. v. 6. who called you into the grace of Christ, that is, through the grace of Christ, or, on account of Christ. Eph. 1. v. 3. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us in every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.v. 4.as he chose us in him before the foundation of the worldvers. 11.in Christ ἐκκληρώθημεν we were called by lot2. Tim. 1. v. 9.God saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the times of the ages. The Syrian, according to the customary Hebraism, rendered it, by the hand of Jesus Christ. But that some refer this προσδιορισμὸν, ἐν Χριστῷ Ιησοῦ to the following ὀλίγον παθόντας, in the sense that we are compelled to endure persecution in Christ, that is, on account of Christ, anyone understands that this is forced, for ὑποδιαστολὴ. ὀλίγον παθόντας. precedes; this is referred to the preceding ὑμᾶς. The Vulgate rendered it, having suffered a little, Erasmus, afflicted for a little while. Some take this 'little' as the opposite of magnitude, in the sense that they are compelled to endure something small in this age. Others, however, take it as the opposite of duration or long length of time, in the sense that every suffering of this life is brief and transitory. Both meanings can be joined, since the adverb ὀλίγον signifies not only 'a little' but also 'a little while' Mark 6. v. 31.rest a little whileLuke 7. v. 47.To whom less is forgiven, he loves less.1. Pet. 1. v. 6.grieved for a little while in various temptations.Rev. 17. v. 11.he must remain a short time; the same judgment regarding the noun ὀλίγος. Matt. 25. 21. ἐπί ὀλίγα you have been faithful over a few and small things.Jas. 4. v. 14. ἀτμὶς πρὸς ὀλίγον φαινομένη, appearing for a short time; and since the afflictions of this life are both light and brief, as the Apostle teaches 2. Cor. 4. vers. 17. τὸ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν καθ' ὑπερβολὴν, εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης κατεργάζεται ἡμῖν, where the weight of heavenly glory is opposed to the lightness of affliction; the eternity of glory is opposed to the momentary duration of affliction.

Ἀυτὸς καταρτίσει ὑμᾶς, στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιώσει. Thus two Royal Codices and others read, which Robert Stephanus annotated, which reading Prosper followed in book 1 de vocat. gent. chap. 24, and the Vulgate translation, explaining the four Greek words καταρτίσει, στηρίξει, σθενώσει θεμελιώσει by three Latin ones, he will perfect, he will confirm, and he will make solid. This reading is also confirmed from the following δοξολογίᾳ, which agrees more with a promise than with a wish. The Verona Codex reads in the optative καταρτίσαι, στηρίξαι, σθενῶσαι θεμελιῶσαι, Which reading Estius prefers to the former, and asserts that those copies which have the future are of less approved faith. But he ought to have feared the thunderbolt of the Council of Trent, which pronounced the Vulgate Latin version authentic, from which it is not permitted to depart under any pretext. It, however, reads in the future, as we have already warned before. Estius indeed warns that the sense is the same, since the Hebrews use futures, not only for preceptive, but also for optative meanings. And that futures are placed for imperatives is customary, especially in precepts, as appears from the Decalogue. Examples also occur in which futures are usurped for the potential mood. 1 Kings 3, verse 8. The people shall not be numbered for multitude, i.e., shall not be able to be numbered. 2 Kings 5, verse 12. Shall I not wash myself in them? i.e., shall I be able to wash myself. Likewise for the mood of beseeching and requesting, that it may be permitted to do something. Num. 20, v. 17. We will pass through thy land, for let it be permitted to us to pass. Jer. 40, verse 15. I will go and smite Ishmael, i.e., let it be permitted to me to go and smite. But that futures are placed for optatives is very rare. Estius ought therefore to have annotated examples of this enallage. Erasmus indeed reads στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιώσει, but reads the fourth word in the optative καταρτίσαι, and does not accept those three as verbs of future tense, but as nouns placed in the ablative case. For thus he reads and translates: αὐτὸς καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιώσει, may he himself perfect you by support, confirmation, foundation. Afterwards he adds: Although I am not ignorant that these three can be accepted as verbs of future tense, he will support, he will confirm, he will found. In the copies of some Greeks these were infinitives, στηρίξαι, σθενῶσαι, θεμελιῶσαι may he confirm, may he corroborate, may he found. But Erasmus confuses the reading of different Codices. For those Codices which read καταρτίσαι, they also read στηρίξαι, σθενώσαι, θεμελιώσει. And conversely, those Codices which read στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιὼσει read καταρτίσαι. The Syriac explains it in the past, or certainly in the present, with the insertion of the word [consult facsimile image] for thus he renders the text: Who gave to us, (or whom he gave to us) that when we have endured these light afflictions, we might be corroborated and confirmed and established (or may we be corroborated, confirmed, and persist) in him (Christ) forever. But in many things he departs from the Greek text. 1. In the Greek the verbs καταρτίσει, στηρίξει etc. are referred to the God of all grace. The Syriac refers them to Christ. 2. In the Greek it is not a matter of the benefit already while receiving, but still in the process of receiving. The Syrian refers to past time. 3. In the Greek εἰς αἰώνιον & ἐν αὐτῳ, is not added; the Syrian adds both. Therefore, the reading of the Greek text is to be preferred as being authentic.

The pronoun ὁ αὐτὸς seems to be redundant from the custom of the Hebrews, among whom relative pronouns are sometimes used idly in the same clause in which the antecedent is, and indeed either placed before the noun Gen. 2. v. 19.cap. 13. v. 16.Ex. 2. v. 6. etc. Matth. 26. v. 24. or placed after the same Gen. 1. v. 27.Lev. 14. v. 6.Matth. 2. v. 41.cap. 12. v. 36.Ioh. 17. v. 2.Rom. 16. v. 27.Apoc. 2. v. 13. which the latter happens in this place. Meanwhile, its emphasis is great. For the Apostle signifies that this preservation in good is to be ascribed uniquely to God alone of all grace, and not to human strengths. But how the significations of these four words, which the Apostle emphatically joins, are to be distinguished, the opinions of the Interpreters vary greatly concerning this. The interlinear Gloss annotates thus: He will perfect i. e. to those virtues which you already have, He will add others; He will confirm for enduring tribulations; He will make solid i. e. He will bring back into the unity of the Church the members dissolved by fear and error. Lyranus proceeds thus: He will perfect, namely, to that for which your virtue does not suffice; He will confirm your fragility, and will make solid the grace given to you. Hugo: He will perfect the reason with full cognition; He will confirm the will with all-manner of peace; He will make solid the memory with continuous and infallible retention of things. Or, He will perfect the rational part with the open vision of God; He will confirm the concupiscible with perfect, integral, true love; He will make solid the irascible with interminable comprehension. The Carthusian: God will perfect that which He began in us; He will confirm in the way through grace, He will make solid in the fatherland through glory. Or, He will perfect the intellect with the reasons of things to be believed and with the understanding of a purified mind; He will confirm the will through the fervor of charity; He will make solid the memory, so that it may be fixed in God. John Huss joins several explanations. Christ Himself will perfect the victory of the battle, which He had so graciously begun. Secondly, He will confirm, regulating the battle until the end of life, and then He will place the seal of victory. Thirdly, He will consolidate in the fatherland, when there will truly be wandering error, but the perpetual fruit of victory. And afterwards: He, who called you, will perfect, supply, you in good; He will confirm, namely, against the evil of fault; He will consolidate, i. e. He will fortify, namely, against the evil of punishment. Or thus, He will perfect, namely, the reason, the cognition of truth;

He will make the concupiscible faculty firm in the love of goodness; he will solidify, namely, the irascible faculty in the detestation of all perversity. Or thus, he will perfect against the world, he will confirm against the flesh; he will solidify against pride. Or, he will perfect against the concupiscence of the flesh; he will confirm against the concupiscence of the eyes; he will solidify against the pride of life. Or, he will perfect, by giving in the present the appetite of executing, he will solidify by giving the operation of completing. Or, he will perfect in the future the rational faculty itself with perfect knowledge, he will confirm the will itself with perfect fruition, he will solidify the memory with secure rest. Some refer this to the mystery of the Trinity. The Father perfects, the Son confirms, the Holy Spirit solidifies. Primaticcius says, we are here perfected by God, giving the will to perfect; confirmed, giving the will to execute; solidified, giving the strength to complete the work: in the future life, when he will give perfect knowledge, love, and retention. But all these proceed from the Vulgate Latin version, which rendered four Greek words with three. The best explanation of all is gathered from the emphasis of the Greek words. καταρτίζειν signifies to perfect, to construct, to adapt, to join together, to restore. Matth. 4. v. 21. Marc. 1. v. 19. it is used concerning the mending of nets. Therefore the Apostle signifies that the web of good works and justice, which we weave, is easily and quickly torn in this life, unless there is added God's καταρτισμὸς. Es ist mit uns in diesem leben eitel Flictwerct und Stu ctwerct. Matth. 21. vers. 16. Roman. 9. v. 22. Hebr. 10. v. 5. it is used concerning preparation. Therefore the Apostle signifies that we are to be prepared by God for good, for which there is no ἱκανότης in us 2. Cor. 3. v. 5. Eph. 2. v. 10. In other places it is taken for perfection or consummation, in which way the Vulgate also rendered it here, he himself will perfect you. Luc. 6. v. 40. 1. Corinth. 1. v. 10. Hebr. 11. v. 3. etc. Therefore the Apostle signifies that it is God who renders us absolute and perfect in the salutary knowledge of himself, in faith and in the pursuit of piety, and who fills us with his gifts, supplies our defects, and completes our blessedness. For thus is that καταρτίσαι explained in places parallel to this one of ours. 1. Thessal. 3. vers. 10. καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν. Hebr. 13. vers. 20. & 21. THE GOD of peace καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς ἐν παντὶ ἒργῳ ἀγαθῷ εἰς τὸ ποιῆσαι τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ. It also signifies καταρτίζειν to replace members in a dislocated body. 2. Corinth. 13. v. 1. καταρτίζεσθε. Be members of one body joined to one another through the bond of charity. Galat. 6. v. 1. If anyone by some fall has been overtaken, him καταρτίζετε as a member light restore the joints. For these things are said with respect to the mystical body of Christ which is the Church. The Apostle therefore signifies that it is God who makes us members in the mystical body of Christ, and if we are overtaken by some fall, he restores us, and as it were resets dislocated members. The LXX use for יסד he founded, he laid a foundation. Psal. 8. v. 3. for כון he prepared, he ordained, he confirmed, for it always imports perfection and firmness. Psalm. 67. v. 10. Psal. 73. v. 17. Psal. 79. v. 16. Psal. 88. v. 36. for עח he fortified, he strengthened Psalm. 8. v. 3. for שות he fashioned, he composed with singular care and industry Psalm. 10. v. 3. for תמך he sustained something from above, lest it fall or perish, or he supported Psal. 16. v. 6. Esa. 4. v. 12. & seqq. cap. 5. v. 3. & 11. which meanings all can be accommodated here. The Syrian has the verb, חיל in Ethpael, he was comforted, he was corroborated. στηρὶξειν signifies to fix, to establish firmly, for it is more than ἵστημι, from which it is derived. Luc. 16. vers. 26. μέγα χάσμα ἐστήρικται, and metaphorically to stabilize, to prop up, Luc. 22. v. 32. στήριξον confirm the brethren, Roman. 1. vers. 11. εἰς τὸ στηριχθῆναι ὑμᾶς, to confirm you in the faith. 1. Thess. 3. v. 1. We sent Timothy εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς καὶ παρακαλέσαι ὑμᾶς περί τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν. where the latter is ἐξηγητικὸν prioris. cap. eiusd. v. 12. May God make mutual charity abound vers. 13. εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας ἀμέμπτους ἐν ἁγιοσόνῃ 2. Thessal. 2. vers. 16. ὁ θεὸς στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς έν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ. cap. 3. v. 3. Faithful is God, ὁς στηρὶξει ὑμᾶς καὶ φυλάξει ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ Iac. 5. vers. 8. Be patient, καὶ στηρίξατε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν 2. Petr. 1. v. 12. ἐστηριγμένους confirmed in the present truth. Apoc. 3. v. 2. στήριξον, confirm the rest, which are about to die. From these passages the genuine meaning of this verb is gathered, namely, that God in the way of faith and piety supports us, lifts up our infirmity, confirms us with the strength of the Spirit, lest we fail from the infirmity of the flesh in such great hatreds of Satan and the world. The LXX use for יצב in Hiphil, he made to stand, he erected. Gen. 28. v. 12. Prov. 15. v. 26. which elsewhere they explain by στερεόω I make firm 1. Reg. 13. v. 21. Thren. 2. vers. 4. στηλόω I stabilize. Iud. 18. v. 16. 1. Reg. 17. v. 16. βεβαιόω Psalm. 40. v. 13. Also for סמך he sustained from above, he supported from above, a person, lest he fall and perish, he propped up, he stabilized, Gen. 27. v. 37. Psalm. 50. v. 13. Psal. 110. v. 7. Psal. 111. v. 7. &c. for סעד he sustained, he made firm, he strengthened Jud. 19. v. 5. & 8.Psal. 103. v. 17. for תמך held, sustained from above, supportedEx. 17. v. 12. for תקע fixed inIsa. 22. v. 25. which all these meanings can be adapted here. The Syrian rendered it by [consult facsimile image] in Ethpael to strengthen in the right, to confirm. σθενοῦν signifies to strengthen, from σθένω, which is I am strong, I am able. σθένειν ἐν πλούτῳ, among Sophocles is to be strong in resources, to be powerful in riches, hence σθένος force, strength, power. Opposed to it is ἀσθένεια weakness of strength. This word does not occur elsewhere in the Scriptures. The Vulgate Interpreter and the Syrian omitted it in this place, or what is more likely, they rendered two Greek words with one Latin and Syriac one.

Θεμελιοῦντε signifies to found, whence θεμέλιος foundation.Matt. 7. v. 25.Luke 6. v. 48. θεμελιώται that house was founded upon a rock,Eph. 3. v. 18. ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐῤῥιζομένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι. Col. 1. v. 23. τῇ πίστει τεθεμελιωμένοι καὶ ἑδραῖοι, καὶ μὴ μετακινούμενοι ἀπὸ τῆς ἐλπίδος τοῦ εὐαγγελίου Heb. 1. v. 10. In the beginning the earth ἐθεμελίωσας, so that it might stand firm and immovable. From these passages the genuine meaning of this word is gathered, namely that it is God who founds and makes us solid, so that we may be constant in faith and charity, and not be overturned by any winds of temptations, or waves of persecutions, or rains of adversities. The LXX use it for יסר founded, laid a foundation,Josh. 6. v. 26.1. Kings 6. v. 36.chap. 7. v. 10. etc. for כוז confirmed, established, constructed, which imports perfection and firmness Psal. 8. v. 4.Psal. 47. v. 8.Psalm. 86. v. 5. etc. The Syrian has the word [consult facsimile image] in Ethpael confirmed. It is gathered therefore from this word θεμελιοῦν, that this whole passage is metaphorical. For just as for the construction of a fortress it is required that it be founded on a firm rock, that it be stabilized with columns, that it be propped up with beams, so that it may not collapse, that it be fortified and surrounded with ramparts, that it be covered, so that it may not be damaged by rains, so in the spiritual building God provides all these things for us out of grace, He founds and stabilizes us in faith, He restores us in virtues, He instructs us with the strength of the Spirit, so that our renewal may take increments day by day; He arms us for sustaining the temptations of Satan, He preserves and confirms us in true piety, so that we may be able to stand against all the insults of the Devil, the world, and the flesh, and not by any threats or terrors suffer ourselves to be moved away from the true faith and piety. In summary, whatever pertains to the beginning, middle, and end of our salvation, all that the Lord Peter comprehends in these four words. Cajetan, following the Greek text, accepts four words, and by the word of perfecting he wishes it to be signified that the temptations of the Devil conduce to perfection; and that it pertains to this, that God may support with moral virtues, confirm with the strength of faith, and stabilize or make solid with His assistance.

Latin:

DEUS AUTEM OMNIS GRATIAE, QUI VOCAVIT NOS IN AETERNAM SUAM GLORIAM IN CHRISTO IESU, MODICUM PASSOS IPSE PERFICIET, CONFIRMABIT, SOLIDABITQUE.

Connexio. 1. Plerique Interpp. Conclusionem Epistolae ab hoc versiculo inchoant, quam exemplo Epistolarum Paulinarum pio voto concludi existimant. Sed quia in hoc versiculo proponitur aliud argumentum consolationis, contra persecutiones propter Evangelii confessionem sustinendas, & quia in v. 14. demum sequitur votum conclusivum, ideò rectiùs ad ipsam Epistolae ἐργασίαν hic versiculus refertur.

2. Quidam haec verba accipiunt, ut pium votum, ac seriam precationem. Existimant enim, Apostolum optare fidelibus, ad quos scribit, tum consummationem seu perfectionem, h. e. plenam divinae voluntatis cognitionem, ac plenam facultatem agendi, quae Deo placent: tum constantiam in fide. Itemque precari iisdem, ut Deus per Spiritum sanctum eain cordibus ipsorum operetur, ad quae ipsos exhortatus fuerat hactenus, ex quo colligunt, Apostolum fidelis Ministri, & Doctoris Ecclesiae officio fungi voluisse; quippe cuius sit, non solùm sanam fidei doctrinam proponere, & ad constantiam in fide, ac reliquas virtutes Christianas exhortari, sed etiam à Deo incrementum petere. Sed rectiùs dicitur, contineri in his verbis argumentum consolationis, in persecutionibus mundi, & tentationibus Satanae, firmâ fide amplectendae, desumtum à promissione Dei, quod in tentationibus & cruce, divinâ suà voluntate nos velit roborare & confirmare. Itemque à brevitate illarum afflictionum, quòd sint exiguae ac transitoriae.

3. Lyranus talem tradit connexionem: Quia talis resistentia contra Diabolum indiget divinâ afsistentiâ, ideò subdit: Deus autem omnis gratiae &c. Nimirum Dei auxilium & praesidium contra omnes Satanae tentationes, contra mundi odia & persecutiones, contra carnis illecebras & seductiones, nos invictos reddit.

4. Iohannes Huss dicit, Apostolum in hac generali exhortatione tria ab omnibus fidelibus requirere. 1. quòd à conspectu debeat esse mentis humiliatio. 2. quòd adversus Diabolum debeat esse attenta vigilatio. 3. quòd de beneficiis debeat esse gratiarum actio, quod membrum tertium in hoc versiculo contineri asserit. Sed rectiùs dicitur, non tàm exhortationis, quàm consolationis ergò hanc sententiam prioribus esse annexam.

Dispositio: Varia in hoc versiculo continentur consolationis adversùs Satanae tentationes, & mundi persecutiones argumenta. 1. à divinae gratiae ubertate. Deus, qui vos elegit, vocavit, iustificavit, quemque iuxta revelatum verbum agnoscitis, invocatis, colitis &c. est Deus omnis gratiae. Ergò suâ gratiâ & auxilio in cruce vobis aderit. 2. à divinae vocationis benignitate. Vocavit vos DEUS in aternam suam gloriam in Christo Iesu. Ergò quod in vobis coepit opus bonum, benignissimè perficiet. 3. à passionum brevitate. Modicum est, quod in hac vita sustinetis, tàm respectu magnitudinis, quàm respectu diuturnitatis. Ergò patienter illud omne ferendum. 4. à beneficiorum divinorum varietate. Ipse vos perficiet, sulciet, roborabit & solidabit. Ergò nihil eorum, quae ad constantiam infide & perseverantiam requiruntur, vobis deerit.

Expositio. ό δε θεὸς πάσης χάριτος. Sicut Paulus 2. Cor. 1. v. 3. Deum vocat θεὸν πάσης παρακλήσεως, quia omnis solida & vivisica consolatio ab ipso unicè descendit, sic Petrus eum hoc loco vocat Deum omnis gratiae, quia scil. est fons omnis gratiae & omnium bonorum, non solùm temporalium & corporalium, sed etiam ac vel maximè spiritualium & aeternorum. Syrus omisit nomen πάσης, ac verba haec à sequentibus disiunxit, textum sic reddens: Deus autem gratiae est, qui vocavit nos &c. Sed vocula πάσης est hoc loco emphatica. Quia Deus Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi est Deus omnis gratiae, òmnis boni salutaris ab ipso expectandi, ideò in tentationibus & persecutionibus non subtrahet vobis suam gratiam, suum praesidium & auxilium. Emphaticum quoque illud, quod in Graeco textu haec verba, ὁ δὲ θεὸς πάσης χάριτος coniunguntur cum sequentibus αὐτὸς καταρτίσει. Ostendit enim Apostolus, ex eodem gratiae fonte & primam ad gloriam coelestem vocationem, & ultimam huius beneficii consummationem, videl. conservationem in bono, & introductionem in gloriam coelestem provenire.

Ὁ καλέσας ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον αὐτοῦ δὸξαν ἐν Χριστῷ Ιησοῦ. Quidam Codices legunt ἡμᾶς, quomodo etiam legit vulgatus Interpres & Syrus paraphrastes. Eandem lectionem secutus est B. Lutherus in versione vernacula, quâ ratione Apostolus seipsum per ἀνακοινωσιν associaret iis, qui patiuntur & divinum auxilium in cruce experiuntur. Apoc. 1. v. 9.Ego Iohannes frater vester, & particeps in tribulatione & regno & patientia in Christo Iesu. Alteri lectioni, quae in secunda persona habet ὑμᾶς, suffragatur, quod in sequentibus huius versiculi verbis eodem modo omnes legunt ὑμᾶς. Exprimit autem in his verbis Apostolus primò vocationis principium sive causam efficientem, quae est Deus, de quo 2. Tim. 1. v. 9.quod vocaverit nos vocatione sancta. Secundò causam impulsivam, quae est gratuita Dei misericordia, quam innuit Apostolus, quando Deum, qui nos vocavit, appellat Deum omnis gratiae. Utique ergò etiam gratia vocationis unicè ab ipso descendit. Tertiò vocationis obiectum, quod sunt credentes in Christum, quos paulo antè iusserat, esse στερεοὺς τῇ πίστει. Quartò vocationis terminum, qui est gloria coelestis & aeterna. Syrus περιφραστικῶς reddidit, vocavit vos in gloriam, quae est in aeternum, Emphaticè autem vocat gloriam illam aeternam Dei gloriam, non solùm quia gloria Dei in beatitudine electorum vel maximè elucebit, sed etiam quia Deus aeternae suae gloriae electos certâ ratione participes faciet. Respicit Apostolus ad v. 1. huius capitis, in quo se vocaverat testem passionum Christi & eius, quae aliquando revelabitur, gloriae consortem. Quintò vocationis causam meritoriam, quae est Christus. Potest quidem ille προσδιορισμὸς salvâ fidei analogiâ referri tùm ad voculam ὑμᾶς: Vocavit vos existentes in Christo Iesu, sc. per fidem, quia non nisi perseveranter in Christum credentes aeternae illius gloriae reddentur participes, tùm ad αἰώνιον θεοῦ δόξαν, quia aeterna gloria non nisi in Christo i. e. propter Christum finaliter obtinetur, sicut Rom. 6. v. 23. dicitur, vitam aternam esseχάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν χριστῷ, Sed simplicissimè refertur ad participium καλέσας, quia vocatio ad aeternam gloriam propter Christi meritum nobis obtingit, quippe cui accepta ferenda sunt omnia beneficia spiritualia, quorum primum est aeterna electio, & in tempore vocatio, ultimum aeterna glorificatio. 1. Cor. 1. v. 2.sanctificatis in Christo Iesu, vocatis sanctis.Gal. 1. v. 6.qui vos vocavit in gratia Christi, id est, per Christi gratiam, sive, propter Christum.Eph. 1. v. 3.Benedictus Deus & pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nos in omni benidictione in coelestibus in Christo Iesu.v. 4.sicut elegit nos in ipso ante mundi constitutionemvers. 11.in Christoἐκκληρώθημενsorte vocati sumus2. Tim. 1. v. 9.Deus liberavit nos & vocavit vocationi sancta, non secundum opera nostra, sed secundum suum propositum & gratiam, quae data nobis est in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia. Syrus iuxta usitatum Hebraismum reddidit, per manum Iesu Christi. Quod vero quidam hunc προσδιορισμὸν, ἐν Χριστῷ Ιησοῦ referunt ad sequentia ὀλίγον παθόντας, sensu eo, quod in Christo i. e. propter Christum persecutionem sustinere cogamur, illud coactum esse, quilibet intelligit, praecedit enim ὑποδιαστολὴ. ὀλίγον παθόντας. refertur hoc ad praecedens ὑμᾶς. Vulgata reddidit, modicum passos, Eras nus, parumper afflictos. Quidam hoc modicum accipiunt ut oppositum magnitudini, sensu eo, quod exiguum quid in hoc seculo sustinere cogantur. Alii vero accipiunt ut oppositum diuturnit ati sive longae durationi, sensu eo, quod brevis & transitoria sit omnis huius vitae passio. Potest utraque significatio coniungi, cum adverbium ὀλίγον non solùm significet parùm, sed etiam paululùm Marc. 6. v. 31.requiescite paululùmLuc. 7. v. 47.Cui minùsremittitur, minùs diligit.1. Petr. 1. v. 6.modicum contristati in variis tentationibus.Apoc. 17. v. 11.oportet eum breve tempus manere; idem iudicium de nomine ὀλίγος.Matth. 25. 21.ἐπί ὀλίγαsuper pauca & exigua fuisti fidelis.Iac. 4. v. 14.ἀτμὶς πρὸς ὀλίγον φαινομένη,ad breve tempus apparens; cumque afflictiones huius vitae & leves sint & breves, docente Apostolo 2. Cor. 4. vers. 17.τὸ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν καθ' ὑπερβολὴν, εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης κατεργάζεται ἡμῖν, ubi levitati afflictionis opponitur pondus coelestis gloriae; momentaneae durationi afflictionis opponitur aeternitas gloriae.

Ἀυτὸς καταρτίσει ὑμᾶς, στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιώσει. Ita legunt Regii Codices duo & alii, quos annotavit Robertus Stephanus, quam lectionem secutus est Prosper lib. 1. de vocat. gent. cap. 24. ac vulgata translatio, quatuor verba Graeca καταρτίσει, στηρίξει, σθενώσει θεμελιώσει exponens per tria Latina, perficiet, confirmabit, solidabitque. Confirmatur etiam haec lectio ex subiuncta δοξολογίᾳ, quae magis congruit promissioni quàm voto. Codex Veronensis legit in optativo καταρτίσαι, στηρίξαι, σθενῶσαι θεμελιῶσαι, quam lectionem Estius priori praefert, ac exemplaria illa, quae habent futurum, minùs probatae fidei esse asserit. Sed metuere debehat fulmen Concilii Tridentini, quod vulgatam versionem Latinam pronunciavit authenticam, à quâ non liceat ullo praetextu discedere. Ea vero in futuro legit, ut iam antè monuimus. Monet quidem Estius, sensum esse eundem, cum Hebraei futuris utantur, non solùm pro praeceptivis, sed etiam pro optativis. Atque futura pro imperativis poni, usitatum est, maxime in praeceptis, ut apparet ex Decalogo. Occurrunt etiam exempla, in quibus futura usurpantur pro modo potentiali. 1. Reg. 3. vers. 8.Populus non supputabitur prae multitudine, i. e. non poterit supputari. 2. Reg. 5. vers. 12.an non lavabo me in illis, i. e. lavare me potero. Item pro modo obsecrandi & petendi, ut liceat aliquid. Num. 20. v. 17.Transibimus terram tuam, pro liceat nobis transire.Ierem. 40. vers. 15.Ibo & percutiam Ismaëlem i. e. liceat mihi ire & percutere. Sed futura pro optativis poni rarissimum. Debebat igitur Estius exempla huius enallages annotare. Erasmus legit quidem στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιώσει, sed quartum verbum legit in optativo καταρτίσαι, ac tria illa non accipit pro verbis futuri temporis, sed pro nominibus in casu auferendi positis. Sic enim legit & vertit. αὐτὸς καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιώσει,ipse perficiat vos fulturâ, confirmatione, fundatione. Postea addit. Quanquam non ignoro, haec lria posse pro verbis accipi futuri temporis, fulciet, confirmabit, fundabit. In nonnullorum Graecorum exemplaribus haec erant infinita,στηρίξαι, σθενῶσαι, θεμελιῶσαιconfirmet, corroboret, fundet. Sed confundit Erasinus diversorum Codicum lectionem. Qui enim Codices legunt καταρτίσαι, illi etiam legunt στηρίξαι, σθενώσαι, θεμελιώσει. Et vicissim, qui Codices legunt στηρίξει, σθενώσει, θεμελιὼσει legunt καταρτίσαι. Syrus in praeterito, vel certè in praesente exponit, inserto verbo [consult facsimile image] sic enim textum reddit: Qui dedit nobis, (vel quem dedit nobis) ut cum sustinuerimus has afflictiones modicas, corroboraremur & confirmaremur & stabiliremur (vel corroboremur, confirmemur ac perstemus) in eo (Christo) in perpetuum. Sed in multis discedit à textu Graeco. 1. In Graeco verba καταρτίσει, στηρίξει &c. referuntur ad Deum omnis gratiae. Syrus ea refert ad Christum. 2. In Graeco non agitur de beneficio iam dum accepto, sed adhuc accipiendo. Syrus refert ad tempus praeteritum. 3. In Graeco non additur εἰς αἰώνιον & ἐν αὐτῳ, Syrus utrumque addit. Praeferenda igitur Graeci textus utpote authentici lectio.

Pronomen ὁ αὐτὸς abundare videtur ex Hebraeorum consuetudine, apud quos quandoque in eodem colo, in quo est antecedens, otiosè relativa adhibentur, & quidem vel praeposita nomini Gen. 2. v. 19.cap. 13. v. 16.Ex. 2. v. 6. &c. Matth. 26. v. 24. vel eidem postposita Gen. 1. v. 27.Lev. 14. v. 6.Matth. 2. v. 41.cap. 12. v. 36.Ioh. 17. v. 2.Rom. 16. v. 27.Apoc. 2. v. 13. quod posterius hoc loco contingit. Interim magna eius est emphasis. Significat enim Apostolus, soli Deo omnis gratiae, non autem humanis viribus hanc conservationem in bono esse unicè adscribendam. Quomodo vero quatuor horum verborum, quae emphaticè Apostolus coniungit, significationes sint distingvendae, de eo plurimùm variant Interpretum sententiae. Gloss. interlin. sic annotat. Ipse perficiet i. e. illis virtutibus, quas iam habetis, super addet alias; confirmabit ad perferendas tribulationes; solidabit h. e. membra timore & errore dissoluta in unitatem Ecclesiae reducet. Lyranus sic progreditur: Ipse perficiet sc. ad quod vestra virtus non sufficit; confirmabit vestram fragilitatem, solidabitque gratiam vobis datam. Hugo. Perficiet rationem plena cognitione; confirmabit voluntatem omnimoda pace; solidabit memoriam continuâ & infallibili rerum retentione. Vel, perficiet partem rationalem visione Dei apertâ; confirmabit concupiscibilem dilectione perfectâ, integrâ, verâ; solidabit ir ascibilem interminabili comprehensione. Carthusianus. Perficiet Deus id, quod incepit in nobis; confirmabit in via per gratiam, solidabit in patriâ per gloriam, Vel, Perficiet intellectum rationibus credendorum & purificatae mentis intelligentia; confirmabit voluntatem per caritatis fervorem: solidabit memoriam, ut sit in Deo fixa. Ioh. Huss plures explicationes coniungit. Ipse vero Christus persiciet victoriam pugnae, quam tàm gratiosè inceperat. Secundò confirmabit regulans pugnam usque ad finem vitae, & tunc ponet sigillum victoriae. Tertiò consolidabit in patria, quando verè erit vagus error, sed perpetuus fructus victoriae. Et postea. Ipse, qui vocavit vos, perficiet, supple, vos in bono; confirmabit sc. contra malum culpae; consolidabit i. e. fortificabit, scil contra malum poenae. Vel sic, perficiet sc. rationem, cognitionem veritatis;

mabit concupiscibilem in amore bonitatis; solidabit scil. irascibilem in detestatione totius perversitatis. Vel sic, perficiet contra mundum confirmabit contra carnem; solidabit contra superbiam. Vel, perficiet contra concupiscentiam carnis; confirmabit contra concupiscentiam oculorum; folidabit contra superbiam vitae. Vel, perficiet, dans in praesenti appetitum exequendi, solidabit dans operationem consummandi. Vel, persiciet in futuro ipsam rationalem perfectâ cognitione, confirmabit ipsam voluntatem perfectâ fruitione, solidabit memoriam securâ quietatione. Quidam referunt ad mysterium Trinitatis. Perficit Pater, confirmat Filius, solidat Spiritus sanctus. Primaticcius dicit, nos hic à Deo persici, dante voluntatem perficiendi; confirmari, dante voluntatem exequendi; solidari, dante robur opus consummandi: in futura vita, cum dabit perfectam cognitionem, dilectionem, retentione. Sed haec omnia procedunt ex vulgata versione Latina, quae tribus verbis Graeca quatuor reddidit. Omnium optima explicatio colligitur ex emphasi Graecorum verborum. καταρτίζειν significat perficere, construere, adaptare, coagmentare, instaurare.Matth. 4. v. 21.Marc. 1. v. 19. usurpatur de sarciendis retibus. Significat ergò Apostolus, telam bonorum operum & iustitiae, quam teximus, facilè ac citò in hac vita rumpi, nisi accedat Dei καταρτισμὸς.Es ist mit uns in diesem leben eitel Flictwerct und Stu ctwerct.Matth. 21. vers. 16.Roman. 9. v. 22.Hebr. 10. v. 5. usurpatur de praeparatione. Significat ergò Apostolus, à Deo nos esse ad bonum praeparandos, ad quod nulla in nobis est ἱκανότης2. Cor. 3. v. 5.Eph. 2. v. 10. In aliis locis accipitur pro perfectione sive consummatione, quo modo etiam vulgata hîc reddidit, ipse perficiet vos.Luc. 6. v. 40.1. Corinth. 1. v. 10.Hebr. 11. v. 3. &c. Significat ergò Apostolus, Deum esse, qui nos absolutos & perfectos reddat in salutari sui cognitione, fide ac studio pietatis, quique donis suis nos impleat, defectus nostros suppleat, & beatitudinem compleat. Ita namque exponitur illud καταρτίσαι in locis huic nostro parallelis. 1. Thessal. 3. vers. 10.καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν.Hebr. 13. vers. 20. & 21.DEUS pacisκαταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς ἐν παντὶ ἒργῳ ἀγαθῷ εἰς τὸ ποιῆσαι τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ. Corinth. 13. v. 1.καταρτίζεσθε.Sitis membra unius corporis per caritatis nexum invicem coniuncta.Galat. 6. v. 1.Si quis lapsu aliquo fuerit praeoccupatus, illumκαταρτίζετεtunquam membrum lux artus reponite. Dicuntur enim haec respectu mystici corporis Christi quod est Ecclesia. Significat ergò Apostolus, Deum esse, qui nos essieit membra in corpore Christi mystico, ac si lapsu aliquo praeoccupamur, nos instaurat, ac velut luxata membra reponit. Θεμελιοῦντε significat fundare, unde θεμέλιοςfundamentum.Matth. 7. v. 25.Luc. 6. v. 48.θεμελιώταιfundata est illa domus supra petram,Eph. 3. v. 18.ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐῤῥιζομένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι.Col. 1. v. 23.τῇ πίστει τεθεμελιωμένοι καὶ ἑδραῖοι, καὶ μὴ μετακινούμενοι ἀπὸ τῆς ἐλπίδος τοῦ εὐαγγελίουHebr. 1. v. 10.In principio terramἐθεμελίωσας,ut stet firma & immobilis. Ex his locis genuina significatio huius verbi colligitur, videlicet Deum esse, qui nos fundet atque solidet, ut in fide & caritate constantes simus, nec ullis tentationum ventis, vel persecutionum fluctibus, vel adversitatum pluviis evertamur. LXX. utuntur pro יסרfundavit, fundamentum posuit,Ios. 6. v. 26.1. Reg. 6. v. 36.cap. 7. v. 10. &c. pro כוזconfirmavit, constituit, construxit, quod perfectionem & firmitatem importat Psal. 8. v. 4.Psal. 47. v. 8.Psalm. 86. v. 5. &c. Syrus habet verbum [consult facsimile image] in Ethpael confirmavit. Colligitur ergò ex hoc verbo θεμελιοῦν, totum hunc locum esse metaphoricum. Quemadmodum enim ad arcis extructionem requiritur, ut ea fundetur in firma petra, ut stabiliatur columnis, ut fulciatur tignis, ne corruat, ut muniatur & circumvelletur aggeribus, ut tegatur, ne à pluviis laedatur, sic in spirituali aedificio Deus haec omnia ex gratia nobis praestat, in fide nos fundat ac stabilit, in virtutibus instaurat, Spiritus robore nos instruit, ut renovatio nostra in dies incrementa sumat; ad tentationes Satanae sustinendas nos armat, in vera pietate nos conservat & confirmat, ut adversùs omnes Diaboli, mundi & carnis insultus consistere possimus, nec ullis minis vel terriculamentis à vera fide & pietate nos dimoveri patiamur. Summatim, quicquid ad salutis nostrae principium, medium & finem pertinet, illud omne D. Petrus quatuor hisce verbis comprehendit. Caietanus, textum Graecum secutus, quatuor verba accipit, & perficiendi verbo vult significari, tentationes Diaboli conducere, ad perfectionem; ad hanc vero spectare, ut Deus fulciat virtutibus moralibus, confirmet robore fidei, stabiliat sive solidet assistentiâ suâ.

## 5:11
TO HIM BE GLORY AND DOMINION FOREVER AND EVER. AMEN.

Connection. 1. Those who take the preceding words as a wish and a prayer say that δοξολογίαν this was therefore added by the Apostle, so that he might show that this wish of his, this prayer, has been heard. But we showed above that not so much a prayer as a promise is contained in the preceding words.

2. As in other Apostolic sayings parallel to this one of ours, to the commemoration of benefits already received δοξολογία is subjoined Galat. 1. v. 5.Apoc. 1. v. 6. so in this place to the promise of benefits yet to be conferred δοξολογία is subjoined, which we also see happening in other places parallel to this one of ours. Rom. 16. v. 25.Now to Him who is able to confirm you, according to my Gospel etc. v. 27. To the only wise God through Christ Jesus, to whom be glory forever.Ephes. 3. vers. 20.Now to Him who is able to do all things superabundantly more than we ask or understand etc.v. 21.to Him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus unto all generations of the age of ages Amen.2. Tim. 4. vers. 8.The Lord will save me into His heavenly kingdom, to whom be glory forever and ever Amen.Hebr. 13. vers. 21.May God καταρτίςαι fit you in every good thing, that you may do His will, doing in you that which is pleasing before Him through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever, Amen.Iudae Epist. v. 24.To Him who is able to keep you without sin, and to set you before the sight of His glory blameless in exultation.v. 25.To the only wise God our Savior be glory and magnificence, dominion and power, both now and unto all ages, Amen. Truly, they are as certain on the part of God, inasmuch as His τὰ χαρίσματα & κλῆσις are ἀμεταμέλητα Rom. 11. v. 29. the benefits promised and yet to be conferred, as those which have already been received, and therefore the pious, by the example of the Apostle, ought to give thanks to God for both.

3. Therefore also the Apostle, from the consideration of divine benefits, as well those received, such as the calling to the eternal glory of God in Christ, as those promised, such as κατάρτισις, στήριξις, σθένωσις and θεμελίωσις in sufferings, breaks forth into this thanksgiving, so that not only from the certainty and infallibility of the promise, but also from the divine power, which is signified by the name τοῦ κράτους, a greater confidence in God may be excited in the souls of the faithful, who are subject to sufferings.

4. He also shows by this δοξολογίᾳ a heart burning and prompt in confirming those subject to the cross and persecutions in this life.

5. Finally, he warns them not to claim for themselves any praise and glory on account of victory against Satan, or on account of patience in afflictions, or on account of perseverance in the stadium and study of piety, but to acknowledge that all these things descend from divine kindness, and therefore all praise and glory are owed to Him alone. He had said, God καταρτίζειν, στηρίζειν, σθενοῦν and θεμελιοῦν: us; for this, a great κράτος, is required, which he teaches must be sought and expected from God alone, by whose power and protection alone we may overcome that most powerful enemy of ours, endure in afflictions, and persevere in good, to whom also on this account eternal thanks are owed by us.

6. As Peter began this Epistle with a doxology, saying: Blessed be God &c. so he ends in the same, saying: To Him be glory &c. so that he may teach that the praise of God ought to be the beginning, middle, and end of our actions.

Disposition, The parts of the verse are two. 1. Doxology. 2. Clause of asseveration.

Exposition. Ἀυτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος. earlier cap. 4. vers. 11. he had said, ᾧ ἐστὶν ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος; but in this place he pronounces absolutely, αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα, so that there may be understood either a verb of the indicative mood ἒστι, or a verb of the optative mood ἒστω. It is more fitting, however, that the indicative ἒστι, be understood, because these things are added to confirm the certainty of the promise. By τὸ κράτος John Huss understands empire. For thus he annotates on this place. To Him be glory from you and empire in you, as regards the saints. But can The customary meaning of τοῦ κράτους is to be retained, and joined with that metonymical explanation by which κράτος is understood as dominion. For the Apostle looks to that strength of divine power which God exerts in perfecting, establishing, strengthening, and grounding us, concerning which he had announced cap. 1. huius Epistolae v. 5. in the power of God you are kept through faith unto salvation. Prosper, book 1, de vocat. gent. chapter 24, citing this passage, reads it thus: To whom is virtue and power. But although κροτος can be explained by power, yet δόξα does not signify virtue. It seems, therefore, that Prosper, having omitted the noun δόξης τὸ κράτος, rendered it by virtue and power. The Syrian places three things in this place, rendering the text thus: To whom is [consult facsimile image] ( praise, glory, majesty, Matt. 19. v. 28. c. 24. v. 30. from the root [consult facsimile image] he praised, he glorified, he affected with honor, he gave thanks, Matth. 15. v. 36. [consult facsimile image] ( strength, power, possession, dominion, from the root [consult facsimile image] he apprehended, he held, he possessed; 2. Corinth. 6. v. 18. GOD is called [consult facsimile image] all-holding, παντοκράτωρ, commanding all things, possessing all things) [consult facsimile image] ( & honor from the root [consult facsimile image] which in Pahel signifies to hold someone as heavy or precious, τιμᾷν to honor Act. 28. v. 9.)

Ἐις τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Concerning the word αἰῶνος, Damascenus discourses thus in book 2, de fide, chapter 1, in the beginning: It is worth the effort to know that the name αἰῶνος is πολύσημον. For an age is called the life of each individual man. Again, an age is called a period of a thousand years. Again, an age is called the entire present life, and ὁ αἰὼν μέλλων the future life after the resurrection, to be closed by no end. Again, an age is called not time nor a part of time, measured by the motion and course of the Sun, namely constituted by days and nights, but τὸ συμπαρεκτεινόμενον, that which is coextended with things everlasting; like a certain temporal motion and space, ὅπερ γὰρ τοῖς ὑπὸ χρόνον ὁ χρόνος τοῦτο τοῖς αἰδίοις ἐστὶν αἰών. There are also said to be seven ages of this world, namely from the creation of heaven and earth until the common consummation and resurrection of men, etc. But the eighth age is that which is to come. Before the foundation of the world, however, when the Sun was not yet, dividing the day from the night, there was no measurable age, but that which is comprehended by the everlasting, as a certain temporal motion and space. And according to this there is also some age, according to which God is called αἰώνιος eternal, nay even προαιώνιος before the age, for he himself made the age. For he alone ἄναρχος existing without beginning, is himself the maker of all things, and of the ages, and of all things that are. But they are called αἰῶνες αἰώνων ages of ages according to that, that there are seven ages of this world, namely many ages containing the lives of men: and one age is the container of all ages, and the age of the age is called the present and the future; but eternal life and eternal punishment show τὸ ἀτελέυτητον τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος that the future age is without end. On which passage of Damascenus, Clichtoveus comments thus. By the name of age any duration, whether having a beginning and an end, or having obtained a beginning without an end, or lacking both, is found to be expressed and signified. For indeed age is frequently taken in the sacred writings for the present life, which is closed by a beginning and an endMatth. 28. v. 20.Luc. 20. v. 34. etc. Age is also often placed for the desires and lusts of this life.Rom. 12. v. 2. But indeed age is frequently found in the Scriptures for the future life, which is interminable, and having a beginning lacks an end, etc. Finally, age is often taken also for eternity immune from beginning and endPsal. 90. v. 1. And in this meaning taken, the age is the container of all ages, because eternity encompasses and over-encompasses all ages, etc. Furthermore, the same doubled expression, whether in the singular or in the number of the multitude, designates perpetuity lacking an end.Apoc. 4. v. 10. etc. That very thing, namely, that by the phrase into the ages of ages eternity lacking all end is signified, Augustine elegantly demonstrates from the comparison of Apoc. 20. v. 10. with Matth. 25. v. 41. What is said there, he says, eternal, here is said into the ages of ages, by which words divine Scripture is accustomed to signify nothing, except that which has no end of time. Concerning the little word Ἀμὴν it was spoken above cap. 4. vers. 11.

Latin:

IPSI GLORIA & IMPERIUM IN SECULA SECULORUM. AMEN.

Connexio. 1. Qui praecedentia verba accipiunt ut votum, & precationem, dicunt, δοξολογίανhanc ideò esse ab Apostolo additam, ut ostendat, hoc suum votum, hanc precationem esse exauditam. Sed ostendimus superiùs, non tàm precationem, quàm promissionem in verbis praecedentibus contineri.

2. Ut in aliis dictis Apostolicis huic nostro parallelis commemorationi beneficiorum iamdum acceptorum δοξολογία subiungitur Galat. 1. v. 5.Apoc. 1. v. 6. ita hoc loco promissioni beneficiorum adhuc conferendorum δοξολογία subiungitur, quod etiam fieri videmus in aliis locis huic nostro parallelis. Rom. 16. v. 25.Ei autem, qui potens est, vos confirmare, iuxta Evangelium meum &c. v. 27. Soli sapienti Deo per Christum Iesum, cui sit gloria in seculaEphes. 3. vers. 20.Ei autem, qui potens est omnia facere super abundanter plusquam petimus aut intelligimus &c.v. 21.ipsi gloria in Ecclesia & in Christo Iesu in omnes generationes seculi seculorum Amen.2. Tim. 4. vers. 8.Dominus salvum me faciet in regnum coeleste, cui gloria in secula seculorum Amen.Hebr. 13. vers. 21.Deusκαταρτίςαιaptet vos in omni bono, ut faciatis eius voluntatem, faciens in vobis, quod placeat coram se per Iesum Christum, cui gloria in secula seculorum, Amen.Iudae Epist. v. 24.Ei qui potens est vos conservare sine peccato, & constituere ante conspectum gloriae suae immaculatos in exultatione.v. 25.Soli sapienti Deo Salvatori nostro gloria & magnificentia, imperium & potestas, & nunc & in omnia secula, Amen. Nimirum tàm certa sunt ex parte Dei, utpotè cuius τὰ χαρίσματα & κλῆσις sunt ἀμεταμέληταRom. 11. v. 29. beneficia promissa & adhuc conferenda, quàm quae iamdum sunt accepta, ac proinde pii pro utrisque exemplo Apostoli debent gratias Deo agere.

3. Ideò quoque Apostolus ex consideratione beneficiorum divinorum tàm acceptorum, quale est vocatio ad aeternam Dei gloriam in Christo, quàm promissorum, qualia sunt κατάρτισις, στήριξις, σθένωσις ac θεμελίωσις in passionibus, in hanc gratiarum actionem erumpit, ut non solùm ex promissionis certitudine & infallibilitate, sed etiam ex divina potestate, quae τοῦ κράτους nomine significatur, maior in Deum fiducia in animis fidelium, passionibus subiectorum, excitetur.

4. Ostendit etiam hac δοξολογίᾳ pectus ardens & promtum in confirmandis cruci & persecutionibus in hac vita subiectis.

5. Denique praemonet, ne quidquam laudis & gloriae ob victoriam adversus Satanam, vel ob patientiam in afflictionibus, vel ob perseverantiam in pietatis stadio atque studio sibi vendicent, sed agnoscant, haec omnia ex divina benignitate descendere, ac proinde ipsi uni ac soli omnem laudem & gloriam deberi. Dixerat, Deum nos καταρτίζειν, στηρίζειν, σθενοῦν ac θεμελιοῦν: ad hoc requiritur magnum κράτος, illud à solo Deo petendum & expectandum esse docet, cuius solius virtute & praesidio hostem illum nostrum potentissimum superemus, in afflictionibus perduremus, & in bono perseveremus, cui etiam hoc nomine sempiternae à nobis debeantur gratiae.

6. Uti Petrus inchoavit hanc Epistolam à doxologia, dicendo: Benedictus Deus &c. ita in eadem desinit, dicens: Ipsa gloria &c. ut doceat, Dei laudem debere esse principium, medium & finem nostrarum actionum.

Dispositio, Partes versiculi duae sunt. 1. Doxologia. 2. Asseverationis clausula.

Expositio. Ἀυτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος. superiùs cap. 4. vers. 11. dixerat, ᾧ ἐστὶν ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος; sed hoc loco absolutè pronunciat, αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα, ut subintelligi possit, vel verbum indicativi modi ἒστι, vel verbum optativi modi ἒστω. Magis tamen congruit, ut subintelligatur indicativum ἒστι, quia ad confirmandam promissionis certitudinem haec subiiciuntur. Per τὸ κράτος Iohannes Huss intelligit imperium. Sic enim ad hunc locum annotat. Ipsi gloria à vobis & imperium in vobis, quoad sanctos. Sed potest usitata significatio τοῦ κράτους retineri, ac cum metonymica illa explicatione, quâ per κράτος imperium intelligitur, coniungi. Respicit enim Apostolus ad robur illud divinae potentiae, quod exerit Deus in nobis perficiendis, stabiliendis, roborandis, & fundandis, de quo pernunciaverat cap. 1. huius Epistolae v. 5.in virtute Dei custodimini per fidem in salutem. Prosper lib. 1. de vocat. gent. cap. 24. citans hunc locum, sic legit: Cui est virtus & potestas. Sed quamvis κροτος per potestatem exponi possit, tamen δόξα non significat virtutem. Videtur igitur Prosper omisso nomine δόξης τὸ κράτος per virtutem & potestatem reddidisse. Syrus tria hoc loco ponit, textum sic reddens: Cui est[consult facsimile image] ( laus, gloria, maiestas,Matt. 19. v. 28. c. 24. v. 30. à rad. [consult facsimile image]laudavit, glorificavit, honore affecit, gratias egit,Matth. 15. v. 36.[consult facsimile image] ( robur, potentia, possessio, dominium, à rad. [consult facsimile image]apprehendit, tenuit, possedit;2. Corinth. 6. v. 18. DEUS vocatur [consult facsimile image]omnitenens,παντοκράτωρ,omnibus imperans, omnia possidens) [consult facsimile image] ( & honor à rad. [consult facsimile image] quod in Pahel significat aliquem gravem vel preciosum habere,τιμᾷνhonorareAct. 28. v. 9.)

Ἐις τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. De voce αἰῶνος sic disserit Damascenus lib. 2. de fide cap. 1. in prine. Operae precium est cognoscere, quod nomenαἰῶνος sit πολύσημον.Seculum enim dicitur, uniuscuiusque hominum vita. Dicitur rursus seculum tempus mille annorum. Dicitur rursus seculum universa praesens vita, &ὁ αἰὼν μέλλωνfutura vita post resurrectionem nullo fine claudenda. Dicitur rursus seculum non tempus neque temporis pars, Solis latione & cursu mensur atae, per dies videlicet & noctes constituta, sedτὸ συμπαρεκτεινόμενον,quod coextenditur sempiternis; instar cuiusdam temporalis motus & spacii,ὅπερ γὰρ τοῖς ὑπὸ χρόνον ὁ χρόνος τοῦτο τοῖς αἰδίοις ἐστὶν αἰών.Dicuntur etiam septem secula mundi huius, à coeli videlicet & terrae creatione uque ad communem hominum consummationem & resuscitationem &c. Octavum autem seculum est, quod futurum est. Ante vero mundi constitutionem, cum Sol nondum erat, diem à nocte dirimens, non erat mensurabile seculum, sed quod comprotenditur sempiternis, veluti quidam temporalis motus & spacium. Et secundùm hoc etiam est aliquod seculum, secundùm quod Deus diciturαἰώνιοςaeternus, quin &προαιώνιοςante seculum, ipse enim seculum fecit. Solus enimἄναρχοςsine principio existens, omnium ipse est factor & seculorum, & omnium quae sunt. Dicuntur autemαἰῶνες αἰώνωνsecula seculorum secundùm id, quod huius mundi septem secula sunt, multa secula videlicet vitas hominum continentia: & seculum unum omnium seculorum contentivum est, & seculum seculi dicitur praesens & futurum; aeterna autem vita & aeternum supplicium ostenduntτὸ ἀτελέυτητον τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνοςquod futurum seculum sit sine fine. In quem Damasceni locum Clichtoveus sic commentatur. Seculi nomine quaevis duratio, sive principium habens & finem, sive sortita principium sine fine, sive carens utroque, exprimi & significari comperitur. Enim vero seculum pro vita praesenti, quae principio & fine clauditur, frequenter in sacris literis accipiturMatth. 28. v. 20.Luc. 20. v. 34. &c. Seculum etiam saepenumerò pro huius vitae desideriis, cupiditatibusque ponitur.Rom. 12. v. 2.At verò seculum pro futura vita, quae intermina est, & principium habens fine taret, invenitur frequenter in Scripturis &c. Demum pro aeternitate quoque principii & finis immuni saepe sumitur seculumPsal. 90. v. 1.Et in hoc significatu sumtum seculum seculorum omnium contentivum est, quod aeternitas omnia praeambiat & super ambiat secula &c. Porrò geminata eadem dictio sive in singulare, sive in multitudinis numero perpetuitatem designat fine carentem.Apoc. 4. v. 10. &c. Idipsum videlicet, quod per phrasin in secula seculorum significetur aeternitas omni fine carens, eleganter demonstrat Augustinus ex collationeApoc. 20. v. 10. cum Matth. 25. v. 41.Quod ibi, inquit, dictum est aeternum, híc dictum est in secula seculorum, quibus verbis nihil Scriptura divina significare consuevit, nisi quod finem non habet temporis. De vocula Ἀμὴν dictum superiùs cap. 4. vers. 11.

## 5:12
BY SILVANUS, A FAITHFUL BROTHER TO YOU, AS I SUPPOSE, I HAVE WRITTEN BRIEFLY, BESEECHING AND TESTIFYING THAT THIS IS THE TRUE GRACE OF GOD, IN WHICH YOU STAND.

Connection. 1. From this verse begins the conclusion of the whole Epistle, which consists of four parts, ἀνακεφαλαιώσει, ἀσπασμοῖς, προτροπῇ & εὐχῇ. Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις is proposed in this verse, ἀσπασμοὶ, προτροτὴ & εὐχὴ in the two following verses.

2. Ἀνακεφαλαιώσει the commendation of the Epistle is included, through which the Apostle seeks benevolence among those to whom he writes, just as through ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν he strives to excite attention in them.

Disposition. John Huss proceeds thus. Four things make this Epistle commendable. 1. The faithfulness of the messenger delivering it. 2. The brevity of the Epistle sent. 3. The truth of the Epistle itself. 4. The charity of those greeting. The first three are proposed in this verse, the latter or fourth in the following verse. The Apostle commends this Epistle of his. 1. by its pleasing brevity. 2. by the majesty of its contents. He signifies that he has done two things in it, namely 1. that he has exhorted those to whom he writes. 2. that he has testified concerning the truth of the Evangelical doctrine. He implies that both, since they have proceeded from an Apostolic and divine Spirit, are deservedly to be highly esteemed.

Exposition of the text. Διὰ Σιλουανοῦ ὑμῖν τοῦ πιστοῦ ἀδελφοῦ (ὡς λογίζομαι) δι' ὀλίγων ἔγραψα. The Vulgate rendered it. By Silvanus, a faithful brother to you, as I suppose, I have written briefly. The Greek properly has. By Silvanus to you a faithful brother, as I suppose, I have written in few words. According to the Greek text, the pronoun ύμῖν seems to be referred to the little word τοῦπιστοῦ, so that the sense may be: By Silvanus the brother, who performs a faithful ministry to you. According to the Latin version, the pronoun to you seems to be referred to the verb I have written, so that the sense may be. By Silvanus a faithful brother, as I suppose, I have written briefly to you. The Syrian paraphrast, as in other things, so also in this part seems to have followed the Latin version more than the Greek text, for thus he rendered it: These few things, as I think, I have written to you by Silvanus, a faithful brother. But the Greek text, as being the only authentic one, is deservedly preferred to both the Latin version and the Syriac paraphrase.

Πᾳρακαλῶν καὶ ἐπιμαρτυρῶν ταύτην εἶναι ἀληθῆ χάριν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς ἣν ἑστήκατε. Παρακαλῶν the Vulgate rendered beseeching. We have warned, however, above, that παρακαλεῖν signifies: 1. to exhort. 2. to beseech. 3. to console. In this place it is placed in the first signification, as is gathered from the argument of the Epistle, which the Apostle here embraces in brief. For he shows that a double end or scope had been proposed to him in this Epistle. First διδασκαλικὸν, for he wished to confirm those to whom he writes in the faith and to testify that the Evangelical doctrine concerning the grace of GOD through Christ, which they had embraced, and in whose faith and profession they stood, is infallibly true. Secondly νουθετικὸν and παραινετικὸν, for he earnestly and gravely warned them that they should lead a life worthy of that profession, and adorn the doctrine with holy morals. Bede warns that the word παρακαλῶν can be referred either to the preceding or to the following things. That he says beseeching, he says, can be referred to the things above, because, namely, he wrote briefly, not commanding, but beseeching them to persist strong in the faith. It can also be rightly coupled to the following things, so that it may be understood not only to testify that this is their true grace, which he proclaims by writing, because indeed there is no salvation in any other, in whom it behooves us to be saved, but also to beseech them that they may make this to be their true grace, with which they are imbued in Christ. But anyone sees that it is more elegant that it be referred to the following things, which the very argument of the Epistle also proves.

Ἐπιμαρτυρῶν. The Vulgate rendered, testifying. But the preposition ἐπὶ added to the simple verb μαρτυρὲω is emphatic, so that the sense is, not only exhorting, but furthermore also attesting. The LXX Interpreters use the word ἐπιμαρτύρομαι in that signification, so that it includes also exhortation. Nehem. 9. v. 29. ἐπεμαρτύρω αὐτοῖς you testified against them, that they might return to your lawv. 30.you testified against them in your Spirit by the hand of the Prophets, and they did not hear.cap. 13. v. 15. ἐπεμαρτυράμην I have testified on the day of the sale of provisions. This meaning can be beautifully applied to this passage. For the Apostle wished to testify that this is the true grace in which they stood, so that, being convinced of its truth, they might constantly persevere in it.

By χάριν some understand faith with its fruits, but more correctly, through a certain species of metonymy, it is understood as the doctrine of the Gospel, in which the grace of God promised through Christ is offered to all and conferred upon believers. Lyranus on this passage: Grace here signifies the Catholic faith. The sense, therefore, is: I have written to you for this reason, not only to exhort you to the pursuit of piety and holiness, but also that by my testimony I might confirm that doctrine and religion which you have embraced, and which you profess in persecutions, to be that one true doctrine and religion by which God wills to be and can be rightly worshipped, and which leads its confessors to eternal life. Thus, therefore, in a few words, the Apostle vigorously explains both the end of his writing, why he wrote this Epistle to the elect strangers of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, etc., and the argument of the Epistle, what he has primarily done in it. Some recall the end of the writing to constancy in faith alone, so that the sense may be: I have written these things to exhort you to persevere in the faith once received, and to remain constant in the acknowledged truth of the Gospel, testifying as a faithful witness and Apostle of Christ that this grace of faith, which you have received through my preaching and that of my fellow Apostles, and in which you have stood until now and still stand, is the true grace of God, by which, namely, you can truly be and remain pleasing to God unto eternal life. But because the Apostle joins τὸ παρακαλεῖν & τὸ ἐπιμαρτυρεῖν, therefore a twofold end of writing and a twofold argument of the Epistle is more correctly established, which opinion the matter itself confirms, since the Apostle exhorts those to whom he writes not only to constancy in faith, but also to other Christian virtues. Bede explains the truth of that grace thus: The Apostle beseeches them to make this, with which they are imbued in Christ, to be their own true grace. For the grace of Christ becomes the grace of those who receive it with a pure heart. For he who spurns the grace of God does not diminish the grace itself, but makes it not to be his own, that is, he makes it not to profit him. These things are indeed rightly said, but perhaps not according to the mind of the Apostle. For the Apostle is not dealing with the first reception or apprehension of grace, but with constancy in the profession of grace once apprehended, that is, of the Evangelical truth once acknowledged and received, as It is manifest from the added προσδιορισμῷ. εἰς ᾓν ἑστὴκατε.. Moreover, there is a Hebraism in the words of this προσδιορισμοῦ, because εἰς ἣν is placed for ἐν ᾗ,, just as the Syrian also rendered [consult facsimile image] in it. for ἑστήκατε. Two Royal Codices and another read στῆτε you stood, so that it may be an exhortation to constancy. Phil. 4. vers. 1.Gal. 5. vers. 1. The word ἑστήκατε stands in the more approved Codices, and it stands Rom. 5. vers. 2. we have access εἰς τὴν χάριν, ἐν ᾗ ἑστήκαμεν.. The sense therefore is, in which you have been established.
