For ἑστήκατε you stood, some maintain that it was written formerly and therefore ought to be read ἑστήκετε you stand. But we are compelled by no necessity to establish a corruption of the text here. The past tense being placed for the present is a customary Hebraism. Lyranus, in which you have been rooted. The Syrian has the participle [consult facsimile image] in which you standing, sc. are.

Latin:

PER SYLVANUM FRATREM VOBIS, UT ARBITROR, BREVITER SCRIPSI, OBSECRANS & CONTESTANS HANC ESSE VERAM GRATIAM DEI, IN QUA STATIS.

Connexio. 1. Ab hoc versiculo incipit conclusio totius Epistolae, quae constat quatuor partibus, ἀνακεφαλαιώσει, ἀσπασμοῖς, προτροπῇ & εὐχῇ. Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις proponitur in hoc versiculo, ἀσπασμοὶ, προτροτὴ & εὐχὴ in versiculis duobus sequentibus.

2. Ἀνακεφαλαιώσει inclusa est Epistolae commendatio, per quam Apostolus apud eos, ad quos scribit, benevolentiam captat, sicut per ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν attentionem in ipsis excitare satagit.

Dispositio. Ioh. Huss sic progreditur. Quatuor faciunt hanc Epistolam commendabilem. 1. nuncii deferentis fidelitas. 2. Epistolae missae brevitas. 3. ipsius Epistolae veritas. 4. Salutantium caritas. Priom tria in hoc versiculo, posterius sive quartum in seq. vers. proponitur. Commendat Apostolus hanc suam Epistolam. 1. à grata brevitate. 2. â contentorum maiestate. Significat se in ea duo egisse, videlicet 1. eos, ad quos scribit, esse exhortatum. 2. de veritate doctrinae Evangelicae esse testificatum. Utrumque cum fuerit à Spiritu Apostolico & divino profectum, meritò magni aestimandam esse innuit.

Textus expositio. Διὰ Σιλουανοῦ ὑμῖν τοῦ πιστοῦ ἀδελφοῦ (ὡς λογίζομαι) δι' ὀλίγων ἔγραψα. Vulg. reddidit. Per Silvanum fidelem fratrem vobis, ut arbitror, breviter scripsi. Graeca propriè habent. Per Silvanum vobis fidelem fratrem, ut arbitror, paucis scripsi. Iuxta textum Graecum pronomen ύμῖν referendum videtur ad voculam τοῦπιστοῦ, ut sit sensus: Per Sylvanum fratrem, qui fidele vobis ministerium praestat. Iuxta versionem Latinam pronomen vobis referri videtur ad verbum scripsi, ut sit sensus. Per Sylvanum fidelem fratrem, ut arbitror, breviter vobls scripsi. Syrus paraphrastes, ut in aliis, ita quoque hac in parte videtur magis secutus versionem Latinam, quàm textum Graecum, sic enim reddidit. Haec pauca, quemadmodum arbitror, scripsi vobis per Sylvanum fratrem fidelem. Sed Graecus textus, utpote solus authenticus & Latinae versioni & paraphrasi Syriacae meritò praefertur.

Πᾳρακαλῶν καὶ ἐπιμαρτυρῶν ταύτην εἶναι ἀληθῆ χάριν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς ἣν ἑστήκατε. Παρακαλῶν vulgata reddidit obsecrans. Monuimus autem superiùs, παρακαλεῖν significare. 1. exhortari. 2. obsecrare. 3. consolari. Hoc loco positum est in prima significatione, ut colligitur ex argumento Epistolae, quod brevibus Apostolus hîc complectitur. Ostendit enim, duplicem sibi in hac Epistola propositum fuisse finem sive scopum. Primo διδασκαλικὸν, voluit enim eos, ad quos scribit, in fide confirmare & testificari, doctrinam Evangelicam de gratia DEI per Christum, quam amplexi erant, & in cuius fide ac professione stabant, esse infallibiter veram. Secundò νουθετικὸν ac παραινετικὸν, feriò enim ac graviter eos monuit, ut vitam professione illâ dignam agerent, & doctrinam sanctis moribus exornarent. Beda monet verbum παρακαλῶν vel ad praecedentia vel ad sequentia referri posse. Quod ait obsecrans, inquit, potest ad superiora referri, quia vid. breviter scripserit, non imperans, sed obsecrans eos, fortes in fide persistere. Potest & ad sequentia rectè copulari, ut intelligatur non solùm contestari, hanc esse veram eorum gratiam, quam scribendo praedicat, quia nimirum nòn est in alio aliquo salus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri, sed etiam obsecrare eos, ut hanc esse veram suam gratiam faciant, quâ imbuti sunt in Christo. Sed quilibet videt, concinniùs esse, ut referatur ad sequentia, quod ipsum etiam probat Epistolae argumentum.

Ἐπιμαρτυρῶν. Vulg. reddidit, contestans. Sed praepositio ἐπὶ simplici verbo μαρτυρὲω addita, est emphatica, ut sit sensus, non solùm exhortans, sed insuper etiam attestans. LXX. Interpp. verbo ἐπιμαρτύρομαι utuntur in ea significatione, ut includat etiam exhortationem. Nehem. 9. v. 29.ἐπεμαρτύρω αὐτοῖςcontestatus es eos, ut revertèrentur ad legem suamv. 30.contestatus es eos in Spiritu tuo per manum Prophetarum, & non audierunt.cap. 13. v. 15.ἐπεμαρτυράμην contestatus sum in die venditionis alimentorum. Haec significatio pulchrè accommodari potest huic loco. Ideò enim testificari voluit Apostolus, eam esse veram gratiam, in qua stabant, ut de veritate illius convicti constanter in eadem perseverarent.

Per χάριν quidam intelligunt fidem cum suis fructibus, sed rectiùs per speciem quandam metonymiae intelligitur doctrina Evangelii, in qua gratia Dei per Christum promissa omnibus offertur, & credentibus confertur. Lyranus in h. l. Gratia significat hîc fidem Catholicam. Sensus igitur est, Ideò vobis scripsi, ut non solùm vos exhortarer ad studium pietatis & sanctitatis, sed etiam ut testimonio meo confirmarem doctrinam & religionem illam, quam amplexi estis, & quam in per secutionibus profitemini, solam esse veram illam doctrinam & religionem, quâ Deus rectè coli velit & possit, quaeque confessores suos ad vitam aeternam perducit. Sic ergò paucis verbis nervosè explicat Apostolus tùm scriptionis finem, eur hanc Epistolam electis advenis dispositionis Ponti, Galatiae &c. scripserit, tùm Epistolae argumentum, quid in ea potissimùm egerit. Quidam revocant scriptionis finem ad solam in fide constantiam, ut sit sensus. Haec scripsi, ut vos exhortarer, ut per severetis in fide semel suscepta, & veritate Evangelii agnita constantes, testificans tanquam fidelis testis & Apostolus Christi, hanc quam per meam & Co Apostolorum meorum praedicationem suscepistis fidei gratiam, & in qua hactenus stetistis, & adhuc statis, veramesse Dei gratiam, per quam scil. verè Deo grati esse, & manere possitis ad vitam aeternam. Sed quia Apostolus τὸ παρακαλεῖν & τὸ ἐπιμαρτυρεῖν coniungit, ideò rectiùs duplex scriptionis finis & duplex Epistolae argumentum statuitur, quam sententiam res ipsa confirmat, cum non solùm ad constantiam in fide, sed etiam ad alias virtutes Christianas eos, ad quos scribit, Apostolus exhortetur. Beda veritatem illius gratiae sic explicat. Obsecrat Apostolus eos, ut hanc esse veram suam gratiam faciant, quâ imbuti sunt in Christo. Gratiae enim Christi eorum fit gratia, qui hanc mundo corde suscipiunt. Nam qui gratiam Dei spernit, non ipsam gratiam minuit, sed hanc suam non esse, id est, sibi faciat non prodesse. Haec rectè quidem dicuntur, sed fortè non ad mentem Apostoli. Neque enim de prima gratiae susceptione sive apprehensione Apostolus agit, sed de constantia in gratiae semel apprehensae, id est, veritatis Evangelicae semel agnitae ac susceptae professione, ut manifestum est ex addito προσδιορισμῷ. εἰς ᾓν ἑστὴκατε. Est autem in verbis huius προσδιορισμοῦ Hebraismus, quia εἰς ἣν ponitur pro ἐν ᾗ, sicutetiam Syrus reddidit [consult facsimile image]in eâ. pro ἑστήκατε Regii duo Codices & alius legunt στῆτεstetis, ut sit exhortatio ad constantiam. phil. 4. vers. 1.Gal. 5. vers. 1. Verbum ἑστήκατε in probatioribus extat Codicibus, & extat Rom. 5. vers. 2.habemus accessumεἰς τὴν χάριν, ἐν ᾗ ἑστήκαμεν. Sensus igitur est, in qua stabiliti estis. Pro ἑστήκατεstetistis, quidam statuunt olim scriptum fuisse & proinde legendum esseἑστήκετεstatis. Sed nulla necessitate cogimur, corruptelam textus hic statuere. Praeteritum poni pro praesente, Hebraismus est usitatus. Lyranus, in quaradicati estis. Syrus habet participium [consult facsimile image]in quavos stantes, sc. estis.

## 5:12-14 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place: 1. Who was that Sylvanus, of whom the Apostle makes mention in v. 12.? Jerome, in Epistle 14 to Damasus, determines that he was the one who, with Paul and Timothy, wrote both Epistles to the Thessalonians. 1. Thess. 1. ver. 1.2. Thess. 1. ver. 1. For he was a colleague of Paul in preaching the Gospel and συνεργὸς, called Silas by a Hebrew name. Acts 15. ver. 40.chap. 16. ver. 19.25.29.chap. 17. v. 4.10. & 14. It must be known, says Jerome in the said place, that Silas, the colleague of Paul, is called an Apostle in the Hebrew tongue, who writes some Epistles with him, and Sylvanus is read erroneously for Silas, since Sylvanus in We do not read in the Acts of the Apostles. Oecumenius establishes the same in his commentary on this place. Among the Papist writers, Lorinus in chapter 15 of Acts and Cornelius à Lapide on this place establish the same. According to this hypothesis, it could be thought that Peter wished to use the work of Silvanus in this Epistle, either in writing it or in delivering it, because rumors were spread that Peter was announcing another Gospel different from the doctrine of Paul. Galat. 2. vers. 2. Therefore, in order to counter these false rumors, Peter writes this Epistle to the elect strangers of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, etc., he records in it the sum of the doctrine preached by him up to that point and announced to them, and he takes care that the same be delivered to them by Silvanus, a colleague of Paul, so that every suspicion concerning the diversity of his own and Pauline doctrine might be removed. But because in Greek Silas is written by but Silvanus by υ, and because the Syrian retains the name Silvanus unchanged, it is therefore more likely that this Silvanus was someone other than Silas, of whom mention is made in the Acts of the Apostles. Peter calls him a faithful brother to them, to whom he writes; therefore, he undoubtedly served them in the preaching of the Gospel. Dorotheus in his Synopsis and the Menologium of the Greeks on August 1 clearly distinguish Silvanus from Silas.

Q. 2. Whether the Apostle used the work of this Silvanus in writing out this Epistle, or in delivering it? Some affirm the former, establishing that this Epistle was dictated to Silvanus as an amanuensis. Lyranus on this place shows through whom he writes, so that those receiving it might be more certain that it emanated from Peter, not from false Apostles. But some bring forward the latter, establishing that this Epistle was handed over to be delivered by Silvanus as a legate or messenger, so that the sense is: I have written this Epistle to you to be sent through Silvanus. The interlinear gloss: Through Silvanus, who was necessary to me, but for your sake I sent him away. The ὑπογραΦαὶ of the Pauline Epistles have the same sense. Thus, the Epistle to the Romans is said to be written from Corinth through Phoebe, a minister of the Cenchrean Church. The first to the Corinthians was written from Philippi through Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus and Timothy; and so in others, that is, it was sent through them, just as the Vulgate Latin version also explained at the end of the first and second to the Corinthians, the Epistle to the Galatians, and the second Epistle to the Thessalonians. This latter opinion is more likely, because the Epistle to the Romans is said to be written through Phoebe, that is, through her it was sent, since in drafting it Paul used the work of a certain Tertius as an amanuensis. Roman. 6. vers. 22. For this reason also he wished to use the work of Silvanus, a faithful minister, in delivering this Epistle, because he could at the same time inculcate with a living voice the same doctrine, the summary of which the Apostle repeats. This part therefore contains ἐπαινισμὸν or a commendation both of Silvanus as a faithful minister in the Gospel, and of the Epistle itself, as having been transmitted through such a man.

Q. 3. Whether that parenthetical, ὡς λογίζομαι, pertains to the epithet πιστοῦ, or whether it should be referred to the added προσδιορισμὸν δι' ὀλίγον? Calvin annotates that parenthesis thus. This exception was added either for the sake of modesty, or so that they might know for certain that he speaks from the feeling of his own mind. But it was absurd for them not to subscribe to the judgment of such an Apostle. Estius in almost the same way. That, as I judge, is not referred to the faithfulness of Silvanus, for thus it would rather give an occasion for doubting his faith, but to the brevity of the Epistle, and it was added for the sake of modesty. Cajetan determines the same, and the Syriac Interpreter, who arranges the text thus. These few things, as I judge, I have written to you through a faithful brother &c. But it is more correctly said to be referred to the epithet πιστοῦ, so that the sense may be, I have written to you through Silvanus a faithful brother, as I have hitherto found him to be, and I am thoroughly persuaded that he will be such also in the future. For τὸ λογίζεσθαι declares something more seriously than τὸ οἴεσθαι or even ἡγεῖσθαι, for it signifies to establish something firmly as if collected by reasons drawn up within oneself, and therefore it has the meaning not of a doubtful opinion, but of a firm persuasion. Rom. 3. v. 28.cap. 6. vers. 11.cap. 8. v. 18.Hebr. 11. v. 19.Sap. 8. v. 18. The Syriac has the word [consult facsimile image] he thought, he judged.Act. 7. v. 25. The parallel places are. Rom. 15. v. 14. Πέπεισμαι I am persuaded (the Vulgate rendered it, I am certain) and I myself concerning you, that you also are full of love &c.Gal. 5. v. 10. I πέποιθα εὶς ὑμᾶς trust in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else.2. Thess. 3. v. 4. πεποίθαμεν, We trust in you in the Lord, that what we have commanded you both do and will do.2. Tim. 1. v. 5. πέπεισμαι I am persuaded, that in you dwells faith not feigned.

Q. 4. Why does the Apostle add, δι' ὀλίγων I have written to you? Some wish, this was added for the sake of excuse, lest with weariness this Epistle Let them read, so that it may be the sense. I have written to you in few words, so that it may not be troublesome to read in what sense almostHebr. 13. v. 22. the Apostle speaks. ἀνέχεσθε, receive the word with an even mind τῆς παρακλήσεως, καὶ γάρ διὰ βραχέων ἐπέστειλα ὑμῖν, for I have written to you in very few words; I could have exhorted you with more, but I wished to study pleasing brevity. Lyranus at this place annotates thus. I have written to you in few words, so that he may be better able to retain it, and fulfill it in work. It can also be referred to the affection of the writer and of those to whom it is written, so that it may be the sense. This Epistle will without doubt seem brief to you, just as to those who receive letters from their dearest friends, and indeed written about the most serious matters, even a long Epistle is accustomed to seem brief.

Q. 5. Does the Apostle mystically understand Rome by Babylon? They affirm 1. from the ancients Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis, and from him Eusebius, book 2 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 15. The Hierapolitan, he says, Bishop, by the name of Papias, says that mention is made of this Mark (who wrote the Evangelical History) by Peter in his former Epistle, which they say was composed at Rome, and that the city of Rome is tropically called Babylon by the same, which is signified from that which he says. The church that is in Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you, and so doth my son Mark. Jerome in the catalogue of Ecclesiastical writers on Mark. Peter also makes mention of this Mark in his first Epistle, figuratively signifying Rome by the name of Babylon. Bede in his commentary on this place. He calls Rome Babylon typically, namely on account of the confusion of manifold idolatry, in the midst of which the holy Church, already raw and very small, was shining, according to the example of the Israelite people, who once small in number and captivated, sitting upon the rivers of Babylon, bewailed the absence of the holy land, nor was it able to sing the Song of the Lord in a strange land. And afterwards. In the time of Claudius both Peter and Mark came to Rome, and Mark himself, having written his Gospel at Rome, was sent to Alexandria, whence it is gathered that this Epistle was written at Rome in the time of Claudius. Similar things occur in Oecumenius in his commentary on this place. 2. From the Papists Baronius, volume 1 of the Annals, Year 45, number 16. That the (former) Epistle was written by Peter at Rome, all the Fathers who have had discourse about that matter have expressly testified, which they also gathered from those words of the same Epistle, in which it is said without: The church that is in Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you. For that he understood Rome by Babylon, they confirm without any doubt.

But the Innovators dissent from these, because they take it very ill that the arrival of Peter at Rome is rendered testified even from the canonical and divine Scriptures. But first, let us demonstrate by the authority of the ancients that Rome was signified by Peter through Babylon, and subsequently, we shall clearly reveal how remarkably they rave who contend that those words were said about another Babylon. Afterwards he brings forward the sayings of Eusebius and Jerome just now cited, and adds the following arguments for this opinion. First, that in the Apocalypse of John, chap. 17. it is noted by the same name, is confessed among all, so that I may speak hyperbolically, since otherwise there are very many who interpret the whole kingdom of the Devil through Babylon. Furthermore, among the ancients, Tertullian against the Jews, chap. 9. and book 3 against Marcion, chap. 13. Thus also Babylon in our John bears the figure of the Roman city, and therefore also of the great and proud kingdom and the conqueror of the saints. One and the same Spirit, by whom the holy men of God were inspired and spoke, signified Rome by the same symbolic name, etc. Secondly. Nor indeed, he says, no. 17, do I think I shall speak imprudently if I add to these that Peter did not use the proper name of the city, because having escaped from prison in Jerusalem, he did not wish it to be perceived by all where he was acting, etc. Indeed, Josephus signifies that the Emperor Claudius had been very eager for Agrippa, King of the Jews, who had bound Peter, soon to be slaughtered before the people, when otherwise it seems to have been customary among the Apostles to call men by changed names, whence no one doubts that Paul, when he says 2. Timoth. 4. I was delivered from the mouth of the lion, signified Nero by the lion. Thirdly, that Rome was signified by Babylon, even if one is unwilling, he is compelled to confess. For since Peter says: The Church which is gathered in Babylon greets you: since it can in no way be understood of that Babylon which is among the Assyrians, since it is established by the authority of Josephus book 18. antiq. cap. 12. that at the same time of Gaius Augustus, when the Jews, both Alexandrian and Palestinian, were suffering such dire things, those who were acting in Babylon and among the Assyrians were Jews who had been expelled and finally slaughtered, it is necessary to affirm that Peter understood Rome by Babylon. Nor is there another Babylon of which Peter could have spoken. For that which was Babylon among the Egyptians was a clearly obscure place, not worthy of the name of a town, it is named a fortress by Strabo book 17. and others, thus indeed so called because it had been erected by certain Babylonians, a place fortified by nature. But to wish to say that Peter understood this as being situated in Egypt is truly a remarkable foolishness and an overly absurd thing, since, while many other things forbid one from holding this opinion, this one thing in particular forbids it in a certain way: that it is established that no gathered Church is found in Babylon, which is in Egypt. For although many Councils are found published with the addition of the names of Egyptian Bishops, in none of these, nor in other monuments of writers, is a Bishop of Babylon in Egypt found named anywhere except after 500 years. Salmero, Disp. 8 on the first Epistle of Peter, likewise maintains that by Babylon here Rome is understood, and he says it is through the remarkable μείωσιν. For the other Babylon of Mesopotamia, and that which was called Babylis and Memphis in Egypt, were scarcely in the nature of things at that time. He also urges that Apocalypse c. 17 John understands Rome by Babylon. Likewise the meaning of this name. To which, he says, can the name of Babylon, i.e., of confusion, be more appropriate than to that one, concerning which Leo in his sermon on the Birthday of the Apostles Peter and Paul says that, being ignorant of the author of its own advancement, while it dominated almost all nations, it served the errors of all nations, and seemed to have assumed a great religion for itself, because it had rejected no falsehood. Finally he exclaims: Where in the nature of things is the seat of Peter shown except at Rome, and the death of the cross, by which he glorified God, or the holy and venerable relics of his body are exhibited to be viewed by pious believers, except at Rome? Where, therefore, are those so impudent and rash, who with a brazen forehead dare to deny that Peter was ever at Rome? Note also, he says, that just as the Apostle in chapter 1 of Romans celebrates with praises the faith of the Roman Church, so the prince of the Apostles, Peter, testifies that the Roman Church was chosen by God, so that these great Apostles might also agree with one another in this matter. He proves that this Epistle cannot be understood as having been written from the true Babylon of Assyria from the fact that no author has handed down to memory that blessed Peter was ever in it. But that he preached at Rome, and ruled that Church for many years, there is almost no one among the ancient and good writers who has not left that attested. Lorinus comments on this passage thus: All, as many Catholic Interpreters as I have read, understand the Roman Church, because the city of Rome, from where Peter was writing, was at that time full of the confusion of idolatry, which is the etymon of Babylon, and had vexed the faithful just as Babylon once did the Hebrews, and just as that one was great and the seat of Empire, and in it there was a mixing of all languages as if in a common fatherland, etc.

Furthermore, Papias in Nicephorus, book 2, Hist. chap. 15, and Eusebius, book 2, Hist. chap. 15, Jerome in Catal. Script. Eccles. and in chap. 47 of Isaiah, Bede in the preface to Mark, and concerning a similar matter in John in the Apocalypse chap. 17, v. 5, Tertullian in the book against the Jews chap. 9, and book 3 against Marcion chap. 13, because it is a kingdom of the proud, a conqueror of the saints of God (Orosius in book 7, chap. 1, also makes a varied comparison between both even in external matters, and Augustine in book 18 of the City of God, chaps. 2 and 22, makes some comparison), Andrew of Caesarea, Arethas, and others who interpret the Apocalypse, lead to this same conclusion. Furthermore, Jerome in Epist. 16 and 151, q. 11, book 2 against Jovinian, in chap. 24 and 27 of Isaiah, and the prologue to the book of Didymus on the Holy Spirit, whom Ribera cites and follows in chap. 14 of the Apocalypse, Ludovicus Vives in book 18 of Augustine's City of God, chap. 22, Marianus Victorius in Epist. 17 of Jerome, Sixtus Senensis in book 2 of the Bibliotheca under the word Harlot, Lindanus in book 4 of the Panoplia, chap. 82, Horantius in book 6 of the Catholic places, chap. 12, Bellarmine in book 2 on the Pontiff, chap. 2, and book 3, chap. 13. Add Nicholas Sander in book 8 on the visible Monarchy of the Church, chap. 8, Baronius in vol. 1 of the Annals, Thomas Madzoda in book 2 on the Antichrist, chap. 16, and book 4, chap. 5 (even if he would not want the passage of the Apocalypse to be understood in this way), Rhodiginus in book 8, chap. 11, Sonnius in book 1 of the demonstration, Tract. 1, chap. 5, Vatablus Mich. 4. n. 38, Pintus in chap. 36 of Ezekiel, Cantapratensis in book 3 of the hypot., chap. 2, Pamelius on Tertullian in the said place, Thomas Bozius in book 17 on the marks of the Church, chap. 6, who confirms the same with certain places of the O.T., Genebrard in the Chronicle, Peter Damian in sermon 2 on St. Mary, Luis de León on Obadiah, Dominicus Bagnensis 2. 2. q. 1. art. 10. dub. 1, Turrianus in book 1 on the Church and its Pastor against Antonius Sadeel, chap. 16, Mutius Iustinopolitanus against Peter Viret on the Papacy, chap. 1. Similar things occur in Estius in the commentary on this place and Cornelius à Lapide ibid. Estius adds, that through Apostolic preaching Rome was converted from Babylon into the Holy Jerusalem and the new Zion. Cornelius à Lapide says, Peter by this nomenclature alludes to Abraham, the parent of the Synagogue, of faith, and of the faithful. For just as God chose Abraham in Babylon and led him out of Ur of the Chaldeans into the promised land; so St. Peter at Rome converted St. Clement, St. Pudens, St. Linus, St. Celsus, and other most illustrious men, who were the leaders and nobles of the Church. Secondly, he alludes to the Babylonian captivity. For then the people of God and the Synagogue of the Jews lived in Babylon captive, and was converting many Babylonians to the faith of the true God, whence there was then in Babylon an elect Church of God. In a similar way, Saint Peter converted very many from gentilism at Rome, and thus established there the citadel and head of the Christian Church. We determine as follows regarding this matter. 1. This question, whether the name of Babylon is to be taken properly for that most famous metropolis of the first Chaldean monarchy in the Scriptures, or for the city of the same name in Egypt, which is called Cairo today, or indeed mystically and figuratively for the city of Rome, does not concern any article of faith, therefore it is permitted to dissent about it without the crime of heresy. Luther, in his commentary on this place, written in the year 23, which exists in volume 1 of his German works, does not greatly object if anyone wishes to understand Rome mystically by Babylon in this place. Ich achte / spricht er / weiss aber dennoch nicht fu r war / dass er die Epistel von Rom geschrieben. He is moved by that argument, that Babel has its name from confusion, and indeed at that time a collection of vices was reigning in Rome, of which the Apostle also makes mention chapter 4, verse 4. 2. If it be granted as much as possible that this Epistle was written at Rome, and consequently that Rome is to be understood by Babylon, yet the primacy of either Peter or the Roman Pontiff is not thereby proven. Paul wrote several Epistles at Rome, yet the Papists do not on that account attribute a monarchical primacy to him. We do not greatly deny that Peter was at Rome. Chemnitz, in Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 50, page 277: There are great contentions among the learned, whether Peter was at Rome, at what time he came there, and how long he was there. And all historians agree that he was at Rome. But at what time he came there, the annotations are most confused. That seems to agree most simply with the History of the Acts, which Origen in volume 3 on Genesis and Nicephorus note, that Peter came to Rome toward the end of his life in the last years of Nero. But this is what we deny, that Peter exercised a monarchical dominion at Rome for 25 years in the Papal seat. 3. Lorinus on this place, page 593, annotates thus: All argue well that it does not hinder the primacy of Peter at all, even if he had never been at Rome, since it does not necessarily depend on that city. From this we conclude thus: The primacy of Peter does not necessarily depend on the city of Rome. Therefore, even if Peter wrote this Epistle at Rome, yet the primacy of either Peter or the Roman Pontiff is not proven from it. 4. Not all Papists agree that Rome is to be understood by Babylon here. Erasmus in his paraphrase on this place: The congregation of Christians, which God chose for Himself together with us in Babylon, greets you, and in in the midst of impious idolaters he follows evangelical piety, in the midst of those living most corruptly he embraces purity of life, in the argument of the Epistle It appears this was written from Babylon, for he bids them greet them with the words of this Church, if the fiction about Rome does not please anyone. Costerus in Enchir. cap. 3. It is not inappropriately said that his former Epistle was written from the Babylon of Egypt. 5. We are compelled by no necessity to depart here from the literal property and to flee to a mystical signification. Bellarm. lib. 1. de Eucharist. cap. 12. § Sed tota &c. Why we should follow the literal sense, our adversaries ought not to ask of us. For it would be similar as if someone were to ask of those who are on a journey, and are following a common and beaten path, why they enter through the door, and not through the window. lib. 1. de Missa cap. 12. §. Sed ista. It is not fitting to deny the proper and genuine sense of the letter without a most urgent reason. Toletus in cap 10. Luc. when the literal sense can be had from the proper signification of the words, one must not have recourse to a figure. 6. In the Babylon of Chaldea there were many Jews, therefore Peter betook himself there, and preached the Gospel to them by virtue of the agreement entered into with Paul. Gal. 2. v. 7. It is consistent, therefore, with the Apostleship of Peter to establish that this Epistle was written from the Babylon of the Assyrians. 7. If Peter had written this Epistle from Rome, it does not seem that a sufficiently just and suitable cause is brought forward why he would have wished to conceal its name, since Paul adds the name of the city in all his Epistles. 8. Peter had Mark as a companion at that time when he wrote this Epistle, as is evident from this very salutation. Therefore he was not at Rome then, for they report that Mark died at Alexandria in the eighth year of Nero, but Peter was killed by Nero at Rome six years later. But if Mark established the Alexandrian Church, and for a long time performed the office of Bishop there, he could not have been at Rome with Peter. 9. The arguments which are brought forward to the contrary are not cogent. For first, concerning Papias the Hierapolitan Bishop, who is the first author of this exposition, the same Eusebius testifies in lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 36. that he invented certain foreign fables and doctrines of the Savior along with some other fabulous things, in which he feigned that there would be millenarians after the resurrection. Therefore his authority in the Church is not great. Secondly, Baronius himself departs from Jerome quite often. In tom. 1. Ann. 69. he teaches that Jerome had fallen into a manifest error concerning the time of the martyrdom of Peter and Paul. ann. 51. n. 8. concerning the time of the Council of Jerusalem; Ann. 62.

No. 52. Concerning the reception of the Epistle to the Hebrews, rejected by the Latins, he departs from Jerome. What of the fact that Alph. de Castro, book 6 against heresies, under the word Bishop, Medina reporting, Gregor. de Valent. in the book on the difference between Bishops and Presbyters, chapter 3, Bellarm. book 1 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 8, attribute manifest errors to Jerome. Beda and Oecumenius followed Jerome's opinion. Thirdly. The remaining Fathers, brought forward as teaching that Babylon is to be understood as Rome, do not speak of this Apostolic passage, but of chapter 17 and 18 of the Apocalypse. However, it does not follow: By Babylon in the Apocalypse, Rome is mystically understood. Therefore, also in this Petrine passage. For it is an argument from a particular. John shows clearly enough that his discourse is about Babylon mystically so called, for he says chapter 17, v. 5 And upon her forehead a name written, Mystery. He also shows that his discourse is about Rome, for he says chapter 17, v. 18 The woman, which you saw, is the great city, which has the kingdom over the Kings of the earth. v. 9 The seven heads are seven mountains, upon which the woman sits. But we are destitute of such guidance in this Apostolic passage. Add that the Antichristian rather than the Roman Empire is expressed by the name of Babylon in the Apocalypse, as is shown in its place. Fourthly, it is said gratuitously that Peter, having escaped from prison by flight, did not want it to be known where he was acting. The Apostles did not seek hiding places, but what they had heard in the ear from Christ, they preached on the housetops Matthew 10, v. 27 not fearing those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul v. 28 It had to be proven first that Peter acted as Bishop of Bishops at Rome, and wrote this Epistle there, then finally one could look into the reason why he did not want to express it by his own name. Fifthly, nothing absurd is said, whether this Epistle is said to have been written from the Babylon of Assyria, or from the Babylon of Egypt, concerning which matter Funccius in his Chronology discourses thus. One Babylon was in Chaldea, most famous in Scripture. That Peter came to it does not seem alien to the truth. For since it is manifest from the Acts that he acted for some years in Syria, it could happen that he also went to that Babylon. Furthermore, another Babylon was in Egypt, in which many Jews were gathered. Peter, therefore, since he had been called to the preaching of the Gospel among the Jews, could also have come there. And this seems very likely. For since Mark, the disciple of Peter, who wrote the Gospel, was established at Alexandria of Egypt, it does not seem foreign that Peter spent some years in Egypt. Sixth, even if there were no mention in the Scriptures or in Ecclesiastical writers of the individual Babylon of Egypt, that Peter taught in it, it is nevertheless sufficient that there was a Church in Egypt gathered for Christ, concerning which no one can doubt. For all historians agree that Mark was the first Bishop of the Alexandrian Church in Egypt. Compare Bynting in Itinerar. lib. 2. p. 61. Seventh, although Gaius may have expelled the Jews from the Babylon of the Chaldeans, it cannot be inferred from that, however, that all Christians whatsoever were expelled from the same. Nor does this argument militate against the Babylon of Egypt, which, however much it may be called an obscure fortress, comparatively, that is, with respect to other magnificent cities, that does not prevent Peter from having been able to dwell there for a time, and to write this epistle in the same place. Eighth, Gregory Cortesius, Cardinal, in the treatise against the Persuader (Udalricus Velenus) written to Adrian 6, rightly warns, Even if Peter were to ascribe greeting to the Pontics in the name of the Babylonian Church properly so called, it is not therefore necessarily the case that he wrote from Babylon, just as Paul did not write in all the Churches, when he sent the greeting of all the Churches to the Romans Rom. 16. v. 21. & when he sent to the Corinthians those which were in Asia 1. Cor. 16. v. 19. he did not at the same time draft the Epistle in all of them, which Lorinus establishes is aptly gathered in this way by Cortesius in h. l. Therefore, even if we were to grant that Peter greets the Pontic Christians in the name of the Roman Church, it would not follow that he wrote this Epistle from Rome: and conversely, even if it cannot be shown that Peter was in Babylon in Egypt, he could nevertheless have greeted the Pontic Christians in the name of the Babylonian Church properly so called.

Q. 6. In what sense does the Apostle call the Babylonian Church co-elect? Cornelius à Lapide thinks that regard is had to the synagogue of the Jews. The people of God, he says, and the Synagogue of the Jews dwelt captive in Babylon, and converted many Babylonians to the faith of the true God, whence there was then in Babylon a Church of God elected. In a similar way, Saint Peter converted very many from paganism at Rome, and thus established there the citadel and head of the Christian Church. There was therefore at Rome a Church co-elect by God, i. e. elected equally as the Synagogue of the Jews was once. If we embrace this hypothesis, it will be more elegant to take the name of Babylon properly for the most famous city of Chaldea. For Peter would refer the Jews converted in Babylon, living under a foreign magistrate, to the memory of the Babylonian captivity, which their ancestors once experienced in the same city and region, but from which they were liberated by divine kindness, with whom they constitute one people of God, one Church. But we warned above that Peter looks to the fact that cap. 1. v. 1. he had called the Pontics elect; therefore, with respect to them, he calls the Babylonian Christians co-elect, indeed. You are not alone, God has his elect everywhere, a few indeed, but exquisite nurseries for the Church to be more widely propagated in the future, as Erasmus speaks in his paraphrase. You are also not alone, you who sustain persecutions on account of the profession of the Gospel, who are exposed to the injuries of all, but the Babylonian Church is elect with you for the same hardships, and for the same glory that will follow those hardships in its own time.

Q. 7. Whether Mark was the natural, or indeed the spiritual son of Peter? Peter had a mother-in-law Matth. 8. v. 14. and led about a sister, a woman, in the Apostleship, 1. Cor. 9. v. 5. Clement of Alexandria, book 3, Strom. p. 210, Peter and Philip begat children. It is not absurd, therefore, to posit that this Mark was the natural son of Peter, from which it could be gathered that the prohibition of marriage, with which the Pope has burdened priests, is not conformable to the doctrine and deed of Peter. But it is more correctly said that this Mark was the spiritual son of Peter, whom he begat in Christ through the preaching of the Gospel 1. Cor. 4. v. 15. Philem. v. 10. in which sense Paul calls Timothy γνήσιον τέκνον ἐν πίστει 1. Tim. 1. v. 2. τέκνον σου ἀγαπητὸν καὶ πιστὸν ἐν Κυρίῳ 1. Corinth. 4. 17. of whom he bears this excellent eulogy, that as a son with a father he served with him in the Gospel Phil. 2. v. 22. Damasus in the life of Peter calls Mark a son by Baptism. Jerome in chapter 65 of Isaiah, near the end, Apostles and Apostolic men begat sons in such a way that they instructed them from the holy Scriptures. Paul [begat] Timothy, Luke and Titus, and many others; Peter [begat] Mark the Evangelist. The same in the Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers under the word Mark. Mark the disciple and Interpreter of Peter. Theodoret reports the same in the preface to the History of the Holy Fathers. The interlinear gloss to this place, Mark greets you, baptized by me, and taught by me. Oecumenius refutes the opinion of those who posit that Mark was the carnal son of Peter, with the argument that Peter, having been freed from the Jerusalem prison, betook himself into the house of Mark, the son of Mary.

Q. 8. Who this Mark was. Resp. 1. Some establish that this Mark is the same as John, the son of Mary and cousin of Barnabas, who was surnamed Mark, of whom mention is made Acts 12:12 Peter came to the house of Mary the mother of John, who was surnamed Mark. Col. 4:10 Mark the cousin of Barnabas greets you, concerning whom you received instructions; if he comes to you, receive him. 2 Tim. 4:11 Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for the ministry. Nicephorus, book 2, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 15: Mark, whom Peter calls his son, Luke in the Acts calls John. 2. But it is more likely that the Mark who wrote the Evangelical History is meant. For first, he who is treated in Acts 12:12 Col. 4:10 2 Tim. 4:11 adhered more to Paul and Barnabas than to Peter. Second, he is said to be surnamed Mark, but the Evangelist was simply called Mark. Third, the Evangelist Mark was a companion of Peter and by his will wrote the Evangelical History. Eusebius, book 2, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 15: Such a splendor of piety shone upon the minds of those who heard Peter at Rome, that they were not satisfied with having heard him once, nor were they content with the unwritten doctrine of the divine preaching, but they besought Mark, whose Gospel is circulated, with every kind of entreaty, that he would leave them written commentaries of the doctrine which they had received delivered by word of mouth, nor did they desist until they had persuaded the man, and thus gave the cause for the writing of the Gospel which is named according to Mark. They say, moreover, that the Apostle, when he had learned this by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, was delighted with the will of these men, and confirmed this written Gospel for the Churches to be read by his own authority. Clement in the sixth ὑποτυπώσεων hypotyposeis sets forth this history. Moreover, the Bishop of Hierapolis, Papias by name, also attests to him, who says that mention is made of this Mark by Peter in his former Epistle. Jerome in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical writers under the word Mark: Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, according to what he had heard Peter relating, being asked by the brethren at Rome, wrote a short Gospel, which when Peter had heard, he approved, and gave it to the Church to be read by his authority, just as Clement writes in the sixth book, and Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis. Peter makes mention of this Mark in his first Epistle, etc.

Q. 9. What kind of kiss of charity that was, of which mention is made. Resp. Baronius, vol. 1, Annals, year 45, no. 13, from the custom of the Romans, [derives] the origin of these kisses he thinks it draws. Formerly, he says, it was received by custom to greet one another with a kiss, as often as friends met while walking, which custom, as being very troublesome and frequently bringing disgust through encounters, the Emperor Tiberius took care to have abolished by a sanctioned law, in Suetonius, Tiberius, chapter 34. Such kisses were symbols of peace and love, which the Apostles took care not to abolish, but to moderate among Christians, while they often admonished them that they ought to greet one another with a holy kiss. Paul, Rom. 16. v. 16. 1. Cor. 16. v. 20. 2. Cor. 13. v. 12. 1. Thess. 5. vers. 26. & Peter in this place. But we showed above that this custom of kissing flowed into the Christian Church rather from the custom of the Orientals, especially the Hebrews. Ecclesiastical writers of the same make frequent mention of it. Justin Martyr in his oration to the Emperor Antoninus: Prayers being finished, we greet one another with a kiss, he relates in the same place that the administration of the Eucharist follows after the kiss. Origen in chapter 16 to the Romans: From this speech of Paul (Greet one another with a holy kiss) the custom was handed down to the Church, that after prayers the brothers receive one another with a kiss, and the Apostle calls this a holy kiss, by which name he teaches first, that the kisses which are given in the Churches should be chaste: then that they should not be feigned, as was that of Judas. But a faithful kiss should first be chaste, then have peace in itself and simplicity in love unfeigned. Tertullian, book on prayer, calls that kiss the seal of prayer, either because it was accustomed to be used in sacred assemblies with the addition of the greeting of those words, Peace be with you, or because it was accustomed to be fixed upon one another after public prayers were finished before departure. Athenagoras in his oration to Christ: It is necessary to temper the kiss, or rather the adoration of the greeting, so accurately, lest if in any way the mind has been even a little polluted, the Word may proscribe it from eternal life. Cyril of Jerusalem, mystagogical catechism 5. When he had remembered the ancient rite, by which the Deacon in the Mass said: Embrace and kiss one another, he adds. Nor should you take this in such a way, as if that kiss were of the kind that is accustomed to be among all friends in the marketplace, for it is not such. Therefore this kiss reconciles minds to one another, and promises them the oblivion of all evils. This kiss is therefore a sign of the reconciliation of minds, and of the entire memory of injuries being deleted. And afterwards: Therefore this kiss, which we use in sacred things, is a reconciliation, and therefore holy, of which Paul also speaks. Greet one another in a kiss. And Peter says, in a kiss of love. Basil, book on true virginity: The Apostle exhorts that we greet one another with a holy kiss, i.e. by a certain as it were breathing of the kiss of the flesh, joining these things to one another in the most pure burning of the Holy Spirit. Chrysostom homily 30 on 2 Cor. 13 We are the temple of Christ. Therefore we kiss the vestibules and entrance of the temple when we kiss one another. Do you not see how many men even fix a kiss upon the vestibules of this temple, partly with bowed head, partly holding with the hand and moving the hand to the mouth? And through these gates and doors Christ has entered, and enters to us, when we communicate. For you know, you who are participants in the mysteries, what I say. For our mouth is not affected with any common honor when it receives the body of the Lord, and for that reason especially we then join mutual kisses. Let those who speak obscene things and who utter insults hear, and let them shudder thinking what kind of mouth they defile and disgrace. Let those who speak obscene things hear, etc. Augustine q. 87 on Genesis It was the custom (among the Hebrews) especially in that simplicity of the ancients, that relatives should kiss relatives, and this is done today in many places. From this custom the holy kiss took its origin, concerning which the same man in sermon 83 on diverse subjects discourses thus. After the Lord's Prayer, which you have received and returned, it is said, Peace be with you, and Christians kiss one another in a holy kiss, which is a sign of peace, if what the lips show, may it be done in the conscience i.e. just as your lips approach the lips of your brother: so let your heart not depart from his heart. This kiss is called first of charity, because it is a sign of sincere love, from which among the Greeks it has the name τὸ φίλημα from φιλέω, among the Latins basium from the base of love. Secondly holy, for the sake of distinction. 1. From an unchaste kiss, such as that of those who love basely. Proverbs 7 v. 13 such as also sometimes mingled itself with holy kisses, as is evident from the passage of Athenagoras cited above and from the words of Clement of Alexandria book 3 of the Paedagogus. There is, he says, also another kiss, incestuous, full of poison, simulating holiness. Do you not know that even spiders, if they only touch with the mouth, bring grave pains to men? To meet which evil, the Apostles and Apostolic men seem to have ordained that men should not thus indiscriminately greet women and women men by imparting a kiss to one another, since formerly in the Church men were accustomed to act separately from women. Baronius on the same place n. 26. 2. From any carnal or civil kiss whatsoever, which does not proceed from Christian and fraternal charity. 3. From an adulatory kiss, such as was that of Absalom, binding the Israelite people to himself with a kiss and aspiring to the kingdom 2 Sam. 15 verse 5 4. From a simulatory and hypocritical kiss, such as was that of Joab to Amasa of one kissing 2. Sam. 20. v. 9. 5. of a treacherous kiss, such as was that of Judas, kissing Christ. Matth. 26. vers. 49. From all those the holy kiss ought to be distinct, and entirely such as befits the saints, which may be a symbol of chaste, sincere, spiritual, holy, and divine love, which we call charity. Bede in this place: Greet one another with a holy kiss, a true kiss, a peaceful kiss, a dove-like kiss, not deceitful, not polluted, such as Joab used to kill Amasa, such as Judas used to betray the Savior, such as those use who speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts. Therefore, they greet one another with a holy kiss who love not in word, nor in tongue, but in deed and in truth. Lyranus in this place: Not an adulatory one, just as Absalom used to kiss the people; not a feigned one, just as Joab [kissed] Amasa; not a treacherous one, just as Judas [kissed] the Lord; not an unchaste one, just as the adulterous woman [kissed] the young man, but a holy kiss, which is a sign of charity and its incentive.

Q. 10. What meaning does the particle Ἀμὴν; have in this place? Resp. Above in the doxologies chapter 4. v. 11. Ἀμὴν is a particle not so much of one wishing, as of one asserting and confirming, as is evident from the particle ἐστὶ added in chapter 4. v. 11., in which meaning it is used John 16. v. 23.2. Cor. 1. v. 20. and elsewhere throughout. Here, however, it is at once a particle of one wishing and confirming. For it is employed: 1. for the confirmation and approval of that which is said, and it is the same as ἀληθῶς truly. 2. for a wishing, and it is the same as γένοιτο, let it be; in which meaning it is used Nehem. 8. v. 6.Psal. 41. v. 14.Tob. 9. v. 12.1. Cor. 14. vers. 16.Apoc. 7. v. 12. of which meaning ἐξηγήσεις there exist 1. Kings 1. v. 36. Amen, so may the Lord God of the King say. Jerem. 28. v. 6. Amen, so may the Lord do, may He confirm thy words, that it may be so done, as thou hast prophesied. Luke 1. vers. 38. Be it done to me according to thy word. In this meaning some wish Amen to be an imperative passive of the first conjugation, but some [wish it] to be a future with the first letter, Nun, removed, so that the sense may be, truly let this be done, let it be ratified, let it be confirmed, let this very thing be established.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, I have written briefly. vers. 12. But Peter wrote only two Epistles. Resp. Erasmus in the argument which he placed before the paraphrase of this Epistle, and in the very paraphrase of the last chapter, maintains that Peter, before these two which still exist, wrote another Epistle and indeed to the same [people], for the reason that he says here: By Silvanus I have written to you briefly Cramerus in the argument of chapter 5 says, that Peter in this Epistle briefly repeats those things which he had previously written to them through Silvanus. Some from the loss of this Epistle and of other sacred books strive to prove the imperfection of Scripture. But I respond: 1. those words which exist in 2. Epist. 3. vers. 1 manifestly refute this opinion. This behold, dearest, I write to you as a second Epistle: for he ought not to have said second, but third, if he had already written two before. 2. Therefore, when he asserts that he wrote through Silvanus, he is not speaking of another, but of this very Epistle transmitted through Silvanus, which a comparison of other places of Scripture shows. Paul 1. Cor. 5. v. 9. says: I wrote to you in an Epistle, not to associate with fornicators, where, however, he understands not another, but that very Epistle, as Chrysostom proves in his Commentary. Hebr. 13. vers. 22. διὰ βραχέων ἐπέστειλα ὑμῖν, certainly in that very Epistle. 2. Iohan. vers. 12. Having more things to write to you, I did not wish to do so by paper and ink. 3. Thence the Syrian paraphrast rendered this place of ours emphatically thus [consult facsimile image] These few things I have written to you, manifestly showing that Peter is not speaking of some other Epistle.

2. The Church in Babylon, co-elect, greets you. v. 13. And yet not all the citizens of that Church were elect. I respond: Lorinus explains, concerning the calling or temporal election to the fellowship of the Church. But we warned above that Peter here looks back to that which cap. 1. v. 1. & 2. he had called the Pontics, to whom he wrote, elect according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father etc., where it is evident from the parallel place 2. Thess. 2. v. 13. that it is a matter of eternal election to Salvation. Therefore, the reconciliation given above in the explanation of cap. 1. v. 2. must be repeated, that Peter calls the Pontic Church elect, the Babylonian co-elect, not by reason of all those who were in the external society of those Churches, but by reason of the true and living members, who belonged to the invisible Church.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Peter not only preached the Gospel with a living voice, but also wished to inform the Church with writings. He did both from the impulse and internal command of the Holy Spirit, otherwise his Epistles themselves would not be a part of Apostolic and Canonical Scripture. Therefore, it is false what the Papists assert, that the Apostles did not have a command to write. Bellarm. lib. 4. de verbo DEI cap. 4. §. Secundò, Pistorius in hodeg. p. 33.

2. Peter wrote to this end, that he might testify that this is the true grace of God, in which they stood v. 12. that is, that the Church of all times and places might know what is the true doctrine of the Gospel concerning the grace of God announced by the Apostles with a living voice, namely that very same which they consigned to writing, lest under the pretext of traditions they should suffer the inventions of men to be thrust upon them. Luke 1. verse 1. Irenaeus lib. 3. against heresies cap. 2. The Apostles and Evangelists, what they first proclaimed with a living voice, afterwards by the will of God they reduced into the Scriptures, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith. It is false, therefore, what the Papists teach, that Scripture is imperfect, and only a certain memorandum. Bellarm. lib. 4. concerning the word of God cap. 12. §. Reply to the Major.

3. Peter wrote this epistle from Babylon in Chaldea or Egypt. Therefore he did not sit at Rome for twenty-five years, exercising monarchical dominion over the universal Church, as the Papists attempt to prove with great effort.

4. If by the name of Babylon Rome is understood, therefore Peter gave the key by which the mysteries of the Apocalypse are opened, so that by Babylon we understand Rome, and therefore we do rightly that we separate ourselves from the Roman Church, for of Babylon it is said Apoc. 18. v. 4. Go out from her. Bellarmine objects lib. 2. concerning the Roman Pontiff cap. 2. that the city of Rome is understood, such as it was in the time of John. But the circumstances of the text do not permit this. It is a question of Rome as a spiritual harlot, who made all kings and nations drink of the wine of her fornication Apoc. 14. v. 8. c. 17. v. 2. c. 18. v. 3. But Rome under the heathen Emperors was rather inebriated by the wine of the prostitution of other nations. Hence many of the Papists acknowledge, that Rome will be the seat of Antichrist around the end of the world. Anglokem on cap. 17. Apoc. It can happen not inconveniently, that that great Antichrist may have his seat at Rome. Ribera on cap. 14. Apoc. n. 39. John speaks in the Apocalypse of Rome, such as it was under the heathen Emperors, and such as, after it shall have fallen away from the Roman Pontiff, it will be at the end of the age. Blasius de Viega on cap. 17. Apocal. comm. 1. sect. 3. The name of Babylon is to be transferred to that Rome which, before it received the faith of Christ, served idols, and to that which will be in the time of Antichrist, which John in this chapter 17 and the following commemorates as about to fall away from the supreme Pontiff, and thus from the faith.

5. John Huss on v. 14. annotates thus. From this place in the Church The kiss of peace has grown obsolete among the people of God, which all the faithful of Christ were previously accustomed to perform, kissing one another and giving peace, and receiving it mutually in a holy kiss during the solemnities of the Mass, but now they have decided to kiss not faces, but painted tablets, not on account of peace, but because of the sons of Belial.

6. Bede on the same verse writes thus: The Apostle began the Epistle with grace, finished it in grace, and sprinkled the middle with grace, so that he might condemn the Pelagian error in every part of his speech, and teach that the Church of Christ could not be saved except through His grace.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Lorinus on v. 12 annotates thus: Testifying that this is true grace, that is, so efficacious that it can immediately bring those departing from here to glory, which was by no means granted before the coming of Christ. Resp. 1. These things arise from the gaps of the Scholastics concerning the limbo of the Fathers. But that limbo of the Fathers is not only ἄγραφος, but also ἀντίγραφος.. Scripture of both the O.T. and N.T. enumerates only two receptacles of souls after this life, namely, heaven and hell. Abraham the father of all believers Roman. 4. v. 11. before the death of Christ was in that place to which Lazarus was carried by the Angels, Luc. 16. v. 22. where he received consolation v. 25. and which place was separated from hell most greatly v. 23. and 26.. Moses and Elias appearing in the transfiguration of Christ are not drawn out from the bosom and bowels of the earth, or from some dark prison, but appear in glory and light, Matth. 17. vers. 5. Luc. 9. vers. 31.. The soul of the converted thief, who died before Christ's descent into hell, was taken into Paradise Luc. 23. vers. 43. 2. That grace of God, by which believers in the N.T. are saved, also saved those who in the V.T. awaited the promised Messiah with true faith. Actor. 15. vers. 11. we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also (our Fathers in the O. Testament). August. Epist. 157. to Optatus. Our faith and theirs is the same, since they believed that this would happen, which we believe has happened. If therefore they also believed that they were saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, it is manifest that this grace also made the ancients live by faith. 3. The virtue of the merit of Christ also redounded to the fathers of the V.T. since the Lamb is said to be slain from the foundation of the world Apoc. 13. vers. 8. not only by reason of the decree, the promise, and the types in the sacrifices, but also by reason of efficacy and fruit, and since Christ Jesus is said to be the same yesterday and today and forever. Hebr. 13. v. 8.

2. The same Lorinus writes thus in the same place. The reason for justifying grace in any state whatsoever is of exactly the same nature, as Augustine teaches in book I against the two Epistles of the Pelagians, ch. 7 & 21, book 1 on the merit and remission of sins, ch. 11, and in every law, the reason for justification consists in an internal gift of grace, and not in a certain imputation alone before the Evangelical law, as Arias Montanus seems to have taught in some place. Therefore, the Evangelical law is deservedly accustomed to be called absolutely the law of grace, since in it is the fullness of grace, as the same Father speaks in Epistle 157. Response 1. If the reason for justifying grace in any state whatsoever (that is, as much in the Old as in the New Testament) is of exactly the same nature, then certainly the reason for salvation in both Testaments is also of exactly the same nature, and therefore just as believers of the New Testament, justified by faith in Christ exhibited, arrive immediately from death to the beatific vision of GOD: so also believers of the Old Testament, justified by faith in Christ promised, arrived immediately from death to the beatific vision of GOD. If the salvation and blessedness by which believers in the New Testament after the passion and death of Christ are made saved and blessed is the same as that by which the Fathers of the Old Testament were once saved, as Peter explicitly asserts Acts 15. v. 11., how were either these made saved without the beatific vision of GOD, or those in the same way in which these are saved? 2. The reason for justification does not consist in an infused gift of grace, but in the gratuitous remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ. Which very thing, if Arias Montanus taught it, he taught it rightly and in accordance with the Scriptures. Rom. 4. v. 6. 3. Grace in the article of justification does not denote an infused habit, but the gratuitous mercy and favor of GOD, φιλανθρωπίαν,, out of which He freely forgives sins to those believing in Christ, as was demonstrated in its own place from συνωνυμία,, from the opposition, from ἑτυμολογία,, from the effects and circumstances of grace. On Justification §. 18. & following. 4. The fullness of grace in the New Testament does not prove that the Fathers who lived in the time of the Old Testament were destitute of justifying grace, a thing which Lorinus himself is forced to admit.

3. Piscator in his scholia on this verse teaches that the doctrine of the Gospel μετωνυμικῶς is called the grace of GOD, because it is a testimony concerning the grace of GOD through Christ unto all believers. Response. These things are indeed said truly, but insufficiently. For the Gospel is not only a testimony concerning the grace of GOD through Christ, but also an efficacious medium through which the grace of GOD is offered to all men and conferred upon those believing in Christ, whence it is called the word of eternal life John 6. v. 68.

& the power of GOD unto salvation to every one that believeth; nay, it is even an efficacious medium, through which the Holy Spirit wills to kindle faith in the hearts of men, by which they may embrace the grace promised in the word of the Gospel.

4. Dionysius the Carthusian on the same verse determines, that the Apostle speaks of charity, and of grace making one pleasing, together with Catholic faith. But that he says that those to whom he writes stand in these things, he knew that very thing certainly through divine revelation, or knew it otherwise through evident signs, this is very probable, or in general concerning all, although not so in particular. Resp. 1. No mention is made in the Scriptures of a divine revelation, through which Peter knew a priori the faith of others, their perseverance in faith, and election to eternal life. 2. But he judged concerning them a posteriori from the effects, namely from the study of the word and a holy conversation of life, from patience in persecutions, etc. 3. Therefore also this judgment was not an infallible judgment of faith, but a probable judgment of charity, from which it happened that when he called Silvanus faithful, he added προσδιορισμὸν, ὡς λογίζομαι. 4. Weighing which, Lorinus on this place comments thus. I do not think that anyone will believe that Peter either knew, or even if he had known, that he wished to affirm concerning all that they were in grace making one pleasing, etc. He renders them certain that, being established within the Church, they have a certain method of obtaining salvation.

5. Estius from v. 13 gathers, that Peter was at Rome and sat there, which he says is impudently denied by certain Sectarians. Resp. 1. That Babylon is understood in this place as Rome has not yet been apodictically proven. 2. It is one thing to have been at Rome, another to have sat at Rome, that is, to have erected a Papal see there. The former can be conceded, while the latter is denied. 3. The name Bishop is accepted in two ways. Firstly broadly for a function with the authority of ruling the Church Epiph. haeres. 27. At Rome the first were Peter and Paul, the same being Apostles and Bishops. Secondly strictly for a certain Ecclesiastical function below the Apostles, 1. Tim. 3. v. 1. Peter was a Bishop not in the latter, but in the former signification.

6. The same Estius ibid. writes thus: By Apostolic preaching and institution it was finally brought about that Rome was converted from Babylon into a holy Jerusalem and a new Sion, such as it remains to this day. Lorinus on v. 13. As formerly the name of Babylon rightly suited Rome on account of idolatry of every kind, so afterwards it deservedly is to be called a holy and city of God, of which it could be said glorious, writes Arnolphus the Count In Henry Canisius, vol. 2. of Ancient Readings, for the sake of the cultivation of religion and truth. He reports indeed an incredible multitude of sacred buildings and pious works, which were being done there in his time, that is, in the year of Christ 100. But without doubt the number of such things in the city is far greater in this our age, as I myself also testify, who for more than twenty years have seen them in person with great pleasure. Resp. 1. That the modern doctrine of the Roman Church differs in many things from that which publicly sounded at Rome in the time of Paul and Peter can be manifestly proven from a comparison of modern doctrine with the Epistle of Paul written to the Romans, with the Epistles of the same man written from Rome to other Churches, namely to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, the latter to Timothy, to Philemon, and to the Hebrews; as also from this very Petrine Epistle, which the Papists claim was written at Rome. 2. If Rome is still today the holy Jerusalem, the new Zion, the holy city of God, whence come so many complaints of the Papist writers themselves concerning the corrupted state of the Roman Church? The Fathers of the Council of Trent, session 6, on reform, chapter 1, confess that Ecclesiastical discipline has collapsed greatly, and that morals in the Clergy and Christian people have been depraved, and that the ancient canons have almost gone into disuse through the injury of the times. Alphonsus de Castro, book 1, against heresies, 4. Because of this kind of heretics (the Lutherans) it has come about that, having abandoned certain trifles to which men have given themselves up for three hundred years until now, they have transferred themselves to better studies, whereby it is that the Church now possesses many more learned men than it has had for four hundred years past until now. 3. Many of the Papists confess that Rome toward the end of the world will be the nest of the Antichrist. 4. In that sense Rome can still today be called a holy city, in the sense in which Jerusalem in the time of Christ and the Apostles was called a holy city Matt. 4. v. 5. on account of the holy seed and certain holy remnants of the faithful people still preserved there.

7. Cornelius à Lapide on the same verse annotates thus. The first, and that a singular and excellent one, was the election of the faithful Romans and of the primitive Roman Church, inasmuch as it, drawing the firstfruits of the Spirit from Christ through St. Peter and Paul, flourished with heroic faith, sublime hope, ardent charity, and therefore it continuously sprouted forth so many hundreds of thousands of Martyrs through three hundred years of persecution. Wherefore many Princes, Kings, and Queens for the sake of devotion set out for Rome with great journeys and expenses, that they might religiously visit the holy places, etc. Indeed Christ the Lord appearing to St.

Brigid, as her life has it in Surius 23. of July, commanded her to travel to Rome, saying. Set out for Rome, for there the streets are paved with gold, and reddened with the blood of the saints: there, on account of the pardons or Indulgences, which the saints have merited, one comes to heaven by a short cut. She obeyed and having set out for Rome, she attained such holiness there, that dying in the same place, in the Year of the Lord 1373. she merited to be inscribed in the catalogue of saints with solemn rite, and so her house, having been converted into a temple, is religiously visited by tenants and pilgrims. Resp. 1. The Apostle speaks of election to glory, which does not have degrees, but is one and equal for all who persevere in faith until the end of life. 2. If we should even wish to take this Apostolic passage concerning election to grace or concerning vocation, nevertheless the election of the Roman Church was not singular and exceptional, but that of the Jerusalem Church. 3. The assertion of Cornelius rests on the hypothesis concerning the Papal see erected at Rome by Peter, which is demonstrated to be false in its own place. 4. Ecclesiastical Histories record that if not more, yet an equal number of Martyrs died at Antioch as at Rome, whence it was celebrated by the proverb, that there were more Martyrs at Antioch than tiles on the roofs. 5. c. Multi dist. 40. The place does not sanctify the man, but the man the place. Gregory to Anastasius the Priest. Not places or orders make us close to our Creator, but our good merits join us to Him, or bad ones separate us. The same, homily 9 on Ezekiel. If the Spirit is lacking, the place does not help. Lot was holy in Sodom, he sinned on the mountain. That places do not change the mind, the first parent of the human race himself testifies, because he fell in Paradise. For if a place could have saved, Satan would not have fallen from heaven. 6. Martin Delrio, book 4, disquis. Magic. chapter 1, q. 3, §. 4, writes thus. Henry of Hesse and Sibyllinus, both Catholics, both religious, but somewhat bold, deny that the Revelations of St. Brigid ought to be held as undoubtedly true, with moral certainty, and they contend this with many arguments. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola brings another argument, namely that in those Revelations there are contradictions.

8. Lorinus annotates on the same verse thus. ( The cause of such great love in Peter towards Mark, that he called him son, is believed to be because he had baptized him and instructed him and used him more familiarly, as an Interpreter. He was so perfect, that he later instituted the Monastic life in Egypt, of which they think Philo speaks in his book on the suppliants. Cornelius à Lapide ibid. Mark erected a Church at Alexandria, with such great continence flourishing with holiness, so that his disciples were surnamed Essenes, that is, holy and pious. Resp. 1. Thomas quodlib. 7. art. 17. and 2. 2. 187. art. 3. admits that in the times of the Apostles monasticism had not yet been instituted. Polyd. Virgil. lib. 7. de rer. invent. cap. I. writes, that Anthony was the first monk in Egypt, Basil in Greece, Hilarion in Syria, Benedict of Nursia in Italy. Bellarm. lib. de Monach. cap. 5. §. Nunc quod &c. Anthony was truly the Prince of Hermits, inasmuch as he neither learned from another, and he himself taught all. 2. The Essenes are referred to by Josephus lib. 18. antiq. cap. 2. and lib. 15. cap. 13. among the Jewish sects. But if anyone objects that those who lived in Egypt were Christians, the judgment of Sozomen concerning them in lib. Hist. Eccles. c. 12. is to be noted. Philo the Pythagorean (he says) relates that the most excellent of the Hebrews from everywhere were gathered into a place at Lake Mareotis situated on a hill, and dedicated themselves to a pious and severe manner of life. Whose dwellings, manner of sustenance, and institution of life he reports to be such as we see observed even at this time by the monks in Egypt &c. While Philo narrates these things in this manner, he seems to signify those Hebrews who in his own age had indeed professed the Christian religion, yet still followed the custom of the Jews somewhat in their life and kept their institutions. For among others this manner of life is not found. Whence I conjecture that among the Egyptians it flourished from that time. The Greek words are thus. Philo understands τοὺς κατ᾽ αὐτὸν ἐξ ἐβραίων, χριστιανίζοντας, ἐπὶ Ιουδαϊκώτερον ὀικοῦντας καὶ τὰ ἐκείνων ἔθη φυλάττοντας. Nicephorus repeats the same explanation lib. 2. Hist. Eccl. cap. 15. They say, he says, that Mark gave laws to that solitary life of Christian monks which is in Egypt. cap. 16. Philo not only pursues the institution of that time of the Apostolic men, sprung, as it seems, from the Jews, but he also approves it by his own judgment, although even then very many customs of the ancient Jews prevailed. Sophonius in the life of Mark. Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, seeing the first Church at Alexandria Judaizing, wrote concerning their conversation as if in praise of his own nation.

9. Baronius Ann. 45. n. 26. Since nevertheless with that caution applied (that not all, to wit, indiscriminately, but men should kiss men, and women women) some fraud by the art of the Devil still seemed to have crept in at times between those kissing one another, whether men or women, in some churches custom changed to kissing a sacred tablet, and indeed Praiseworthy. Resp. Estius in chapter 16 of Romans writes thus: Some think it probable that Paul (as also Peter) using this form of speech (Greet one another with a holy kiss) speaks of the kiss of peace, which is shown at the time of the sacrifice before the perception of the mysteries. Bellarminus in book 2 of the Mass, chapter 15, discourses thus concerning the ceremony of the kiss in the celebration of the Mass: The Priest frequently kisses the altar itself, then the book of the Gospel, then his Minister, and through him diffuses peace to the whole Clergy and people, etc. Moreover, there is a double reason for this kiss. For we kiss the altar and the book as a sign of reverence, but the brethren as a sign of charity and peace. Therefore, it is not the tablet, but the kiss of the brethren that is conformable to the salutation by a holy kiss, which was customary in the primitive Church, a thing which John Huss already warned of long ago, whose words were recited above in index 5.

Observations. 1. It is the duty of a true and faithful Minister of the Church not only to teach, but also to παρακαλεῖν exhort to constancy in the faith. Rom. 12. v. 7. & 8. For hearers are in need of such exhortations, lest they be carried about with every wind of doctrine in the wickedness of men. Eph. 4. v. 14. As to sin, so also to errors is the nature of men prone, miserably corrupted by the fall of the first parents. There is added the πανουργία, of Satan, the persecutions and hatreds of the world, the infirmity and drowsiness of the flesh.

2. The little word ἐπιμαρτυρῶν admonishes us concerning the office of the Apostles, that they were constituted by God as witnesses of Christ and the Gospel, which testimony they not only faithfully deposited, but also sealed with their own blood. Iohan. 15. vers. 27. Act. 1. v. 8. cap. 10. v. 39. & 42. 1. Iohan. 1. v. 3.

3. The Apostles had to testify concerning Christ and the truth of the Gospel not only by living voice, but also by writings. Iohan. 21. vers. 24. This is that disciple, who bears witness of these things and wrote these things. 1. Ioh. 1. vers. 3. That which we have seen and heard, we announce to you. vers. 4. And these things we write to you. Apocal. 1. vers. 2. John testified to the word of GOD, and the testimony of Christ. vers. 3. Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this prophecy.

4. Charity is not suspicious, it hopes all things. 1. Corinth. 13. vers. 7. It thinks no evil of anyone. vers. 5. Just as it is difficult for someone to be suspicious evil, who is good: Thus he who is evil himself finds it difficult to suspect that anyone is good.

5. It is for Christians to stand, not to waver, much less to slip. They must stand entirely, both through constancy in faith, and through patience in adversities and persecutions, and through resistance to temptations. Ex. 14. v. 13.Stand and see the salvation of the LordRom. 5. v. 2.we stand in grace.1. Cor. 16. v. 13.stand in the faith, act manfully.Gal. 5. vers. 1.Stand in liberty,Eph. 6. v. 14.stand having your loins girt &c.Phil. 4. vers. 1.stand in the Lord most dear.2. Thess. 2. v. 15.Brethren stand.

6. Christian charity is fostered by mutual greetings, which are a sign of friendly affection and a pious wish for the salvation of one's neighbor.

7. In Babylon, that sink of all idolatry and wickedness, God was able to gather for Himself a holy Church through the preaching of the Gospel. Indeed, there is no region, no city so corrupt, but that the word preached in it brings forth some fruit there Esa. 55. vers. 10.

8. What else is this whole world but Babylon, that is, a confusion of tumults, desires, business, and secular disturbances? In this Babylon the Church has a place, which is holy Jerusalem, seeing peace, and serving GOD in peace. Aug. in sent. sentence 222. Two loves make two cities in the whole world. The love of GOD makes Jerusalem, the love of the world makes Babylon. Let everyone therefore ask himself, and he will find from where he is a citizen.

9. The Babylonian Church was co-elect with the Pontic Church; indeed, among the pious citizens of the holy city, the spiritual Jerusalem, there flourishes a communion of spiritual benefits. This truly confirms the pious in faith not insignificantly. It is a great thing that, through the preaching of the word, men from places so remote and distant are gathered into one Church.

10. Let senior theologians embrace students of the sacred letters with fatherly love as sons, and let these in turn revere theologians who are outstanding in age, erudition, piety, and experience as parents.

11. The holy kiss is a kiss of charity; not of carnality, not born on the lips, but proceeding from the breast. Clement of Alexandria, book 3, paedag. Love is not judged by a kiss, but by benevolence. Those but do nothing else with a kiss than disturb the Churches, since they do not have friendship itself within. For this certainly stirred up a shameful suspicion and slander, that they would impudently use a kiss, which ought to be mystical, which the Apostle called holy. Having worthily tasted the Kingdom, let us show the benevolence of the soul with a modest and closed mouth, through which the gentleness of character is most exerted. Bede in h. l. Those greet one another with a holy kiss, who do not love in word nor in tongue, but in deed and in truth.

12. A kiss offered by an inferior is a symbol of reverence and obedience; from an equal, it is a symbol of concord and mutual love. Durandus lib. 4. Ration. div. offic. cap. 53. A kiss in Holy Scripture signifies union, charity, peace, and reverence. Concerning the kiss of union it is said Cant. 1. Vers. 1. Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Concerning the kiss of charity Isaac says to his son Genes. 27. v. 26. Come near to me, and give me a kiss. Concerning the kiss of peace the Apostle says 1. Corinth. 16. v. 20. Greet one another with a holy kiss. Concerning the kiss of reverence the Lord says Luc. 7. Vers. 45. You gave me no kiss.

13. The author of the book on friendship, chapter 6, in Augustine, volume 4, teaches, that that holy kiss is a sign of reconciliation, peace, charity, joy, and Catholic communion. The interlinear gloss likewise teaches, That holy kiss is fixed as a sign of common faith. It is called the kiss of charity, because the Apostle requires that Christians not only show themselves humane and benevolent in words and countenance, but that they declare a sincere and pious affection of the heart toward their neighbor through the duties of charity.

14. In Cyprian, Epist. 59, mention is made of an ancient custom, also accepted among the Heathens, by which kisses were given to infants newly born, which that Fidus, to whom he writes, shuddered to do. And if, he says, an infant is still new from birth, it is not, however, such that anyone ought to shudder to kiss him in the bestowing of grace and in the making of peace, when in the kiss of an infant each one of us, for the sake of his religion, ought to consider the very hands of GOD, still fresh, which we in a way kiss in a man just formed and newly born, when we embrace that which God has made.
